articles.text: An earthquake was felt throughout Piedmont and the rest of the East Bay early Monday morning. Residents woke up in the night to feel rumbling at 2:56 a.m. on Monday, September 22. The 4.3 magnitude quake was centered in Berkeley a few blocks south of the UC Berkeley Campus. Piedmont Firefighters felt the quake, assessing the Fire Station for damage and found no problems. In spite of the sharp and loud jolt and the brief rumbling sound, the earthquake did not result in any calls for service. Piedmont Public Works received no calls regarding the earthquake as well. “This earthquake is a good reminder to review your household emergency communication plan and home disaster supply kit and make sure you know what to do when you feel shaking – drop, cover, and hold on,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. The earthquake’s origin point was close to the Hayward Fault, which experts estimate has a one in three chance of experiencing a 6.7 magnitude earthquake in the next 30 years, according to an earthquake outlook published in 2019. The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) has an aftershock predictor that indicates about an 18% chance of another earthquake greater than magnitude 3.0 in the surrounding region in the next week. Chances of a more significant event drop off quickly, though there is about a 2% probability of an aftershock greater than magnitude 4.0 in that same time. Resources are available online to help residents prepare for natural disaster at www.piedmont. ca.gov/disaster. Car Show Organizer Police Officer Tyler Petit
articles.title: Earthquake rocks Piedmont houses

articles.text: On September 19th students at Piedmont Middle School held the Medieval Faire. New 7th graders looked forward to it as a fun way to tie in their newfound knowledge of the Middle Ages after learning about it the few weeks prior. This event included a medieval banquet, where core classes performed skits and dances. Ms. Brenneman’s AM core class did a Maypole dance, a traditional medieval performance. They took ribbons and wrapped them around a pole, which signifies fertility, spring, and community. Mr. Scherman’s AM class carried out a skit which taught everyone about table manners. Ms. Kelly’s class even did a dance with sticks, hitting them together and doing moves that mimic sword fighting. “The performances were very fun and coordinated, everyone did so well!” said 7th grader Nina Stock. Additionally, there were also fun booths that other core classes ran. Overall, the function was full of fun and games, and needless to say, 7th graders enjoyed the hour and a half long entertainment. articles.text: In the time it takes to enjoy a cup of coffee, your family can become more confident and prepared for a wildfire. As fall begins, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to set aside time to complete a simple, easy-to-follow at-home wildfire evacuation exercise with their household. Follow i ng step -by-step instructions and discussion prompts provided in a short video, families, housemates, and neighbors can transform their wildfire “what ifs” into a tangible, actionable plan. In less than an hour, this exercise helps you spot gaps, talk through decisions, and walk away more confident about what to do if a wildfire comes. What to expect • A realistic, local wildfire scenario based on conditions in Piedmont • Simple, pause-and-discuss prompts for each stage of evacuation • A downloadable worksheet to capture your household’s plan and next steps • A calm, supportive narrator to walk you through the process • Total time: 30-45 minutes Watch the video and download the worksheet at piedmont.ca.gov/ WildfireDrill. Find additional wildfire preparedness resources at piedmont.ca.gov/Wildfire. Building a more prepared community The at-home evacuation exercise is one part the Piedmont Fire Department’s broader work partnering with community members to build a safer, more resilient Piedmont. This summer, the Department conducted a practical evacuation drill for the Blair/Scenic/Alta neighborhood, giving them a hands-on opportunity to test their own evacuation plans. Firefighters also provide yearround public education, coordinate training with regional partners, and offer home visits to help residents understand steps they can take to harden their properties. Last year the Department also led development of Piedmont’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, engaging residents in a collaborative process to create a 5-year roadmap that identifies steps the City could take to reduce the impacts of disasters before they happen. Each household that completes the at-home exercise adds another layer of readiness to these efforts – strengthening not just their own plans, but our community’s resilience as a whole.
articles.title: Fire Dept. asks residents to complete at-home wildfire evacuation exercise

pages.text: 2 2 Wednesday, September 24, 2025 Opinion Observations of off-leash dog areas The following letter was sent to Piedmont Mayor Betsy Andersen and Nancy Kent. Editor: My mother’s family lived in Piedmont in the 1920s, and my family has been here since 1983, 42 years. We live in the home built by my grandparents’ best friends, where they raised my father’s business partner and best friend. We all have always had dogs. I use the off-leash paths at Piedmont Park. Very few of the dogs ever leave the concrete paths. Those that do are mainly labs and goldens wading in Bushy Dell Creek. No damage to the park. And the dogs really love running, romping and visiting each other. We could use a bench down by the softball field, facing the park, not the baseball diamond. The dogs mainly play down there not up where the benches are now. Dracena Quarry is mostly just the asphalt path down the middle. Dogs have always been banned from the lawns at the top and bottom. Most dog activity at the park across from Beach School is on the concrete paths. If the dirt area were resod, I am guessing that the very limited sunlight and the activity of dogs would destroy it. The dirt area is too steep for most of us to enjoy anyway, so leaving that large dirt area under the bridge is not really depriving humans. Meanwhile, those who do not want to share our parks with our dog friends have all the lawns at Piedmont Park. Bear Park, the lawns at both the top and bottom of Dracena Quarry, and all the sports fields. The off-leash portion of Piedmont Park along Bushy Dell Creek and the asphalt path at Dracena Quarry are very little to turn over to our best friends, and they so enjoy it. –Dana Sack Fire Dept. asks residents to complete at-home wildfire evacuation exercise By Tony Simons In the time it takes to enjoy a cup of coffee, your family can become more confident and prepared for a wildfire. articles.text: Work has progressed on the Grand Avenue Repavement Project, with bulb-outs on Fairview Avenue, and completion of new green infrastructure. Part of the completed work includes a new bioswale, a channel of plants that filters pollutants from run-off, reducing the waste that goes into storm drains. “The construction of the bioswale is an exciting component of the Grand Ave Paving and Pedestrian Safety Construction crews operate a Steam roller to pack down the new pavement. A worker smooths out freshly laid asphalt on Grand Avenue. Improvement Project,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “It is the first, true, green infrastructure project in Piedmont, and it is also a great example of how these types of projects can simultaneously enhance safety while improving the aesthetics of the neighborhood. With paving on Grand Avenue finally underway, we are excited to approach the final stages of this construction project.” Intersection paving on Grand and Fairview Avenues was completed on Friday, September 12. The newly installed bioswale on Grand Avenue filters pollutants from run-off, reducing the waste that goes into storm drains.

articles.text: People-lover two-year-old Ariana was found in the streets as a stray. Oakland Animal Services staff and volunteers say Ariana thrives on human connection. At 53-pounds, she is not grande and will try to climb into your lap. On a recent field trip with a volunteer, Ariana walked politely on leash, was easy to handle, and had a calm, steady presence. She was a quiet rider in the car, took treats gently, and demonstrated her gentle energy. She enjoyed watching the world go by, relaxing in the grass, and napping by the volunteer’s side. Though she’s tolerant of other dogs, Ariana clearly prefers the company of people and would do well as a solo dog. She’s a great fit for a lower-energy home looking for a loving, affectionate companion. Come meet Ariana at Come meet Ariana at Oakland Animal Services. Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 7 pm, or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 pm. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Ariana must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information about adoption or fostering, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com. articles.text: The following is an abridged version of the Piedmont Pulse, a bi-weekly update, published by the Superintendent of Piedmont Unified School District, Jennifer Hawn. The unabridged version is available at Smore.com/n/gt0zk September 22 Dear PUSD Families & Staff: Last week I had a chance to attend the 6th grade new family night, the 7th grade new family night, and the City’s new families night. Building community is at the heart of Piedmont, and I firmly believe that when we bring our parents together, our kids also build stronger relationships with each other. Speaking of our kids, I hosted a lunch for our high school students to hear their thoughts on how the cell phone policy is going at PHS/MHS. Our kids are so wise and had many effective arguments for the use of phones at the high school level. Some students (well...only a few) also commented that the new policy is something they can live with, but expressed concern about a more restrictive policy next year. Hearing the experiences of parents and our students reminds me of the importance of listening to all members of our school community: students, staff, and parents, in our efforts to offer the finest education possible. I encourage our families to continue to engage in the many community opportunities below to share perspective on our school programs. Your voice matters. In Partnership, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent High School Courses Two weeks ago, I wrote [smore. com/n/nas4p6] about the challenges of the high school schedule of courses, including our efforts to offer courses according to student interest and need. To further improve our efforts, we held a Board workshop on September 12th to explore options that could improve course opportunities for students, including transitioning to graduation requirements that reflect the UC A-G course admission requirements. At this workshop, we defined courses according to the California State high school graduation requirements, the UC A-G course requirements, and reviewed our PUSD high school graduation requirements [docs.google. com/spreadsheets/d/16ut-_GwBwAu7iKswzRXchvId2CBDKcTwhwDjCkXiDq0/edit?usp=sharing]. All three sets of requirements are different, and we discussed PUSD courses that we may want to change from a requirement to an elective option. Semester courses under consideration include the following: • Computer Studies • Ethnic Studies • Health To be clear, the rationale for moving these courses from a requirement to an elective option is to allow students more flexibility to pursue courses that reflect their interests and needs. At the workshop, we also reviewed enrollment in elective courses, with consideration of criteria to use when we determine we should not offer a course. We currently have under-enrolled elective courses that prompted a discussion of the cost to offer a course, which comes to a minimum of 24 students. That is, when we offer courses under 24 students, the revenue we receive for each student does not cover the cost of the course. We already cover the cost of many courses that have under 24 students for some core and other required courses, and so it is not financially sustainable to offer elective courses that are under-enrolled. In order to ensure a balance between providing robust course offerings and financial sustainability, we are developing a rubric to use for elective courses. This rubric will take into account various criteria, including course requests, lab courses, access for alternative learners, new courses, cost, and actual enrollment in the current year and over time. A review of this year’s course options revealed challenges for students to access the courses they requested. Enrollment for some elective courses is unsustainably low; however, we have heard from teachers that enrollment does not reflect student interest. Conversely, we have courses that have high demand, sometimes over-enrolled and unavailable, leaving students forced to choose courses they did not request, including “Unscheduled” free periods and/ or TA periods instead of electives students want. At the September 24th Board meeting, we will follow up on information the Board requested. No decisions will be made at this meeting; however, we will provide additional information from the 9/12 Board workshop on how we can move forward with improving our process for offering high school course options that meet the interests and needs of our students.

articles.text: Screens are everywhere – phones, tablets, TVs, laptops, Children today are surrounded by them from a very young age. While technology brings many benefits, from virtual storybooks to video calls with grandparents, parents often wonder: How much screen time is too much? And what does it mean for my child’s speech and language development? What the research tells us Studies have shown that children under the age of two learn best through real-life, face-toface interactions. Talking, playing, and reading with caregivers provide the foundation for language development. When screen time replaces these interactions, children may miss out on valuable opportunities to practice back-and-forth communication. For preschool and school-age children, the effects are more nuanced. Educational programs and interactive apps can support learning, but passive viewing— like watching videos alone— doesn’t promote the same level of language growth as conversation-rich activities. In fact, children who spend more time in front of screens may have smaller vocabularies and weaker social communication skills. Quality matters more than quantity It’s not just about how much time children spend on screens— it’s about how they use them. A video chat with a grandparent, where your child responds and asks questions, is very different from passively watching cartoons. “Co-viewing” (watching together and talking about what you see) makes a big difference. For example, if your child is watching a show about animals, pause and ask, “What sound does that lion make?” or “Which animal do you like best?” This turns screen time into an interactive language-building experience. Guidelines for families The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) offers helpful recommendations: • Under 18 months: Avoid screen time, except for video chatting. • 18–24 months: If you introduce screens, choose high-quality programming and watch together. • Ages 2–5: Limit screen time to about one hour per day of quality content, with co-viewing encouraged. • Ages 6 and up: Place consistent limits on time and content, ensuring screen use doesn’t replace sleep, physical activity, or family interaction. Practical tips for parents • Prioritize Face-to-Face: Even short bursts of play and conversation during daily routines (mealtime, bath time, car rides) support language more than passive screen use.

articles.text: With Homecoming approaching this Saturday, Piedmont High School kicked off Spirit Week on Monday. Spirit Week is a long-standing PHS tradition designed to rally students in the lead-up to Homecoming, culminating in Friday’s Purple Out and the highly anticipated Homecoming football game Friday evening. The week not only celebrates school pride but also encourages friendly competition and creativity among students across grade levels. The daily themes are: PJ Day, Mountain vs. Beach, Upperclassmen as Seniors vs. Underclassmen as Babies, Wild West vs. West Coast, and a Friday Purple Out. Students are encouraged to dress according to each theme. ASB decorated the school’s interiors over the weekend to spark excitement and build school spirit. Often, however, ASB struggles to fully engage the entire student body. Even though they visit classrooms the week before Spirit Week and post engaging videos to remind students of the themes and encourage participation, turnout and enthusiasm during the week often fall short of expectations. Many students seem less motivated to dress up or join in the rally activities compared to past years, making it a challenge for ASB to generate the same level of school spirit from previous Spirit Weeks. “I feel like Spirit Week is really fun, but sometimes the themes repeat a lot because ASB has limited options, so people don’t always get excited,” said PHS senior Amelia Carter. “I’ve also noticed that if seniors don’t participate, underclassmen follow suit. Last year, the current sophomore class didn’t participate much, which is a little frustrating. They might think they’re too cool for it, even though dressing up can be really fun.” Monday’s theme is “PJ Day” giving everyone a comfortable option to start the week. “I think seniors need to lead the charge so more students will join in and I’m actually really excited to dress up for every theme. On the bright side, ASB’s publicity has improved, so hopefully that helps boost participation,” added Carter. Spirit Week will culminate with the entire city piling on the community spirit as the Piedmont Highlander football teams hosts Arroyo High at Witter Field at 7:00 p.m. on Friday. Photo by Evolette Mak Seniors Rachel Young (left), Meher Baccher, Chloe Koh, Stephanie Lee, Elisha Bell, Elena O’Connell, and Sacha Andrews show off their Pajamas for Piedmont High School’s Spirit Week.
articles.title: Homecoming starts with Spirit Week

Stop by for a full day of fun and exploring the out-of-this-world exhibits. Older kids will love the shows in the planetarium and megadome, the boldest way to experience space and science on the biggest of big screens. Every Friday and Saturday night the Chabot Observatory Deck has free telescope viewing as well, weather permitting. Oakland Museum of California Museumca.org 1000 Oak Street, Oakland; 318-8400 The museum’s Nature Playspace, built in 2022, allows little learners to unleash their curiosity and imagination a built for kids arena. Located in the Gallery of California Natural Sciences, the playspace is focused on the unique needs of children ages 2 to 5, along with their families and caregivers. Children under 12 years of age can visit the Museum for free as long as they are accompanied by an adult over 18 years old. OMCA is open Wednesday-Sunday 11:00 a.m.-5:00 p.m. and hosts a kid friendly, and free concert every Friday evening. Tilden Steam Train Visitberkeley.com/directory/tilden-park-steam-train 2481 Grizzly Peak Blvd, Orinda 548-6100 The Tilden Steam train has been in operation since 1952 and is open weekends from 11:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. weather permitting. Grab a $4.00 ticket to ride a real-life Thomas the Tank Engine. Enjoy panoramic views of the Bay and try to hold your breathe through the tunnel. Kids will love hopping on the miniature steam train chugging along on 15-inch gauge tracks. Sit in an open-air cabin, ride the caboose or sit inside the luxurious miniature dining car. Exploratorium Exploratorium.edu Pier 15, San Francisco, (415) 528-4444 The Exploratorium is a favorite destination for curious scientists of all levels. Come see the interactive exhibits that will amaze and stun guests. Amongst the center’s mind-blowing exhibits are the Aeolian Harps, Anamorphic Benches, the Bacteriopolis, and the Chaotic Pendulum. The Exploratorium has more exhibits, features and activities than can be seen in one day, so consider a membership. On Saturday, September 27 they host an annual Engineering Day with interactive activities, and hands-on exhibits.

Stop by for a full day of fun and exploring the out-of-this-world exhibits. Older kids will love the shows in the planetarium and megadome, the boldest way to experience space and science on the biggest of big screens. Every Friday and Saturday night the Chabot Observatory Deck has free telescope viewing as well, weather permitting. See Chabot’s website for visibility status. Oakland Museum of California Museumca.org 1000 Oak Street, Oakland; 318-8400 The museum’s Nature Playspace, built in 2022, allows little learners to unleash their curiosity and imagination a built for kids arena. Located in the Gallery of California Natural Sciences, the playspace is focused on the unique needs of children ages 2 to 5, along with their families and caregivers. Children under 12 years of age can visit the Museum for free as long as they are accompanied by an adult over 18 years old. OMCA is open Wednesday-Sunday 11:00 a.m.-5:00 p.m. and hosts a kid friendly, and free concert every Friday evening. Tilden Steam Train Visitberkeley.com/directory/tilden-park-steam-train 2481 Grizzly Peak Blvd, Orinda 548-6100 The Tilden Steam train has been in operation since 1952 and is open weekends from 11:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. weather permitting. Grab a $4.00 ticket to ride a real-life Thomas the Tank Engine. Enjoy panoramic views of the Bay and try to hold your breathe through the tunnel. Kids will love hopping on the miniature steam train chugging along on 15-inch gauge tracks. Sit in an open-air cabin, ride the caboose or sit inside the luxurious miniature dining car. Exploratorium Exploratorium.edu Pier 15, San Francisco, (415) 528-4444 The Exploratorium is a favorite destination for curious scientists of all levels. Come see the interactive exhibits that will amaze and stun guests. Amongst the center’s mind-blowing exhibits are the Aeolian Harps, Anamorphic Benches, the Bacteriopolis, and the Chaotic Pendulum. The Exploratorium has more exhibits, features and activities than can be seen in one day, so consider a membership. On Saturday, September 27 they host an annual Engineering Day with interactive activities, and hands-on exhibits. Homecoming starts with Spirit Week By Evolette Mak With Homecoming approaching this Saturday, Piedmont High School kicked off Spirit Week on Monday. Spirit Week is a long-standing PHS tradition designed to rally students in the lead-up to Homecoming, culminating in Friday’s Purple Out and the highly anticipated Homecoming football game Friday evening. The week not only celebrates school pride but also encourages friendly competition and creativity among students across grade levels. The daily themes are: PJ Day, Mountain vs. Beach, Upperclassmen as Seniors vs. Underclassmen as Babies, Wild West vs. West Coast, and a Friday Purple Out. Students are encouraged to dress according to each theme. ASB decorated the school’s interiors over the weekend to spark excitement and build school spirit. Often, however, ASB struggles to fully engage the entire student body. Even though they visit classrooms the week before Spirit Week and post engaging videos to remind students of the themes and encourage participation, turnout and enthusiasm during the week often fall short of expectations. Many students seem less motivated to dress up or join in the rally activities compared to past years, making it a challenge for ASB to generate the same level of school spirit from previous Spirit Weeks. “I feel like Spirit Week is really fun, but sometimes the themes repeat a lot because ASB has limited options, so people don’t always get excited,” said PHS senior Amelia Carter. “I’ve also noticed that if seniors don’t participate, underclassmen follow suit. Last year, the current sophomore class didn’t participate much, which is a little frustrating. They might think they’re too cool for it, even though dressing up can be really fun.” Monday’s theme is “PJ Day” giving everyone a comfortable option to start the week. “I think seniors need to lead the charge so more students will join in and I’m actually really excited to dress up for every theme. On the bright side, ASB’s publicity has improved, so hopefully that helps boost participation,” added Carter. Spirit Week will culminate with the entire city piling on the community spirit as the Piedmont Highlander football teams hosts Arroyo High at Witter Field at 7:00 p.m. on Friday. Photo by Evolette Mak Seniors Rachel Young (left), Meher Baccher, Chloe Koh, Stephanie Lee, Elisha Bell, Elena O’Connell, and Sacha Andrews show off their Pajamas for Piedmont High School’s Spirit Week. articles.text: This year’s Medieval Faire had a variety of costumes worn by nobles and knights, peasants and merchants. This year’s King, Kai Chiles, and Queen, Sophie Messina, wore extravagant costumes, with shining crowns and luxurious robes, making their presence very noticeable in the dining hall. Lords and Ladies who sat at the front table had some noticeable costumes themselves. It seems that some had a lot of effort and planning in them. The nobles had flashy robes, and some, tiaras, and other luxurious accessories. One Lord, Oliver Dewar, took noblewear to the next level, wearing shades of purple, black, and gold with a black dotted lustrous robe. A very common and simple type of costume was that of a merchant. A baggy linen shirt with some kind of leather vest, and a nice leather belt with pants was a popular costume for the average citizen (and this author). Although people were very creative about it! Some wore green pants, some wore dark green pants, some wore brown, some wore light brown, and even red! The dining hall was full of merchants! Though there were a lot of merchants and peasants, there were also bakers. Miles Croan Smolko and Zain Shah were bakers and called themselves Big Little Bakery! A white apron, stained with chocolate or baking flour, spread across the face of this dessert disher costume. Teachers had some costumes to be reckoned with as well. Many had impressive dresses or gowns with green or other medieval colors. The most intriguing costume I saw was Mr. Scherman, who used a brown robe with a rope for a belt and was a friar! Incredibly creative costume! Although there were some basic costumes, there were many amazing ones that had a lot of thought put into them. Overall, for this Medieval Faire, the costumes were a win. Like I said, from nobles and knights to peasants and merchants, these medieval costumes are the best part of the faire. Staff Photos Scherman’s Morning Manor teaches the entire medieval gala about good table manners. Wesley Kolstad (left), Gabriel Garrigues, Curtis Broome (with mic), Ezra Schwartz (with book) and Emi Ito and Olive Abelson Lindsey wait for a chance to douse their favorite teachers. The most popular activity was the olliebollen-on-a-string contest, which entails competitors racing to eat an olliebollen attached to a piece of thread. An olliebollen is a fourteenth-century name for a doughnut. After the contenders had faced their doughnuts, there was no trace of the sugary snack left, just a sprinkling of crumbs. Cornhole, fortune telling, and the marriage booth were also fun and popular additions to the activities of the faire.

articles.text: Alive with energy and excitement, the Medieval Festival was filled with a variety of games meant to indulge students in the fun of medieval life. Par ticipants wanting to unlock their inner jester participated in stilt walking. In medieval times, stilts were used for maneuvering through marshes and flooded land, but here at Piedmont Middle School, they were used for fun. Students enticed by more dangerous activities gravitated to sword fighting. The rules are simple: two opponents are handed weaponry, pool noodles, and fight for a serving of seafood (Swedish fish). Whoever hits their rival twice with their pool noodle sword under the shoulders wins and is rewarded. The festival also included the traditional medieval practice of public humiliation and physical punishment. Volunteering teachers were locked in wooden pillories and exposed to public ridicule, scorn, and wet sponges in a game of soak-a-bloke. Likely a punishment for giving a few too many homework assignments. Students stood in long lines to Ansh Jagirdar (left) and Burton Mandel sword fight for servings of “seafood.”

pages.text: Wednesday, September 24, 2025 9 Medieval Faire Continued from page 8 Our King, Queen, and Others By Salma Bendix Before the Medieval Faire even took place, we elected our nobility. Our class, Mr. Scherman’s 5/6 Core, and other classes alike may have drawn names of people who volunteered or simply raised a hand to cast a vote. This election was to determine our “manor’s” Lord and Lady. The Lord and Lady from each “manor” would attend a meeting during lunch to then choose the King and Queen. On the day of the faire, we watched the mesmerizing Maypole dance take place while the Photo by Anne Smith King, Kai Chiles (left) and Queen, Sophie Messina preside over the Maypole Dance. king and queen sat on chairs at the highest point. During the banquet, lords and ladies took their seats above the rest at their “C” shaped table facing the crowd, while the royalty was welcomed into the hall with another dance. They sat upon their thrones and welcomed everyone in the room. Nobles took the responsibility of giving a speech thanking the king and queen and calling the manor’s citizens to stand and cheer. After the delightful entertainment provided by the citizens of multiple manors and the informative etiquette lesson, the king and queen called for the beginning of the feast. Among the citizens feasting, their roles were quite simple, like peasants. Obviously, there were many a pope, priest, and plague doctor playing out their roles perfectly. Aside from the medieval roles people took on, we were also able to volunteer to work at faire booths. While working these jobs, students really got into character like a fortune teller who told my fortune, Winne Schickedanz, who played her role perfectly. These were just some of the few things I took away from roles for this event, and I know there was a lot more happening behind the scenes to make the Medieval Faire possible. ® R&S OVERHEAD R&S OVERHEAD GARAGE DOOR, INC. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Staff Photos Massimo Mittone makes one of his two interceptions against Aragon. Piedmont’s football team got the job done on Friday, September 19 at Aragon in San Mateo, beating the Dons 36-16 to even their record after games to 2-2. The Highlanders played complementary football in every sense, where the defense and special teams frequently set up the offense with good field position. “The defense and special teams put us in good positions. We still need to clean some things up for sure and be a little tighter on the offensive line. We were down at one point with a very young team that could easily shut down, but they didn’t. We’re super proud of them after a game like this,” said PHS coach Jordan Seiden. After trailing 14-7 in the second quarter, Piedmont ran off 23 unanswered points before Aragon recorded a 2-point safety. Xavier Henderson also notched two touchdowns against Aragon, giving him six over the past two weeks after scoring four TDs in Piedmont’s 45-12 win over Berean Christian on September 12. “[After opening] the season with two losses, the defense was going through it. We knew we had to set up the offense, get our stops, and let the offense do its job. I didn’t get a lot of touches [at running back] last year, but this year, I’m going to punch one in when we need it,” linebacker and running back Xavier Henderson said. Friday night also marked the Mattias Seelenberger hit the longest field goal for Piedmont in the last decade with a 41-yarder. Cash Panico makes an athletic catch on down the sideline. He had a 68-yard touchdown reception against Aragon. longest field goal for Piedmont High in the past decade. In the second quarter, sophomore kicker Mattias Seelenberger converted a 41-yard field goal to give PHS its 16-14 advantage. Ten years ago to the day Josh Landheer hit a 42-yarder in a win over Salesian. Seelenberger is in his first varsity season. With his soccer background he is applying his skills on the football gridiron. “I missed a PAT and I was pretty nervous. I’ve hit one from further in practice, so I stayed calm took a deep breath. I’ve been playing soccer for years. When I started kicking field goals I realized how different it is than soccer,” Seelenberger said. With Piedmont’s strong defensive game, sophomore linebacker Massimo Mittone recorded two interceptions in the fourth quarter. “Football is new to me. I had no idea what I was doing when I first came to practice last year. It’s all been a learning experience, I’ve only been playing outside linebacker for two weeks,” Mittone said. Offensively, Jimmy Lagios continues to show confidence and poise as the team’s new starting quarterback. He tossed two touchdowns against Aragon, including a 68-yard bomb to Cash Panico, who made a couple of acrobatic catches despite having a broken thumb. “Toward the beginning of the season, I was still learning how the plays looked in the game, but I’ve picked up a lot of things on how to read defenses. Cash had a great game. I knew Cash is fast and can beat his man, so I trusted that,” Lagios said. Game Recap Piedmont scored the game’s opening touchdown a couple of minutes into the game when Rehan Mumtaz turned a reverse 60 yards for the score. However, Aragon answered on their next drive to even it up at 7-7 at the 7:19 mark. After a few trades of possession, the Dons scored their final touchdown at 8:19 in the second quarter, scoring on 4th-and-10 with a 32-yard catch and run, making it 14-7. On Piedmont’s next series, Lagios found Panico on a streak down the sideline for a 68-yard touchdown in a 3rd-and-18 situation with 7:06 left in the half. A missed extra point put Piedmont back 14-13. After forcing a punt, Seelenberger hit his 41 yarder at the end of a nine-play drive with 2:53 left, putting PHS ahead for good 16-14. Piedmont came out hot in the third, scoring on its opening drive by capping off with a direct snap to Henderson from the three-yard line, 23-14, with 9:35 left. After back and forth possessions, PHS scored again with 10:17 left in the fourth quarter. This time, Henderson punched in a six-yard carry to make it 30-14. Aragon got its safety with 3:52 remaining, but Piedmont got another score on an 18-yard pass to Jack Meyjes with 1:51 left. Aragon blocked the final extra point, making it 36-16. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-2 overall) hosts Arroyo for Homecoming Night this Friday, September 26 at Witter Field at 7:00 p.m.
articles.title: Highlanders roll over Aragon 36-16

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team took third place at the Vintage Valley Tournament in Napa over the weekend. Piedmont High took third place at the 2025 Vintage Valley Water Polo Tournament at Vintage High School in Napa last weekend, September 19-20. Piedmont opened the tournament with an 11-9 win over Roseville, lost 17-7 to Liberty, and beat Carmel narrowly 14-13 to close. It was a strong game for Henry Stein against Carmel with six goals in their win to claim third place. Elles Kreickhaus was important in a 11-9 win over Roseville, leading the team with four goals. The batch of games brings Piedmont’s record to 6-5 overall. They now look ahead to the start of their league schedule in the Western Alameda County Conference. Piedmont faced league rival Berkeley on Tuesday and will visit Castro Valley on Thursday, September 25. 14-13 over Carmel Piedmont led 5-2 after the first quarter and held an 8-5 lead by halftime. Carmel narrowed the deficit to 11-9 in the third quarter and outscored the Highlanders 4-3 in the fourth quarter but PHS scored the game-winner with 55 seconds left. In the first quarter, Carmel scored quickly after just 22 seconds, but the Highlanders scored four straight goals with three straight by Henry Stein to claim an early hat trick, and one by Rylan Patty to give PHS a 5-1 lead with 37 seconds left. Carmel got one back with 17 seconds remaining. Piedmont drew a man-advantage after 33 seconds in the second quarter, leading to another goal by Stein. After a pair of Padre goals, Elles Kreickhaus scored at the 1:38 mark. Carmel scored with 31 seconds left, but 12 answered on the ensuing possession with six seconds on the clock. Carmel scored to open the third with a goal after 30 seconds, but the Padres committed a foul, leading to Stein scoring his fifth. Carmel scored the next two goals to cut Piedmont’s lead to 9-8 with 2:56 remaining, but PHS responded with two straight goals by Kreickhaus and Ben Kappas. The Padres scored once more with 29 seconds remaining, making it 11-9. In the fourth, Carmel scored quickly to cut the lead to one. But with 4:20 left, Piedmont scored with a man-advantage for a 12-10 lead. But the Padres knotted things up at 12-12 with 3:09 remaining. Colin Amen scored with 1:43 left, but Carmel tied it just 13 seconds later. With 55 seconds left in the game, Patty launched in the eventual game-winner, and Piedmont held on defensively. Final stats: Stein had six goals, Patty scored three, Kreickhaus had two, and Kappas had one. 17-7 loss to Liberty Piedmont kept things close in the first quarter, going into the second down 4-3. However, Liberty, a Div. I school, extended its advantage to 9-5 in the second Photos by Lynne Wright Henry Stein logged six goals against Carmel to help PHS win a razorthin victory, 14-13.
articles.title: Piedmont takes 3rd in water polo tourney in Napa

articles.text: Staff Photos Samantha Huyhn runs in for a forehand. She’s competing at the No. 1 doubles spot alongside Emma Chan. Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team split its two matches over the past week. They recently defeated Western Alameda County Conference foes Castro Valley 6-1 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Thursday, September 18, but lost 6-1 to North Coast Section rival Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco the previous day. “All of the matches against Castro Valley were fairly one sided. We had chances to win against Lick. All three doubles matches went to the 10 point breaker but we couldn’t pull any of them out,” said coach Jim Landes. Samantha Huyhn and Emma Chan appear to have locked down the No. 1 doubles spot. The pair beat Castro Valley 6-4, 6-1, and fell in a narrow three-set battle to Lick-Wilmerding 6-3, 2-6, 10-3. Huyhn is a three-year varsity starter and performed well last year with Emma Eisemon. She also was the doubles partner of senior Maddie Tran as a sophomore. “I haven’t played with Emma [Chan] since before this season, but we’ve known each other for a long time and know each other’s playing style. As a doubles player, being able to adapt to so many different people, it really helps improve my game,” Huyhn said. “It’s been going well. Obviously, I haven’t played with Samantha until this season, but it feels like we’ve been a team for longer. It’s been coming natural, we set each other up and close out points really well,” Chan added. Kate Jumper won Piedmont’s only match against Lick-Wilmerding at the No. 2 spot in three sets, 6-3, 5-7, 11-9. She also won 6-3, 6-2 against Castro Valley. “Kate Jumper played excellent tennis against Lick’s Maahir Gupta and won the 10 pointer Emma Chan, a junior, is another part of Piedmont’s No. 1 doubles team. articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled to Concord’s Newhall Community Park on Saturday, September 20 for the De La Salle Invitational with more than 200 runners in both girls’ and boys’ races. The Highlanders’ girls’ team came away with a 13th place finish of 34 teams, while the boys were 24th of 39. “Our varsity girls had some trouble committing to getting out early and wound further back through the first mile than they probably should have been. Leighton, Skylar, Amalia and Cora still executed pretty well on the back half of the course to save their days,” assistant coach Reece Proctor said, who was filling in for head coach Steve Zirkelbach. Leighton Mand led the way for the girls’ squad, finishing 62nd of 230 runners with a time of 20:26.40 on the three-mile course. Four spots behind her in 66th was Skylar Best, clocking a time of 20:35.10. Amalia Gray finished 83rd with a time of 20:53.90, Cora Brozowski Schrader came in 95th in 21:08.40, while Viviane Oesterer rounded out the Highlanders’ best five runners in 104th in 21:21.20. As for the boys’ side, Alex Schleuning led things for the squad in 77th of 275 athletes, finishing with a time of 16:59. He time marked a personal record for three mile races by 10 seconds. Behind Schleuning was Aaron Bennett in 107th, coming across the finish line in 17:17.60. His time in the three-miler marked a personal record by one minute and 27 seconds. Dylan Wallway, a freshman, placed 142nd in 17:51.80 to be Photos by Jenni Tsoi Best Skylar Best placed 66th of 230 in 20:35.10 at the three-mile course of the De La Salle Invitational. Piedmont’s third-best runner. It marked the first three-mile race of his high school career. Rounding out Piedmont’s best five runners were Devon Thai in 163rd and Ian Chung right behind him in 164th, clocking respective times of 18:07.60 and 18:08.60. It marked a personal record of near five seconds for Thai and 13 seconds for Chung. “Aaron was definitely the performance of the day to take 1:27 off his three-mile personal best on a more challenging course. Five of our six varsity boys ran new personal bests. Dylan also raced really well and went 17:51 to finish 3rd for the team. Alex Schleuning also did well to break 17 minutes by a hair,” Proctor said. articles.text: Pouyan “Coach P” Assadi is the Head Coach of both Junior Varsity Football and Varsity Track and Field at Piedmont High School. A modern-day Renaissance man, he plays the violin, speaks fluent Farsi and French, holds a degree in Biomedical Engineering from the University of Minnesota, and is an award-winning product manager at a leading software company. In high school, Coach P was a recruited track athlete and also played football, experiences that gave him firsthand insight into the discipline, hard work, and sacrifice required of student athletes as they balance academics, athletics, and personal growth. He brings that perspective to every practice and uses it to guide and mentor the athletes he coaches. Coach P leads with a “players first” philosophy and relentless energy. He inspires athletes to push past their limits and build their conditioning both in-season and out. Under his leadership, the track program has reached unprecedented heights. The boys’ team captured the first league titles in school history, and more than twenty athletes have earned spots on college rosters. Off the field, he is a proud Minnesotan, a lifelong Vikings fan, a husband, and a new parent. Known as one of the best time managers around, Coach P balances his family life, a demanding career, and his coaching responsibilities. He always makes time for his players, whether it is answering a late-night text, checking in, or showing up when it matters most. unteered at Big Brothers Big Sisters in Minneapolis. Then when I moved to San Francisco, I joined BBBS’s Bay Area chapter. At the same time, I had friends who coached and really enjoyed it, so in 2019 I signed up to coach at Burlingame High School, which is where my physical work location was. Once COVID happened, the track season ended abruptly in March 2020, and soon after my wife and I moved out of San Francisco and bought a house in Piedmont. One day I was working on a house project and a pack of boys wearing Piedmont gear jogged past me, and it was a reminder to get back into coaching now that I was settled into my new home. From there I reached out to the school, and a few short weeks later I was coaching! Q: How do you think your coaching helps players prepare for varsity? Coach P: To properly learn any skill set, you need to build your initial foundational understanding, then add layers over time. For most athletes, starting at the JV level allows them to learn at their own pace, and over time we teach them skills that layer on top of each other. We start with proper form, safety, and basic play calling. Then we see that young athletes become more smooth in their motions, putting together multiple pieces of their learning into one fluid motion, and being able to understand more complex plays across a more comprehensive playbook. Then when they are ready, they go up to the next level where they are well prepared and are able to adjust more easily to the varsity game. Q: What inspired you to start coaching, and how did you get involved with Piedmont High School athletics? Coach P: Volunteering has always been a part of my life. When I was in junior high and high school, I would volunteer at senior homes, as well as play my violin at different events. Once I graduated from college, I volQ: How has your experience as a track coach influenced your approach to coaching football, and vice versa? Coach P: You quickly learn that most athletic movements and mental preparation are some version of the same, regardless of Coach Pouyan Assadi sport, but how you teach each area varies. What is interesting is that through coaching a more diverse set of physical activities, not just football and track and field but also the sub-domains within track and field, you see how athletes learn best. For example, I found that JV football athletes benefit most from film study, so I started videotaping track athletes’ critical motions and sharing with them. The results were clear. It expedited their ability to fix their core mechanics, which is part of why we are seeing our JV track and field athletes hitting marks that only top tier PHS varsity athletes used to hit just a few years ago. Q: Can you share a memorable moment or game from your first JV season? Coach P: I distinctly remember the St. Patrick-St. Vincent game from the 2022 season, as it was the first game we consolidated our varsity down to JV. I had already gotten to know varsity level guys like Markos [Lagios] and Sam [Shelby], but that week I was able to spend time with them and get to know them more. Beyond that I was concerned about the former JV starters losing significant playing time, but the varsity staff did a good job of rotating everyone in, and it helped that we won by 40. articles.text: Harvest Festival patrons flocked to Piedmont Park on Sunday, Sept. 21, to enjoy the beautiful last day of summer weather and welcome the autumn season. Community Hall came to life early, accepting entries for the Edibles Contest starting at 7:30 a.m. The fun, highlighted by jazz music, scarecrow sculptures and food, lasted well into the afternoon. Now in its 27th year, Piedmont’s Harvest Festival has continued to expand. A watermelon-eating contest was added last year, and an apple cider press brought new joy this year. articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) will present the first major retrospective of painter Suzanne Jackson, entitled Suzanne Jackson: What Is Love, opening September 27 and running through March 1, 2026. Organized in collaboration with the artist, the exhibition spans six decades of Jackson’s multifaceted career. Featuring more than 80 works, including paintings, drawings, and a new large-scale commission, the show explores Jackson’s novel approach to color, light, and structure, as well as her deep connection to nature, poetry, and performance. Jackson is known for her ethereal early canvases and her recent three-dimensional “floating” acrylic paintings that challenge traditional notions of painting. The exhibition also examines her interdisciplinary background as a dancer, poet, and theater designer, highlighting how these influences and her ties to radical artist communities shaped her art. “Suzanne Jackson: What Is Love promises to be a groundbreaking exhibition,” said Christopher Bedford, SFMOMA’s Helen and Charles Schwab Director. “Jackson continues to innovate by extending paint into three dimensions and embedding it with found materials to reflect on personal and cultural histories.” “Suzanne Jackson’s life has been driven by an insistent search for creative freedom and a bohemian spirit that is indebted to the San Francisco ethos in which she was raised,” added Jenny Gheith, curator of the exhibition and SFMOMA’s Interim Head of Painting and Sculpture. “What Is Love captures the curiosity, wonder and resilience of Jackson’s life’s work.” Jackson will participate in an artist talk at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art on Thursday, September 25 at 5 p.m. with scholar Kellie Jones, chair of the African American and African Diaspora Studies Department at Columbia University. In her conversation with Jones, Jackson will reflect on her creative process, her experience across artistic disciplines and her relationship to the Bay Area. On Friday, September 26 SFMOMA will invite several speakers to discuss different aspects of the artist’s work for the Suzanne Jackson and Friends program. The event begins at 6 p.m. Visit sfmoma.org or call 415.357.4000 for more information. Artist Suzanne Jackson

articles.text: The Exploratorium in San Francisco hosts its 26th annual Engineering Day, with events conducted in Spanish and English, this Saturday, September 27. Engineering Day offers hands-on activities and cultural experiences aimed to spark children’s curiosity in science and technology. This year’s programming focuses on electrical, structural, mechanical, aerospace, and biological interactive activities, including a build-your-own catapult workshop, a presentation on bridge structural integrity, and a hands-on water quality test alongside experts from Engineers Without Borders. The Exploratorium is partnering with the Society of Hispanic Professional Engineers, the local Bay Area chapter of the National Society of Black Engineers and the Stanford UniPhoto courtesy of The Exploratorium Experts from Society of Hispanic Professional Engineers, the National Society of Black Engineers and the Stanford University chapter of the American Indian Science and Engineering Society offer presentations at the event. Photo courtesy of The Exploratorium Interactive activities for kids of all ages will be STEM focused. versity chapter of the American Indian Science and Engineering Society for this event. Engineers and STEM educators from these groups will offer presentations and offer guests an opportunity to ask questions and connect with experts in the field. “Engineering Day is such a unique opportunity for young people to not only tinker and build, but to imagine themselves as future scientists and engineers,” said Ivan Torres, Exhibit Engineer at the Exploratorium. “It’s an important and powerful thing when they see people who share their language, culture, or background thriving in STEM careers; it helps them recognize that they belong in these fields too.” Live music will be performed by BULULÚ, a San Francisco-based band known for its vibrant blend of traditional Latin music and modern influences. San Francisco Public Library partners with the Exploratorium to offer young attendees a bilingual storytime and free book giveaway while supplies last. Admission to Engineering Day is included with museum admission. Visit www.exploratorium.edu to purchase tickets. The event is all-day, with events beginning at 10 a.m.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will present two performances of Dead Man Walking at the War Memorial Opera House from September 26 and 28, marking the 25th anniversary of the opera’s world premiere. Commissioned by San Francisco Opera and first performed in 2000, Dead Man Walking is composed by Jake Heggie with a libretto by Terrence McNally. The opera is based on the 1993 memoir by Sister Helen Prejean, which recounts her experiences with a death-row inmate. Since its premiere, the work has been staged over 80 times globally and is now considered the most performed contemporary opera in the repertoire. “This production of Dead Man Walking represents one of the most astonishing, full-circle moments of my career,” Heggie said in a press release. “It’s hard to believe it was 25 years ago when the opera premiered here to phenomenal acclaim. No one could have predicted the journey it would make, with more than 80 international productions to date.” The 25th-anniversary presentation features mezzo-soprano Jamie Barton as Sister Helen Prejean and bass-baritone Ryan McKinny as Joseph De Rocher, the condemned inmate. Susan Graham, who originated the role of Sister Helen in 2000, returns to the opera as Mrs. Patrick De Rocher. Patrick Summers, who conducted the premiere, returns to lead the San Francisco Opera Orchestra and Chorus. The production is directed by Leonard Foglia, with set designs by Michael McGarty and costume design by Jess Goldstein. The staging, originally developed by a consortium of American opera companies, is owned by Lyric Opera of Chicago and is being presented at the War Memorial Opera House for the first time this year. Additional cast members include Brittany Renee as Sister Rose, Raymond Aceto as George Benton, Rod Gilfry and Caroline Corrales as Owen and Kitty Hart, and Nikola Printz and Samuel White as Jade and Howard Boucher. Dead Man Walking is performed in English with English supertitles. Performance dates are September 26 (7:30 p.m.) and 28 (2 p.m.). Call the San Francisco box office at (415) 864-3330 or visit sfopera.com to purchase tickets. Dead Man Walking is based on the 1993 memoir by Sister Helen Prejean, which recounts her experiences with a death-row inmate.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Shotgun Players Christopher Chen’s The Motion premiered on the Ashby Stage September 13. Shotgun Players presents the world premiere of Christopher Chen’s The Motion, playing at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley now through October 12. Obie Award–winner Christopher Chen blurs the line between performance and participation in his newest play The Motion, where a heated debate slips down a kaleidoscopic ‘rabbit hole’ engaging audience members as voyeurs and accomplices. Theater guests are given voting cards and are invited to take part in the experience as it happens on stage. The Motion is a unique play that entwines clever comedy, sharp dialogue, and science fiction to create a fractal pattern of moral dilemmas. “The Motion, which riffs on the debate format before spinning into different worlds, is one of the most ambitious plays I’ve written,” said Chen. “There’s a particular thrill when you feel yourself being swayed from one side to another then back again, because it feels like you’re activating the deepest part of your humanity,” he continues. “It’s like a Russian nesting doll. You open one and there’s another inside… It’s one surprise after another,” added Shotgun Players Director Patrick Dooley. “A dominant theme that emerges in this story aligns with others that are addressed in the season, which is, what it means to be human.” Cast includes Erin Gould as Moderator/Jack Donovan, David Sinako as Dr. Alan James, Erin Mei-Ling Stuart as Dr. Sarah Matthis, Soren Santos as Professor Neel Serrano and Gabrielle Maalihan as Professor Lily Chan. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https://shotgunplayers.org/show/the-motion/.
articles.title: The Motion playing on Ashby Stage now through Oct. 12

articles.text: The internationally acclaimed Bennewitz Quartet will perform at Kohl Mansion in Burlingame on October 19. Music at Kohl Mansion, the longest-running chamber-music-only presenter on the San Francisco peninsula, hosts the event. The program will feature quartet members Jakub Fiser and Stepan Jezek on violin, Jiri Pinkas on viola, and Stepan Dolezal on cello. Founded in 1998 and based in Prague, the Bennewitz Quartet has become one of the leading ensembles in international chamber music. The group received early recognition after winning top prizes at the Osaka Chamber Music and Festa (2005) and the Premio Paolo Borciani competition in Italy (2008). In 2019, the quartet was awarded the “Classic Prague Award” for Best Chamber Music Performance. Recent seasons have included performances at major European venues such as Wigmore Hall in London, Laeiszhalle in Hamburg, and Konzerthaus in Berlin. The ensemble has also appeared in the U.S., making its debut in cities including Providence, Houston, and Tucson, and returning to the Music and Beyond Festival in Ottawa and the Harvard Musical Association. In their home country, the Bennewitz Quartet recently completed a series of concerts featuring the complete string quartets of Antonín Dvořák as part of the Dvořák Prague Festival. A pre-concert talk by Stanford cellist and educator Christopher Costanza is held at 6 p.m., and the concert begins at 7 p.m. A complimentary wine and dessert reception follows the concert at 9 p.m. For more information, and to purchase tickets, contact the Box Office at (650) 762-1130, or purchase online at https://musicatkohl.org/. Bennewitz Quartet

articles.text: Piedmont artists and Art Walk veterans Irene Nelson, Chris Harvey, and Larraine Seiden will participate in the 51st annual ArtSpan San Francisco Open Studios later this month. The three will exhibit together as guest artists at Miro Studios, 744 Alabama St., San Francisco, on Sept. 27–28, 11 a.m.–5 p.m. The monthlong event, running Sept. 20–Oct. 19, invites the public to explore hundreds of artists’ studios across San Francisco neighborhoods. Visitors can connect directly with creators, discover new work, and experience the city through its thriving art community. Admission is free. A full guide is available at artspan.org. Artist Spotlights Irene Nelson creates abstract paintings as acts of discovery, blending memory, imagination, and experimentation. Her work has been shown at the de Young Museum, the Contemporary Jewish Museum, and the Crocker Art Museum, and is held in public and private collections worldwide. articles.text: Open through Oct. 13, 11–2 p.m. Slavic Art Exhibit The Center for Slavic Arts and Culture is proud to present its very first exhibition, Kaleidoscope. The show brings together 17 artists from five Slavic countries, including a photographer and a jewelry designer, each sharing their talent and creative vision. In challenging and uncertain times, art reminds us of beauty, resilience, and the strength of our community. Kaleidoscope is a celebration of creativity, and a reminder of how art can connect, uplift, and inspire us all. This exhibition will be open weekend days from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. until mid-October. CSAC celebrates Slavic culture’s rich heritage and vibrant traditions, and works to preserve and promote the art, history, and unique identities of the twelve Slavic nations, fostering appreciation and understanding across diverse communities. Come to explore a world of creativity, tradition, and inspiration. Saturday, September 27, 7:30 p.m. Extraordinary Vocal Soirée Fundraiser Feeling sad, frustrated and frightened with the news these days? You’re not alone. Come listen to some healing music that inspires comfort, peace, and joy. The program, called You’ll Never Walk Alone, will include popular opera, musical theater and sacred music to soothe the soul and lift your spirits. The well-known professional singers have been or are currently involved with SF Opera Chorus, SF Symphony Chorus, Oakland Symphony Chorus, West Edge Opera, Festival Opera, Livermore Opera, Opera San Jose, Opera Parallèle, Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra, and American Bach Soloists, featuring mezzo-soprano Christine Abraham, sopranos Hope Briggs, Amy McKenzie, and Christa Pfeiffer, tenor Joe Meyers, and baritone Daniel Cilli, among others, and accompanied by pianists Paul Dabb, Jerome Lenk, and Stephen Main. This event is free with donations, which the organizers will contribute to a national charity. Write to christapfeiffer17@gmail.com for more information. Sunday, September 28, 4:00 p.m. Festival Opera Vocal Recital Festival Opera’s Salon Series concludes with a thrilling afternoon celebrating the vocal brilliance of the Bel Canto age. Performing the works of Rossini, Bellini, Delibes, and Meyerbeer; experience the magic of Shawnette Sulker and Sara Couden’s virtuosic voices as they bring to life the dazzling duets and soaring melodies that define the art of beautiful singing. This salon setting offers a rare opportunity to be up close with the artistry and vocal fireworks that make this repertoire unforgettable. Don’t miss this exquisite musical journey—where voices reign supreme: Bel Canto Forever! Tickets are at https://zeffy.com/ticketing/salon-series-bel-canto-forever. Sunday, October 5, 5:00 p.m. Spruce Ritual Ensemble Concert Experiencing Lucian Balmer’s ensemble Spruce Ritual is to feel a greater depth of humanness, heart, and soul. Through sublime melodies and intricate compositions, they take the listener on a heartfelt musical journey, mixing the wisdom, knowledge, and spirit of two great ancient cultures: eastern Hindustani music and western classical music, and infusing their own sacred spirit to create music that is achingly beautiful, human and transformational. Accompanying Lucian will be: Charith Premawardhana (viola), Robin Reynolds (cello), Will Marsh (sitar), Souryadeep Bhattacharyya (sarod), Srishti Biyani Oswal (bansuri/ vocals), and Josh Mellinger (tabla). Experience an immersive evening where music and motion converge - the unique sound of Spruce Ritual intertwined with the storytelling grace of kathak dancer Karishma, a Bay Area-based performer, and dance educator with over 20 years of experience, weaving ancestral roots with contemporary ritual. articles.text: A River Runs Through It, released in 1992, is a gently told period drama, beautifully photographed by Oscar-winning Philipe. Rousselot. It is set in Missoula, Montana, during a time that stretches from the end of WWI to the beginning of the Great Depression. The narrative, with voiceover by director Robert Redford, is based on the 1976 autobiography by Norman Maclean. The film follows the Maclean brothers, Norman (Craig Scheffer) and Paul (Brad Pitt), who as youngsters thrived in the bucolic surrounds of rural Missoula. They were taught the discipline, if not the art, of fly fishing on the nearby Blackfoot River by their Presbyterian minister father (Tom Skerritt) who gently merged religion with the early mornings the three spent standing in the rippling river, casting their lines out onto the eddying, rippling surface. Their time together, often spent sitting among the Ponderosa pines on the river’s banks, or finding a metronomic rhythm as they fished, moments when the morning light shimmered off the wet rocks, all of it a metaphor for their union, captured in the lyrical words of Maclean and spoken Tom Skerritt, Craig Sheffer and Brad Pitt in A River Runs Through It

articles.text: John Greenleaf Whittier observed: “for all sad words of tongue or pen, the saddest are these: “it might have been.” Sounds like a hymn to regret. But not if you learn an important lesson from Dr. Ephraim Engleman. To him, life was a football field with an open field ahead of him. Prepare to be amazed and inspired. Born in San Jose in 1911, he was a musical child prodigy on the violin and the piano. He found early success playing music in silent film houses to accompany the silent films. Then the sound films made the scene, ending his nascent musical career. His parents suggested a medical career. That sounded good. But this child genius found it tough going. He made it through Stanford Medical School, but it was not as easy as playing music. Success and fame did come. Music and medicine have had a long connection. Consider the many doctors’ orchestras in our country. Dr. Engleman became a famous rheumatologist. His office at the University of California Medical Center overlooked San Francisco‘s Kezar Stadium. This was just the place to entertain contributors to his Rosalind Russell-Ephraim Engleman Research Center. The symbiosis of medicine and music continued until his 104th year. He died at his work desk. His enthusiasm for life was unbated. He believed that life was to be enjoyed and music was one of the most important aspects. He played his violin every day. Along the way, he met many famous musicians. Early on, he played string quartets with the illustrious violinist Misha Elman. He also acquired a collection of famous violins. Whether it was a Stradivarius or a Guarnerious, Eph had one. He also had a childlike enthusiasm which some mistook for boasting. For example, just about every famous violinist who came to San Francisco telephoned Eph and asked to come to visit him. Naturally, they tried the famous violins om jis collection, and a free concert ensued. The names of these musicians comprise a veritable Who’s Who of the music world. Somehow, this busy doctor found time to write an autobiography, many musical plays, and also compose popular songs. He also found time to play jazz piano and of course the regular chamber music sessions. Towards the end of his 104 years, Engleman offered some “commandments” for a good life. If I remember correctly, the first commandment was: “Choose your parents wisely.” Another was: “Never retire.” And be sure to enjoy everything that you do. Dr. Ephraim Engleman
articles.title: It might have been

articles.text: A scene from Happy Feet Happy Feet is charming and playful, making this rollicking tale of a unique penguin named Mumble (Elijah Wood) seem decidedly fresh. Apparently, every Emperor penguin sings a unique song called a “heartsong,” used to attract a mate. If the males’ song matches the females’ song, well, they mate, which is what occurred with Mumble’s parents, Norma Jean (Nicole Kidman) and Memphis (Hugh Jackman). As a result, Norma Jean lays an egg, which she leaves in the care of Memphis while she and the other females go off to fish. It’s a harsh winter, and Memphis accidentally drops the egg. When the new chick, Mumble, is finally born, the parents discover that he can’t sing, but can tap dance. Mumble soon becomes a young adult whose feet never stop moving; however it’s the elders, led by Noah (Hugo Weaving), who grumpily take exception to Mumble’s dancing and ridicules him, in his Scottish brogue, for being different. Meanwhile, he does have a secret crush on the talented Gloria (Brittany Murphy), but doesn’t have the “heartsong” that is so necessary to find a companion. Meanwhile, Mumble meets a group of mini-Mexican Adelie penguins, called “the Amigos,” whose leader is Ramon Lovelace (Robin Williams) who is willing to help Mumble court Gloria (Ramon sings “My Way” while Mumble lip-synchs). Naturally, Gloria falls for him. Soon all the young penguins are singing and tap dancing to “Boogie Wonderland.” Of course the elders are appalled. Mumble is ordered to stop, but refuses, and is exiled from the flock, blamed for what has been a lean fishing season. And so Mumble’s the adventure begins, one that takes him all the way to Australia where he ends up in a marine sanctuary where kids, one girl in particular, can stand and watch him swimming behind massive panes of glass pool. The girl taps on the glass and Mumble, with his beak, taps back, hoping to communicate with the humans. Event ually, Mumble is released from the sanctuary and finds his way home to his flock. It’s upon his return that he challenges the elders and prevails, and soon everyone is dancing and celebrating, most especially Mumble and Gloria and Ramon. Happy Feet. Directed by George Miller. With voices of Elijah Wood, Robin Williams, Brittany Murphy. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG. Released in 2008. Streaming on Prime/Apple tv/Fandango/ YouTube

articles.text: To take a closer look at the Piedmont housing market, the Post sat down this week with accomplished real estate agents Brenda Schaefer and Karen Starr. Both are intimately familiar with Piedmont, both as realtors and as residents – Starr raised her daughter in Piedmont and Schaefer raised her kids as fourth-generation Piedmonters. Schaefer and Starr work together as partners at the Grubb Company, a full-service boutique real estate brokerage that represents buyers and sellers in Oakland, Piedmont, Berkeley, Kensington, El Cerrito and Albany. Founded by Donald J. Grubb Sr., the Grubb Company has been a locally owned brokerage since 1967. The company boasts a team of skilled agents, in-house legal counsel, and leading-edge marketing techniques. The Starr-Schaefer team has been together for more than 14 years. Schaefer has a background in escrow, having worked as an escrow officer. Starr brings a legal background with her work as a residential attorney. The pair say they are strong, strategic competitors who possess a deep understanding of the process, thanks to their combined skill set. As a local company, the Grubb Company emphasizes a deep understanding of market trends and the nuances of neighborhoods. The firm also hosts weekly meetings every Tuesday, where the team is updated on new statutes, local and state laws, listings and more by broker John Karnay. “It’s just amazing, the level of continuing education that we get at our Tuesday meetings,” said Starr. “...like during COVID, we had to pivot constantly about what the requirements were about showing houses and protecting clients – the sellers and the buyers.” The pair is well-connected in the real estate community, keeping up with colleagues and friends across agencies. articles.text: by Robert Redford. “In the slanting sun of the late afternoon the shadows of great branches reached from across the river, and the trees took the river in their arms. The shadows continued up the bank until they included us.” Regrettably, Norman Maclean passed away before the film was completed; however, his words frame a final, touching moment as Maclean, now nearing the end of his life, stands at the edge of the river, and with trembling hands slowly ties a fly to his line, and seemingly lost in the moment gazes off into the distance. “Eventually, all things merge into one, and the river runs through it. The river was cut by the world’s great flood and runs over rocks from the basement of time. On some of the rocks are timeless raindrops. Under the rocks are the words, and some of the words are theirs. I am haunted by waters.” It was only later that I learned that Robert Redford, at the age of 89, had died. And though I knew that decades had passed since I sat in a theater and watched Barefoot in the Park (1967), a romantic comedy with Jane Fonda, I took his timeless presence on the screen for granted. I gave little thought to the span of his career that began with an unaccredited role in 1960 and did not conclude until 2018 with his last leading role in the film The Old Man and the Gun. Yet he seemed to defy the gravity of aging. He would always be the Hubbell Gardiner in the film The Way We Were. His filmography is stunning,

pages.text: 28 Wednesday, September 24, 2025 Features Walking on Wednesday From Havens’ estate to SB 9 homes: walkers trace Piedmont’s past and future By Dick Carter Last Wednesday was what locals call a hot day in Piedmont with temperatures in the 80s. The Walking on Wednesdays group stayed in the central part of town to avoid steep climbs. Even in the heat, 42 walkers and two K-9 best friends turned out at the Exedra for the weekly outing. A month earlier on August 6 the group had toured shaded Wildwood Gardens, once part of Frank C. Havens’ early-20th-century Wildwood Estate. That day they covered the two lower loops but ran out of time before reaching the upper section. Last week’s walk was a chance to complete it. Before setting out, walkers heard a quick refresher on Havens. Born in 1848 into a founding family of Shelter Island, New York, he left home at 16 to work as a cabin boy and sailed around Cape Horn to California. He spent time in Honolulu and China before arriving in San Francisco in 1866. Havens worked in banking, became an Oakland attorney, and emerged as a leading East Bay real estate developer, leaving a mark on Oakland, Berkeley and Piedmont. Construction is never far away in Piedmont, and the walkers saw plenty of it. They first detoured down Magnolia Avenue to the city’s new aquatics center. Earlier this month, both pools were filled and system testing began. Through the fencing, walkers could glimpse the sparkling pools, landscaping, and workers putting on final touches. Four water-blue letters spelling SWIM stood ready to welcome future visitors. The group followed a scenic path through upper Piedmont Park, past the Tea House and along Highland and Wildwood avenues to the old Wildwood Gardens entrance, still marked by two partially hidden stone columns. Skipping the lower loops from their August walk, they continued uphill. One stop was at a lot where foundation work for a new accessory dwelling unit had just begun. A deep pit carved into the hillside caught their attention. A worker, Octavio, explained that roughly 1,500 cubic yards of soil were being removed and that temporary piers and retaining walls kept the slope stable. He expected foundation work to wrap up by year’s end, with the house completed by late 2026. The walkers then continued past a backyard treehouse to the seldom-visited Wistaria Way loop. A nearby parcel had once been part of a larger home. After the owner died earlier this decade, the lot was donated to a church and sold in 2022. Two proposals that year for a single-family house were denied after objections from neighbors and the city about size. The owners then turned to Senate Bill 9, California’s 2022 law that lets homeowners split lots and build up to four units on parcels zoned for single-family homes. Their application, to divide the lot and build two homes plus an ADU, was approved by Piedmont planners in December 2023. Building permits followed in July 2024, and work started immediately. Today, the modern, glass-fronted structures are largely framed. Some finishing remains, but they already stand out. On a Wistaria walk last fall, owner Geoff Gibson told the group he hoped to spend Christmas 2025 there with his family. From the looks of progress, that may happen. The walk wrapped up by climbing Woodland Way to Lafayette Avenue, then back to the Exedra via Crocker, Wildwood, Sheridan and Highland avenues. It was a warm morning, with equal measures of local history, construction updates and neighborhood views. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets each Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland and Magnolia) at 10:30 a.m. All are welcome, including dogs. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Last week’s walkers included Brenda Ferrero, Bill Ahern, Priscilla Wanerus, Edith Lee, Marion Lim Yankowithz, Kat Lang, Mary Carter, Dan Scdoris, Phil Witte, Karen Palmer, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Silva Fones, Albert Chen, Tina Shum, Don Fones, Stella Houston, Judy Sokoloff, Liz Dalyrmple, Mary Ann Barnes, Sanghi Wagner, Laura Dudell-Foley, Denny McGee, Kim Kuo, Joyce Ahern, Sherry Jacobs, Irene Thompson, Debbie Powell, Cathy Laymon, Peggy Shultz, Chuck Oraftik, Judy Love, Jasmine Cai, Mike Gallent, Claudine Bach, Ken Hubbert, Rick Eigenbrode, Deborah Kurtin with her K-9 best friend Brie, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased Leila Deacon was visiting from Great Britian and walking with her father, Jack Fischrup, and their K-9 best friend Kojak.
