articles.text: Coach Pouyan Assadi with members of the Piedmont track team Q: How do you balance being a football coach and a track coach? Coach P: The two seasons as well as offseasons do not overlap, so while it has been a challenge balancing my personal life along with the two sports, the sports themselves have not been too tough to balance. At times there are overlaps in the football spring workout plans and important track meets, but that is really it. The two sports complement each other quite well, and it is no coincidence that we have had a new level of success the last couple of years and buy-in from key athletes in our year-round football-track cycle. Q: What’s the most unforgettable game or meet you’ve coached so far? Coach P: The 2024 game against Newark is a game I will remember for a long time. That was the most prep I put into any game thus far, and our athletes came out and had our best week of practice all season. It was our last game of what was a historic season, so we wanted to make sure we came out ready to end the season on a positive note and also set the tone for varsity, who was also looking to secure their backto-back league title. I remember tons of nuances about the game, but a play that still gives me goosebumps is when we were up 13-7 late in the 4th quarter with Newark driving. They were on our 22-yard line, 2nd and 2, in position to score. But then here comes Max [Fujimoto], jumping an out route, picking it off, and going 80 yards for the pick six go-ahead touchdown. Game, set, match, and we ended the season on a five-game winning streak. Q: What were some challenges you faced in your first year, and how did you overcome them? Coach P: Football is an intense sport where coaches are required to make many tough decisions within a matter of seconds. Play calling, personnel decisions, time management, people management, and much more. It took me a bit to ramp up, but like I mentioned about properly learning any skill set, I built a foundation, understood expectations, practiced by adding layers to build my skill set, and now I feel pretty comfortable with where I am at. I also have not been shy about asking questions to the varsity staff, who have been very helpful in my growth. Q: How have you built relationships with your players since joining the program? Coach P: I believe in understanding athletes as individual people first and foremost, and building that relationship is fundamental to creating a successful program. I have done my best to take time to chat with our kids to learn who they are, their hobbies, what gets them excited, and more. As coaches, we are fortunate to meet these boys when they are rambunctious freshmen, and over time your bond strengthens and you chat about more than just football or track. It is always fun when kids, now young adults, come back from college and ask to meet up for lunch and simply talk about life or even ask for advice. Q: Where do you see the JV football and track programs in the next few years? Coach P: JV football is still in its “crawl” stage of the crawlwalk-run process, but I feel pretty comfortable saying we are crawling really fast. At times there are overlaps in the football spring workout plans and important track meets, but that is really it. The two sports complement each other quite well, and it is no coincidence that we have had a new level of success the last couple of years and buy-in from key athletes in our year-round football-track cycle. Q: What’s the most unforgettable game or meet you’ve coached so far? Coach P: The 2024 game against Newark is a game I will remember for a long time. That was the most prep I put into any game thus far, and our athletes came out and had our best week of practice all season. It was our last game of what was a historic season, so we wanted to make sure we came out ready to end the season on a positive note and also set the tone for varsity, who was also looking to secure their backto-back league title. I remember tons of nuances about the game, but a play that still gives me goosebumps is when we were up 13-7 late in the 4th quarter with Newark driving. They were on our 22-yard line, 2nd and 2, in position to score. But then here comes Max [Fujimoto], jumping an out route, picking it off, and going 80 yards for the pick six go-ahead touchdown. Game, set, match, and we ended the season on a five-game winning streak. Q: What were some challenges you faced in your first year, and how did you overcome them? Coach P: Football is an intense sport where coaches are required to make many tough decisions within a matter of seconds. Play calling, personnel decisions, time management, people management, and much more. It took me a bit to ramp up, but like I mentioned about properly learning any skill set, I built a foundation, understood expectations, practiced by adding layers to build my skill set, and now I feel pretty comfortable with where I am at. I also have not been shy about asking questions to the varsity staff, who have been very helpful in my growth. Q: How have you built relationships with your players since joining the program? Coach P: I believe in understanding athletes as individual people first and foremost, and building that relationship is fundamental to creating a successful program. I have done my best to take time to chat with our kids to learn who they are, their hobbies, what gets them excited, and more. As coaches, we are fortunate to meet these boys when they are rambunctious freshmen, and over time your bond strengthens and you chat about more than just football or track. It is always fun when kids, now young adults, come back from college and ask to meet up for lunch and simply talk about life or even ask for advice. Q: Where do you see the JV football and track programs in the next few years? Coach P: JV football is still in its “crawl” stage of the crawlwalk-run process, but I feel pretty comfortable saying we are crawling really fast. We are getting buy-in from families sooner, a larger contingent of freshmen has joined us more consistently for summer workouts, and more families are marking their calendars for the 2026 Tahoe camp than ever. We need to continue moving the process upstream to Piedmont Middle School, where I know [Coaches] Bo (Pou) Tauaho and Isaac (Oskie) Tauaho are working to get younger kids excited about football in general, but also building their foundation sooner, especially for the offensive and defensive lines, so when they enter the JV program we can start polishing their skills instead of building them up from step one. The 1st–8th grade summer camp was another step in the right direction, and hopefully we are in the “walk” stage sooner rather than later. For track and field, we are in the early stages of “run” (no pun intended). We have sent 20 kids to college for track and field during my time with the team, have won the league title, and attended the CIF State Championship three of the last four years. This last year we even qualified and competed at Nike Nationals. Now we just need to be more consistent and raise the ceiling a little higher to be considered a real premier track and field team. Coach P: I came into coaching almost purely as a people motivator and sports enthusiast, but those two attributes have now fused together and my skill set has grown dramatically. Even when I watch football on Sundays, or professional track during the summer season, I watch it differently. For football I can identify coverages and see patterns, and for track I know what a time or mark is going to be halfway through an event. Beyond that, I have learned how to listen to all the solicited and unsolicited advice and find the best solution to implement in order to create the best experience and the most successful program possible. Add in the relationships and bonds that have formed, and I can say with confidence that I am a better person today than I was before I started coaching. And I’m happy that folks that have put so much labor and love into these vehicles are able to show them off. It’s incredible.” Along with the impressive lineup of classic and custom vehicles, Coast Construction Company brought a track car system for kids and parents to race their favorite cars in miniature. Residents also enjoyed food from a taco truck and conversations among the many car enthusiasts. “This is the result of hundreds of hours from five knuckleheads,” laughed resident Peter Gaylord about his car – a charmingly eclectic Dodge Colt plastered with stickers, racing colors, and several brass instrument horns. Gaylord, along with fellow resident Luis Zuniga, were at the event representing a group of friends who built the car to race in the 24 Hours of Lemons – a racing event for cars under $500. Officers came to support the car show from the Alameda County Sheriff’s Department, including the Alameda County Sheriff Yesenia Sanchez and District Attorney Ursula Jones Dickson. Residents and police officers enjoy the wide array of classic and custom vehicles at the 4th annual Coffee, Cars and Cops car show in Piedmont on Saturday, September 20. articles.text: Housing Plan adjusted for community feedback After a long meeting on Monday, September 8, the Piedmont Planning Commission voted unanimously to pass a recommendation to the City Council to adopt the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan – a housing plan for developing City-owned land in Moraga Canyon into a new neighborhood of up to 197 multi-family housing. The controversial housing plan would provide space to develop buildings up to six stories either in the Blair Park area or in the hillside near Coaches Field. The plan includes 137 market-rate housing units and 60 low-income housing units, as well as road safety improvements and an expansion to Coaches Field. The City has received over 70 written comments on the Draft Specific Plan since it was released for review in April. Based on community comments, staff recommended several changes to the Draft Specific Plan, including: • Clarifying the type of flashing beacons that will be used to warn motorists of traffic signals and pedestrian crossings • Requiring the specific traffic safety analysis be conducted at the time of a development agreement to ensure appropriate “stopping sight distance” at intersections and at time of initial design review for driveways • Providing more flexibility
articles.title: Planning Commission moves forward with Moraga Canyon Housing recommendation

articles.text: Piedmont elementary school students have been hard at work creating dozens of scarecrows for Sunday’s Harvest Festival. Many groups stopped by the office of the Piedmont Post for old newspapers to mold their imaginative creations into form via papier-mâché. Piedmont Education Foundation will host an auction during the Harvest Festival for community members to bid on and take home the scarecrows. Last year’s auction sales and Kid’s Carnival receipts generated $28,000 for Beach, Havens and Wildwood schools. articles.text: Consumer Affairs Reporter After considering its options in response to the Republic Services strike this past summer, and after having requested that Piedmont citizens fill out questionnaires regarding the lack of garbage pickups for one to two weeks, the City has decided on a course of action: do nothing. According to Deniz Ergun, the city’s Sustainability Manager, the City Council did not make a formal decision on the matter. Rather, the course of action is more of a “we’ve talked to other cities affected and no one is doing anything either” sort of thing. She told me that individual customers affected by the strike – in other words, the owners of the 3,737 single family residences in the city – call Republic Services directly to negotiate a credit. However, a random, unscientific check showed that other cities were indeed taking actions on behalf of their residents. The City Manager’s Office in Richmond told this reporter that right after the strike was settled, the City sent a formal letter to Republic requesting a citywide credit for missed services. While Richmond has not yet resolved the matter, they assured me that this was an ongoing matter and would not simply be dropped or ignored. The Daly City Utilities Billing Department told me that credits had already been issued to residential customers. I have left messages with other cities’ Public Works Departments and am waiting for their responses. So why didn’t Piedmont do the same? As usual, the devil is in the details. Speaking with the Customer Service Manager at Republic Services, I learned that Piedmont has a different kind of contract than other cities. Absent force majeure, Republic is required to provide us with contracted services. So, according to them, management personnel staffed the trucks and did the Piedmont routes. In fact, Republic thinks that everyone in Piedmont had their garbage and recycling picked up during the strike. articles.text: City Council heard a proposal to update Planning & Building permit fees and adopted a formal cost recovery policy at their regular meeting on Monday, September 15, 2025, adjusting building permit fees with attention to a residential solar panel rebate program. New permit fees will go into effect January 1, 2026. The proposed updates follow a fee study conducted earlier this year. The study found that current fees only recover 73% of the cost of permit services, resulting in an under-recovery of more than $400,000 per year. articles.text: two weeks without pickup. Here is where technology comes to the rescue. Republic’s trucks are equipped with GPS, the results of which can be downloaded and reviewed. So, if someone says they did not get service, it can be verified by comparing their address with the GPS tracking from the trucks. However, this does require every customer who did not receive the contracted services to individually call Republic to request a credit. As a long-time computer geek, I suggested that Republic download its GPS results and use a spreadsheet or database to electronically compare the GPS results to the list of streets in Piedmont, thereby determining the streets that were missed, and then automatically generating credits to affected customers. The reaction I received was the audio equivalent of a deer in the headlights. So, if you didn’t receive your normal service during the strike, you need to call Republic at 800- 320-8077 and let them know. Do it while it is fresh in your mind and before September 30th bills are generated. “Ask and you will receive”, because the City will not do it for you. Finally, we do need to ask why Piedmont decided to sweep this matter under the rug, especially after asking residents to fill out online questionnaires (remember them?) about service levels during the strike. City personnel certainly must have known that streets were missed based on the input from residents. Perhaps they chose to accept Republic’s assertion that there were no service disruptions, or perhaps they simply chose the path requiring the least effort. In any case, they had a responsibility to notify residents, either on the Piedmont website, via the Piedmont Post, or with some other sort of communication. It is disappointing that they chose not to do so.

articles.text: Amazon is a dog with a big heart currently in a medium-sized package. At 44-pounds and 8-months-old, this playful Doberman Pinscher/Mixed Breed has been the star of his shelter playgroups where he loves zooming around with his friends in games of chase. Shelter staff and volunteers describe him as goofy and friendly. He recently moved into a foster home and his fosters report he is trustworthy while uncrated and enjoys socializing with their resident dogs. Amazon will thrive with an active adopter who is ready to dedicate time to training and providing him with daily mental and physical exercise. He would do well in a multi-canine household, or as a solo pulp. Meet Amazon at Oakland Animal Services If you’re looking for a smart energetic puppy, complete an adoption questionnaire on Oakland Animal Services webpage and his foster will contact you to arrange a meet-and-greet at the shelter. For more information about adoptions and fostering, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: The 27th annual Harvest Festival will kick off the fall season on Sunday, September 21, in Piedmont Park. Piedmont Community Center will host the Edibles Contest and display the many entries, including produce, prepared dishes and baked goods, and products of the bountiful gardens and creative kitchens of Piedmont. Anyone who lives or works in the City of Piedmont may submit an entry; group entries are allowed and up to four entries may be made per category. To enter the contest, bring a labeled item and entry form to Community Hall between 7:30 and 10:00 a.m. Founded in 1998 by Bill Drum and Susan Hill, the contest now has 27 categories, including: best curds and butters, pies, pesto, most unusual vegetable and three categories for baked bread. Entries will be gauged by a panel of judges composed of city council members, city staff, and various volunteers. Ribbons and prizes will be awarded and a full list of winners will be detailed in next week’s Piedmont Post. A Marianna’s Peace heirloom tomatoes grown by The Question Man. These and many other edible foods will be on display in the Edibles Contest on Sunday September 21. articles.text: Piedmont residents meet officers and admire impressive cars at last year’s Cops, Coffee and Car show. The Piedmont Police Department is gearing up for its 7th annual car show, complete with hot coffee and even hotter automobiles this Saturday, September 20, from 9:00 a.m. to noon near the Exedra. The event brings cops, coffee and cars to the center of Piedmont as a part of the department’s outreach efforts. Excitement is revving up as nearly 100 vehicles have been entered in this year’s event. Officer Tyler Petit, organizer of the car show, anticipates more than 120 unique cars to be on display this year. To accommodate the growing turnout, the event will expand from the Community Center parking lot down Magnolia Avenue to the base of Piedmont High School. This year’s car will be an opportunity for Piedmont residents to meet the city’s new Police Chief, Frederick Shavies, along with members of the police department. Along with the impressive lineup of classic and custom vehicles, a taco truck will be on-site. The Cops, Coffee and Car Show was pioneered by former Piedmont Police Sergeant Steve DeWarns in collaboration with Officer Petit in 2018. In its second year, the car show had 44 cars in 2019, and since then has had approximately 100 showroom worthy cars since 2021. To enter a vehicle in the show, e-mail officer Tyler Petit at coffeecarscops@piedmont. ca.gov. Be sure to include your name, phone number and e-mail address, and the name, make, model and year of the vehicle. articles.text: Superintendent Jennifer Hawn’s original unabridged September 8, 2025 Piedmont Pulse is available online at App.smore. com/n/nas4p6 Dear PUSD Families & Staff: As you know, on September 4 an intruder entered the Beach campus by climbing over a fence with the intent to play basketball. While we were fortunate that the individual did not pose a threat beyond making a poor decision, the incident prompted our team and community to reflect on how we can strengthen security and safety measures on our campuses. Our schools have safety plans that outline how we respond to a variety of potential threats. Staff are trained in these protocols, which include close coordination with the Piedmont Police Department (PPD). We also encourage students and community members to follow the “See something, say something” principle to help keep our campuses safe. The recent Beach incident illustrates these protocols in action: when an intruder entered campus, the Principal was immediately notified, the school was placed on lockdown, and PPD arrived within minutes to remove the individual. Thanks to these swift actions, students and staff remained safe throughout the incident. Following this incident, we reviewed our protocols, including feedback from parents, and we will use both the text and email systems to communicate with families when there is a campus emergency. We are also thoughtful about the impact of these events, even when the result is all are safe. Thanks to our School Psychologist, Diana Cooksey for a helpful resource at: Childmind. org/guide/helping-children-copeafter-a-traumatic-event/ for staff and parents. A special thanks to the Beach staff, including the leadership of Principal Anne Valva, for keeping our students safe, along with PPD for their quick response to this safety incident. Finally, thank you to our students and parents for your partnership in safety. In Partnership, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent Honoring Chris Stevens As September 11 [passes], we remember those who lost their lives, including Piedmont High School alumnus, Class of 1978, Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens, who dedicated over two decades to the U.S. Foreign Service and was known for his commitment to diplomacy, connection, and democratic ideals. On September 11, 2012, Ambassador Stevens, along with Navy SEALs Glen Doherty and Tyrone Woods and State Department officer Sean Smith, lost their lives during attacks on U.S. facilities in Benghazi, Libya. Their sacrifice highlighted the courage required of those who serve our nation abroad. The loss was felt deeply in Benghazi, where residents mourned Stevens as a trusted friend, and in Piedmont, where our community honored his legacy by naming the high school library the Ambassador Christopher Stevens Memorial Library in 2013 in his memory. His life and service continue to inspire, reflecting the Piedmont High School motto, “Achieve the Honorable.” Learn more about the life of Chris Stevens at: https://out. smore.com/e/nas4p6/XALcm6?__$u__ AC Bus Route Service — Community Advocacy Needed Thank you to the students and parents who took our survey [three] weeks ago and who wrote to AC Transit officials to restore Bus 33 service to upper Piedmont. To those surveyed families, I recently sent out an opportunity to write to AC Transit to restore service. If you would like to join in this letter-writing effort, we could use your help to advocate for this critical transportation need. Linked at: Out.smore.com/e/ nas4p6/RbirFR?__$u__ is information below to assist you in sending a letter via email to the AC Transit staff and Board. We believe advocacy from our PUSD community can make a difference in calling attention to this important matter and potentially leading to the restoration of bus service to upper Piedmont. For high school Juniors and Seniors, this opportunity to advocate locally can earn students the PUSD State Seal of Civic Engagement on a student’s transcript and diploma for college admissions purposes. For Seal Criteria see https://out.smore.com/e/nas4p6/ pLRR4s?__$u__ The AC Transit Board meeting [was] Wednesday, Sept. 10th at 5pm. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich [provided] students dinner and [planned] to meet in Room 30A at PHS to join the AC Transit Board meeting. High School Scheduling During the first several weeks of school, we heard from some parents regarding scheduling issues, including courses that are at capacity and unavailable to students. This moment reminded me of a post I wrote in August 2023 (linked at Out.smore.com/e/ nas4p6/mUaEpc?__$u__) about similar challenges. Two years ago, we experienced uneven enrollment in courses, which prompted me to take a look at the PHS master schedule, in terms of courses offered and how the master schedule of courses was built. Fast-forward to this year, and we experienced similar issues, especially related to courses that are at capacity with no room for additional students. Moreover, two years ago we had approximately 30 additional students over what we have today, with essentially the same courses available to students. One would conclude that we should be able to accommodate most or all of our students’ requests. However, the concerns remain, and we will need to consider more effective ways to build a master schedule of courses for our high school students. Several reasons for the challenges are as follows: TA & Free Periods: Building a student-centered schedule means offering courses they are likely to take. This year, one challenge we faced was the timing of when courses were offered. While our scheduling software is designed to maximize student course preferences, other factors also shape the master schedule, such as the limited number of course sections, teacher availability, and specific course requirements. pages.text: 6 Wednesday, September 17, 2025 SchOOLs September 8 Piedmont Pulse By Jennifer Hawn Superintendent Jennifer Hawn’s original unabridged September 8, 2025 Piedmont Pulse is available online at App.smore. com/n/nas4p6 Dear PUSD Families & Staff: As you know, on September 4 an intruder entered the Beach campus by climbing over a fence with the intent to play basketball. While we were fortunate that the individual did not pose a threat beyond making a poor decision, the incident prompted our team and community to reflect on how we can strengthen security and safety measures on our campuses. Our schools have safety plans that outline how we respond to a variety of potential threats. Staff are trained in these protocols, which include close coordination with the Piedmont Police Department (PPD). We also encourage students and community members to follow the “See something, say something” principle to help keep our campuses safe. The recent Beach incident illustrates these protocols in action: when an intruder entered campus, the Principal was immediately notified, the school was placed on lockdown, and PPD arrived within minutes to remove the individual. Thanks to these swift actions, students and staff remained safe throughout the incident. Following this incident, we reviewed our protocols, including feedback from parents, and we will use both the text and email systems to communicate with families when there is a campus emergency. We are also thoughtful about the impact of these events, even when the result is all are safe. Thanks to our School Psychologist, Diana Cooksey for a helpful resource at: Childmind. org/guide/helping-children-copeafter-a-traumatic-event/ for staff and parents. A special thanks to the Beach staff, including the leadership of Principal Anne Valva, for keeping our students safe, along with PPD for their quick response to this safety incident. Finally, thank you to our students and parents for your partnership in safety. In Partnership, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent Honoring Chris Stevens As September 11 [passes], we remember those who lost their lives, including Piedmont High School alumnus, Class of 1978, Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens, who dedicated over two decades to the U.S. Foreign Service and was known for his commitment to diplomacy, connection, and democratic ideals. On September 11, 2012, Ambassador Stevens, along with Navy SEALs Glen Doherty and Tyrone Woods and State Department officer Sean Smith, lost their lives during attacks on U.S. facilities in Benghazi, Libya. Their sacrifice highlighted the courage required of those who serve our nation abroad. The loss was felt deeply in Benghazi, where residents mourned Stevens as a trusted friend, and in Piedmont, where our community honored his legacy by naming the high school library the Ambassador Christopher Stevens Memorial Library in 2013 in his memory. His life and service continue to inspire, reflecting the Piedmont High School motto, “Achieve the Honorable.” Learn more about the life of Chris Stevens at: https://out. smore.com/e/nas4p6/XALcm6?__$u__ AC Bus Route Service — Community Advocacy Needed Thank you to the students and parents who took our survey [three] weeks ago and who wrote to AC Transit officials to restore Bus 33 service to upper Piedmont. articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) presented a record-breaking check for $4,116,427 to the Piedmont School Board on Wednesday, September 10. This grant is the largest in the foundation’s history and reflects a full year of fundraising through the Giving Campaign and other programs, such as Spring Fling, Harvest Festival, Dress Best for Less, business sponsorships, and a distribution from the PEF Endowment Fund. Co-chairs of the Giving Campaign Catie Osborn and Kim Hunter added their thoughts and thanks on the record-breaking gift. “This incredible achievement is only possible because of the generosity of our community,” said Osborn, “Our donors make it clear, year after year, that supporting our schools is a shared priority.” “We’re especially proud that 94% of this grant directly funds the people who make Piedmont schools exceptional: our classroom teachers, librarians, paraeducators, classroom aides, intervention specialists, technology coordinators, counselors, nurses, psychologists, athletics staff, and special education professionals,” said Hunter. The impact of that support stretches back decades. “PEF was founded 50 years ago by parents and neighbors who believed that strong schools are the heart of our community,” said PEF Board Chair Bridget Schreiber. “Half a century later, we are still building on that legacy, and this grant is a powerful example of what we can accomplish together.” That spirit of celebration continues this fall. The 2025–26 Giving Campaign began yesterday, September 16. PEF’s Board of Directors and the PUSD School Board are vying to see who will reach 100% Giving Campaign participation first this year. Every gift brings Piedmont schools one step closer to the resources they need. To join this year’s campaign and make your impact, visit PiedmontEdFoundation.org/donate. Piedmont Education Foundation board members Ashish Patel (front, left), Catie Osborn, PEF Executive Director Heather Frank, PEF Board Chair Bridget Schreiber, and Kim Hunter present this year’s PEF Grant to PUSD Board Members Lindsay Thomasson (back, left), Susy Struble, Ruchi Medhekar, Max Roman, Michael Malione, Student Board Members Saniyah Johnson and Hunter Fasteau, and PUSD Superintendent Dr. Jennifer Hawn.

articles.text: For more than 140 years, Chabot Space & Science Center has inspired Bay Area learners of all ages to explore the universe beyond classroom walls. Since opening its telescope doors in 1883, Chabot has stayed true to its mission: sparking curiosity, discovery, and wonder. Today, that mission continues through free and paid programs that connect science to everyday life— right here in Oakland. A Tradition of Looking Up Free telescope viewings are at the heart of Chabot’s history. Every Friday and Saturday night, volunteers open the domes and guide visitors through the night sky. The tradition connects generations of neighbors, families, and stargazers—and reminds us that learning doesn’t end when the school day does. Step Into Nature: Hike & Sip For a deeper connection to the natural world, Chabot’s Hike & Sip program combines science, history, and reflection. Guests hike through the surrounding redwoods with Chabot’s Science Associates, learning about the cultural and natural history of the Oakland Hills. Afterward, they gather on the observation deck for refreshments and telescope viewing. Family Nature Adventures Young scientists get an early start with Family Nature Adventures, designed for families with children ages 3–8. Each month features a new theme—owls, fungi, reptiles, and more— brought to life through playful, hands-on exploration. Parents and children learn together, showing that science belongs to everyone. Investing in the Next Generation This year marks 25 years at Chabot’s Skyline Boulevard location. The center’s commitment to education includes programs like the Oakland Space Academy, which offers workforce development opportunities for high school students and beyond. Exhibit Technician and Engineering Instructor Ben Tagami explains: “I’m most excited about creating an informal learning environment where students can develop both creativity and engineering skills. There’s something valuable about stepping away from traditional classroom structure and giving students time and space to explore and tinker.” side technical skills, Chabot helps prepare the next generation for STEM careers while keeping curiosity at the center. Oakland’s Place for Space, Science, and Discovery Whether stargazing through a historic telescope, hiking in the redwoods, or watching a child discover the wonders of nature, Chabot Space & Science Center offers countless ways to learn outside the classroom. For more information about Chabot Space and Science Center, 510-336-7300 or go to our website at chabotspace.org. Chabot Space & Science teaches kids outside the classroom.

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Art department will open an art fundraiser today, in collaboration with Piedmont artist Will Mouat. The Piedmont dad created a cartoon poster map of Piedmont, and the sale of each giclee 24”x36” archival print will be donated to the school’s art program. Mouat’s piece compiles dozens of culture icons representing the City of Piedmont and everything within sight from the top of Blair Avenue. The piece captures Piedmont’s landmarks and popular annual events, including the 4th of July Parade, the Turkey Trot, and the Scout Tree Lot. The piece contains details of individual homes and neighbors’ parked vehicles to create a cultural snapshot of Piedmont. “I didn’t really make it to sell,” said Mouat. “I made it because I wanted my kids to have something.” Mouat, a resident for 12 years, started the piece with paper and pencil, moved to ink, then digitized the piece to do the coloring with an iPad. Work on the iPad alone required more than 80 hours of coloring and 80,000 brush strokes. “It’s as if you’re at the top of the hill looking down. It took a lot of mental gymnastics since that’s the wrong angle, but I really wanted SF in the background,” said Mouat. This is the first printing of Mouat’s art piece, and he will have the original on display this weekend in Piedmont Park at both the annual Car Show on Saturday and the Harvest Festival on Sunday. “Our goal is to raise at least $3000 to cover the cost of tuning one kiln and replacing the other,” said Piedmont High School Art Department chair Gillian Bailey. Donors of $150 or more to the PHS Art Materials Fund will receive a hand signed giclee print poster while helping fund art materials for the art department. Prints will be custom printed at East Bay Giclee, a local printer, and should be ready in November. The fundraiser will continue until October 5. With the sale of 20 posters, the Art Department can replace their Ceramics kiln, which broke last week and will be more expensive to repair than replace. New Ceramics teacher Sarah Houchin and her students would benefit greatly from working equipment. Donations will support students in Ceramics 1,2,3,4 and AP 3D Design. Donations may be made online at Buy.stripe.com/3cscMR5nya2TbOE289. To donate to the PHS Studio Arts and Ceramics fund, open the camera app on your phone or go to the link above. Piedmont Artist Will Mouat is selling 24” X 36” giclee prints of this map of Piedmont to support the PHS Art Department.

pages.text: 10 10 Wednesday, September 17, 2025 Piedmont High School’s class of 2005 reunites for its 20th reunion. By Jay Russell Members of Piedmont High’s graduating class of 2005 came together again for their twentieth reunion on Saturday, August 30. The reunion was hosted by Class President Jeff Dang along with Kera Bartlett Binns, Alexandra Constantine and Mike Haralambides. Around 50 graduates and a handful of spouses made it back to their hometown for the event hosted at the Bartlett’s manor, which is no stranger to big parties. PHS Class of 2005’s 20th Reunion If this reporter’s memory serves, the same home, with sprawling views and lawns hosted a memorable 6th grade Halloween party for much of the grade, in 1998. Hostee Kara Bartlett Binns described a majority of those that made it to the reunion as largely currently living in the Bay Area. “There was both a sense of delight to discover so many of us lived nearby, and an eagerness to get together more often in less formal ways,” said Binns. Class of 2005’s Caitlin Anderson was impressed by graduates that traveled at great lengths, from Los Angeles, Washington D.C. and Chicago, to attend the reunion. The event was catered by La Mediterranee and Viridian supplying tasty morsels for conversations with long lost, and now found, friends as the sun slipped over the Pacific Ocean. Some people looked exactly the same as graduation day, prompting people to question their need for a name tag. “We all knew each other half a lifetime ago. We did so much Sophia Chew (left), Claire Neumann, Cullen Ready and Jeff Dang Jackie Espana (left), Sarah Moore and Myles Fisher Ivana Yu (left), Jeff Dang and Jeff Sweet PHS’s class of 2005 gathers for its 20th reunion. Shane Thygeson (left), Elizabeth Tom, and Addison Duke growing up together, but now we have grown up even more,” added Andersen. Many conversations on the evening recounted how the pandemic impacted the graduates of 2005. “Many of us had to pivot in a time of chaos, and are now looking at a new career, a young family, or even questioning whether we want to continue on the path we are currently walking. I enjoyed the candor and gentle honesty in those moments, [about] things weren’t necessarily sunny, [that] we wouldn’t share with a stranger,” said Andersen. The evening’s fun spilled over afterhours, prompting groups to look for a new home to continue the party. Although now, 20 years after high school, graduates weren’t asking each other “Is your house open, are your parents out of town?” All grown up, the discussion could easily continue down the street at The Kona Club, on Piedmont Avenue. A venue most of the grads couldn’t legally get into 20 years ago when it was the King’s X. “I still, now a week later, feel such warmth when I think about the reunion, with gratitude that all my childhood friends are really doing okay in this crazy moment of the world,” said Anderson. “Hearing about who married who, meeting spouses, fawning over pics of kids and pets [made] it such a great event for restoring hope in the future.”

articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled to Hidden Valley Park in Martinez for the 40th annual Ed Sias Invitational on Saturday, September 13. Competing in the small school’s category, the girls’ team placed fourth of 23 schools while the boys were 11th of 24. “The varsity girls’ team had a very good team performance on Saturday in a more competitive field than they faced the previous weekend,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “Once again, the close distance between the first and 5th runner continues to be their strength. “ The boys’ team was missing lead runner Sebastien Swain, and senior captains Noah Sohn and Alex Schleuning. The girls’ team finished equal on points with third place Las Photos by Jenni Tsoi Best Piedmont’s girls’ team placed fourth of 23 schools at the Ed Sias Invitational. Pictured are Mara Kemp-Malone (left), Leighton Mand, Skylar Best, Amalia Gray, Nikita Gorelik, Viviane Oesterer, and Cora Brozowski Schrader. Lomas at 139, but were narrowly edged out when factoring in the Knights’ sixth runner. Leighton Mand led Piedmont’s girls, placing 19th of 158 runners. Ian Chung (1559) led the boys’ team. He was 56th out of 168 runners. “We were reminded of the importance of every member of a squad. Our top five girls actually tied Las Lomas for third, but their sixth runner was two spots ahead of Nikita Gorelik, which gave them the edge,” Zirkelbach said. Piedmont’s best five runners finished within 38 seconds of each other. Leighton Mand led the way, placing 19th of 158 athletes, recording a time of 13:15 on the two-mile course. Behind Mand was Skylar Best in 29th, clocking a time of 13:29.4. Junior Amalia Gray was 33rd in 13:43.2, while Viviane Oesterer was right behind her in 34th, 13:45.8. Cora Brozowski Schrader rounded out their best five in 38th, 13:52.5. PHS’ sixth runner was Nikita Gorelik, clocking a 14:13.5 to finish 53rd. Boys’ team The PHS boys finished in the top half of the field despite being without top runners like Noah Sohn and Alex Schleuning, while former honorable mention for Athlete of the Year Sebastien Swain misses time as he recovers from surgery. articles.text: Henderson leads Highlanders with 4 touchdowns Piedmont’s football team captured its first win of the season, beating the visiting Berean Christian Eagles 45-12 for their home opener at Witter Field. The Highlanders were coming off back-to-back losses to Salesian and Middletown where they were in tightly contested games in the third quarter before falling behind in the fourth. This time Piedmont kept the gas pedal down for all four quarters. The previous week, PHS last lost to Middletown 34-17, which the Eagles opened their season against in a 22-14 victory. For coach Jordan Seiden and his players, it felt like Piedmont finally put everything together. “The offense got things going, and most importantly, the defense got it together. They were tackling much better and they had better communication. It was one of those games where every player on the roster contributed,” Seiden said. It was a big evening for Xavier Henderson, who scored four touchdowns. “Xavier had a big game. He’s a ball player. In Piedmont, not a lot of kids grow up playing football and it’s a big teaching process. Xavier has played football since he was five or six, so it’s second nature to him. When he’s in his prime shape, he’s one of the best players in the Bay Area. There may be people who are bigger and faster than him, but his instincts, his nose for the ball, and skill set is great,” Seiden said. Junior running back Rehan Rehan Mumtaz scored on a 30-yard touchdown run. Photos by Sajid Mumtaz Xavier Henderson (right) and Dash Waters Worthen celebrate a touchdown. Henderson scored four times against Berean Christian. Mumtaz also had a solid game, scoring on a 30-yard touchdown early in the fourth quarter. “Rehan Mumtaz had the first 100-yard game of his career and scored his second touchdown. He’s incredibly fast and tends to rely on his speed, Seiden said. Seiden has also been impressed by kicker Mattias Seelenberger who converted a 37-yard field goal in the third quarter, while pinpointing a wellplaced kickoff which led to a recovery by Piedmont. “Our kicker made a 37-yard field goal. He’s three for three on field goals and 10 for 10 on PAT attempts. We recovered a kickoff and we’ve always put a heavy emphasis on special teams,” Seiden said. Game Recap After recovering a fumbled snap at the 50-yard line, Piedmont drove six plays to the end zone. On their first play, Mumtaz took a reverse 19 yards to the BC 32, while Jimmy Lagios found Jack Meyjes on a 28-yard reception to the five. After a five-yard penalty, Henderson broke two tackles on a 10-yard touchdown run—making it 7-0 around the 8:50 mark in the first quarter. Henderson scored again on an 18-yard touchdown reception on a screen play at the very end of the first quarter. Berean Christian got one back on a long touchdown pass on fourth down early in the second quarter, making it 14-6 after a botched extra point. After Jason Shum recorded an interception, Piedmont drove to the 14 yard line before Henderson shed another couple of tackles on his way to the end zone, bringing their lead to 21-6 midway through the second quarter. Near the end of the second quarter, quarterback Jimmy Lagios found Jack Meyjes for a 27-yard touchdown pass down the sideline, 28-6. After George Saunders intercepted a pass early in the third, Piedmont drove seven plays to score, capping off with a one-yard touchdown by Henderson for a 35-6 lead. Seelenberger later hit a 37-yard field goal to make it 38-6. After BCHS scored early in the fourth quarter, Piedmont’s final touchdown came on a 30-yard touchdown carry by Mumtaz. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-2 overall) visits Aragon in San Mateo this Friday, September 19 at 7:00 p.m. Jason Shum nabs an interception in the second quarter.

articles.text: Staff Photos Allyson Huyhn lands one of her eight kills against Lick-Wilmerding. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team is on a roll, capturing two wins in the past week to create a three-match winning streak. They have improved their record to 6-3. The Highlanders recently beat Lick-Wilmerding in a clean 3-0 sweep at Binks Rawlings Gym on Thursday, September 11. They also defeated Urban in San Francisco 3-1 two days earlier. The results mean Piedmont has now doubled last year’s win total after just nine matches. “We’re young, but we have confidence. It’s had a domino effect on the entire team in the best way possible,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. It’s a night and day difference than previous years. With 11 matches remaining in the regular season, the Highlanders are one win away from matching their win total in 2023, and five wins away from the last time the team qualified for the North Coast Section playoffs in 2018. “The connection between all the girls is just insane this year,” stated senior Stella Wilk. “We’re all really putting in the work and you’re seeing all the work in practice coming through in games.” “When I first played on varsity as a sophomore, I looked up to all the older girls. This year, we’re really young so it’s exciting to see them bring the energy,” added senior Mira Sachs. 3-0 over Lick-Wilmerding Piedmont won its clean sweep by scores of 25-16, 25-14, and 25-13. In the first set, the Highlanders dominated with 10 kills, taking advantage of the Tigers’ offensive and defensive errors. Sofia Meyer led the way with four, while, Wilk, Maika Ting, and Allyson Huyhn had two each. The second set was even more one-sided with 16 kills to their credit, allowing many starters to rest in the third set. Ting landed five spikes, Izara Dando had four, Sachs had three, Huyhn and Wilk had two, while Jasmine Houlder had one. In the third set, Lick-Wilmerding actually kept it a close contest at 12-8, but Piedmont only allowed five more points from then on. From there, PHS scored five straight puts to jump ahead 17-8, then scored eight of the final 13 points. Huyhn, a usual setter, scored the final two points of the match with back-to-back kills. Final stats: Huyhn led the way with eight kills, Wilk had five kills, Sachs had four, Ting had seven, Dando had four kills and two blocks, and Meyer had four. Maika Ting had 14 kills against Urban and seven against Lick-Wilmerding. Daisy Tran lines up a spike against Lick-Wilmerding.
articles.title: Piedmont wins third straight, improves record to 6-3

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team bashed Albany 24-11, improving their record to 4-2. Piedmont High’s girls’ water polo team traveled to Albany on Thursday, September 11, beating the Cougars in a one-sided 24-11 victory. The result improves Piedmont’s record to 4-2 through six matches. Piedmont led 5-3 by the end of the first quarter and extended the gap to 11-7 by halftime. The Highlanders took over in the third quarter with five goals while allowing two, making it 16-9. PHS added on eight goals in the final period and held Albany to two. It was an impressive game by Esme Krumins and Rachel Young, each scoring five goals on the night. Match Recap Piedmont opened to a 5-3 lead in the first quarter with two goals by Rachel Young, and individual scores by Esme Krumins, Mava Pisani, and Havia Leonard. Official times of goals were not tracked throughout the match. In the second quarter, Young opened with a goal, but Albany responded quickly on their next possession—6-4. PHS then ran off three unanswered goals, all coming from Krumins to make it 9-4 before Albany’s next score. After a pair of goals by the Cougars, Young got back on the scoreboard, while Abigail Jacoby netted another a minute later to make it 11-6. Albany got one back right before halftime, 11-7. Jacoby got Piedmont on the board first in the third quarter, 12-7. Soon after, PHS drew an exclusion penalty on Albany, leading to a quick goal by Young to extend their lead to 13-7. Piedmont then rallied off three straight goals by Sydney Olson, Pisani, and Leonard to make it Staff Photos Vivian Burke scored a hat trick against Albany. Rachel Young scored five goals against the Cougars. a comfortable 16-7 advantage. Albany scored twice in the final minutes of the third, 16-9. In the final going, Piedmont drew a player advantage, leading to Krumins scoring seconds later. Vivian Burke then added back-toback goals over the next couple of minutes, 19-9. Albany scored after drawing a player advantage, but Burke netted another soon after, 20-10. Celeste Dickason made it 21-10, then Leonard added another. After one more goal by the Cougars, Piedmont’s final goals were scored by Young and Leonard, bringing the final score to 24-11. Final stats: Krumins and Young led with five goals. Leonard had four goals. Burke had three goals. Pisani, Olson, and Jacoby had two goals. Dickason scored an individual goal.

articles.text: Piedmont wins consolation bracket at James Logan Tournament Staff Photos Faith Chin won all six of her matches over the past week. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team wrapped up a busy week with six matches in four days, winning the James Logan Tournament’s consolation bracket in the process. At the tourney in Union City on Friday and Saturday, September 12-13, the Highlanders defeated Moreau 7-0 and lost 5-2 to Cal High on the opening day. On Day 2 they beat Emerald 5-2 and of note, Berkeley 6-1. Prior to the tournament, they lost 6-3 to Acalanes in Lafayette on Wednesday, September 10 and swept San Leandro 7-0 on Tuesday, September 9. “We played a lot of tennis. We took home first place in the James Logan Tournament consolation ladder. We’re now 5-5 with 12 matches remaining in the season, not counting WACC and NCS,” said coach Jim Landes. 6-1 victory over Berkeley Piedmont beat their Western Alameda County Conference rivals by winning three of four matches at singles and all three doubles matches. The result does not count toward their league schedule because it was in tournament play. At singles, all of Piedmont’s wins were nearly clean sweeps. Kate Jumper won 6-0, 6-1 at No. 2, Faith Chin won 6-1, 6-1 at No. 3, and Arianna Kortum won 6-0, 6-1 at No. 4. PHS’ only loss was at No. 1 singles, where freshman Ella Ruthven lost in three sets, 6-4, 4-6, 10-7. All doubles matches at the tournament were played in eightgame single sets. Maddie Tran and Samantha Huyhn won 8-2 at No. 1, Emma Chan and Chiara Silvio won 8-2 at No. 2, while Amalia Angulo and Amelia Oldrin won 9-7 at No. 3. 5-2 over Emerald Piedmont only lost one singles and one doubles match against Emerald HS from Dublin. At singles, Jumper won 7-6 (9-7), 6-3 at No. 2, Chin won 6-1, 6-1 at No. 3, and Kortum won 6-0, 6-1 at No. 4. Ruthven lost in three sets at No. 1, 4-6, 6-4, 10-7. At doubles, Chan and Silvio won 8-4 at No. 2 while Ella Thomasson and Lila Rosen won 8-3 at No. 3. articles.text: Piedmont High’s flag football team pulled out a 6-0 shutout over Western Alameda County Conference opponents Mt. Eden on Thursday, September 11 at Witter Field. The result improves Piedmont’s record to 3-2 overall and 2-0 against league opponents. Piedmont got its game-winning touchdown with 1:35 remaining in the first quarter when quarterback Edie Elmquist found Kate Tong for a five-yard pass on an out route. It was also a big game on the defensive side for Brynne Jones, who finished with four tackles for loss and a quarterback sack. Dahlia Osman had an interception, and Elspeth Grippando led the team with 12 tackles. The Highlanders look ahead to another league battle when visiting Arroyo in San Lorenzo on Thursday, September 18. Game Recap After two trades of possession in the first quarter, Piedmont scored on an eight-play drive. It featured Elmquist hitting receiver Malia Williams on a big 26-yard reception on 3rd-and-16 to the Mt. Eden 30. Elmquist then found Tong on a 15-yard reception. After a Monarchs penalty put the Highlanders at the five, Elmquist passed to Tong for the touchdown reception on second down with 1:35 on the clock. After a failed one-point conversion, Piedmont led 6-0. PHS forced a punt on Mt. Eden’s next possession, including a tackle for loss by Brynne Jones. Both teams traded the ball on multiple three-and-outs through the remainder of the first half, but highlights include another tackle for loss by Jones and a 29-yard reception by Williams. Mt. Eden drove to the Piedmont 32 to open the third quarter, but another tackle for loss by Jones led to a turnover on downs. After a three-and-out by Piedmont, senior safety Dahlia Osman nabbed an interception with 3:17 left in the third. Both teams continuously traded possession in the fourth quarter until the final whistle. Jones recorded a sack, leading to a turnover on downs at the Piedmont’s 29. articles.text: Coach Jordan Seiden was named head coach of Piedmont varsity football in 2022, taking over at a time when the program’s future was in doubt. He brought more than 25 years of coaching experience, having led teams at Skyline High School in Oakland, Capuchino High School in San Bruno, and Castro Valley High School. With deep roots in local gridiron history, he has made it his mission to restore Highlander pride through leadership grounded in hard work, respect, and camaraderie. Since his arrival, coach Seiden has led a remarkable turnaround. Piedmont football was on the brink of collapse after COVID decimated participation and raised questions about the future of the program. Under his leadership, the team has rebounded with renewed pride and energy, climbing back to win back-toback league titles. A Bay Area native, coach Seiden played at St. Mary’s High School and graduated from Berkeley High in 1991. He continued his football journey at Diablo Valley College and UC Davis before studying kinesiology at St. Mary’s College in Moraga. Off the field, coach Seiden has devoted his career to supporting young people in challenging situations. He worked at Alameda County’s juvenile hall and later with the Oakland Unified School District, helping students stay in school or return after time away. For him, the true measure of success is helping young people grow into responsible citizens as well as athletes. Coach Seiden continues to inspire players, families, and the wider community with a vision built around discipline, teamwork, respect, and lasting Highlander pride. Jordan Seiden talks over the growth of Piedmont High’s football program and his philosophy as a coach. articles.text: Autumn Lights Festival, an art-filled and family-friendly fundraising event for the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt (FGLM), returns this year on Thursday, October 16. The festival has drawn more than 12,000 art and nature enthusiasts to Lake Merritt since 2012 and celebrates its 13th anniversary over three nights, October 16 through 18. Patrons will experience more than 50 locally-produced illuminated art displays, some of which were presented at Burning Man desert events, throughout Oakland’s seven-acre municipal gardens. Filma Collective, a coworking artists’ space based in Berkeley, is one of over a dozen featured artist organizations this year. “This is a very special show for us as it’s the only botanical installation we do, a fusion of art and nature,” Filma Collective artists wrote in a statement. “The festival is a yearly fundraiser for the public gardens in Oakland’s Lake Merritt which are a beloved Autumn Lights Festival 2023 pillar of the local community. We’ve been in love with the gardens for years and feel blessed we’re able to participate in helping it remain available to all our The event is family-friendly and includes activities for young visitors. Courtesy of Gardens at Lake Merritt friends in the community.” Ticket purchases benefit the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt, a volunteer organization formed in 2004. FGLM volunteers provide much needed maintenance assistance as the City of Oakland’s gardening staff has been dramatically reduced over time. The nonprofit partners with the City of Oakland to support the maintenance, revitalization, and programming of the seven-acre collection of themed gardens within Lakeside Park on the shores of Lake Merritt, including a bonsai garden, a Sensory Garden, a Toddler Garden, an Urban Edible Garden, and more. The Autumn Lights festival is FGLM’s biggest annual fundraiser. Tickets are on sale now and can be purchased by visiting https://gardensatlakemerritt.org/ autumn-lights-festival-2025/.
articles.title: Autumn Lights Festival returns to Lake Merritt Oct. 16 - 18

articles.text: Yeny Valdés Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) welcomes Cuban music artist Yeny Valdez accompanied by Team Bahia this Friday as part of the museum’s free “Friday Nights” series. Valdés is a renowned Cuban singer with five Latin Grammy nominations and was the lead vocalist of Los Van Van, one of Cuba’s most iconic bands, for 16 years. She will perform contemporary Cuban music with a high-energy mix of timba, salsa, son, and tropical fusion. She is joined by Team Bahia, a group of musicians who specialize in soul and rhythm. Their performance invites everyone to dance, celebrate, and feel the energy of Caribbean music. “Friday Nights” is a free community-gathering evening event series held every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout spring and summer, featuring live music, immersive arts activities and late-night museum access with the purchase of a museum ticket. Concerts begin at 7 p.m. Bring a blanket and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s large lawn, where live music and entertainment takes place throughout the evening. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from a stationed food truck on-site. A rotating list of vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon Streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. Friday Night events are always free and open to the public, but late-night museum access requires a ticket purchase. Visit https://museumca.org/event/friday-nights-at-omca-with-yenyvaldes-teambahia/ to learn more about this week’s lineup.
articles.title: Yeny Valdés performs free concert at OMCA this Friday

articles.text: Marin Theatre Company (MTC) is extending its run of Jonathan Spector’s Eureka Day, now ending on September 28. The play is set at the Eureka Day School in Berkeley, California, portrayed as a “bastion of progressive ideals with a board of directors that values inclusion above all else.” The majority of the play takes place during meetings between parents and administrators concerning requirements for vaccination after an outbreak of mumps at the school. These meetings prompt school leadership to reconsider its liberal vaccine policy in comedic and dramatic ways. The New York Times called Eureka Day and Jonathan Spector’s “lively portrait of a debate over mandatory vaccinations” as the “the perfect play for our age of disagreement.” MTC’s production of Eureka Day is presented in partnership with Aurora Theatre Company, where the play had its world premiere in 2018, two years before the COVID-19 pandemic and the discourse over required vaccinations that followed. Marin Theatre Company’s production features nearly all its original cast members from the 2018 world premiere. The cast includes Howard Swain as Don, Lisa Anne Porter as Suzanne, Leontyne MbeleMbong as Carina, Charisse Loriaux as Meiko, Teddy Spencer as Eli, and Kelsey Sloan as Winter. Eureka Day features assistant direction by Molly Aaronson-Gel, scenic design by Richard Olmsted, costume design by Maggie Whittaker, lighting design by Jeff Rowlings, sound design by Ray Archie, and video content by Teddy Hulsker. Nick Carvalho is the stage manager with Mona Jean Ortiz as Assistant Stage Manager A pre-show presentation from MTC’s stage designer is held on Thursday, September 18. Eureka Day is appropriate for audience members 14 and older. Visit https://purchase.marintheatre.org/EventAvailability?EventId=49801 to purchase tickets. Cast of Eureka Day
articles.title: Marin Theatre extends Eureka Day to Sept. 28

articles.text: Smuin Ballet Company presents its fall season, entitled “Extremely Close,” on September 19 and 20 at the Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek. Smuin’s 32nd season is directed by Amy Seiwert and is inspired by Alejandro Cerrundo’s art installation and movement drama Extremely Close, set to a score by Philip Glass and Dustin O’Halloran. Fall performances include the West Coast premiere of choreographer Justin Peck’s Partita, set to Caroline Shaw’s Pulitzer Prize-winning “Partita for 8 Voices,” a unique number featuring eight dancers in sneakers. Smuin Ballet will be the first company outside of New York City Ballet to perform the work since it premiered in 2022. The final piece being performed in this season’s fall programming is A Long Night choreographed by Seiwert, a former mentee of the late Michael Smuin. Seiwert reimagines Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream with humor and heartfelt storytelling that honors George Balanchine’s original choreography. A Long Night premiered in 2023 for BalletX in Philadelphia and is set to songs by Patsy Cline, Pink Martini, Harry Nilsson, and more. “To have Justin’s [Peck] and Alejandro’s [Cerrundo] work in my first curated season is an honor and a thrill,” said Seiwert. “Justin’s creative path reminds me a bit of our founder Michael Smuin’s. His work in film and on Broadway informs the distinctive style he brings to his creations for the concert dance stage. And Alejandro’s work exemplifies how extraordinary contemporary dance can be: musical and theatrical, with a mystery that will take your breath away.” Smuin Ballet hosts two performances at Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek September 19 through 20: Friday at 7:30 p.m. and Saturday at 2 p.m. The company’s fall season concludes at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts in San Francisco September 26 through October 5 with eight performances scheduled: Friday, September 26 at 7:30 p.m.; Saturday and Sunday, September 27 and 28 at 2 p.m.; Thursday, October 2 at 7:30 p.m.; Friday, October 3 at 7:30 p.m.; Saturday, October 4 at 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.; and Sunday, October 5 at 2 p.m. Single-day tickets are available at www.smuinballet.org. Smuin Ballet dancers prepare for the company’s fall season. ®

articles.text: Where the Crawdads Sing is a southern gothic story based on the 2018 best-selling novel by Della Owens. As of this writing, it has sold more than 12 million copies worldwide and has developed a passionate fan base, hence it was inevitable that it would find its way to the screen. Set in the small North Carolina town of Barley Cove, the story spans some 20 years, from the 1950s to the 1970s. The film, which doesn’t quite follow the narrative plot of the book, opens with a young woman, Kya Clark (Daisy Edgar-Jones), also called “the Marsh Girl,” on trial for murder. She is charged with killing Chase Andrews (Taylor John-Smith), a popular young man from a wealthy and prominent family. Her defense counsel is retired attorney, Tom Milton (David Strathairn), who has known Kya since she was a child and is committed to her innocence. The tale is told in a series of flashbacks, beginning with Kya as a young girl who lives on the edge of a stretching marsh with her mother, siblings, and abusive, drunken father. After a violent episode, her mother, suitcase in hand, silently walks away, soon to be followed by her brother and sisters, and Kyra finds herself left with her father. But before long he vanishes as well. Barely a tween, she finds herself abandoned, alone, living in the shack, struggling to survive, while relying on Daisy Edgar-Jones in Where the Crawdads Sing her knowledge of the marsh, her innate intelligence, and remarkable resourcefulness. And so Kya develops into a fiercely independent young woman who wanders the marsh in her father’s old boat, and sells mussels to a local store-owner in exchange for needed supplies. She did go to school, for one day, but was laughed at by the children when she stood before them barefooted and uncombed and ridiculed. It’s only years later that she is taught to read by a local boy, Tate Walker (Taylor John-Smith), who has known Kyra since they were children (they are now in their teens). Once she discovers books, a new and astonishing world opens up to her, and she begins to read about the marsh animals and soon sketches them in her notebooks, demonstrating an extraordinary descriptive talent. Where the Crawdads Sing gradually develops into two love stories involving Tate and Chase (it’s Chase that Kyra is accused of killing). But the essence of the film is the isolating solitude of the marsh and the small shack where Kyra has lived alone, shunned by the judgmental townspeople. Time and place, as well as the splendor of the marsh, become as central to this story as its characters. Those who loved the book will embrace the film. Others may find it less intense than it might have been, especially the trial. But as a whole, it is engaging and at times irresistible. Where the Crawdads Sing, Directed by Olivia Newman. Starring Daisy Edgar-Jones, Taylor John-Smith, Harris Dickinson. 2 hrs., 5 min. PG-13. Streaming on Disney+/Roku/ HBO-MAX/Fandango/Prime. The animation is flawless, the attention to detail breathtaking, and the story a let’er rip adventure that takes a retired, square-faced, bespectacled curmudgeon, Carl Fredricksen (Ed Asner), 78, and his uninvited sidekick, Russell (Jordan Nagai), 8, to the jungles of South America. As a young boy, sitting in darkened movie houses, watching newsreels of the famous explorer, Charles Munz, Carl dreamed of having a great adventure. One afternoon, walking home from the matinee, he meets Ellie who, he discovers, has exactly the same spirit. They grow up nurturing the belief that some day they will stand together in an exotic spot, surrounded by vast jungles and cascading waterfalls. Alas, life got in the way and in a wonderfully crafted four minute montage, Carl and Ellie’s life together is revealed: years quickly pass, countless moments of joy and sadness are shared. In a moment of inspiration, Carl ties some 20,000 helium balloons to the top of his house, forming a magnificent bouquet of colors, and early one morning floats away. Unbeknownst to Carl, Russell, an earnest, well- equipped Wilder ness Explorer, happened to be on his front porch at the moment of lift-off. And so the journey begins with the unlikely pair riding on the southerly winds, headed toward South America. There they will meet talking dogs; a very old Charles Munz; a large, chocolate-loving bird named Kevin; and take an unexpected ride on a vintage dirigible. You can’t make this stuff up. Well, actually, in the case of Pixar, you can, and that is exactly what these filmmakers do with unbridled imaginations and an inexhaustible well of stories that captivate and entertain. In Up they even manage to work in a few life lessons for Carl and Russell, Carl’s being that poignant aphorism about how life is what happens while you are waiting to really live (and go to South America). UP. Directed by Pete Docter and Bob Peterson. Voiced by Ed Asner, Jordan Nagai and Christopher Plummer. Pixar animated film. 1 hr., 38 min. Rated PG. Released in 2014. articles.text: Open through Oct. 13, 11–2 p.m. Slavic Art Exhibit The Center for Slavic Arts and Culture is proud to present its very first exhibition, Kaleidoscope. The show brings together 17 artists from five Slavic countries, including a photographer and a jewelry designer, each sharing their talent and creative vision. In challenging and uncertain times, art reminds us of beauty, resilience, and the strength of our community. Kaleidoscope is a celebration of creativity, and a reminder of how art can connect, uplift, and inspire us all. This exhibition will be open weekend days from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. until mid-October. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, September 17, 2025 The Musical Gourmet Music and athletics By Joseph Gold The world of music is a very competitive place - overt and covert. In reality, the two terms are rather similar. Competition is intense. Musicians are athletes of the arts. Timing is imperative and stamina is also. The general public does not realize how much energy it takes to play a concert. Think of a concert as a musical marathon. The performer needs nuanced musical abilities in combination with complete and total concentration. The public enjoys experiencing perfection. In the past, it was the music that was important. Now an ostentatious display has usurped integrity. Classical musicians have adopted the superficial world of the pop music scene. Famous ballet dancers like Rudolf Nureyev were incredible athletes. Can you imagine how good a ballet dancer Romanian gymnast Nadia Comaneci would have been had she so desired? Interestingly enough, both ballet dancers and gymnasts use professional choreographers. Their music is selected with great care. Opera singers have always been very popular with the public. They are generally known by their excessive girth given that the only exercise they do is eatThe Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet ing. But don’t be fooled. Singing on the opera stage is very physically taxing. Star concert performers must keep themselves in good shape physically. Local violinist Stuart Canin has had an amazing career. He is almost 100 years old and has continued to play well into his late 90s in admirable style. Yehudi Menuhin has always practiced yoga. Another violin prodigy from San Francisco was Ruggiero Ricci. He could have been an outstanding gymnast on the parallel bars. Guys I know who served with him in the army said that he could do chin-ups with great rapidity and ease. Violinist Jascha Heifetz competed in tennis, table tennis and pistol shooting. The greatest players always kept themselves an excellent physical shape. It was also a pleasure to learn their philosophy. They believed that the musical score was the most important thing. As interpreters, they were at the service of the music. Things are very different now. Conductors have lived long lives. Their form of exercise is very much like aerobics. Sincerity should also figure as a very important aspect of music. The virtuoso musician makes things look easy and effortless. Given that technique is the cornerstone of any art, nuance must come into play. Despite all the superficialities that we see from “superstar” musicians, the rules of music are very simple. The great American musician Albert Spalding stated it as: “sincerity, sincerity, sincerity.“ I have always admired football coach Vince Lombardi. Can you imagine him as a conductor of an orchestra? He would have been marvelous. He espoused sincerity and respect in every way. He saw the entire picture and conveyed it to his teams. But in reality, “the team that controls, the line of scrimmage wins the game.” That’s the way it should be in music. Violinist Joseph Gold as a young man on the USC wrestling team. Among the fragments he discovers a small envelope with the name “Black” written on it. Inside he finds an unusual, corrugated key. Oskar holds the key in his hand, and it is in that moment that he becomes convinced that the key fits a lock, a box perhaps, that contains a message from his father. And thus we learn, through flashbacks, that over the years Thomas has created what he called “reconnaissance expeditions,” a scavenger hunt of sorts, which sends Oskar out into the streets of New York in search of what they call “the sixth borough.” And so attaching the key to a lanyard, which he wears around his neck, Oskar is inspired to begin a similar expedition. He starts by looking through a massive NYC phone book, and finds that there are 472 Blacks listed. His mission, kept a secret from his mother, is to visit all of them, asking if they recognize the key. His first stop is at the home of Abby Black (Viola Davis), and it’s during his conversation with her that he mentions he has been tested for Asperger’s Syndrome with inconclusive results. We know that Oskar is precocious, at times brusque, highly verbal, but we soon learn that Thomas’ expeditions were about much more than simply a sixth borough hunt, but a way of sending his son into a world in which he is inherently uncomfortable. Abby has no idea about the key, and so Oskar continues, from Black to Black, showing each of them the key, and using his father’s vintage camera takes their photograph, which he keeps in a notebook. To refer to Extremely Loud & Intensely Close as a work of art may verge on hyperbole. And yet, doesn’t it represent the use of images and narrative as only film can, to explore the depths of grief and loss while focusing on the emotions of a young boy who struggles to find meaning in what he angrily judges is meaningless. The key becomes a metaphor for Oskar’s arduous and at times fraught search for answers to questions that are timeless: to what purpose? To what end? And ultimately, why? articles.text: How deep pressure therapy from a service dog can improve mental health The psychiatric service dog has emerged as a potentially effective way to manage stress, despite being one of the least pioneered innovations in mental health. Although emotional support animals were banned from traveling in cabins outside carriers, the Americans With Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990 allows service dogs trained to actively mitigate disabilities full public access. These disabilities can be visible or invisible. One task psychiatric service dogs can perform is deep pressure therapy, which involves more than just a dog laying on its owner. To effectively perform this task, the dog must be trained to tighten its core to maintain balance while dropping its weight onto the owner. This requires impressive stamina, as well as intense focus on the handler. Deep pressure therapy can be incredibly effective for individuals struggling with anxiety, depression, ADHD, obsessive, compulsive disorder (OCD), and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The dog acts as a weighted blanket, providing calming and grounding pressure that can lift mood, decrease anxiety, increase focus, and stabilize the handler. Despite skeptics who claim the dog is merely laying there for comfort, service dogs trained for deep pressure therapy actively respond to specific cues to legitimately aid their handler. Many people assume they don’t qualify for a service dog due to their invisible or seemingly minor disability. However, a service dog can greatly improve quality of life, even with a simple task like deep pressure therapy. Pairing this task with alert task training may decrease the need for psychotherapy sessions, reduce dependency on psychiatric medication, and even help handlers wean off long-term medication entirely. As a holistic approach to addressing the mental health epidemic, psychiatric service dogs offer a promising solution. With increased stress affecting many lives, deep pressure therapy from a trained service dog could provide much-needed relief. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com.

articles.text: About 36 walkers and four K-9 companions gathered at the Exedra last Wednesday for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays outing. The Wednesday before, the group enjoyed a historical tour led by Nancy DeRoche through her neighborhood above Oakland Avenue. The highlight was the Blair Avenue house where Jack London wrote The Call of the Wild in 1902–03. In about 1910, the house was moved two lots up the street to make way for the Sutro Mansion — a reminder of how homes were once relocated by rolling them across logs pulled by horses, mules, or oxen. While common a century ago, such methods would not be permitted under today’s regulations. Sacramento Star Piedmont Tax Article dated 01-28-1914 Hugh Craig Another relocated home with a central place in Piedmont’s history is the Craig House at 55 Craig Avenue. Built in 1879 by Hugh Craig, it is the city’s second-oldest residence and a large Stick Italianate Victorian that remains striking even today. From the Exedra, the walkers made their way up Mountain Avenue to visit the site and learn more about Craig’s influence on Piedmont. Craig was a pivotal figure during Piedmont’s early years. Born in Sydney, Australia, in 1841 to Scottish parents, he grew up in New Zealand before moving to Oakland in 1874 to work for the New Zealand Insurance Company in San Francisco. He purchased five acres in Piedmont and built his home in 1879 on Vernal (now Highland) Avenue. Following the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, many families relocated across the Bay, swelling the populations of Oakland and Piedmont. Oakland, pressed for revenue, sought to annex Piedmont to expand its tax base. But some Piedmont residents wanted self-determination.
