articles.text: A record turnout of 26 readers showed up at Piedmont Community Center in Piedmont Park on September 8 for the First Mondays Reading Group discussion. Participating were Sue Backer, Sarah Johnson, Bill Ahern, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Ken Young, Mike Henn, Karin Fetherston, Heidi Schmidt, Laura Goldman, Peggy Shultz, Hilary Honore, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Pat McMahon, Nancy Henn, Adrienne Hamlin, Alicia Rivera, Martin Levy, Orrel Lanter, Gerry Gregg, Darby Gregg, Linda Sigel, Mary Carter, Bella Almanzan, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. The group was pleased to have Rose Byrne with them for the first time. The group was there to talk about The Women by Kristin Hannah, an author of more than 20 historical fiction novels. Hannah’s books are known for their character development, historical depth, and themes of love, loss, and female friendship. Her best-selling work, The Nightingale, has sold over 4.5 million copies worldwide and has been published in 45 languages. The Women is Hannah’s most recent novel. It was published in 2024 and tells the story of Frances “Frankie” McGrath, a privileged, young woman who defies her conservative parents to become an Army nurse during the Vietnam War. The book debuted at number one on The New York Times fiction best-seller list, was at number one for 10 weeks, and was one of the most borrowed titles in American public libraries at the time. It’s the story of Frankie’s incredibly hard nursing experiences in Vietnam, the deep bonds she forms with other nurses, and her difficult return to an America where the sacrifices and trauma of its returning female veterans were not understood or appreciated. In January 2024, Warner Bros acquired the book’s screen rights for a film adaptation, and a movie is in the works. The Women generated a lot of First Mondays Reading Group discussion. Some members of the group had many issues with the book and even questioned whether it was “serious literature.” The story seemed like a soap opera with one horribly bad thing after another happening to Frankie. One reader wondered if any character could be less innocent. The group believed that the issues Frankie experienced did happen to those involved in the Vietnam war, but was it possible for all these problems to happen to one person? Some readers felt that “the bones of the book” were good, but the storytelling was so “flowery” that they were turned off. The war experiences packed into the first part of the book seemed like a MASH television episode, but they weren’t funny. Dead men coming back into Frankie’s life was almost expected by the readers. For some of them it became silly. Many readers were also disappointed with the story’s hard to believe ending, For one male reader this was “a book by a woman, about women, for women.” Some readers would have preferred a non-fiction history of peoples’ real Vietnam War experiences rather than this fiction. Readers felt The Women missed an opportunity to tell the tragic story of this war more credibly. Additionally, the book at 470 pages seemed long. However, some readers had more positive things to say about the book. They felt they got a lot out of the novel. It brought back their Vietnam experiences, many of which were hard. The book generated memories and provoked emotions that are important for people, and especially younger people, to understand. Additionally, Hannah’s message that there is a lack of understanding and appreciation of women’s contributions during the Vietnam War is an important one. Another enjoyable part of the discussion was the readers sharing their different experiences during this Vietnam War period. This conversation took on a life of its own and it was interesting to hear how people wanted to contribute in different ways based on their motivations and consciences during the war. The readers had to be reminded to come back to talk about the book. The group seemed to accept that The Women has flaws but it does address an important historical issue regarding the lack of understanding of the role of women in the Vietnam War. The group had previously selected The Wright Brothers by David McCullough for October’s read and Euphoria by Lily King for their November book. After Dick Carter’s presentation of three non-fiction candidates, the readers chose Differ We Must by Steve Inskeep for their December read. With all their business done, they took a group photo in the circle outside the Community Hall. The group will meet on the patio outside the Community Hall in Piedmont Park on October 6th at 1:30 PM for their next discussion. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. Go to https://bit.ly/3R86PP4, or call the Recreation Department at 510 420-3070, to register. The First Monday Reading Group will meet on the patio outside the Community Hall in Piedmont Park on October 6th at 1:30 PM for their next discussion.

The truly giant parks are woods containing multiple gardens, fields, lakes, trails for riding horses and bicycles, and paths for runners and hikers. Britain after he visited Portugal in 1903 to strengthen the relationship between the two countries and reaffirm their alliance. The park has a central strip of grass and an intricate hedge work, flanked by long walkways to the left and right. At the observation deck at the top of the park, you can see a statue of Marquês de Pombal and the Tagus River off in the distance. Praça do Marquês de Pombal is a roundabout and square dedicated to the Portuguese statesman and diplomat who effectively ruled the Portuguese Empire from 1750 to 1777 as chief minister to King Joseph I. From there, you venture down Avenida da Liberdade, a shaded and beautiful 1,100 meter avenue down the center of Lisbon that could draw comparisons to the Champs-Élysées in Paris. The avenue is lined with numerous monuments to several historical Portuguese figures and events. The largest monument is dedicated to the fallen soldiers in World War I. Avenida da Liberdade comes to an end at Monumento aos Restauradores, or Monument to the Restorers, which was made to memorialize Portugal’s victory in the Portuguese Restoration War of 1640-1668 and erected in 1886. The route veers slightly toward the Estátua do Rei Dom Pedro IV, another town square with two fountains and the Column of Pedro IV in between. The monument is dedicated after Pedro I, who was the first ruler of the Empire of Brazil. But before you reach the column, take a tasty detour after the Monumento aos Restauradores by turning left (right if coming the opposite direction) to A Ginjinha for a further dive into Portuguese culture. A Ginjinha is a historic open-front bar that opened in 1840—where you can sip Portugal’s famous cherry Staff Photos liquor. The location was helped publicized by travel journalists like Anthony Bordain and Rick Steves. From the Column of Pedro, head down R. Augusta avenue, where you can find several gift shops and restaurants on its way to the Arco da Rau Augusta and Commerce Square. In the center of Praça do Comércio is a monument to King José I, created in 1775. Your journey ends across the street from Commerce Square at Cais das Colunas, a pier named after the two columns on the edge of the Tagus River. The location played as a welcoming point to several prominent figures, like Queen Elizabeth II in 1957. From there you can see Ponte 25 de April, a bridge with a striking similarity to the Golden Gate, with Santuário de Cristo Rei to its left. Take off your shoes and dip your weary feet in the water after a day of walking around Lisbon. Take a detour to A Ginjinha, a historic watering hole to drink Portugal’s famous ginjinha — a cherry infused liquor. The location was created in 1840. The path is nearing its end down R. Augusta avenue to the Arco da Rau Augusta. Our trail ends at Cais das Colunas, where you can take in a view of Ponte 25 de April and Santuário de Cristo Rei to its left.

articles.text: This fall, Stagebridge—Oakland’s pioneering center for creative aging—is inviting older adults back for another season of classes that spark curiosity, laughter, and connection. Beginning the week of September 22, the schedule includes everything from storytelling and acting to dance, improv, and clowning. Stagebridge has long believed that staying active and engaged is key to thriving in later years. Science agrees: picking up new skills and keeping socially connected can improve memory, boost mood, and even support physical health. But the real magic shows up in the community itself. Toby, a Stagebridge teacher who recently returned after some time away, described the experience this way: “I had such a wonderful time with my cohort. They were openhearted, delightful, funny, poetic, and kind—and did I mention FUNNY? When I first walked back into the church, I felt a whiff of sadness, missing my great clown sister Joan Mankin. But that soon dissolved into pure joy when the actual magic of Stagebridge took over. All I know is you have an enchanted island there, one where I made fantastic new friends and reconnected with old ones.” For many, that sense of “enchanted island” is what makes Stagebridge unique. Students come not only to learn but also to find camaraderie, to reconnect with creativity, and to share in the humor and wisdom that flourish in later life. Teachers, many of whom are artists still active in the Bay Area, bring both skill and heart to their work, creating spaces where every participant feels welcome. A quick look at Stagebridge’s event calendar shows how alive this community really is, from performances to storytelling nights that bring members together both in and beyond the classroom. Interested in joining the fun? Learn more about Stagebridge and all upcoming fall classes at www.stagebridge.org. Stagebridge is America’s oldest performing arts nonprofit for older adults. Based in Oakland, CA | www.stagebridge.org | info@stagebridge.org | (510) 210-3773 Stagebridge Summer Camp: where bold costumes meet even bolder personalities. When the rhythm hits, the feet don’t stop—Stagebridge keeps the beat alive.

articles.text: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has a list of 20 common fraud schemes on its “Scams and Safety”1 web page, including credit card theft. The thief makes small purchases with your stolen credit card number and sees if they go through, if they do, then they hit your account for bigger purchases. You should have an email, text message, or phone alert set up with your credit card company, so that the bank will contact you if there are any unusual spending items, if there are illegitimate charges, you must report to the bank as soon as possible so you won’t be charged for those items. The bank will lock your account and send you a new card in the mail. This can be frustrating when you have set up monthly withdrawals to be charged against your card. You’ll have to go to those companies’ websites and change the card numbers you use for those charges. How to protect yourself from Internet scams and fraudulent schemes. The FBI says protect your computer2 by keeping systems and software up to date and install a strong reputable anti-virus program. Also, ou will pay a yearly fee for antivirus, antispyware, and firewall software services, but the safety they provide makes it well worth the cost. Be careful when connecting to a public Wi-Fi network and create a strong and unique passphrase for each online account you hold and change them regularly. If you’ve been the victim of a scam, file a complaint with your local/state police department’s cybercrime unit and file a complaint with the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3).3 Forewarned is forearmed. The more you know about e-scams and fraudulent schemes, the safer you will feel. Another way to protect yourself is by regularly visiting the Federal Trade Commission’s (FTC’s)4 website for updated information and warnings. Its function is to protect America’s consumers by educating and taking consumer complaints on everything from identity theft to unwanted telemarketing solicitations by phone or by email. It runs the National Do Not Call Registry,5 which you should sign up for. Once you are on the do-not-call list for at least 31 days, the calls/emails should stop, and if they don’t then you can file a complaint with the FTC. You can register each phone number that you have, and your registration won’t expire. You can check the FTC’s website if your phone number is still registered.5 Remember, it’s not OK for companies to leave recorded voicemails on your phone, so you can file a complaint if you receive unwanted telemarketing robocalls. Once you are registered on the do-not-call list, it’s illegal for those telemarketers to continue to call you. Use your common sense. If you don’t recognize the area code or the phone number on your caller ID, chances are it’s a telemarketing call. Don’t answer it, or if you do, insist that they take you off their call list. To keep up to date on current scams that are plaguing consumers, the FTC has an email alert system that you can sign up for.6 This educational, third-party article is provided as a courtesy by Liz Lummis O’Neil, Agent (CA Ins. Lic. #4282724) New York Life Insurance Company. Be careful when connecting to a public Wi-Fi network and create a strong and unique passphrase for each online account you hold and change them regularly. If you’ve been the victim of a scam, file a complaint with your local/state police department’s cybercrime unit and file a complaint with the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3).3 Forewarned is forearmed. The more you know about e-scams and fraudulent schemes, the safer you will feel. Another way to protect yourself is by regularly visiting the Federal Trade Commission’s (FTC’s)4 website for updated information and warnings. Its function is to protect America’s consumers by educating and taking consumer complaints on everything from identity theft to unwanted telemarketing solicitations by phone or by email. It runs the National Do Not Call Registry,5 which you should sign up for. Once you are on the do-not-call list for at least 31 days, the calls/emails should stop, and if they don’t then you can file a complaint with the FTC. You can register each phone number that you have, and your registration won’t expire. You can check the FTC’s website if your phone number is still registered.5 Remember, it’s not OK for companies to leave recorded voicemails on your phone, so you can file a complaint if you receive unwanted telemarketing robocalls. Once you are registered on the do-not-call list, it’s illegal for those telemarketers to continue to call you. Use your common sense. If you don’t recognize the area code or the phone number on your caller ID, chances are it’s a telemarketing call. Don’t answer it, or if you do, insist that they take you off their call list. Dear MacMama, I know this is the time of year when new iPhones come out. I have an iPhone 13. Do you think this is a good time to upgrade? I really enjoy the camera on my iPhone and I understand that the new ones have much better cameras. I love to take photographs not only of my family but of flowers and landscapes. So which one would you recommend for me? Ellen, Rockridge Dear Ellen, I think this is an excellent time to upgrade. There are four versions of the iPhone 17, and I’ll give you a quick description of each. If the camera is most important, I’d recommend the iPhone 17 Pro or Pro Max. At this writing, all are available for pre-order and should be in Apple stores on Friday, Sept. 19. If you order now, expect a wait of several weeks—new iPhones usually take six to eight weeks before supply catches up. All models include Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is three times more scratch-resistant, and the new Center Stage front camera that can shoot with both front and rear cameras simultaneously. • iPhone 17: The “basic” model isn’t basic at all. It comes in five colors and features a 48-megapixel dual fusion camera with .5x, 1x, and 2x zoom. Apple claims all-day battery life. It should be 50% faster than your iPhone 13, with a 6.3-inch Super Retina XDR display. Prices range from $799 (256 GB) to $999 (512 GB). • iPhone 17 Air: New this year, this is the thinnest iPhone yet at 5.6 mm, with a 6.5-inch titanium body. It has a 48-megapixel main camera and up to 2x zoom, but fewer features than the Pro models. It’s designed for people who want a sleek, futuristic look. Available in four colors, it ranges from $999 (256 GB) to $1,399 (1 TB). • iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max: If photography is your priority, these are the ones. Both have forged aluminum bodies and three 48-megapixel rear cameras, including a new telephoto with up to 8x optical zoom. They support ProRes Raw video and offer the best battery life yet. The Pro has a 6.3-inch display and costs $1,099 to $1,499. The Pro Max, at 6.9 inches, has even more features and a new 2 TB option, ranging from $1,199 to $1,999. Each phone serves a different audience: • The iPhone 17 offers strong performance at a lower price. • The Air is for those who prize design and portability. • The Pro and Pro Max deliver professional-quality photos, longer battery life, and expanded storage. Apple also introduced new watches and AirPods Pro 3. A notable feature is live translation in beta, currently supporting English, French, German, Portuguese, and Spanish, with more languages coming soon. Remember: you can trade in your old iPhone, finance with the Apple Card at no interest, or use Apple’s yearly upgrade program. Carriers will also launch promotions starting Sept. 19. Q: How do you build trust with your players, especially when you are holding them to a high standard? A: Consistency. Hold everyone accountable and to a certain standard. Make sure that they understand what is expected of them and what is acceptable and what is not. Both on and off the field. Q: What legacy do you want to leave as a coach? A: One that everyone involved gets remembered for. This took a lot of help and cooperation from a lot of people, from parents and players to the coaches and other people that have supported us along the way. This was a true team effort. Q: When someone asks what makes Piedmont football different, what do you say? A: The closeness of the kids and the community. So many of the players have grown up together that there can be a different sense of ownership and commitment when you are also doing it for your brother because you know he’s doing the same. After visiting Craig House, the walkers continued a longer loop through neighborhood streets. They admired the Ronada-Ramona Triangle — a landscaped parklet dedicated in 2014 through the efforts of nearby residents, the city, and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation — and paused to note a modern infill home at 26 Ronada. The group then wound south on Grand Avenue, up Manor Drive, and along Holly Place, before crossing through Dracena Park and returning to the Exedra. Their final stop was at the newly filled pools of the soon-to-open Piedmont Aquatics Center. The combination of local history and community camaraderie has become a hallmark of Walking on Wednesdays. Each week, participants not only enjoy fresh air and exercise but also deepen their connection to Piedmont’s past. The walks begin every Wednesday at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra (Highland and Magnolia Avenues). All are welcome to join, including friendly dogs. Participation is free, but registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at tinyurl.com/3ethkehu or by calling (510) 420-3070. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department is inviting community members to kick off the Harvest Festival weekend by joining for a park screening of Migration (2023). The movie starts at 7:15 p.m. in Piedmont Park, though families can arrive as early as 6:30 p.m. to enjoy food and reserve a spot for a blanket on the lawn. This month’s Movie in the Park is sponsored by Piedmont Cub Scouts. Families enjoy a Movie in the Park screening on the Piedmont Park lawn. articles.text: Droves of Piedmont families gathered at Beach Elementary School last Sunday, September 7, to play, dance and draw at the 24th Annual Chalk Art Festival. The school’s blacktop was divided into 100 squares for kids to draw everything from dragons and aquatic animals to their favorite movie and video game characters. “It went great!” said event organizer Jon Schleuning. “We had great weather, great turnout as always. It was a lot of fun just seeing the blacktop explode into color.” Squares of “cement canvas” were available to purchase for $20, with all proceeds going to support art programs in Piedmont Schools. The event was aided by five student volunteers from the high school. Attending artists enjoyed music from DJ Criddy. “We sold pretty much all of our squares,” said Schleuning. “We had great involvement from kids and parents and families – we have people that come back every year, even after the kids have graduated from Beach.” Founded in 2002 by Havens art teachers Raul Jorcino and Karen Stanton, the event was moved to Beach School in 2008 Two kids collaborate on a chalk drawing at the 24th Annual Chalk Art Festival on the Beach School playground.
articles.title: Chalk Art Festival – where imagination soars

articles.text: Long-awaited pool project begins final testing period The Piedmont Community Pool project entered its final stage of completion last week as workers plastered the new competition and activity pools before filling them with water. The project now moves into the final system testing period known as commissioning. The pool’s project budget remains at $34.9 million, after being funded by $25.1 million in bonds and interest from measure UU which was approved by voters in November 2020. “Seeing water in the pools is extraordinary,” said City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore. “With this milestone complete, our focus now shifts to commissioning – the critical, behind-thescenes work that prepares us for a safe and successful opening.” Commissioning is expected to last as long as six weeks while the pool equipment, filters, and heating are stress-tested. Commissioning can take as little as Piedmont’s new competition pool, complete with diving boards

articles.text: Editor: I attended the Pancake Breakfast at Beach Elementary today. It was the 20th such celebration and my face is sore from so much smiling! The savory pancakes were highlights as always — that recipe could win a national competition! The appearance of the Fire Truck was also a treat, it’s amazing how many valves, knobs and capabilities those trucks have. But the thing that seemed new this year was a dunk tank where attendees could have extra fun by dunking people in a refreshing cold tub. I spat out a bite of my breakfast when the first person was dunked into the water. Piedmont has such a wonderful community feeling and events like the Pancake Breakfast reinforce how much community can matter. I would also like to propose that more events have dunk tanks, whether to celebrate, settle competitions or surprise guests! I can’t wait for the Wildwood Crab Feed and the Havens Game Night. I just hope if Wildwood has a dunk tank at their Crab Feed they don’t store the crabs in that dunk tank. –James Bohanion 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall Executive Editor: Misha Edel City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Tony Simons Evolette Mak, Intern Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Jay Russell SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: The Pardee Home Museum continues its Salon series on Sunday, September 14 at 4 p.m. with a presentation about poet Joaquin Oakland’s own Victorian poet was a walking, talking symbol of the Golden West. We remember him for his frontier ethics and bad boy antics but don’t fully understand his uplifting magnetism. Kristen Caven, the California Writers Club Writer in Residence at Joaquin Miller Park, will paint us a new picture of Joaquin Miller as America’s late romantic by introducing us to the many fascinating women who loved him. From the legendary Paquita, his Indian bride, to the “White Witch of Oakland,” his daughter Juanita, we’ll meet poets, actresses, heiresses, and the nation’s wealthKristen Caven is a creative dervish: as an author, playwright, cartoonist, lyricist, and independent historian, she is known as a dancer, poet and impresario, but her work is grounded in the field of mental health and wellness from a family perspective. Her unique perspectives on Oakland have given us fresh takes on Mills College (with her cartoon history, “Inside the Mills Revolution”), Oaktoberfest (with her animated play, “The Dirndl Diaspora” and her “Dirndl Diversity” fashion shows and movement), Lake Merritt (with her Pergola play, “Be Mused”), and her song, “Joaquin Miller Went Walkin’.” She’s also lectured to the Art Deco Societies of San Francisco and Miami Beach on the Virtures of Vintage Cookbooks. Her most recent book is The Uplift Family Playbook, an illustrated companion to The Winning Family: Where No One Has to Lose, and you can watch her last lecture, “Reconsidering Joaquin Miller” on the Oakland Public Library Youtube channel. You can find her books and follow her blogs, “Walkin’ with Joaquin” and “Generous Muse” on www.kristencaven.com. California Writers Club Writer in Residence at Joaquin Miller Park, Kristen Caven The event includes champagne & snacks. Covered parking is available at City Center West Garage, 12th & MLK. articles.text: Piedmont High alum Kera Bartlett Binns is the lead organizer of Sun Day, a major clean energy event in Berkeley. The event will be held on Sunday, September 21 from 2:00–5:00 p,m, at the Willard Park Clubhouse, 2720 Hillegass Ave, Berkeley. RSVP to https://actionnetwork.org/events/sun-day-community-celebration-berkeley With many of the federal clean energy tax incentives sunsetting this year, now is a crucial time for Bay Area homeowners to learn how to electrify. This event demystifies the process in a fun, family-friendly way. It’s also a great fit for Piedmont residents looking for hands-on inspiration and access to local rebates and programs. The event includes: • Clean Energy Engagement Zone with expert clean energy guidance, demos of induction cooktops, portable solar panels, EV chargers, heat pumps, and more. • E-bike Try-It Zone on a closed section of Hillegass Avenue with test rides from Rad Power Bikes, Access Trikes, and Bay Wheels. • Speaker Panel featuring Rahul Young of Rewiring America, plus local homeowners, and non-profit leaders sharing reallife electrification stories • Kidical Mass Bike Ride, solar-powered s’mores, smoothie bikes, and hands-on kids’ activities • Food trucks and a community picnic Confirmed Engagement Zone Exhibitors (18+): Ava Community Energy City of Berkeley Office of Energy & Sustainable Development Sierra Club QuitCarbon Gradient Climate Health Now Acterra 350 Bay Area Ecology Center. For more information contact KeraBBinns@gmail.com.

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department is gearing up for its 7th annual car show, complete with hot coffee and even hotter automobiles on Saturday, September 20, from 9:00 a.m. to noon near the Exedra. The event brings cops, coffee and cars to the center of Piedmont as a part of the department’s outreach efforts. Excitement is revving up as nearly 100 vehicles have signed up to participate. Officer Tyler Petit, organizer of the car show, anticipates more than 120 unique cars to be on display this year. To accommodate the growing turnout, the event will expand from the Community Center parking lot down Magnolia Avenue to the base of Piedmont High School. This year’s show offers a chance for residents to meet the city’s new Police Chief, Frederick Shavies, along with members of the police department. The show promises to be a great opportunity to connect with local first Car Show organizer Officer Tyler Petit (left) with Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies. responders while enjoying a family friendly day surrounded by impressive cars and community spirit. Along with the impressive lineup of classic and custom vehicles, a local taco truck will be on site. The Cops, Coffee and Car Show was pioneered by retired Piedmont Police Sergeant Steve DeWarns in 2018. In its second year, the car show had 44 cars in 2019, and has had approximately 100 show worthy cars since 2021. To enter a vehicle in the show, e-mail officer Tyler Petit at coffeecarscops@piedmont. ca.gov. Be sure to include your name, phone number and e-mail address, and the name, make, model and year of the vehicle. An aerial view of the car show from a drone

articles.text: A good Samaritan brought Dougie into the Oakland Animal Services shelter after he was found on the road having been hit by a car. Since having his severely broken back leg amputated, one-year-old Dougie has been recovering in a foster home and is getting better every day. Dougie is a sweet, social pup who loves to hang out with his foster family, but does just fine when left alone. He is house-trained and has been slowly but surely learning to navigate the world on three legs. He loves to snooze on his comfy dog bed (especially if it’s in the sun) and snuggle up with his humans so they can rub his chin. Dougie will need an adopter who can help him continue to build his confidence as he heals. He would do well with an appropriately matched canine sibling, or as a solo dog with Come meet Dougie at Oakland Animal Services. some pup friends. Submit your adoption questionnaire online at Oakland Animal Services (oaklandanimalservices.org/adopt/dogs/ foster-dog-adoption-questionnaire/) to meet Dougie and you will be contacted by his foster who can arrange a meet-andgreet with you and Dougie at the shelter. Follow Dougie in foster with @adopt.from.oas on Instagram. For more information, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@gmail.com. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District’s (PUSD) school board will convene tonight at 7:00 p.m. for a regularly scheduled meeting. This will be the second meeting of the school year and will be back in its usual location of City Hall at 120 Vista Avenue. A presentation will be made with a State of the School report for Millennium High School (MHS). Principal Irma Muñoz Daniels will provide a history lesson on MHS which was originally established in the early 1980’s and officially was named in 2000. The report is especially timely as the MHS Falcons are celebrating 25 years this year. The main discussion item of the evening will address Interdistrict Attendance and the district’s current policy and practice to enroll students who live on split parcels in Piedmont and Oakland. Legal counsel will be provided from the law firm of Danis Woliver Kelley. “There are split parcels all along the boundary line between Piedmont and Oakland because the boundary was based on sewer lines rather than property lines, which was what distinguished the Piedmont area from the neighboring areas at the time of incorporation,” the board background document reads. There will also be two review and action items on the agenda concerning the school’s budget, an Unaudited Actuals report and a Gann Spending Limit resolution. Also of importance is a resolution which would offer different health care options for district employes. The district will consider the change which promises lower rates overall with opt-outs permitted.

articles.text: In my last article, I introduced the idea of Slow Made, a creative counter-movement to the AI fast lane. Much like the slow food revolution reminded us to savor the process of preparing and eating our meals, Slow Made is about reclaiming the joy and richness of the creative process. Sure, AI can whip up a “poem” or “paint” a picture in seconds. But if we shortcut the making, we miss out on the magic and the mess. We lose the process of wandering and discovering. The “I don’t know where this is going, but I’m going to let it unfold in front of me.” That’s the stuff creativity is made of. And that’s the part our brains actually need! And it’s not just for making art. It’s what we need for problem-solving, empathy, innovation, and connection. So the big question is: how do we keep the creative process alive and well in a world that wants everything done yesterday? Let’s talk about what Slow Made looks like in real life at work, at home, with kids, even on vacation. At Work: Think Before You Automate It’s tempting to let AI do the first draft of everything. Have an email to write? A proposal or report due? Even creative brainstorming for the next big idea can be outsourced these days. But what if, every once in a while, you started from scratch? Give yourself time to think. To sketch. To write something badly and then make it better. You’ll be surprised what ideas emerge when you allow for the imperfect. In fact, that’s where real innovation starts. It’s not in the perfect output, but in the messy in-between. Try this: Block 30 minutes of “blank page” time each week. Pick something you’d normally outsource to AI and don’t. Let your brain do the heavy lifting, even if it’s clunky at first. At Home: Create Before You Consume We all scroll. We all binge. But making something before you consume media can shift your whole day and your brain chemistry. Write a haiku on a sticky note and leave it for your spouse on the refrigerator door. Doodle while you make your breakfast. Play three chords on the piano in the corner. Try a new way to make sourdough. Make your brain produce before it absorbs. Try this: Start your morning with 10 minutes of making instead of 10 minutes of checking your phone. No rules. Just make. I keep a doodle journal and pens next to my bed so I can just make some fun shapes in interesting colors first thing in the morning. With Kids: Show the Process, Not Just the Product Kids are naturally Slow Made thinkers. They love the process. And then we start rushing them. (“Okay, great drawing, now let’s clean up!”) Instead, give them permission to follow their natural instincts. Sit down and draw with them. (Even if you think you “can’t draw”) Ask what happens next in their story. Let them see you creating too. Try this: Set up a “messy zone.” This could be a table or corner where creativity can happen without needing to be cleaned up right away. Celebrate the half-finished creation, the scribbled start of a story, the open-ended building project. Kids won’t finish most of what they start…that’s why they are creative geniuses! On Vacation: Make Time to Wander Vacations are prime territory for Slow Made thinking, but only if you stop scheduling every second. Give yourself unstructured time. Pack a sketchpad. Write in a travel journal. Capture moments in your own words, not just your camera roll. Wander a new city with no google maps. Sit and admire a sunset, watching all the way until the last speck of color is gone. Try this: Choose one creative ritual for your trip, for instance, journaling, sketching, photographing textures or doors or foliage…and do it daily. Not for Instagram, just for your own enjoyment. The Slow Made Mindset At its core, Slow Made isn’t about being anti-tech or going off the grid. It’s about being intentional. It’s about choosing to engage with the process and being open to whatever outcome does or does not manifest. When we create slowly, we reconnect with ourselves and each other. We open space for noticing and insight. So let’s give ourselves permission to go slow. Let’s make things. And those things might be terrible or beautiful or messy or all three. A creative life isn’t something you can rush. It’s something you make, one slow step at a time. Nina Meehan is a Communication and Creativity Speaker and Coach. https://ninameehan. com/
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Slow Made: Keeping the Creative Process Alive and Well

Crab Cove Visitor Center Ebparks.org/parks/visitor-centers/crab-cove 1231 McKay Avenue, Alameda; 544-3187 Visit Crab Cove Beach and the Doug Siden Visitor Center in Alameda to learn about creatures of the Bay. Join Fish Feeding viewings Wednesdays from 3:00-3:30 p.m. to get an up close view of Crab Cove’s crabs, flounder, perch, and other species while being feed by the Center’s biologist. No registration is required, drop-ins welcome. The center is open Wed - Sun: 10:00 a.m.-5:00 p.m. (March - Oct.). Lindsay Wildlife Center Lindsaywildlife.org 1931 First Ave. Walnut Creek; (925) 935-1978 Check in on Lindsay Wildlife’s 60 animal ambassadors. Exhibit Hall hours are Wednesday to Sunday from 10:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. The center also offers outdoor programs like Raptor Recess, in which kids can meet hawks and owls in the Raptor Redwood Grove. The Animal Ambassadors program lets kids get up close and personal with their favorite animal ambassadors on the outdoor campus. Stop by for a full day of fun and exploring the out of this world exhibits. Older kids will love the shows in the planetarium and megadome, the boldest way to experience space and science, on the biggest of big screens. Every Friday and Saturday night the Chabot Observatory Deck has a free telescope viewing as well, weather permitting, check their website for visibility status. Slow Made: Keeping the Creative Process Alive and Well By Nina Meehan In my last article, I introduced the idea of Slow Made, a creative counter-movement to the AI fast lane. Much like the slow food revolution reminded us to savor the process of preparing and eating our meals, Slow Made is about reclaiming the joy and richness of the creative process. Sure, AI can whip up a “poem” or “paint” a picture in seconds. But if we shortcut the making, we miss out on the magic and the mess. We lose the process of wandering and discovering. The “I don’t know where this is going, but I’m going to let it unfold in front of me.” That’s the stuff creativity is made of. And that’s the part our brains actually need! And it’s not just for making art. It’s what we need for problem-solving, empathy, innovation, and connection. So the big question is: how do we keep the creative process alive and well in a world that wants everything done yesterday? Let’s talk about what Slow Made looks like in real life at work, at home, with kids, even on vacation. At Work: Think Before You Automate It’s tempting to let AI do the first draft of everything. Have an email to write? A proposal or report due? Even creative brainstorming for the next big idea can be outsourced these days. But what if, every once in a while, you started from scratch? Give yourself time to think. To sketch. To write something badly and then make it better. You’ll be surprised what ideas emerge when you allow for the imperfect. In fact, that’s where real innovation starts. It’s not in the perfect output, but in the messy in-between. Try this: Block 30 minutes of “blank page” time each week. Pick something you’d normally outsource to AI and don’t. Let your brain do the heavy lifting, even if it’s clunky at first. At Home: Create Before You Consume We all scroll. We all binge. But making something before you consume media can shift your whole day and your brain chemistry. Write a haiku on a sticky note and leave it for your spouse on the refrigerator door. Doodle while you make your breakfast. Play three chords on the piano in the corner. Try a new way to make sourdough. Make your brain produce before it absorbs. Try this: Start your morning with 10 minutes of making instead of 10 minutes of checking your phone. No rules. Just make. I keep a doodle journal and pens next to my bed so I can just make some fun shapes in interesting colors first thing in the morning. With Kids: Show the Process, Not Just the Product Kids are naturally Slow Made thinkers. They love the process. And then we start rushing them. (“Okay, great drawing, now let’s clean up!”) Instead, give them permission to follow their natural instincts. Sit down and draw with them. (Even if you think you “can’t draw”) Ask what happens next in their story. Let them see you creating too. Try this: Set up a “messy zone.” This could be a table or corner where creativity can happen without needing to be cleaned up right away. Celebrate the half-finished creation, the scribbled start of a story, the open-ended building project. Kids won’t finish most of what they start…that’s why they are creative geniuses! On Vacation: Make Time to Wander Vacations are prime territory for Slow Made thinking, but only if you stop scheduling every second. Give yourself unstructured time. Pack a sketchpad. Write in a travel journal. Capture moments in your own words, not just your camera roll. Wander a new city with no google maps. Sit and admire a sunset, watching all the way until the last speck of color is gone. Try this: Choose one creative ritual for your trip, for instance, journaling, sketching, photographing textures or doors or foliage…and do it daily. Not for Instagram, just for your own enjoyment. The Slow Made Mindset At its core, Slow Made isn’t about being anti-tech or going off the grid. It’s about being intentional. It’s about choosing to engage with the process and being open to whatever outcome does or does not manifest. When we create slowly, we reconnect with ourselves and each other. We open space for noticing and insight. So let’s give ourselves permission to go slow. Let’s make things. And those things might be terrible or beautiful or messy or all three. A creative life isn’t something you can rush. It’s something you make, one slow step at a time. articles.text: More than 30 children’s authors will fill Children’s Fairyland with storytelling magic on Saturday, September 20 as the park celebrates books and 75 years of imagination. Fairyland’s Children’s Book Festival runs from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., welcoming more than 30 beloved and emerging children’s authors, illustrators, and storytellers from across the Bay Area. The festival brings together young readers, writers, and artists for a joyful day of storytelling, meet and greets, book signings, and interactive programming, all included with general admission. Throughout the park, families can meet authors and illustrators, hear stories read aloud by the creators themselves, watch illustration demos, and shop for books from the Books on B pop-up shop. “The Children’s Book Festival, originally known as Turn the Page, gives young readers a chance to meet the people behind the pages, discover new favorites, and feel the joy of being a part of a community that values literacy and the art of storytelling,” said Angela Moffett, Fairyland’s librarian. “For children who love books, and all lovers of children’s literature, the book festival at Fairyland is truly the best day of the year.” The festival also spotlights Fairyland’s Youth Writers’ Workshop, where young authors (ages 8–12) will share their original stories in an anthology, presenting alongside their mentor, local author, illustrator, and educator, Rob Liu-Trujillo. Speakers for the 2025 Children’s Book Festival: • Shawn Harris, Caldecott Honor recipient, known for his First Cat in Space graphic novel series, a phenomenon so beloved that fans pack soldout launches • Malik Sickstein, multi-genre author, graphic novelist, and spoken word creator • Jamaica Stevens, educator, musician, yoga instructor, and author of Yoga Adventure • Nidhi Chanani, award-winning graphic novelist of Pashmina • Dev Petty, acclaimed author of I Don’t Want to Be a Frog The event will be emceed by educator Peter Limata, host of Storytime with Mr. Limata. Additional community programming includes hands-on activities from local literacy partners, art-making stations, and family literacy resources. The first 75 families in attendance will receive a limited-edition Book Festival tote bag. For more information visit: Fairyland.org/event-calendar/ book-festival/ Oakland-based author Aida Salazar read her book “Jovita Wore Pants” during the 2024 Children’s Book Festival. Kids read aloud stories from the Emerald City Stage during the 2024 festival.

articles.text: Tacos at Senior Fest This year’s Senior Fest at Piedmont High School took place on Friday, September 5, and celebrated the PHS Class of 2026 with a day full of activities. Organized by Assistant Principal Joseph Marik and supported by parent volunteers, Hampton Field was transformed into a lively festival space featuring a bouncy house, mechanical bull, arts and crafts tables, and sports equipment. Seniors arrived at 9:30 a.m. to find a snack table before kicking off the day with a classwide game. Split into groups by wristband color, students raced to complete challenges designed to encourage bonding among peers who might not usually interact. Afterward, seniors enjoyed a variety of activities, from pickleball, volleyball, and spikeball to airbrush tattoos and bracelet making. The highlight of the afternoon was an all-you-can-eat taco lunch paired with Italian ice, Seniors enjoy Italian ice at Senior Fest. perfect for the warm weather. Whether testing their skills on the mechanical bull or relaxing with friends, students had plenty of ways to celebrate together. At 2 p.m., seniors were excused, wrapping up a successful and memorable day of community and fun. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School. Senior girls enjoy the warm weather at Senior Fest. ®
articles.title: Senior Fest a raging success

articles.text: Piedmont High School held its annual Club Day on Wednesday, Sept. 3, drawing hundreds of students eager to join campus organizations and connect with their peers. The event, coordinated by ASB leaders Grace Alonigreen and Dahlia Strub, featured more than 40 clubs, from established groups like Red Cross and Key Club to unique offerings such as Bio-Mart and the Food Blogging Club. Tables lined the breezeway as club leaders competed for attention with candy, hats, frisbees, and other giveaways. Identity-based organizations also played a prominent role this year. African Affinity Student Union, Advocacy for Asian Americans, GSA, and JSU all continued their missions of creating space for their respective communities. However, the Hispanic Student Union was notably absent. For many students, Club Day serves as both a launchpad for building community and a chance for leaders to help their organizations grow. The event’s popularity also brought challenges. Roughly a dozen clubs were not on the official lineup, some due to missing the registration deadline and others simply because of limited space, missing the chance to showcase their offerings to potential members. In particular, Flow Club, the group responsible for supplying menstrual products in the girls’ bathrooms, did not have a table. The absence of such groups raises broader questions about whether all student organizations are given equal opportunities to connect with their peers, and how those opportunities might extend beyond a single day. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School. Students check out a club during PHS Club Day.
articles.title: Club Day draws a big crowd

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team couldn’t get the job done on the road in Middletown on Friday, September 5, losing 34-17. The Highlanders kept the game close early in the third quarter, trailing by just one point 18-17, but things fell apart after that. It was similar to the Highlanders’ Week 1 loss to Salesian, where they trailed 21-17 in the third quarter, but gave up 20 unanswered points at the end. In Friday’s game, Middletown ran off 16 unanswered points after halftime. Middletown opened the scoring in the first quarter with 5:47 left to lead 6-0 after a missed extra point. Piedmont then got on the board with a 27-yard field goal by Mattias Seelenberger after the team drove to the five-yard line. The Mustangs extended the lead to 18-3 in the second quarter, but Piedmont got one back with a four-yard touchdown carry by Rehan Mumtaz before halftime. After recovering an onside kick to start the third quarter, Piedmont drove 50 yards to go ahead at 18-17 after a five-yard touchdown pass from Jimmy Lagios to Jack Meyjes. However, the game fell apart from there. Game Recap Piedmont opened with possession and drove to Middletown’s 44 yard line before the drive stalled out, failing to convert a 4th-and-4. The Mustangs then got on the board first after nine plays, all runs, with 5:47 left in the first quarter. On the ensuing possession, Piedmont’s Jimmy Lagios found Diego Hurwitz on a streak down the sideline, getting knocked out around the two-yard line. On 1st-and-Goal, PHS allowed a loss on a run, while Jack Meyjes was called for a penalty on a potential touchdown reception on second down. At the 10 yard line, Lagios nearly found Meyjes again in the back of the end zone, but the receiver was called out on another potential touchdown grab. The Mustangs then drove 54 yards on five plays on their next possession to score in the final minute of the first quarter (official times weren’t available), including a long 27-yard carry to cap things off—bringing the score to Staff Photos Quarterback Jimmy Lagios had one touchdown pass against Middletown. After two trades of possession, Middletown took over at their 30 in the middle of the second. On the first play, the Mustangs took a reverse to the house for a 70-yard score, 18-3 after another missed extra point. Xavier Henderson took the next kickoff to the 48, leading to a three-play touchdown series. It started with an 18-yard grab by Dash Waters-Worthen, followed by a 29 yard screen to Henderson. Piedmont opened the third quarter with a big swing of momentum when recovering an onside kick at the 50. After six plays, Lagios found Meyjes on a five-yard touchdown, making it 18-17 early in the third. But things unraveled from there. Middletown scored on a 22-yard pass to make it 24-17. Piedmont then drove 51 yards on the next drive, but a penalty led to 4th-and-25 from the Middletown 30, leading to a turnover early in the fourth quarter. The Mustangs got their final score on a 10-play, 70-yard drive, capping off with a 17-yard touchdown run. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-2 overall) hosts Berean Christian on Friday, September 12 at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Staff Photos Edie Elmquist runs into the end zone for a touchdown against Miramonte Piedmont High’s flag football team claimed its first win of the season on Thursday, September 4 at Witter Field, beating the Miramonte Matadors in a defensive battle, 12-6. Piedmont scored the game’s opening touchdown thanks to a fumbled snap by Miramonte deep on their side of the field. On a punt attempt, the Matadors’ center snapped the ball over the punter’s head, leading to a dead ball at the four yard line. It led to quarterback Edie Elmquist finding Stephanie Lee for a touchdown moments later. “It’s rare for us to go up first, so I think we felt the mental energy from that. Miramonte made some adjustments, and our players responded with their own adjustments,” said PHS coach Beth Black. The Highlanders increased their lead to 12-0 with 2:34 left in the second quarter on a two-yard carry by Elmquist. The sophomore quarterback has proven to be the leader of Piedmont’s offense, using her speed to break the pocket, and an arsenal of moves to make flag-pullers miss. Now in her second year as the team’s quarterback, Elmquist is showing a deeper knowledge of the game, poise, and quick thinking to make plays. She credits her rapid development to playing club flag football. “At the end of last season, I just thought, ‘I need more.’ So all summer and softball season I worked to get better. I was running, I was lifting, and played with another team. That gave me a lot of confidence,” Elmquist said. Senior safety Dahlia Osman had two interceptions, one in the first quarter and another in the third. She has recorded a pair of interceptions in all three games this season. Osman moved to safety during her junior season in 2024 after playing at cornerback as a sophomore. Using her speed and flag pulling ability, Osman is in the perfect spot, roving the field as the defense’s playmaker. “I like playing back there and being an interrupter,” Osman said. “Last year, I was switched into playing safety during the season after starting out at corner. This year, I’ve become much more comfortable back there and I know what to watch for.” Game Recap Both teams traded possession in the first quarter, leading to Miramonte’s botched punt attempt. Taking over at the four, Piedmont scored on second down when Elmquist found Lee for the touchdown with 2:03 left. Elspeth Grippando (left) celebrates after recording an interception. Dahlia Osman recorded two interceptions against Miramonte, giving her six this season.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team lost two matches on the road over the past week. They lost 8-1 to Campolindo in a non-league match in Moraga on Wednesday, September 3, before losing a close 4-3 battle with North Coast Section rival Marin Academy at Dominican University in San Rafael the following day. “Campo has a very strong team and our only victory was by Chiara Silvio and Inara Mehta at No. 2 doubles,” said coach Jim Landes. “The Marin Academy match was much tighter. We won three out of the four singles, but Marin swept the doubles.” Standout freshman Ella Ruthven continues to leave her mark atop Piedmont’s singles order, winning in a heated three-set match against Marin Academy’s top starter Ann McDermott, 6-7, (8-6), 6-4, 10-7. “Ella Ruthven had a very good win against one of the McDermott twins, pulling it out in the super breaker 10-7. Ella used her strong forehand but also mixed in some nice slices on her backhand that befuddled her opponent,” added Landes. 4-3 loss to Marin Academy At singles, Ruthven won her match at the No. 1 spot in three sets, 6-7, (8-6), 6-4, 10-7. Faith Chin won her match at No. 3 in straight sets, 6-1, 6-3, while Arianna Kortum had a clean sweep of her opponent at No. 4 in a shutout score, 6-0, 6-0. Kate Jumper was Piedmont’s only loss at singles, 6-3, 6-4. “Faith Chin and Arianna Kortum both played very well winning in decisive straight sets. Kate Jumper also played well but came up against a very good lefty Staff Photos Inara Mehta helped win Piedmont’s only match against Campolindo at No. 2 doubles with Chiara Silvo (not pictured). opponent and lost in two good sets,” Landes said. At doubles, Samantha Huyhn and Emma Chan lost 6-0, 6-4 at the No. 1 spot. Chiara Silvo at No. 2 lost a close match, while Ella Thomasson and Leela Sivakumar lost 6-4, 6-3 at No. 3. 8-1 loss to Campolindo Piedmont played nine total matches against Campolindo, given they play in the top division of North Coast Section while the Highlanders are D2. The Highlanders’ lone win came at No. 2 doubles by Silvo and Mehta in three sets, 1-6, 6-2, 10-1. “Inara and Chiara got off to a slow start, losing the first set, but then rebounded strongly winning the second set and lost just one point in the 10 point super breaker. Both girls played really well hitting strong ground shots and moving a lot at the net,” Landes said. PHS lost all six matches at singles. Ruthven and Jumper both lost 6-0, 6-0 at No. 1 and No. 2 respectively. Chin played a close match at No. 3, losing 7-6 (7-4), 7-5. Kortum lost 6-2, 6-4 at No. 4, Lila Rosen fell 6-0, 6-1 at No. 5, and Sivakumar lost 7-5, 6-2 at No. 6. At doubles, Silvo and Mehta won the only match of the day at No. 2. Huyhn and Chan lost 7-5, 6-3 at No. 1, while Thomasson and Maddie Tran had a close three-set match at the No. 3 spot, losing 6-4, 4-6, 10-8. Tuesday vs. San Leandro Piedmont traveled to San Leandro for their first Western Alameda County Conference match of the season on Tuesday, September 9. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-3 overall) visits Acalanes in Lafayette today, Wednesday, September 10, for a match at 3:30 p.m. They are also set to compete at the James Logan HS Tournament in Union City on Friday and Saturday, September 12-13. Ella Ruthven, a freshman, had a three-set win over Marin Academy’s top singles starter. Faith Chin won her match at No. 3 singles against Marin Academy.

articles.text: Photos by Jenni Tsoi-Best Skylar Best (1401), Leighton Mand (1413) and Viviane Oesterer (1414) ran as a pack at the start of the St. Mary’s Invitational. Piedmont High’s cross-country teams has a strong start of the season at the St. Mary’s Invitational in Moraga on Saturday, September 6. The girls’ team ran to a second-place finish out of 15 schools, while the boys placed third of 21 teams. “Both of the varsity teams had really solid performances,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “The varsity girls team finished in 2nd place, in large part due to the small spread between our first and fifth runners. On the boys’ side, all of the varsity boys ran very good races in this first outing. Only 35 seconds separated our top finisher and the fifth runner.” Strong pack running for girls All five of runners finished within 20 seconds of each other. Leighton Mand led with a 17th place finish in a field of 110 runners with a time of 12:42.15 on the two-mile course. Running nearly side by side was Skylar Best, finishing 18th in 12:48.06. In 20th was Viviane Oesterer, clocking a 12:56.31, Amalia Gray was 21st in 12:57.70, while Cora Brozowski Schrader rounded out their best five times in 13:02.31 to finish 24th. “Only 20 seconds passed between when Leighton Mand crossed the finish line and when Cora Brozowski Schrader, our fifth scorer finished. Viviane had the most even splits of the varsity girls, running only six seconds slower for the second mile. The top five girls all performed well and appeared to have executed on the plan to go out conservatively and pass as many people as possible in the second half of the race,” Zirkelbach said. Boys’ results The boys’ team impressed even though it was without lead Leighton Mand led the way for Piedmont’s cross-country team, placing 17th of 110 runners. runner Sebastien Swain. Sohn led the way for the Highlanders, finishing in 13th of 147 athletes with a time of 10:37.6. “The team was led by senior captain Noah Sohn, whose performance demonstrated his canny ability to race and to manage his tactical strategy,: said Zirkelbach. Behind Sohn was Alex Schleuning finishing 20th with a time of 10:45.39, Ian Chung was six spots behind him in 26th in 10:53.57, Aaron Bennett placed 30th in 10:55.02, and senior Devon Thai rounded out their best five times in 42nd, clocking a time of 11:12.27. NEXT UP Piedmont looks ahead to the 40th annual Ed Sias Invitational at Hidden Valley Park in Martinez, the traditional first race of the season. Events start at 9:00 a.m.; Piedmont’s boys’ varsity team runs at 10:15 a.m., while the girls’ take the course at 10:40 a.m. Noah Sohn (1442) led the way for the boys’ cross-country team finishing 13th of 147 runners.

articles.text: Staff Photos Fiona Olsen led Piedmont with 12 kills and a block against Hayward. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team appears to be turning the corner after sweeping Hayward 3-0 at the Farmers’ gym on Thursday, September 4 by scores of 25-18, 25-14, and 25-18. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 4-3 through seven matches, which eclipses last year’s season total of 3-19. “We’re such a young team, but we’re going to give our league a run for their money,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. “Today wasn’t the best display, but there’s something about us that gives us a spark. We can see potential at the end of the tunnel,” If all goes well for the Highlanders, they are likely to finish this season with a winning record and possibly their first North Coast Section berth since 2018. “There are seven sophomores to fill important roles. We have the skill and have more wins than last year,” Cardenas said. Maika Ting, one of eight new players, recorded eight kills against Hayward. “It’s been really amazing to be a part of this team. We have a bunch of sophomores who I know really well. Everyone and is really encouraging,” Ting said. Against the Farmers, the home side was able to keep things close in each set until Piedmont powered home the win. Piedmont clung to a narrow 15-13 advantage before limiting Hayward to just one point to finish the second set. In the third there were eight lead changes until the Highlanders went ahead for good at 17-16. Match Recap It was a dominant first set for Piedmont’s Fiona Olsen, landing eight kills in their 25-18 win. Ting also scored on five spikes, while Izara Dando had three. Maiki Ting, a sophomore, had eight kills against Hayward. In the second set, both teams traded points back and forth for the better half of the set. With Piedmont holding to a 15-13 lead, they added three straight points before Hayward’ next point to hold an 18-14 advantage. That turned out to be the Farmers’ last point of the set, with PHS scoring seven straight to claim the win, including two kills by Ting, a kill and an ace by Stella Wilk, and one spike by Dando. As for the final set, the Farmers kept things competitive with eight lead changes before the Highlanders took control. Hayward held a 16-14 lead after scoring three straight points, but Piedmont powered back with seven straight points to jump ahead 21-16, including kills by Mira Sachs, Daisy Tran, and a block by Olsen. From there, the Highlanders scored four of the final six points to take the 25-18 win, while Wilk put away the match with the winning kill. Final stats: Olsen led the way with 12 kills and one block. Dando had six kills and one block. Ting had eight kills, Wilk had three, Sachs had three, Tran and Julia Stokes had two, and Charlie Panico had one. Mira Sachs goes up for a spike. She had three kills against the Farmers.
articles.title: Girls’ volleyball eclipses 2024 win total after 7 matches

pages.text: Wednesday, September 10, 2025 15 HIKING WITH JON Hiking with elephants through a Thailand sanctuary By Jonathan Comeaux [From August 2023] When visiting Chiang Mai and the northern province of Thailand, it’s clear to see the region’s cultural ties to elephants with countless merchants having trinkets, clothing, and jewelry of elephants on display. If you’re visiting Chiang Mai, travelers are bound to run into offices for sanctuaries looking to lure in tourists, so it is important to do your research to ensure you’re investing your experience with the right company which treats its elephants ethically. With that, the Post visited Into The Wild The Post visited an elephant sanctuary on the outskirts of Chiang Mai, Thailand. Elephants coating themselves with dirt to cool off while on the trail. Walking through a thick jungle in Doi Inthanon National Park Elephant Camp on the outskirts of Chiang Mai. In Thailand, elephants are tied to the nation’s history in religion and royalty. They are considered guardians of Buddha, Earth and Thailand’s temples. They were also used in ancient wars to defend the country, while ownership of them was considered a sign of status. However, the species has decreased from the 300,000 wild elephants during the 20th century to an estimated 3,084-3,500 now with an estimated 4,000 in captivity. When choosing an elephant sanctuary to visit, it’s important to decide against places that host rides, keep their elephants in enclosed areas, and has a proper diet for the elephants—all of which is considered animal cruelty. Elephants, which have a typical lifespan of 60-70 years, can have a severe drop in life expectancy when kept in improper conditions, with some cases as high as a 50 percent drop. Into The Wild Elephant Camp have seven elephants in a large encampment about 40 miles outStaff Photos An elephant searching to see if the Post’s journalist had any treats. side of Chiang Mai in the Doi Inthanon National Park. Their elephants are in an open space alongside the Mae Tian River, allowing you to learn about the species, its history, and natural habitat. As the guides at Into The Wild explained, it is difficult to release domesticated elephants back into the wild given they are intelligent creatures with good memories, meaning they will seek out humans in order to get food. Into The Wild specializes in finding other domesticated elephants that may have not had ideal living conditions in its previous home. “Elephants have been living with people for many generations, so they generally rely on people. It’s really difficult for them to return to the wild by themselves. They have a really big brain, so when they are used to being fed by people, it’s hard for them to find their own food because they know humans will feed them,” explained Mike, a guide at Into The Wild. After feeding the elephants, they offered a brief hike through the jungle alongside the elephants, observing how they naturally live in the wild—finding dirt pits to throw on themselves and trees to topple over as they scratch their backsides. Guides also point out edible foliage for foraging and how local tribes have used different species of plants for uses like medicine, insect repellent, and cuisine. The hike puts you in close quarters with the Thailand wilderness. articles.text: Black Gold: Stories Untold, a major art exhibition highlighting the transformative impact of Black communities on California’s cultural, social, and political worlds, is now on view at Fort Point National Historic Site in the Presidio. Black Gold features artwork by 17 contemporary artists and collectives who lived in California from the Gold Rush to the Reconstruction period following the Civil War, including never-before-seen commissions by Akea Brionne, Demetri Broxton, Adrian L. Burrell, Adam Davis, Cheryl Derricotte, Mildred HowBrian Kemble, curator of Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek Ruth Bancroft Gardens is honoring its longtime curator and horticulturist Brian Kemble on Thursday, September 25. Kemble has worked with the gardens for 45 years and oversees thousands of cacti and succulent species that grow on the garden’s three acres. As curator, he is in charge of hybridizing plants or finding two plants that have complementary characteristics and combining them to create new species. Kemble worked closely with Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, who was ahead of her time in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public. Kemble will be in conversation with Dick Turner, the garden’s first Executive Director, and will share stories of working alongside the Bancroft, how he’s seen the garden transform over the decades and his reflection on what he wants his enduring legacy to be. Guests are invited to stay for a reception with beverages and light fare following the presentation and conversation. Ticket holders may join in to raise a glass to Kemble’s legacy and work. All ticket sales help fund Kemble’s “Bed 12” project, the first flower bed Ruth worked on in the garden. Donations and ticket proceeds benefit the restoration and revitalization of Bed 12. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/event/an-evening-with-brian-kemble/. New commissions explore themes of African American resilience during a pivotal era in the American West, including the fight for legal rights within the “free” state of California, the successes of early Black entrepreneurs and the experiences of African American Army regiments known as the Buffalo Soldiers. The exhibition also features recent works by Carla Edwards, Isaac Julien, Alison Saar, and Hank Willis Thomas. The exhibition is presented by FOR-SITE, a nonprofit organization dedicated to the cultural arts, and curated by Cheryl Haines, the nonprofit’s founding executive director. “Black Gold is a collaborative effort that brings together the work of an array of artists, thinkers, and community leaders to reveal narratives that are historically significant and continue to resonate today,” Haines said in a press release. “I am thrilled to shed light on this important part of California’s story.” The exhibition remains on view through November 2. Admission is free. Fort Point National Historic Site is located 201 Marine Drive in San Francisco. For more information, visit www.for-site.org. Photo by Claudine Gossett

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco unveils Unbound: Art, Blackness, and the Universe, a group exhibition exploring connections between Blackness and spiritual cosmologies, on October 1. The new exhibition, organized by Key Jo Lee, MoAD Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs, highlights the similarities between the Black existence and “cosmic Blackness,” or Afrofuturism. Unvound includes paintings, glass sculptures, and installations celebrating the modern artistic genre. The exhibition features artists David Alabo, Renee Cox, Oasa DuVerney, Torkwase Dyson, Allison Janae Hamilton, Barkley L. Hendricks, Cullen B. Washington Jr., M. Carmen Lane and Sidra Bell, Michi Meko, Gustavo Nazareno, Rashaad Newsome, Chris Ofili, Mikael Owunna, Harmonia Rosales, Lorna Simpson, Didier William, and Fred Wilson. “For the past 20 years, MoAD has proudly embarked on a journey to ensure that Black creative expression is embraced, elevated, and seen by international visitors and those that call the Bay Area home,” said Monetta White, Executive Director and CEO. “The artistic depth of UNBOUND A new exhibition at MoAD was organized by Key Jo Lee, Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs. will bring intergenerational African Diasporic voices together under an innovative curatorial framework that shifts the focus through which we understand and appreciate contemporary art.” “This exhibition is a celebration of the vast conceptual capacity of Blackness, and treats Black existence with the same imaginative and intellectual openness we apply to thinking through metaphysics and the cosmos,” Lee added. “In doing so, it makes a radical claim that Blackness is not marginal, but central to how we comprehend being, time, and the universe itself.” For more information, visit https://www.moadsf.org.

Black Gold features artwork by 17 contemporary artists and collectives who lived in California from the Gold Rush to the Reconstruction period following the Civil War, including never-before-seen commissions by Akea Brionne, Demetri Broxton, Adrian L. Burrell, Adam Davis, Cheryl Derricotte, Mildred HowBlack Gold exhibition now on view at Fort Point ard, Tiff Massey, Umar Rashid, Trina Michelle Robinson, Bryan Keith Thomas, and Cosmo Whyte. New commissions explore themes of African American resilience during a pivotal era in the American West, including the fight for legal rights within the “free” state of California, the successes of early Black entrepreneurs and the experiences of African American Army regiments known as the Buffalo Soldiers. The exhibition also features recent works by Carla Edwards, Isaac Julien, Alison Saar, and Hank Willis Thomas. The exhibition is presented by FOR-SITE, a nonprofit organization dedicated to the cultural arts, and curated by Cheryl Haines, the nonprofit’s founding executive director. “Black Gold is a collaborative effort that brings together the work of an array of artists, thinkers, and community leaders to reveal narratives that are historically significant and continue to resonate today,” Haines said in a press release. “I am thrilled to shed light on this important part of California’s story.” The exhibition remains on view through November 2. Admission is free. Fort Point National Historic Site is located 201 Marine Drive in San Francisco. For more information, visit www.for-site.org. Brian Kemble, curator of Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek By Allyson Aleksey Ruth Bancroft Gardens is honoring its longtime curator and horticulturist Brian Kemble on Thursday, September 25. Kemble has worked with the gardens for 45 years and oversees thousands of cacti and succulent species that grow on the garden’s three acres. As curator, he is in charge of hybridizing plants or finding two plants that have complementary characteristics and combining them to create new species. Kemble worked closely with Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, who was ahead of her time in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public. Kemble will be in conversation with Dick Turner, the garden’s first Executive Director, and will share stories of working alongside the Bancroft, how he’s seen the garden transform over the decades and his reflection on what he wants his enduring legacy to be. Guests are invited to stay for a reception with beverages and light fare following the presentation and conversation. Ticket holders may join in to raise a glass to Kemble’s legacy and work. All ticket sales help fund Kemble’s “Bed 12” project, the first flower bed Ruth worked on in the garden. Donations and ticket proceeds benefit the restoration and revitalization of Bed 12. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/event/an-evening-with-brian-kemble/. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s 2025 season opens with The Reservoir, a new play by Jake Brasch, which will be shown now through October 12. The heartfelt, dark comedy follows Josh, an aimless, queer, neurotic young adult who moves home to Colorado to get sober while on medical leave from New York University. Josh struggles with memory loss and fatigue as well as shame and regret associated with his alcoholism but comes to find unlikely allies in his four unpredictable grandparents. The Reservoir explores how dementia and alcoholism affect a family with tenderness and humor. The play made its world premiere at the Denver Center in Colorado early this year on January 17. Mike Donahue directs the Berkeley Repertory Theatre production. The cast includes Michael Cullen, Ben Hirschhorn, Barbara Kingsley, Pamela Reed, Peter Van Wagner, Brenda Withers, and Nancy Carlin. “I can’t imagine a better launch to the new season than Jake’s play, which is such a smart, Playwright Jake Brasch funny, touching celebration of family, identity, human fallibility, and the hard work it takes to live life in a fully present way,” said Berkeley Rep Artistic Director Johanna Pfaelzer. “I’m delighted to welcome Jake and Mike to Berkeley Rep, and to have Pamela Reed, who our audiences fell in love with in our world premiere of Becky Nurse of Salem, back on stage in the Peet’s Theatre.” Face masks are required for performances on September 14 (matinee and evening), September 16, and September 21 (matinee). A docent-led post-show discussion is held after every matinee performance. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep. org to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep season opens with The Reservoir

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony opens its 54th season this Sunday, September 14, at 4:00 p.m. at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley with a new addition to their Symphonic Series, Visions of Elysium. Led by guest conductor Dina Gilbert of the Montreal Symphony, the concert invites the audience on a quest for transcendence that spans from tranquility to triumphant heroism. Gilbert has received critical acclaim for her energy, presence on the podium, and the breadth of her repertoire. Cellist Gabriel Cabezas Conductor Dina Gilbert The evening opens with Samy Moussa’s otherworldly vision of Elysium, the paradisiacal afterlife of Grecian heroes. Next, cello soloist Gabriel Cabezas leads listeners through shadow and fog in Alyssa Weinberg’s Caligo and to emotional heights in Tchaikovsky’s Pezzo capriccioso. The evening concludes with Ludwig van Beethoven’s Symphony No. 3, a bold declaration of humanity’s aspiration toward an ideal world. Tickets start at $15. Tickets are available now at https://www. berkeleysymphony.org/event/ visions/.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony opens season this Sunday

articles.text: Oakland Ballet Company performs Luna Mexicana, a ballet celebrating Dia de los Muertos and traditional Mexican dance, on Saturday, November 1 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Tickets are available online now. Luna Mexicana is an original work by Oakland Ballet Company’s Artistic Director Graham Lustig and is one of the Bay Area’s most celebrated events honoring Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, a holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico and Latin America. Lustig’s production features a young woman whose ancestors “dance” back to life in the form of teetering skeletons, skirt-swishing ladies and a bride and groom duet. In 2018, Oakland Ballet Company premiered Viva la Vida, co-choreographed by Lustig and Martín Romero of Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza. The dance celebrates the life and artistry of iconic Mexican artist Frida Kahlo and is now included in annual presentations of Luna Mexicana. The program is presented in two acts with an intermission and features a selection of Mexican contemporary and folkloric dance as well as music curated by Lustig. Past performances have included the Aztec ensemble Nahui-Ehekatl and Co. and dancers from Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza. Light bites and refreshments will be served. Audience members of all ages are encouraged to attend in Day of the Dead costume. Luna Mexicana is a family-friendly event and ideal for audience members ages 7 and up. Visit https://oaklandballet.org to purchase tickets. Photo of Luna Mexicana performed in 2017 Photo by Stephen Texeira
articles.title: Tickets available now for Oakland Ballet’s Luna Mexicana
