articles.text: Maggie’s Plan is a film that relies on engaging, spot-on dialogue, lots of it. Writer/director Rebecca Miller has a remarkably well-tuned ear for conversation, especially that which is embedded in New York academia, inserting such memorable phrases as, “Nobody unpacks commodity fetishism like you do.” And seriously suggests that there is an academic niche known as “ficto-critical anthropology.” Really? In contrast to the esoteric pursuit of post-structural posturing is the guileless, winsome, early thirties Maggie (Gretta Gerwig), a New School of Social Research academic administrator. She decides that while she can’t seem to sustain a relationship with a man for longer than six months, she wants to be a mother and is prepared to go it alone. She just needs a sperm donor and asks an old college friend, Guy (Travis Finnel), an artisanal pickle entrepreneur and a gifted mathematician. He agrees and they arrange a delivery time. Meanwhile she meets John (Ethan Hawke), a married academic (he’s the ficto-anthropologist) and a budding novelist. He asks Maggie if she would mind reading the first chapters of his novel, something his wife, Georgette (Julianne Moore), a chilly, successful professor at Colombia, has little interest in doing. They do have two children, but John is perpetually discontent and feels neglected by Georgette. His solipsistic narcissism – nicely disguised behind his charm and impulse to write and create – is only gradually revealed as the narrative evolves. And so begins a satirical, funny, Three-time Academy Awards winner Paul Haggis wrote and directed The Next Three Days. It is gripping and unrelenting and a non-stop thriller wrapped in a mystery. The narrative is predicated on a question that treads its way throughout: what would you do, what risks would you be prepared to take if your spouse were convicted of a murder she did not commit and sentenced to life in prison? You, John Brennan (Russell Crowe), have hired lawyers, paid dearly to submit appeals, spent weeks in desperate discussions regarding options overlooked, managed to sustain a fragile hope that SCOTUS, the final arbiter, might at least review the trial, and for almost three years you have worried that your wife, Lara (Elizabeth Banks), will reach a point where she can no longer summon the will to face prison absent any hope of ever being released. You have now run out of runway. And so you, John, a mild-mannered, soft-spoken college professor of English, begins to construct an improbable, high-risk plan to break Lara out of prison, knowing that the odds are against his success, meaning if caught he will either be killed or go to prison himself, leaving his son without both parents. articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Big Hero 6 Disney’s animated Oscar nominated Big Hero 6 will appeal to an audience of kids and family. The narrative, a derivative of Marvel’s superhero characters, features 14-year-old Hiro Hamada (Ryan Potter), a nerdy, robotics obsessed kid. He lives in the futuristic Asian-like city of San Fransokyo, where he hangs out with a cohort of extraordinary friends: GoGo Tanago (Jamie Chung), Wasabi (Damon Wayans, Jr.), and Honey Lemon (Genesis Rodriguez). Hiro, who graduated from high school at the age of 14, spends his days submerged in techie stuff. At night, however, he engages in illegal robotic fight games. His older brother, Tadashi (Daniel Henney), worries about Hiro’s night-time antics, so with the encouragement of both Hiro’s aunt, Cass (Maya Rudolph), and Tadashi, he agrees to visit the cutting-edge Institute of San Fransokyo. It’s also an amazing technical achievement, created by some 40 animators, working with stop-motion claymation, real props, three dimensional sets, with a cast of chickens with perky dialogue and personalities to match. The story is set on a bleak chicken farm in Yorkshire, England, run by a cranky (bordering on sadistic) commandant, Mrs. Tweedy (Miranda Richardson). She rants and screeches about the lack of egg production, and is working on a Rube Goldberg plan to turn all the chickens into pot pies if things don’t pick up. Among the chickens is Ginger (Julia Sawahla), a spunky prize hen, who is not about to simply give in to Mrs. Tweedy, unlike her complacent peers. Brash, overly confident, he convinces the hens that he can teach them to fly as well. Of course, Rocky also falls for Ginger, and as a result the two begin to hatch a plan for a prison-break. articles.text: Sunday, Sept. 14 – Oct. 13, 11–2 p.m. Slavic Art Exhibit The Center for Slavic Arts and Culture is proud to present its very first exhibition, KALEIDOSCOPE. The show brings together 17 artists from five Slavic countries, including a photographer and a jewelry designer, each sharing their talent and creative vision. In challenging and uncertain times, art reminds us of beauty, resilience, and the strength of our community. Kaleidoscope is a celebration of creativity, and a reminder of how art can connect, uplift, and inspire us all. This exhibition will be open weekend days from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. until mid-October. CSAC celebrates Slavic culture’s rich heritage and vibrant traditions, and works to preserve and promote the art, history, and unique identities of the twelve Slavic nations, fostering appreciation and understanding across diverse communities. Come to explore a world of creativity, tradition, and inspiration. Sunday, September 14, 4:00 p.m. Circadian String Quartet Gala concert To celebrate the release of their first studio album, Circadian String Quartet invites you to an album release party at their annual Gala. Celebrate the release of the Quartet’s first studio album, Circadian Stories. Every guest will receive a copy of this exciting new album, which features original Circadian arrangements from all over the world, compositions written by Iranian-born Sahba Aminikia, and the vocal stylings of Lily Storm. Join musical guests Lily Storm and the Shiraz Choir and Ensemble, directed by Amin Assadi, for a Gala fundraiser with an afternoon of music, elegant food and wine, and giving. The program includes music by Astor Piazzolla, Philip Glass, Parviz Meshkatian (arranged by Sahba Aminikia), music from Studio Ghibli by Joe Hisaishi and music by our own David Ryther. Request an invitation by email to: circadianstringquartet@gmail.com Saturday, September 27, 7:30 p.m. Extraordinary Vocal Soirée Fundraiser Feeling sad, frustrated and frightened with the news these days? The program, called You’ll Never Walk Alone, will include popular opera, musical theater and sacred music to soothe the soul and lift your spirits. articles.text: Critics are a curious lot. They are necessary for a variety of reasons. If you are a performer, you want a critic’s “stamp of approval” that legitimizes the performer. You hope for a good review. But sometimes a terrible review becomes a “cause célèbre”. That was the case when the Tchaikovsky Violin Concerto was premiered in Vienna. The most important music critic said of this concerto that “It stank on the ears of the listeners”. His review is memorable because he was completely wrong. Tchaikovsky‘s Violin Concerto has become one of the most popular and appreciated pieces in the entire repertoire. The famous sports columnist Howard Cosell was proud to declare: “I never played the game.” Did he mean that he was proud that he was never on the field of battle or did he mean “playing the game” in a figurative way? Both viewpoints are equally important to consider. Understanding all aspects of performing is an important virtue. A brief introducThe Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet tion told us many things about the composer as well as his composition. This critics’ ear was delighted. We were treated to a melancholy three-way conversation, a lively scherzo somewhat in the manner of Mendelssohn, an expressive valse Russe. and a brilliantly jumping saltarello. All three players played with full confidence. Next came Piano Trio No. 1 by the contemporary Russian-born composer Lera Auerbach. While it is a contemporary work, combining modern harmonies, there is great depth and imagination in the work. We were told that the composer is a woman of wide-ranging interests. She knows how to organize chaos in a way that fits together quite nicely. I was impressed by a melodic wildness, which was thrilling. Another movement offered a sense of foreboding. Sunday’s concert concluded with a formidable performance of a trio by Beethoven. Good vibes were everywhere. Victoria Ehrlich told the audience “that’s why musicians enjoy playing in the Piedmont Center for the Arts.” The performing musicians played with a great understanding which is paramount for performers. John is still writing his original novel, Maggie is working, raising their daughter, and playing backstop for his two kids. Suddenly she begins to wonder if perhaps John was a mistake and thus arrives the essence of Maggie’s Plan: she settles on a scheme to send the purloined John back to Georgette. Right child, wrong guy she’s concluded. It’s Shakespearean in a kind of screwy, comedic way. John observes at one point that in every relationship one person is the gardener and the other the rose. And, of course, when it comes to love and initial passion, well the best laid plans, so to speak, ultimately end in a series of unintended consequences, no matter how urbane those involved may be. At no time does writer/director Rebecca Miller (daughter of Arthur Miller), to her credit, try to explain in any kind of esoteric jargon exactly what “ficto-anthropology” is. articles.text: A strong turnout of 44 walkers and a record six K-9 best friends were on hand last week. Nancy DeRoche had offered to take the group on a historical tour of her neighborhood above Oakland Avenue, which includes the historic Blair and Scenic Avenues. Nancy told the group she became interested in the history of her neighborhood after she learned that noted architect Albert Farr once lived in her Oakland Avenue home for many years. Nancy said she draws on the research that Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi has done. Walker and Piedmont historian Meghan Bennett had previously created a website dedicated to the Bourgeois Bohemians in “Boho Piedmont” that Nancy also drew upon. Meghan’s site is https:// www.paintingpiedmont.com/ Nancy explained that the area above Oakland Avenue was a bit of a Bohemian neighborhood from about 1890 to 1910. It was rural and sparsely populated. Writer Jack London and painter Xavier “Marty” Martinez lived there in some unique homes. Some of these creative types built their own homes. Nancy led the group across Highland Avenue and went up to Oakland Avenue. They turned up Oakland and stopped at 2010 Oakland, which was once the home of George Sterling, Frank C. Havens’ nephew. Sterling worked for Havens, and married Havens’ wife’s sister. Sterling was a frustrated artist and poet and traveled in a circle of artists. He met Jack London and encouraged him to live in Piedmont. The walkers backtracked a few houses and went up the one-block Hardwick Avenue to the steep Blair Avenue. As the walkers were making their climb of Blair, Nancy pointed out the Sutro Mansion at the top of the street, hidden by other homes. Nancy told the group that the mansion is not the first house built on this hilltop site. Initially, a much smaller, craftsman-style home was built there in 1876-77 by architect Joseph Worcester. He was not the architect for whom the University of California, Berkeley’s architecture department building is named. That’s Wurster Hall. This house has another, special claim to fame. It was the house that Jack London rented and lived in when he wrote his classic, The Call of the Wild, in 1902-03. However in about 1910 after London no longer lived there, it was moved two lots up the street so that the Sutro Mansion could be built on the site and have expansive views of the Bay. The group walked up to see the smaller house. It has a lovely, redwood shake shingle exterior and was enlarged after it was moved by adding a new first floor. It is reported to have been the first redwood shake exterior home built on the West Coast, and the walkers took a group photo in front of it. London was a prominent part of the artist colony that occupied this part of Piedmont in the early 1900s. He was a free-spirited man who sailed to the Orient, drank freely, and had at least three important women in his life. The success of The Call of the Wild provided him with considerable wealth. He built a separate home for first wife, Bessie, and their two daughters further up the hill on Scenic Avenue. pages.text: Wednesday, September 10, 2025 21 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers explore Piedmont’s connection to Jack London By Dick Carter A strong turnout of 44 walkers and a record six K-9 best friends were on hand last week. Nancy DeRoche had offered to take the group on a historical tour of her neighborhood above Oakland Avenue, which includes the historic Blair and Scenic Avenues. Nancy told the group she became interested in the history of her neighborhood after she learned that noted architect Albert Farr once lived in her Oakland Avenue home for many years. Nancy said she draws on the research that Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi has done. Walker and Piedmont historian Meghan Bennett had previously created a website dedicated to the Bourgeois Bohemians in “Boho Piedmont” that Nancy also drew upon. Meghan’s site is https:// www.paintingpiedmont.com/ Nancy explained that the area above Oakland Avenue was a bit of a Bohemian neighborhood from about 1890 to 1910. It was rural and sparsely populated. Writer Jack London and painter Xavier “Marty” Martinez lived there in some unique homes. Some of these creative types built their own homes. Nancy led the group across Highland Avenue and went up to Oakland Avenue. They turned up Oakland and stopped at 2010 Oakland, which was once the home of George Sterling, Frank C. Havens’ nephew. Sterling worked for Havens, and married Havens’ wife’s sister. Sterling was a frustrated artist and poet and traveled in a circle of artists. He met Jack London and encouraged him to live in Piedmont. The walkers backtracked a few houses and went up the one-block Hardwick Avenue to the steep Blair Avenue. As the walkers were making their climb of Blair, Nancy pointed out the Sutro Mansion at the top of the street, hidden by other homes. Nancy told the group that the mansion is not the first house built on this hilltop site. Initially, a much smaller, craftsman-style home was built there in 1876-77 by architect Joseph Worcester. He was not the architect for whom the University of California, Berkeley’s architecture department building is named. That’s Wurster Hall. This house has another, special claim to fame. It was the house that Jack London rented and lived in when he wrote his classic, The Call of the Wild, in 1902-03. However in about 1910 after London no longer lived there, it was moved two lots up the street so that the Sutro Mansion could be built on the site and have expansive views of the Bay. The group walked up to see the smaller house. It has a lovely, redwood shake shingle exterior and was enlarged after it was moved by adding a new first floor. It is reported to have been the first redwood shake exterior home built on the West Coast, and the walkers took a group photo in front of it. London was a prominent part of the artist colony that occupied this part of Piedmont in the early 1900s. He was a free-spirited man who sailed to the Orient, drank freely, and had at least three important women in his life. The success of The Call of the Wild provided him with considerable wealth. He built a separate home for first wife, Bessie, and their two daughters further up the hill on Scenic Avenue. He Jack London died at the early age of 40 in 1916. Just before this house is a 163-foot set of steep stairs up to the upper portion of Scenic. The walkers started the climb, but just then Eliza White, the current owner of Bessie’s former home, came out to tell the group about the house. There are 57 steps up to the front door. Some windows are original, and owners selling the house pass along a letter written by Jack London to the buyers. The walkers thanked Eliza and continued up to the top of the stairs for a little rest. There Nancy told them about painter Martinez, another famous member of the Piedmont Bohemian community, and showed them pictures of some of his paintings. Nancy led the group down the appropriately named Scenic Avenue with its wonderful views of San Francisco to what was Martinez’s rustic bungalow home at 324 Scenic, built in 1908. Festive parties with his friends, including poet Joaquin Miller were held there. Martinez later moved to CarmelXavier Marty Martinez Self Portrait by-the-Sea, but his daughter and artist, Kai Martinez, inhabited this home until her death in 1989. The group made their way down this narrow part of Scenic and decided to have another adventure on their way home. This was descending the hill via Piedmont’s longest pedestrian pathway and set of stairs, the 281-foot Blair and Scenic Path. Its steep stairs go as far as the eye can see, and thankfully there is a handrail the entire way. All of the walkers safely got back to Blair, and then down to Pacific and Mountain Avenues to the Community Hall parking lot. The group gave Nancy a round of applause at the walk’s end for the wonderful tour of her historic neighborhood. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Paul Simonson, a resident of Piedmont passed away at home on August 9, 2025 after an extended illness. Born Paul Sterling Simonson in Eugene, Oregon on November 6,1946, he was raised in Springfield, OR, Duluth, MN and Sioux Falls, SD. The son of a Lutheran minister, he was devoted to a life of service as he saw role modeled by his parents. It seemed to come naturally to him to be both a good listener and a good storyteller. He was generous and authentic when sharing his time, attention and wonderful sense of humor with others. One of his guiding principles was that everything that lives is sacred. From that came his profound sense of responsibility and commitment to others. Paul earned a BA degree in history and political science from Augustana College in Sioux Falls, SD. While in college he had a part-time job writing articles for the Associated Press and for the sports department at the Argus Leader newspaper in Sioux Falls. He earned an MA degree in theology and philosophy from Hartford Theological Foundation in Hartford, CT, and taught American government and history at Austin School, a private girls academy in Hartford. Later he taught in the philosophy department at California Lutheran College in Thousand Oaks, where he was also the cross-country coach. Paul met his beloved wife, Lonnie, in their freshman year at Augustana College. Partners for 48 years, he and Lonnie celebrated their marriage in 1988 at Rock Lake in northern Minnesota. They welcomed their son, Leif, into the family in 1990. Always a dedicated volunteer, Paul served as a Den leader with the Cub Scouts and took part in many Boy Scout events over the years. He worked with the adult teams from Piedmont Community Church that went annually to build houses in Mexico, developing deep friendships with other adults and young people from the church. He was also committed to helping with the Altar Guild, tutoring and with the children’s education program. A highlight every August was time spent at the family’s remote cabin on Rock Lake. This was a place of rest and renewal for Paul. He was an expert fisherman and caught many a northern pike, walleye and largemouth bass at Rock Lake. There was ample time for reading, hiking, swimming, and enjoying his family and friends that came to share this magical place. Paul and Jon Boshard cofounded Richards and Sterling and several Italics retail stores in 1985. The company imports beautiful tile and stone from Italy and Turkey. Paul loved to travel and was able to make many trips to Italy, often with Lonnie and Leif, to visit the factories where Paul Simonson, a longtime Piedmont resident, died on August 9, 2025. the tile was made. Paul is survived by his loving wife, Lonnie, their son, Leif, his siblings, Alice (Robert) LaBarre, Stephen (Linda) Simonson and Mary (Dean) Andrews and many cherished family and friends. A memorial service will be held on Thursday, September 18, 2025, at 11:00 AM at Piedmont Community Church. Memorial gifts may be made to Children Rising, a tutoring program in the elementary schools of Oakland, online or by mail. To donate online, visit: www. children-rising.org/donate. Under “Dedicate” check yes and follow the instructions. Checks made out to Children Rising may be mailed to: 2633 Telegraph Ave. #412 Oakland, CA 94612. Memo: Paul Simonson Memorial Gift.

articles.text: “Paddle!” yelled the coxswain at the back of the canoe, “You’re doing great, keep going!” Scouts had woken up at 4:30 a.m. to pack up and head back to camp from a night sleeping under the stars on Parsons Beach. They had to paddle the mile and a half on the ocean to get back before breakfast was served. Most were tired, many were sunburned, and everyone was hungry. “Keep paddling!” encouraged the coxswain. It was the last full day of summer camp at Camp Emerald Bay on Catalina Island, and the Piedmont Scouts in Troop 11 had had a week full of adventure. Some Scouts flew down the weekend before and spent the night on the USS Iowa. That Sunday morning, they were up early to catch the ferry. So many early mornings… The first day of camp included orientation and the swim test. Scouts and adult leaders jumped into the ocean and swam 100 yards, demonstrating the proficiency needed for a week’s worth of snorkeling, stand-up paddleboarding, kayaking, sailing, swimming, and miles of canoeing. Ryan, Elisa, Rob, Andrew and Jack take the lead on the caterpillar crawl. Scouts took a tour of the USS Iowa en route to summer camp. articles.text: Dr. Kathy Hull of Piedmont was recently awarded an Honorary Doctorate at Santa Clara University for her years of public service as the Founder and Staff Psychologist at George Mark Children’s House. Following the conferring of the degree by the University President, Dr. Julie Sullivan, Hull gave the commencement address to the Class of 2025 of the Graduate School of Counseling Psychology and Education, from which she had received a Master’s degree in 1980. Dr. Hull had been asked by the Dean to share the legacy of GMCH as an organization which has had a profound impact on Bay Area communities, and beyond, for over twenty years. She focused her remarks on three words that were inspirational both in her career and the actualization of GMCH: Possibility, Curiosity and Hope. To begin, she gave the graduates a description of George Mark and the lovely difference it makes in the lives of its young patients: “The House, named after my two brothers who died when they were young, is located capable hands and take a break from their demanding and relentless responsibilities,” she said. Twenty years since its inception, George Mark House has helped hundreds of families through the challenging journey of illness and death in a way that has allowed them comfort, dignity, unlimited bereavement support, and connection to other families who have shared a similar experience. They are supported in being able to reengage with life. All of the services are provided at no charge to the families who stay there. In closing, Hull encouraged the graduate to seek purposeful work. ‘You have been given the foundation to go from this campus with self-confidence and build lives of meaning. You will never regret speaking up for injustice or going out of your way to help the less fortunate. Better is possible. It just takes a willingness to try.” – Dr. Kathy Hull Founder George Mark pediatric hospice on five acres of beautifully landscaped gardens. It is a tranquil and nurturing place where families, with sick or dying children, can spend quality time together supported by the love and attention of extraordinary volunteers and caretaking staff. Wednesday morning - Piedmont Center for the Arts 9:00am - 10:00am Wednesday evening - online 7:30pm - 8:15pm Free ~ No experience needed ~ Drop ins always welcome For more info and Zoom link: Mark Herrick ~ herrickmark@icloud.com ~ 415-706-2000 Ages 12 and older welcome Sudoku Puzzle Sudoku by Myles Mellor 6 2 3 2 9 7 7 5 9 1 Kathy Hull presented with Honorary Doctor’s degree by Santa Clara University Dr. Kathy Hull of Piedmont was recently awarded an Honorary Doctorate at Santa Clara University for her years of public service as the Founder and Staff Psychologist at George Mark Children’s House. Following the conferring of the degree by the University President, Dr. Julie Sullivan, Hull gave the commencement address to the Class of 2025 of the Graduate School of Counseling Psychology and Education, from which she had received a Master’s degree in 1980. Dr. Hull had been asked by the Dean to share the legacy of GMCH as an organization which has had a profound impact on Bay Area communities, and beyond, for over twenty years. She focused her remarks on three words that were inspirational both in her career and the actualization of GMCH: Possibility, Curiosity and Hope. To begin, she gave the graduates a description of George Mark and the lovely difference it makes in the lives of its young patients: “The House, named after my two brothers who died when they were young, is located capable hands and take a break from their demanding and relentless responsibilities,” she said. Twenty years since its inception, George Mark House has helped hundreds of families through the challenging journey of illness and death in a way that has allowed them comfort, dignity, unlimited bereavement support, and connection to other families who have shared a similar experience. They are supported in being able to reengage with life. All of the services are provided at no charge to the families who stay there. In closing, Hull encouraged the graduate to seek purposeful work. ‘You have been given the foundation to go from this campus with self-confidence and build lives of meaning. You will never regret speaking up for injustice or going out of your way to help the less fortunate. Better is possible. It just takes a willingness to try.” “Better is possible. It just takes a willingness to try.” – Dr. Kathy Hull Founder George Mark pediatric hospice on five acres of beautifully landscaped gardens. It is a tranquil and nurturing place where families, with sick or dying children, can spend quality time together supported by the love and attention of extraordinary volunteers and caretaking staff. Almost everyone went snorkeling to look for garibaldis, crab, and other sea life. Other classes offered at the camp included wood carving, archery, environmental science, basic Scout skills, and lots of time at the waterfront. A few Scouts even built an underwater ROV and practiced driving it in the cove. The last full day of camp included the aquacade, a campwide competition that included five Scouts in a rowboat built for two, racing without a paddle, or five Scouts swimming a rowboat (still without paddle) with SPL Kajsa Benson was one of the Scouts participating in the ROV Exploration class Tired Scouts successfully making it back to camp before breakfast an adult volunteer attempting to stand up inside. Don’t forget the sandbuilding competition, or the Scoutmaster belly flop. It wrapped up with a relay that included canoeing, kayaking, swimming, and a sprint to compete a trivia challenge. A final ferry ride took the Scouts back to their bus for a long, quiet, ride back home to Piedmont. articles.text: Piedmont Makers co-founder Dave Ragones is stepping down as president this year, while continuing his role in the popular STEAM education group as treasurer. Ragones is making the transition after guiding Piedmont Makers from inception through huge growth, and seeing more than 1000 kids getting involved with the Makers program. “It was time for the next generation, if you will,” said Ragones. “My kids are older – they’re in high school, or just graduated from high school, and they’re not as involved in the programs.” Taking the helm as Co-Presidents of the Makers Board are Ben Stein and Kevin Clark. Stein and Clark have both been active on the Makers Board for years, with Stein having served as ComPiedmont Makers Co-Founder Dave Ragones at the 2024 Piedmont Maker Faire.
articles.title: Piedmont Makers President Dave Ragones steps back after 10 years

articles.text: Children’s Fairyland has been celebrating for the last 75 years, and pumped up the volume with a raucous 75th birthday party on Monday, September 1. The Labor Day event drew upwards of 2,800 patrons, to enjoy and honor the establishment that has set the international standard for children’s theme parks since 1950. Throughout the day kids explored the park via Old Mother Hubbard’s shoe arch entrance, with beaming wide eyes. The controversial housing plan would provide space to develop residences of up to five stories either in the Blair Park area or on the hillside near Coaches Field. The plan includes 137 market-rate housing units and 60 low-income housing units, as well as road safety improvements and an expansion to Coaches Field. articles.text: The Beach Dads Club will celebrate 20 years of philanthropy this Sunday, September 7, with its popular annual Pancake Breakfast. Beach dads are preparing for an unforgettable anniversary full of new features and fun with the usual delicious flapjacks, bacon, coffee and joy starting at 9 a.m. on the Beach Elementary School playground. Rob Doebelin, this year’s Dads Club president (Padre Grande), is chomping at the bit for the big party. The Dads will soon be prepping gallons of their secret recipe to fix up a mean breakfast consisting of thousands of pancakes, countless sausage links, and more than 100 pounds of bacon. “We’re honoring Beach, our kids, and all the Padre Grandes who’ve kept this tradition alive. From stacks of pancakes to new Fun Zone surprises, to celebrating the people who make this community special — with staff, teachers, firefighters, and police eating free — we want this year’s breakfast to feel like both a thank-you and a kickoff to the next 20 years of fun, friendship, and community spirit,” said Doebelin. LETTERS - MAIN Serious concerns remain on Moraga Canyon housing Editor: On Sept. 8, 2025, the Piedmont Planning Commission is scheduled to vote on a recommendation to the City Council on the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan (MCSP). The MCSP calls for building 197 housing units on Moraga Ave. (either in Blair Park or on the steep hillside above and around Coaches Field.) The housing would be 5-story structures with 60 low-income and up to 137 market rate units. Some of us who have followed the Plan’s development for 3 years have questions and serious concerns for Piedmont’s future if it becomes a reality. Here are a few. Disaster Evacuation: Piedmont Fire Dept. cites Moraga Canyon as a “high risk wildfire” area and predicts a wildfire is “highly likely.” The Canyon is also less than 1 mile from the Hayward Fault. Moraga Ave. is a designated emergency evacuation route and is the only way out for the estimated 400 to 1,000 new Canyon residents, as well as for many existing nearby Oakland and Piedmont residents. The Plan expects people to walk or bicycle in a disaster. How likely is that? How will emergency crews reach the Canyon if Moraga Ave. is gridlocked as residents desperately try to leave? Remember the 1991 Oakland hills fire. Does Piedmont want to risk its residents’ lives? Financial Risks: The MCSP requires the market-rate developer to pay all infrastructure costs, including widening Moraga Ave., adding sidewalks and bike lanes, new stormwater drains and sewer lines, undergrounding all utilities – and expanding Coaches Field. What if the developer declines or defaults part way through development? Does this cost fall on the City and Piedmont taxpayers? Will new residents be able to get fire insurance? Known Obstacles: The Plan itself acknowledges constraints to the development, stating that hydrology “could cause dangerous road conditions on Moraga Ave. during significant rain and cause local flooding.” Stormwater storage basins at both site options may have to be replaced. And “due to the presence of steep slopes (above Coaches Field), much of this land is not conducive to development.” The City wants to declare Blair Park, a designated Piedmont City park, as “surplus land” in order to develop it. articles.text: As the weather turns hotter and vegetation dries out, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to prepare their yards for fire season by trimming trees and shrubs, clearing flammable materials, and removing dead vegetation around their property. Even if these steps were taken earlier this summer, PFD advises another round of clearing as fall nears. The East Bay hills have had significant wildfires in September and October multiple times in the last 150 years. Communities are best protected when everyone takes steps to manage the vegetation around their homes, which helps to reduce the spread and severity of fires when they start. Residents can do their part by taking a few simple protective measures in their yards every fall. The Fire Department asks residents to make time in the next few weeks to prepare their properties: Clear debris Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around the yard. Clear leaves and pine needles from roofs, gutters, and the ground. Remove flammable materials, such as paint or propane containers from under decks and away from buildings. Trim plants of dead material It’s important to keep all plants in the yard watered and well-maintained. Remove any dead or dying vegetation. If you have trees that shed bark or leaves such as eucalyptus in the yard, remove any shed debris. Create space between plants and home Remove branches that hang over the roof or are within 10 feet of the chimney. Prune plants away from buildings. This buffer area will help protect the house and give firefighters an area to work in to defend your home during a fire. Create space between plants Trim trees so the lowest branches are at least six feet from the ground, or three times the height of any shrubs beneath the tree. This helps prevent fire from moving from the ground to the treetops, where it can spread more quickly. Download a checklist for preparing your yard at piedmont. ca.gov/YardChecklist. Find more information and links to additional resources on preparing your property for fire season at piedmont.ca.gov/vegetation. If you need help identifying what needs to be done on your property, call the Fire Department at (510) 420-3030 to request an inspection.
articles.title: Time to prepare for wildfire season

articles.text: The best practice in vegetation management is to remove all vegetation within five feet of your home. Even if this is not currently feasible for you, taking protective measures in your yard will increase your home’s chance of surviving a wildfire and reduce risk to our whole community. Use this checklist to prepare your yard. CREATE SPACE Maintaining adequate space between plants, structures, and other objects on your property makes it harder for a fire to spread. Trim trees so that the lowest branches are at least 6 feet from the ground, or 3 times the height of any shrubs beneath the tree. Trim trees so that branches are 10 feet apart from other trees. Remove branches within 10 feet of your chimney. Remove branches that hang over your roof. Remove or prune plants and shrubs near windows. Move patio furniture, wood piles, etc. away from plants. CLEAR DEBRIS & FLAMMABLE MATERIAL Clear leaves, pine needles, and other debris from roofs, gutters, and the ground. Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around your property. Remove plant debris and other flammable materials, such as propane containers and paint from under decks. KEEP PLANTS WELL MAINTAINED Whether you have natives or non-natives, the most important thing is to keep all plants in your yard watered and well-maintained. Trim any dead or dying material from plants. Keep plants watered - especially any plants located within five feet of your home. If you have Eucalyptus trees, remove any shedding bark and leaves. Minimum Vertical Clearance: Avoid Fire "Ladders" 3X X Trim trees so the lowest branches are 3 times the height of shrubs below. For example, if a 5 foot shrub is growing near a tree, the lowest branch should be be 15 feet above it - 20 feet from the ground. We're here to help! If you have questions or need assistance, call us at (510) 420-3030. Lack of vertical space between shrubs and trees allows fire to move from the ground to treetops like a ladder, leading to more intense fires. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Piedmont City Hall will be closed on Thursday, September 4, while PG&E replaces an outdated electrical transformer as part of the City’s 911 Dispatch Center replacement project. Replacing the obsolete transformer will allow the Police Department to connect to a new, independent electrical system and backup generator, ensuring continuous operations during outages. This milestone is critical for the project, which began during summer 2024. City Hall services will be unavailable but there will be no interruption to public safety. Thursday, September 4: • Public safety services will continue uninter r upted. Police, Fire, and Dispatch functions will be powered by generator. • City Hall will be closed. Services typically received at the Planning, Building, and Public Works permit counter or the City Clerk counter will not be available by phone or email. • Power will also be out at 801 • • Magnolia, Veterans Hall, and the tot lot bathroom in Piedmont Park. Recreation Department offices at 385 Hillside Avenue will remain open. KCOM will be off the air during the outage. The online meeting video archive will remain available. City Hall services will resume on Friday, September 5. Dispatch center replacement Dispatch functions as the nerve center for the City of Piedmont’s public safety response, fielding more than 13,000 calls each year for Police and Fire services. The old facility was severely undersized, unable to accommodate modern technologies, and located in an area that had not been seismically retrofitted, posing a risk to continued operations in a catastrophic event. The new dispatch center is intended to provide a much larger, seismically safe space, as well as featuring state-of-the-art call answering equipment that improves cell phone location accuracy and offers real-time, on-screen translation in multiple languages. It will also allow dispatchers to continuously monitor automated license plate readers and public safety cameras via large, wall-mounted screens. The electrical upgrade will provide the Police Department with an independent, reliable source of power and a backup generator, while allowing City Hall and 801 Magnolia to remain operational during future outages using the old, shared backup generator. Once energized, the dispatch center will include installing servers, cabling, and related equipment in the new Police Department IT room, configuring new networking and telecommunications infrastructure, and installing the next-generation dispatch workstations. A phased transition from the temporary dispatch center to the new facility is expected later this year. Concurrent with the physical space improvements, the City recently augmented dispatch staffing for the first time since 1978. articles.text: Grant Program expands to rentals The California Residential Mitigation Program (CRMP) announced today its second Earthquake Brace + Bolt (EBB) grant registration period for 2025, running from August 20 through October 1. This seismic retrofit program offers up to $3,000 for older homes, now expanding to include rentals and other non-owner-occupied residential properties. For the first time, this open registration expands eligibility to include non-primary residential properties, giving landlords and other property owners the opportunity to apply for seismic retrofit grants to strengthen woodframed homes built before 1980 with raised foundations against earthquake damage. Following the successful registration of nearly 19,000 homeowners during the January registration period, CRMP is initiating a second registration phase. With more than 1,100 eligible ZIP Codes across the state - including 303 added earlier this year - qualified homeowners can apply for grants of up to $3,000 to help cover the cost of bolting houses to their foundations and bracing crawl space walls. These seismic retrofit upgrades help to reduce earthquake damage and provide more resilient housing in high-risk areas. More than $20 million in grant funding will be available to help offset the cost of seismic retrofits. Since the 2013 EBB program launch, more than 32,500 California homeowners have received grant assistance for strengthening their homes against earthquake damage. The EBB grant program is administered by CRMP, a Joint Powers Authority between the California Earthquake Authority (CEA) and the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES). “Offering a second registration period this year is a valuable opportunity in helping us meet the strong demand we’ve seen for earthquake retrofit assistance,” said Janiele Maffei, Chief Mitigation Officer, California Earthquake Authority. “By opening eligibility to include non-owner-occupied residential properties, we are helping ensure more of California’s older homes, including rentals, can be strengthened against earthquake damage. Retrofitting is one of the most effective ways to reduce the risk of severe damage in a major quake, protecting both residents and the communities they call home.” Income-eligible homeowners may also qualify for supplemental grants. Up to $7,000 in additional grant funds are available for households with an annual income at or below $89,040, which may provide up to 100% of the funds needed to cover a seismic retrofit. Grants are contingent upon meeting eligibility requirements and available funds. “Earthquake retrofits create a safer and more resilient California. Expanding retrofit grants to rental properties means CRMP will provide even greater protection for California’s housing stock and the families who call these properties ‘home,’” said Tom Welsh, Chief Executive Officer of the California Earthquake Authority. “Each retrofit brings us one step closer to a better-prepared California.” Beginning August 20 and running through October 1, 2025, eligible homeowners can register for a retrofit grant at EarthquakeBraceBolt.com, where they can also find detailed program information, select a trained California-licensed general contractor and view the full list of ZIP Codes and program areas. About Earthquake Brace + Bolt (EBB) Established by the California Residential Mitigation Program, EBB offers up to $3,000 to help California homeowners retrofit their house to reduce potential damage from earthquakes. A residential seismic retrofit makes a house more resistant to earthquake activity, such as ground shaking and soil failure, by bolting the house to its foundation and adding bracing around the perimeter of the crawl space. For more information, please visit: EarthquakeBraceBolt.com. About the California Residential Mitigation Program (CRMP) CRMP was established in 2011 to help Californians strengthen their homes against damage from earthquakes. CRMP is a joint powers authority created by the California Earthquake Authority and the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services. For more information, please visit crmp.org.

City Hall will be closed Sept. 4 for installation of new Dispatch Center Transformer By Tony Simons Piedmont City Hall will be closed on Thursday, September 4, while PG&E replaces an outdated electrical transformer as part of the City’s 911 Dispatch Center replacement project. Replacing the obsolete transformer will allow the Police Department to connect to a new, independent electrical system and backup generator, ensuring continuous operations during outages. This milestone is critical for the project, which began during summer 2024. City Hall services will be unavailable but there will be no interruption to public safety. Thursday, September 4: • Public safety services will continue uninter r upted. Police, Fire, and Dispatch functions will be powered by generator. • City Hall will be closed. Services typically received at the Planning, Building, and Public Works permit counter or the City Clerk counter will not be available by phone or email. • Power will also be out at 801 • • Magnolia, Veterans Hall, and the tot lot bathroom in Piedmont Park. Recreation Department offices at 385 Hillside Avenue will remain open. KCOM will be off the air during the outage. The online meeting video archive will remain available. City Hall services will resume on Friday, September 5. Dispatch center replacement Dispatch functions as the nerve center for the City of Piedmont’s public safety response, fielding more than 13,000 calls each year for Police and Fire services. The old facility was severely undersized, unable to accommodate modern technologies, and located in an area that had not been seismically retrofitted, posing a risk to continued operations in a catastrophic event. The new dispatch center is intended to provide a much larger, seismically safe space, as well as featuring state-of-the-art call answering equipment that improves cell phone location accuracy and offers real-time, on-screen translation in multiple languages. It will also allow dispatchers to continuously monitor automated license plate readers and public safety cameras via large, wall-mounted screens. The electrical upgrade will provide the Police Department with an independent, reliable source of power and a backup generator, while allowing City Hall and 801 Magnolia to remain operational during future outages using the old, shared backup generator. Once energized, the dispatch center will include installing servers, cabling, and related equipment in the new Police Department IT room, configuring new networking and telecommunications infrastructure, and installing the next-generation dispatch workstations. A phased transition from the temporary dispatch center to the new facility is expected later this year. Concurrent with the physical space improvements, the City recently augmented dispatch staffing for the first time since 1978. Two new dispatcher positions were added last year, a staffing increase made possible by the March 2024 passage of Measure F. articles.text: More than 100 girls, parents, and siblings gathered at Beach Playfield in Piedmont for another successful Try It Out Tuesday event on August 23. The free event, coordinated by the Recreation Department’s Eva Phelan, continues to offer Bay Area girls+ the opportunity to explore new sports in a supportive and inclusive environment, with a focus on empowering girls through athletics. This month’s session gave participants the chance to rotate through three different stations: powerlifting, golf, and pickleball. Preston Pinckney of Ace Golf provided hands-on swing instruction, while members of the Piedmont Pickleball Group introduced the rules and fundamentals of their fast-growing sport. At the ever-popular powerlifting station, Piedmont High School seniors Robyn Kim and Layth Haddawy guided girls through beginner-friendly deadlifts and squats, “It looked so heavy, but it really helping many to try the sport for the first time. Kim, the 2025 U.S. National Powerlifting Champion, demonstrated powerlifting to a large audience of young female athletes at last spring’s Play It Like a Girl+ event and said she was excited to return for another opportunity to inspire girls in the community. “When I first started lifting, I didn’t see many girls in the sport,” she explained. “Now I get to show them that being strong and powerful is part of playing like a girl. It’s not about competing with anyone else; it’s about seeing what you can do and surprising yourself.” “I didn’t know girls could be powerlifters,” said Mattie Grohmann, a fifth-grade student at Beach Elementary, moments before completing a deadlift that exceeded her own body weight. A line of girls work at perfecting their golf swing at Try It Out Tuesday. Kids race around the court, enjoying a game of pickleball. A young girl learns powerlifting technique.

One creates comfort and connection; the other jolts us into laughter we’ll remember years later. Why Families Need Play Now Family life today runs fast. Parents juggle work, carpools, and endless logistics; children navigate school, screens, and constant structure. Play is what interrupts that treadmill, what reminds everyone that life isn’t only about the next task or achievement. Shared play gives families breathing room, a spark of connection, and a memory that lasts far longer than the Tuesday evening routine. Lightly Through Life As the school year takes over, play isn’t something to grow out of. It’s something to grow into. Shaw’s reminder rings true, but play can also be a way of being — a lighter way of moving through the ordinary days. So this week, schedule 20 minutes of play. Be whimsical. Be ordinary. Be together. Normal life will keep its routines without you for half an hour. And as Peter Pan warned, “Once you’re grown up, you can never come back.” But perhaps you can — not to childhood itself, but to the spirit of it, carried lightly into the present. Randall Grayson P.h.D (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over twenty years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about summer program, family camps, and twoweek sessions can be found at www.campaugusta.org. READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: The SAT has been administered in a digital format since last year. It is taken by millions of students worldwide as part of the college application process. At Piedmont High School, more than 120 students sit for the exam each year. The test is divided into four sections, two in reading and two in math, and typically lasts about two hours. Along with the ACT, the SAT remains a key factor for colleges that require standardized testing and can significantly influence admissions outcomes. This year, the SAT exam on August 23 proved to be one of the most chaotic yet. With over 30 PHS students testing that day, it’s no surprise that the San Francisco test centers, where most Bay Area juniors and seniors choose to take their exams, were packed with thousands of students. Students driving into San Francisco quickly found themselves stuck in standstill traffic as tens of thousands of cars clogged the streets. In fear of being late to the SAT, some students abandoned their rides altogether, sprinting along streets and weaving through red-light intersections. When they finally reached their test sites, they were met with crowds of students just like themselves, spilling across sidewalks and entryways. At the Moscone Center alone more than 4,000 students were crammed inside, facing unprepared staff and mounting confusion. What made the experience even more overwhelming was the crowd of parents pressed against the glass outside and the airport-like atmosphere inside. After half an hour of confusion, students were funneled into halls that had been hastily divided into sections. While most students were eventually able to take the exam without major issues, some areas faced Wi-Fi failures that left students sitting at their desks for hours, scrolling on their phones, only to be told they would not be able to test at all. PHS senior Mina Dao-Hoang was unable to take the August SAT due to Wi-Fi issues. “It took an hour and a half to sit down, and only a few could use Wi-Fi so they started, but the rest of us were talking and seated. People had phones out to text their parents but we could only leave around 11:30 after not being able to take it.” she said. Dao-Hoang was one of more than 600 students who never got the chance to test, and one of a few from PHS. When asked how she felt about the situation, she explained, “I didn’t study, but I can imagine that if people did, they would be really mad. The SAT is important because more schools are requiring it and if you do well, you have a higher chance to get into a prestigious school. We basically lost the opportunity to take both an August and a September SAT before college applications.” Senior Elena O’Connell, on the other hand, was able to complete the exam, but the disruptions still weighed on her. “It felt different than the other SAT I took because there were a lot more people. While you were taking the test you could hear the other proctors from the other sections through the speakers, so it was hard to focus,” said O’Connell. For both students, and for many others across the Bay Area, the August SAT may have taken away what should have been a crucial opportunity to get ahead in the college application season. The biggest update for those who were unable to test is that they now have to go out of their way to retake it this Saturday at Union Square in San Francisco. “I’m going to have to take it and then the September one in two weeks,” Dao-Hoang noted. For students already overwhelmed by the pressures of college applications, the chaos of this year’s August SAT only added another layer of stress to an already high-stakes process. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern writer with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: PHS students vs. the SAT: August’s battle

articles.text: Earlier this summer, 37 eighth grade students capped off their time at Piedmont Middle School with a parent-led trip to Yosemite National Park that was organized by Judy Lin and Michelle Abernathy. As Chief Operating Officer of NatureBridge, a non-profit that runs outdoor schools in national parks, Judy uniquely understands the power of outdoor education. Michelle is a former teacher who took her students to NatureBridge and is also a mom and wife to NatureBridge alums. “We’re passionate about outdoor ed. Great things happen when students are learning out in nature together and we wanted our kids to have that experience with their classmates. Michelle and I knew we wanted to make a NatureBridge trip happen,” said Judy. What began as an idea last fall became a reality in early June as a busload of rising ninth graders and parent chaperones arrived in Yosemite Valley for their weeklong program. The trip leaders organized everything from travel logistics to finances and chaperone support to make their vision for the trip come true. The result was an unforgettable outdoor adventure. Led by NatureBridge educators, the students hiked miles around Yosemite Valley, learned Thirty-seven recent Piedmont Middle School graduates in front of Half Dome science, and got to know their classmates through team building activities. The kids challenged themselves and gained confidence throughout the week, from crawling through narrow caves to wading in cold rivers to completing their challenge hike to the top of the Mist Trail in 95 degree heat. Ben McMurtry reflects, “I liked exploring with my friends and doing cool team building activities. Not having phones meant we could do all kinds of other stuff together.” Henry Van Den Bos and his trailmates try to figure out the team challenge. A team-building exercise included being blindfolded to learn about trust and communication. Zayda Weber leads the group in a closing campfire activity.
articles.title: Inaugural eighth grade outdoor education trip to Yosemite

pages.text: Wednesday, September 3, 2025 9 Eighth Grade Continued from page 8 “An important goal for our trip was for it to be completely tech-free,” Michelle added. “I think that no tech felt like a challenge for these kids but it ended up being a highlight for them.” Students passed the time on long bus rides by talking and playing games. They made friendship bracelets and bonded over card games and chess after their days on the trail. The kids played hide and seek and “pinecone baseball” in Curry Village and rediscovered the joy of sitting around and simply hanging out with friends - all without screens. “It felt like the kids were able to let down their guards and be themselves. There was a lot of silliness and laughter and also some real introspection and serious appreciation for the environment around us,” said parent Becca Posamentier. Most students knew each other before the trip, but this shared outdoor experience that included sleeping in tent cabins and mixed trail groups allowed for wider and deeper connections. Penelope Hopper says, “Being in a different environment with people I normally see at school was definitely a bonding experience. It was so much fun, and I’ll never forget the random memories we all created together.” The kids left Yosemite with a stronger sense of community that they can hopefully carry into high school. The success of this first eighth grade trip has inspired plans for more. Judy and Michelle hope to make this trip a tradition for younger siblings. “Meaningful experiences in nature are more important than ever for kids. This trip will hopefully be something that our kids and their classmates will always remember about middle school,” said Judy. articles.text: In early August a group of nine Piedmont Scouts from Troop 15 and two adult leaders completed a seven-day, 60+ mile backpacking adventure in the High Sierra, including summiting Mt. Whitney at 14,505 feet, the highest The group entered at the Cottonwood Lakes trailhead in the John Muir Wilderness at 10,000 feet, each night ascending to higher alpine lakes, including Long Lake at 11,200 feet and Guitar Lake at 11,500 feet. After ascending to New Army Pass at 12,300 feet, the group joined the Pacific Crest Trail and John Muir Trail in Sequoia National Park to reach Mt. Whitney. On the morning of the summit attempt, scouts broke camp at 5 am and started their 3,000- foot ascent in the dark lit by headlamps. As the sun rose, the scouts hiked the ridgeline below the peak, navigating exposed ledges, fields of snow, and technical traverses. By 9 am, the group reached the summit, celebrating with group photos and handstands. All the scouts are current Piedmont High students including six Life Scouts who are nearing the end of their scouting journey as they complete their Troop 15 Scouts on top of Mt. Whitney on Wednesday, July 30. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo team got its season started at the Labor Day Bash tournament at James Logan in Union City on Friday and Saturday, August 29-30. Winning one of four games. The Highlanders opened with a 12-5 loss to Washington on the first day but beat host school James Logan 12-11 later on. They next day, Piedmont faced two Western Alameda County Conference foes, losing 14-9 to Castro Valley and 20-10 to Alameda. Piedmont’s game with Washington marked a rematch of last year’s Division 2 North Coast Section Quarterfinals, which PHS ultimately lost in a 14-11 barnburner. This time, the Huskies were able to take a lead and hold it for a victory thanks to a large batch of returning upperclassmen. 12-5 to Washington The Huskies got out to a commanding 7-2 lead through the first quarter. Although Washington was held scoreless in the second quarter, Piedmont was only able to gain one goal. In the third quarter, Washington added three more goals to the tally while allowing one. Piedmont was held scoreless in the fourth quarter, allowing two to Washington. Final stats: Elles Krieckhaus and Henry Stein scored twice. Zach Dupree scored once. Goalie Luke McAuliffe had four saves, while Dylan Jerez had three saves in the fourth quarter. Staff Photos Elles Krieckhaus scored had four goals against James Logan and five against Castro Valley. Rylan Patty had four goals against James Logan and three vs. Alameda. Henry Stein led with four goals against Alameda. 12-11 victory vs. James Logan It was a back and forth game against James Logan with both teams holding a 2-2 tie at the end of the first quarter. Piedmont trailed 6-5 going into halftime after scoring three goals but allowing four. The Highlanders turned things around in the third quarter, scoring four and allowing just two to take a 9-8 lead to start the fourth. Both teams scored three goals in the final going. Final stats: Krieckhaus led the way with four goals and one assist. Rylan Patty also scored four goals. Stein had two goals, one assist, and one steal. Ben Kappas had a goal, assist, and two steals. Nick Riordan scored once. McAuliffe finished with 11 saves and one steal. 14-9 loss to Castro Valley Castro Valley led 4-2 through the first quarter and extended the gap to 10-4 by halftime. Piedmont clipped away at the lead in the third quarter with four goals and allowed two, trailing 12-8 to start the fourth. The Trojans added two more goals in the final going while allowing one. Final stats: Krieckhaus led scoring with five goals. Patty had two goals and a steal. Stein had two goals. Alameda prevails 20-10 It was a high-scoring opening quarter with the Hornets logging 10 goals, while Piedmont kept things interesting with six of their own. However, Alameda added another five in the second quarter to Piedmont’s two in both the second and third quarters. The Hornets scored three in the fourth, holding the Highlanders scoreless in the process. Final stats: Stein led the way with four goals, one assist, and one steal. Patty scored three goals. Krieckhaus had two goals and an assist. Kappas had one goal, and Riordan had one assist. McAuliffe had five saves. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-3 overall) travels to San Marin in Novato on Wednesday, September 10. The starting time has not been confirmed.

articles.text: It was a tough matchup against Salesian to start Piedmont’s football season on Saturday, August 30 in Richmond, losing 41-17. Despite the defeat, the Highlanders kept things close through three quarters and trailed by just four-points with 8:08 left. The Pride also beat Piedmont last year 46-14 and returned some of their top talent, like receiver Carlton Perrilliat and running back Tyler Sadler. “It felt like last year, when we had a lead on them. But you have to play four quarters of football and your true colors show up in hard times,” said Piedmont coach Jordan Seiden. “I don’t care about the score, I care about the effort. We need to give ourselves our best chance through effort.” For a while, it looked like Piedmont was punching well above its weight class with an almost entire new roster on offense, defense, and special teams. Trailing 28-17, the Highlanders were driving downfield to Salesian’s 29, but a blown assignment led to an interception and quick score by the Pride. “Yeah, we’re a new team, but the other team doesn’t care about that. We had a missed assignment and that led to the interception,” Seiden said. Despite the disappointing result, there were some bright spots as Piedmont went up against last year’s Div. 5 North Coast Section No. 2 seed and eventual semifinalist. Sophomore quarterback Jimmy Lagios didn’t shy from the moment, looking poised navigating the pocket to elude pressure and rolling out to find receivers. Lagios connected with two teammates for touchdowns. Hurwitz, who led last year’s JV team in scoring, had an impressive 53-yard touchdown after fighting through two defenders. George Saunders scored a 25-yard touchdown, breaking a tackle on his way to the end zone. “Jimmy stepped up and played as good a game as we could ask. He was scrambling and made some plays. He got the ball out and our receivers made some nice plays. The great side of things is [that] young guys stepped up,” Seiden said. Piedmont will travel 100 miles to Middletown in Lake County for a game on Friday, September 5. Last year, PHS beat the Mustangs 42-21 at Witter Field. Game Recap After a couple possessions, Salesian scored first on a 12 yard pass with 1:42 left in the first quarter. The Pride added another touchdown with 4:19 left in the second quarter to go up 14-0. Piedmont assumed possession at its own 47-yard line after a failed onside kick. On 3rd-and-10, Lagios hurled a ball downfield to Hurwitz, who athletically fought off pass interference and two defenders to turn up field and score with 3:51 left in the second quarter, making it 14-7. Salesian scored on their ensuing possession with 1:03 left. PHS drove 60 yards in the remaining time, including a 26 yard reception by Jack Meyjes and an 11 yard catch by Saunders. Xavier Henderson (#13) defends a pass while covering Salesian’s top receiver, Carlton Perrilliat.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s flag football team opened up its season with a 27-6 loss to St. Mary’s on Thursday, August 28 at Witter Field. Despite the loss, there were still bright spots as Piedmont adjusts to the sport’s new rules. “That was the best loss we ever had. We started out focused and they adjusted. As the game went on, we were still energized and excited about how we played. Of course, you want to win, but we’re still feeling very positive,” said coach Beth Black. Sophomore quarterback Edie Elmquist did well, using her speed to break the pocket for rushing yards, while also finding open targets when rolling out. “Edie was phenomenal on the run; she’s utilizing her speed. She knows every route and has the confidence to dance back there. She’s showing confidence,” Black said. Senior safety Dahlia Osman also made an impact, recording two interceptions, including one in the end zone. “Dahlia is Dahlia; she’s a force back there,” Black said. Piedmont scored the final touchdown of the game when Malia Williams ran the ball 25 Staff Photos Edie Elmquist lines up for a pass in Piedmont’s second opener against St. Mary’s. yards into the end zone. Black discussed some of the work that needs to be done. “We’re going to work on flag pulling from the outside hip. We want to work on screen blocking, and just building more connections on the field,” Black said. The Highlanders look ahead to hosting Miramonte tomorrow, Thursday, September 4. Five days later, PHS opens its league schedule in the Shoreline Division of the Western Alameda County Conference against Tennyson on September 9. Dahlia Osman makes one of her two interceptions. Piedmont celebrates Malia Williams’ (middle) touchdown. Game Recap After Piedmont went threeand-out on the first possession, Saint Mary’s drove 43 yards on three plays to go up 6-0 with 8:40 left in the first quarter following a failed extra point conversion. On the next drive, Elmquist had a completion to Cory Minor while Elmquist also broke runs of five and 12 yards. However, PHS elected to punt on 4th-and-5 at their 35 yard line. After two trades of possession, Saint Mary’s drove to the 21 yard line, but Osman thwarted their series by nabbing an interception. The Panthers got the ball back with 11:15 to go in the second quarter, driving 33 yards to the end zone—making it 13-0 with 7:22 left. Piedmont’s next drive featured a 15 yard reception by Kaylani Spieckerman and a 10 yard carry by Elmquist, but the drive stalled out two yards past midfield at the St. Mary’s 38 with 26 seconds left in the half. In the third quarter, Osman had a critical takeaway by grabbing her second interception, this time jumping a route in the end zone with 4:34 on the clock. However, Piedmont’s offense punted after three plays, leading to another St. Mary’s score with 39 seconds left—19-0. The Panthers later forced a safety in the fourth quarter with 6:52 remaining in the game, 21-0. Piedmont got on the board late after just three plays. It featured Anjali Bowers recording a nine yard reception before Williams took a carry 25 yards to the house. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-1 overall) hosts Miramonte on Thursday, September 4 at 7:30 p.m. They also host Tennyson on Tuesday, September 9 at the same time.

articles.text: Photos by Jenni Tsoi Leighton Mand, the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2024 is back for her junior season. Piedmont High’s cross-country team returns to action this week at St. Mary’s College in Moraga on Saturday, September 6 at the St. Mary’s Invitational. They’ll compete with 31 other schools, with many teams from the North Coast Section. It’s shaping up to be a potentially strong season for the girls’ squad, led by returning runners, Leighton Mand and Amalia Gray. Both reached last year’s CIF State Championship. The Post named Mand its 2025 Sophomore of the Year following her cross country and track campaigns. She finished 74th of 201 athletes at the State Championship, while she was sixth of 127 at the NCS Championship. “Leighton is a cornerstone runner of the girls’ team. She’s consistent and competitive. She wants to work hard and race hard. She’s also shown she can look out for other members of the team,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. Gray was among last year’s breakout stars as a sophomore as well. She was 101st at State and finished 14th at NCS. Alongside Gray and Mand, Piedmont has a very strong group of eight runners who could all make an impact. Skylar Best enters her senior year, while sophomores Viviane Oesterer and Nikita Gorelik also made an impact in their debut in 2024. Senior Cora Chun, senior Mara Kemp-Malone, and junior Cora Brozowski Schrader are three runners who should help. “Skylar is a senior and one of our captains and Amalia went to the State meet last year. Viviane is a sophomore and was one of our top runners last year at the WACC Championship and North Coast. Cora Chun is another senior captain, Cora Brozowski Schrader is looking strong as well. Nikita had a really strong track season, I’m looking forward to her being in the running,” Zirkelbach said. In total, Zirkelbach sees a girls’ group who could potentially make it to State if all goes well. “The girls look very promising if everyone can stay healthy. They have a shot to possibly make it to the State meet,” Zirkelbach. The boys’ will have to go much of the season without star runner Sebastien Swain, who underwent surgery over the offseason on a lingering injury. He was our 2025 honorable mention for Athlete of the Year. the Post’s’ first boys’ sophomore to do so. Zirkelbach is hopeful Swain can recover in time for the 2025 Western Alameda County Conference Championship near the end of the season. “Sebastien had surgery early in the summer. He’s back doing easy rehabilitation running. He’s easing back into it, and we’re hoping he can be back by the WACC Championship,” Zirkelbach said. Zirkelbach named junior Alex Schleuning as someone who is doing well, and senior Noah Sohn Amalia Gray was a breakout star as a sophomore, reaching last year’s CIF State Championship.

Game Recap After Piedmont went threeand-out on the first possession, Saint Mary’s drove 43 yards on three plays to go up 6-0 with 8:40 left in the first quarter following a failed extra point conversion. On the next drive, Elmquist had a completion to Cory Minor while Elmquist also broke runs of five and 12 yards. However, PHS elected to punt on 4th-and-5 at their 35 yard line. After two trades of possession, Saint Mary’s drove to the 21 yard line, but Osman thwarted their series by nabbing an interception. The Panthers got the ball back with 11:15 to go in the second quarter, driving 33 yards to the end zone—making it 13-0 with 7:22 left. Piedmont’s next drive featured a 15 yard reception by Kaylani Spieckerman and a 10 yard carry by Elmquist, but the drive stalled out two yards past midfield at the St. Mary’s 38 with 26 seconds left in the half. In the third quarter, Osman had a critical takeaway by grabbing her second interception, this time jumping a route in the end zone with 4:34 on the clock. However, Piedmont’s offense punted after three plays, leading to another St. Mary’s score with 39 seconds left—19-0. The Panthers later forced a safety in the fourth quarter with 6:52 remaining in the game, 21-0. Piedmont got on the board late after just three plays. It featured Anjali Bowers recording a nine yard reception before Williams took a carry 25 yards to the house. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-1 overall) hosts Miramonte on Thursday, September 4 at 7:30 p.m. They also host Tennyson on Tuesday, September 9 at the same time. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s cross-country team returns to action this week at St. Mary’s College in Moraga on Saturday, September 6 at the St. Mary’s Invitational. They’ll compete with 31 other schools, with many teams from the North Coast Section. It’s shaping up to be a potentially strong season for the girls’ squad, led by returning runners, Leighton Mand and Amalia Gray. Both reached last year’s CIF State Championship. The Post named Mand its 2025 Sophomore of the Year following her cross country and track campaigns. She finished 74th of 201 athletes at the State Championship, while she was sixth of 127 at the NCS Championship. “Leighton is a cornerstone runner of the girls’ team. She’s consistent and competitive. She wants to work hard and race hard. She’s also shown she can look out for other members of the team,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. Gray was among last year’s breakout stars as a sophomore as well. She was 101st at State and finished 14th at NCS. Alongside Gray and Mand, Piedmont has a very strong group of eight runners who could all make an impact. Skylar Best enters her senior year, while sophomores Viviane Oesterer and Nikita Gorelik also made an impact in their debut in 2024. Senior Cora Chun, senior Mara Kemp-Malone, and junior Cora Brozowski Schrader are three runners who should help. “Skylar is a senior and one of our captains and Amalia went to the State meet last year. Viviane is a sophomore and was one of our top runners last year at the WACC Championship and North Coast. Cora Chun is another senior captain, Cora Brozowski Schrader is looking strong as well. Nikita had a really strong track season, I’m looking forward to her being in the running,” Zirkelbach said. In total, Zirkelbach sees a girls’ group who could potentially make it to State if all goes well. “The girls look very promising if everyone can stay healthy. They have a shot to possibly make it to the State meet,” Zirkelbach. The boys’ will have to go much of the season without star runner Sebastien Swain, who underwent surgery over the offseason on a lingering injury. He was our 2025 honorable mention for Athlete of the Year. the Post’s’ first boys’ sophomore to do so. Zirkelbach is hopeful Swain can recover in time for the 2025 Western Alameda County Conference Championship near the end of the season. “Sebastien had surgery early in the summer. He’s back doing easy rehabilitation running. He’s easing back into it, and we’re hoping he can be back by the WACC Championship,” Zirkelbach said.
