articles.text: JV offense gets ready for Salesian game with Offensive Coordinator Darnell Reed. Players are Jonah Cha-Foster, Gus Leonard, Max Watson, Aidan Shartsis, Kayode Zuberi, Cyrus Emanuelson, Jed Gilbert, Travers Kemp, Mason Gray, Ernie Hildreth, and Vaha Mafi. Photo by JC Curran Piedmont’s JV football team came away with a narrow 12-6 victory at Salesian Prep to open its season on Saturday, August 30 in Richmond. The team entered its season with 18 freshmen, eight sophomores, and three juniors who knew they had a lot of talent but hadn’t yet seen how it translated in a real game. Piedmont’s offensive line gave quarterback Jonah Cha-Foster enough time to find his receivers as he finished the game with two passing touchdowns, one to Mason Gray, and another to Mateo Long, who made a diving catch in the end zone for the catch. Cha-Foster finished the day with 100 passing yards, as well as another 40 yards on the ground. After a strong first half, Piedmont had a shaky start to the second half, giving up an onside kick which immediately resulted in a Salesian touchdown on a 40-yard carry. It seemed to cause some nerves from Piedmont after nearly relinquishing an onside kick, but the Pride was penalized for illegal touching. Piedmont went on a long drive on the ensuing possession but ultimately turned the ball over on downs at Salesian’s 12-yard line. When Salesian got the ball back, Piedmont forced a turnover on downs but failed to take advantage. With four minutes left in the game, Salesian regained possession. With two minutes left and Salesian threatening to score, outside linebacker Cyrus Emanuelson read the quarterback’s eyes to snatch an interception and secure Piedmont’s Week 1 victory. Additional key players in this game included running back-linebacker Vaja Mafi who had some explosive rushing plays on offense as well as some bruising tackles on defense. Tight end Jed Gilbert also had a good game securing a couple of catches and making effective blocks to help open up run lanes. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0 overall) travel to Middletown to take on the Mustangs this Friday, September 5, at 4:00 p.m. Photo by Alex Shartsis. JV Quarterback Jonah Cha-Foster flies for extra yards.
articles.title: JV Highlanders hold on to beat Salesian 12-6

articles.text: It was a difficult second match of the season for Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team, falling 7-0 to University in Golden Gate Park in San Francisco. Despite the one-sided score, Piedmont had some close matches throughout the day. No. 4 singles starter Arianna Kortum took University’s Lauren Connor to three sets, with each set only separated by two games or less. No. 3 doubles team Ella Thomasson and Chiara Silvo also took their match to three sets, while both of Kate Jumper’s sets at No. 2 singles were separated by two games. “We did have a few close matches. Arianna Kortum, and Ella Thomasson and Chiara Silvio each went to the deciding 10-point breaker, ”said coach Jim Landes. Thomasson and Silvo are both sophomores and new varsity starters. The duo played together as freshman last year. “Chiara and Ella played together last year. They play very well together. There’s a chance that they can move up in the lineup, but they are good at No. 3. Chiara has a nice serve and Ella can swing well too,” Landes said. The Highlanders look ahead to a match at Campolindo today, September 3, in Moraga. One day later they will travel to Dominican University in San Rafael to play Marin Academy. Match Results At singles, freshman Ella Ruthevin fell to Piper Lim at the No. 1 spot, 6-0, 6-0. Jumper fell in a close two-set match at No. 2 singles, 7-5, 6-4. Faith Chin lost 6-1, 6-2 at No. 3 to Nina Jayaraman, while Kortum fell in her three-set match, 7-5, 5-7, 10-8. At doubles, Samantha Huyhn and Emma Chan lost 6-2, 6-0 at the top spot to University’s Annabelle Allessio and Sophie McFadden. Maddie Tran and Inara Mehta lost 6-1, 6-3 at No. 2. Thomasson and Chiara Silvo battled to a three-set loss at No. 3 doubles, 6-4, 6-7 (7-5), 10-7. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-1 overall) visits Campolindo in Moraga today, September 3, at 3:30 p.m. They also travel to San Rafael to play Marin Academy at Domincan University on Thursday, September 5 at the same time. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team opened its 2025 campaign in strong fashion, winning three of five matches last week. They opened with a 3-1 loss to Head-Royce at home on Tuesday, August 26, but bounced back to beat San Leandro 3-2 in the Pirates’ home gym on Thursday, August 28. They also won two of three matches at the Highlander Varsity Tournament in its first year on Saturday, August 30. The tournament was played in a best of three sets (regular season matches are best of five). PHS defeated AIMS College Prep 2-0 and also swept Sonoma Valley 2-0, but lost in the championship game to Granada 2-1. Piedmont’s three wins matches their total victories last year. 2-1 to Granada It was a close three sets against Granada with each set finishing with a separation of five points or less. Piedmont won the opening set 25-20, but lost 25-21 in the second set. In the 15-point tiebreaker, Granada pulled off the 15-11 victory. Final stats were not provided. 2-0 over Sonoma Valley It was a dominant two sets for Piedmont, winning 25-15 and 25-14. The Highlanders recorded 11 kills in the first set on their way to the victory. Senior Mira Sachs powered down three spikes, while fellow senior captain Wilk had three as well. Fiona Olsen had one, while sophomores Izara Dando and Sofia Meyer had two. In the second set, sophomore Maika Ting took over with five kills. Dando, Meyer, and Wilk each recorded two. Final stats: Wilk had four Staff Photos Piedmont opened its season strongly with three wins in five matches. kills, Sachs had three, Ting had five, Olsen had one, Dando had four, and Meyer had four. 2-0 over AIMS College Prep Piedmont won their opening round match of the Highlander Varsity Tournament in quick fashion, holding AIMS to sub-10 points in both sets, winning 25-6, 25-9. Final stats: Jasmine Houlder had five kills, Ting logged four kills, Stokes had three kills and a block, while Olsen also had five kills. 3-2 over San Leandro San Leandro actually opened with two straight wins to go up 2-0, holding an opportunity to win the match. However, Piedmont went on the offensive, winning the final three sets 25-17, 25-19, and 15-12. Highlanders powered down eight kills in the start of their comeback in the third set. Ting too over the match in the fourth set, logging six of her 12 kills. In the final set, PHS was mightily efficient with their swings, notching 11 kills in the 15-point set. Final stats: Ting led with 12 kills, Wilk had eight, Olsen had three, Sachs had nine, Dando had six, Allyson Huyhn had two. 3-1 loss to Head-Royce All four sets against the Jayhawks also finished with each set finishing within a five-point gap. Piedmont opened with a 25-21 win, but lost three straight sets by scored of 25-20, 25-22, and 25-22. Final stats: Wilk had seven kills and one block. Ting had had nine kills. Olsen had six kills and two blocks. Stokes had four kills. Sachs had four kills and a block. Dando had 10 kills and two blocks. articles.text: Historic House and Gardens launch fall festivities Sept. 22 Fall activities are coming to Filoli this month. Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside ends its Summer Night events on September 18, and ushers in seasonal autumn festivities beginning September 22. Summer Night events include guided hikes on select evenings, live music and performances, a selection of rotating food vendors and after-hours estate access. Filoli closes its grounds at 5 p.m., but on Wednesdays and Thursdays through September 18, visitors can explore the historic house and gardens well into the evening. Located 30 miles south of San Francisco and nestled at the foot of the Santa Cruz Mountains, the scenery provides for an idyllic backdrop to view the setting sun on a pleasant summer evening. Filoli will then launch its popular lineup of fall activities, beginning with ‘Filoli Fall Tea’ on September 22. Guests are invited to a cozy afternoon tea seating in the serene Garden House, featuring seasonal ingredients and festive fall decor. A kid-friendly companion event, entitled ‘Witches Tea,’ begins October 3. Kids can snack on sweet treats and taste ‘bubbly brews’ while enjoying storytime readings. Accompanying adults get a complimentary drink with ticket purchase. The estate will revive its ‘Nightfall’ series of events on October 3, transforming the house into a haunted mansion and the gardens into a pumpkin-filled wonderland. These halloween-based events return after a successful launch last year. “Our Nightfall event offers a unique way to experience the enchanting beauty of Filoli after dark,” said Kara Newport, CEO and President of Filoli. “We look forward to welcoming families, couples, and friends to immerse themselves in this magical Halloween celebration.” Beginning October 18, estate guests will have the opportunity to taste harvested products from local vendors. A marketplace of artisans will be stationed in Filoli’s outdoor Woodland Court, where ticket holders can sample ciders, wines, handcrafted pies, jams and jellies and more. For more information and Summer and Fall activities, visit Filoli at https://filoli.org/. ®

articles.text: The 2025 World Arts West Dance Festival returns for its third and final weekend at Tunnel Tops in the Presidio in San Francisco this Sunday, September 7. The festival’s finale includes live dance perfor mances, hands-on workshops and family-friendly activities, and is free to attend. This year’s festival theme is “Dance as Health and Healing,” and features performances by Dimensions Dance Theater, one of Oakland’s most iconic Black dance companies, as well as Alleluia Panis/ KULARTS, which will present “Lakbai Diwa,” a Filipino diasporic spirit cultural ceremony and living dance prayer. The event concludes with a Haitian dance workshop hosted by Laurie Fleurentin, who will share the role of music and dance in Haitian culture. “This year we close the gap between artists and audience members where the public gets to create, move and sing right along with the artists,” Andréa Spearman, Associate Programs and Community Engagement Manager of World Arts West, said in a press release. “They get to leave with something tangible.” This is the fourth year the Presidio has hosted World Arts West, and this finale is expected to bring together a diverse community of attendees, artists, and families from across the Bay. “We are honored to welcome World Arts West back to the Presidio,” added Aya Tacdol, Community Partnerships Manager at the Presidio Trust. “The festival shares the richness of global dance traditions and reinforces our shared commitment to making the Presidio a welcoming, inclusive space for all.” The festival begins at 1 p.m. and concludes at 4 p.m. Advance registration is not required. For more information, visit https:// www.worldartswest.org/. Photo courtesy of World Arts West Alleluia Panis/KULARTS will present “Lakbai Diwa,” a Filipino diasporic spirit cultural ceremony and living dance prayer.

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is hosting an artist talk with Korean-Canadian playwright Ins Choi, director of the play Kim’s Convenience, on Thursday, September 11. Choi’s award-winning comedy drama Kim’s Convenience opens at American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) on September 18. The play is based on Choi’s experiences working at his own family’s convenience store, Kim’s Grocer, in Scarborough, Toronto, and follows family patriarch Mr. Kim as he faces a changing neighborhood landscape and the gap between his values and those of his Canadian-born children. Choi called the play a “love letter to his parents and to all first-generation immigrants who call Canada their home.” Kim’s Convenience debuted on July 6, 2011 at the Toronto Fringe Festival to wide critical acclaim and inspired a popular Netflix series of the same name. Choi, creator of the play and Artist Ins Choi the Netflix show inspired by it, will be in conversation with Pam MacKinnon, Artistic Director for American Conservatory Theater, in a limited-seating discussion. MacKinnon said she is “thrilled to be bringing Ins Choi, as playwright and actor, in his beautifully crafted and deeply personal prodigal son story Kim’s Convenience to A.C.T.” Seating is first-come, firstserved, and general admission ticket purchase is required. The event begins at 6 p.m. For more information, visit https://calendar.asianart.org/ event/artist-talk-with-ins-choi/.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum hosts talk with ACT director Ins Choi Sept. 11

By Allyson Aleksey Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside ends its Summer Night events on September 18, and ushers in seasonal autumn festivities beginning September 22. Summer Night events include guided hikes on select evenings, live music and performances, a selection of rotating food vendors and after-hours estate access. Filoli closes its grounds at 5 p.m., but on Wednesdays and Thursdays through September 18, visitors can explore the historic house and gardens well into the evening. Located 30 miles south of San Francisco and nestled at the foot of the Santa Cruz Mountains, the scenery provides for an idyllic backdrop to view the setting sun on a pleasant summer evening. Filoli will then launch its popular lineup of fall activities, beginning with ‘Filoli Fall Tea’ on September 22. Guests are invited to a cozy afternoon tea seating in the serene Garden House, featuring seasonal ingredients and festive fall decor. A kid-friendly companion event, entitled ‘Witches Tea,’ begins October 3. Kids can snack on sweet treats and taste ‘bubbly brews’ while enjoying storytime readings. Accompanying adults get a complimentary drink with ticket purchase. The estate will revive its ‘Nightfall’ series of events on October 3, transforming the house into a haunted mansion and the gardens into a pumpkin-filled wonderland. These halloween-based events return after a successful launch last year. “Our Nightfall event offers a unique way to experience the enchanting beauty of Filoli after dark,” said Kara Newport, CEO and President of Filoli. “We look forward to welcoming families, couples, and friends to immerse themselves in this magical Halloween celebration.” Beginning October 18, estate guests will have the opportunity to taste harvested products from local vendors. A marketplace of artisans will be stationed in Filoli’s outdoor Woodland Court, where ticket holders can sample ciders, wines, handcrafted pies, jams and jellies and more. For more information and Summer and Fall activities, visit Filoli at https://filoli.org/. articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s 103rd season opens this Friday, September 5 with the company’s annual opera ball, featuring Music Director Eun Sun Kim conducting Verdi’s Rigoletto. A revival of Verdi’s masterpiece is running September 5 through 27 at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco. Baritone Amartuvshin Enkhbat stars as the tormented titular character Rigoletto and Romanian soprano Adela Zaharia sings Gilda, with Yongzhao Yu making his San Francisco Opera debut as the Duke of Mantua. Mezzo-soprano J’Nai Bridges stars as Maddalena and bass Peixin Chen takes on the role of Sparafucile. The cast also includes Aleksey Bogdanov (Monterone), Stella Hannock (Giovanna), Olivier Zerouali, Samuel White, Jongwon Han, Caroline Corrales, and Elisa Sunshine. Jose Maria Condemi directs Rigoletto with sets inspired by the surrealist paintings of Giorgio de Chirico. Conductor and historian Jessica Bejarano will present an introduction to Rigoletto an hour before curtain at each performance. Music Director Kim will host a talkback after a September 21 matinee performance. San Francisco Opera’s annual ball, the company’s biggest fundraiser, kicks off the 2025-26 season on September 5, held at both City Hall and the War Memorial Opera House with proceeds benefiting the artistic initiatives of San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Opera Guild’s education programs. Guests will be greeted with a festive cocktail reception followed by a dinner crafted by local chefs served in San Francisco City Hall’s rotunda. The opening night performance of Verdi’s masterpiece Rigoletto closes out the evening. The opening weekend celebrations continue on Sunday, September 7 when Kim conducts the orchestra at Golden Gate Park, featuring stars from the fall season for the popular Opera in the Park concert, now in its 50th year. Opera subscriptions and single tickets for concerts this year are available at (415) 864-3330 and sfopera.com. Opera ball tickets may be purchased online at https://www.sfopera.com/seasons/opera-ball/. Photo by Gabrielle Lurie for the San Francisco Chronicle Eun Sun Kim conducts the orchestra at Golden Gate Park this Sunday.
articles.title: Free SF Opera concert in Golden Gate Park this Sunday

articles.text: Shotgun Players presents the world premiere of Christopher Chen’s The Motion, playing at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley on September 13. Obie Award–winner Christopher Chen, the playwright, blurs the line between performance and participation in his newest play The Motion, where a heated debate slips down a kaleidoscopic ‘rabbit hole’ engaging audience members as voyeurs and accomplices. Theater guests are given voting cards and are invited to take part in the experience as it happens on stage. The Motion is a unique play that entwines clever comedy, sharp dialogue, and science fiction to create a fractal pattern of moral dilemmas. “The Motion, which riffs on the debate format before spinning into different worlds, is one of the most ambitious plays I’ve written,” said Chen. “There’s a particular thrill when you feel yourself being swayed from one side to another then back again, because it feels like you’re activating the deepest part of your humanity,” he continues. “It’s like a Russian nesting doll. You open one and there’s another inside… It’s one surprise after another,” added Shotgun Players Director Patrick Dooley. “A dominant theme that emerges in this story aligns with others that are addressed in the season, which is, what it means to be human.” The cast includes Erin Gould as Moderator/Jack Donovan, David Sinako as Dr. Alan James, Erin Mei-Ling Stuart as Dr. Sarah Matthis, Soren Santos as Professor Neel Serrano and Gabrielle Maalihan as Professor Lily Chan. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https://shotgunplayers.org/show/the-motion/. Playbill cover for Christopher Chen’s The Motion, premiering on the Ashby Stage on September 13
articles.title: Shotgun Players premieres The Motion on Sept. 13

articles.text: Play leaves theater next Saturday San Francisco Playhouse’s production of My Fair Lady, based on the film adaptation of George Bernard Shaw’s 1913 play Pygmalion, leaves the theater next Saturday, September 13. Single-day tickets for showtimes Tuesday through Sunday are available online now. My Fair Lady originally premiered on Broadway in 1956, telling the story of Eliza Doolittle, a Cockney flower girl who is given speech lessons from Professor Henry Higgins, a phonetician, so that she may pass as a lady. The legendary original production received unanimous glowing reviews since its opening and won six Tony Awards, including Best Musical. It ran for 2,717 performances, the longest-running musical in Broadway history at the time. The musical features a beloved score including classic songs “I Could Have Danced All Night,” “Get Me to the Church on Time,” “Wouldn’t It Be Loverly,” “On the Street Where You Live,” “The Rain in Spain,” and “I’ve Grown Accustomed to Her Face.” The score of My Fair Lady was among the most successful ever to emerge from the American musical theatre with more than five million copies of the Broadway-cast recording sold. San Francisco Playhouse’s production is directed by Artistic Director Bill English, with music direction by Dave Dobrusky and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The ensemble in4cludes Jillian Smith as Eliza Doolittle and Adam Magill as Henry Higgins, with Julio Chavez, Heather Orth, Jill Slyter, Jura Davis, Kareem Jenkins and Andy Collins rounding out the ensemble. The show is on stage six days a week; Tuesday through Sunday. For showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/2024-2025-season/my-fair-lady/. The cast in San Francisco Playhouse’s production of My Fair Lady Photo by Jessica Palopoli
articles.title: Last chance to see My Fair Lady at SF Playhouse

articles.text: Piedmont native Tyler Joseph Ellis is starring in the Tony Award-winning musical comedy Shucked, with four weeks of performances scheduled in San Francisco. The show, which The Wall Street Journal calls “flat out hilarious,” will play at the Curran Theatre beginning September 9 with performances through Sunday, October 5, 2025. Tickets for all performances are on sale now at www.broadwaysf.com. The play is set in Cobb County, a town flanked on all sides by the corn fields of Somewhere, America. No one ever goes in or out of Cobb County, content as they are with their daily lives revolving around corn. When the corn fields start dying, however, the town’s way of life is threatened. In the face of this crisis, one brave young woman leaves the town and accidentally enlists the help of a con-man to save her hometown. Chaos and hilarity are sure to ensue. Shucked features a book by Tony Award winner Robert Horn, music by Grammy Award winning country musicians Brandy Clark and Shane McAnally, and directed by three-time Tony Award winner Jack O’Brien. “By the end of my run, I’ll have done it over 300 times,” laughed Ellis about his role in Shucked. Playing the role of Storyteller 2, Ellis acts as the charming narrator. Before he found himself performing eight shows in a week, Ellis got his start in Piedmont schools. He attended Wildwood Elementary School, where every 5th grade class put on a musical. Originally aiming for the role of the Sheriff of Nottingham, Ellis ended up as Robin Hood in the lead role. “It was a profound experience, as a fifth grader,” said Ellis. “I remember being in the bathroom, getting into costume and feeling so nervous but so alive.” Ellis next was in a Piedmont High School production of Oklahoma! in the role of “Slim.” Ellis credits Piedmont School staff with helping him find the passion that would later become his career. “In leaving Piedmont High School, you realize how lucky you had it,” said Ellis. “Piedmont School District and Piedmont High School has such a robust theater culture.” Ellis particularly appreciated PHS Theater Director Kim Taylor’s “state-of-the-art” acting classes and comprehensive theater curriculum. “Piedmont is a rare gift in terms of its focus on the arts, specifically the performing arts. I think the infrastructure, especially for a public school, is sort Tyler Joseph Ellis of unheard-of, and I give so much credit to the faculty and staff that keep it alive,” said Ellis. With his passion for performance ignited, Ellis pursued theater and entertainment wholeheartedly – including his representation of the Pacific Loon in the 50th Annual Leonard J Waxdeck Bird Calling Competition. Ellis graduated from the University of Southern California in 2020 with a major in Theatre and a minor in Marketing. When he’s not on a Broadway tour, his home base is New York City, where he balances a life of comedy content creation, writing, and acting for both stage and screen. Ellis has been featured in co-star roles for the first seasons of HBO Max’s “The Sex Lives of College Girls” and NetPhoto by Matthew Murphy and Evan Zimmerman Maya Lagerstam (left) as Storyteller 1 and Piedmont Native Tyler Joseph Ellis (right) as Storyteller 2 in the North American Tour of Shucked. flix’s “That 90’s Show.” He also co-wrote and starred in the short film “Co-Star,” which has just finished a film festival run and will be available to stream at home soon. One of Ellis’ more nervewracking roles was a July 2023 one-man show titled Tyler’s Quarter-Life Crisis, an autobiographical play about growing up in Piedmont and moving to New York to pursue theater. Ellis is currently writing a new musical comedy with composers Jacob Ryan Smith and Dan Mertzlufft entitled The (Disaster) Marathon of 1904. The show was selected as part of the 2024 New Musicals Lab, and won the third ever Broadway Shark Tank, which gives writers an opportunity to present their shows to a panel of industry judges. “To pursue theater, and to prioritize it in your life, doesn’t need to mean that it’s your entire life,” advised Ellis. “I think there’s a common misconception that if you’re going to be pursuing acting or theater that there is no room for anything else.” For young adults with a passion for acting and theater, Ellis offered some advice. “If you’re feeling it, follow that – because you don’t want to regret not having pursued something that interests you,” said Ellis. “...If you have a strong passion for something, don’t let anyone tell you that’s not worthy of pursuing, in any way, shape or form.” Audiences can see Ellis perform in Shucked for four weeks, September 9-October 5, at the Curran Theater. Tickets may be purchased at www.broadwaysf. com/events/shucked/. For more information on the play, visit www.shuckedmusical.com. Create, Learn, Code. Intro to Micro:bit Thursday, September 04 — 3:30 p.m. – 4:30 p.m. Join us for a free, four-week, hands-on workshop series this September and learn the basics of coding Microsoft MakeCode with the BBC micro:bit, a pocket-sized programmable computer. This program is for kids ages 7-12. We will explore fun, interactive projects each week while building real coding skills using Microsoft MakeCode (similar to Scratch). Space is limited, make sure to register online! Knitting & Crochet Circle with Susan Segal! Tyler Joseph Ellis as a freshman ay Piedmont High in a production of Oklahoma! Monday, September 08 — 11:00 a.m. –1:00 p.m. Join us every second and fourth Monday of the month for a delightful early afternoon of yarn, needles, and good company at our Adult Knitting & Crochet Circle! Settle into a warm and inviting space where creativity and conversation intertwine. If you need assistance with anything or have questions, Susan is here to help. Join us and make the most of your knitting/crochet experience with us! What to Bring: • Your current knitting or crochet project • Your preferred yarn and needles/hooks • A smile and a willingness to connect with fellow crafters Whether you’re a seasoned pro or just starting, everyone is welcome. While we’d love to accommodate everyone, keep in mind that space availability will be on a first-come, first-served basis. Birds of the East Bay - East Bay Regional Parks Presents Wednesday, September 10 — 2:00 p.m. – 3:00 p.m. Join us to explore the fascinating world of birds, from soaring raptors to tiny songbirds. Examine what they leave behind (with the option to dissect an owl pellet) and uncover their vital role in keeping ecosystems healthy. No live animals will be present. This program is tailored for kids (ages 5-12) but open to all! articles.text: Since the end of WWII, stories of quiet defiance and astonishing bravery have continued to surface, each one reminding us of the resilience of the human spirit. The Courageous Heart of Irena Sendler tells one such story. Set in German-occupied Poland, the film centers on the Warsaw Ghetto, a grim enclosure where 450,000 Jews were forced to live in crushing conditions. From there, families were deported by train, their destinations whispered to be “work camps” but feared to be something far worse — death camps. For many, that possibility was too horrific to grasp. Yet outside the ghetto walls, some refused to look away. Among them was Irena Sendler, a Catholic social worker who disguised herself as a nurse. This guise allowed her to slip past checkpoints, carrying with her not medicine but hope. At staggering personal risk, Irena organized an underground network that smuggled Jewish children out of the ghetto. She used forged papers, hidden exits, tunnels, sewers, even wheelbarrows and trucks. Each journey was fraught with danger, the threat of discovery constant. Perhaps the most heartwrenching task was convincing parents to let go. Irena had to persuade mothers and fathers that entrusting their child to a stranger was the only chance of survival. The weight of those moments — Anna Paquin in The Courageous Heart of Irena Sendler the tears, the fear, the impossible choice — is one of the film’s most powerful threads. Determined to preserve each child’s identity, Irena recorded their names and foster placements on scraps of paper, burying them in jars for safekeeping. She dreamed that parents who survived would one day be reunited with their children. Her mission did not go unnoticed. Near the end of the war she was betrayed to the Gestapo, arrested, and brutally tortured in Warsaw’s notorious Pawiak Prison. Though sentenced to death, she refused to reveal any names. Members of the Polish underground ultimately bribed her guards, and she was freed just before her scheduled execution. She spent the remainder of the war in hiding, continuing her work under a false identity. When the war was over, the true scale of her efforts emerged: 2,500 children rescued. Decades later, in 2007, Irena Sendler was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize — and in real life, she had already been honored in 1965 by Yad Vashem as one of the Righteous Among the Nations, Israel’s recognition of non-Jews who risked everything to save Jews during the Holocaust. The film honors her story with restraint and respect, reminding us that in humanity’s darkest hours, even a single, steadfast heart can make an immeasurable difference. articles.text: Martin Scorsese’s The Irishman is framed by memory and betrayal. At its center is Frank Sheeran (Robert De Niro), a truck driver who becomes a foot soldier for the mob and later a close ally of Teamsters leader Jimmy Hoffa (Al Pacino). The film, drawn from Charles Brandt’s 2004 book I Heard You Paint Houses, traces Sheeran’s life from chance encounter to lifelong entanglement, and finally to isolation in old age. The story opens in a rest home, with a long tracking shot leading to Sheeran in a wheelchair, white-haired and alone, speaking to someone off camera. From there, the narrative unfolds in flashbacks, beginning in the 1950s. Sheeran, hauling meat across Pennsylvania, meets Russell Bufalino (Joe Pesci), a seemingly benign older man who turns out to be a powerful mob boss. That meeting leads to Sheeran’s introduction to Hoffa, a friendship that will shape his life and tether him to the mob-union alliance. The film uses a road trip to Detroit as its spine. Sheeran and Bufalino, traveling with their wives, make stops along the way, each serving as a doorway into memory. These digressions show the mechanics of mob life: loans from the union’s pension fund, favors traded, silence enforced, and the euphemisms that stand in for violence. Sheeran himself becomes a man who “paints houses,” code for killing on command. What emerges is less a riseand-fall story than a study in loyalty and self-deception. Sheeran substitutes the mob for family, giving himself to an organization that promises brotherhood but is, at its core, transactional. Beethoven’s Piano Trio Op. 70, No. 2 , will close out the program with elegant interplay and bursts of playful energy revealing a masterpiece of chamber dialogue.

articles.text: The children’s classic Black Beauty, written by Anna Swell in 1887, has managed to endure for well over a century, and has been told and retold in books and on the screen. But note that the film I’m recommending in this review was released by Disney+ in 2020 and represents a complete reimagining of the story. Where the original narrative by Sewell is set in Dickensian Victorian England, and Black Beauty is a male mustang (voiced in the 1994 film by Alan Cummings), this most recent release flips the gender of Black Beauty now voiced by Kate Winslet. The story begins in the American West where the young colt (not yet named) roams free with her mother in the Onaqui Mountains of Utah. Free that is until some cowboys round up the wild horses, and in the process separate the youngster from her mother; the two never to be reunited. As it turns out, the young mustang catches the attention of horse trainer John Manley (Iain Glen) who takes her to a horse sanctuary named Birtwick. Though the horse likes Manley, it is nevertheless rebellious and uncooperative, trying the patience of the trainer. At the same time, Manley receives the tragic news that his sister and her husband have been killed in a traffic accident and he is asked to care for his young niece, Jo Green (Mackenzie Foy), Mackenzie Foy in Black Beauty a teenager. Though Jo makes it clear to her uncle that she is unhappy with the situation, and still grieving, the black mustang catches her attention, and wisely Manley puts the difficult horse in the care of Jo, asking her also to work in the stables. As it turns out, the horse (which Jo names Black Beauty) and the teen become close, recognizing that each has suffered an extraordinary loss. And so begins act two. To Jo’s distress, Manley tells her that because Birtwick is in need of money, Black Beauty may have to be sold. Jo makes a deal with the owner of the sanctuary that she will work extra hours and earn enough money to buy Black Beauty. Nevertheless, the horse is sold, and thus the setting of the film shifts dramatically from Utah to England. And so the story evolves: Jo searches for Black Beauty, and the horse ends up being sold several times, first to an upper class English family, to a farmer, then to a New York carriage driver. Meanwhile the Beauty and Jo yearn to be reunited and the search continues. As an aside, a version of Black Beauty was released in 1994 and would make for an interesting comparison. But note that the film I’m recommending in this review was released by Disney+ in 2020 and represents a complete reimagining of the story. Where the original narrative by Sewell is set in Dickensian Victorian England, and Black Beauty is a male mustang (voiced in the 1994 film by Alan Cummings), this most recent release flips the gender of Black Beauty now voiced by Kate Winslet. The story begins in the American West where the young colt (not yet named) roams free with her mother in the Onaqui Mountains of Utah. Free that is until some cowboys round up the wild horses, and in the process separate the youngster from her mother; the two never to be reunited. As it turns out, the young mustang catches the attention of horse trainer John Manley (Iain Glen) who takes her to a horse sanctuary named Birtwick. Though the horse likes Manley, it is nevertheless rebellious and uncooperative, trying the patience of the trainer. At the same time, Manley receives the tragic news that his sister and her husband have been killed in a traffic accident and he is asked to care for his young niece, Jo Green (Mackenzie Foy), Mackenzie Foy in Black Beauty a teenager. Though Jo makes it clear to her uncle that she is unhappy with the situation, and still grieving, the black mustang catches her attention, and wisely Manley puts the difficult horse in the care of Jo, asking her also to work in the stables. As it turns out, the horse (which Jo names Black Beauty) and the teen become close, recognizing that each has suffered an extraordinary loss. And so begins act two. To Jo’s distress, Manley tells her that because Birtwick is in need of money, Black Beauty may have to be sold. Jo makes a deal with the owner of the sanctuary that she will work extra hours and earn enough money to buy Black Beauty. Nevertheless, the horse is sold, and thus the setting of the film shifts dramatically from Utah to England. And so the story evolves: Jo searches for Black Beauty, and the horse ends up being sold several times, first to an upper class English family, to a farmer, then to a New York carriage driver. Meanwhile the Beauty and Jo yearn to be reunited and the search continues. As an aside, a version of Black Beauty was released in 1994 and would make for an interesting comparison. articles.text: The Indie Next List has fresh reading recommendations every month. Check out their newest iteration of hot-off-the-press works of literature, recently published by respected writers. This month has particularly interesting titles in the historical fiction and fantasy genres. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received praise from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small book store culture. This book has the lush fantasy and romance readers crave as well.” —Laura Kendall, Second Flight Books, Lafayette, IN folded into. There is a courage that exists in the ability to stay. It is brave to plant roots and dig into your people.” —Taylor Smith, Left Bank Books, St. Louis, MO A Truce That Is Not Peace Publishing, Memoir “In this brilliant memoir, Toews explores her grief and guilt about her sister’s suicide. As in her fiction, she balances profound sorrow with humor, reflecting the contradictions we all encounter as we traverse life.” —Nancy Sims-West, Raven Book Store, Lawrence, KS You Weren’t Meant to Be Human Saga Press, Horror “Andrew Joseph White’s adult debut is possibly his best book yet. articles.text: It was the hottest day of the summer as I pulled into Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena. The old carriage house housed the bottles for the charity auction and the winery tables were arranged around the green lawn under the shade of the old oak trees. This was my second time attending the annual Taste of Mt. Veeder event put on by the Mount Veeder Winery Association and I was excited to revisit some old friends and discover some new wineries. Nature wasn’t making it easy for the wineries to show off their new releases. The wines left out on the table tended to be too warm and the wines pulled from the ice buckets too cold, but the stouthearted vintners pressed on and at the end of the day I was excited to find some really great wines to write about. Mount Veeder is an American Viticultural Area (AVA) among the Mayacaymas Mountains west of Napa and Yountville. The mountain was named after Peter Veeder a Dutch Presbyterian minister who was one of the first non-natives to explore the area. The area has been producing wines since the 1860’s and is the only hillside appellation in Napa Valley that adjoins the cool, bayside Carneros, benefiting from the cooling influence of San Pablo Bay. Mount Veeder is an island of ancient seabed pushed up into a mountain surrounded by volcanic soils that typify the rest of Napa Valley. The rugged mountain terrain of extremely steep slopes above the fog, renders shallow topsoil and minimal water retention, resulting in tiny berries with intense flavor and concentration. The Mount Veeder AVA is small with only about 35 wineries producing 40,000 cases per vintage or about 1.3% of total Napa Valley production. This year’s Taste of Mt. Veeder event featured 26 wineries pouring their new releases. The following wines were the cream of the crop – the best of Mt. Veeder. • 2021 Yates Family Fleur de Veeder $80 Coming from a vineyard that has been continuously farmed since 1880 the Yates Family Merlot has an earthy nose with herbal notions over a core of cassis, plums and blackberries with hints of cedar and menthol. Quite mineral in the medium-bodied mouth it has soft tannins and just enough freshness, finishing long and earthy. Great job. • 2021 Mi Sueno Cabernet Sauvignon Lynne’s Vineyard $105 The deep garnet colored Mi Sueno Cabernet sashays out of the glass with provocative warm blueberry and raspberry scents with an undercurrent of violets and forest floor. The full-bodied palate is laden with fragrant black and blue fruits, framed by firm, finely grained tannins and seamless freshness, finishing long and perfumed. This wine should improve for up to two decades in the cellar. • 2022 Robert Craig Cabernet Franc Amenet Vineyard $118 Cabernet Franc is a grape that requires lots of sun to avoid being vegetal and Robert Craig has found the right spot on Mt. Veeder. The wine shows beautiful blueberry and cassis fruit, a cool, almost floral note, medium to full body and sensational purity and texture found in this big boned classic mountain wine. This is a beauty of finesse and restraint, yet intensity. Drink over the next 25 years. • 2023 Baker Canyon Cabernet Sauvignon $250 Only 300 cases of the wine were produced by this new winery at the northern tip of the Mt. Veeder appellation. The Baker Canyon Cab possesses an uncommonly dense black/purple color, and a sweet nose of licorice, underbrush, blackcurrants and toast. Amazingly extracted, yet somehow retaining its elegance, this wine offers the essence of black fruits in its long, rich, full-bodied flavors. There are Baker Canyon Winery is a new winery on Mt. Veeder The Taste of Mt. Veeder happened on the hottest day of the year

Veeder. The wine shows beautiful blueberry and cassis fruit, a cool, almost floral note, medium to full body and sensational purity and texture found in this big boned classic mountain wine. This is a beauty of finesse and restraint, yet intensity. Drink over the next 25 years. • 2023 Baker Canyon Cabernet Sauvignon $250 Only 300 cases of the wine were produced by this new winery at the northern tip of the Mt. Veeder appellation. The Baker Canyon Cab possesses an uncommonly dense black/purple color, and a sweet nose of licorice, underbrush, blackcurrants and toast. Amazingly extracted, yet somehow retaining its elegance, this wine offers the essence of black fruits in its long, rich, full-bodied flavors. There are enough acidity and ample tannin but the wine’s extraordinary purity and equilibrium are hallmarks of this smashing effort. (Not yet released.) • 2022 Grape Culture Cabernet Sauvignon Nosotros Vineyard $150 This was my first introduction to Grape Culture. The wine shows typical mountain fruit characteristics. On the nose you have lovely cassis, violets, plums plus hints of baking spices. Full-bodied and firmly structured, it is ripe, vibrant and wonderfully layered with lively, crunchy fruit and fine-grained tannins, finishing long. Great partner to a grilled ribeye steak. • 2021 Mount Veeder Cabernet Sauvignon Michael and Arlene Bernstein were the first to plant vines on Mt. Veeder when they established the Mount Veeder Winery in 1970. This wine continues their tradition of intense mountain-style Cabernet. Blended with a portion of Merlot to soften the tannins it offers a nose of cigar box, fragrant earth, cloves and chocolate over a core of blackberry and plums plus a touch of expresso. Medium-bodied and packed with intense black fruit, cedar and spice box flavors, it has good freshness finishing long and perfumed. Beautifully balanced it will last for decades in the cellar. • 2022 Rudd Crossroads Mountain Blend $90 Very deep garnet-purple colored, the Rudd Crossroads Mountain Blend leaps from the glass with vibrant black currant and cherry scents with touches of black pepper, sage and roses. The medium to full-bodied palate has a solid structure of firm, chewy tannins supporting the muscular fruit finishing with great freshness and plenty of latent depth. Give it another 2-3 years in the bottle and drink it over the next 30. • 2020 Mayacamas Cabernet Sauvignon $185 Mayacaymas is a historic and iconic winery that paved the way for others to explore Mt. Veeder. They have always made lean, structured Cabernets that can age for many decades. The 2020 is all red fruits, flowers, iron and leather. Firm tannins provide the backbone for a powerful structured Cabernet that is notable for its restrained intensity. Sweet floral notes appear on the finish adding lift and polish. This beautifully crafted classic mountain Cabernet needs at least 5 years in the cellar to show its true potential. • 2021 Brandlin Cabernet Sauvignon $110 Brandlin is a sister estate to Cuvaison in Carneros and is made there. The wine opens with aromas of plums, cherries and underbrush with touches of lavender, tar and truffles. Medium to full-bodied, plush, rich and seductive in the mouth, there is a lovely perfumed/spicy character that emerges in the long finish. • 2020 Sky Mt. Veeder Syrah $50 It was so nice to find a mountain-grown Syrah at this Cabernet dominated tasting. Sky is a venerable winery that has been around for a long time somewhat flying under the radar. The Syrah is youthfully dense with aromas of blackcurrants, leather and black pepper. The full-bodied palate is Baker Canyon Winery is a new winery on Mt. Veeder The Taste of Mt. Veeder happened on the hottest day of the year packed with blueberry fruit and its rounded tannins and mouthwatering acidity enliven its concentrated savory fruit and its long, latent finish. Medium to full-bodied, it is elegant, fresh, and very perfumed in the mouth with a firm, fine-grained structure and a long, spicy finish. • 2022 Hess Collection “The Lion” $225 This is a beautiful example of Mt. Veeder Cabernet Sauvignon with its blue and black fruits (raspberries, blueberries interwoven with honeysuckle). The wine has a wonderful, sweet kiss of delicate oak and forest floor. It is full-bodied and rich with supple tannins. It is a classic wine that is approachable, and frankly irresistible already, but promises to evolve gracefully for another 30 years. It is a blend of Sauvignon Blanc, Semillion, Viognier, Albarino, Riesling and Chardonnay. It is bright and sassy, layered with saline notes, lemon pith, chalk, and melon. articles.text: Among those participating in Wednesday’s Walk were Carolyn George, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Brenda Ferrero, Alicia Rivera, Karen Palmer, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Irene Thompson, Mark Davis, Tina Shum, Judy Love, Phil Witte, Stella Houston, Greg Slattoff, Peggy Shultz, Greg Keller, Pat Keller, Sherry Jacobs, Bonnie Sherwood with K-9 best friend Zippy, Mary Ann Barnes, Lori Austin, Helen Dong, Dave DeRoche, Mary Carter, Noemi Alvarado, Bill Ahern, Dan Scdoris, Albert Chen, Edith Lee, June Yee, and Dick Carter. The Walking on Wednesdays group had a good turnout of about 40 walkers and four K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday for their weekly walk. The City of Piedmont re-opened the Linda Pickleball courts in early August after resurfacing and marking them exclusively for pickleball. The courts are closed on Wednesdays so the walkers could inspect the courts without interrupting anyone’s play. Piedmont Recreation Department’s Liam Kelly was to meet them at the courts. The group went down Magnolia and up to the seldom traveled MacKinnon Place, a culde-sac. A hidden 110-foot set of about 48 steep stairs took them down to Arbor Drive. The group went up to Oakland Avenue and went down to Linda Avenue wot see the newly resurfaced pickleball courts. Liam Kelly asked the walkers if they could remember what the space had previously been used for. Dick Carter remembered playing softball on it as an elementary school student in the late 1950s. The site had also been basketball courts and most recently a pair of undersized tennis courts. The project was initially funded to be completed in 2023, and the popularity of pickleball exploded. Trials were conducted and temporary courts were set up at different locations, but the demand for pickleball was evident. How this demand could be met became a controversial issue. The Piedmont Recreation Commission made a recommendation to the City Council that the Linda Tennis Courts be converted into pickleball courts. This led to a lawsuit from neighbors who cited concerns about the noise associated with pickleball play and the impact on nearby residents. Accommodations and sound mitigation efforts have been made. The courts are open from 9 to 6 weekdays, 9 to 3 on Sundays, and closed on Wednesdays. There are no lights. Low-noise balls are provided in a large bin and there is a list of low noise rackets at the courts. There are no reservations needed and there are no fees. The Piedmont Public Works Department began the $60,000 project to reconstruct, resurface, and restripe the Linda Pickleball Courts in April. The project was originally expected to take two months, but there were delays in receiving court equipment. In addition, two trees whose roots were causing uneven court surfaces had to be removed. The transformation was a challenge, but the result is impressive. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.
articles.title: Wed. Walkers head to the courts

articles.text: So, it’s fall, 1959, and when you walk into your staid New England prep school English class for the first time, your teacher asks you to stand on your desk. You do. It’s both exhilarating and alarming. Is this higher learning? What in the world could come next? High school junior Todd Anderson finds out fast from John Keating, a new addition to the faculty, who, when he himself was a student there years ago, belonged to something called “The Dead Poets Society.” One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. This month’s selection is 1989’s Dead Poet’s Society, directed by Peter Weir and starring Robin Williams as the unorthodox teacher, Keating, and Ethan Hawke as his student, Todd. The school, Welton Academy, is an all-boys prep school known for its ancient traditions and high standards. A breath of fresh air, Keating uses unorthodox methods to reach out to the teenage boys, who face enormous pressures from their parents and the school. With Keating’s help, students Todd Anderson, his friend Neil Perry (Robert Sean Leonard) and others learn to break out of their shells, pursue their dreams and seize the day. The film received mixed reviews from critics, but it’s been an audience favorite for years. Attendees polled by CinemaScore gave the film a rare “A+” grade. Time Magazine said, “Williams, who has comparatively little screen time, has come to act, not to cut comic riffs, and he does so with forceful, ultimately compelling, simplicity,” and Pauline Kale said, “Robin Williams’ performance is more graceful than anything he’s done before. He’s totally, concentratedly here. He reads his lines stunningly, and when he mimics various actors reciting Shakespeare, there’s no undue clowning in it; he’s a gifted teacher demonstrating his skills.” Dead Poet’s Society will be screened on September 11 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 1:00 p.m. Sponsored by the Rec Department, the film series continues on the second Thursday of each month. Doors will open at 12:45. The event is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP is encouraged. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch.
articles.title: Dead Poets Society comes to Piedmont

articles.text: Organizations that provide adult recreational activities inside the city of Piedmont are invited to participate in the second annual Piedmont Adult Recreation EXPO. The EXPO will be held on Sunday, November 16, from 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Veterans Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue. This event will showcase recreational programs from the Piedmont Recreation Department, the Piedmont Adult School, the Piedmont Center for the Arts, and other organizations. Representatives will table at the event and explain to attendees how they can get involved in the different groups’ fall 2025 and winter 2026 recreational programs, activities, or classes. There is no fee to participate in or attend the EXPO. The event will be open to all adults, Piedmont residents and non-residents. Last year’s EXPO in November was highly successful with approximately 200 people participating. This community service event is being conducted by Piedmont volunteers. The event is supported by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the Piedmont Adult School, the Piedmont Center for the Arts, and a limited number of corporate sponsors. In 2023 an Older Adult Recreation Report concluded that there was a broad range of recreational opportunities available for older adults in Piedmont from many organizations, however people often were unaware of them or did not know how to get involved. The EXPO addresses this opportunity and increases adult participation in Piedmont recreation of many different types. Groups that provide recreation for adults within the city of Piedmont and want to participate in the EXPO should contact Lisa Gardner at lgardner555@gmail. com or Dick Carter camktgrp@ comcast.net to register or get more info. Patty Dunlap (right) the President of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation talks about the group during last year’s Expo. Last year’s Piedmont Adult Recreation Expo in Veteran’s Hall
articles.title: 2nd annual Piedmont Adult EXPO set for Nov. 16

articles.text: Noticing grey hairs on your furry friend’s muzzle? It could be time to switch up your care routine to better support the needs of an aging dog. While we can’t make them live forever, implementing a few key changes can help extend your canine companion’s golden years. This goes beyond just slowing down on walks; their medical and nutritional needs require some increased attention at this stage of life too. Be sure to consult with your vet to determine the best care for your senior pup. When your dog shows signs of aging, consider adjusting their diet. Senior dogs often become less active and lose body weight, so they need a boost from their food. Senior dog food typically contains higher percentages of fat, protein, and ingredients to support joint health and cognitive function. Prescription diets can also be life changing or even life extending for dogs with medical conditions. While they come at a premium cost, it is worth it to see the dramatic improvement in your dog’s quality of life. Dietary supplements can also be beneficial. Glucosamine and fish oil are two supplements that may improve the lives of senior dogs struggling with arthritis and hip dysplasia. These supplements can support mobility and joint health, reduce inflammation, and increase joint lubrication. Consider adding one tablet of glycoside or a pump of fish oil to your senior dog’s meals. Making your home more senior-dog friendly is an essential step. Consider providing an orthopedic bed for joint support and adding nonslip surfaces or paw stickers to prevent slipping. If your dog has poor eyesight, covering sharp corners with protective foam can help prevent accidents. Choose toys that are gentle on aging teeth. And finally, consider getting a ramp to help your large breed dog into your car while avoiding injuries to both dog and human from attempting to lift them. While your dog may slow down, exercise and mental stimulation remain crucial. Hydrotherapy can be a great way to provide exercise while soothing joint pain and maintaining muscle mass. Clipping nails regularly and avoiding steep inclines on walks can also help. Many dogs develop a stronger sense of smell as they age, so consider adding scent-based games to your routine like sniff mats or AKC’s Virtual Scentwork program. As your dog ages, you can significantly enhance their comfort and quality of life by tailoring their diet, supplements, home environment and exercise routine to be more senior-friendly. With love and patience, you can ensure that your furry friend’s golden years are filled with the same joy and companionship they’ve given you for so long. The joy, love, and care we felt today is what has kept the magic alive for 75 years and will carry Fairyland forward for 75 more,” said Morgan Rothenbaum, Fairyland’s Senior Director of Marketing & Communications. Fun knew no limits at the big celebration, Fairyland brought out Daisy the Clown to make balloon animals and dazzle children with a knee slapping performance blending balloon twisting, magic, and chaos at play. The Prescott Circus, who also performed at the Piedmont Food Fest, dazzled birthday party guests with a live show of acrobatics, juggling and clown antics at Fairyland’s Aesop’s Playhouse. “Tío Conejo’s Big Wish,” Fairyland’s first fully bilingual puppet show, drew enormous crowds at the Puppet Theater for the show’s premiere. Performances of the show will run daily at Fairyland until October 26 at 11 a.m., 2 p.m., and 4 p.m. The warm Oakland weather prompted many families to pack their own coolers, allowing them to stay hydrated and energized enough to chase toddlers up and down Alice’s Rabbit Hole. A truck with shaved ice also brought relief and sugar rushes to the masses of children at the birthday bash. The idea for creating a storybook theme park in Oakland began in 1948, when local nursery owner Arthur Navlet envisioned a place for children to play freely and safely in a world built just for them. With support from the Lake Merritt Breakfast Club, Oakland Parks Superintendent William Penn Mott Jr., and a dedicated group of community members, the dream for Children’s Fairyland took shape. On September 2, 1950, Children’s Fairyland opened as the first storybook theme park in the country. The park’s winding paths, whimsical handcrafted sets, rides, theatre space, and focus on imaginative play were so influential that Walt Disney himself visited the park while planning the creation of Disneyland. All the details were covered and highlighted in gold on the afternoon, the paint was bright, the balloon arches were enchanting and kids got to take home goodie bags containing yoyos, mini-whoopie cushions and magic bottles of bubble solution. Instantly the water is saturated with blood as she tumbles against the bottom, hitting sharp coral and rocky sand. In 2014, Ragones and Piedmont Makers partnered with Piedmont Schools to hold the first Piedmont School Maker Faire, which has become a beloved community event to showcase STEAM education and community projects. PUSD was the first school district in the nation to host an official K-12 School Maker Faire in partnership with Maker Education, providing a template for other schools to follow in Piedmont’s footsteps. Piedmont Makers has since become a driving force behind the growth in robotics education in Piedmont, with the program expanding from a single high school robotics team of ten kids in 2015 to 125 robotics teams with over 900 kids. “It’s always rewarding to be able to meet so many different families and kids that are in the program, and see kids that started ten years ago that are now graduating and doing engineering, and pursuing STEM careers in college and beyond,” said Ragones. Continuing this dedication to education, Ragones and Piedmont Makers helped PUSD on a fundraising campaign in 2020 for the new Engineering Lab in the school STEAM building, raising $420,000 to outfit the lab with world-class equipment. The Engineering Lab was up and running in January 2022, providing a capstone facility for teachers, students, and the world championship-qualifying Highlander Robotics Team. Ragones was honored by the Piedmont Unified School District for his impact on local education as the recipient of the 2023 Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award. “All-in-all it’s been a great experience,” said Ragones. “and I’m not going anywhere – I’m still on the board, I’m still the treasurer, so I’ll continue to give back in that way.” In addition to Piedmont Makers, Ragones has also served on the board of the Piedmont Baseball/Softball Foundation, as well as on the board of the Piedmont Education Foundation. He is a long-time Piedmont youth sports coach for baseball, soccer and softball, and has built a 25-year career in technology working for companies such as Salesforce and NVIDIA. The final act returns to Sheeran in care, reflecting on a life hollowed out. Hoffa is gone. Bufalino is gone. His peers are dead or imprisoned. His daughters have vanished from his orbit. What remains is a man talking into silence, telling his story not to friends or family but to strangers, and perhaps to investigators. Regret creeps in, though even here it seems partial, muted, as if the habit of denial never left him. Scorsese has often examined worlds defined by violence and codes that stand outside the law — Mean Streets, Goodfellas, Casino. The Irishman belongs to that lineage but feels more like a coda. Its characters are driven forward without reflection, their choices narrowing until only loss remains. Notably, women appear only at the edges, representing bonds that are ignored or abandoned. Family exists, but it is repeatedly set aside for business. The performances carry the story’s weight. De Niro gives Sheeran an unassuming surface that conceals the choices he makes. Pacino embodies Hoffa with volatility and conviction, while Pesci, long associated with explosive roles, plays Bufalino with restraint that is all the more chilling. Together they anchor a film that spans decades and shows the cost of living by a code that erases the individual. The Irishman runs three and a half hours but never drifts from its course. It is both expansive and intimate, a story of power and corruption told through the life of one man who mistook obedience for belonging. In the end, the story is not about the mob, or even Hoffa, but about the solitude left behind when loyalty proves empty. The Irishman. Directed by Martin Scorsese. The Shallows is a taut thriller, absent any dialogue to speak of. What that means is that all that is emotive about this nicely drawn film depends on the considerable ability of Lively, who must now endure a long, cold night while ever aware that with the arrival of high tide in the morning her place on the rock will gradually become more and more precarious. Being in the water, even the shallows, will mean all but certain death. As the sun sets she waits and shivers in the dark and grimaces from the pain of not only her severe leg injury, but countless coral cuts and abrasions. Lively’s performance is spot-on as the camera tightly follows her tenacious attempt at resisting a mind numbing panic, fighting to be resourceful and brave. Her expressions, the clench of her jaw, the look in her eyes, the pep talks she gives herself saturates her situation with an abiding verisimilitude. The role also required a tour de force of demanding athleticism. Clearly, The Shallows is an adrenaline-inducing movie that will grip you from the moment you reach for that first handful of popcorn until the end credits. That nudging, nascent feeling of dread builds, ultimately filling every frame and becomes unrelenting. The Shallows. Directed by Jerome Collet-Serra. articles.text: Dear PUSD Families & Staff: As we begin a new school year, I am thoughtful about recent initiatives that reflect our district’s commitment to supporting students’ growth—both academically and personally. I have been observing the implementation of the new mobile device policy, especially at our high schools, and I want to complement our students on their effort to follow the new policy, which limits use of mobile devices (cell phones and all devices that connect to the internet). My observations at brunch and passing periods where cell phone use is now restricted indicate that students are not using devices. In fact, I have not really seen a lot of use at lunch either. Thank you to our students and staff for implementation of this new policy. I will be gathering feedback from students, staff, and parents this fall about the effectiveness of the new policy, particularly on students’ sense of wellness. I also want to encourage parents with children in elementary and middle school to explore the Wait Until 8th campaign [at WaitUntil8th.org] which encourages families to delay giving children smartphones until at least 8th grade. We recognize there may be a need for some cell phone access at the high school level; however, research indicates that waiting until at least 8th grade benefits children’s mental health, improves sleep, and creates space for students to build stronger face-to-face relationships, all of which support stronger academic achievement. As a community, we can help reduce the social pressure on students to be online too soon and instead encourage meaningful human connections. In Partnership, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent AC Bus Route Service – Please Consider Writing a Letter Thank you to the students and parents who took our survey two weeks ago and who wrote to AC Transit officials to restore Bus 33 service to upper Piedmont. To those surveyed families, I recently sent out an opportunity to write to AC Transit to restore service. If you would like to join in this letter-writing effort, we could use your help to advocate for this critical transportation need. Linked [below] is information to assist you in sending a letter via email to the AC Transit staff and Board. Docs.google.com/document/d/120iauuCe2mJkpRM8PI16E1sDEtpYoO3YbEs_JcSds0E/ edit?tab=t.t0g81pkp30oh. We believe advocacy from our PUSD community can make a difference in calling attention to this important matter and potentially leading to the restoration of bus service to upper Piedmont. Take a look at Canva.com/design/ DAGul8Pir8Y/DXJSDet8l_CFIi9N_6BA6g/edit Thanks to Jay Russell and our administrators for their help in taking these amazing photos of our students, staff, and families. articles.text: Editor: In my opinion, the state legislature should not have viewed the solution to our housing shortage based on individual cities. A regional approach to this problem is far more rational. It is my understanding that no consideration was given to the available space that each city has to accommodate new high density housing. In the case of Piedmont, the only available open sites are our very limited parks and recreational fields. I think we should pursue having the state legislature have a carve out for cities, such as Piedmont, instead of having to sacrifice or precious, open green space of which we have so little. Our city officials and the citizens at Piedmont need to contact our state legislators. It’s obvious that in recent years we have seen a tremendous number of residential housing units built in Oakland and Berkeley, San Leandro and Hayward, El Cerrito and Richmond, which have the open space needed to accommodate this high density housing. Some people prefer living in a high density housing situation. I am not one of them, and I don’t think most people in Piedmont are either. Putting 160 units in Blair Park is an absolute abomination. This project will change the whole feel of the Morgen Canyon. Na is an obscenity. This is a natural green corridor and should be preserved forever and not degraded in order to comply with a poorly thought out housing mandate from the State of California. This particular site gets very little natural sunlight. Moraga Avenue of course is a major thoroughfare for emergency access and egress from the hills should there be another fire, and this will be significantly compromised . The Coaches Field location is at least a little bit more removed and we’ll have less of an impact on the canyon because of this. It is also a more expensive project which would make it less likely to be built Again, I think we need our city officials to pursue the idea that to carve out for cities that have no open space, parks and green belts should be off limits. A regional approach to this problem is far more rational. It is my understanding that no consideration was given to the available space that each city has to accommodate new high density housing. In the case of Piedmont, the only available open sites are our very limited parks and recreational fields. I think we should pursue having the state legislature have a carve out for cities, such as Piedmont, instead of having to sacrifice or precious, open green space of which we have so little. Our city officials and the citizens at Piedmont need to contact our state legislators. It’s obvious that in recent years we have seen a tremendous number of residential housing units built in Oakland and Berkeley, San Leandro and Hayward, El Cerrito and Richmond, which have the open space needed to accommodate this high density housing. This project will change the whole feel of the Morgen Canyon. Na is an obscenity. This is a natural green corridor and should be preserved forever and not degraded in order to comply with a poorly thought out housing mandate from the State of California. articles.text: I recently lost a ring. It was a simple gold band with small ridged edges. It was my mother’s original wedding band, She had given it to me at the beginning of my sophomore year of high school. In other words, that simple golden ring had been with me on my pinky finger for the majority of my life in high school. Any time I felt myself becoming anxious before an exam, nervous before a tennis match, or even when I was just fidgety, I would start to twirl the ring that sat on my pinky finger. The ridged edges would contrast the smoothness of the band itself, and I would become grounded in the feeling of twisting it around my finger. Facing ever-changing friend groups, failed assignments, choir rehearsals, late night froyo runs with my best friend, and even the death of my grandmother, my mother’s ring was on my finger. In essence, while the world around me failed to stay consistent, the ring on my finger never changed. Its weight was a reassurance for whatever I faced next. It had traveled with me around the world and back. From Edinburgh, Scotland to Cancun, Mexico to Tahoe City, California. Through customs, airports, airplanes, hotels, bus rides, cab rides, museum explorations, dinners by the beach, roller coasters, and so many other experiences, the ring stayed firmly on my finger. I leave for college in five days. The thought that the ring wouldn’t come with me hadn’t even entered my mind — why would it? The ring had gone everywhere with me, what was one more adventure? In my panic to find the ring, I realized my panic wasn’t solely about misplaced jewelry, but instead a projection of my fear of leaving for college. It was the fear of change; change on such a monumental level. The next four years of my life would be spent nearly 5,120 miles away from home. The ring would be a reminder of home, of my family. This fear kept me tossing and turning in the stale air of my bedroom most of the night. As much as I want to go to college and experience what many label as “the best four years of their life,” I have to admit that I am scared. I have spent 18 years in the same house, in the same room, surrounded by the same people talking about the same things. The fear of starting over is strong and can be paralyzing. But the fear of not trying my best to make the most of my brand new start is stronger still. Ring or no ring, I am going to college. And while I consider myself to be deeply superstitious (irrational), and just slightly religious (rational), I briefly took the ring’s disappearance as a bad omen. That line of thinking came from the superstitious part of me, but the religious side tells me the loss of a material item doesn’t translate to something bad happening. I now find myself faced with a dilemma. I can either remake the ring with unused gold jewelry from my mother, or I can just move on. The rational part of my brain tells me that there are so many material things that remind me of home that I can’t take with me to college. For example, the flickering street lamp on Hagar Ave where my best friend and I watched the sunset, or the cutting boards that had Slavic imagery on the backs that my mother would use when she cooked, or even the painting hanging on my wall of an antique Italian car race advertisement that my father got for me. There are so many things that I can’t take with me; I can only take their memory and their significance, knowing they are waiting for me to come back home. But I have the opportunity to take the ring with me, even though I know it won’t be the one I had. So the new question is, do I remake the ring and take the familiar weight on my pinky with me to college, or do I go to college and start anew without its company? I think only Plato has an answer. But unfortunately for me, he is long dead and I don’t speak Greek. To channel some of my own philosophy, I say that this decision is inconsequential. Compared to what I will one day inevitably be faced with, this is child’s play. In six months my life will be so drastically different this decision won’t matter. So I say, a ring is just a ring. Whatever memories I had with it aren’t exclusively tied to that piece of gold. They exist in my mind. And if I remake the ring, it’s because I miss the jewelry itself and not the made-up significance in my mind. While I didn’t end up remaking the ring, I admit I did buy a replacement. I will never forget my mother’s wedding band and its comforting presence throughout the highs and lows of high school. But the new ring serves as a clean slate, ready to experience new adventures – and new memories. Larissa Edel has been a contributing writer with the Post for six years and soon will begin college at University of St. Andrew’s in Fife, Scotland.
articles.title: Ringing in a new chapter

articles.text: The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has published a Draft Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for an upcoming Pacific Gas & Electric (PG&E) power-line replacement project. To provide information about the proposed project, CEQA process, and provide an opportunity to submit verbal comments, the CPUC will hold two virtual meetings on Wednesday, September 3, at 2:00 p.m. and at 5:00 p.m. The Draft EIR evaluates potentially significant adverse environmental impacts that could be associated with the Project and identifies project components, mitigation measures, and project alternatives that would avoid, reduce, or eliminate significant impacts. The EIR ends its 45-day comment period on Friday, September 26. Officially called the “PG&E Moraga-Oakland X 115 Kilovolt (kV) Rebuild Project,” the proposed project is a maintenance project intended to replace older existing 115 kV power line equipment that has reached the end of its useful life. Upon completion of construction, the structures currently in place would be replaced with more fire-resistant structures and conductors. Citizens may attend the virtual meetings on September 3 with the following Zoom links: • 2 p.m. - https://us02web.zoom. us/j/84794642276 • 5 p.m. - https://us02web.zoom. us/j/89981865478 Project Background The proposed project involves upgrades to approximately five miles of overhead 115 kV power lines between Moraga and Oakland X substations in the City of Orinda, unincorporated areas of Contra Costa County, and the cities of Oakland and Piedmont A map shows the length of power line to be replaced in the proposed plan. within Alameda County. The project seeks to rebuild the four overhead lines into four hybrid lines, with both overhead (about 4 miles) and underground (about 1 mile) segments. Existing towers, poles and conductors would be replaced either with overhead rebuild or underground components, and minor modifications would occur within the existing substations. Some recently replaced power line structures would be reused or reused with some modification. The CPUC is the lead agency responsible for environmental review of the project in compliance with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). According to the CPUC, the operation of new overhead and underground power lines in this project would reduce the risk of wildfire compared to existing conditions. Written comments may be submitted for inclusion in the final EIR via email at MOX@ aspeneg.com before September 26. Comments should reference the Moraga-Oakland X Project, A.24-11-005. Before including an address, phone number, email address, or other personal identifying information in their comment, residents should be aware that their entire comment will be placed in the Project file and shall become part of the public record. Comments are also posted online as part of the public record. The CPUC cannot approve requests to withhold contact information from the public record. articles.text: The Piedmont Planning and Building Department hosted an open house on Thursday, August 21, at the Veterans Hall to inform community members on a variety of projects related to housing development, sustainability, and wildfire resilience. The event had five informational stations with displays with information on multiple policy development initiatives, allowing residents to drop in throughout the event and learn how they can provide input on projects before decisions are made. At each station, attendees were able to speak directly with City staff, ask questions, and get more information about project timelines and opportunities for input. Featured projects included: • Moraga Canyon Specific Plan: A comprehensive plan for developing city-owned land along Moraga Avenue into a new neighborhood featuring affordable and market-rate housing, road safety improvements, and an expanded Coaches Field. • Objective Design Standards: Clear, measurable design rules that will govern new residenSenior Planner Pierce MacDonald (left) answers a resident’s questions at the Open House last Thursday. • • tial construction, including accessory dwelling units and SB9 developments. Streamlined Business Permitting: Proposed zoning updates that will allow certain types of businesses to open through a ministerial process, avoiding a lengthy public hearing process. Building Electrification Strategy: A roadmap for how the City can support residents to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from their homes by replacing gas appliances with clean, electric alternatives. • Building and Fire Code updates: Local amendments to state building codes to support wildfire-resistant construction and update Piedmont’s energy efficiency “Reach Codes.” “[Residents] should definitely subscribe to the planning and building newsletter, because we do send out monthly newsletters telling people about every ongoing planning and building project,” said Senior Planner Gopika Nair.
