articles.text: On Monday, September 1 Children’s Fairyland turns 75 and will celebrate with a full day of family fun from 10 a.m.- 4 p.m. The Labor Day event will feature performances by DJ Lance Rock, Prescott Circus, Daisy the Clown, with hands-on activities, interactive art, a brand-new bilingual puppet show, giveaways, special guests, and a parade through Oakland. “This isn’t just a birthday party, it’s our love letter to the generations of families that have supported Children’s Fairyland,” said Kymberly Miller, CEO of Fairyland. “For 75 years, Fairyland has been a place where kids and families fall in love with storytelling, make cherished memories, and feel safe to play, explore, and connect. This celebration honors our past, reflects on our growth, and opens a new chapter in Fairyland’s story.” The 75th Birthday Party kicks off at 9:30 a.m. with a Parade to the Birthday Party, co-hosted by BART and Fairyland. Starting at the 19th Street BART Station, the parade winds its way to Lake Merritt and ends at the Fairy Gates. DJ L a nce Ro ck , t he Emmy-nominated host of the hit Nick Jr. Series “Yo Gabba Gabba!,” brings his signature mix of music, storytelling, and dance to Fairyland’s Festival Stage. He’ll perform live twice, at 1:00 p.m. and 3:00 p.m., each followed by a meet and greet. Learn more about DJ Lance Rock at www. djlancerock.org. The birthday party will also premiere “Tío Conejo’s Big Wish,” Fairyland’s first fully bilingual puppet show based on a folktale from Cuba. The show will run through October 26, with daily performances at 11:00 a.m., 2:00 p.m., and 4:00 p.m. A live show by Prescott Circus at noon featuring Oakland youth performers showcasing acrobatics and juggling. A bubble-filled performance by Daisy the Clown at 2:30 p.m., blending balloon twisting, magic, and playful chaos. Daisy is a beloved performer known for creating interactive and creative fun for kids of all ages. Puppet Playdates with Quercus, Fairyland’s fuzzy mascot, occur at 11:20 a.m. and 2:20 p.m. Children’s Theatre interactive performances of “Teddy Bear’s Wish” start at 11:30 a.m. and 12:30 p.m. Plenty of activities, including interactive art stations, a giant birthday card for Fairyland, a community-painted mural, a Birthday Adventure Passport activity, where kids collect stamps after completing activities and prompts, then turn it in for a limited-edition 75th anniversary button. All kids will take home special goodie bags. On September 2, 1950, Children’s Fairyland opened its gates as the country’s first storybook theme park, built specifically for young children. Fairyland quickly became a cherished part of Oakland’s identity and cultural landscape, igniting imaginations, shaping childhoods, and inspiring countless theme parks around the world. The idea for creating a storybook theme park in Oakland began in 1948, when local nursery owner Arthur Navlet envisioned a place where children could play freely and safely through a world built just for them. With support from the Lake Merritt Breakfast Club, Oakland Parks Superintendent William Penn Mott Jr., and a dedicated group of community members, the dream for Children’s Fairyland took shape. Since then, Fairyland has remained a cherished part of Oakland’s cultural landscape, attracting nearly 200,000 visitors annually to explore the park’s 10 acres. Over the years, it has grown to include cultural celebrations, literacy programs, puppet education, summer camps, and one-of-a-kind performances that reflect the diverse cultural heritage of the Bay Area. The park has remained true to its roots over the decades, providing hands-on, screen-free experiences that inspire imagination, creativity, confidence, and a lifelong love of learning. Buy tickets in advance at Fairyland.org Celebrate 75 years of Fairyland on Labor Day, September 1.
articles.title: Children’s Fairyland celebrates 75th birthday on Labor Day

articles.text: Piedmont Makers has kicked off another exciting STEAMfilled year, with over 900 K-12 kids participating in youth robotics this fall, a 20% increase over 2024. While Piedmont remains the largest participant, the most dramatic growth occurred in neighboring communities, with Oakland registrations jumping 16% and Berkeley increasing its participation by 44%. The FIRST LEGO League Challenge division for older students (4th-8th grade) led the surge with nearly 40% growth from 257 to 350+ participants, demonstrating both strong community appeal and the magnetic pull of hands-on STEM education that extends far beyond Piedmont’s borders. This year will mark a change in leadership, as long-time co-founder Dave Ragones stepping down from the presidency. While continuing to participate as Treasurer, Ragones leaves an indelible mark as co-founder and leader of the Piedmont Makers. Ragones’s efforts are well known within the community, as highlighted by PUSD’s recognition in 2023, honoring Ragones with the Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year award. Ragones was an instrumental force in helping to create the now well-established School Maker Faire in 2014, fundraising for the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab in the Piedmont High School STEAM building, and growing the FIRST youth robotics program in Piedmont from a single team to one of the largest youth-serving organizations in Piedmont and beyond. articles.text: From therapy sessions to healthy snacks, the PUSD Wellness Center plays a vital role in student well-being. This year’s fundraiser will help ensure these services remain free and accessible for Piedmont middle and high school students. The Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) Wellness Center has officially launched its 2025 fundraising campaign, aiming to raise $50,000 to continue providing essential mental health services to Piedmont’s middle and high school students. This year’s campaign is off to a strong start thanks to lead donors Tom Snyder and Anne Bisagno, who opened the campaign with a $10,000 contribution. Their early support sets the tone for a community-wide effort to ensure the PUSD Wellness Center can maintain its current level of care. The Wellness Center (WC) is a vital resource for Piedmont High School, Millennium High School, and Piedmont Middle School students, offering therapeutic support for challenges such as stress, anxiety, depression, grief, conflicts, and substance use concerns. During the 2024–2025 school year, one in three students at Piedmont and Millennium High Schools and one in four at Piedmont Middle School visited the Wellness Center. Last school year, WC therapists provided more than 2,000 therapy sessions, while over 150 students received ongoing, individualized support. The Center also offered more than Staff photo Wellness Center therapists Emily Goodwin (left), Kimmy Demkovich and Umara Hansen, Wellness Center co-founder Brooke Zimmerman and Wellness Center therapist Jen Blau 3,500 healthy snacks to students, provided practitioner training led by top mental health experts, and remained a trusted place for both scheduled and drop-in care. “The availability of a free, on-campus Wellness Center is an essential resource for our students,” said School Board President Lindsay Thomasson. “It removes significant barriers to accessing mental health care, including the difficulty of finding an available provider, scheduling appointments, and managing outof-pocket expenses.” The Wellness Center operates on a minimal budget, with community donations funding critical staff stipends, program supplies, and student support activities. Every contribution, large or small, helps support this safe space for Piedmont students to seek support and build resilience. While she may have given up the 8:00-3:00 in-class schedule, her passion for art, teaching, life, and language typifies the saying: once a teacher, always a teacher. Bjork started teaching in 1990, in the inaugural year of Teach for America, through which she took a position teaching Spanish at a middle school located in North Carolina. With mixed emotions she recalled the chaos of the program before it became an established institution. “There were about 32 of us [teachers in North Carolina], and we had a two bedroom apartment, so we were all sleeping on the floor,” said Bjork. Many of the schools initially contracted with Teach for America had budgets that dried up, and so Bjork considered herself lucky to get a contract with a school early on, and a ticket out of the crowded apartment. Her willingness to adapt allowed her to teach many different subjects including 7th grade Language Arts and Reading and Special Education in the 2004-05 year. Bjork then taught middle school Spanish until 2016, before switching to teach her first passion, Art. Her final teaching post took her to Piedmont High School as the Ceramics and Art 1 teacher. “I loved that, and it was really fun to work with older kids and, [take on] new challenges,” she said. “At the middle school we were balancing adolescent growth and really prioritizing the whole child in that way. I loved the challenge of [switching to PHS Art]. I loved having that opportunity to really work at something that I’m passionate about,” she said. Bjork found a friend at PHS in the Art department, Gillian Bailey, whom she called, “the most A ceramic piece by Hannah Bjork Hiking in Oregon in July this summer Student art from Bjork’s Gnome project. fantastic art teacher that I’ve ever known.” “[Gillian] and I had a lot of fun, lots of good jokes, a lot of good times, and we’ll stay friends. I know that for a fact; we still are,” said Bjork. Bjork, continues to keep in touch with former students as well. This summer in Maine she visited a former Piedmont 6th grade student, now a midwife and mom of two. Bjork’s future plans include gardening, baking her famous cakes and lots of travel with beloved husband Bob Shireman. “We’re going to Germany. We’re going kayaking on the Columbia River with a travel group and probably going back to Mexico,” she said. Travel for her husband’s job will also take the couple to New York, Washington D.C., Los Angeles and Colorado, all before the winter holiday. articles.text: Piedmont football returns this Saturday with a season-opening game at Salesian. Piedmont football is back this Saturday, August 30 with an opening game at Salesian in Richmond to kick off its 10-game season. The Highlanders return after going 10-2 in 2024 with a senior-laden squad that won its first North Coast Section game since 2017. It sought its second straight Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division title and won its third league banner in as many years. “We’re still in the middle division with Hayward and Newark Memorial. It’s going to be a physical year just like it was last season. Hayward brings a similar team but is new in some spots. They are already talking a lot,” said Piedmont coach Jordan Seiden. Piedmont lost 16 players to graduation in the Class of 2025, requiring obvious overhauls to both offensive and defensive units. “15 of those 16 players were two-way starters. Now it’s a whole new cycle. We’re doing a lot of teaching like we did the first couple of years. It’s a young group, but they are going to be good,” Seiden said. For a fourth year, Piedmont will have a Lagios at quarterback wearing No. 4. This time, sophomore Jimmy Lagios steps into the starting role following the graduation of his older brother, Markos. Incoming quarterback Jimmy Lagios talks things over with coach Jordan Seiden. Rehan Mumtaz carries the ball in running back drills at practice. Staff Photos “Jimmy had a great year on JV, we want to see his growth and development. As that’s happening, he’s going to be a huge part of anything we’re able to do. It’ll look differently offensively. He’s not as mobile as Markos was, but he’s a natural smooth thrower. Same number, they look alike, but he’s taller. They are different and similar at the same time,” Seiden said. On offense, PHS must replace starting running back Tommy Ashton and star receiver Sam Shelby, an honorable mention for the Post’s Athlete of the Year award. At running back, Piedmont could have a formidable threeheaded monster with Xavier Henderson, Colby Hong, and Rehan Mumtaz. Hong and Henry Brennan will also fill into the inside linebacker spot vacated by Ashton, while Henderson will continue at linebacker as well. Jack Meyjes and Dash WatersWorthen will take the lead at receiver, Meyjes will also play defensive back. “Xavier is one of our more vocal leaders. We also need Colby and Henry to be the quarterbacks of our defense and be vocal. That leadership will manifest itself. We’re young, so people will have to step up as leaders,” Seiden said. Despite losing the vast majority of starters from last year, Piedmont will still have leadership with eight seniors from the previous team. Adrian Kondakov and Bill Ashton make two critical pieces to their offensive and defensive lines. “We have a great coach in Oski Tauaho, and Adrian has fed off of Oski’s energy and the teaching he’s gotten from him. Adrian is one of my four-year kids and he doesn’t say much, but he leads by example,” Seiden said. After visiting Salesian this Saturday, Piedmont will travel to Middletown on September 5 and have their home opener at Witter against Berean Christian on September 12. NEXT UP Piedmont plays Salesian in Richmond on Saturday, August 30 at 1:00 p.m.

articles.text: Ryan Tripp (left) details his rowing career after his boat with Dartmouth won the silver medal at the IRA National Championships. Ryan Tripp graduated from Piedmont High in 2020 and closed his collegiate career at Dartmouth in monumental fashion. He helped his college lightweight eight win the silver medal at the Intercollegiate Rowing Association National Championships on June 1. Dartmouth finished less than a boat length behind Harvard in a field of six schools. Following nationals, Tripp was among three nominees for the inaugural Oarsman of the Year Award, considered the Heisman Trophy of rowing. Helped by Tripp, Dartmouth’s silver medal is a testament to their perseverance as a program. It was the school’s first medal in the event in 12 years. Back in 2020 Dartmouth dropped the lightweight rowing team amidst budget deficits caused by COVID-19. It was reinstated in 2021. “When we came into the fall of 2021, we took on a lot of novices and people who were trying out rowing for the first time. My freshman year was a season with a lot of ups and downs. We saw some glimmers, like placing fifth at the Head of the Charles,” Tripp explained. “We were steadily making progress on paper, but I don’t think we won a race as a freshman or as a sophomore. We had to keep a level head and slowly build a culture that loved training and supporting one another. We knew we’d have to weather losses and hard times,” he added. Tripp was the only senior in Dartmouth’s silver medal winning boat. After the National Championship race, head coach Trevor Michelson spoke of Tripp’s leadership helping propel their boat to the podium. Tripp said he tried to replicate things he learned from captains before him. “One of the great gifts is being able to learn from everyone you train with. There’s something really unique with how we cared for one another. It was so clear that we had a shared commitment, so I wanted to keep harping that and making sure everyone felt extremely supported,” Tripp said. In the weeks that followed, Tripp wrote a detailed reflection of his 10-year rowing career, offering unique insights that could prove valuable to other young athletes. He wrote about the importance of genuinely caring about the wellbeing of teammates, a shared unwavering fixation on setting records at Dartmouth, grounding yourself by reflecting on your past, and the various mentalities related to sport. “We used that metaphor to keep medaling at national championships on our horizon for a very long time. We were focused with the training. The team was motivated and you have to be comfortable rowing in those competitive scenarios,” Tripp said. Tripp wrote about times in his rowing career that he dreaded race day, figuring out that he had to find a “relaxed joy” when competing. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, August 27, 2025 Sports Football returns this Saturday at Salesian Ryan Tripp, Dartmouth win silver medal at National Championships Piedmont football returns this Saturday with a season-opening game at Salesian. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont football is back this Saturday, August 30 with an opening game at Salesian in Richmond to kick off its 10-game season. The Highlanders return after going 10-2 in 2024 with a senior-laden squad that won its first North Coast Section game since 2017. It sought its second straight Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division title and won its third league banner in as many years. “We’re still in the middle division with Hayward and Newark Memorial. It’s going to be a physical year just like it was last season. Hayward brings a similar team but is new in some spots. They are already talking a lot,” said Piedmont coach Jordan Seiden. Piedmont lost 16 players to graduation in the Class of 2025, requiring obvious overhauls to both offensive and defensive units. “15 of those 16 players were two-way starters. Now it’s a whole new cycle. We’re doing a lot of teaching like we did the first couple of years. It’s a young group, but they are going to be good,” Seiden said. For a fourth year, Piedmont will have a Lagios at quarterback wearing No. 4. This time, sophomore Jimmy Lagios steps into the starting role following the graduation of his older brother, Markos. Incoming quarterback Jimmy Lagios talks things over with coach Jordan Seiden. Rehan Mumtaz carries the ball in running back drills at practice. Staff Photos “Jimmy had a great year on JV, we want to see his growth and development. As that’s happening, he’s going to be a huge part of anything we’re able to do. It’ll look differently offensively. He’s not as mobile as Markos was, but he’s a natural smooth thrower. Same number, they look alike, but he’s taller. They are different and similar at the same time,” Seiden said. On offense, PHS must replace starting running back Tommy Ashton and star receiver Sam Shelby, an honorable mention for the Post’s Athlete of the Year award. At running back, Piedmont could have a formidable threeheaded monster with Xavier Henderson, Colby Hong, and Rehan Mumtaz. Hong and Henry Brennan will also fill into the inside linebacker spot vacated by Ashton, while Henderson will continue at linebacker as well. Jack Meyjes and Dash WatersWorthen will take the lead at receiver, Meyjes will also play defensive back. “Xavier is one of our more vocal leaders. We also need Colby and Henry to be the quarterbacks of our defense and be vocal. That leadership will manifest itself. We’re young, so people will have to step up as leaders,” Seiden said. Despite losing the vast majority of starters from last year, Piedmont will still have leadership with eight seniors from the previous team. Adrian Kondakov and Bill Ashton make two critical pieces to their offensive and defensive lines. “We have a great coach in Oski Tauaho, and Adrian has fed off of Oski’s energy and the teaching he’s gotten from him. Adrian is one of my four-year kids and he doesn’t say much, but he leads by example,” Seiden said. By Jonathan Comeaux Ryan Tripp graduated from Piedmont High in 2020 and closed his collegiate career at Dartmouth in monumental fashion. He helped his college lightweight eight win the silver medal at the Intercollegiate Rowing Association National Championships on June 1. Dartmouth finished less than a boat length behind Harvard in a field of six schools. Following nationals, Tripp was among three nominees for the inaugural Oarsman of the Year Award, considered the Heisman Trophy of rowing. Helped by Tripp, Dartmouth’s silver medal is a testament to their perseverance as a program. It was the school’s first medal in the event in 12 years. Back in 2020 Dartmouth dropped the lightweight rowing team amidst budget deficits caused by COVID-19. It was reinstated in 2021. “When we came into the fall of 2021, we took on a lot of novices and people who were trying out rowing for the first time. My freshman year was a season with a lot of ups and downs. We saw some glimmers, like placing fifth at the Head of the Charles,” Tripp explained. “We were steadily making progress on paper, but I don’t think we won a race as a freshman or as a sophomore. We had to keep a level head and slowly build a culture that loved training and supporting one another. We knew we’d have to weather losses and hard times,” he added. Tripp was the only senior in Dartmouth’s silver medal winning boat. After the National Championship race, head coach Trevor Michelson spoke of Tripp’s leadership helping propel their boat to the podium. Tripp said he tried to replicate things he learned from captains before him. “One of the great gifts is being able to learn from everyone you train with. There’s something really unique with how we cared for one another. It was so clear that we had a shared commitment, so I wanted to keep harping that and making sure everyone felt extremely supported,” Tripp said. In the weeks that followed, Tripp wrote a detailed reflection of his 10-year rowing career, offering unique insights that could prove valuable to other young athletes. He wrote about the importance of genuinely caring about the wellbeing of teammates, a shared unwavering fixation on setting records at Dartmouth, grounding yourself by reflecting on your past, and the various mentalities related to sport. “We used that metaphor to keep medaling at national championships on our horizon for a very long time. We were focused with the training. The team was motivated and you have to be comfortable rowing in those competitive scenarios,” Tripp said. Tripp wrote about times in his rowing career that he dreaded race day, figuring out that he had to find a “relaxed joy” when competing. articles.text: Piedmont’s flag football team returns for its third year. Piedmont High’s flag football team returns for their third year of action, getting their season started this Thursday, August 28 against St. Mary’s of Berkeley at Witter Field. The sport has quickly become arguably the most popular sport at the school with more than 50 athletes on varsity and two separate junior varsity squads. “We had over 50 girls tryout and we have enough girls to field a varsity and two junior varsity teams. One of the JV teams is an all-freshman team and will compete in the same league because there are no other freshman teams,” coach Beth Black said. “As we expected, girls who picked up the football found out how quickly they liked the game. We’re running a supportive environment and want to teach kids how to play,” she added. The Highlanders went 6-10 last season and will have to replace All-League players Miya Fujimoto and Dorothy Nemeth. Black expects Malia Williams to continue making an impact on both offense and defense. “Malia is a great playmaker for us at receiver. Our running back position is fluid, we’ve been trying a lot of different girls at a lot of different positions. Our belief system is every girl should be learning every position,” Black said. Sophomore quarterback Edie Elmquist returns for her second year as a starter. She’s a two-sport athlete with softball, putting her strong arm to work. Black said Elmquist has made improvements Staff Photos Edie Elmquist returns as Piedmont’s starting quarterback. Dahlia Osman is Piedmont returning tackler and pass defender. She’s a three-year starter. rolling outside of the pocket and putting use to her mobility. “Edie is back and she’s looking strong. It’s hard to believe she’s a sophomore, she just has a lot of maturity to her. She’s learned to read where the ball goes and she’s moving around a lot in and out of the pocket. I’m impressed with her ability to just want more out of herself,” Black said. Defense carried the weight for Piedmont last season. Senior leader Dahlia Osman is back in the fold, navigating the secondary as the team’s leading tackler and pass defender for the last two years. She’s been a starter for all three years of the flag football program. “Dahlia is a force. Our seniors are really cohesive and that’s been a lot of fun to see,” Black said. Elspeth Grippando became an X factor for Piedmont’s defense as a pass rusher, chasing down quarterbacks for sacks. She’ll be doing the same thing, once again, this season, but with an added wrinkle; teams are now allowed to have multiple rushers. It’s one of many big rule changes from the California Interscholastic Federation and National Federation of State High School Associations. “You can rush as many as you want. You can rush from one yard and there is no longer a no-run zone, so you can run the ball in short-yardage situations. In past years, you couldn’t run within five yards of the line to gain a first down,” Black said. Changes by CIF Thus season the CIF (State) and NFHS made sweeping changes to the game’s playing structure. Multiple rushers are now allowed. With that, quarterbacks are now allowed to run at all times. No-run zones are eliminated, meaning teams can now call run plays at any time. Spin moves, jumping, and dives are now fully permitted. Offenses can now use screen-plays, but blocking must still be considered non-contact without hands/arms being extended. Teams now must decide to punt on fourth downs, rather than deciding to relinquish possession. The changes essentially make it a brand new ball-game. “It’s a big shift but I think it’s going to work out just fine,” Black said. NEXT UP Piedmont hosts St. Mary’s on Thursday, August 28 at 7:30 p.m. They also host Las Lomas on Tuesday, September 2 at the same time at Witter Field.

articles.text: For some children, the toughest part of going back to school isn’t meeting a new teacher, finding their classroom, or making friends — it’s speaking up. Answering a question, asking for help, or joining in at lunch can feel overwhelming when communication anxiety takes over. As a pediatric speech-language pathologist, I often meet students who are lively talkers at home but become quiet, hesitant, or even silent in the classroom. The causes vary shyness, past experiences, perfectionism, or a speech and language difference. The good news? With patience, understanding, and a few simple strategies, parents and teachers can help children build confidence. 1. Shyness or Anxiety? Shyness is a personality trait that often eases once a child warms up. Communication anxiety is different: it lingers and can cause kids to avoid speaking altogether. Signs include refusing to raise a hand, freezing or whispering when called on, saying “I don’t know” when they do, and showing physical distress such as fidgeting, blushing, or tearing up before speaking. If these behaviors appear often in school, they may point to more than shyness. 2. Practice in Safe Spaces Role-play common school situations at home: asking to use the restroom, ordering lunch, answering a question. Start small, maybe practicing with stuffed animals or siblings, then build up to a few friends or relatives. The key is gradual exposure in low-pressure settings. 3. Exposure, Not Pressure Telling a child to “just speak up” usually backfires. Instead, set up small wins. Ask for a single word, then a short phrase, then a full answer. Over time, these small successes reduce fear and grow confidence. 4. Build Self-Advocacy Even young children can communicate needs without words. A simple cue card: “I need help” or “I need a break”, allows them to express themselves while reducing stress. As confidence builds, swap cards for spoken requests. 5. Partner Early With Teachers If your child struggles, loop in their teacher at the start of the year. Share strategies: call on your child only for questions

pages.text: Wednesday, August 27, 2025 15 Back to School in Piedmont Helping Kids Find Their Voice at School By Katie Pengilly For some children, the toughest part of going back to school isn’t meeting a new teacher, finding their classroom, or making friends — it’s speaking up. Answering a question, asking for help, or joining in at lunch can feel overwhelming when communication anxiety takes over. As a pediatric speech-language pathologist, I often meet students who are lively talkers at home but become quiet, hesitant, or even silent in the classroom. The causes vary shyness, past experiences, perfectionism, or a speech and language difference. The good news? With patience, understanding, and a few simple strategies, parents and teachers can help children build confidence. 1. Shyness or Anxiety? Shyness is a personality trait that often eases once a child warms up. Communication anxiety is different: it lingers and can cause kids to avoid speaking altogether. Signs include refusing to raise a hand, freezing or whispering when called on, saying “I don’t know” when they do, and showing physical distress such as fidgeting, blushing, or tearing up before speaking. If these behaviors appear often in school, they may point to more than shyness. 2. Practice in Safe Spaces Role-play common school situations at home: asking to use the restroom, ordering lunch, answering a question. Start small, maybe practicing with stuffed animals or siblings, then build up to a few friends or relatives. The key is gradual exposure in low-pressure settings. 3. Exposure, Not Pressure Telling a child to “just speak up” usually backfires. Instead, set up small wins. Ask for a single word, then a short phrase, then a full answer. Over time, these small successes reduce fear and grow confidence. 4. Build Self-Advocacy Even young children can communicate needs without words. A simple cue card: “I need help” or “I need a break”, allows them to express themselves while reducing stress. As confidence builds, swap cards for spoken requests. 5. Partner Early With Teachers If your child struggles, loop in their teacher at the start of the year. Share strategies: call on your child only for questions they’re prepared to answer, or let them rehearse responses in advance. Teachers appreciate knowing how to help without adding pressure. When to Seek Extra Support If communication anxiety persists for months or interferes with friendships, learning, or daily life, it may be time for outside help. A speech-language pathologist can provide strategies tailored to your child. Sometimes a counselor or psychologist is also useful, especially if anxiety reaches beyond communication. The Takeaway Back-to-school season can be exciting and nerve-racking for children with communication anxiety. With empathy, gentle practice, and a supportive team, kids can learn to find and use their voice in the classroom and beyond. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. articles.text: California College of the Arts invites teens to explore art & design This fall, California College of the Arts (CCA) is opening its doors to local high school students who want to dive into the world of art and design. From hands-on workshops to the prestigious Scholastic Art & Writing Awards, there are many ways for young artists to explore their passions and showcase their talent. All high school students ages 14 to 18 are welcome to join CCA’s fall Atelier programs. These non-credit weekend intensives and multi-week classes run from October 1 through December 15. Each course is designed to be flexible, inspiring, and taught by practicing artists and designers who understand how to connect with high school students. Atelier classes encourage students to experiment with new materials, sharpen their skills, and create pieces they can proudly include in future art and design school applications. Studios include 2D Portfolio Development, Animation, Architecture and Interior Design, Fashion, Figure Drawing, Illustration, and Industrial Design. Registration is now open, and spots are available on a first-come, first-served basis. For students eager to share their creativity, the Scholastic Art & Writing Awards offer a chance to shine. This national competition is open for submissions from October 1, 2025, through January 6, 2026. Middle and high school students in grades 7 through 12 can enter work in 28 art and writing categories, and high school seniors may also submit complete art portfolios. CCA is proud to host the Bay Area regional chapter for the fourth year in a row and has been inspired by the vision and passion of students who are shaping the future of the creative world. The regional competition concludes with a spring pop-up exhibition at CCA, where award-winning students present their work to friends, family, and the community. Submissions can be entered at artandwriting.org. Students preparing for college Instructor supporting an Atelier student as they build a concept board for their upcoming fashion design project. have another important opportunity this fall. On November 9, 2025, CCA will host National Portfolio Day, featuring more than 30 leading art and design colleges accredited by the National Association of Schools of Art and Design. Representatives will provide in-person and virtual portfolio reviews, answer questions about their programs and admissions, and offer guidance on building a portfolio that stands out. This season is full of possibilities for young artists to learn, create, and take exciting steps toward their future. Join CCA’s vibrant community and watch your teen’s confidence and creativity grow. Contact Information: California College of the Arts Youth Programs & Continuing Education youthprograms@cca.edu cca.edu/youthprograms (415) 551-9224 College representatives reviewing portfolios with high schoolers eager to turn their creative passions into college degrees.

articles.text: R e c r e a t i o n Back-to-school season fills calendars fast - carpools, practices, late-night homework, endless drop-offs. For Piedmont parents, that means less time for home projects. Honey Homes, founded in Lafayette by parents, pairs you with a reliable handyman so your house keeps running smoothly while you focus on the important things (or other to-dos!). Here are a few smart ways our members are preparing their homes this fall: If you’re a Piedmont homeowner with a list of “I’ll get to it later” projects, let us help. We’re offering a complimentary trial: a 30-minute walk-thru to review your list, plus a 1.5-hour working visit with our expert Piedmont handymen team. Book your free trial by September 6th: https:// honeyh.co/piedmontpost 1. Install hooks or cubbies Give backpacks, coats, and sports gear a designated spot. A few simple hooks or cubbies can turn a morning scramble into a smoother routine. 2. Add motion-sensor lighting Dark evenings come quicker this time of year. Motion-sensor lights near garages, driveways, or side yards keep your family safe and your home secure. 3. Hang bike racks in the garage Between sports gear and scooters, garages can get crowded. Wall-mounted bike racks free up space and keep things tidy. 4. Patch dents and wall scuffs From summer playdates to extra foot traffic, walls and doors need some extra TLC. A quick touch-up keeps your home looking fresh. 5. Secure loose pavers or steps Busy schedules mean more in-and-out. Make sure your entry is safe for kids, guests, and neighbors. With Honey Homes, you don’t have to squeeze these projects into an already packed week. articles.text: Claude, the iconic American alligator with albinism at the California Academy of Sciences, will be celebrating his 30th birthday (or hatch day) this September. The museum is marking the occasion with a month of daily festivities including merch giveaways, Mascot Claude photo-ops, special programs, and a splashy cupcake party on September 14 to celebrate the reptile who’s captured the hearts and minds of millions. Thirty may sound old, but in human care alligators can live well into their sixties. Claude currently weighs 278 pounds and is over 10 feet long. But back when he first hatched from his egg, Claude was only about the size of a banana. Claude’s pale color is due to albinism, a rare genetic mutation that prevents the production of a pigment called melanin. American alligators are typically black or dark green, but because of his albinism, Claude’s skin is translucent and appears white. Albinism affects his eyes as well, giving him low vision. Claude’s eyes look pinkish red, as the blood vessels in the back of his eyes are visible through his clear irises. Because of his albinism, Claude would not have been able to camouflage well in a natural swamp habitat and would be vulnerable to predators. Many Academy visitors see Claude lying perfectly still in his habitat and wonder if he is real. While he may often look like a Claude will be celebrating his 30th birthday (or hatch day) on September 14 at the California Academy of Sciences. statue, this behavior is typical and advantageous for an alligator. Alligators are ambush predators, relying on camouflage and stealth to save energy by lying in wait until prey comes close enough to lunge. Claude is also a reptile, which means he is ectothermic, or cold blooded, and uses minimal energy to maintain his body temperature. He uses so little energy that he only needs to be fed once a week, and likes to eat fish heads and tails, chicks, rats, and micronutrient gel. In their natural habitat, alligators can go months without eating. American alligators are only found in the Southeastern United States, and are an example of a conservation success story. In the 1960s, commercial hunting and habitat loss drove American alligator populations into decline, and they became an endangered species. But communities near swamps advocated for habitat preserves and hunting regulations, and scientists began alligator breeding programs and investigated alligator biology as well as their role in swamp ecosystems. With these combined efforts, alligator populations slowly began to recover. In 1987, they were removed from the endangered species list and have been doing well ever since. Although he may not move much, Claude is adored by many and offers the opportunity to learn about his species’ conservation story and just how special animals with differences can be. Guananí Gómez-Van Cortright is a Public Presenter at California Academy of Sciences. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse’s production of The Addams Family, based on the macabre 1964 television series and The New Yorker cartoon that inspired it, premieres next Friday, September 5. Directed by Mel Martinez, with music direction by Erika Oba and choreography by Cat Delos Santos Reyes, The Addams Family is a comedic musical that’s fun for the whole family with themes of family dysfunction, being true to oneself, and celebrating love in all its forms. Christian Arteaga stars as patriarch Gomez Addams with Tielle Baker playing the great Morticia Addams, supported by Serene Hammami as the mischievous Wednesday and Keenan Moran and William Spitz playing Pugsley. “The Addams Family is a musical that at its core is about love, family, and being true to who you are, and our Addams Family truly embraces their Latin Culture with nods to the Mexican Gothic aesthetic in our design,” said Director Mel Martinez. “Much like me, our Gomez is both Spanish and Mexican and we wanted to lean into the MexSerene Hammami is Wednesday Addams in Berkeley Playhouse’s The Addams Family. ican representation. It is important to me to show that brown is beautiful, and joyful, and full of heart,” he added. “The heart of the show is how close this family is. Every decision they make is because they love each other.” Performances run Friday through Sunday, and select weekday evenings, beginning September 5. For tickets, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org.
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse’s The Addams Family premieres Sept. 5

articles.text: Unique event celebrates 10th anniversary The San Francisco Botanical Garden will host its 10th annual Flower Piano interactive festival beginning September 12 in Golden Gate Park. This unique event merges botanical beauty and classical tunes against the backdrop of San Francisco’s most famous park. Flower Piano Lounge transforms San Francisco Botanical Garden into an alfresco concert hall where everyone and anyone is invited to play and listen. A dozen pianos will be placed across the 55-acre garden, inviting visitors to explore San Francisco’s collection of diverse plants and foliage while seeking out the hidden instruments’ location. At each of the pianos, there will be scheduled professional and community partner performances as well as open play time for anyone to sit down and play. The event has enjoyed nine successful years of turn-out, and took a pause in 2020 due to gathering restrictions. Sunset Piano, which hosts the event in partnership with the garden, places Grand pianos and Baby-Grands throughout the gardens where musicians and artists will play an eclectic range of genres, from Jazz to classical to AfroCuban. A limited number of Pianist Christian Tumalan performs on opening night, September 12. chairs, as well as lawn seating, is available and guests are encouraged to bring their own blankets or foldable chairs. This year, the Celebration Garden in the San Francisco Botanical Garden will be transformed into the “Flower Piano Lounge,” featuring an upgraded musical landscape and priority entry to the festival. Guests may attend special performances from local headliners and enjoy access to premium bars, food from local makers, lounge seating, restrooms, and flexibility to relax and enjoy all areas of the festival. Festivities begin on September 12 with the 10th anniversary opening night event, featuring Montuno Swing Salsa Band with Grammy Award-Winning Pianist Christian Tumalan. The festival ends on Sunday, September 21 with a special event featuring long-time Flower Piano star, Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble, at the Flower Piano Lounge in the San Francisco Botanical Garden. Other featured artists this year include Amy Norman, Dawn Oberg, Sojourn Duo, Wavefront Manifold, and more. On Fridays, the Flower Piano Lounge will host family-friendly and sensory-friendly daytime performances featuring the San Francisco Ballet and a puppet show. For a full list of programming, visit https://gggp.org/event/flower-piano-2025/.
articles.title: SF Botanical Garden’s ‘Flower Piano’ launches Sept. 12

articles.text: Festival offers discounted and free showings at local venues Bay Area Theatre, one of the largest regional performing arts service organizations in the U.S., announced the return of its popular Bay Area Theatre Week festival running September 12 through 22. The ten-day event offers free and discounted events organized by local theatres, including discounted tickets for American Conservatory Theater’s (A.C.T.) production of Kim’s Convenience and Berkeley Playhouse’s The Addams Family. Play w r ight I ns Choi’s award-winning comedy drama Kim’s Convenience is based on his own experiences working at his family’s convenience store, Kim’s Grocer, in Scarborough, Toronto, and follows family patriarch Mr. Kim as he faces a changing neighborhood landscape and the gap between his values and those of his Canadian-born children. The Addams Family, currently showing at Berkeley Playhouse, also follows the quirks and eccentricities of family life. Directed by Mel Martinez, with music direction by Erika Oba and choreography by Cat Delos Santos Reyes, The Addams Family is a comedic musical that’s fun for the whole family with themes of family dysfunction, being true to oneself, and celebrating love in all its forms. Bay Area Theatre Week 2025 includes over thirty events hosted by more than twenty regional theatres, including Berkeley Repertory Theatre, Center Repertory Theatre, Shotgun Players, Marin Theatre and more. Theatre Bay Area is expanding Bay Area Theatre Week to incorporate social mixers and arts classes in addition to discounted shows. Proceeds benefit the nonprofit Theatre Bay Area, whose mission is to unite, strengthen, promote and advance the theatre community in the San Francisco Bay Area. “Arts and culture are fueling San Francisco’s comeback,” said San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie in a press release. “From concerts to theater productions, the arts bring people to our city, fill our hotels, and create joy in our communities. I encourage everyone to take advantage of Bay Area Theatre Week and experience the world-class performances that make San Francisco vibrant.” For a full list of offerings, visit www.TheatreBayArea.org/ BATW25.
articles.title: Bay Area Theatre Week is Sept. 12 - 22

articles.text: Performances in Mountain View, Walnut Creek & San Francisco Smuin Ballet Company presents its fall season, entitled “Extremely Close,” on September 12 with three performances at Mountain View Center for Performing Arts, followed by events in Walnut Creek and San Francisco. Smuin’s 32nd season is directed by Amy Seiwert and is inspired by Alejandro Cerrundo’s art installation and movement drama Extremely Close, set to a score by Philip Glass and Dustin O’Halloran. Fall performances include the West Coast premiere of choreographer Justin Peck’s Partita, set to Caroline Shaw’s Pulitzer Prize-winning “Partita for 8 Voices,” a unique number featuring eight dancers in sneakers. Smuin Ballet will be the first company outside of New York City Ballet to perform the work since it premiered in 2022. The final piece being performed in this season’s fall programming is A Long Night choreographed by Seiwert, a former mentee of the late Michael Smuin. Seiwert reimagines Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream with humor and heartfelt storytelling that honors George Balanchine’s original choreography. A Long Night premiered in 2023 for BalletX in Philadelphia and is set to songs by Patsy Cline, Pink Martini, Harry Nilsson, and more. “To have Justin’s [Peck] and Alejandro’s [Cerrundo] work in my first curated season is an honor and a thrill,” said Seiwert. “Justin’s creative path reminds me a bit of our founder Michael Smuin’s. His work in film and on Broadway informs the distinctive style he brings to his creations for the concert dance stage. And Alejandro’s work exemplifies how extraordinary contemporary dance can be: musical and theatrical, with a mystery that will take your breath away.” Smuin Ballet Company’s fall season opens at the Mountain View Center for the Performing Arts September 12 with performances through September 14: Friday and Saturday at 7:30 p.m., with two additional matinees Saturday and Sunday at 2 p.m. Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek hosts two performances September 19 through 20: Friday at 7:30 p.m. and Saturday at 2 p.m. The company’s fall season concludes at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts in San Francisco September 26 through October 5 with eight performances scheduled: Friday, September 26 at 7:30 p.m.; Saturday and Sunday, September 27 and 28 at 2 p.m.; Thursday, October 2 at 7:30 p.m.; Friday, October 3 at 7:30 p.m.; Saturday, October 4 at 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.; and Sunday, October 5 at 2 p.m. Single-day tickets are available at www.smuinballet.org. pages.text: Wednesday, August 27, 2025 19 Arts & Entertainment SF Botanical Garden’s ‘Flower Piano’ launches Sept. 12 Unique event celebrates 10th anniversary By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco Botanical Garden will host its 10th annual Flower Piano interactive festival beginning September 12 in Golden Gate Park. This unique event merges botanical beauty and classical tunes against the backdrop of San Francisco’s most famous park. Flower Piano Lounge transforms San Francisco Botanical Garden into an alfresco concert hall where everyone and anyone is invited to play and listen. A dozen pianos will be placed across the 55-acre garden, inviting visitors to explore San Francisco’s collection of diverse plants and foliage while seeking out the hidden instruments’ location. At each of the pianos, there will be scheduled professional and community partner performances as well as open play time for anyone to sit down and play. The event has enjoyed nine successful years of turn-out, and took a pause in 2020 due to gathering restrictions. Sunset Piano, which hosts the event in partnership with the garden, places Grand pianos and Baby-Grands throughout the gardens where musicians and artists will play an eclectic range of genres, from Jazz to classical to AfroCuban. A limited number of Pianist Christian Tumalan performs on opening night, September 12. chairs, as well as lawn seating, is available and guests are encouraged to bring their own blankets or foldable chairs. This year, the Celebration Garden in the San Francisco Botanical Garden will be transformed into the “Flower Piano Lounge,” featuring an upgraded musical landscape and priority entry to the festival. Guests may attend special performances from local headliners and enjoy access to premium bars, food from local makers, lounge seating, restrooms, and flexibility to relax and enjoy all areas of the festival. Festivities begin on September 12 with the 10th anniversary opening night event, featuring Montuno Swing Salsa Band with Grammy Award-Winning Pianist Christian Tumalan. The festival ends on Sunday, September 21 with a special event featuring long-time Flower Piano star, Kev Choice Chamber Ensemble, at the Flower Piano Lounge in the San Francisco Botanical Garden. Other featured artists this year include Amy Norman, Dawn Oberg, Sojourn Duo, Wavefront Manifold, and more. On Fridays, the Flower Piano Lounge will host family-friendly and sensory-friendly daytime performances featuring the San Francisco Ballet and a puppet show. For a full list of programming, visit https://gggp.org/event/flower-piano-2025/. Berkeley Playhouse’s The Addams Family premieres Sept. 5 By Allyson Aleksey Berkeley Playhouse’s production of The Addams Family, based on the macabre 1964 television series and The New Yorker cartoon that inspired it, premieres next Friday, September 5. Directed by Mel Martinez, with music direction by Erika Oba and choreography by Cat Delos Santos Reyes, The Addams Family is a comedic musical that’s fun for the whole family with themes of family dysfunction, being true to oneself, and celebrating love in all its forms. Christian Arteaga stars as patriarch Gomez Addams with Tielle Baker playing the great Morticia Addams, supported by Serene Hammami as the mischievous Wednesday and Keenan Moran and William Spitz playing Pugsley. “The Addams Family is a musical that at its core is about love, family, and being true to who you are, and our Addams Family truly embraces their Latin Culture with nods to the Mexican Gothic aesthetic in our design,” said Director Mel Martinez. “Much like me, our Gomez is both Spanish and Mexican and we wanted to lean into the MexSerene Hammami is Wednesday Addams in Berkeley Playhouse’s The Addams Family. ican representation. It is important to me to show that brown is beautiful, and joyful, and full of heart,” he added. “The heart of the show is how close this family is. Every decision they make is because they love each other.” Performances run Friday through Sunday, and select weekday evenings, beginning September 5. For tickets, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org. Smuin Ballet opens 32nd season on Sept. 12 Performances in Mountain View, Walnut Creek & San Francisco By Allyson Aleksey Smuin Ballet Company presents its fall season, entitled “Extremely Close,” on September 12 with three performances at Mountain View Center for Performing Arts, followed by events in Walnut Creek and San Francisco. Smuin’s 32nd season is directed by Amy Seiwert and is inspired by Alejandro Cerrundo’s art installation and movement drama Extremely Close, set to a score by Philip Glass and Dustin O’Halloran. Fall performances include the West Coast premiere of choreographer Justin Peck’s Partita, set to Caroline Shaw’s Pulitzer Prize-winning “Partita for 8 Voices,” a unique number featuring eight dancers in sneakers. Smuin Ballet will be the first company outside of New York City Ballet to perform the work since it premiered in 2022. The final piece being performed in this season’s fall programming is A Long Night choreographed by Seiwert, a former mentee of the late Michael Smuin. Seiwert reimagines Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream with humor and heartfelt storytelling that honors George Balanchine’s original choreography. A Long Night premiered in 2023 for BalletX in Philadelphia and is set to songs by Patsy Cline, Pink Martini, Harry Nilsson, and more. “To have Justin’s [Peck] and Alejandro’s [Cerrundo] work in my first curated season is an honor and a thrill,” said Seiwert. “Justin’s creative path reminds me a bit of our founder Michael Smuin’s. His work in film and on Broadway informs the distinctive style he brings to his creations for the concert dance stage. Bay Area Theatre Week is Sept. 12 - 22 Festival offers discounted and free showings at local venues By Allyson Aleksey Bay Area Theatre, one of the largest regional performing arts service organizations in the U.S., announced the return of its popular Bay Area Theatre Week festival running September 12 through 22. The ten-day event offers free and discounted events organized by local theatres, including discounted tickets for American Conservatory Theater’s (A.C.T.) production of Kim’s Convenience and Berkeley Playhouse’s The Addams Family. Play w r ight I ns Choi’s award-winning comedy drama Kim’s Convenience is based on his own experiences working at his family’s convenience store, Kim’s Grocer, in Scarborough, Toronto, and follows family patriarch Mr. Kim as he faces a changing neighborhood landscape and the gap between his values and those of his Canadian-born children. The Addams Family, currently showing at Berkeley Playhouse, also follows the quirks and eccentricities of family life. Directed by Mel Martinez, with music direction by Erika Oba and choreography by Cat Delos Santos Reyes, The Addams Family is a comedic musical that’s fun for the whole family with themes of family dysfunction, being true to oneself, and celebrating love in all its forms. Bay Area Theatre Week 2025 includes over thirty events hosted by more than twenty regional theatres, including Berkeley Repertory Theatre, Center Repertory Theatre, Shotgun Players, Marin Theatre and more. Theatre Bay Area is expanding Bay Area Theatre Week to incorporate social mixers and arts classes in addition to discounted shows. Proceeds benefit the nonprofit Theatre Bay Area, whose mission is to unite, strengthen, promote and advance the theatre community in the San Francisco Bay Area. “Arts and culture are fueling San Francisco’s comeback,” said San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie in a press release. “From concerts to theater productions, the arts bring people to our city, fill our hotels, and create joy in our communities. I encourage everyone to take advantage of Bay Area Theatre Week and experience the world-class performances that make San Francisco vibrant.” For a full list of offerings, visit www.TheatreBayArea.org/ BATW25. Blake Garden is a little known treasure located at 70 Kenyon Rd. in Kensington, just a 25-minute drive from Piedmont. The Garden is 100 years old and exists because Anson Styles Blake and Anita Day Blake agreed to sell their Berkeley home and property to UC Berkeley so the California Memorial Stadium could be built. The Blakes then chose to move to the very barren hills of a newly identified area called Kensington, where they built a magnificent new home on 10+ acres of very undeveloped land. Upon completion of the house they were joined by Anita’s sister, Mabel Symmes. Mabel, like her sister and brother-in-law, was a graduate of UC Berkeley where she was a student of Landscape Architecture. Together the sisters set out to design and plant beautiful gardens containing water features, pocket gardens with statuary, Oak trees, a small canyon with Redwood trees, controlled creeks and much, much more. In 1962, following the deaths of Anson (1959), Anita (1962) and Mabel (1962), at Blake’s bequest, the House and Gardens became the property of University of California and under the management of its Department of Landscape Architecture and Environmental Planning. Today the garden has an estiBlake Garden is a hidden gem in Berkeley. Photos by Lester Ellis mated 1500 plant species, a Redwood grove with 80-foot-tall trees, a large Koi pond, quiet creeks, extensive winding gravel paths, rugged stone walls, huge rock outcroppings, spacious lawns ideal for picnics, spectacular views and the original estate home. The Garden is both a teaching and plant research center for UC faculty and students. It is a very tranquil place to visit. The home, designed by Walter Danforth Bliss and completed in 1924, was last occupied as the home of the Presidents of the University of California. That use ended in 2008. The house is now in very poor condition. Staff at the University are studying numerous options for the future of the house. Hopefully it can be saved. Entry to the garden is free as is the parking. articles.text: Festival Opera continues its 2025 season on August 24 and September 28.with an innovative Salon Series of Sunday afternoon concerts at Piedmont Center for the Arts featuring some of the Bay Area’s rising stars and critically acclaimed artists. The series offers intimate, artist-curated performances that highlight rare repertoire and virtuosic collaboration between talented singers and musicians alike. At the conclusion of each concert, the audience is invited to stay for a post-performance reception with the artists. Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin commented, “This new format encourages programming a broader variety of vocal music: art song, arias and scenes from operas, solo cantatas, complete short operas, and even some gems from genres outside of the classical music spectrum. The artists and programs we present this year are all very dear to me, and the singers are absolute stars of their respective voice types. They are sure to offer memorable and impactful performances which our audience can witness up-close in this chamber music venue.” American Song Cycles Last Sunday, August 24, the newly inaugurated Festival Opera Salon Series continued with an afternoon of music by renowned soprano Carrie Hennessey and acclaimed pianist Daniel Lockert featuring two magnificent works by American composers. Concert goers had the chance to experience encore performances of Julia Seeholzer’s Portraits of Disquiet, a reflection on our modern world first performed in Festival Opera’s online recital series during the pandemic, and Jake Heggie’s At the Statue of Venus, a poignant and humorous journey of anticipation and self-discovery which was a part of the company’s 2021 mainstage production. Bel Canto Forever On Sunday, September 28 at 4 p.m., Festival Opera plans a celebration of soaring vocalism with soprano Shawnette Sulker and contralto Sara Couden, accompanied by Zachary Gordin at the piano. The program includes the 19th century Bel Canto music of Rossini, Bellini, Delibes and Meyerbeer with dazzling duets, arias, soaring melodies and vocal fireworks that define the art of bel canto, beautiful singing. Individual tickets for each Salon concert are priced at $40 and available online at www.festivalopera.org. Carrie Hennessey Shawnette Sulker Sara Couden Residency at the Mac In addition to the Salon Series, Festival Opera announces a new residency at Point Richmond’s historic Hotel Mac, presenting a series of “First Fridays” at the newly renovated Biancoverde Restaurant with its menu of sumptuous Italian fare. Zachary Gordin shared, “The series will feel like fun and casual operatic ‘jam sessions’ for the restaurant and bar patrons, bringing favorite opera artists from the Bay Area and beyond to the Mac, performing hits from opera, Broadway, and more.” Upcoming “First Fridays” are scheduled for 6:30 p.m. on September 5, October 3, November 7, and December 5. Artists and programs will be announced. There is no cover charge, but advance reservations are recommended. The iconic Hotel Mac, which originally opened in 1911, is located at 50 Washington Avenue in Point Richmond. For more details and reservations, visit festivalopera.org/at-the-mac.

articles.text: Saturday, August 30, 7:00 p.m. Temescal Quartet & Friends Temescal String Quartet is a San Francisco Bay Area ensemble, established in 2004 by musicians of the SF Opera and Ballet Orchestras. Founding member violinist Barbara Riccardi was joined by cellist Nancy Bien in 2016. The members share a great love of music, deep friendship, and great joy in playing music together. This event will include a viewing of art works by cellist Nancy Bien, and a wine and cheese reception will follow the concert, provided by David Konigsmark of Circadian Cuisine. Purchase your advance tickets soon at https:// www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6696869. Sunday, August 31, 4:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Players concert A sextet of leading members of the home-town Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, including music director Marty Stoddard on flute, will present a concert entitled Summer Winds, including music by Mozart, Francis Poulenc, Georges Barboteu, and Carl Nielsen. Free tickets are available on Eventbrite, and donations are encouraged also: https://www.eventbrite.com/e/1510592706449. Saturday, September 6, 6:00 p.m. Slavic Art Exhibit The Center for Slavic Arts and Culture is proud to present its very first exhibition, Kaleidoscope. The show brings together artists, a photographer, and a jewelry designer from five Slavic countries, each sharing their talent and creative vision. In challenging and uncertain times, art reminds us of beauty, resilience, and the strength of our community. Kaleidoscope is a celebration of creativity, and a reminder of how art can uplift, connect, and inspire us all. This exhibition’s opening reception will take place from 6 to 8 p.m., and the show will then be open weekend days from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. until mid-October. Sunday, September 7, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Fall Celebration To celebrate the Fall Equinox and Mexican Independence Day, the jazz and pop piano trio will present a full program centered around Autumn Leaves. There is a narrative that ties each tune into the theme for the month. For Autumn Leaves, for example, many of the tunes, such as Autumn Leaves (1947), September in the Rain (1937), Autumn In New York (1934), Early Autumn (1949), and September Song (1938), have an obvious connection to the autumn theme. Other tunes such as I’ve Got the World on A String (1932) and Wrap Your Troubles in Dreams (1931) do not have such an obvious connection. The narrative ties these tunes and all the tunes on the show into the autumn theme. As another summer passes, don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of a Sunday late afternoon in the Classic Jazz Club with the trio. Doors open at 4:15 PM. Tickets $25 at https:// brownpapertickets.com/e/6214927 or $30 at the door, cash or check ONLY. Sunday, September 7, 7:30 p.m. Fath Chamber Players concert Violinist Josepha Fath, cellist Victoria Ehrlich, and pianist Amy Zanrosso will present a rich musical journey beginning with Frank Bridge’s Miniatures for Piano Trio, charming vignettes full of grace, wit and melodic warmth, followed by Lera Auerbach’s Piano Trio No. 1 to provide a modern counterpart with brooding lyricism, dramatic surges and kaleidoscopic textures. Beethoven’s Piano Trio Op. 70, No. 2, will close out the program with elegant interplay and bursts of playful energy revealing a masterpiece of chamber dialogue. Come experience and enjoy this Bridge to Beethoven with $30 tickets at the door or $25 advance tickets from https://brownpapertickets.com/e/6699441. articles.text: Director Joshua B. Porter Piedmont natives Karyn and Kevin Yarris, alongside director Joshua B. Porter, are set to begin filming their upcoming indie feature film I’ve Got You next month. I’ve Got You is a story of love, loss, hope, redemption, and the enduring power of family. Produced by Piedmont natives Karyn and Kevin Yarris under their Wildwood Entertainment banner, the film promises to deliver an emotionally rich and visually stunning cinematic experience. The romantic drama, written by Kevin Yarris, is now in pre-production and is set to begin filming in Calaveras County in September. “We are thrilled to have Josh at the helm of this project,” said Karyn Yarris. “His vision and passion align perfectly with the heart of this story, and we can’t wait to bring it to life.” Featured in the starring roles are Aaron Dominguez, who acted in Hulu’s Only Murders in the Building and current star of the horror film Witchboard, and Nicholas Cirillo, who boasts credits in Black Mirror, Outer Banks, and She-Hulk: Attorney at Law. The film follows brothers Tyler (Dominguez) and Kyle (Cirillo) on a journey to discover their purpose in life. Along the way, they find themselves and, unexpectedly, love. Karyn Yarris previously served as an executive producer on the feature film Blowback, starring Randy Couture and Cam Gigandet, while Kevin Yarris contributed as a writer on the film. In addition to his work on I’ve Got You, Josh’s debut feature film No Evidence of Man has garnered acclaim winning best screenplay at the Madrid Film Festival and Best Cinematography at the 2025 Golden State Film Festival. For more information, visit ivegotyouthemovie.com. Co-star Aaron Dominguez Producer Karyn Yarris Co-star Nicholas Cirillo Writer/Producer Kevin Yarris

articles.text: Registration is open for the Fall 2025 session of Piedmont Adult School. The session will start September 8 and run through December 20. The fall session will include a wide range of classes in Art, Business, Computers/Tech, Cooking, Exercise, Language, Music, Philosophy and more. Among the new classes offered this fall is “Philosophy for Life,” taught by Stephen Szczepanek. The course will cover the teachings of philosophers ranging from Plato to Descartes to Kant, giving students a solid grounding in philosophical thought and a basis to explore independently. “Philosophy is a way for us to engage deeply with the most difficult questions of human existence: who we are, what our purpose is on this planet, and what it means to live a fulfilled, authentic life,” said Szczepanek. A native of England, Szczepanek holds Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees in Philosophy from the University of Oxford. He will also be teaching Conversational Intermediate Spanish for the Adult School. In addition to Spanish, he speaks French, Italian, Greek and Polish. Stephen Szczepanek will teach a course at Piedmont Adult School titled Philosophy for Life, an overview of world philosophers. “Teaching new ways to communicate and understand the world is a real joy for me,” said Szczepanek. “That’s why I love to share the gift of philosophy and languages.” Come learn something new, expand your horizons, and meet great people in a friendly, lowstress environment. Check out all the classes and register online at Piedmontadultschool.org, or by calling 594-2655. Classes do fill up, so register right away for best availability. articles.title: Piedmont Walkers tour city landmarks with new Police Chief

pages.text: 28 Wednesday, August 27, 2025 Walking on Wednesday Piedmont Walkers tour city landmarks with new Police Chief By Dick Carter There was a strong turnout of 45 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s weekly Walking on Wednesdays outing. The group also welcomed two special first-time walkers: new Piedmont Police Chief Frederick W. Shavies II and his assistant, April Fitzgerald. Before the walk began, Chief Shavies was introduced. He grew up in Oakland and attended Fremont High School, where he was an All-City football player. He went on to Washington State University, playing defensive end and appearing in the Rose Bowl. After graduation, he joined the Oakland Police Department in 2006, rising to Deputy Chief. He Walking on Wednesday group in motion was appointed Piedmont’s police chief in July. Shavies has children in Piedmont schools and has already embraced the community. He registered with the Recreation Department for Walking on Wednesdays and plans to walk with the group when his schedule allows. The walkers started behind the Exedra, past Community Hall and the Tea House, and up the Highland-Guilford steps in Piedmont Park. The $155,000 project, completed in 2023 with support from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, replaced wooden railroad ties with concrete steps, landings and handrails. The steps now provide a handsome entrance to the park. The group emerged on Highland Avenue, where Chief Shavies helped them cross, and continued up Sierra Avenue. On Sierra, a Julia Morgan-designed home was undergoing major foundation work. From there the group walked Sheridan Avenue, Wildwood Avenue, the Hall Fenway, Crocker Avenue and Hampton Road, stopping for a photo with the chief at King Avenue. They continued on to Hampton Park and up Hampton to Lexford and Huntleigh Roads. At LaSalle Avenue, they entered the St. James Woods Terrace neighborhood, marked by its early 20th-century white pillars and distinctive terracotta tile sidewalk inlays. At Lexford and Hampton, the group saw one of two designated Piedmont Heritage Tree Southern magnolias, with the second located nearby on Huntleigh. The Heritage Tree Program, established in 2018 by the City Council on the Park Commission’s recommendation, has recognized 28 trees citywide. The walk also featured a 1939 Storybook-style brick home on Lexford Road, designed by architect and engineer Carr Jones. The house features a circular chimney, a wavy brick wall, a terracotta and slate roof, and a turret that gives it a castle-like appearChief Shavies walks with Dick Carter ance. A sign at the door reads, “The rooster crows, but the hen delivers.” Architect and walker Jim Kellogg shared details about the house, including its unique brick garage addition and pool in the back. The owner, Eric Tupper, came out to greet the group, explaining that it was his wife’s childhood home. Their children built the brick maze in the yard during the pandemic. He added that the home’s radiant heating is its best feature. The group enjoyed meeting Tupper and learning about the home before heading back through Hampton, LaSalle and St. James Drive, and returning to the town center. It was a longer walk than usual, but especially memorable with Chief Shavies and Fitzgerald joining in and providing a police escort throughout. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra (Highland and Magnolia Avenues). Everyone is welcome to join, and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially encouraged. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu or by calling (510) 420-3070. New Piedmont Police Chief Frederick W. articles.text: Carleton Denis “Denny” Mathewson passed away peacefully at home on August 6, 2025, at the age of 88. Denny was born in San Francisco on November 21, 1936 – Big Game day – a fitting beginning for someone who loved college football and whose life would be marked by spirited optimism, light hearted humor, and unwavering love for his family and friends. Denny began his education at St. Dominic’s Elementary School, with a formative three-year stay in Eureka while his father served in World War II. He later attended St. Ignatius High School in San Francisco and graduated from Stanford University in 1958 with a degree in Economics. After college, he served in the U.S. Army before starting his professional life at The Emporium, which sent him to New York on a special assignment. After a year in New York, he returned to California and established a long and respected career in commercial real estate. In retirement, he served on the Piedmont Education Foundation Board and volunteered for Experience Corps as a tutor, working with kids in Oakland schools. Denny approached life with a positive outlook, a sense of humor, and a curiosity in others. He had a natural ease and all felt welcome in his presence. A gifted storyteller, he had a knack for bringing people together through laughter, memory, and warmth. He had a deep appreciation for life’s simple pleasures and was happiest spending time on the ski slopes or at the beach with his friends and family. He Denny Mathewson passed away at the age of 88. and his wife, Jan, shared a love of travel and saw much of the world together. More than anything, Denny adored his family. He was a proud and devoted husband, father, and grandfather, and found true joy in the lives and accomplishments of his children and grandchildren. He is survived by his wife Jan; daughters Hilary Anne Conrad and Lindsey Ziegler; son-inlaw Brad Ziegler; and beloved grandchildren Clemens and Bay Conrad, and Clara and Cameron Ziegler. He was preceded in death by parents, Dr. Carleton Mathewson, Jr. and Catherine Daly Mathewson and sisters Anne Mathewson Wood and Shelagh Mae Denning. A celebration of life will be held in October. In lieu of flowers, the family encourages donations to The Cancer League, Inc. or the Piedmont Education Foundation in Denny’s memory.

Moraga Canyon Housing The open house included a display with information about the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, a potentially controversial housing plan that would create as much as 132 units of multifamily housing in Moraga Canyon. Opinions on the plan’s community feedback page range from the plan being “well thought out” to serious concerns of traffic congestion during a fire evacuation. “Almost all of the people who live in the district area that would be impacted by this addition of density are opposed to this plan,” said one online comment. To view or share comments on the plan, visit its community feedback page at https://communityfeedback.opengov.com/portals/ piedmontca/Issue_14422. So, their pool is out of commission,” Krumins said. “Mentally, for myself, the coaches, and the players; we’ve been here before. It’s nothing new, but what I like about this team is they are relentless and just want to get in the water. For me, it’s about consistency and having consistent workout times. If we can get consistent pool time, wherever that is, we’re going to be fine,” he added. With a talented team, Krumins hopes they can recapture the magic of their NCS title-winning team in 2023, who did it all without a pool to call home. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council accepted a $748,000 grant for the Moraga Avenue Pedestrian Safety Project at their Monday, August 18 Council meeting. The project will include the installation of bulb-outs, flashing beacons, and other pedestrian and bike improvements at four intersections along Moraga Avenue. Both the 2014 Piedmont Bike/ Pedestrian Master Plan and the 2021 Safer Streets Plan recommended pedestrian safety improvements to the following intersections on Moraga Ave. • Ramona Ave. • Highland Ave. • Mesa Ave. • Red Rock Rd. The improvements also include a proposed “No right turn on Red” sign from Moraga onto Highland, heading uphill. This follows complaints from cyclists about cars at the intersection. The City applied for the grant last fall with the Alameda County Transportation Commission (ACTC). Council approved a resolution of support for staff to file the application on October 7, 2024.
articles.title: Piedmont to receive $748,000 for pedestrian improvements on Moraga Avenue

articles.text: Kiran Bawa working at her desk in City Hall. Now back at work for the City of Piedmont, Finance Director Kiran Bawa has been adjusting well to work in the California weather. With over two decades of public sector finance experience, Bawa began her service with the City on July 2, 2025. As Finance Director, Bawa oversees citywide finance functions, including accounting, payroll, auditing, purchasing, investments, and the development of the City’s annual budget. Bawa is taking over after the retirement of Finance Director Mike Szczech. The appointment marks a return to Piedmont for Bawa, who previously served as Piedmont’s Finance Director from 2016-2017. For the past eight years, she has been Finance Director for the City of Falls Church, VA, where she oversaw a $137 million General Fund budget. Before joining Piedmont in 2016, Bawa served as Budget Director for the City of Oakland, where she implemented budget balancing measures to expand services while addressing financial obligations, and as Manager of Capital Planning & Grants at AC Transit, where she was responsible for the District’s $500 million capital budget. “I’m really, really grateful – deeply grateful for the opportunity to be able to come back [to Piedmont],” said Bawa. Bawa found out the City was hiring while referencing some of the work she did during her last stay in Piedmont. My hope is that we continue to come together to solve these challenges together. –James Bohanion Improve Business License efficiency in Piedmont Editor: The City recently published an article in The Exedra declaring that it is going to pursue residents over business taxes. I have a feeling a huge percentage of residents are not abiding by this law and had – and still have – no idea. Many are about to get hit with extra paperwork and a tax bill of thousands of dollars. I urge the Mayor and City Council to immediately, retroactively, end this unnecessary bureaucracy. Simply institute a reasonable minimum threshold, below which no registration is required or tax due – like what San Francisco recently did. Piedmont requires anyone doing business here – even consultants or home-based small business of any size – to get a license and report gross receipts each year. This is a burden for a large number of residents who either operate small businesses or are consultants and who are still required to comply with this arcane law. The minimum fee of $100 is meaningless to the city’s budget and just a waste of time for residents. The percentage fee is unfair to contractors, which is where the world is heading.
