articles.text: All businesses operating in Piedmont – including home-based operations, independent contractors, consultants, freelancers, online storefronts – are required to obtain a City business license. Businesses currently operating without a required license may soon receive a letter providing information about how to register and pay applicable taxes. Businesses that have not previously registered may be responsible for back taxes for the last three years. However, penalties typically associated with late registration will be waived if businesses register and pay within 90 days from the date on their notification letter. Business owners can now register and pay applicable taxes quickly and easily through a new online system at piedmont. hdlgov.com. Support is available through a dedicated customer support line at (510) 250-1975, with experts available to guide business owners through the registration process and help calculate taxes based on individual business structures. Businesses requiring a license include: • Home-based businesses (includes 1099 self-employment) • Online storefronts or “influencers” with a Piedmont business address • Landlords operating long- • term or short-term rentals Contractors and consultants working in Piedmont, even if located elsewhere Notification letters to unregistered businesses are part of the compliance audit recommended by the City’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee. The audit follows a public education campaign conducted earlier this year to raise awareness of existing laws among community members. Businesses that need assistance or have questions about their registration status can contact customer support at (510) 250-1975 or visit piedmont. ca.gov/ComplianceLetter. She is also excited to see construction finish on the Community Pool Project, having grown up in swimming sports herself. With the pool project projected to come to a close this month, Bawa addressed concerns of the pool’s perceived cost overrun. “The cost did go up, but not any more than [the City] can handle,” said Bawa. “With the Measure UU funds and the contributions and the grants that we have received, the pool is slated to finish within the budget.” The pool project was initially approved for a bond of $19.5 million through Measure UU. The total cost budget of the pool is now $34.9 million. With the budget for City projects racing into the tens of millions, managing Piedmont’s Finances is difficult, highly detailed work. Luckily, Bawa is no stranger to managing bonds. Among her achievements while working in Virginia Bawa was credited with architecting the bond referendum to finance a new $120 million high school, maintaining the City’s AAA bond ratings, and helping to craft a revenue sharing agreement between the government and the schools. Bawa believes that the most important traits for a Finance Manager are accountability, integrity, job knowledge, teamwork and collaboration. She also stresses the importance of longterm financial stability and proper infrastructure maintenance. “Finance is such a field that it doesn’t flow naturally to a lot of people – and it’s very crucial in making decisions,” said Bawa. She recounts long hours in the past, working sometimes until 3 a.m. with Council Members and Committees during her time with the City of Oakland.

articles.text: Share feedback by Friday, August 22 The City is inviting residents to share comments on its Draft Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) – a roadmap showing what Piedmont could do now to reduce or avoid potential damages from natural hazards like earthquakes, wildfires, and severe weather – by Friday, August 22. Residents can read the draft LHMP online at piedmont.ca.gov/ LHMP and submit comments online at https://communityfeedback.opengov.com/portals/piedmontca/Issue_14549 or by email to LHMP@piedmont.ca.gov. The draft LHMP identifies 21 actions that could help reduce risk to Piedmont, including: • Strengthening resilience of IT infrastructure through redundancy and backup systems • Retrofitting or replacing critical facilities to meet modern seismic safety codes • Annual fire fuel mitigation on City property • Strengthening local building and fire codes to require wildfire-resistant construction and more stringent vegetation management standards Since the draft LHMP was existing and new projects to improve evacuation routes • Backup power projects to ensure redundancy • Storm drain upgrades and other drainage improvements Including an action in the LHMP does not guarantee that it will happen. Rather, it positions the City to apply for state and federal mitigation grants that could support implementing that project. About the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) identifies the natural hazards that pose greatest risk to Piedmont and documents how each hazard would be likely to impact Piedmont if it were to occur. It then seeks to identify and prioritize actions the City and community could take now that would prevent or reduce those impacts. Getting community input on the draft LHMP is the final step before finalizing the document and submitting it to Cal OES for approval. Learn more about the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update process and read the draft plan at piedmont.ca.gov/LHMP. Residents can read the draft LHMP online at piedmont.ca.gov/LHMP published, the project team identified an additional 16 projects to include in the final document based on community input, including: • Establishing a Red Flag Weather policy for Piedmont • Additional wildfire mitigation measures such as enhancing vegetation management programs for private property and adding fire hydrants for better coverage • Considering inf rast r ucture improvements to roads, sidewalks and paths during
articles.title: Survey: City roadmap for reducing damage from natural disasters

articles.text: On Aug. 27, 2025, the Beacon Grand Hotel will host Elegance Meets Impact, a fashion show and auction benefiting George Mark Children’s House. Legendary designer Lily Samii, known for dressing senators, royals and Hollywood stars, will step out of retirement for the one-night-only event. Samii will present 20 gowns from her private collection, each selected for the show and auction. “I thought my days of runway shows were behind me, but the children of George Mark called me back,” Samii said. “Each gown I’ve chosen carries a piece of my heart. If my work can bring comfort and care to even one child, then it is worth every moment out of retirement.” Founded more than 20 years ago, George Mark Children’s House is the first freestanding pediatric palliative care center in the United States. It provides respite, end-of-life care and family support in a setting that blends the warmth of home with hospital-level expertise. Parents are given space to rest, siblings receive counseling, and children take part in art, music and play therapy. Guests at Elegance Meets Impact will see San Francisco leaders, philanthropists and community figures walk the runway in Samii’s designs. A raffle will also award two United Airlines Premium Economy roundtrip tickets to Europe, valued at $17,000. Proceeds from the evening will go directly to compassionate care for children and families. That includes medical support, grief counseling, meals, overnights for parents and programs that focus on quality of life. The impact of support from Lily Samii will participate in a one-night-only fashion show and auction benefiting George Mark Children’s House on August 27. the event will be felt directly at George Mark Children’s House. Funds raised will help provide respite care so parents can rest while children receive expert medical support, end-of-life care in a home-like setting, bereavement and grief counseling for families and siblings, play and art therapy that give children joy and connection, and comprehensive family support such as meals and overnight stays. The event itself will take place Wednesday, Aug. 27, 2025, at the Beacon Grand Hotel in San Francisco’s Union Square. A VIP reception begins at 5:30 p.m., followed by general admission at 6 p.m. Seating is limited, and tickets can be reserved at georgemark.org/elegance-meets-impact.
articles.title: Lily Samii Returns to the Runway for George Mark Children’s House

articles.text: Piedmont’s school board will convene tonight, Wednesday, August 20, in a new location – the second floor of the Alan Harvey Theater in the Drama classroom. The regularly scheduled meeting begins at 7:00 p.m.; community members are invited to participate in the proceedings remotely via Zoom.us/j/88189454401 or in-person, in the theater at 800 Magnolia Avenue. The meeting will be the first of the new school year and the first since June 25, and there will be plenty of business to discuss. Following Dr. Elise Marks and the teachers union’s comments, CSEA employees will have time at the microphone. After remarks from Piedmont Education Foundation, community members will have the chance to speak to any item not listed on the agenda. Superintendent Jennifer Hawn’s remarks will include a slide show of the first day of school, and board members will also give their individual board reports. New student board members will be introduced and formally appointed to the board. For the fall semester Saniyah Johnson will be the student representative to the board for Millennium High School (MHS) and Hunter Fasteau will represent Piedmont High School (PHS). In the spring, Charli Panico will be the student leader on the board for PHS and Ben Ramakrishnan will represent MHS. Presentations tonight will provide details on the “State of the Adult School” and provide a “45- Day Budget Revision” following Governor Newsom’s final State Budget Act. “Not later than 45 days after the Governor signs the annual Budget Act, the school district shall make available for public review any revisions in revenues and expenditures that it has made to its budget to reflect the funding made available by that Budget Act,” states Education Code 42127(h). The meeting will also approve a resolution allowing temporary borrowing from Alameda County. A first reading will be conducted on PUSD employees’ use of technology. As student

articles.text: Piedmont Middle Schoolers are invited to audition for this year’s fall musical, Cats: Young Actors’ Edition. All 6th, 7th, and 8th graders enrolled at Piedmont Middle School are invited to audition for the school’s fall musical, Cats: Young Actors’ Edition, with music by Andrew Lloyd Webber. The musical is based upon Old Possum’s Book Of Practical Cats by T.S. Eliot. Performances are scheduled for Friday to Sunday, October 24-26. Rehearsals are three times a week, Tuesdays (3:45-5:45 p.m.) as well as Wednesday and Thursday evenings (6:30-8:30 p.m.). Audition submissions are due by 8:00 p.m. on Monday, August 25 and should be submitted via Google form. Callbacks are in person on Thursday, August 28 from 4:00-8:30 p.m. More information about auditions will be made available to PMS students. For questions, contact director Amy Moorhead at amoorhead@piedmont.k12. ca.us. High School For Piedmont High School and Millennium High School students, Moorhead will direct and produce the musical Grease. Jim Jacobs and Warren Casey wrote the book, music and lyrics for this rollicking musical evoking the look and sound of the 1950s. PHS/MHS performances are Thursday, January 29, at 7:00 p.m., Friday, January 30, at 7:00 p.m., Saturday, January 31, at 7:00 p.m. and Sunday, February Piedmont High School and Millennium High School students will produce the musical Grease. 1, at 4:00 p.m. Auditions for Grease are open to all students enrolled in Piedmont High School or Millennium High School. Online audition submissions are due the week of September 15 with callbacks later that week. Full information about auditions will be made available to all PHS/MHS students in midlate August.

articles.text: Piedmont High School began the 2025–26 school year with notable changes on campus, namely a newly implemented ban on cell phones during class. Students are no longer able to access their phones at school, excluding lunch time, a change that students are still adjusting to. With last year’s seniors having graduated, the halls feel different without the Class of 2025’s familiar presence. On the first day, seniors and freshmen were celebrated with donut holes before going to their first classes. As always, the shift from summer break to textbooks, long classes, and lectures feels jarring for both teachers and students, but over the first week, a sense of cohesion among the student body has begun to take shape. The week ended with a schoolwide assembly, which included introductions of Dr. David Yoshihara, the principal, and Joseph Marik, the assistant principal, and the ASB representatives for the year. Dr. Yoshihara has also announced the continuation of the Highlander Hunt and a surprising new addition to PHS school spirit – our new mascot in the form of a purple and gold lion. Students found the mascot walking around and greeting them at the front door. The school is currently looking for suggestions of a name for the new mascot. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern writer with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: Life at PHS gets rolling for new school year

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, August 20, 2025 SchOOLs School Board Meeting tonight By Jay Russell Piedmont’s school board will convene tonight, Wednesday, August 20, in a new location – the second floor of the Alan Harvey Theater in the Drama classroom. The regularly scheduled meeting begins at 7:00 p.m.; community members are invited to participate in the proceedings remotely via Zoom.us/j/88189454401 or in-person, in the theater at 800 Magnolia Avenue. The meeting will be the first of the new school year and the first since June 25, and there will be plenty of business to discuss. Following Dr. Elise Marks and the teachers union’s comments, CSEA employees will have time at the microphone. After remarks from Piedmont Education Foundation, community members will have the chance to speak to any item not listed on the agenda. Superintendent Jennifer Hawn’s remarks will include a slide show of the first day of school, and board members will also give their individual board reports. New student board members will be introduced and formally appointed to the board. For the fall semester Saniyah Johnson will be the student representative to the board for Millennium High School (MHS) and Hunter Fasteau will represent Piedmont High School (PHS). In the spring, Charli Panico will be the student leader on the board for PHS and Ben Ramakrishnan will represent MHS. Presentations tonight will provide details on the “State of the Adult School” and provide a “45- Day Budget Revision” following Governor Newsom’s final State Budget Act. “Not later than 45 days after the Governor signs the annual Budget Act, the school district shall make available for public review any revisions in revenues and expenditures that it has made to its budget to reflect the funding made available by that Budget Act,” states Education Code 42127(h). The meeting will also approve a resolution allowing temporary borrowing from Alameda County. A first reading will be conducted on PUSD employees’ use of technology. As student usage of cell phones has been restricted this year, this item will provide community members, teachers and staff the opportunity to discuss policy around their own usage of technology including cell phones, computers and AI software. Currently, no changes to the policy are recommended for employees. The consent calendar includes an extensive Personnel Action Report which contains new hires, extra compensation and resignations by teachers and school staff members that have occurred since the end of June. articles.text: On August 19 Chabot Space & Science Center marked a remarkable milestone – 25 years atop Oakland’s Skyline Boulevard. Perched amid the largest stand of coastal redwoods in the East Bay, the nonprofit Center has become a hub for hands-on space and science learning, community engagement, and cosmic inspiration. The journey to Skyline began long before the current facility opened its doors in 2000. Founded in 1883 as an astronomical observatory in Oakland, Chabot has a 142-year legacy of inspiring curiosity about the universe. Its move to its current 13-acre site in Redwood Regional Park allowed the institution to expand its vision: a science center that connects learners of all ages to the wonders of space and our planet. When the new Chabot Space & Science Center opened on August 19, 2000, visitors encountered two historic refracting telescopes—Leah (1883) and Rachel (1916)—alongside a full-dome planetarium, classrooms, and interactive exhibits. In 2003, the 36-inch reflecting telescope called Nellie joined the sky-watching family, making Chabot home to the largest public observatory complex in the Western United States. These telescopes have not only delighted amateur astronomers but also contributed to research, including Near Earth Object studies and even relaying information to NASA during the Apollo 13 descent. Over the past quarter century, Chabot has expanded both its facilities and its reach. In 2005, new classrooms and teacher preparation spaces opened with Measure G funding. In 2008, the Center celebrated its 125th anniversary with a year of public programs, and in 2018, Measure WW funded the Observation Deck expansion that added 3,200 square feet of outdoor viewing space. Chabot’s mission has always been to make science and space accessible to all. Today, the center offers a vibrant mix of planetarium shows, workshops, tinkering spaces, lectures, community events, and school programs. Its education team partners closely with Oakland and Contra Costa County schools, emphasizing inquiry-based learning, inclusion, and collaboration—fostering the critical thinking skills essential for the 21st-century workforce. In 2021, a groundbreaking partnership with NASA Ames Research Center brought the NASA Ames Visitor Center to Chabot, complete with hands-on activities, mission artifacts, and exhibits on cutting-edge research. This collaboration also laid the groundwork for the Oakland Space Academy, a workforce development pathway for local youth. As Chabot heads into the rest of 2025 and beyond, the focus is on deepening connections with the community. “Times of transition can be powerful and catalytic moments,” said Adam Tobin, Executive Director and CEO. “When I consider these milestones, reflecting on all that we have accomplished and the impact that we have had, I firmly believe that Chabot’s best days are still to come. In so many ways, Chabot is as well positioned as we have ever been to fulfill our dream of making science inspiring, accessible, and empowering for all.” To celebrate its 25th anniversary on Skyline Boulevard, Chabot will offer programs, events, and activities designed to engage the community, build relationships, and give back to the people of the area that have supported it for the past quarter century. From its 19th-century beginnings to its 21st-century innovations, Chabot remains committed to a simple yet profound mission: to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the Universe and Planet Earth. As the next chapter begins, the view from Skyline has never looked brighter. We hope you’ll join us up on the hill as we celebrate the next 25 years and all that is to come. For more information about Chabot Space and Science Center, 510-336-7300 or go to our website at chabotspace.org. Photo by Mostly Harmless Photos A young boy peers through Rachel, the historic 20-inch refractor telescope, watching the night sky unfold before him. 4426 Piedmont Avenue, Oakland • www.fentonscremery.com • 568-7000

articles.text: Beach 4th grade teacher Ben Spencer offers after-school enrichment class on Mondays Blacktops & Books students play a real-life version of Hungry, Hungry Hippos. Beach Elementary School 4th grade teacher Ben Spencer is offering an after-school enrichment class, Blacktops & Books, for 3rd-5th grade students. The class begins with 50 minutes of high-energy outdoor games and activities and then moves inside for another 50 minutes, where students will complete their homework and participate in academic activities and games. “Parents can expect their kids to have a unique, fun, and academic experience when they participate in Blacktops & Books,” said Spencer. “I’m most looking forward to the kids having fun, developing a love for playing games, and making lifelong, meaningful friendships.” Kids will get a chance to have exercise and will be given an opportunity to get a majority of their weekly homework finished. “Students really benefit from being in a class that is made up of 3rd, 4th, and 5th graders. They all learn from each other. The older ones learn to be leaders and mentors. They also learn how to be patient. The younger kiddos learn valuable social skills and are able to gain a lot of academic confidence because they get support from the older students at Beach. It’s a win-win,” said Spencer. Spencer, who also is the Piedmont High School boys’ basketball coach, and has a knack for making academic work fun and organizing the most fun of outdoor, athletic activities. Enrollment is now open for Blacktops & Books. The first class begins at 3:10 p.m. on Monday, September 8 and the program runs through Monday, November 17. Parents can also sign up their kids for just the first hour of outdoor activities at a discounted price. Visit Homeroom.com/activities/63276 to enroll or email bspencer@piedmont.k12.ca.us. Students are shown playing Banana Tag at Beach School.
articles.title: Blacktops & Books

articles.text: Samantha Pell recently completed the requirements to be an Eagle Scout. She is a member of Piedmont’s Troop 1, and currently is studying in England for her high school sophomore year. Her Eagle Project was a mural of the Earth at Thornhill Elementary School in Montclair, surrounded by handprints of the outgoing fifth grade class. The mural occupies a wall that has been left empty for the past 10+ years. It surrounds one of the main gardens, adjacent to the playground. What was once a gaping hole in the vibrant and lush environment has now been transformed into a part of the overall environment, adding joy and engagement to the space. Additionally, my dedication serves to encourage the graduating class to return even after they leave, to care for the garden that they are now connected to on another level. On another note, the mural also serves to be a catalyst to Thornhill’s extensive environmental and sustainability programs which greatly benefit the Troop 1 Eagle Scout Samantha Pell K-5 children. This includes the school wide gardening classes taught by Alexis Lavine-Moore with whom Samantha worked on the mural. “It was my goal to help the garden become an even more special space for students, like the garden during my time at Havens Elementary School,” Pell added. Samantha Pell’s Eagle Project was a mural at Thornhill Elementary.
articles.title: Samantha Pell achieves Eagle

During the assembly, PHS Association of Student Body (ASB) representatives, from each grade, led their respective classes in class dances and chants, coalescing each grade into synchronism. ASB reps also took to center court with ASB Director Haley Adams to perform their own dance choreography. A highlight of the assembly Freshmen cheer during the assembly. got students active by having ASB reps compete in a miniature scavenger hunt against the other grades. ASB reps surveyed the stands of their classmates for the items and then ran to center court with the requested item. “Bring me a water bottle with a straw,” one round of the scavenger hunt requested. One student rep, found a water bottle near the locker room, opened it to check for a rubber straw, and then ran to the center court with the lid and straw. articles.text: With the new school year approaching, the Class of 2026 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. If there is an athlete you’d like to see featured, email news@ piedmont-post.com. P.J. BRAYER Basketball, Lacrosse P.J. Brayer is a two-sport athlete in basketball and lacrosse. He earned All-League honors in both sports, receiving an honorable selection in basketball and a firstStaff Photos P.J. Brayer was an All-League recipient in basketball and lacrosse. team selection in lacrosse. On the basketball team Brayer was a forward and proved to be a tone-setter for Ben Spencer’s squad that reached the North Coast Section championship game. In addition to providing a presence on the boards, he’s capable of playing outside and knocking down 3-pointers. He had 12 points in Piedmont’s CIF State tournament game with No. 8 Natomas, nine points in Piedmont’s NCS 78-69 win over No. 9 Bethel, and 10 points in a narrow 59-58 league win over Castro Valley. On the lacrosse team, Brayer is a long stick midfielder. Similar to the basketball team, Brayer plays a critical role on defense and offense. He had one goal and five assists in a heated 8-7 win over archrival Bishop O’Dowd and one goal and three ground balls in a 9-3 win over Dublin Stella Wilk was a leading outside hitter on last year’s girls’ volleyball team. STELLA WILK Volleyball Stella Wilk is set to be a twoyear starter on the volleyball team. She proved to be one of Piedmont’s leading outside hitters in 2024. The girls’ volleyball team went 3-19 last season, a rebuilding year with two freshmen and six sophomores. She will be the only senior starter from last year’s team. She was a critical part of Piedmont’s 3-0 shutout win over Alameda, recording eight kills in their 25-13, 25-13, 25-22 victory. Adrian Kondakov is a leader on Piedmont High’s football team as an offensive and defensive lineman. ADRIAN KONDAKOV Football Adrian Kondakov will line up as a starting defensive tackle and offensive tackle. He earned an honorable mention for AllLeague honors last year. Kondakov returns to the lineup as the only full-time starter on the offensive line. He has a unique leadership role and will help lead four other starting offensive linemen, while also playing as a defensive lineman. Piedmont’s football team finished last season with a 10-2 overall and won the Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division title. It was the second league title in a row after winning the Shoreline in 2023. He was a starter on the Highlanders’ North Coast Section semifinal appearance and helped give the school its first NCS win since 2017 when they beat No. 6 Fortuna 42-46 in the first round as the No. 3 seed.

articles.text: Briana Webb to play at Fresno State Piedmont High’s basketball program has established a reputation for sending athletes students to the collegiate level. Luke Barrett, PHS Class of 2020, recently signed a professional contract to play for Arka Gdynia of Poland. On the girls’ side, 2025 graduate Briana Webb is now set to continue her basketball career at Fresno State. in the Round of 64, but fell to No. 2 Alabama 80-66 the following round. He played a critical part in SMC’s opening round win over Vandy. He sent a pair of assists for 3-pointers in the second half, including one to Augustas Marčiulionis give his team a 53-50 lead with 4:33 left. He also knocked down a 3-pointer to give St. Mary’s a 56-50 lead with 2:01 left. He finished with a double-double against Vanderbilt with 12 points, 10 rebounds, and two assists. Against Alabama, he played 37 minutes, logging six points, seven rebounds, and an assist. The Gaels finished the season with a 29-6 record. Photo courtesy of St. Mary’s Athletics Luke Barrett, PHS Class of 2020, has signed with Arka Gdynia of Poland’s Orlen Basket Liga. LUKE BARRETT Luke Barrett recently finished as a senior leader at St. Mary’s College and has joined Arka Gdynia in Poland’s Orlen Basket Liga. He graduated from Piedmont High after leading the school to the D4 North Coast Section title, which remains the last Section championship for the boys’ basketball team. Arka is a nine-time championship winning team and have had several former players appear in the NBA. They start their season on September 29 with the regular season ending in May. Gdynia is a city on the Baltic coast of northern Poland, resting along the Gulf of Gdansk with a population of 257,000. “I’m getting ready to get to Gdynia. I can’t wait to meet the team, get to work, and have a great season… I’m beyond excited and grateful to be in Poland for the first time. I’m ready to see this beautiful country,” Barrett said in the team’s announcement of his arrival. Barrett is joining the team on a month-long trial before potentially landing his first full-time professional contract. “Luke agreed to a month-long trial, which really impressed me as a coach. This shows that he is confident in his abilities. Together with the coaching staff, we will carefully evaluate his performance in person,” Arka head coach Mantas Česnauskis said. Barrett joins Arka after helping St. Mary’s earn the No. 7 seeded team in the eastern bracket of the NCAA Tournament. The Gaels beat No. 10 Vanderbilt 59-56 in comeback fashion Staff Photo Briana Webb, PHS Class of 2025, is set to continue her basketball career at Fresno State. BRIANA WEBB Briana Webb recently graduated from Piedmont High after joining the school as a senior. She had an instant impact on Bryan Gardere’s basketball team, earning one of our Breakout Player of the Year mentions. She was a first-team All-League recipient and was named Athlete of the Month in January. She joins a Division 1 program at Fresno State, which plays in the Mountain West Conference. The Bulldogs went 19-15 last season and reached the MWC Semifinals as the No. 6 seed before losing to No. 2 Wyoming 57-45. Webb logged a double-double in Piedmont’s 70-48 win over Salesian in the NCS Open Division’s Fifth-Place Final. She also led scoring with 15 points in a 50-47 regular season win over arch rival Bishop O’Dowd. She had important performances in some of Piedmonts more critical games, including 13 points in Piedmont’s overtime 61-52 win over Clayton Valley on, she logged 19 points and eight rebounds in their 54-44 win over Alameda, had 19 points and seven boards in their narrow 53-51 loss to Antelope, and led scoring Webb also led scoring with 22 points in an 81-66 loss to Centennial, a top three rated team in Nevada.

articles.text: Kids are back to school, and student-athletes are getting back into their groove ahead of the upcoming fall sports season. Piedmont High will field nine teams for the fall season with both cross-country teams, girls’ volleyball, girls’ tennis, football, flag football, girls’ golf, and both water polo teams. Here’s a look at three key athletes for the upcoming season. JIMMY LAGIOS Football Jimmy Lagios continues a new family tradition, inheriting Piedmont High’s varsity football team’s starting quarterback role from his brother, Markos, who graduated earlier this year. He’ll wear the same No. 4. In addition to playing the junior varsity football team as a freshman, Lagios earned starting minutes on the varsity boys’ soccer team and varsity baseball team. We named Lagios our honorable mention for our 2025 Freshman of the Year award for his contributions to the boys’ soccer team reaching the D4 NCS Final as the top seed and winning the D5 CIF NorCal championship with the No. 5 seed as a freshman starter. Lagios was credited with three assists and one goal as a key cog in coach Ben Russell’s central midfield. He logged one of his assists in Piedmont’s 4-2 win over No. 9 Urban in NCS, helping give his team a 2-1 lead when laying off a pass to Logan Faucher. He scored his lone goal on a header in a 3-1 Staff Photos Jimmy Lagios is set to be the football team’s starting quarterback as a sophomore. win over Hayward during the regular season. Soccer finished its season with a 13-4-9 (W-T-L) record. In baseball, Lagios had two appearances as a pitcher and struck out five batters. LEIGHTON MAND Cross Country Leighton Mand is entering her third year as a varsity runner for the cross country team. She earned out 2025 Sophomore of the Year award and was our honorable mention for 2024 Freshman of the Year. She was our Athlete of the Month in November and our honorable mention for October. Mand reached the CIF State Cross Country Championship last year, where she finished 74th of 201 athletes with a time of 19:52.7. At the NCS Championship, Mand placed sixth of 127 runners to qualify for State. She also finished fifth out of 40 runners at the WACC Championship in 19:16.8. She is a distance runner on the track team in the spring. Last season, Mand reached the NCS Meet of Champions in the 1600 meters and was a member of the 4x800 relay team. In the 1600, Leighton finished the season 17th of 24 at the Meet of Champions with a time of 5:23.46. To get there, she was sixth of 23 at the NCS Bayshore Championship in 5:24.42, while she finished fourth of 37 at the WACC Championship in 5:25.80. On the 4x800 team alongside Nikita Gorelik, Skylar Best, and Caroline Taylor, the team finished 12th of 16 at the Meet of Champions with a time of 10:07.23. They also placed third of 11 teams at the League meet Bayshore in 10:13.46. LUKE MCAULIFFE Water Polo Luke McAuliffe is entering his third year as the Highlanders’ starting goalie this fall. We named him the Post’s 2024 Sophomore of the Year after he helped lead the school to its first-ever North Coast Section championship. Last season, PHS finished 16-10 and reached the Division 2 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 4 seed. They lost a heated 14-11 game to No. 5 Washington in NCS, but bashed No. 13 Freedom 17-9 in the opening round. In 2023 as a sophomore McAuliffe was instrumental in the school’s only NCS title. As the No. 4 seed PHS beat No. 5 Newark Memorial 12-9 in the quarterfinals, upset No. 1 Marin Academy 13-9 in the semifinals, and defeated league rival No. 3 Alameda 10-8 for the championship. Photo by Becky Spies Leighton Mand enters her junior year on the cross country team. She was our 2025 Sophomore of the Year and our honorable mention for 2024 Freshman of the Year. Staff Photos Luke McAuliffe is entering his third year as Piedmont’s starting goalie on the water polo team.

In this week’s edition of Piedmont athletes in college, we take a look at Claire Dean of Stanford’s gymnastics team, Julien Lee of Colorado College’s cross country and track teams, and Perséas Gioukaris of San Francisco State’s basketball team. CLAIRE DEAN Gymnastics Stanford University Claire Dean, PHS Class of 2022, is entering her senior year on Stanford’s gymnastics team. She helped the Cardinal win the 2025 ACC Championship and reach the second round of the NCAA Regional Championships. Stanford finished with a 19-6 overall record in 2025. The Cardinal beat North Carolina by just .55 of a point, beating the Tarheels 197.775-197.225. For the ACC Championship, Dean recorded a score of 9.850 on the balance beam and a 9.900 on the floor exercise. In 2024, Dean helped Stanford finish fourth in the Pac-12 Championships and reach the NCAA Championships semifinals. Photo courtesy of SFState Athletics Perséas Gioukaris, PHS Class of 2023, earned Academic All-District honors with San Francisco State. PERSÉAS GIOUKARIS Basketball JULIEN LEE, TRACK Cross-country Colorado College Julien Lee, PHS Class of 2024, is entering his sophomore year on Colorado College’s cross country and track and field teams. Last year, Lee competed in four different 8K meets in cross country and another seven in track. In cross country his best time came at the 2024 Roadrunner Invitational in Denver, clocking a 28:15.3 to finish 136th of 187 runners. Another productive run was at the 2024 Colorado Springs Open, where he placed 96th of 130 with a time of 28:29.4. Lee made it to the Southern Collegiate Athletic Conference Track and Field Championship in San Francisco State Perséas Gioukaris, PHS Class of 2023, finished her sophomore year on San Francisco State’s basketball team. She earned College Sports Communicators Academic All-District last season. San Francisco State finished 2025 with a 9-18 record with Gioukaris playing a role. She appeared in all 26 games and started twice for 291 total minutes. She finished the season with 47 points, 25 rebounds, 12 assists, 16 steals and two blocks. Known for her quick hands on defense, she had a season-high three steals in an 84-70 loss to Chico State. She was a starter on Piedmont’s 2023 Division 4 North Coast Section and Western Alameda County Conference championship team. With Piedmont, she earned first-team All-League honors after being forced to miss her junior year due to CIF transfer rules. She had 12 points and two steals in Piedmont’s 75-49 win over Branson for the NCS title. Photo courtesy of Colorado College Athletics Julien Lee, PHS Class of 2024, will be a sophomore on Colorado College’s cross country and track teams.

She earned College Sports Communicators Academic All-District last season. San Francisco State finished 2025 with a 9-18 record with Gioukaris playing a role. She appeared in all 26 games and started twice for 291 total minutes. She finished the season with 47 points, 25 rebounds, 12 assists, 16 steals and two blocks. Known for her quick hands on defense, she had a season-high three steals in an 84-70 loss to Chico State. She was a starter on Piedmont’s 2023 Division 4 North Coast Section and Western Alameda County Conference championship team. Athletes to watch this fall at Piedmont High By Jonathan Comeaux Kids are back to school, and student-athletes are getting back into their groove ahead of the upcoming fall sports season. Piedmont High will field nine teams for the fall season with both cross-country teams, girls’ volleyball, girls’ tennis, football, flag football, girls’ golf, and both water polo teams. Here’s a look at three key athletes for the upcoming season. JIMMY LAGIOS Football Jimmy Lagios continues a new family tradition, inheriting Piedmont High’s varsity football team’s starting quarterback role from his brother, Markos, who graduated earlier this year. He’ll wear the same No. 4. In addition to playing the junior varsity football team as a freshman, Lagios earned starting minutes on the varsity boys’ soccer team and varsity baseball team. We named Lagios our honorable mention for our 2025 Freshman of the Year award for his contributions to the boys’ soccer team reaching the D4 NCS Final as the top seed and winning the D5 CIF NorCal championship with the No. 5 seed as a freshman starter. Lagios was credited with three assists and one goal as a key cog in coach Ben Russell’s central midfield. He logged one of his assists in Piedmont’s 4-2 win over No. 9 Urban in NCS, helping give his team a 2-1 lead when laying off a pass to Logan Faucher. He scored his lone goal on a header in a 3-1 Staff Photos Jimmy Lagios is set to be the football team’s starting quarterback as a sophomore. win over Hayward during the regular season. Soccer finished its season with a 13-4-9 (W-T-L) record. In baseball, Lagios had two appearances as a pitcher and struck out five batters. LEIGHTON MAND Cross Country Leighton Mand is entering her third year as a varsity runner for the cross country team. She earned out 2025 Sophomore of the Year award and was our honorable mention for 2024 Freshman of the Year. She was our Athlete of the Month in November and our honorable mention for October. Mand reached the CIF State Cross Country Championship last year, where she finished 74th of 201 athletes with a time of 19:52.7. At the NCS Championship, Mand placed sixth of 127 runners to qualify for State. She also finished fifth out of 40 runners at the WACC Championship in 19:16.8. She is a distance runner on the track team in the spring. Last season, Mand reached the NCS Meet of Champions in the 1600 meters and was a member of the 4x800 relay team. In the 1600, Leighton finished the season 17th of 24 at the Meet of Champions with a time of 5:23.46. To get there, she was sixth of 23 at the NCS Bayshore Championship in 5:24.42, while she finished fourth of 37 at the WACC Championship in 5:25.80. On the 4x800 team alongside Nikita Gorelik, Skylar Best, and Caroline Taylor, the team finished 12th of 16 at the Meet of Champions with a time of 10:07.23. They also placed third of 11 teams at the League meet Bayshore in 10:13.46. LUKE MCAULIFFE Water Polo Luke McAuliffe is entering his third year as the Highlanders’ starting goalie this fall. We named him the Post’s 2024 Sophomore of the Year after he helped lead the school to its first-ever North Coast Section championship. Last season, PHS finished 16-10 and reached the Division 2 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 4 seed. They lost a heated 14-11 game to No. 5 Washington in NCS, but bashed No. 13 Freedom 17-9 in the opening round. In 2023 as a sophomore McAuliffe was instrumental in the school’s only NCS title. As the No. 4 seed PHS beat No. 5 Newark Memorial 12-9 in the quarterfinals, upset No. 1 Marin Academy 13-9 in the semifinals, and defeated league rival No. 3 Alameda 10-8 for the championship. RAVI SILVERBERG Basketball Piedmont High Class of 2025 Macalester College Class of 2029 Ravi Silverberg graduated from Piedmont High with the Class of 2025 after leading the basketball team to the North Coast Section title game as the squad’s leading scorer. He was the Post’s Athlete of the Month in January and February. In the post-season Silverberg scored 18 points in Piedmont’s 87-49 win over Ukiah in the first round, scored 25 points in their 78-69 quarterfinals finals win over Bethel—scoring his 1,000th career point in the process. He scored 17 points in their semifinals’ 60-53 win over Windsor and finished with 33 points in the Highlanders’ 75-70 loss to St. Patrick in the championship game. He also scored 18 points in PHS’ 84-71 loss to Natomas in the D4 CIF State first round. Ravi details his workout regimen ahead of his freshman season on Macalester College’s basketball team. What was your workout program this summer? This summer, my routine included weightlifting five times a week and playing basketball every day. I’ve been especially focused on getting a high volume of shots up during each session in the gym. What were your fitness goals for the summer? My main goals were to build strength, improve my athleticism, and become more consistent with my shooting. I’ve been working on extending my range and becoming more fluid shooting three-pointers off the dribble. How are you measuring your development? I track my progress by gradually increasing the difficulty of my workouts. Each week, I challenge myself with more advanced drills to push my limits and see growth. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I usually train with teammates and friends. I also apply techniques and guidance I’ve received from previous coaches, adapting them to create a personalized routine that suits me best. What was a recent milestone that you accomplished? A recent milestone was bench pressing 225 pounds which is something I’ve been working toward for a long time. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Half the battle is just showing up. Always be confident and trust the work you put in. articles.text: R e c r e a t i o n Dear PUSD Families & Staff: Congratulations on a wonderful first day of school! We are so excited to have students back, and it has been a day of joyful reunions between friends, teachers, and staff. Welcome back! We have a great year planned ahead, with many opportunities for our community to come together to discuss topics of focus for our district. We gathered feedback toward the end of last year, and there were many comments related to a desire for more rigor and focus on academics in our schools, across grade levels. This year, we will examine our Strategic Priority “Investing in Outstanding Academics” in staff and community meetings, reviewing our data, our current programs, and exploring ways in which we may improve or refine our programs. We look forward to a community process in which the voices of our staff, students, and parents come together to ensure the finest educational options for our students. Further down in this newsletter, you will see the list of meetings where you can voice your ideas. I also want to highlight our work in establishing a policy to adhere to the State’s new law, AB 3216, the Phone-Free Schools Act. At our elementary schools and middle school, mobile devices (phones, earbuds, watches, and other internet connected devices) are not permitted for use on campus during the school day. At our high schools, phones are permitted at lunch only. We recognize there are varying opinions on use of mobile devices, and we will hold meetings with students, staff, and parents throughout this year to continue to gather input on the impact of this policy on student well-being and academic success. Speaking of input, one emerging topic on which we could use input is related to the AC Transit change of bus routes, including the elimination of the upper Piedmont route, which impacts our students’ access to and from our campuses. Below you will find a “Pulse Check” quick survey to gather input. Enjoy these first days of school, and I look forward to connecting with you and our students throughout this school year. In Partnership, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent Pulse Check - AC Transit Bus Route Elimination As I shared above, AC Transit has changed their bus routes, including the elimination of the Upper Piedmont/Piedmont Estates route. We will be meeting with officials of AC Transit to discuss this change and advocate for reinstatement of this important transportation option for our families. We recognize the importance of public transportation to and from our schools, and we will share this information with AC Transit. In order to provide information on the impact of this change, we could use more information on how many families are impacted by the elimination of this bus route. We encourage you to offer your input in this short “Pulse Check” survey linked below. Out.smore.com/e/ad9xjq/ sIcrh9?__$u__ Welcome Back 2025! articles.text: This fall, Piedmont Council’s Cub Scout Packs welcome new families to join. Cub Scouts is Scouting America’s program for all youth in kindergarten through 5th grade. Parents and youth are invited to visit the Packs at your elementary school’s welcome back night and their first meeting of the year in September. Come by to meet the Pack leadership and see what Cub Scouts is all about! Cub Scouts delivers a unique program that gets kids outdoors, encourages their expression, and promotes character. “I love that Cub Scouts is open to any child from anywhere of any ability,” says Pack 4 Cubmaster Brad Cardon. “All that is required is an open mind, a sense of adventure, and to embrace the Cub Scout Motto: ‘Do Your Best.’” Families interested in joining Cub Scouts can stay tuned to the Council’s landing page for up-to-date information on Pack meetings and informational events: https://piedmontscouting. org/2025/08/12/which-pack-willyou-choose/. For Pack contact information and scheduling, or general Cub Scout questions, contact Piedmont’s District Executive Eris (eturner@piedmontbsa.org, 510- 844-4752) or stop by our office at 10 Highland Way. 2025 Day Camp sack race

articles.text: As children return to school this fall, singers with the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) are preparing for another season of music, joy and community. Children ages 5 to 18 can discover their voices, build confidence and make lasting friendships at PEBCC. The youngest singers, in Kinder Choir, are introduced to choral music in a nurturing and playful environment. In the Training Department, students learn fundamentals such as pitch, tempo, rhythm and phrasing. A typical rehearsal includes vocal warmups, group repertoire, music theory, vocal games and choreography. Singers learn how to blend with others while developing their musicianship. forming Department, students are ready for the highest level of children’s choral training. They take on advanced repertoire, sharpen stage presence and prepare for performances and collaborations in the Bay Area and beyond. Besides weekly rehearsals, students experience music through summer camps, workshops, combined rehearsals and collaborations with other choirs. Performing Department members serve as ambassadors for the Choir and the East Bay through local concerts, professional partnerships and appearances at international festivals. Two advanced choirs tour domestically and abroad each year, with recent trips to Finland, Estonia, England and Canada. In 2024, PEBCC won first prize at the Llangollen International Eisteddfod in Wales, earning the title “Young Choir of the World.” Tours often include homestays with local families, giving singers a chance to immerse themselves in a different culture. PEBCC also hosts the Golden Gate International Choral Festival every three years. The festival will return in July 2026, bringing choirs from around the world for a week of workshops, concerts and shared musical experiences. Every rehearsal at PEBCC is about learning, exploring and connecting. Singers grow through each level of the program, building skills, confidence and musical understanding along the way. Classes meet once or twice a week, with multiple schedule options to fit families’ needs. PEBCC is enrolling now for the 2025–26 season. Please contact Anastasia Fegbeitel-Finn, Program Director, Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir: afegbeitel-finn@piedmontchoirs.org Every Voice Belongs

articles.text: Parents, come learn about Girl Scouts and how to get started. Do you want your daughter to discover her confidence, explore the outdoors, learn to problem solve, improve her community and build lifelong friendships? We will have leaders available at an open house to share their experiences, answer questions and help get you organized and started. Girl Scouts is for all school age girls. articles.text: Marin Theatre Company (MTC) premieres Jonathan Spector’s Eureka Day on August 28, featuring nearly all its original cast members from the 2018 world premiere. The play is set at the Eureka Day School in Berkeley, California, portrayed as a “bastion of progressive ideals with a board of directors that values inclusion above all else.” The majority of the play takes place during meetings between parents and administrators concerning requirements for vaccination after an outbreak of mumps at the school. These meetings prompt school leadership to reconsider its liberal vaccine policy in comedic and dramatic ways. MTC’s production of Eureka Day is presented in partnership with Aurora Theatre Company, where the play had its world premiere in 2018, two years before the COVID-19 pandemic and the discourse over required vaccinations that followed. The New York Playwright Jonathan Spector Times called Eureka Day and Jonathan Spector’s “lively portrait of a debate over mandatory vaccinations” and “the perfect play for our age of disagreement.” An opening night post-show reception will be held on Tuesday, September 2. A pre-show presentation from MTC’s stage designer is held on Thursday, September 18. Eureka Day is appropriate for audience members 14 and older. Visit https://purchase.marintheatre.org/EventAvailability?EventId=49801 to purchase tickets.

articles.text: SFJAZZ opens its 2025- 26 season, curated by Executive Artistic Director Terence Blanchard, on September 4. Keyboard master, jazz organist and GRAMMY-nominated composer Cory Henry returns to SFJAZZ with his band the Funk Apostles on September 4 and 5, launching the company’s new season. Henry is a former member of Snarky Puppy and toured with many mainstream artists including Bruce Springsteen, Michael McDonald, Boyz II Men, Kenny Garrett, and The Roots. He launched his solo career in 2018 and released his debut single, “Trade It All”, with his band The Funk Apostles. Both Thursday and Friday concerts begin at 7:30 p.m. Henry also appears as a guest musician with the gospel group Blind Boys of Alabama on September 6 and 7. The nine-month season features over 350 concerts and includes performances by jazz luminaries as well as emerging young voices shaping the genre’s future. articles.text: Pianist Yuja Wang opens 2025-26 season The San Francisco Symphony begins its 2025-26 season with its annual opening gala on September 12, featuring pianist Yuja Wang and Seoul Philharmonic conductor Jaap van Zweden. The evening’s program features Piotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s Piano Concerto No. 1, John Adams’s Short Ride in a Fast Machine, and Ottorino Respighi’s Pines of Rome. The company’s opening gala concert is one of three programs Zweden conducts with the San Francisco Symphony this season. Wang, a renowned Chinese-born classical pianist from Beijing, made her San Francisco Symphony debut in 2006 and toured Asia with the company and its former conductor Michael Tilson Thomas in November 2012. She has since become a recurring guest pianist at Davies Symphony Hall and has performed with the Berlin Philharmonic, Oslo Philharmonic, Toronto Symphony Orchestra and more. Guests are invited to a complimentary preconcert reception featuring a celebratory toast, light bites, and entertainment in the orchestra lobby from 5:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. Specialty cocktails are available for purchase at the orchestra level bar following the gala concert until 9:30 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2025-26/Opening-Gala. Yuja Wang

articles.text: A scene from Kim’s Convenience which debuted in 2011 at the Toronto Fringe Festival. American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) premieres Playwright Ins Choi’s award-winning comedy-drama, Kim’s Convenience, opening Thursday, September 18. The play is based on Choi’s experiences working at his own family’s convenience store, Kim’s Grocer, in Scarborough, Toronto, and follows family patriarch Mr. Kim as he faces a changing neighborhood landscape and the gap between his values and those of his Canadian-born children. Choi called the play a “love letter to his parents and to all first-generation immigrants who call Canada their home.” Kim’s Convenience debuted on July 6, 2011 at the Toronto Fringe Festival to wide critical acclaim and inspired a popular Netflix series of the same name. “I’m very excited about bringing this production to A.C.T.,” said Choi. “Some of my nieces and nephews live in the Bay Area and have never seen me perform or this play which was co-inspired by their grandad’s store back in Toronto long ago. So this will be very special.” A.C.T. Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon said, “I am thrilled to be bringing Ins Choi, as playwright and actor, in his beautifully crafted and deeply personal prodigal son story Kim’s Convenience to A.C.T.” A.C.T. will present Our Store, Your Story, a photo and essay series that features San Francisco immigrant family-owned businesses, alongside showings. A revamped pre- and post-show party celebrating LGBTQ pride within the theater community will be held on Wednesday, October 8, and an aftershow Q&A session with actors and artists will take place on September 30, October 5 and October 8. Kim’s Convenience is directed by Weyni Mengesha. The cast includes Ins Choi as Appa, Esther Chung as Umma, Ryan Jinn as Jung and Kelly Seo as Janet. Understudies include Frank Chung, Jeffrey Kim, Ngabo Nabea, and Rosie Simon. The play is performing at A.C.T. ‘s Toni Rembe Theater from Thursday, September 18 through Sunday, October 19. Single tickets are on sale now at the A.C.T. Box Office at 415-749- 2228 or online at act-sf.org/kims.
articles.title: A.C.T. premieres Kim’s Convenience Sept. 18

articles.text: Paul McCartney: Photographs 1963–64: Eyes of the Storm, currently on view at Legion of Honor in San Francisco, has been extended through October 5. The never-before-seen exhibition drew more than 100,000 visitors. The exhibition includes more than 250 of McCartney’s personal captures as well as video clips, archival materials and more that offer a behind-thescenes look at the meteoric rise of one of the world’s most celebrated and popular bands. Images span December 1963 through February 1964 and chronicle the Beatles’ journey to megastardom. Photographs were taken by McCartney with a single-lens reflex camera, which were introduced in the 1950’s as part of a new generation of handheld cameras. Sally Martin Katz, Legion of Honor Assistant Curator of Photography, said that McCartney acquired the camera in 1963 at a time “when many were experimenting with this newly popularized medium.” “The technology of the 35mm handheld camera allowed for a spontaneity in picture-taking, leading to the emergence of a snapshot aesthetic that embraced imperfection,” Katz said. “McCartney’s pictures reflect this new spirit in photography, as well as the literal blur of travel that The Beatles were experiencing, rapidly moving from one place to another.” Katz added that the exhibition, which includes photographs printed for the first time, captures “Beatlemania in full force.” “They depict the frenzied crowds chasing the band down the New York City streets, for example, and the swarms of people greeting them at the Miami airport,” she said. “The Beatles were at the eye of the storm they created: thousands of eyes were looking to capture that storm, and McCartney, with his camera, returned their gazes.” Visit https://www.famsf.org/ exhibitions/paul-mccartney-photographs to learn more. Paul McCartney: Photographs 1963–64: Eyes of the Storm exhibition display at Legion of Honor, San Francisco.
articles.title: Legion of Honor exhibition Paul McCartney: Photographs extended through Oct.

articles.text: Weekends until August 25, 11–2 p.m. Nepal art exhibit This exhibition brings together Nepali artists living in the USA as first-generation immigrants. The body of works displayed explores the paradoxes of diasporic life—particularly the process of building identity amid pressures to conform to dominant cultures and homogeneous identities. Drawing inspiration from everyday life and personal experiences, this exhibition reflects the tension between strong attachment to the culture left behind and the process of assimilating into a new society. As the result of seven months’ research on Nepali Diaspora artists and their works, based in the Bay Area and beyond, by Fulbright Visiting Scholar Swosti Rajbhandari Kayastha with San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum, the show has provided a platform for artists to express their unique experiences and perspectives, often highlighting the complexities of navigating multiple cultures and identities. The gallery will be open to the public without charge on Saturdays and Sundays from July 26 to August 25, from 11 AM until 2 PM each weekend day. Sunday, August 24, 4:00 p.m. Festival Opera Vocal Recital Salon Festival Opera’s 2025 Salon Series continues with a powerful evening of music by renowned soprano Carrie Hennessey and acclaimed pianist Daniel Lockert featuring two magnificent works by American composers. Experience encore performances of Julia Seeholzer’s Portraits of Disquiet, a gripping reflection on our modern world first performed in FO’s online recital series during the pandemic, and Jake Heggie’s At the Statue of Venus, a poignant and humorous journey of anticipation and self-discovery which was a part of Festival Opera’s 2021 mainstage production. Don’t miss this rare opportunity to be moved and inspired by two extraordinary works performed by artists who bring every note and word to life. Join us for an unforgettable evening of artistry and storytelling through song! Advance tickets are strongly recommended and available at http://bit. ly/4ouNZlR. Saturday, August 30, 7:00 p.m. Temescal Quartet & Friends concert Temescal String Quartet is a San Francisco Bay Area ensemble, established in 2004 by musicians of the SF Opera and Ballet Orchestras. Founding member violinist Barbara Riccardi was joined by cellist Nancy Bien in 2016. The members share a great love of music, deep friendship, and great joy in playing music together. This event will include a viewing of art works by cellist Nancy Bien, and a wine and cheese reception will follow the concert, provided by David Konigsmark of Circadian Cuisine. Please purchase your advance tickets soon at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6696869. Sunday, August 31, 4:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Players concert A sextet of leading members of the home-town Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, including music director Marty Stoddard on flute, will present a concert entitled Summer Winds, including music by Mozart, Francis Poulenc, Georges Barboteu, and Carl Nielsen. Free tickets are available on Eventbrite, and donations are encouraged also: https://www. eventbrite.com/e/1510592706449. Sunday, September 7, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Fall Celebration To celebrate the Fall Equinox and Mexican Independence Day, the jazz and pop piano trio will present a full program centered around Autumn Leaves. There is a narrative (story line) that ties each tune on the program into the theme for the month. The narrative ties these tunes and all the tunes on the show into the autumn theme. As another summer passes, don’t miss the relaxed pleasure of a Sunday late afternoon in the Classic Jazz Club with the trio. Doors open at 4:15 PM. articles.text: Exhibition leaves museum Sept. 14 Kunié Sugiura: Photopainting, an exhibition featuring over 60 works by Japanese American photoartist Kunie Sugiura, leaves the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) on September 14. Japanese native Sugiura pioneered a unique category of artistic expression by blending photography with painting, drawing and other mediums. She also experimented with the photogram technique, one of the earliest forms of photography dating back to 1839. Kunié Sugiura: Photopainting, her first survey exhibition in the U.S., features over 60 artworks spanning her sixty-decades long career. “Throughout her career, Kunié Sugiura has subverted traditional notions of photography, bravely bucking trends to produce a distinctive body of work that is unmistakably her own,” said Erin O’Toole, SFMOMA’s curator and head of photography. “Sugiura’s many experiments and explorations with the photographic medium upend our notions of what photography can be,” added SFMOMA Director Christopher Bedford. “We look forward to engaging our communities with KuniéSugiura’s art and are honored to open the first survey exhibition of her work in the U.S.” Sugiura moved to the U.S. in 1963 to study at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago where she was a mentee of conceptual artist and photographer Kenneth Josephson. A major retrospective of her art was on display at the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum in 2018. From 1986 to 2008 she produced a column entitled “New York Report,” in which she reviewed gallery and museum exhibitions, for the Japanese-language magazine Bijutsu Techo. “I am very happy I found a way of life that has interested me and has kept my focus for so long,” Sugiura said in an interview with Cristina Chan, SFMOMA’s Managing Editor. “Over my career, I have had a few people and audiences who have supported my art. This time, I feel like more people are understanding my ideas and art.” Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/kunie-sugiura-photopainting/ to learn more. Kunié Sugiura
articles.title: Last chance to see Kunié Sugiura exhibition at SFMOMA

articles.text: In 1946, with London still marked by the Blitz, a letter arrived from a small island in the Channel. It draws writer Juliet Ashton into a world shaped by occupation, loss, and an unlikely book club: The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society. Juliet, played with quiet strength by Lily James, is a novelist whose own life has been scarred by the war. Encouraged by her editor Sidney Stark (Matthew Goode), she sets out to write about the solace books provide. The timing proves uncanny: a farmer from Guernsey, Dawsey Adams (Michiel Huisman), reaches out seeking a volume she might help him find. In his letter, he mentions the society, a group formed during the German occupation that survived on reading, and on each other. Curious, Juliet travels to Guernsey. What she imagines will be a quick visit turns into something else entirely. The island’s beauty hides darker memories, and the society’s eccentric name conceals a tragic story waiting to be told. At first, she observes as a guest, reading to the members at their gatherings and listening as they recall the war years. But soon, her connection deepens. Dawsey, kind and steady, emerges as more than just a correspondent. The bond between them quietly complicates Juliet’s engagement to an Lily James and Michiel Huisman in The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society American officer, Mark Reynolds (Glen Powell). articles.text: There is a side story to everything. When I was teaching in the San Francisco public schools, kids wanted me to teach them rap. I responded that rap was something they could do on their own. They needed to explore the world, and music was the best way to do it. Every one of my students learned to read music with proficiency, sing the music of many lands and understand their cultures, recognize all the instruments of the Orchestra by sight and by sound, play the recorder with proficiency, and learned how to listen. These are just a few of the things that they learned – and they had fun doing it. Learning should be fun. In my opinion, music is one of the best ways to learn “cultural awareness“. At the same time that we become culturally aware, we learn geography among many other things. Why are different cultures attracted to their representative music? Let’s take a quick tour around the world. Perhaps we should start with one of the most vilified peoples of our world. These are the Romany people. They are also known as gypsies and Zigeuner. When they left their land of origin, they brought with them enthusiasm for music. Where would Hungarian or Romanian music be without the Zigeuner? Their musical voice was the violin and the cymbalom. When they went to Spain, flamenco music flourished and became the most characteristic music of the Iberian peninsula. The guitar was the voice of flamenco. Needless to say, it has become a very popular instrument internationally. Italy is known as the land of opera and the birth of the violin family. Every country has adapted opera in its own way. Might there be a connection between Italian opera and Chinese opera? And the violin? Here in America, Dixieland music became popular. The most characteristic instrument of the Dixieland jazz band is the clarinet. Originally it was the violin that carried the melody. Note that country fiddling style is closely aligned with the Italian violin technique of the 18th century. In particular, there is the light and rapid bowing technique and the low position of the violin. Many of our greatest singers began their careers singing in church. articles.text: Elizabeth Banks and Russell Crowe in The Next Three Days succeed; one mistake ends it all. Meanwhile, the police sense that something is building, tightening the net even before John makes his move. The film’s suspense comes not from elaborate set pieces but from watching each decision John makes narrow the margin between success and disaster. A professor buying tools under the counter, practicing timing on city streets, and hiding money in the house is hardly the image of a criminal mastermind, yet that is the point. The interest lies in seeing someone without the usual resources of the genre attempt what seems impossible. Crowe plays John with restraint, showing a man whose calm exterior masks mounting urgency. Banks gives Lara a mix of defiance and exhaustion that makes clear why John cannot abandon her. Neeson, in his brief appearance, embodies the world John is about to enter: precise, unsentimental, and dangerous. Haggis directs without flourishes. The story moves forward step by step, allowing the audience to understand both the mechanics of the plan and the human cost behind it. The question the film leaves hanging is less whether John will succeed than whether his choice can be justified. Three Days has not only delivered the tension of an escape but also raised a more enduring issue: how far love and loyalty can bend the boundaries of law, reason, and survival. The Next Three Days. articles.text: Few films capture the magic of childhood summers as vividly as The Sandlot. Released in 1993 but set in the summer of 1962, it is less about baseball than about belonging, friendship and the timeless rituals of growing up. Scottie Smalls (Tom Guiry), 13, is the awkward new kid who has just moved with his mom (Karen Allen) and stepdad (Denis Leary) to the San Fernando Valley. Encouraged to make friends, he stumbles onto a dusty sandlot where a group of neighborhood boys spend their days playing ball. Smalls can barely throw or catch, but team leader Benny Rodriguez (Mike Vitar) takes him under his wing. By summer’s end, the game has given Smalls more than skills. It has given him a place in the world. The boys’ universe revolves around the field, but their imaginations reach far beyond it. A snarling dog known only as “the Beast” guards the junkyard next door, swallowing every home-run ball that clears the fence. When Smalls accidentally offers up his stepdad’s prized Babe Ruth– signed ball, the team faces a quest that feels larger than life. The film’s humor is stitched together with moments anyone who grew up in a neighborhood pack will recognize: the first crush (Squints and lifeguard Wendy Peffercorn), tall tales told under streetlights, long afternoons that feel endless until school looms again. These vignettes make The Sandlot as much a memory piece as a sports film. A scene from The Sandlot 801 MAGNOLIA AVENUE, PIEDMONT, CA 94611 Violinist Josepha Fath, cellist Victoria Ehrlich, and pianist Amy Zanrosso will present a rich musical journey beginning with Frank Bridge’s Miniatures for Piano Trio , charming vignettes full of grace, wit and melodic warmth, followed by the slow movement from Schubert’s Piano Trio in Eb Major, Op. 100 . Lera Auerbach’s Piano Trio No. 1 will provide a modern counterpart with brooding lyricism, dramatic surges and kaleidoscopic textures. Beethoven’s Piano Trio Op. 70, No. 2 , will close out the program with elegant interplay and bursts of playful energy revealing a masterpiece of chamber dialogue.

articles.text: The Right Program Simplifies Training What if the key to moving with ease, aging with strength, and having more energy for the things you love wasn’t hours of cardio or a restrictive diet—but learning how to lift? Strength training isn’t about chasing a certain look. It’s about building a body that feels good, moves well, and keeps up with the life you want. Why Lean Muscle Matters Lean muscle is your body’s engine. The more you build, the more efficiently you burn energy—even at rest. That means: • A faster metabolism • Stronger bones and joints • More daily energy • Confidence in how you move Unlike quick-fix programs, strength training creates lasting change: better posture, injury protection, and vitality at every age. And it works no matter where you are on your fitness journey. “But I’m a Beginner …” Here’s the truth: you don’t need to know what you’re doing before you start. And you don’t need to start out fit. articles.text: If your dog pulls on the leash, you’re not alone. It’s probably the number one thing people complain to me about. Puppies might learn “heel” pretty quickly with treats, but once they hit about six months — what I like to call the raptor phase — everything changes. Suddenly every smell, every squirrel, every blowing leaf is more exciting than you, and walking feels like being dragged behind a sled. So, what do you do? First, get the right gear. If your dog is pulling hard on a flat collar, swap it out. A front-clip harness — like the PetSafe Easy Walk — works well because it gently turns the dog back toward you instead of letting them dig in. Don’t bother with back-clip harnesses; those just give your dog more leverage. Some folks like the Gentle Leader, which goes over the muzzle. It can work wonders, but you have to be gentle with it. Don’t yank — that can hurt. Next, the leash. Keep it simple: a plain six-foot nylon, leather or biothane leash. No retractables, no bungees. Those teach dogs to lean into the tension, which makes pulling worse. Now, here’s the trick I use all the time: Mike Wombacher’s “Pay Attention Exercise.” It doesn’t take treats, just a bit of focus. Put your dog on your left, hold the leash in your right, and let a little loop cross your body. Start walking with purpose. Then, without warning, turn sharply away from your dog. The leash will tighten for just a second and the dog will have to catch up. As soon as they do, gather the loop, keep moving, and then turn again. Praise when they follow on a loose leash. The key here is pace. Don’t dawdle. Keep your feet moving and make your dog pay attention to you, not the other way around. If you’re using a Gentle Leader, give it a split second longer before the turn so you’re not snapping the dog’s neck. Most dogs figure this out after a few turns, sometimes even in the first session. It’s not magic, but it works — especially if you stay consistent. Pair the right tool with this exercise, and those exhausting, frustrating walks start to feel a lot calmer. Before long, it won’t be you following your dog, it’ll be your dog following you. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.text: There was a strong turnout of 48 walkers and four K-9 best friends for last week’s Walking on Wednesdays outing organized by the Piedmont Recreation Department. Along the way, the group visited Piedmont Community Church, where members shared the story of a new meditation garden. The idea for the stop began when walker and church member David Haecker told the group about the garden, which includes a labyrinth and fountain. The space is dedicated to church member Judy Wright’s late husband, Bob, who died in 2024. Wright, along with her daughter Lisa Fuller, church members Paul Schroeder and Suzie Skugstad, and many volunteers helped bring the garden to life. Much of the inspiration came from Sonja ten Grotenhuis, a church member who will attend Boston University this fall. Sonja created the garden as her Girl Scout Gold Award project, which requires more than 80 hours of work. With donations from church members and friends, and Schroeder’s heavy labor removing a concrete wall, the garden was transformed from a patch of weeds into a peaceful retreat. “Bob loved labyrinths,” Wright told the walkers. “This was the perfect way to honor him.” Sonja explained that the labyrinth and fountain are meant to bring nature into people’s lives and encourage reflection. She and Skugstad selected the stone for the fountain, while new benches and tree lights make the space welcoming both day and night. Like all Gold Award projects, Sonja said, the garden is designed to have a lasting community impact. The space is open to the public for quiet meditation and contemplation. Before heading to the garden, walkers heard about the church’s long history. Founded as the Piedmont Sunday School in 1900, it became the Piedmont Community Church in 1912. Philanthropist Wallace Alexander and his wife, Mary, donated land for the present site, and the Albert Farr designed church building was dedicated in 1918. Later additions included the Christian Education Building, dedicated in 1949. After visiting the garden, walker and church member Dottie Hutch led the group on a tour of the church. They stopped in the youth chapel to admire its stained glass, visited the courtyard and Guild Hall, and finished in the sanctuary. The dog friendly space impressed walkers with its woodwork, high ceiling trellises and a pipe organ with 3,000 pipes. Haecker, Hutch and Schroeder also shared more about the church, which has about 300 active members attending in person and online. As the oldest nondenominational church west of the Mississippi, its mission has long been one of service to the community and the wider world. For the walkers, the visit was uplifting and memorable. The new meditation garden, like the church itself, stands as another gift of beauty and reflection to the Piedmont community. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required. Those interested should go to https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or contact the Piedmont Recreation Department at (510) 420-3070 for more information. Historical picture of the church. Among those participating were Bill Ahern, Brian Henderson, Claudine Bach, Chuck Oraftik, Mary Henderson, Joyce Ahern, Larry Olsen, Nancy Olsen, Priscilla Wanerus, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Kathleen Parkerton, Karen Palmer, Adrienne Hamlin, Alicia Rivera, Mark Davis, Caskey Weston, Holly Trief, Judy Sokoloff, Cathy Laymon, Eric Behrens, Ken Hubbert, June Yee, Martin Levy, Brian Hamlin, Sean Brient with K-9 best friend Pip, Dottie Hutch, Sherry Jacobs, Joyce Hicks with K-9 best friend Mocha, Dave DeRoche, Nancy Henn, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Stella Houston, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Tina Shum, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, David Haecker, Peggy Shultz, Kat Lang, Pat Keller, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Judy Love, Marianne Jukas, Mary Carter, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased Sunny Bostrom-Fleming was with them for the first time.
