articles.text: Cuvaison winery is south of Napa, about one hour from Piedmont. My recent visit to Napa’s Carneros wine region brought me full circle. In the early 1980’s as a graduate student in Berkeley I would often make forays to the wine country to explore the fascinating new world of wine I was discovering. One of my most memorable early trips was prompted by an issue of Robert Parker’s wine magazine where he listed California’s greatest Pinot Noir producers. One winery that received special acclaim was Kent Rasmussen Winery in the Carneros region. It was there in that wild, remote wind-swept region that I first tasted great Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. (And also met a life-long friend.) In those days Carneros was the up-and-coming area for Pinot and Chardonnay. In the years since then other regions have captured some of the attention away from Carneros. The Russian River showed it was capable of world class Pinot Noir, then the Santa Lucia Highlands came into vogue. The high elevation vineyards in the Sonoma Coast region also gained notoriety. But the world’s attention seems to be returning to Carneros. Driving through Carneros recently there was a hive of activity and numerous new wineries I had never heard of in addition to some high-end resorts and restaurants that dot the landscape. Los Carneros AVA is an American Viticulture Area that spans across parts of Napa and Sonoma counties. It is known for its relatively cooler temperatures due to the marine fog and breezes coming in off San Pablo Bay. It is unique among American appellations in that it spans both Napa and Sonoma counties. Carneros is composed of a series of low rolling hills that sit above the San Pablo Bay and beneath Mount Veeder. The soils are predominantly sandy loam over clay. Because of the cooling influence of the Bay and regular fog and ocean breezes, Carneros is widely considered to be “Napa’s Burgundy” as Pinot Noir and Chardonnay thrive here. It could also be called “Napa’s Champagne” because multiple sparkling houses have set up shop here and produce truly world-class sparkling wine. I have known of the Cuvaison brand for many years but until recently I have never had the chance to visit the winery. Founded in 1969, Cuvaison is one of the pioneering wineries that helped put Napa Valley onto the global stage. In 1979 Cuvaison was acquired by the Schmidheiny family of Switzerland who still own the winery today. The Schmidheiny family cemented Cuvaison’s focus on Chardonnay and Pinot Noir by acquiring 400 acres of land north of San Pablo Bay on the Napa side of Carneros. In 2009 Cuvaison built a new 32,000 square foot winery. Steve Rogstad has been the head winemaker since 2002. In 2016 Dan Zepponi was named president and CEO of Cuvaison. Dan grew up in the wine industry as his father was co-founder of ZD winery. Dan graciously offered his time to guide me through a flight of the Cuvaison current releases. He was warm and gregarious and had a story or two on every topic. (It was also fun to talk with Dan about his sideline of playing guitar in the All-vintners country rock band, the Silverado Pickups.) Sustainability and concern for the environment are core values for Cuvaison and there is a care and thoughtfulness evident in the layout of the winery and vineyards. The high-ceilinged glass-walled tasting room is bright and airy and sits on a hilltop with a stunning panoramic view of the vineyards and a beautiful reservoir. The Schmidheiny family cemented Cuvaison’s focus on Chardonnay and Pinot Noir by acquiring 400 acres of land north of San Pablo Bay on the Napa side of Carneros. In 2009 Cuvaison built a new 32,000 square foot winery. Steve Rogstad has been the head winemaker since 2002. In 2016 Dan Zepponi was named president and CEO of Cuvaison. Dan grew up in the wine industry as his father was co-founder of ZD winery. Dan graciously offered his time to guide me through a flight of the Cuvaison current releases. He was warm and gregarious and had a story or two on every topic. (It was also fun to talk with Dan about his sideline of playing guitar in the All-vintners country rock band, the Silverado Pickups.) Sustainability and concern for the environment are core values for Cuvaison and there is a care and thoughtfulness evident in the layout of the winery and vineyards. The high-ceilinged glass-walled tasting room is bright and airy and sits on a hilltop with a stunning panoramic view of the vineyards and a beautiful reservoir. Wine tasting takes place inside the tasting room, on the expansive patio and Napa native Dan Zepponi is President and CEO of Cuvaison. in two boat houses perched over the reservoir. One of the offerings of the inexpensive Vineyard Tasting ($40) offers three wines on the patio. Unlike many wineries, Cuvaison welcomes children. • 2021 Cuvaison Brute Rose Method Champenoise, $60 This refreshing copper-colored sparkling wine is scented of apples, mushrooms and fresh baked bread with nutty tones. The palate balances bright berry fruits and savory tones, supported by creamy mousse, bright freshness and flinty tones on the bone dry finish. • 2023 Brandlin Sauvignon Blanc, $50 Cuvaison has a sister estate on Mt. Veeder named Brandlin that The glass-walled tasting room overlooks the vineyards. produces Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc. This wine is fermented in oak barrels and has a pleasing vanilla note. It is full-bodied, concentrated and dense on the palate with a fleshy core of fruit and a generously extracted structure. It concludes with a long, dense oak-inflected finish showing great harmony and balance. It is a dead ringer for a top-class white Bordeaux. • 2023 Cuvaison Sauvignon Blanc Methode Beton, $50 Totally opposite in style from the previous wine this is made in a concrete egg fermenter with no oak exposure. It has pretty aromas of citrus blossoms, kiwi and stone with lots of alluring herbal accents emerging. The medium-bodied palate offers electric energy from its juxtaposition of tangy acidity and a round mouth-coating texture. The perfect wine for fish or shellfish. • 2022 Cuvaison Chardonnay Estate, $35 Made in a clean stainless-steel style with no malolactic fermentation. It has a lovely bouquet of pears, apple and lemon zest, it is medium-bodied, textural yet racy, with lovely tension and a long, mineral finish. Very Chablis like. • 2022 Cuvaison Chardonnay Kite Tail, $70 This is an oakier, bigger style of Chardonnay more like Mersault or Montrachet than Chablis. It features scents of peaches, cashew, honeysuckle and beeswax. The full-bodied palate’s expansive, satiny texture is complimented by bracing acidity and it offers concentrated, perfumed fruit that lingers impressively on the finish. • 2022 Cuvaison Estate Pinot Noir, $45 The estate Pinot has slowly unfolding aromas of cherry, plums and mint, becoming more floral as it airs in the glass. The palate is layered with woodsy, earthy flavors. It’s structured by silky tannins and vibrant acidity and boasts a flourish of spicy accents on the finish. • 2022 Cuvaison Pinot Noir Spire, $80 Made in a Burgundian oldworld style this impressive wine has a complex perfumed nose of raspberries, black cherries, earth, tobacco and leather. Fleshy and full-bodied with smooth tannins, good acidity and purity the berry fruit flavors linger in the mouth and emerge in a long, savory, satisfying finish. Would be a perfect partner to grilled salmon. The Cuvaison logo Cuvaison Winery 1221 Duhig Road, Napa, CA 94559 707 942 2455 carnerostasting@cuvaison.com The entrance to Cuvaison tasting room. The Spire Pinot Noir was the favorite wine of the tasting.

articles.text: BBQ Without Borders returned to the Oakland Museum of California earlier this month. Their event on August 2 was presented by the organization No Immigrants No Spice (NINS), and was a celebration of food and an affirmation of the often unacknowledged contributions of immigrant communities to the nation’s cultural richness and social fabric. “In a time when the narratives around immigration are often distorted, BBQ Without Borders offers a tangible space with a delicious counter-narrative,” said Dr. Vibha Gupta, a Piedmont resident and founder of No Immigrants No Spice. “We believe that by coming together over food, we can bridge divides, celebrate the cultural richness immigrants bring, and directly support those who are building our communities from the ground up.” This year’s event, themed “Toward A Greener Future,” looked to highlight the economic and cultural impact of immigrants. The food tents this year provided a culinary journey, with an array of flavors from a celebrated lineup of Bay Area immigrant chefs, including: • Anthony Salguero of Popoca: Bringing Salvadoran-inspired delights to the forefront. • Maria Marquez of Tacos Mama Cuca: Offering traditional and modern Mexican flavors from Sonora. • Cafe Colucci: Serving up renowned Ethiopian cuisine and seasonings. • Third Culture Bakery: Sweet Indonesian and Taiwanese inspired desserts from the bakery behind the Mochi Muffin. Beyond the mouth-watering food, BBQ Without Borders raised over $25,000 for the East Bay immigrant community, channeled through The Unity Council, an Oakland non-profit. The event also featured live music, dance, and a Silent Auction with artwork and photography. “What we have here today is the America I want to live in. Thank you for being here,” Gupta told the crowd. NINS is keeping its resilience fund open for donations until September 1. To donate, visit Photos by Scott Hoag A chef from Tacos Sinceros, led by Chef Sincere Justice, makes tacos at Oakland Museum on August 2. Displays in the museum plaza detail the history of the restaurants, along with the chefs behind the meals. A cook at Preeti’s Pani Puri Party, a live cooking demonstration and tasting with award-winning chef Preeti Mistry. noimmigrantsnospice.org/donate. All funds will be distributed in the form of micro-grants to immigrant families in Oakland, through NINS’ collaboration with The Unity Council. No Immigrants No Spice (NINS) is a non-profit organization that uses food as a vehicle to highlight the positive impact immigrants have on culture and society. Through events and initiatives like BBQ Without Borders, NINS aims to foster understanding, celebrate diversity, and provide critical support to immigrant communities, including the distribution of micro-grants. Learn more at https://noimmigrantsnospice.org/. This culinary force of cooks represented the Salvadorian restaurant Popoca, led by Chef Anthony Salguero. articles.text: Monday, August 11 signaled the start of another school year in Piedmont. Piedmont kids, teachers and parents have pronounced summer vacation finished, and school in session. A dreary sky hung over the first morning of school before the first bells rang at 8:30 a.m. Many kids and parents beamed as kids wore their best and brightest outfits with new haircuts and new backpacks. One big change this year for all Piedmont elementary students will be the switch to Fishtank Learning for the English Language Arts curriculum. This year’s elementary music curriculum is being called a bridge year according to the school district, to be used to perfect a more permanent change coming in 2026- 27 . This year, Piedmont fourth graders will take Theater Arts instead of music and 5th graders will essentially double up on their music instruction time. At Beach Elementary, Principal Anne Valva has quickly become the most tenured principal in the district. Valva and PMS’s Karen Shipp both became principals in 2022. Valva has quickly found a home leading her school, with the support and respect of her staff and students. On the three elementary school campuses, parents said goodbye and took photos beneath purple and white balloon arches, holding signs with friends. “And what’s your name?” a Beach teacher asked one of her new students. “I don’t think I’m ready for this,” a Beach mom said while holding the hand of a three-year old. At Wildwood, new Principal Amy Fry got off to a fast start. “The first day was great,” she said. “I enjoyed seeing so many students and families excited to return to school. I’m looking forward to working with the community to help continue to make Wildwood a wonderful place to learn and grow.” Havens students now only need to remember one important name: Reed. New Principal Susanne Reed and office Administrative Assistant Melanie Reed share the name and look to form an administrative synergy as well. Tender goodbyes and enthusiastic I-love-yous were seen on the playgrounds of all three schools. At Beach, those farewells visibly had more immediacy and lingered on longer, towards the lower side of the playground, where the youngest students’ Kinder and T-K journeys begin. Hugs and kisses from moms and dads started the day off. At 8:30 a.m. students filled into their new classrooms, with new knowledge to be imparted, friends to be made and memories to form. The first day of school by and large is a reunion for students in Piedmont between friends formerly long lost, but now reunited.
articles.title: It’s a new year for elementary schools

pages.text: 2 2 Wednesday, August 13, 2025 Opinion By Jay Russell QUESTION: What are you excited about for this upcoming school year? Asked on Friday, August 8, at Piedmont Middle School walkthrough registration. RONAN PRICE, 8th grade I’m excited to hang out with my friends and being an 8th grader having classes on the top floor of the school. By Pastor Jim Hopkins Dear Lala: You are four and one half years old now and on Monday you are going to start T-K (Transitional Kindergarten). You have gone to your new school many times before but now it is not only their school; it is your school. YaYa and I simply want to say that we hope you will have the time of your life and that we think it is very likely that you will. You know that Hop Pop works at a church. Sometimes you come and sit on the steps with me when I talk to the kids and tell them stories. Sometimes you go with the other kids and Miss Yvonne while the big people stay in church. Sometimes you stay with your mom and dad and listen to the people sing and to Hop Pop talk. Sometimes when I’m doing that, we give each other a little wave. The Big Book I read from tells us that God creates each and every one of us, that God knows us and that we are “fearfully and wonderfully made.” I don’t expect you to understand those words, I don’t understand them completely myself, but I hope you will remember that their message is that you are magnificent, precious and irreplaceable. You will not always go to Hop Pop’s Church but if you ever go to another church that, for whatever reason, tells you that you are not magnificent, precious and irreplaceable, please get out of that church as fast as you can. The world we live in can be very hard. That is one of the lessons we learn when we watch Bluey together. Sad things happen. We make mistakes and messes. So do other people. Still, hard and sad things are not all there is. There is family, there is laughter, there is imagining and there is love. I don’t know what your favorites things to learn about and do will be. Take a good long time to figure that out. Try lots of things. Don’t worry if it isn’t easy. Remember the Bluey episode “Baby Race” where everybody was worried about who did what first? It didn’t really matter, did it? What mattered was trying, learning and accepting that everyone was different. Another thing the Big Book that Hop Pop reads from says is that God doesn’t give everyone the same talent but that everyone is given a gift. I think you will probably have more than one gift, but that is what Hop Pops are for, to tell you that you are amazing. Some days, you won’t feel like it, but you are. I look forward to you telling me about T-K. I hope you have the time of your life. Love you forever, Hop Pop Hop Pop is Pastor Jim Hopkins, Senior Pastor at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, Lakeshore Avenue & Mandana Boulevard in Oakland. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is surveying residents on potential programs to help transition homes from natural gas to clean electricity. Feedback will guide which pilot programs, like bulk purchasing or smart panels, should be prioritized. Residential natural gas use accounts for roughly half of Piedmont’s greenhouse gas emissions. Piedmont’s Sustainability Division is working with a community task force to understand existing barriers to home electrification and create a practical, equitable framework for solutions – a potentially vital part of achieving the city’s climate goals. The online survey builds on earlier community input that identified the biggest barriers to home electrification in Piedmont. Now, the task force is exploring possible programs the city could pursue to help address those barriers. Feedback on these concepts will help determine which ideas to prioritize for further analysis. The survey asks for input on four program concepts: • Organizing neighborhood electrification projects to lower costs through bulk purchasing. • Providing short-term appliance loans while property owners make upgrades needed to support electric equipment. • Launching a pilot program to test “smart panel” devices that help residents electrify their homes without expensive panel upgrades. 2025 Sustainability James Glauber talks about his induction cooktop, which heats pans directly and efficiently. Residents can check out the City’s Induction Cooktop Lending Program to try out this cooking technology for free. For each program, the survey asks: • How well could this help address common barriers to home electrification? • Which program would be most helpful for you personally? • If the city could only do one of these programs, which would you prioritize? The survey should take about five minutes to complete and is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ ElectrificationSurvey. Piedmont’s climate goals Natural gas use in residential buildings accounts for roughly half of Piedmont’s in-territory greenhouse gas emissions. Because much of Piedmont’s housing stock is old and large, homes are on average less energy efficient than those in neighboring communities. Transitioning these buildings from natural gas to renewably sourced electricity not only has health, safety, and cost benefits, it is a critical part of meeting the City Council’s adopted goal of climate neutrality by 2045. The city has convened an Electrification Task Force of community representatives— covering a broad range of expertise and experiences—who are working with sustainability staff to develop a roadmap for supporting all community members in switching to electric appliances. For more information on the Electrification Strategy and Electrification Task Force, including meeting materials, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ElectrificationStrategy. With questions, contact Sustainability Program Manager Deniz Ergun at dergun@piedmont.ca.gov. 2025 Sustainability Awards Winner James Glauber shows his home battery and heat pump. articles.text: Editor: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council. My husband David and I, and our neighbors, are very concerned about the safety ramifications of the Moraga Canyon housing plan, mainly: 1. Evacuation route: Moraga Ave. is a principal evacuation route for Piedmont and Oakland. We can’t imagine 900 additional daily trips on top of the existing 11,000. Last night at the Planning Commission meeting, your outside consultant said that the bike lane would be used as an emergency third lane. Very dangerous for any pedestrians/bikers escaping in an emergency. Not safe! 2. We worry about potential fire insurance increases/insurability denials for both Oakland and Piedmont neighbors as a result of packing in 197 units in a fire zone. 3. How will you provide parking for 197 units on the Blair side of Moraga? Your diagram shows 130 units. 4. An alternate site would be to consolidate 3 elementary schools into 2. pages.text: Wednesday, August 13, 2025 3 Survey: Home Electrification programs to ease transition By Tony Simons The City of Piedmont is surveying residents on potential programs to help transition homes from natural gas to clean electricity. Feedback will guide which pilot programs, like bulk purchasing or smart panels, should be prioritized. Residential natural gas use accounts for roughly half of Piedmont’s greenhouse gas emissions. Piedmont’s Sustainability Division is working with a community task force to understand existing barriers to home electrification and create a practical, equitable framework for solutions – a potentially vital part of achieving the city’s climate goals. The online survey builds on earlier community input that identified the biggest barriers to home electrification in Piedmont. Now, the task force is exploring possible programs the city could pursue to help address those barriers. Feedback on these concepts will help determine which ideas to prioritize for further analysis. The survey asks for input on four program concepts: • Organizing neighborhood electrification projects to lower costs through bulk purchasing. • Providing short-term appliance loans while property owners make upgrades needed to support electric equipment. • Launching a pilot program to test “smart panel” devices that help residents electrify their homes without expensive panel upgrades. 2025 Sustainability James Glauber talks about his induction cooktop, which heats pans directly and efficiently. Residents can check out the City’s Induction Cooktop Lending Program to try out this cooking technology for free. For each program, the survey asks: • How well could this help address common barriers to home electrification? • Which program would be most helpful for you personally? • If the city could only do one of these programs, which would you prioritize? The survey should take about five minutes to complete and is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ ElectrificationSurvey. Piedmont’s climate goals Natural gas use in residential buildings accounts for roughly half of Piedmont’s in-territory greenhouse gas emissions. Because much of Piedmont’s housing stock is old and large, homes are on average less energy efficient than those in neighboring communities. Transitioning these buildings from natural gas to renewably sourced electricity not only has health, safety, and cost benefits, it is a critical part of meeting the City Council’s adopted goal of climate neutrality by 2045. The city has convened an Electrification Task Force of community representatives— covering a broad range of expertise and experiences—who are working with sustainability staff to develop a roadmap for supporting all community members in switching to electric appliances. For more information on the Electrification Strategy and Electrification Task Force, including meeting materials, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ElectrificationStrategy. With questions, contact Sustainability Program Manager Deniz Ergun at dergun@piedmont.ca.gov. 2025 Sustainability Awards Winner James Glauber shows his home battery and heat pump. articles.text: The Alameda County Environmental Health Department (ACEHD) has issued a work notice about upcoming environmental investigation activities at the former Shell service station at 29 Wildwood Avenue in Piedmont. Work will include soil, vapor, and groundwater testing as part of cleanup oversigh. Beginning Aug. 14, Wayne Perry, Inc. and Shell will conduct environmental surveys over three days. The work will be carried out in accordance with permits from the Alameda County Public Works Agency and overseen by ACEHD. Work will take place from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., Monday through Friday, and will include the use of a limited-access direct push rig and support vehicles. The site, which Shell plans to redevelop into an electric vehicle charging station, is currently regulated by ACEHD under a Leaking Underground Storage Tank case and a Cleanup Program Site case. To confirm that current site conditions in the soil, soil vapor, and groundwater are protective of utility workers and nearby properties, crews will install five soil vapor probes six inches beneath the building foundation and five more probes four feet deep inside and outside the existing building. Once this work is complete, the site will be secured until ACEHD approves the removal of the building foundation and hydraulic hoists. A separate work notice will be issued before demolition and lift removal. Based on investigation results, ACEHD may require cleanup actions. Residents will be notified of any further environmental work through fact sheets and public meetings. Community protection measures The work notice outlines the following protective steps during the investigation: • Plastic sheeting will protect the work area and prevent soil transfer to asphalt. • Inspect and/or clean vehicle wheels before leaving the site. • Maintain straw bales to stop dirt, silt, or slurry from entering storm drains • Maintain fencing and posted signage with a phone number for complaints. According to the notice, dust and odors will be controlled. Residents with concerns may call Tracy Craig at 510-334-4866 for a prompt response. The notice also invites residents to review the case file for the 29 Wildwood Avenue project, including all technical documents, online at the State Water Resources Control Board GeoTracer website at https://geotracker.waterboards.ca.gov and searching for the address “29 Wildwood Avenue, Piedmont.” map of the site boundary and sample locations at 29 Wildwood Ave.

articles.text: 1-year-old, 57-pound Sway is turning heads and winning hearts. This Husky mix is a mix of young-dog energy and older-dog obedient. He’s house-trained, waits politely for meals, and respectful in his Oakland Animal Services-arranged foster home. Sway knows the sit, shake, and down commands, and is eager to learn more (especially if treats are involved). He’s got a go-with-the-flow temperament and would thrive with someone who loves walks, runs, or just backyard play sessions. He enjoys chase games with other dogs and could be a great match for a playful pup, or would be content as your oneand-only. Sway is affectionate without being clingy, and his foster family calls him a, “gentleman with just the right mix of calm, curiosity, and charm.” While he’s still building confidence with some new experiences (stairs and loud Come meet Sway at Oakland Animal Services. noises are a work in progress), he adjusts quickly and is brave at heart. To meet Sway, fill out an adoption application online on Oakland Animal Services’ website and you will be contacted by his foster who will arrange a meet-and-greet with Sway. For more information, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@gmail.com /(415) 845- 1999. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department is gearing up for its 7th annual car show, complete with hot coffee and even hotter automobiles on Saturday, September 20, from 9:00 a.m. to noon near the Exedra. The event brings cops, coffee and cars to the center of Piedmont as a part of the department’s outreach efforts. The Cops, Coffee and Car Show was pioneered by now retired Piedmont Police Officer Steve DeWarns in 2018. In its second year, the car show had 44 cars in 2019, and since then has had approximately 100 showroom worthy cars since 2021. To enter a vehicle in the show, e-mail officer Tyler Petit at coffeecarscops@piedmont. ca.gov. Be sure to include your name, phone number and e-mail address, and the name, make, model and year of the vehicle. Car Show organizer, Officer Tyler Petit (left) with Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies.

The local Ken Betts Suds Machine Car Wash and gas station on the corner of Piedmont Avenues and Pleasant Valley is back in business after more than a year of upgrades required by state regulators. Betts held a grand reopening party to celebrate its return to servicing local car owners on April 19-20, with a balloon arch, free ice cream from Mister Softee, and a guitarist playing music on the shaded patio. You know, these guys have to work in the heat and in bright sunlight… so we’re putting up two sun shades—one as you exit the car wash and one before that.” The first shade structure is currently being installed, while the other is awaiting permits, she said.

articles.text: Annual kickoff party on August 23 PCSC has become known for providing tiny houses for local organizations that serve unhoused youth. PCSC has raised the funds to cover the material costs, roughly $60,000 for the four tiny houses! co-VP Communications, PCSC Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is hosting its annual kickoff party to start the 2025-26 crew year on Saturday, August 23, from 4:00 to 6:00 p.m. PCSC is a youth-led organization that has served Bay Area communities for over 20 years. Comprised of nearly 150 high school students (or middle school aged from the affiliated Piedmont Service Club), the crew volunteers at weekly events which are planned, organized, and funded through its members. Popular activities range from building Tiny Houses for unhoused youth to cooking for the food-insecure. In addition, an ongoing program of weekly tutoring helps underserved children in East Oakland. The annual kickoff party acts as an open house where crew advisor Ken Li and the 14 youth leaders share their experiences and answer questions regarding PCSC. This meeting is a great opportunity for prospective non-members to learn about joining PCSC and for current members to reconnect with the crew community. All parents, middle, and high school students regardless of whether active in the crew are welcome to attend. If interested in attending, please complete this event registration form (https://forms. gle/4w3Lw6djUVvevEiu5). A response with the location in Piedmont will then be sent. If you have any questions, please visit the website PCServiceCrew. org or email any of the following three: Ken Li, PCSC advisor and founder (ken.i.li@sbcglobal. net), Elena O’Connell, co-President (elenafoc26@gmail.com), or Stephanie Lee, co-President (stephanieww08@gmail.com). Chloe Koh is co-VP Communications with the Piedmont Community Service Crew, a Venturing unit of Piedmont Scouts. One of the most popular types of service work that PCSC does is to cook for the food insecure. PCSC’s fundraising team raises money that covers the cost of the meals that we prepare. articles.text: Students returned to the Piedmont Middle School campus last week with walkthrough registration in the Buzz Redford Gym. On Friday, August 8, students had their photos taken for school ID cards wearing brand new shirts, picked up schedules and happily ran into classmates from days gone by. PMS Principal Karen Shipp stood in the doorway of the gym taking it all in. Shipp said there wasn’t much new about walkthrough registration this year, but that there is always such excitement and energy every year as students reunite with their friends. New 6th-8th graders received their class assignments and compared schedules with friends not seen since before summer vacation. Inside the gym students also got Scots Camp t-shirts, and visited a variety of tables for signups for extracurricular activities. The sports sign up table was staffed by basketball coach Colin Dagdagan and cross country coach Minori Tsuge. The duo said this year saw increased interest in girl’s flag football. “I think because it’s now a varsity sport at the high school there are a lot of girls excited to play in middle school,” said Tsuge. Outside the gym, students got their hippocampuses working, while trying to guess the number of gummy worms and jelly beans inside of mason jars. The closest guesses were announced on Monday, winning the candy and instant envy of classmates. For many new sixth graders, any anxiety about Friday’s walkthrough, was eased by the 6th grade Boot Camp which ended a couple of days earlier on August 6. Seventh grade teacher Ted Scherman and P.E. teacher Tim Wisnewski hosted the orientation with enormous success again. This year’s camp had 110 incoming 6th graders enroll in the optional summertime course. Prepped for the new year, middle schoolers were able to walk off campus after the Friday afternoon registration with knowledge and peace of mind to help them enjoy the final days of vacation, say goodbye to summer and hello to school. Seventh graders JoJo Shim (left) and Ezra Schwartz volunteer at the giveaway spinner wheel which gave students prizes including affirmation pins, pom pom keychains, pencils, and emoji erasers. articles.text: Football season opens August 30 Piedmont High’s football team is back on the field with helmets cracking and pads smacking as they build toward their August 30 season opener at Salesian. The Highlanders opened padded practice on Monday, August 11, officially turning the page on last year’s 10-2 result and the WACC Mission Division title. Piedmont won their second straight league title in 2024 after winning the 2023 Shoreline Division crown. They reached the Division 7 NCS Semifinals as the No. 3 seed before losing to No. 2 Ferndale, but a 42-46 NCS win over No. 6 Fortuna marked the school’s first postseason win since 2017. “I’ve been waiting for this day since last November,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “We want to get that taste out of our mouth. We have a really different team; it’s going to require a lot of teaching this year.” Last year’s team concluded a cycle that saw 16 seniors graduate. Offensive and defensive lineman Adrian Kondakov is set to start at left tackle and is the only returning starter from last year’s offensive front. “It’s difficult having four new people to teach but it’s fun being with a new group,” Seiden said. “I’m trying to teach them to have a gritty mentality and to push themselves when they are tired. As long as guys come every day to practice with the mentality of getting better, they’ll become a good varsity player.” Kondakov is expected to lead by example. Seiden describes him as a man of few words. Staff Photos Adrian Kondakov is the only returning starting offensive lineman from last year and will start at left tackle. “The only senior in that group is Adrian. He’s a silent leader. He’s one of my four-year kids and I’ve maybe heard him say 10 words. He nods his head and goes to work. He’s very intelligent and loves football after never playing before coming to high school,” Seiden said. Of the 16 graduates from 2025, Piedmont faces the task of replacing three-year starting quarterback Markos Lagios. As it turns out, the school will continue having a Lagios in the No. 4 slot at quarterback. The position will be filled by Markos’ younger brother, Jimmy Lagios, who. is taller than his older brother and slings the ball with as much spin and velocity. Jimmy was the Post’s honorable mention for 2025 Freshman of the Year. “The irony of him being Markos’ brother isn’t lost on me. But he’s just scratching the surface. He played really well on JV, so we Jimmy Lagios is stepping into the starting quarterback role, wearing the same number as his older brother Markos, who as the quarterback last year. Xavier Henderson enters his senior year as a key playmaker on offense, defense, and special teams. just want to see his progression. As that’s happening. He’s going to be a huge part of whatever we’re able to do,” Seiden said. With a vast number of starters to replace on both offense and defense, Piedmont’s running game could become a strong point. Xavier Henderson looks like the Highlanders’ feature back, while Colby Hong provides downhill power and Rehan Mumtaz adds speed to the mix. Henderson came to the school last year and made an instant impact. He’s now one of the leaders om the team. “I look at it with a positive outlook. My mentality is really no different from last year, it’s just about showing up and wanting it more – the type of player who goes all out and becomes a different person on the field. I’m looking to carry that on this year,” Henderson said. Henderson was a playmaker for Piedmont in all three phases. He had 169 rushing yards and one touchdown, to go with 19 pass receptions for 312 yards and six touchdowns last year. He also led the team in tackles for loss, and had two kickoff returns for touchdown. Yet he is entering the 2025 season feeling like he has something to prove. “I have a lot to prove this year. I really want to get a scholarship offer and to just improve overall. I’m just trying to bond with the guys and get better,” Henderson said. The Highlanders’ full football program is looking set to have around 55 athletes spread across varsity and junior varsity, the highest number in years. The varsity program will have around 30 athletes, a far cry from where the program was in 2022 when the varsity was canceled midway through the season. Now, Piedmont can run 11-on-11 practices with both units. “It almost makes you choke up seeing where the program is now, especially the original coaches who have been here the whole time when we had 15 kids,” Seiden said. After back-to-back WACC titles, Piedmont isn’t looking to lay off the gas. If all goes well, the Highlanders could be competing for their second straight Mission Division title. We’ll provide more coverage of the football team ahead of their season-opener.

He’s going to be a huge part of whatever we’re able to do,” Seiden said. With a vast number of starters to replace on both offense and defense, Piedmont’s running game could become a strong point. Xavier Henderson looks like the Highlanders’ feature back, while Colby Hong provides downhill power and Rehan Mumtaz adds speed to the mix. Henderson came to the school last year and made an instant impact. He’s now one of the leaders om the team. “I look at it with a positive outlook. My mentality is really no different from last year, it’s just about showing up and wanting it more – the type of player who goes all out and becomes a different person on the field. I’m looking to carry that on this year,” Henderson said. Henderson was a playmaker for Piedmont in all three phases. He had 169 rushing yards and one touchdown, to go with 19 pass receptions for 312 yards and six touchdowns last year. He also led the team in tackles for loss, and had two kickoff returns for touchdown. Yet he is entering the 2025 season feeling like he has something to prove. “I have a lot to prove this year. I really want to get a scholarship offer and to just improve overall. I’m just trying to bond with the guys and get better,” Henderson said. The Highlanders’ full football program is looking set to have around 55 athletes spread across varsity and junior varsity, the highest number in years. The varsity program will have around 30 athletes, a far cry from where the program was in 2022 when the varsity was canceled midway through the season. Now, Piedmont can run 11-on-11 practices with both units. “It almost makes you choke up seeing where the program is now, especially the original coaches who have been here the whole time when we had 15 kids,” Seiden said. articles.text: Staff Photos I traveled to Bangkok to watch Tottenham Hotspur play a preseason match, but torrential downpour canceled the match. All I got was this crummy picture of Harry Kane, who now plays for Bayern Munich. If you’ve been following the Post’s sports section over the last couple of years, you may remember my recount of a trip to Thailand to watch my favorite European football team, Tottenham Hotspur of North London, for their preseason tour. The trip in 2023 to Bangkok’s Rajamangala Stadium was spoiled by a monsoon, making the pitch sopping wet and unplayable. Parents, coaches, and students at Piedmont High have come to notice me wearing a Tottenham hat or jersey of Heung-min Son and Lucas Moura It’s often been a topic of conversation between and the English-born coaches at Witter Field over the years, like boys’ soccer coach Todd Russell who support Southampton, former boys’ coach Todd Sullivan who is a devout Manchester United supporter, and former girls’ coach Dan Chubbock. In 2022, I traveled to Ibrox Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland to watch Tottenham take on Rangers. It gave me a chance to watch manager Antonio Conte’s new team and see my favorite players, Son and Harry Kane, in person for the first time. As professional sports go, 2022 marked Kane’s final year at the club, finishing his time as Tottenham’s greatest player of all time and its all-time leading goal scorer. Moura was cut loose in May 2023. My focus for my 2023’s preseason trip to Rajamangala Stadium was to say goodbye to the greatest striker the club has ever produced before the English captain was traded to German superpower Bayern Munich. However, Tottenham scheduled the match during Thailand’s monsoon season in late July. Rain began to build an hour before kickoff, resulting in a waterlogged pitch that caused balls to stick like arrows into the grass. With just six crew members A photo of the monsoon rain pouring down at Rajamangala Stadium. It remains one of my fondest travel memories. A photo of Heung-Min Son in 2022 at Ibrox Stadium. He now plays for LAFC of Major League Soccer. working to clean the full 100-plus yard field, locals turned to me and laughed, saying: “Welcome to Thailand.” As the rain poured while we huddled underneath an overhang of Rajamangala Stadium, little did I recognize how vast the changes at Tottenham would occur since I last saw them in person in July 2023. In addition to Kane and Moura leaving before the 2023-24 season, Conte was fired near the end of 2023 after going on a rather comical tirade during a press conference. Tottenham hired Ange Postecoglou as their next manager, known for his attacking brand. Nearly two years later, Postecoglou and Son helped lead Tottenham to the Europa League title in May following a season of frustration. Tottenham finished the Premier League season in 17th of 20 teams, just one spot above the relegation zone, after injuries hobbled the lineup from start to finish. Regardless, Spurs made it to the Europa League Final in Bilbao against Manchester United, winning 1-0 to give Tottenham its first trophy in 17 years. But change was immediately on the horizon. In the weeks after lifting the Europa League trophy, Postecoglou was fired due to their 17th place finish in the Premier League. Since that day in Rajamangala, Spurs have held onto just 13 players out of 40 going into 2025-2026, including both of my favorite players, Son and Kane, now elsewhere. Unfortunately, the Post’s vacation schedule the last two years haven’t lined up with Tottenham’s preseason tour. This year, the club played in Hong Kong against Arsenal and in Seoul versus Newcastle. But more importantly, Son announced he was departing from Tottenham Hotspur following their August 3 match against Newcastle, ending his time with the club after 10 years of service. He now plays for LAFC in Major League Soccer, at least giving me more chances to watch him in person in the U.S., albeit for a different team. The changes throughout Tottenham since my last trip to watch them are an unmistakable reminder of the vicious cycle of professional sports. When asked by European football fans or soccer colleagues, ‘Why Tottenham?’ My response has always been, ‘Because they make you work for it.’ Spurs now go into the 2025-26 season without some of its greatest players, Kane and Son, and its first trophy-winning coach in nearly two decades, Postecoglou. Perhaps new manager Thomas Frank can propel Spurs to greater heights. But one thing is for sure; those memories of watching Kane and Son play in Glasgow and walk in the pouring rain in Bangkok are now much more special.
articles.title: My life as a Tottenham Hotspur supporter in America

articles.text: In this week’s edition of Piedmont athletes in college we take a look at Parker Terrill of the UC Berkeley track and field team, Taylor Rolefson of Bates College’s swim team, and her brother Tom Rolefson on the Hamilton College swim team. In the 50 breast, Tom finished 30th of 48 in 26.87. As for the 100 free, he finished in 48.31 for 51st place. In the 200 medley relay, Hamilton was 18th of 22 with Rolefson as the last leg with a time of 21.06. At Piedmont High, Rolefson earned All-League honors as a senior. His 200 freestyle relay team reached the NCS Championship which placed 11th of 16 teams in 1:28.23. To get there, the team was 13th of 40 in the NCS preliminaries in 1:27.79, which marked a PHS record. Photo courtesy of Cal Athletics Parker Terrill, PHS Class of 2022, reached the 2025 ACC Championship and NCAA Division 1 West events. PARKER TERRILL UC Berkeley Parker Terrill, PHS Class of 2022, is entering his senior year on the University of California’s track and field team. He was our 2022 Co-Athlete of the Year as a record-setting pole vaulter at Piedmont High. He finished his 2025 season by reaching the NCAA Division 1 West First Round in May. He placed 26th of 37 athletes in the pole vault at the event, recording a height of 16 feet, 5.5 inches. He qualified for Nationals by making it to the 2025 ACC Championship, finishing eighth of 17 vaulters at 16 feet, 7.25 inches. Terrell also set a new personal record at the Cal Opener in March, where he recorded a vault of 17 feet, 2.75 inches, finishing third of eight athletes. Photo courtesy of Bates College Taylor Rolefson, PHS Class of 2024, just finished her freshman season on the Bates College swim team. TAYLOR ROLEFSON Bates College Taylor Rolefson, PHS Class of 2024, now a freshman on Bates College’s swimming team, also reached the NESCAC Championship competing in several events. In the 50 butterfly, she was 40th of 48 in 27.27. In the 50 free, she swam a time of 25.39 to finish 44th of 55 swimmers. She also placed 39th of 46 in the 200 freestyle in 1:59.79. She swam the third leg on the 400 freestyle relay team which finished 10th of 22 schools with a time of 53.05. At Piedmont High, Rolefson earned All-League honors as a junior and senior. As a junior, she was a member of PHS’ league championship winning swimming relay team. Their 200 medley relay and 400 freestyle relay teams finished its regular season undefeated and won the WACC title in both events. Photo courtesy of Hamilton College Tom Rolefson, PHS Class of 2024, reached the NESCAC Championship as a freshman. TOM ROLEFSON Hamilton College Tom Rolefson, PHS Class of 2024, is entering his sophomore year at Hamilton College. He reached the New England Small College Athletic Conference Championship meet in February in multiple events as a freshman, including the 50 free, 100 free, 50 breast, and the 200 medley relay. He finished 29th of 60 in the 50 free, logging a time of 21.39.

14 Wednesday, August 13, 2025 Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 18th year. Current and former college athletes as well as high school athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmont-post.com. CHRISTIAN TAYLOR Track and Field Piedmont High Class of 2023 UC Davis Class of 2027 Christian Taylor graduated from Piedmont High in 2023 as a four-year varsity member in both cross country and track and field. He’s set to embark on his junior year at UC Davis. With the Aggies’ track team, Taylor competed in five events last season. He won the 800 at the Aggies Open in March, clocking a time of 1:54.34 in a field of 25 runners. He finished his season in April at the Mike Fanelli Track Classic, placing 37th of 193 in the 800 with a time of 1:54.41, while also finishing 37th of 173 in the 1500, clocking a 3:58.28. He details his workout program ahead of his junior year. What is your workout program this summer? Staff Photo Christian Taylor, PHS Class of 2023, is entering his junior year on the UC Davis track and field team. My workout schedule is the same as it was last year, but with slightly higher mileage. Workouts on Tuesday and Thursday, long runs on Sunday, with Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday being steady runs. I’m going up to 70 miles per week this summer and am currently at 60 miles per week. I am also lifting five days a week. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My main fitness goal is to get my Achilles healed with lots of rehab and some treatment. The secondary goal is to just build back my base fitness to prepare for an intensive winter of training. How are you measuring your development? I track all my mileage and workouts to see what my fitness level looks like, but don’t have any direct metrics other than mileage and workout pace. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working on my own, but with training and rehab given to me by my coaches and athletic trainer. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I think the most impressive thing I’ve done this summer was a 14-mile run in Big Bear (6,700 feet) with 1,700 feet of elevation gain throughout the run. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? I would tell them that discipline is key. You need to be consistent and work out; especially on the days you don’t feel like it. Those days are what separate the top 1 percent from everyone else. NIA KIM Track and Field Get your FREE estimate today from Piedmont’s most trusted auto body shop. UALITY BODY & FENDER (510) 839-3122 www.QualityBF.com Piedmont High Class of 2025 UC Santa Cruz Class of 2029 Nia Kim was breakout star on Piedmont High’s track and field team in her only year as a varsity athlete after joining the squad as a former gymnast. We named her our 2025 Athlete of the Year award winner. Kim became a Western Alameda County Conference champion on May 7 in the 100 meter hurdles with a time of 15.62 seconds and the North Coast Section Bayshore Area champion in 15.19 on May 17. She logged the same time at the Meet of Champions on May 24 to place sixth overall. This all came after Kim and coach Pouyan Assadi discovered hurdles could become her primary event after randomly jumping over a frame during practice. Nia also placed second of 15 at the WACC Championship in the high jump with a height of five feet. She jumped the same height at the NCS Bayshore Area Championship to place third of 18. She also reached the Meet of Champions on two different relay teams. Her 4x100 team was fifth of 21 at the Bayshore in 50.06 and wound up finishing 17th of 24 at the Meet of Champions in 50.18. Her 4x400 team placed second of 14 at the Bayshore in 4:09.20, while they placed 13th of 23 at the Meet of Champions in 4:09.06. Her time of 15.19 sets the standard at Piedmont High, holding the school record with over a second gap to its next best time, which was Elizabeth Korn’s 16.35 in 2019. She details her workout plan ahead of her freshman year at UC Santa Cruz. What is your workout program this summer? I have been doing lots of strength training, sprint workouts, and mobility work about 4-5 days a week. What are your fitness goals for the summer? I am hoping to improve my explosiveness while also keeping up my endurance for longer distances. I am also trying to prevent injury by doing lots of rehab and weight training. How are you measuring your development? I have been timing my sprints and have been progressively overloading my reps at the gym. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I have been training solo, which can make discipline a little harder, but I occasionally run into my high school coaches. Having company can make my workouts a bit easier and boost my motivation. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I’ve felt myself getting stronger in the weight room and that’s carried into my strength on the field. Staff Photo Nia Kim joins UC Santa Cruz after winning the Post’s 2025 Athlete of the Year award. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? I’d recommend taking care of your body by getting enough rest and fuel. Also, trust in the process and in your coaches. It’s helpful to remind yourself that you are your biggest competition, not the people around you. WILL PARKER Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2025 Pomona-Pitzer Class of 2029 Will Parker just graduated from Piedmont High, helping them go 16-10 and reach the NCS Quarterfinals. He earned firstteam All-League honors as a junior and senior and was named the Post’s Athlete of the Month in April. Last season, Parker leads the team with a sterling .400 batting average for 32 hits, 19 RBIs, nine doubles, two triples, and one home run. As a junior, Parker was a big factor in the team compiling a 19-10 overall record and winning the WACC Foothill Division regular season with a 7-3 record. PHS battled to the D4 NCS Championship as the No. 2 seed, losing to No. 4 Justin-Siena. They qualified for the D4 CIF State NorCal tournament for the first time. Earning the No. 1 seed, PHS beat No. 8 Capuchino 13-1, won 5-0 over No. 4 Colusa, but lost 6-0 to No. 2 Bradshaw Christian in the championship game. In 2024, Will led the team with a .375 batting average, recording 33 hits with eight doubles, 24 RBIs and scored 22 runs. What is your workout program this summer? This summer I’ve been hitting, lifting, and doing throwing/ defensive work. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goals are to continue to put on muscle, get stronger, and build explosiveness to get my body in the right shape to get to work on campus in the fall. How are you measuring your development? I usually base my measurement of development on how much harder I’m throwing and hitting, as well as checking my weight on the scale. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I do my lifting on my own in my home gym, mixing in lifts instructions from the strength coach at Pomona-Pitzer, along with my own lifts. I also go to a coach in San Leandro to work on hitting and defense. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I recently hit 240 pounds on the bench press. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? No one should have to push you to get better. The real work happens when no one’s watching. Silent work makes the loudest impact. Staff Photo Will Parker prepares to join Pomona-Pitzer after graduating from Piedmont High earlier this year.

articles.text: Following Monk’s Trail to Wat Pha Lat & Wat Phra That Doi Suthep [From August 2023] Welcome travelers, hikers, and traveling hikers! Thailand is home to some of the thickest jungles in the world. Luckily, the outskirts of Chiang Mai provides a scenic hike through a Thai jungle on its way to a pair of historic Buddhist temples. The Monk’s Trail, also known as the Wat Pha Lat Trail, takes hikers to a hidden temple, Wat Pha Lat, within the Doi Suthep-Pui National Park. The hike to Wat Pha Lat is just 0.8 of a mile but ascends a steep 550 feet in elevation gain. During the hike to Wat Pha Lat, you’ll pass under groves of bamboo with insects making noise around you, while also passing a small waterfall on your way to the temple. Wat Pha Lat translates to “Monastery at the Sloping Rock.” Created during the reign of King Kuena from 1355-1385, the monastery was originally used as a resting spot for people walking up to at Phra That Doi Suthep, the much famous and final location for our hike. Once the road leading to Doi Suthep was established in 1935, Wat Pha Lat became a residency for monks. You’re welcomed to the holy grounds by sculptures of Buddha with a cascading stream of water falling over the sloping rock that bears the monastery’s name. The temple is a serene location in the middle of the bamboo forest; with ancient architecture to awe at. There is a Naga Staircase, two mythical serpent creatures down a stairwell. In Buddhist religion, the Nagas are known as protectors of the temple to ward off evil spirits. There are also three Chedis on the Wat Pha Lat grounds, which are large sacred structures that are known to house precious relics from Buddha or revered monks. There’s also a Viharn to worship Buddha. Stepping inside the building requires patrons to remove their shoes, like all temples in Thailand. Although I spotted many people in shorts, it’s not recommended to wear shorts or cutoff clothing on holy grounds in order to pay respect to Buddha. It’d be wise to keep light pants in your pack. The hike to Wat Pha Lat is a popular one, passing 46 hikers in the 0.8 mile span to the monastery before passing an uncountable Staff Photo The Monk’s Trail leads to Wat Pha Lat, a monastery tucked away in the jungle of Doi Suthep-Pui National Park. articles.text: Northern Light School will host its annual Celebrity Golf Invitational Tournament on Monday, September 22 — an exciting day of sport and social impact that brings together athletes, celebrities, business leaders, and local changemakers in support of educational equity. pages.text: Wednesday, August 13, 2025 15 HIKING WITH JON Temple hunting in a Thailand jungle Following Monk’s Trail to Wat Pha Lat & Wat Phra That Doi Suthep By Jonathan Comeaux [From August 2023] Welcome travelers, hikers, and traveling hikers! Thailand is home to some of the thickest jungles in the world. Luckily, the outskirts of Chiang Mai provides a scenic hike through a Thai jungle on its way to a pair of historic Buddhist temples. The Monk’s Trail, also known as the Wat Pha Lat Trail, takes hikers to a hidden temple, Wat Pha Lat, within the Doi Suthep-Pui National Park. The hike to Wat Pha Lat is just 0.8 of a mile but ascends a steep 550 feet in elevation gain. During the hike to Wat Pha Lat, you’ll pass under groves of bamboo with insects making noise around you, while also passing a small waterfall on your way to the temple. Wat Pha Lat translates to “Monastery at the Sloping Rock.” Created during the reign of King Kuena from 1355-1385, the monastery was originally used as a resting spot for people walking up to at Phra That Doi Suthep, the much famous and final location for our hike. Once the road leading to Doi Suthep was established in 1935, Wat Pha Lat became a residency for monks. You’re welcomed to the holy grounds by sculptures of Buddha with a cascading stream of water falling over the sloping rock that bears the monastery’s name. The temple is a serene location in the middle of the bamboo forest; with ancient architecture to awe at. There is a Naga Staircase, two mythical serpent creatures down a stairwell. In Buddhist religion, the Nagas are known as protectors of the temple to ward off evil spirits. There are also three Chedis on the Wat Pha Lat grounds, which are large sacred structures that are known to house precious relics from Buddha or revered monks. There’s also a Viharn to worship Buddha. Stepping inside the building requires patrons to remove their shoes, like all temples in Thailand. Although I spotted many people in shorts, it’s not recommended to wear shorts or cutoff clothing on holy grounds in order to pay respect to Buddha. It’d be wise to keep light pants in your pack. The hike to Wat Pha Lat is a popular one, passing 46 hikers in the 0.8 mile span to the monastery before passing an uncountable Statues of Buddha greet you as you enter Wat Pha Lat. Staff Photo The Monk’s Trail leads to Wat Pha Lat, a monastery tucked away in the jungle of Doi Suthep-Pui National Park. A pond at Wat Pha Lat that overlooks a view of Chiang Mai through the jungle trees. amount of people walking around the temple grounds. Wat Pha Lat has a parking lot for those disinterested in putting on their hiking boots, while there are also taxis available for those wanting a short-cut to the renowned Wat Phra That Doi Suthep up the road. Venturing from Wat Pha Lat to Wat Phra That Doi Suthep by foot turns a moderate hike into a difficult one; it should only be traversed by skilled hikers ready to get their hands dirty. Although it adds just 1.4 miles of hiking to your day, you’ll pick up nearly 1,500 feet in elevation gain, requiring hikers to bring their knees all the way to your chest on some steep sections. Marching in humidity around 80 percent caused this Bay Area born-and-raised hiker to look like he jumped out of a pool when reaching Doi Suthep. But the path to Doi Suthep is extraordinary and cuts you away from the bounds of foot traffic on the Monk’s Trail to Wat Pha Lat. After hiking up the remainder of the Monk’s Trail, you’ll intersect with Sriwichai Alley (route 1004), walking left to take the Pilgrim’s Path on the opposite side of the road. The Pilgrim’s Path goes for 0.8 of a mile until greeting the road, once again, where you will follow the road up for the remaining half-mile up to Doi Suthep, where you will pass shops, restaurants, and taxi drivers at the bottom of the temple. Created in 1383, Wat Phra That Doi Suthep is named after the mountain which it is located and considered to be the most sacred temple in all of Thailand. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) newest exhibition Students on Strike highlights the 1968 student-led strike at San Francisco State University (SFSU) and other noteworthy movements that established the nation’s first Black Studies Department and first College of Ethnic Studies at the university. The exhibition features historical and contemporary posters and photographs to draw comparisons between the strike at SFSU and the recent campus protests against the war in Gaza. In October 2024, San Francisco University State University students protested the Israel-Hamas war and the statewide school system’s ongoing investments in weapons manufacturers. Student-led demonstrations were seen at campuses across the state and at University of California schools. Museum visitors will be presented with an opportunity to integrate local historical context with more recent student demonstrations, including pro-Palestinian organizations on campuses throughout California. Students on Strike is on view through May 31, 2026. Visit https://museumca.org/ on-view/students-on-strike/ to learn more. articles.text: The Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) presents Routed West: Twentieth-Century African American Quilts in California, an exhibition of more than one hundred quilts by approximately eighty artists, on view now through November. African American Quilts is the most expansive presentation to date of a transformative bequest of African American quilts that BAMPFA received in 2019, and highlights the history of the Second Great Migration where African Americans emigrated from the south fleeing economic and racial oppression. Many families settled in California, bringing quiltmaking traditions from the communities they had left behind. Approximately one fourth of the quilts displayed were completed in the South prior to 1950, while others were created in California during the postwar era. Also featured in the exhibition are nearly a dozen recent artworks by Black quilt artists in the Bay Area, including members of the African American Quilt Guild of Oakland. Curator Elaine Yau, a distinguished folk art specialist who has overseen the collection since 2019, said the exhibition highlights BAMPFA’s multi-year initiative to research, catalog, and conserve the nearly three thousand African American quilts and several hundred unattributed quilts in its care. The exhibition is believed to comprise the largest collection of its kind, according to museum officials. “With Routed West, we’re activating the extraordinary collection of African American quilts at BAMPFA to honor the stories of the individuals and communities whose vibrant artistic traditions are indispensable to, but too often omitted from, the larger narrative of American art history, and of our own history here in California,” Yau said in a press release. “These magnificent quilts carry within them stories of resilience, creativity, self-determination, and ingenuity, [including] narratives that not only define a distinctive period of artistic production but also inform a deeper understanding of the intergenerational ties that continue to sustain Black life in the United States,” she added. The exhibition is on view through November, Wednesdays through Sundays, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. For more information about this exhibition and BAMPFA’s summer season, visit bampfa.org.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse’s production of My Fair Lady, based on the film adaptation of George Bernard Shaw’s 1913 play Pygmalion, is showing onstage now through September 13. My Fair Lady originally premiered on Broadway in 1956, telling the story of Eliza Doolittle, a Cockney flower girl who takes speech lessons from professor Henry Higgins, a phonetician, so that she may pass as a lady. The legendary original production received unanimous glowing reviews since its opening and won six Tony Awards, including Best Musical, and ran for 2,717 performances making it the longest-running musical in Broadway history at the time. The musical features a beloved score including classic songs “I Could Have Danced All Night,” “Get Me to the Church on Time,” “Wouldn’t It Be Loverly,” “On the Street Where You Live,” “The Rain in Spain,” and “I’ve Grown Accustomed to Her Face.” The score of My Fair Lady was among the most successful ever to emerge from the American musical theatre with more than five million copies of the Broadway-cast recording sold. San Francisco Playhouse’s production is directed by Artistic Director Bill English, with music direction by Dave Dobrusky and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The ensemble includes Jillian Smith as Eliza Doolittle and Adam Magill as Henry Higgins, with Julio Chavez, Heather Orth, Jill Slyter, Jura Davis, Kareem Jenkins and Andy Collins rounding out the ensemble. The show is on stage six days a week, Tuesday through Sunday. For showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/2024-2025-season/my-fair-lady/. articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s 103rd season opens on Friday, September 5 with the company’s annual opera ball, featuring Music Director Eun Sun Kim conducting Verdi’s Rigoletto. A revival of Verdi’s masterpiece is running September 5 through 27 at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco. Baritone Amartuvshin Enkhbat stars as the tormented titular character Rigoletto and Romanian soprano Adela Zaharia sings Gilda, with Yongzhao Yu making his San Francisco Opera debut as the Duke of Mantua. Mezzo-soprano J’Nai Bridges stars as Maddalena and bass Peixin Chen takes on the role of Sparafucile. The cast also includes Aleksey Bogdanov (Monterone), Stella Hannock (Giovanna), Olivier Zerouali, Samuel White, Jongwon Han, Caroline Corrales, and Elisa Sunshine. Jose Maria Condemi directs Rigoletto with sets inspired by the surrealist paintings of Giorgio de Chirico. Conductor and historian Jessica Bejarano will present an introduction to Rigoletto an hour before curtain at each performance. Music Director Kim will host a talkback after a September 21 matinee performance. San Francisco Opera’s annual ball, the company’s biggest fundraiser, kicks off the 2025-26 season on September 5, held at both City Hall and the War Memorial Opera House with proceeds beneMusic Director Eun Sun Kim conducts Verdi’s Rigoletto and leads the company’s 2025-26 season. fiting the artistic initiatives of San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Opera Guild’s education programs. Guests will be greeted with a festive cocktail reception followed by a dinner crafted by local chefs served in San Francisco City Hall’s rotunda. The opening night performance of Verdi’s masterpiece Rigoletto closes out the evening. The opening weekend celebrations continue on Sunday, September 7 where Kim conducts the orchestra at Golden Gate Park, featuring stars from the fall season for the popular Opera in the Park concert, now in its 50th year. Opera subscriptions and single tickets for concerts this year are available at (415) 864-3330 and sfopera.com. Opera ball tickets may be purchased online at https://www.sfopera.com/seasons/opera-ball/.
articles.title: SF Opera opens 103rd season with Verdi’s Rigoletto

articles.text: Cal Performances welcomes former artist-in-residence Angelique Kidjo and world-renowned cellist Yo-Yo Ma to UC Berkeley’s historic Greek Theatre in a special Labor Day weekend performance on Saturday, August 30. Kidjo is a four-time Grammy winner and has earned recognition over the years for projects like Yemandja, the artist’s first major foray into stage acting, and a reboot of the Talking Heads’ classic 1980 album Remain in Light, both part of the Cal Performances 2021–22 season. The Benin-born singer was also named one of Time magazine’s “100 Most Influential People of 2021” for her work as a performer, teacher, and cultural ambassador. Her latest recordings incorporate West African music, Afrobeat, Afro-pop, hip hop, and R&B. Ma has performed as a soloist with orchestras around the world. He has recorded more than 90 albums and received 18 Grammy Awards. In addition to recordings of the standard classical repertoire, he has recorded a wide variety of folk music such as American bluegrass music, traditional Chinese melodies, the tangos of Argentinian composer Astor Piazzolla, and Brazilian music, and remains one of the world’s most well-respected cellists. The Labor Day concert is part of Cal Performances’ Illuminations: “Exile & Sanctuary” programming for the 2025–26 season, a theme that aims to “conYo-Yo Ma and Angelique Kidjo nect seven unique performances to academic research” on the UC Berkeley campus, focusing on physical displacement, rupture of identity, and “a stripping away of the familiar that leaves an individual or community without a sense of belonging.” The performance connects centuries of interaction between African musical idioms and western music, highlighting exile and sanctuary as both a refuge and a creative space for artists. Ma and Kidjo use the Baroque sarabande dance form and its possible African antecedent, a dance to worship the Congolese spirit Zarabanda as a method to showcase the qualities that connect different cultures, genres, and musical traditions. “Every day there are moments when all of us can feel we are on the inside of something and also when we feel we are on the outside of something,” Ma said in a statement. “To be able to understand both at the same time and oscillate between the two gives us a larger perspective on the world.” “If your mind is open, and there is no fear, it’s easier to listen, and to question yourself,” Kidjo added. Tickets are likely to sell out fast and are currently available at calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the Zellerbach Hall Ticket Office Tuesday–Friday, 12–5:30 p.m. and Saturday–Sunday, 1–5 p.m.
articles.title: Yo-Yo Ma & Angelique Kidjo at Greek Theatre Aug. 30

articles.text: Consider the still memorable template: The year is 1918. WWI is underway, and for almost two years a pandemic, also known as the Spanish Flu, grips the world. Its origin is still unknown, its impact staggering. Some 500 million were infected and 50 to 100 million died. Panic swept the globe; white masks, a signature image, were ubiquitous. Recall Outbreak, released some years back, which opened with an image of an infected person sneezing in a movie theater. It was a hold-your-breath moment as the small particles went aerosol. Contagion has countless such moments, small and large. The film opens with a dark screen and the sound of a dry, hacking cough. Then the image of Beth Emhoff (Gwyneth Paltrow) comes into focus, her face a sheen of sweat. She’s in a nightclub in Macao, gambling, having drinks with business associates, and talking intimately to someone not her husband on a cell phone. She coughs again and is asked if she feels all right. She insists it’s just jet lag. At that moment, the audience knows more than she does: this will not end well. Everything she touches, every person she comes into contact with, warrants a tight shot, and each image is, as is the movie, chilling. The film also flirts, thematically, with apocalypse, touching on how fragile are society’s rules of law and decorum. It soon becomes evident in Contagion that just beneath the patina of civilization resides the instinct for survival at any cost—a Darwinian response that can, like the virus, be just as lethal. The thread of civility is slender. Of course we live as if it were otherwise. However, one event can change everything. Contagion is about such an event. Contagion. Directed by Steven Soderbergh. Starring Matt Damon, Gwyneth Paltrow, and Marion Cotillard. 1 hr 42 min. Rated PG-13. articles.text: Martin Scorsese has never been afraid to say what he thinks about the art form he’s devoted his life to. But in the age of billion-dollar superhero franchises, his comments about Marvel films landed like a thunderclap—dividing fans, filmmakers, and critics into rival camps. Movies—cinema, film, however we name them—are a technological and artistic wonder, blending writing, acting, photography, costuming, sound, and music into worlds that can thrill, terrify, and move us to tears. They are the modern-day campfire, drawing audiences together to witness stories of danger, triumph, and transformation. And each year, we celebrate the best of them with ceremony, glamour, and awards. It was the question of what best really means that prompted Scorsese to write his controversial New York Times essay, The Dying Art of Filmmaking. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, August 13, 2025 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Martin Scorsese and the Marvel Universe By Chris Honoré Martin Scorsese has never been afraid to say what he thinks about the art form he’s devoted his life to. But in the age of billion-dollar superhero franchises, his comments about Marvel films landed like a thunderclap—dividing fans, filmmakers, and critics into rival camps. Movies—cinema, film, however we name them—are a technological and artistic wonder, blending writing, acting, photography, costuming, sound, and music into worlds that can thrill, terrify, and move us to tears. They are the modern-day campfire, drawing audiences together to witness stories of danger, triumph, and transformation. And each year, we celebrate the best of them with ceremony, glamour, and awards. It was the question of what best really means that prompted Scorsese to write his controversial New York Times essay, The Dying Art of Filmmaking. In it, he set out to define what cinema is—and isn’t. Just before the release of The Irishman—nominated for 10 Oscars and arguably his magnum opus—Scorsese was asked about Marvel movies. He admitted he’d tried to watch a few but found they weren’t for him. “They are closer to theme parks than they are to movies as I’ve known and loved them… and in the end, I don’t think they’re cinema.” By Chris Honoré Consider the still memorable template: The year is 1918. WWI is underway, and for almost two years a pandemic, also known as the Spanish Flu, grips the world. Its origin is still unknown, its impact staggering. Some 500 million were infected and 50 to 100 million died. Panic swept the globe; white masks, a signature image, were ubiquitous. Recall Outbreak, released some years back, which opened with an image of an infected person sneezing in a movie theater. It was a hold-your-breath moment as the small particles went aerosol. Contagion has countless such Contagion a gripping thriller moments, small and large. The film opens with a dark screen and the sound of a dry, hacking cough. Then the image of Beth Emhoff (Gwyneth Paltrow) comes into focus, her face a sheen of sweat. She’s in a nightclub in Macao, gambling, having drinks with business associates, and talking intimately to someone not her husband on a cell phone. She coughs again and is asked if she feels all right. She insists it’s just jet lag. At that moment, the audience knows more than she does: this will not end well. Everything she touches, every person she comes into contact with, warrants a tight shot, and each image is, as is the movie, chilling. The film also flirts, thematically, with apocalypse, touching on how fragile are society’s rules of law and decorum. It soon becomes evident in Contagion that just beneath the patina of civilization resides the instinct for survival at any cost—a Darwinian response that can, like the virus, be just as lethal. The thread of civility is slender. Of course we live as if it were otherwise. However, one event can change everything. Contagion is about such an event. Contagion. Directed by Steven Soderbergh. articles.text: Anne With An E is a wonderful and engaging reimagining of the classic coming-of-age novel Anne of Green Gables by Lucy Maud Montgomery (1908). Set on Prince Edward Island in the late 1890s, the series opens with 13-year-old Anne (Amybeth McNulty) waiting at a rural train station. Matthew (R.H. Thompson), who—along with his sister Marilla (Geraldine James)—had requested a teenage boy from an orphanage to help on their farm, instead finds Anne, a spirited redhead with boundless curiosity and a torrent of words. A mistake has been made, but Matthew reluctantly brings her home, unaware that Anne has not yet truly found a family. Anne is precocious, imaginative, and resilient—traits that both charm and unsettle those around her. Her rich inner world is a refuge from the cruelty and loss she has endured since birth. Across three seasons, the series offers superb performances and tackles themes that remain timely today, extending well beyond the typical scope of an adolescent coming-of-age tale. While particularly resonant for tween and teen girls, it’s a series worth watching together as a family, sparking meaningful conversations. Unless revived by popular demand, there will be no fourth season—but Anne With An E is still not to be missed. Anne With An E. Directed by Moira Walley-Beckett. Starring Amybeth McNulty, R.H. Thompson, Geraldine James. Three seasons. Rated PG. Released in 2017. Now streaming on Netflix. articles.text: Weekends until August 25, 11–2 p.m. Nepal art exhibit Materialized Thoughts This exhibition brings together Nepali artists living in the USA as first-generation immigrants. The body of works displayed explores the paradoxes of diasporic life—particularly the process of building identity amid pressures to conform to dominant cultures and homogeneous identities. Drawing inspiration from everyday life and personal experiences, this exhibition reflects the tension between strong attachment to the culture left behind and the process of assimilating into a new society. As the result of seven months’ research on Nepali Diaspora artists and their works, based in the Bay Area and beyond, by Fulbright Visiting Scholar Swosti Rajbhandari Kayastha with San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum, the show has provided a platform for artists to express their unique experiences and perspectives, often highlighting the complexities of navigating multiple cultures and identities. The gallery will be open to the public without charge on Saturdays and Sundays from July 26 to August 25, from 11 AM until 2 PM each weekend day.
