articles.text: Have you ever returned home to what looks like an explosion of cushion stuffing and trash, courtesy of your furry friend? Destroying items, inappropriate elimination, excessive vocalizing, and obsessive scratching are all symptoms of a common issue known as separation anxiety. Many modern pet parents treat their dogs like family members, taking them everywhere, especially since the Covid-19 pandemic. However, failing to establish the need for occasional alone time can be a disservice to your dog. Dogs are pack animals that respond to their world partially based on the reactions of the one in charge of their safety. Establishing a clear hierarchy helps them understand what’s expected of them and can increase their feeling of safety in your home and with you. A dog that feels responsible for you will spend a great deal of time worrying about making decisions regarding safety, whereas a dog that feels responsible to you knows you can keep them safe. So, how do you address separation anxiety in your dog? Let’s go back to puppy 101; where do we put a puppy to bed before they’ve been house trained? Most would answer correctly: the crate. Crate training can be an effective way to address separation anxiety. The goal is to establish a safe space to which your dog knows you will always return. To start, acquire a crate and leave the door open. Stand a few feet away, toss treats into the crate, and tell your dog to “go to bed.” Let them begin to associate their crate with the yummy things you’re tossing in there. Once your dog is comfortable entering the crate, tell them to lay down, then to stay. Walk away to the other side of the room, and come back to give them a treat. Repeat this process with longer and longer distances. Now it’s time to close the door when you walk away, but make sure to open it 90% of the time when you come back. If your dog cries in the crate or paws at the door, use a firm sharp voice to discourage this behavior. Make sure you never return to the crate unless your dog is quiet to avoid accidentally rewarding poor behavior with your presence. Start with short periods of crate time with you out of sight (like thirty seconds), and gradually increase that time. Never crate a dog for longer than four hours. To make the crate a happy space, leave the door open when not using it and slip delicious tidbits into the crate so your dog feels interested in returning to check for rewards. With patience and consistency, crate training can help your dog feel more secure and reduce separation anxiety. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland. She helped to found the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. Contact her at 510–507–2017, email Sierra109@gmail.com, or visit the website at www.oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com.

articles.text: There was an excellent turnout of 24 readers on the patio outside the Piedmont Community Hall on August 4th for the First Mondays Reading Group discussion. Participating were Peggy Shultz, Sue Backer, Bill Ahern, Judy Love, Martin Levy, Mike Henn, Laura Goldman, Sarah Johnson, Lois Price, Nancy Henn, Lisa Euphrat, Nadean Guffanti, Carol Long, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Orrel Lanter, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Ken Young, Rich Siegel, Alicia Rivera, discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus, Hilary Honore, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to have Heidi Schmidt and Mary Carter with them for the first time. The group was there to talk about their August book, Tender At The Bone: Growing Up At The Table by Ruth Reichl. She is an American chef, food writer, New York Times restaurant critic, and has also written cookbooks, memoirs, and a novel. This debut 1998 memoir is full of life and love, loss and survival, and is especially about food. It was on The New York Times bestseller list several weeks. There are the food stories and recipes that shaped her life, but Reichl also shares stories of her family, friendships, and her journey of self-discovery. She learned early in life that since she wasn’t “pretty or funny or sexy,” but she could attract friends with food instead. Throughout the book there are humorous stories and her favorite recipes. Reichl was raised in Manhattan and Connecticut by a docile father and a mother who suffered from manic depression. She enjoyed the advantages of some family wealth, such as a Christmas in Paris when she was 13, and high school in Canada to learn French. She went to the University of Michigan, earned a graduate degree in art history, married a sculptor, lived in a loft in Manhattan, and then in the 1970s with friends bought a 17-room “cottage” in Berkeley that they turned into a commune and restaurant. The reading group alternates between fiction and non-books. August was a non-fiction month, but at the discussion’s start the possibility was raised that Tender At The Bone is actually fiction. Many of Reichl’s adventures seemed to be exaggerated and embellished. Could her mother really be a notorious food poisoner and known as the “Queen of Mold?” In fact, Reichl confessed the book was mostly true and some was made up for entertaining storytelling. Some readers found the book to be fun and it didn’t matter if all the stories were completely true, but others didn’t want to finish the book. For food-oriented readers the inclusion of recipes was enjoyable and the ones for Reichl’s devil eggs and brownies were considered the best. Members of the group could also relate to Reichl’s experiences in the New York City area, Michigan, and Berkeley, which all seemed accurate and were engaging. There were times when readers laughed out loud at the usual behavior of the Reichl family. The author’s relationships with her parents were particularly interesting. Her mother was mentally ill and her behavior and choices for Reichl when she was young created strange situations. But her father didn’t intervene. He used his work to escape the craziness and Reichl used food to escape too. Readers thought the family was in denial about the mother being bipolar. The fact that both of the father’s two wives were mentally ill said something about him too. However, it was noted that people didn’t fully understand mental illness and didn’t talk about it at that time. Another interesting side discussion was how non-Jews interpret actions by Jews that are considered part of their Jewish identity (e.g., eating pork). It was also fun to note that “old fashion” items like a rotary phone or phonograph record are unknown objects to grandchildren. Readers’ criticisms of the book were many. It didn’t capture their interest. It was repetitive and like a soap opera; it wasn’t exciting. The story was always about her, but not self-revelatory; other characters weren’t well developed. However, it was accepted that this is a memoir and this focus on the author might be expected. There was a desire to know more about Reichl’s later professional life, but that was probably another book too. It was also noted that the book’s title, Tender At The Bone, actually refers to being vulnerable. Reichl was able to overcome the challenges created by her parents though her drive and intellect and also with the support of other family members, the family cook, and business mentors. She came out of her family chaos fine and successful. This was something the readers could all appreciate. The group had previously selected The Women by Kristin Hannah for September and The Wright Brothers by David McCullough for October. After Phyllis Van Kranenburgh’s presentation of three fiction candidates the readers chose Euphoria by Lily King for their November book. Since Labor Day is Monday, September 1, the group will meet on Sept ember 8 at 1:30 p.m. for their next discussion. New readers are welcome and there is no fee to participate. Register at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. There was an excellent turnout of 24 readers on August 4th for the First Mondays Reading Group discussion.

articles.text: The Rockridge district will be rockin’ on Saturday, August 23 with more than 20 street performances, 55 local artists, flea and artisan market, big sales and special offers, kids’ crafts, special menus and tastings, and a pup promenade. Rockridge welcomes everyone to the Rockridge Rock-NStroll enjoy local wares, fine dining, savory sweets, and delicious drinks found only in this magical district. This is not a typical street festival. It’s a 1-mile leisurely stroll loaded with amazing sights, sounds, and experiences on every block. From Broadway to Alcatraz, College Avenue and its side streets will be full of creativity and family-friendly finds. Rock-N-Stroll is a true showcase of one of Oakland’s most creative and vibrant neighborhoods. A vast majority of the musicians and artists participating in the event hail from Rockridge itself, either living or working in the district. These talented artists of all ages will be performing or tabling inside and outside of shops, each matched with a location that best compliments their style. On this one day, the entire district turns into a carefully-curated local arts gallery. “As a proud Oakland resident involved in the art scene here, I am always in awe of the incredible local artists that live in our neighborhoods,” said Marcy Reed, a festival volunteer that who spearheads the outreach for artists. Over 20 street performers will be spread out on nearly every other block of the district to entertain you during your stroll. Representing a range of musical styles from a solo cellist to a 5-piece Tom Petty tribute band, they provide the perfect ambiance for a day of exploring Rockridge. Because there are no stages or street closures, you will want to bring your own lawn chair if you want to park yourself near a band. Stores, restaurants, salons, and other service providers will be offering special promotions for visitors. You can sample free tacos at Belly, grab a free book from the Rockridge Library, paint piggy banks at First Federal Savings & Loan, spin a prize wheel at Market Hall, get 50% off an item from Cole Hardware, along with other offers from over 40 businesses. For more details and a schedule of activities, visit RockridgeDistrict.com/rocknstroll. articles.text: Earlier this summer, longtime Piedmont residents Connie and Mark Herrick released Ripley’s Bird Buddies, the fourth installment of a self-published, illustrated children’s series based on the adventures of their late rescue cat Ripley. The newly-published story became the Herricks’ “own little bird book,” Connie Herrick said, identifying 20 different species of birds that live in Piedmont. It was a natural progression for Ripley’s story, she added, which began in 2021 with Ripley’s World, the Herricks’ first book of the series. Each book features titular character Ripley, a “tiny, feisty, funny, calico kitty with a big imagination,” and is bolstered by her many real-life friends in Piedmont including her German Shepherd “sisters” Kapo and Pele, raccoon twins, baby possums, and a squirrel that plays tag. Ripley’s Bird Buddies celebrates the city’s diverse avian wildlife and was coincidentally released as Piedmont became a hotspot among avid birdwatchers and environmentalists. A pair of great horned owls took up residence in Dracena Park earlier this year, and more recently, a family of bald eagles in a eucalyptus tree on the Piedmont-Oakland border has garnered a sizable, local following for marking the first time in recorded history that the species has successfully raised babies in the city, according to NBC Bay Area. This renewed interest highlights the core message of Ripley’s Bird Buddies, which encourages young readers to “take a moment every day to enjoy and know the birds in your neighborhood.” It includes a lengthy list of bird species that are easily identifiable in Piedmont, the natural setting of all Ripley’s books, including the white-crowned sparrow, California scrub jay, and mourning dove The inspiration for Ripley’s Bird Buddies came organically, Connie explained, from observing birds that have gathered in the couple’s own backyard over the years. Mark Herrick, who illustrates the children’s books, was separately working on paintings of finches and jays that became regulars at their Greenbank house. “I told Mark, these bird paintings that you’re doing are really nice. I think we ought to do a book,” Connie said. “I thought kids would really like to know about [the birds’] little personalConnie and Mark Herrick Mark Herrick at work illustrating Ripley’s Missing Locket, the couple’s second book, in watercolor. Cover of Ripley’s Bird Buddies ities, because they’re very, very distinctive. The way they interact with each other, and their special little quirks, really identify them.” Mark’s illustrations and Connie’s writing describe each species in kid-friendly detail, including their distinctive coloring, favorite garden snacks, and birdsong cadence. “As we were going through these [illustrations] and creating personalities for the birds, we started to block out and storyboard.” Mark said. “It was very organic and unplanned, and we had a lot of fun with it.” Connie said she started “gathering facts” about crows, juncos, hummingbirds and falcons for the story. “I started writing these little vignettes for each bird based on the facts but it was really boring. It was boring to me, and it was certainly going to be boring to the child, so I shifted my focus on their personalities and how they interact with each other,” she said. “For example, the house finch is a bit of a bully,” she said with a laugh. “But the little lesser Goldfinch, the ones that are yellow, those poor things, they just get knocked off.” New characters include Kangee, the American Crow, a “brave, bold, tricky trickster who loves to pull funny pranks,” and Kali, a Dark-eyed Junco, who is a “really good scratcher and digger and can find hidden treats like juicy, wild berries.” They are joined by a pair of “large and powerful” owls, an “aerobatic” Peregrine Falcon, a pair of “shy but friendly” mourning doves and more. The Herricks said they hope Ripley’s Bird Buddies will inspire a new generation of birdwatchers, and admit that they weren’t invested in the hobby until receiving a gift from friend and former Piedmont mayor Patty White, who passed away in 2023. Patty gave the Herricks a birdfeeder when they were mourning the passing of their dog. “That was really the beginning of it all,” Mark said. “We just got so super into it because we just lost Kapo, and were grieving and trying to figure out, do we get another dog or not? Then we set up the feeder, and the birds and squirrels really became like our outdoor pets,” he said. “We just got so much pleasure, sitting there drinking our coffee and getting to know the personalities of these birds. It was a huge, huge positive force in our life.” Copies of Ripley’s Bird Buddies and other books in the series are available online at www. RipleyandFriendz.com. The Herrick’s fifth book, Ripley’s Vet Visit, will be published in 2026.

Ripley’s Bird Buddies celebrates the city’s diverse avian wildlife and was coincidentally released as Piedmont became a hotspot among avid birdwatchers and environmentalists. A pair of great horned owls took up residence in Dracena Park earlier this year, and more recently, a family of bald eagles in a eucalyptus tree on the Piedmont-Oakland border has garnered a sizable, local following for marking the first time in recorded history that the species has successfully raised babies in the city, according to NBC Bay Area. This renewed interest highlights the core message of Ripley’s Bird Buddies, which encourages young readers to “take a moment every day to enjoy and know the birds in your neighborhood.” It includes a lengthy list of bird species that are easily identifiable in Piedmont, the natural setting of all Ripley’s books, including the white-crowned sparrow, California scrub jay, and mourning dove The inspiration for Ripley’s Bird Buddies came organically, Connie explained, from observing birds that have gathered in the couple’s own backyard over the years. Mark Herrick, who illustrates the children’s books, was separately working on paintings of finches and jays that became regulars at their Greenbank house. “I told Mark, these bird paintings that you’re doing are really nice. I think we ought to do a book,” Connie said. “I thought kids would really like to know about [the birds’] little personalConnie and Mark Herrick Mark Herrick at work illustrating Ripley’s Missing Locket, the couple’s second book, in watercolor. Cover of Ripley’s Bird Buddies ities, because they’re very, very distinctive. The way they interact with each other, and their special little quirks, really identify them.” Mark’s illustrations and Connie’s writing describe each species in kid-friendly detail, including their distinctive coloring, favorite garden snacks, and birdsong cadence. “As we were going through these [illustrations] and creating personalities for the birds, we started to block out and storyboard.” Mark said. “It was very organic and unplanned, and we had a lot of fun with it.” Connie said she started “gathering facts” about crows, juncos, hummingbirds and falcons for the story. “I started writing these little vignettes for each bird based on the facts but it was really boring. It was boring to me, and it was certainly going to be boring to the child, so I shifted my focus on their personalities and how they interact with each other,” she said. “For example, the house finch is a bit of a bully,” she said with a laugh. “But the little lesser Goldfinch, the ones that are yellow, those poor things, they just get knocked off.” New characters include Kangee, the American Crow, a “brave, bold, tricky trickster who loves to pull funny pranks,” and Kali, a Dark-eyed Junco, who is a “really good scratcher and digger and can find hidden treats like juicy, wild berries.” They are joined by a pair of “large and powerful” owls, an “aerobatic” Peregrine Falcon, a pair of “shy but friendly” mourning doves and more. The Herricks said they hope Ripley’s Bird Buddies will inspire a new generation of birdwatchers, and admit that they weren’t invested in the hobby until receiving a gift from friend and former Piedmont mayor Patty White, who passed away in 2023. Patty gave the Herricks a birdfeeder when they were mourning the passing of their dog. “That was really the beginning of it all,” Mark said. “We just got so super into it because we just lost Kapo, and were grieving and trying to figure out, do we get another dog or not? Then we set up the feeder, and the birds and squirrels really became like our outdoor pets,” he said. “We just got so much pleasure, sitting there drinking our coffee and getting to know the personalities of these birds. It was a huge, huge positive force in our life.” Copies of Ripley’s Bird Buddies and other books in the series are available online at www. RipleyandFriendz.com. The Herrick’s fifth book, Ripley’s Vet Visit, will be published in 2026.

pages.text: Wednesday, August 13, 2025 27 Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers explore history of Frank Havens By Dick Carter Last Wednesday was a warm day so the Walking on Wednesdays group decided to stay in the central part of Piedmont and the shade of Wildwood Gardens for their weekly walk. Wildwood Gardens was the site of Frank C. Havens’ early 20th Century “Wildwood Estate” so there was lots of Piedmont history to be discussed. There was a historical connection with Frank C. Havens at 801 Magnolia, which is now the home of the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA). The first building at 801 Magnolia was built as a private residence around 1878. It is reported to have been a twin of the Wetmore House up Bonita Avenue at its corner with Vista Avenue and is considered to be Piedmont’s oldest unaltered home. It was built in 1878 for Jesse Wetmore and his family as a summer home. Frank C. Havens was born in 1848 into one of the founding families of Shelter Island, New York. He ran away from home at the age of sixteen and became a cabin boy on a sailing vessel which rounded the Horn on its way to California. He spent two years in Honolulu and went to China. After a year in the China shipping trade, he Wednesday Walkers meet new Piedmont Police Chief, Frederick Shavies. came to San Francisco in 1866. He worked in banking and became an Oakland attorney and real estate developer in the East Bay, particularly in Oakland, Berkeley, and Piedmont. Havens was married twice. His first wife died when she was 33 and his second wife was Lila Mandana Rand. The Havens family lived in the house at 801 Magnolia, which was the home of Blanche Wetmore Sherman. This location was convenient for Havens, as it was across from Piedmont Park which he was developing. Records show that the house was remodeled and converted into a Christian Science Church in 1935. A youth education wing was added in 1964. The Christian Science Church building was purchased by the City of Piedmont in 2003 as part of its Civic Center Master Plan, which later stalled. After sitting vacant for years, the City leased the building to the PCA which began renovations in 2011 for its use as an arts center. In about 1880 Havens founded a stock brokerage and then created the Oakland-based “Realty Syndicate” in 1895 with F.M. “Borax” Smith. Through it Havens and Smith built the Claremont Hotel and other structures. The Syndicate was also originally the parent company of the Key System transit company and accumulated at least 13,000 aces of valuable hilltop land that stretched from near Mills College to the boundary of North Berkeley. The group walked up Highland Avenue and down Wildwood Avenue to the entrance of Wildwood Gardens. Two partially hidden columns mark the former entrance to Havens’ estate. The walkers entered the neighborhood and made their way through its streets. They noted a unique brick storybook home with a curved roof while looking for 101 Wildwood Gardens, Havens’ mansion. Havens owned all the land from Crocker Avenue down to Oakmont Avenue and Oak Road and wanted to build his estate on this land. In 1906 Havens hired Bernard Maybeck to design his home. It was designed as an oriental home of teakwood and fine carvings from India, China and Japan. It took two years to build. Lila Havens was a student of eastern religions, and the EastFrank Havens ern motifs can be seen in the house. Legends say she picked a fight with Maybeck, and he quit. Havens was also a follower of Eastern philosophy and meditation, and the mansion had an opium smoking bed. At the time of the San Francisco earthquake and fire in 1906 Havens resigned from the active management of the Realty Syndicate to become president of the Peoples Water Company. At some point before 1910, Havens and Smith came into conflict for uncertain reasons. On December 9, 1910 it was made public that they had divided their interests. Havens took over the water company and land holdings and Smith acquired the Key Route interests. Sadly, after they had created so much together, they never met or spoke again. In 1911 Havens was sued by shareholders of the Peoples Water Company over his use of assets and he later developed significant financial problems. He had to sell many of his assets and was in debt when he died on February 9, 1918. Lila had to sell the Wildwood land to pay what was owed. The estate’s grounds were sold as the Wildwood Gardens Tract, and the current neighborhood is the result. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Reed steps into the top spot at Havens following the resignation of the last principal from the Randy Booker era in Piedmont, Anne Dolid. Dolid was hired in 2014 by Booker’s predecessor, Connie Hubbard, in her last year as Superintendent. Reed has principal experience, and most recently held the principal role at Rosa Parks Environmental Science Magnet in Berkeley. She knows new Wildwood Principal Amy Fry from their time working together at Malcolm X Elementary School in Berkeley. Another reason Reed is comfortable in the new job at Havens is her pedigree. Her grandmother was a teacher, her mom is a teacher, her sister has been a principal and a teacher, and her brother is a librarian. articles.text: Amy Fry, the new principal of Wildwood Elementary School, took some time to chat with the Post about the defining moments in her career, Piedmont’s new reading curriculum, and what experiences she will rely upon this year. Fry provided poignant answers about her new position and exuded excitement that promises to embrace Wildwood students and families. With the first day of school on Monday, August 11, Fry shared how she expects to feel on that day. “Excited, because I’m excited to meet the kids. The kids are what bring life to the work, right?” said Fry. Fry’s education journey began in upstate New York, where she graduated Magna Cum Laude from SUNY Geneseo before moving to the west coast. Most recently, she was the Vice Principal of Hearst and Mohr Elementary Schools in Pleasanton. With more than 25 years of experience in public education, her past teaching experience promises to be of incalculable worth. articles.text: Piedmont City Council was given an update on the Piedmont Community Pool project and approved a $100,000 for soft costs at their Council meeting on Monday, August 4. According to project leaders, the new pools are expected to be filled with water in the last week of August, which will be followed by 6-8 weeks of system testing known as “commissioning.” The pool’s project budget remains at $34.9 million, after being funded by $25.1 million in bonds and interest from measure UU. The reallocated funds account for special inspections and testing, a mandated safety measure, as well as design services moving forward. “This still falls within our total project budget,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “We think we have a firm understanding of what the hard costs are, and we are moving some of the budget we had allocated [previously] to the soft cost. So it’s like taking from one pocket and putting it in the other.” As of July 30, construction was estimated at 96% complete. The project crossed a milestone on Thursday, July 31, as crews completed the final concrete pour for the activity pool deck, pedestrian bulb-outs at the Magnolia/Bonita intersection, and a sidewalk leading into the pool entrance from Bonita Avenue. articles.text: After nearly two years of public engagement, AC Transit is announcing new changes to their bus network, with changes going into effect on Sunday, August 10. The route changes will discontinue extended school-hour service connecting the Hampton/ Estates Drive area to Piedmont High School, Millennium High School, and Havens Elementary School. “We had been, for a year-anda-half, talking about the line in and service, and never did it come up that this school service might go away,” said Piedmont Mayor Betsy Andersen. A letter was sent to AC Transit to express dismay at this change to Piedmont’s bus service, which could have an effect on students. The letter was sent by Mayor Betsy Andersen, City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, and School Board President Lindsay Thomasson. “This vital school-hour service provides the sole transit connection to local schools for a significant portion of the 1,700 students attending school in the Piedmont civic center,” reads the letter. “Discontinuing this service significantly impacts these students’ access to safe transportation to school and places undue burden on families, especially those with working parents who are unable to provide transportation during school commute times.” The upcoming changes include the removal of the existing line 33, and its replacement with a new line 88 running between Piedmont and Downtown Oakland. “Every decision was guided by three core principles – reliability, equity, and frequency,” said AC Transit External Affairs Representative Maria Henderson in an announcement at Monday’s City Council Meeting. According to Henderson, the new planned bus routes aim to respond to changes in travel patterns since the COVID-19 Pandemic. A full list of changes to all AC Transit bus routes can be found at actransit.org/realign. pages.text: Volume 27, No. 41 Piedmont, California August 6, 2025 91¢ Piedmont Post Piedmont Post A Community Newspaper Serving the Citizens of Piedmont Meet Principal Fry New Wildwood principal sits down with the Piedmont Post By Jay Russell Amy Fry, the new principal of Wildwood Elementary School, took some time to chat with the Post about the defining moments in her career, Piedmont’s new reading curriculum, and what experiences she will rely upon this year. Fry provided poignant answers about her new position and exuded excitement that promises to embrace Wildwood students and families. With the first day of school on Monday, August 11, Fry shared how she expects to feel on that day. “Excited, because I’m excited to meet the kids. The kids are what bring life to the work, right?” said Fry. Fry’s education journey began in upstate New York, where she graduated Magna Cum Laude from SUNY Geneseo before moving to the west coast. Most recently, she was the Vice Principal of Hearst and Mohr Elementary Schools in Pleasanton. With more than 25 years of experience in public education, her past teaching experience promises to be of incalculable worth. Impressively, Fry has been a classroom teacher at every elementary grade level, except for See Principal Fry on page 7 New Wildwood Elementary School Principal, Amy Fry Piedmont to lose school-hour bus service AC Transit bus route changes begin on August 10 By Tony Simons After nearly two years of public engagement, AC Transit is announcing new changes to their bus network, with changes going into effect on Sunday, August 10. The route changes will discontinue extended school-hour service connecting the Hampton/ Estates Drive area to Piedmont High School, Millennium High School, and Havens Elementary School. “We had been, for a year-anda-half, talking about the line in and service, and never did it come up that this school service might go away,” said Piedmont Mayor Betsy Andersen. A letter was sent to AC Transit to express dismay at this change to Piedmont’s bus service, which could have an effect on students. The letter was sent by Mayor Betsy Andersen, City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, and School Board President Lindsay Thomasson. “This vital school-hour service provides the sole transit connection to local schools for a significant portion of the 1,700 students attending school in the Piedmont civic center,” reads the letter. “Discontinuing this service significantly impacts these students’ access to safe transportation to school and places undue burden on families, especially those with working parents who are unable to provide transportation during school commute times.” The upcoming changes include the removal of the existing line 33, and its replacement with a new line 88 running between Piedmont and Downtown Oakland. “Every decision was guided by three core principles – reliability, equity, and frequency,” said AC Transit External Affairs Representative Maria Henderson in an announcement at Monday’s City Council Meeting. According to Henderson, the new planned bus routes aim to respond to changes in travel patterns since the COVID-19 Pandemic. A full list of changes to all AC Transit bus routes can be found at actransit.org/realign. Construction workers install landscaping and sidewalks at the pool site. City Council approves $100,000 in spending for Pool Project leaders “confident” the pool will be filled in August By Tony Simons Piedmont City Council was given an update on the Piedmont Community Pool project and approved a $100,000 for soft costs at their Council meeting on Monday, August 4. According to project leaders, the new pools are expected to be filled with water in the last week of August, which will be followed by 6-8 weeks of system testing known as “commissioning.” The pool’s project budget remains at $34.9 million, after being funded by $25.1 million in bonds and interest from measure UU. The reallocated funds account for special inspections and testing, a mandated safety measure, as well as design services moving forward. “This still falls within our total project budget,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “We think we have a firm understanding of what the hard costs are, and we are moving some of the budget we had allocated [previously] to the soft cost. So it’s like taking from one pocket and putting it in the other.” As of July 30, construction was estimated at 96% complete. The project crossed a milestone on Thursday, July 31, as crews completed the final concrete pour for the activity pool deck, pedestrian bulb-outs at the Magnolia/Bonita intersection, and a sidewalk leading into the pool entrance from Bonita Avenue. Landscaping has begun, with more planting scheduled in the See Pool Update on page 3 Workers pour concrete for a sidewalk at the entrance to the pool. As long as I was throwing lobs to Lebron and KD, I wouldn’t even have to be that good. 1700th Anniversary of Nicene Creed By Pastor Jim Hopkins We Baptists are given to identifying ourselves as “non-creedal’ people, (we like to say that we have no creed but Christ and that the Bible is our only authoritative written word). But even Baptists of long standing, like myself, must admit that the 1700th anniversary of a historic Christian creed is worthy of notice. Seventeen hundred years ago more than 300 bishops and officials participated in the first ecumenical council of the Christian church. It met between May and August 325 in the Byzantine city of Nicea (now Iznek, northwestern Turkey). The council was convoked by Emperor Constantine (r 306-337) to address the Arian controversy that threatened the unity of the early church, and for Constantine who viewed Christianity as the cement of his empire, the health of the empire itself. Using beautiful, majestic and lyrical language – We believe in one Lord, Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, eternally begotten of the Father, God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten not made, consubstantial with the Father. - the Council rejected the Arian argument that the Son was somehow secondary to the Father and provided language that is still used by Christians around the globe to affirm their faith during worship and to define their faith in the public square. It is less well known that the first Nicene Council also took action to set the date of Easter as the first Sunday after the first full moon following the spring equinox. It was a consequential gathering to say the least. As a non-creedal Christian one of the things I value, apart from its longevity, beauty and enduring impact, about the Nicene Creed is its focus on Jesus the Christ as the very heart of the Christian faith. In contrast to many contemporary statements of faith, the creed does not mention the Bible as a focus of belief. Instead, it devotes the great majority of its words to the identity and work of Jesus. In the creed it is Jesus, rather than the Bible, that is the eternal Word of God. The PHS team reportedly gathered for practice at a pool in Berkeley. According to Piedmont parent Elizabeth Mitchell, the team had to cancel all of its clinics planned for this summer due to lack of an available pool. “My plea to the City Council is to possibly speed up the rest of the construction so that there is some chance there will be at least some home games in Piedmont this year,” said Mitchell. “We’ve already lost one of the coaches who can’t commute to wherever [we’ll be practicing].” Other residents are left wondering at the sudden increase in construction activity, questioning the choices that led to delays. “How many millions of dollars are we over budget?” asked Piedmont resident, teacher and water polo coach John Savage. “To build on that question, has anyone been fired, dismissed, removed from the project?” City staff reassured residents that delays, although never wanted, are nonetheless a frustrating reality for both residents and the City. “Certainly [City Council] is doing everything [it] can to support, and we are doing everything we can to expedite,” said Gonzales. “So I think if we’re starting from a place of assuming that is not being done, we’re starting from an incorrect space.” Piedmont City Council Betsy Andersen, Mayor. 604-9864 bandersen@piedmont.ca.gov Conna McCarthy, Vice Mayor 658-9148 cmccarthy@piedmont.ca.gov Jennifer Long 804-539-4250 jlong@piedmont.ca.gov Tom Ramsey 593-6612 tomr@pmainc.com Lorrel Plimier 420-3048 lplimier@piedmont.ca.gov Piedmont School Board Lindsay Thomasson, President 415-666-0268 lthomasson@piedmont.k12.ca.us Ruchi Medhekar, Vice President 393-7540 rmedhekar@piedmont.k12.ca.us Michael Malione Max Roman Susy Struble Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: A Piedmont resident learns about Planning & Building projects at an open house event earlier this year. The City of Piedmont will host an open house to get residents to meet city staff and learn about various projects related to housing development, sustainability, and wildfire resilience. The open house will be held by the Planning and Building Department on Thursday, August 21 from 6:30- 8:30 p.m. at Veterans Hall, 401 Highland Avenue. The event will offer residents a one-stop opportunity to learn about upcoming projects and provide input before decisions are made. Residents may come anytime and move through five informational stations at their own pace. At each station members of the city staff will answer questions and provide details about project timelines. Featured projects include: • Moraga Canyon Specific Plan: A comprehensive plan for developing city-owned land along Moraga Avenue into a new neighborhood featuring affordable and market-rate housing, road safety improvements, and an expanded Coaches Field. • Objective Design Standards: Clear, measurable design rules that will govern new residential construction, including accessory dwelling units and SB9 developments. • Streamlined Business Permitting: Proposed zoning updates that will allow certain types of businesses to open through a ministerial process, avoiding a lengthy public hearing process. A resident has a conversation with a member of the City staff at an open house event. • • Building Electrification Strategy: A roadmap for how the City can support residents to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from their homes by replacing gas appliances with clean, electric alternatives. Building and Fire Code updates: Local amendments to state building codes to support wildfire-resistant construction and update Piedmont’s energy efficiency “Reach Codes.” This event is free, and no registration is required. Light refreshments will be served.
articles.title: City to host Planning & Building Open House

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department is gearing up to host its 7th annual car show, complete with hot coffee and even hotter automobiles on Saturday, September 20, from 9:00 a.m. to noon near the Exedra. The event brings cops, coffee and cars to the center of Piedmont as a part of the department’s outreach efforts. The Cops, Coffee and Car Show was pioneered by now retired Piedmont Police Officer Steve DeWarns in 2018. In its second year, the car show had 44 cars in 2019, and since then has had approximately 100 showroom worthy cars since 2021. To enter a vehicle in the show, e-mail officer Tyler Petit at coffeecarscops@piedmont. ca.gov. Be sure to include your name, phone number and e-mail address, and the name, make, model and year of the vehicle. articles.text: In a show of collaboration between students, teachers and the school board, Piedmont High’s English Language Arts electives courses have been rescued from the chopping block and allowed to continue. During the May 14 School Board meeting students spoke during the open forum in support of Film as Literature, Public Speaking and Creative Writing, which were in jeopardy. When students were selecting their classes for this year, those classes were available and a healthy amount of students selected them. One of the two Creative Writing semester and the lone Film at Literature semester were under threat of being cut prior to the May 14 school board meeting. “The interest in these elective classes really is huge, it is a testament to just what Ms. Foster has done with students the past couple years,” said English teacher Elise Marks. “I have heard many students talk about how Creative Writing, Public Speaking and Film as Lit have made them feel human again, in a way they have lost since COVID. That they found community in those classes that they don’t find in their other classes, they have found their voices again, they have found passion,” said Marks. Mercedes Foster, the English Department chair, spoke in defense of the classes in jeopardy, and asked for the board to reinstate them. Twenty-nine students had signed up for Film at Lit, a class that the Post chronicled in an Inside the Classroom feature on March 15, 2023. Ella Hughes, a recent PHS graduate who will be attending Cal as a Comparative Literature major, spoke in staunch defense of the classes on May 14. “Cutting back on the course selection further than we already have, I know would materially impact potential career paths and interests for dozens of students,” said Hughes. “If you’re into English you just have the core curriculum, we can’t strip back over half the electives available in this area and not expect that’s going to seriously affect any students that are involved in the humanities,” said Hughes. Many students rallied to the lectern during the board meeting. “Humanities electives overall have prepared me for the future better than any APs or grad requirements,” said Sophena Tuli, a 2025 graduate. The passionate pleas of students and staff were heard, and in a show of collaboration those classes have since received funding and remain unhindered. “This one has a happy ending,” exclaimed Marks. “We’re delighted that the Board and superintendent agreed to fund an additional .2 FTE to enable all the students who signed up for Creative Writing, Public Speaking, and Film as Literature to take those courses.” Film as Literature teacher Mercedes Foster talks with 2023 PHS senior Teagan Haddawy about the day’s lesson on long-take, tracking shots.
articles.title: Language Arts electives to continue at PHS

articles.text: As the new school year quickly approaches, rising high school seniors who are college-bound should be finalizing their list of schools to which they will apply. Building a college list should consider a student’s academic goals, social needs and wants, and fit the family budget. Finalizing your college list should begin with a clear understanding of your budget. Use the Net Price Calculator for your intended schools to determine what you should expect to pay. If the anticipated cost of attendance is higher than what your family can afford, do not apply. It is heartbreaking to have a dream crushed by the reality of budget. Doing thorough research about each of your intended colleges should give you the information you need to determine if the school fits your academic goals. Ask yourself the following questions: Does it have the major you want to pursue? Are there opportunities for you to do research? How is the study abroad program, and can you still graduate on time if you do it? Do the schools align with your social needs? Know that there are fantastic colleges of all sizes! But knowing what your options are for residential living, extracurricular activities, intramural sports, or religious-based communities may all factor into your decision of whether a school is right for you. This research about social fit is important to make sure your time in college fuels your personal growth. College admissions are competitive for everyone- even high school valedictorians with perfect SAT or ACT scores don’t have a golden ticket. Your final college list needs to be balanced with regard to reach, target, and likely schools. Make sure that there are financial safeties in addition to academic safeties to avoid disappointment in the spring. Apply only to schools that you would actually consider going to. There is no use applying to more schools just to collect acceptances. Focus your attention and effort on schools you really care about and put forth your best application to each. Your time and energy are valuable. Karen Shopoff Rooff is Director of College Consulting at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. Karen is a former college professor and an experienced coach. For more information please visit www.studysmarter. com, email info@studysmarter. com, or call (510) 350-8444.

I notice what kids are doing, and how they’re interacting with their peers, their teacher, the curriculum.” When Fry was introduced to the community at a Piedmont School Board meeting on March 12. she received high praise from vetted educators including her predecessor, Beth Rhine. “I know Wildwood teachers just adore Beth Rhine, so her recommendation carries a lot of weight,” said Piedmont Teachers Union President Elise Marks. “Beth Rhine told me immediately as soon as she started working here, ‘Amy, I think you would like this place, I think you should check it out’,” said Fry on March 12. Fry was also given high praise by school board members Max Roman and Michael Malione who have children at Wildwood School. “Able to hit the ground running, we really sensed that from you. So I’m thrilled that you are here and you accepted,” said Malione to Fry. The tests and challenges for the first-year principal include navigating new switches in curriculum for all Piedmont elementary students, namely the switch to Fishtank Learning for English Language Arts and changes to the 4th and 5th grade music programming. Fry should be the right woman for this English Curriculum change, having been a Literacy Coach and Response to Intervention Coordinator at Oxford Elementary School in Berkeley Unified for six years. In that role Fry provided reading interventions, coached teachers, and facilitated school-wide initiatives to improve literacy outcomes. “We are going to provide time for teachers to collaborate around [the new English curriculum] and grapple with it, and time for teachers to be okay with learning something new. There’s going to be bumps in the road, and there’s going to be times for them to collaborate and times for them to reflect, and times for them to get ongoing training so they can build confidence around how to teach it,” said Fry. Fry cited one inspirational experience, with one of her 4th grade students in Berkeley, that solidified her career choice to be an educator. After the student’s mom moved out of state, Fry requested to continue with him in 5th grade by taking on his IEP. “The special education teacher said, you know, he’s very challenging. And I said, that’s okay, he’s a child. We’re going to love him, and we’re going to work with him through this. His father and his stepmother worked really closely with the special education team and me, and he made three years of growth in reading in one year,” said Fry. Fry described it as a beautiful experience. “When we can bring together the family, all the educators involved, and the student, we can all be in alignment and get on the same page to listen to each other. When we can work together, we can do incredible things for kids,” she added. Fry described this collaborative approach as an archetype for the work she wants to do as a principal. “It’s bringing together all the stakeholders in the child’s journey, really listening to everybody involved. Then, working collaboratively with that team to making sure you’re all communicating and on the same page so you can really help that child feel good about the progress that they’re making and their success,” said Fry about the work of a principal. Fry lives with her husband and two daughters in Alameda. Their oldest daughter will be a sophomore at University of Texas, and the younger will be a sophomore at Alameda High School. Fry’s willingness to be open promises to bode well for her and everyone at her new home, Wildwood Elementary. Don’t be shy; come in and say hi to Principal Fry. articles.text: Four Piedmont Scouts from Troop 1 returned to the East Bay last month after completing an unforgettable 8-day, 7-night backpacking expedition through the Eastern Sierra Nevada Mountains – a journey that tested their endurance, fostered camaraderie, and brought them face-to-face with some of California’s most awe-inspiring wilderness. Their journey covered over 70 miles on the trail under 40-pound packs and included over 15,000 feet of climbing. The group included brothers Miguel and Mateo Long, Sean Heafey, and Luke Ironside with adults Steve Long, Chad Ironside, and Bryan Houlette. Starting at the 10,200 foot Cottonwood Lakes Trailhead outside of Lone Pine, the Scouts traversed 12,178 foot New Army Pass and settled into their third night of camp at Timberline Lake, where alpine serenity and crisp mountain air rejuvenated their spirits. From there, they tackled the crowning challenge of their adventure – summiting Mt. Whitney, the tallest peak in the contiguous United States at 14,505 feet. Through wind, altitude and miles of switchbacks, they reached the summit with exhilaration and pride. On day six their route led them over Forester Pass, the highest point on the Pacific Crest Trail at 13,200 feet. The southern approach to this pass is dramatic, unlike any other pass in the Sierras. Originally deemed impassable by early trail builders, the pass was finally conquered in 1931 with creativity, determination, and of course, dynamite! One worker lost his life in its creation. A plaque at the site of the accident commemorates his sacrifice. Today, hikers are rewarded with panoramic views stretching north into Kings Canyon National Park and south into the vast Kern River valley flowing through Sequoia National Park. Each Scout was pleasantly surprised to find that parents had hiked in to meet them for the final night. Brendan Heafey, Sara Ironside and Marisa Strong brought new energy and gummy worms to the group. They fished and watched a beautiful sunset across Kearsarge Lake. The group exited via 11,760 foot Kearsarge Pass on day eight, exhausted but triumphant. Their journey was a physical achievement and a lesson in grit and gratitude. Through grueling climbs, freezing nights, starfilled skies, blisters, wind, rain, and thunderstorms, the Scouts returned with stronger leadership skills, tighter bonds, and stories they’ll carry for life. Piedmont Scouts from Troop 1 begin their 8-day, 70-mile trek through the Eastern Sierra Nevada Mountains at the Cottonwood Lakes Trailhead outside of Lone Pine, California. Pictured are Steve Long (left), Chad Ironnside, Bryan Houlette, Miguel Long, Sean Heafey, Mateo Long, and Luke Ironside. An ancient Foxtail Pine, rare and remarkable is found only at elevations at or above 10,000 feet in California in the southern Sierra around Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks. They can live to be more than 3,000 years and are the second-oldest species tree still living on our planet. Troop 1 Eagle Scout Miguel Long shows the California State Fish and namesake of the wilderness that Piedmont Scouts traversed – the Golden Trout Wilderness. Golden Trout are world renowned for their brilliant coloration and high-altitude adaptations. They evolved in only two streams in the southern Sierra Nevada, although they have since been planted in hundreds of lakes and streams across almost every state in the Western United States. Piedmont Scouts from Troop 1 pause for a picture atop 11,760 foot Kearsarge Pass on the final day of an 8-day, 70-mile trek through the Eastern Sierra Nevada Mountains. Pictured are Eagle Scout Miguel Long (left), Luke Ironside, Sean Heafey, and Mateo Long. Piedmont Scouts from Troop 1 enjoy lunch and the view atop 13,200 foot Forester Pass, the dividing line between Kings Canyon and Sequoia National Parks: Bryan Houlette (left), Chad Ironside, Luke Ironside, Mateo Long, Miguel Long and Sean Heafy.

articles.text: As I enter my senior year of high school, it’s the first question everyone asks. But why isn’t the question When do I want to go? Since I was five years old, I’ve spent every August to June in school. The schoolwork and stress that came along with it only worsened as I got older. Now, after years of spending my free time studying, college sounds exhausting. So, instead of jumping into more tedious lectures and late-night essays, a gap year sounds like a much-needed reset. For those who don’t know, a gap year is a break from formal education between secondary school and higher education. When my mom first mentioned the idea of taking a gap year, I immediately shot it down. I, like many others, believed that a gap year would only cause me to lose focus on my goals, fall behind, and appear less appealing to colleges. As it turns out, 60% of students return from their gap years with a more serious outlook on their academics. According to Denver Gap Year, this increased focus leads to gap year students scoring 23% higher grades than students who didn’t take a gap year. This increase in focus can boost a gap year student’s likelihood of being admitted to certain colleges. As a child, I was often asked what I wanted to be when I grew up. My answer never stayed the same. One day I’d want to be a doctor, the next I’d want to be an actress. At 17, I haven’t figured out my dream career path. Many of us don’t know what we want to do with our lives, but are asked to put something down on our college applications. This sort of uncertainty leads to 80% of college students changing their major at least once. Taking a gap year allows students to explore different fields of interest to discover what suits them best. Some may travel the world, develop an interest in a language, and choose to major in it. Some may intern at different businesses and find that they want to work in marketing. Others may paint and gravitate towards art history, or help animals and discover an interest in veterinary studies. Now, unable to decide, I’m planning a gap year that will test drive my interests. Maybe I’ll volunteer at a chimpanzee sanctuary in Africa to see if I want to study zoology. Or maybe I’ll coach tennis in El Salvador to see if I want to be a teacher. Everyone’s gap year can be completely different. It’s up to you. Taking a gap year doesn’t make me lazy or less than. A gap year allows me to dive into my passions, learn practical skills, and grow my perspective of the world. It’s about taking a step back to move forward with purpose. It’s a time to figure out who I am outside of the classroom. When I do enter college, I want it to be with a clearer sense of direction and a stronger understanding of who I am. Choosing what college I want to attend and, moreover, what kind of career I want to have are huge decisions. I want to make sure I make the best decision. For me.

articles.text: Is Piedmont still a tennis school? Pictured is Piedmont’s 2017 NCS title-winning team. Staff Photos When I arrived at the Post in what feels like a lifetime ago, one thing was made clear to me: Piedmont High is a tennis school. At the time, the Highlanders’ girls’ tennis team was pushing one of the longest undefeated league title runs (19 years) in state history led by coach Neil Rothenberg. Moreover, they were robbed of a potential sixth-straight Division 2 North Coast Section team championship because of smoke from the fire in Paradise in November 2018. But now in 2025, how has the school’s top program changed? Is Piedmont High still a tennis school, or have other teams caught up? boys’ team, meanwhile, had won five NCS titles (2009, 2012, 2014, 2015, 2017) in a nine-year span from 2009-2017. Piedmont High hasn’t won a league title, boys or girls, since 2018. Tennis has, however, excelled on an individual basis in recent years. Lucas Smolko is entering his senior year and won the last two WACC singles titles. Tanya Kononova won a WACC singles title in 2022 and reached the 2023 finals. articles.text: In this week’s edition of Piedmont athletes in college, we take a look at three basketball players including Samantha Smith of Macalester College, A.J. Harris of Emory University, and Hannah Govert of Bryn Mawr. Photo courtesy of Macalester College Samantha Smith, PHS Class of 2024, played her freshman year on Macalester College’s basketball team. SAMANTHA SMITH Photo courtesy of Emory University A.J. Harris, PHS Class of 2023, helped Emory University reach the Elite Eight of the Div. 3 NCAA Tournament. games for 825 minutes, scoring 336 points by shooting 45 percent from the field and 33 percent from 3-pointers, to go along with 149 rebounds, 43 assists, 42 steals and seven blocks. Harris notched a career-high of 28 points on December 30 in a 77-71 win over Union College. He finished his illustrious Piedmont High career as the school’s All-Time leading scorer with 1,570 points after playing in just two full varsity seasons and an abbreviated 2021 season due to COVID-19. Harris was named the WACC’s Co-Player of the Year alongside Berkeley’s Samir O’Brien. We named Harris the Posts’ 2023 honorable mention for Athlete of the Year. Macalester College Samantha Smith, PHS Class of 2024, just finished her freshman year at Macalester College. Macalester College finished its season with a 12-13 overall record. Smith appeared in all 25 games and started seven times, playing 16 minutes per game for 57 points, 34 rebounds, 11 assists, six steals, and two blocks. Her best performance was scoring 18 points in an 84-71 loss to Webster. At Piedmont High, she was a two-year varsity member. Smith helped the Highlanders win the 2023 D4 NCS title as a senior and claim back-to-back Western Alameda County Conference firstplace banners. She transferred to PHS as a junior after two years at Dublin. HANNAH GOVERT A.J. HARRIS Emory University A.J. Harris, PHS Class of 2023, finished his sophomore year on Emory University’s men’s basketball team in Atlanta. The Eagles finished its season 23-6 and reached the Elite Eight of the Division 3 NCAA Tournament before falling to Wesleyan University 61-58 in overtime. Harris appeared in all 29 Bryn Mawr College Hannah Govert, PHS Class of 2022, is set to be a senior at Bryan Mawr College after being a four-year member of Piedmont’s varsity basketball team. The Owls went 7-18 last season. Govert started all 25 games, averaging 25 minutes per game. She scored 54 total points, 63 rebounds, 25 assists, 18 steals, and one block. In the 2023/2024 season, Govert appeared in 17 games and recorded a career high of 11 points, to go along with 13 assists and 12 steals. She earned Centennial Conference Academic Honor Roll honors. As a freshman, she averaged 24.8 minutes per game for 54 points and 94 rebounds. With Piedmont as a senior in 2022, Govert helped the Highlanders reach the D4 NCS Championship with the No. 2 seed, losing to No. 1 Marin Academy. Photo courtesy of Bryn Mawr Athletics Hannah Govert, PHS Class of 2022, finished her junior on Bryn Mawr’s basketball team as starting player in every game.

articles.text: Kyla Williams is a two-sport athlete in soccer and track. With only so many end-ofyear awards to go around, some of the mighty contributions made throughout the year tend to get lost on the shuffle. In this article, we reflect on three athletes at the school who were either entering their first year as a starter or getting time in their largest role in their PHS athletic career. Three who made a huge impact included Kyla Williams in soccer and track, Massimo Mittone in baseball, and Savannah Dennig in basketball. Staff Photos KYLA WILLIAMS Soccer, Track and Field Kyla Williams is a rising sophomore and proved to be a spark on the soccer team in the winter and track as a sprinter in the spring. On the soccer team, Williams made a big impact as a forward, typically carving up defenses using her speed down the wing. She scored once in Piedmont’s NCS 5-1 win over No. 16 College Prep in the D4 playoffs. We gave her Athlete of the Week honors in January after scoring twice in Piedmont’s 5-2 regular season win over Castro Valley, while logging a goal and assist in PHS’ 4-3 loss to Alameda. With the track team, Williams earned an honorable mention for All-League honors. She reached the NCS Meet of Champions on the 4x100 relay team, which finished 17th of 24 teams. Massimo Mittone, a sophomore, is a standout pitcher on the baseball team. He didn’t give up a single run through his first four appearances and has established a 1.12 ERA in five appearances for a team-leading 22 strikeouts. He recorded two consecutive complete game shutouts, helping Piedmont win 1-0 over Miramonte on March 11 and 1-0 over San Leandro on March 20. Mittone was in consideration for our Freshman of the Year award before suffering a season-ending injury in late March. SAVANNAH DENNIG Basketball MASSIMO MITTONE Baseball Massimo Mittone has burst onto the scene for the baseball team last season as a freshman pitcher, building a 3-0 record in four starts. We named him The Posts’ honorable mention for Athlete of the Month in March. Savannah Dennig was another key member of Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team becoming one of the best in the state. She proved to be one of PHS’ best defenders, rebounders, and a reliable ball-handler. One of Dennig’s best performances came in the fifth-place final in the NCS Open Division against Salesian, where she put up 18 points and three rebounds in the Highlanders’ 70-48 win. She earned an honorable mention for All-League honors and our honorable mention for Freshman of the Year. Savannah Dennig was a standout freshman on the basketball team.
articles.title: Breakout stars of 2024-25: Kyla Williams, Massimo Mittone, Savannah Dennig

articles.text: Lorena leaped again to stop Jorelyn Carabalí. The result bumped Brazil up to No. 4 in the FIFA World Rankings, while Colombia moved up three spots to No. 18. The United States remains No. 1 despite losing the 2023 World Cup in the Round of 16 to Sweden by way of penalty kicks. It’s a shame that the U.S. Women’s National soccer team doesn’t play in the CONMEBOL federation against the best South American teams like Brazil, Colombia, Argentina, and so on. This year’s Copa America Femenina’s final on Saturday, August 2 between the Canaries of Brazil and Los Cafeteros of Colombia played to a breathtaking penalty shootout, in extra time, with Brazil winning 5-4 after finishing extra time in a heated 4-4 draw. Colombia took the lead three different times, but the Brazilians answered after each score. Linda Caicedo opened scoring for Colombia in the 25th, but Angelina Alonso Costantino equalized with a penalty kick deep into first-half stoppage time at 45+9’. In the second half, Colombia forced an own goal on Brazil to take a 2-1 lead in the 69th minute, but Amanda Gutierres scored on a long-range shot for Brazil just 11 minutes later. With just two minutes of regulation time left, Mayra Ramírez put Colombia ahead at the end of a counter attack in the 88th. But Brazil wouldn’t go away. With the last kick of regulation, 39-year-old Brazilian legend Marta scored the tying goal at 90+6’ in stoppage time. Her shot was an absolute rocket from about seven yards atop the area, taking the attempt on her first touch on the volley. It was a breathtaking shot from Marta, leaving Brazil coach Arthur Elias with his head in his hands and tears of joy running down his cheeks. Colombia’s players stood in pure disbelief. Marta wasn’t done in extra time. In the 105th minute, she gave Brazil their first lead of the game after being left unmarked in front of Colombia’s net. Receiving a cross, Marta redirected the ball into the bottom corner. Then in the 115th with five minutes left in extra time, Colombia responded with another banger of a goal. This time, Leicy Santos arced in a free kick from a few yards atop the penalty area to force penalty kicks. PKs came all the way down. Brazil was once again on its heels after missing their second kick, but it was Brazil goalkeeper Lorena da Silva Leite playing the hero. Lorena saved a shot by Santos to keep Brazil ahead 3-2 despite their early miss, but Marta was stonewalled on the next attempt. With a 5-4 lead, Photo courtesy of Winchester Star Marta was Brazil’s Player of the Match, scoring two goals, including a stunning rocket from distance to force extra time. Photo courtesy of EFE.com Brazil’s goalkeeper, Lorena, made a pair of huge saves in penalty kicks to lift her team above Colombia.
articles.title: Brazil beats Colombia in stunning Copa America final

articles.text: In this week of Hiking with Jon, we delve into our final of six features of trails near Lake Tahoe with the popular urban exploring adventure, Donner Pass near Truckee on the north side of Lake Tahoe. We typically cover Donner Pass in the winter where snow sheds on the abandoned railway give excellent cover from the harsh winters of the Sierra Nevada Mountains. During the spring and the summer, the location is an excellent place to walk for experienced hikers, elder seniors, and young children given the railway’s level surface. The abandoned railway was originally constructed in 1867 for the Central Pacific Railroad’s portion of the first transcontinental railroad. The trek takes you through hollowed out mountain tunnels and snow sheds through the pass surrounding Donner Lake. Aside from the obvious historic railway, the mountain pass is the same area where the DonPhotographed in May 2025, snow still was visible in some sections of the Donner Pass trail. For art lovers, murals and graffiti line the interior of the snow sheds. You can walk through the hollowed-out tunnels at Donner Pass along an abandoned railway that was constructed in 1867. A second China Wall is inside the long tunnel through a mountain.

articles.text: Featured artwork includes Akea Brionne’s ‘Mary Ellen Pleasant,’ 2025, Bryan Keith Thomas’s detail of ‘Heirloom’ Gilded Box, 2025 and Demetri Broxton’s ‘Eyes That Have Seen the Ocean Will Not Tremble at the Sight of the Lagoon,’ 2025. Black Gold: Stories Untold, a major art exhibition highlighting the transformative impact of Black communities on California’s cultural, social, and political worlds, is now on view at Fort Point National Historic Site in the Presidio. Black Gold features artwork by 17 contemporary artists and collectives who lived in California from the Gold Rush to the Reconstruction period following the Civil War, including never-before-seen commissions by Akea Brionne, Demetri Broxton, Adrian L. Burrell, Adam Davis, Cheryl Derricotte, Mildred Howard, Tiff Massey, Umar Rashid, Trina Michelle Robinson, Bryan Keith Thomas, and Cosmo Whyte. articles.text: Stern Grove Festival, the west coast’s longest-running free festival, concludes next weekend with the “Big Picnic Weekend” featuring performances by Damian and Stephen Marley on Saturday, August 16, and Diana Ross on Sunday, August 17. Stern Grove Festival, now in its 88th season, is held annually at the amphitheater at Sigmund Stern Grove in San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. Stern Grove Festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts, including opera, theater, and music. Tickets for picnic table seating are still available for the Big Picnic Weekend, the festival’s annual fundraiser. This year’s fundraiser concludes the summer-long concert series with performances by Damian and Stephen Marley, the multi-Grammy-winning artists and sons of the legendary Bob Marley, and Motown icon Diana Ross. Ross rose to fame as the lead singer of the 1960s pop group the Supremes and earned the title “Queen of Motown Records.” She began her solo career in the 1970s, launching iconic hits like “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” “Touch Me in the Morning,” “I’m Coming Out,” and “Love Hangover.” Visit https://www.sterngrove. org to reserve picnic tables. Table purchases are considered donations to Stern Grove Festival and are non-refundable. Damian and Stephen Marley

articles.text: Shotgun Players’ current production of Terry Guest’s award-winning play The Magnolia Ballet has been extended through Saturday, August 16. The Magnolia Ballet is a southern gothic love story that explores themes of the Black experience, queerness, masculinity, and intergenerational relationships in the American South. Protagonist Ezekiel “Z,” a Black queer teen growing up in rural Georgia, builds a romantic relationship with his white friend, Danny. As their love grows, Z interacts with the ghostly ancestors of his past, including his father Ezekiel Mitchell V. Through these interactions Z reckons with homophobia, toxic masculinity and racism as he comes to terms with his own sexuality. The Magnolia Ballet, directed and choreographed by AeJay Antonis, made its Bay Area debut on the Shotgun Players stage last month. Guest’s play won the 2022 Jeff Awards for Best Production and Best Performer as well as the David Goldman Best New American Play Award. “The complexity of masculine love lies at the heart of this work. Fathers, sons, and friends navigate the razor’s edge between tenderness and violence, fear and vulnerability,” Marquis said in a press release. “Terry Guest writes about people like the men in my family who don’t always get a voice on the theatrical stage.” “He invites us in to see them,” Marquis added. “He doesn’t just make them villains. He cracks them open.” Shotgun Players Artistic Director Patrick Dooley said Guest also captures “that familiar sensation of the fine line between pain and love in our most intimate relationships.” “It’s so rare to read a play that seamlessly weaves poetic imagery and dances into a story with such a strong narrative,” he added. Jaiden Griffin stars as Ezekiel “Z” Mitchell VI with Drew Watkins as his father, Ezekiel Mitchell V. Nicholas René Rodriguez plays Danny Mitchell, Z’s best friend and lover. Devin A. Cunningham, who recently played the role of Juicy in San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Fat Ham, takes on the role of the Apparition. Performances take place at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley, located at 1901 Ashby Ave. Tickets are available online at www.shotgunplayers.org/show/magnolia or by calling the box office at 510-841- 6500 x 303. articles.text: Concerts take place in the meadow on the Filoli historic grounds. Filoli Historic House and Gardens in Woodside launches its series of outdoor summer concerts, featuring six artists over two weeks, on August 17. Performances take place in the meadow on Filoli’s historic estate, combining nature, art and history for a truly unique Bay Area summer experience. Located 30 miles south of San Francisco and nestled at the foot of the Santa Cruz Mountains, the scenery provides for an idyllic backdrop to view the setting sun and enjoy live music on a pleasant summer evening. Gangstagrass, a hip-hop, country and bluegrass fusion band, launches the concert series on Sunday, August 17. Gangstagrass is the brainchild of founder Oscar Owens who had become an in-demand producer and singer/songwriter during the early 2000s. The group has released multiple albums since its formation, competed on America’s Got Talent and produced the Emmy Award-nominated theme song for the FX Network series Justified. All shows will run from 7 p.m. to 8:30 p.m., with check-in beginning at 5:30 p.m. The House and Garden will be open for guests to explore prior to the concert. To view a full list of performers, visit https://filoli.org/summer-stage/. The Summer Stage concert series coincides with Filoli’s Summer Nights events, serving as a time to gather with family and friends and enjoy the sunset and summer blooms. Every Thursday night throughout the summer, the Grove Bar is serving wine and beer in the garden, nestled under the shade of the Olive Grove. The Georgian-style terraces around the historic house offer sweeping views of the Santa Cruz Mountains, a contrast to the 16-acre formal English Renaissance-style garden to the south. Gangstagrass, a bluegrass hip-hop band, launches the concert series.
articles.title: Gangstagrass launches summer concert series

articles.text: The Napa Valley chamber music festival Music in the Vineyards’ (MITV) 31st season continues through August 24. Tickets are available for upcoming performances by Pacifics Quartet, Ariel Quartet and more. The series of live performances traditionally showcases distinguished chamber musicians as well emerging young talent during its four-week season in August, with concerts held at popular wineries and vineyards throughout the valley. Since the festival’s inception in 1995, wineries in Napa Valley continue to lend their space for MITV musicians to perform live, offering a uniquely Northern Californian festival experience. With complimentary wine tastings at each intermission and breathtaking views of the Napa Valley, this unique combination of wine country ambiance and great musicianship allows audiences to experience chamber music in small intimate settings. The multi-Grammy award winning Pacifica Quartet performs next Wednesday, August 13, at Hudson Ranch and Ariel Quartet performs on Wednesday, August 20 at the Hudson House located at Beringer Vineyards. Pavone String Quartet, a group of undergraduate students at the world-renowned Shepherd School of Music at Rice University, perform on August 11. The Pavone Quartet are winners of Music in the Vineyards’ 2025 Fellowship Quartet competition. A finale concert is held on Sunday, August 24, closing the festival with Beethoven’s Archduke trio performed by a trio of virtuosos. A reception dinner under the stars follows. For more information on Music in the Vineyards and to purchase single day tickets, visit www.musicinthevineyards.org. Pacifica Quartet musicians Austin Hartman (second violin) Mark Holloway (viola) Simin Ganatra (first violin) and Brandon Vamos (cello)

articles.text: Vertigo, directed by Alfred Hitchcock, is, as anticipated, a classic psychological mystery-thriller that slowly draws the audience into its tightly scripted narrative from the first frame. Set in San Francisco in the mid-1950s, the story opens with Detective Scottie Ferguson (James Stewart) and a uniformed officer chasing a suspect across the flat, third story rooftops of a downtown building. Scottie slips and goes over the edge of the roof, barely managing to grip the roof’s gutter. Terrified, he is dangling above an alley, three stories below. The officer, leaning forward toward Scottie yells, “Reach up with your hand”…and suddenly he falls down to the concrete below. The impact of that moment results in Scottie developing vertigo, a fear of heights which can result in a disorienting feeling of falling or a fear of heights (aka agoraphobia). It forces the detective to retire from the department. This disabling fear is briefly demonstrated when Scottie visits his ex-fiancé, Midge (Barbara Bel Geddes), a fashion designer, who encourages him to stand on a stepping stool hoping he will, with practice, realize he is on the mend. This failed attempt only reinforces his sense of vertigo and a harrowing sense of losing his balance. The narrative then cuts to Scottie meeting with an old acquaintance, Gavin (Tom HelKim Novak and James Stewart in Vertigo more), a wealthy ship builder. After some minutes of small talk, Gavin explains that he is worried about his wife, Madeline (Kim Novak), who seems detached, acting strangely, seemingly fixated on her great-great grandmother, Carlotta. Gavin wants to hire Scottie, asking him to follow her and report back. At first reluctant, offering other alternatives (a psychiatrist), he agrees. All of the above is act one, slowly compelling; however, it is also the beginning of Hitchcock’s attempt to pull the audience into a perplexing mystery, one that fashions countless questions all while observing Scottie tailing Madeline. Her days include a visit to Carlotta’s grave where she places a small bouquet of flowers near the tombstone, and sits for hours in a museum, looking at an historical painting of this long-ago deceased woman titled “Carlotta.” To go any further would deprive the viewer of what I think of as a long and unexpected reveal; yet, this is, after all, Hitchcock. What is puzzling suddenly becomes a love story that takes a classic turn and stunning twist. Consider the title of the film, Vertigo, a condition which plagues Scottie. It becomes a metaphor for his obsessive need for Madeline while creating a sense of foreboding, which haunts the long and complex act three. Both Stewart and Novak are simply excellent. Both go through a metamorphosis regarding their characters and deliver exceptional performances. Vertigo. Directed by Alfred Hitchcock. Starring James Stewart, Kim Novak, Barbara Bel Geddes. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated PG. Released in 1958. Now streaming on Netflix/Prime/apple/Fandango. Sara Couden, contralto Zachary Gordin, piano

articles.text: The term B movie was long used to refer to those second tier films that ran after the main attraction during the 40s and 50s. In fact, to make sure audiences felt like they received sufficient bang for their buck, going to the movies meant watching a newsreel a cartoon and two feature films. The Bs were hurry-up movies with less well-known stars, small budgets, and were the equivalent of those dime magazines widely popular during the same time period known as pulp fiction. The paper between the covers was rough and cheap (pulpy), the subjects running to gritty detective mysteries, wildly imagined tales of science fiction and melodramatic westerns. This is all to say that instead of calling a film such as Edge of Darkness a B movie (and all the films of that ilk), it might be more accurate to simply call it pulp cinema. That’s not to imply that such films are not entertaining. Indeed, lacking all pretense, with stripped down plots and dialogue, pulpy movies can entertain and then some. If it’s a truism that not all films have to be analyzed, or run through an intellectual colander, then B movies are a good fit. They are rarely ambiguous, or enigmatic or laden with the implied. Edge of Darkness uses the familiar and satisfying trope of revenge to move the plot along at an intense clip.
