articles.text: Lewis MacDougall in A Monster Calls A Monster Calls is extraordinary and a heartfelt surprise. But take seriously its rating of PG-13. While the trailer seems to promise a child’s tale, involving an enormous monster in the humanoid shape of a gnarly yew tree, the British film is so much more. There is not a hint of Disney to be found, and the narrative goes far beyond the familiar palliative, “happily ever after.” At the film’s center is 12-yearold Conor (Lewis MacDougall) who is in a place in his young life that is almost more than he can bear. He is relentlessly bullied at school, haunted by a traumatic nightmare that causes him to wake in the deep of night, and coping with the life-threatening illness that is consuming his mother (Felicity Jones). He is also unable to turn to his rigid and distant grandmother (Sigourney Weaver). His father (Toby Kebbell) has been, for most of his life, absent, living in America and though he arrives briefly due to his ex-wife’s illness, he offers little comfort to Conor. And then one night, as he sits in his room sketching in his notebook, strange things begin to happen, a pencil rolls across his desk, onto the floor. Objects begin to move. And then, there, outside his opened window, stands a monster (the voice of Liam Neeson), a giant man-tree, who suddenly crashes into Conor’s room and speaks to him, insisting that he tell him three stories. Conor is both terrified and combative, wanting to suspend his disbelief, yet boldly resistant to what is but cannot be. articles.text: Freaky Friday is a family friendly comedy, ideal for kids (8+), tweens and teens, but not to forget that parents will find lots to smile at as well. At the center of the story is single mom Tess (Jamie Lee Curtis), widowed several years ago and now on the brink of marrying Ryan (Mark Harmon). Her daughter, Anna (Lindsay Lohan), just 15, is a surly teenager. The two frequently find themselves at odds. Actually they couldn’t be more different. Tess is a multi-tasking, stressed-out psychologist, who either on her cell phone, checking her Palm Pilot, or seeing patients. Anna plays the guitar, is failing English, generally feckless and often in detention. One evening they go out for a Chinese dinner, the meal followed by a fortune cookie. While all seems benign, we soon learn that it wasn’t. Inexplicably, they wake up the next morning having discovered that they have, in effect, well, body-swapped. While it isn’t a new premise, as films go in Hollywood (recall Big with Tom Hanks, for example), Lohan and Curtis do a superb job trying to adjust to this remarkable change. Both stand before the mirror and have that expected “Good grief, what’s happened to me?” moment. Both actors are having fun with their roles, conveying that neither is prepared to walk in the other’s shoes. Tess can’t play the guitar, nor can she do algebra, nor navigate school. Anna stumbles through Tees’ neurotic patient appointments, and even attends a talk show where she tries to sell her mom’s recently published book on aging. Tess has a hilarious problem when she is confronted with the very awkward attention of Anna’s hunky, motorcycle riding boyfriend, Jake (Chad Michael Murray) who doesn’t want to take “no” for an answer. All of this amounts to one hilarious moment after the next, using the fulcrum word “empathy,” all while the story unfolds. Though they were both in constant disagreement, slowly they develop lots of insights into one another. Anna comes to understand what it means to be a mom, and Tess realizes that being a teen is no walk in the park, what with all the changes in moods that define what it means to be an adolescent. Reconciliation is not far off. Freaky Friday. Directed by Mark Waters. Starring Jamie Lee Curtis, Lindsay Lohan, Mark Harmon. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released in 2003. articles.text: Weekends until August 25, 11–2 p.m. Nepal art exhibit This exhibition brings together Nepali artists living in the USA as first-generation immigrants. The body of works explores the paradoxes of diasporic life and reflects the tension between strong attachment to the culture left behind and the process of assimilating into a new society. It is the result of seven months’ research on Nepali Diaspora artists in the Bay Area and beyond, by Fulbright Visiting Scholar Swosti Rajbhandari Kayastha with San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum, the show has provided a platform for artists to express their unique experiences and perspectives, often highlighting the complexities of navigating multiple cultures and identities. The gallery will be open to the public without charge on Saturdays and Sundays from July 26 to August 25, from 11 a.m. until 2 p.m. each weekend. Sunday, August 10, 4:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pops Piano Trio In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, piano; Marshall Perry, upright bass; and Albert Brooks, drums – will perform a concert in tribute to Richard Rodgers, the premier composer of the American musical. This concert will be loaded with jazz and pops favorites dating from the ‘20s through the ‘50s, including eleven songs composed by Richard Rodgers! Tickets, $25 at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6214927, will also be available ($30) at the door with cash or check only. Seating is limited to the first 50 attendees. Experience encore performances of Julia Seeholzer’s Portraits of Disquiet, a gripping reflection on our modern world first performed in FO’s online recital series during the pandemic, and Jake Heggie’s At the Statue of Venus, a poignant and humorous journey of anticipation and self-discovery which was a part of Festival Opera’s 2021 mainstage production. Don’t miss this rare opportunity to be moved and inspired by two extraordinary works performed by artists who bring every note and word to life. articles.text: A performance of HMS Pinafore on Sunday afternoon at the Lesher Center in Walnut Creek drew a disappointingly small crowd. Given that the Lamplighters have been delighting audiences with their top-notch and colorful operettas for about 73 years, the sparse attendance was somewhat surprising. Lamplighter productions are known for their vibrancy and quality, precisely how a Gilbert and Sullivan production should be—and Sunday’s performance was no exception. As I understand it, the performers on stage generously donate their talents and time, while only the orchestra members receive payment. The performance began punctually at 2 PM with the dimming of the lights. From the opening notes of the overture, it was clear that the orchestra, led by the energetic conductor Brett Strader, was playing crisply and with great enthusiasm. This energy was palpable both in the pit and on stage, largely thanks to Strader’s spirited direction. Gilbert and Sullivan operettas achieved widespread popularity for several reasons. First and foremost, they were designed as accessible entertainment. Sullivan’s music, though not particularly groundbreaking, was masterfully composed and always resonated perfectly with Gilbert’s librettos. Sullivan’s musical achievements were so admired in his lifetime that Queen Victoria knighted him. Gilbert, however, had to wait until after the Queen’s death for his knighthood. Victoria had objected to some of his sharp social commentary. Though all members of Sunday’s cast were in fine voice, their diction was notably poor. Ini-

I found myself questioning whether they were singing in a language unfamiliar to me. Despite the English libretto by Gilbert and the provided supertitles, the words were nearly impossible to discern. Audiences should not require supertitles to follow an English operetta. The responsibility falls squarely on the stage director to ensure clear enunciation, a rarity nowadays as actors frequently rush their speech and neglect consonants in song. Gilbert and Sullivan operettas famously stirred audiences with pointed social commentary. HMS Pinafore, for instance, cleverly critiques the inefficiencies of the British Navy, particularly evident in the song “When I Was a Lad.” No wonder Queen Victoria hesitated to bestow knighthood upon Gilbert. The operetta also touches on themes like baby switching, power struggles, and culminates in a vibrant, patriotic finale. Each Gilbert and Sullivan operetta aims to both delight and enlighten, offering ample food for thought. Yet, for actors singing on stage, here’s a friendly reminder: PLEASE ENUNCIATE! articles.text: A series of paintings by Bay Area native artist Kristen Jensen is on display this month, with artwork depicting life during the COVID-19 pandemic. The exhibit, “Social Distancing – Five Years On,” is on display now through August 31 at Studios Eleven Gallery, 560 2nd Street, Oakland. An Artist’s Reception scheduled for August 16, from 1:00-5:00 p.m. Jensen has been painting professionally since 1999, and currently works from her studio at Studios Eleven in Oakland, California. Known for her abstract and representational art, many of Jensen’s paintings include architectural elements that hearken back to her childhood fascination with the blueprints her father Artist Kristen Jensen, a Bay Area native, paints in her studio. Social Distancing, No. 7: Masking Up. Depicted serving the Oakland community during the pandemic, Frederick Shavies would later become Piedmont’s Police Chief. Social Distancing, No. 11: College Life, 2020. Social Distancing, No. 4: The Ballet Lesson. Social Distancing, No. 12: Dreams Deferred. brought home from his architectural practice. Jensen’s work appears in private and corporate collections across the country. Notably, the gallery features a painting of Piedmont’s new Police Chief Frederick Shavies from when he was an officer in Oakland. During the early days of the COVID-19 shelter-in-place, Jensen met Shavies on duty in Oakland, and he kindly agreed to have his photo taken for her painting series. Navigating the fractures and polarization of 2025, Jensen’s painting series offers a space to revisit the unexpected moments of grace and collective perseverance during the COVID-19 pandemic. These paintings hope to reflect a shared experience, capturing the uncertainty, stillness, isolation, grief, resilience and unexpected beauty of those unprecedented times. “I started the ‘Social Distancing’ series as a way to stay connected to the outside world during the COVID-19 shelter-inplace,” said Jensen. “The subjects are mostly people I know or have seen my few trips out into the world, or images that have been shared by friends.” During the pandemic, Jensen used her project as a fundraiser to help people in the Bay Area experiencing food insecurity and kids in underserved communities. Prints and cards of the pandemic paintings were sold, with 100% of the profits going toward the fundraiser. Post-pandemic, Jensen is finally able to put together an in-person art exhibit for the paiting series. Social Distancing, No. 13: Keep Calm and Carry On.

articles.text: This summer, Ensemble from Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) had the honor of representing the United States at Laulupidu, Estonia’s world-famous national song festival. Held every five years in Tallinn, Laulupidu is one of the largest choral gatherings in the world, bringing together more than 30,000 singers and tens of thousands of audience members in a multi-day celebration of music, identity, and cultural pride. For the youth of PEBCC Ensemble, it was an experience of a lifetime. Wearing concert attire alongside choirs from across Estonia, Japan, and beyond, Ensemble joined the Select Children’s Choir – a prestigious group made up of top young singers from Estonia – to perform advanced repertoire beyond the main festival pieces. Singing in perfect Estonian under the soaring arch of the Tallinn Song Festival Grounds, the same place where peaceful singing protests helped bring independence to the country decades ago, PEBCC singers rose to the moment with grace and power. pages.text: Wednesday, August 6, 2025 27 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers visit Hampton Park By Dick Carter The prior week Piedmont Scout Sammy Ragones had given the Walking on Wednesdays group a special tour of two new batting cages at Coaches Field he built in partnership with the City for his Eagle Scout project. Hampton Park is another city park with a sports field known as Hampton Field that has a historical connection to Scouting. The group thought they would go to Hampton to complement their Coaches Field visit. The walkers went up Highland Avenue to Sheridan and Wildwood Avenues, through the Hall Fenway to Crocker Avenue and into Crocker Park. The group stopped in front of a newly planted, fenced garden where a large pine tree once stood, where a page from Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website was shared. There is a picture of an April 1, 1917 Oakland Tribune article with a headline that proclaimed, “Piedmont Improves Park.” The article reported, “Work had begun for the improvement of a city park at Union avenue (the original name of Hampton Road), opposite the residence of Wallace M. Alexander. The ground is a triangular lot … adjoining the residence property of Frederick Hall. This lot was purchased by Alexander and some of his neighbors … and presented to the city of Piedmont for park purposes.” The group went through the park past the granite sculpture of a Bear and Her Two Cubs by noted sculptor Beniamino Bufano in the park's center. The walkers exited the park and went up Hampton Road to Hampton Park. On the park’s front steps more history was shared and a group photo was taken. From Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research the walkers learned that Hampton Park was once part of 50 acres purchased in 1911 by Louis Titus, a Berkeley real estate developer. He intended to build a mansion on this large tract of land, but in 1912 the new city of Piedmont raised property taxes significantly. Titus dropped his plans and left Piedmont. In 1914 James Tyson, a lumber and shipping businessman bought 30 acres of the land for his home. Tyson was a strong supporter of Piedmont Boy Scouts, which began in 1910, and in 1921 he made a portion of his land available to the Piedmont Scouts for their use as an outdoor camp. During the Great Depression in 1938 Tyson also make this land available to the Piedmont schools. A WPA project leveled it with the intention that it would be the site of a future “East Piedmont” school. However, it was never built. In the 1950s and 60s the land was a dusty, sometimes muddy baseball field for young kids. When grass was planted, youth soccer matches were often played there on a soggy field because an underground water flow was an on-going problem. Hampton Park has evolved greatly over the years. It is much different today than what Piedmonters experienced 100, 50, and even 25 years ago. A building was constructed in 2000 to house children's programs that is used by the Piedmont Cooperative Playschool and the Recreation Department. Dramatic improvements were made to the field and park during 2017 in a $2 million public/private partnership that the Piedmont community generously supported. Drainage and artificial turf were installed that made the field more serviceable during the year. In 2019 the baseball backstop was dedicated and named in honor of Oakland Police Officer John Hege. The 41-year-old Piedmont native was one of four officers fatally shot following a traffic stop in East Oakland on March 21, 2009. He was the only one who remained alive long enough to enable his organs to be donated to people in need of transplants. The field is used today for organized baseball, children¹s football, and soccer. The park also has two tennis courts, a backboard, a volleyball court, and six basketball hoops. There is a children's play structure and sand area that are located a few feet from the tennis courts. The walkers took a group photo at the front of the park then went down La Salle Avenue to Indian Road and stayed on LaSalle until reaching Mandana Boulevard in Oakland. A few steps up the street Mandana turns into Crocker Avenue and the walkers were back in Piedmont. They returned to the Exedra via the Hall Fenway, Wildwood, Sheridan, and Highland Avenues. It was noted that the Hall Fenway is named to honor Herbert Hall, a descendant of Frederick Hall named in the 1917 Oakland Tribune park article. In the early 1960s Herbert Hall convinced the City to accept this property that was previously a Key System 10 Line Train right-of-way, and he worked with neighbors and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation to raise funds for its acquisition. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: In 2003, Harvard undergrad and computer genius Mark Zuckerberg began work on a new concept that eventually turned into the global social network known as Facebook. Six years later, he was one of the youngest billionaires ever, and, for better or worse, he’s still filthy rich and still in the news. His fame got a bump in 2010 when the director David Fincher and the writer Aaron Sorkin made a movie about his rise and his travails. It’s called The social Network and you can catch it next week in Piedmont. One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The Social Network stars Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg. Aaron Sorkin won an Oscar for his screenplay. The film was released in the United States on the weekend of October 1, 2010, debuting at Number One, with widespread critical acclaim. Rotten Tomatoes gave it an approval rating of 96%, followed by this critical consensus: “Impeccably scripted, beautifully directed, and filled with fine performances, The Social Network is a riveting, ambitious example of modern filmmaking at its finest.” Roger Ebert named it the best film of the year. “David Fincher’s film has the rare quality of being not only as smart as its brilliant hero, but in the same way. It is cocksure, impatient, cold, exciting and instinctively perceptive,” Ebert said. And Rolling Stone also named it the movie off the year, adding “ Fincher and Sorkin triumph by lacing their scathing wit with an aching sadness that defines the dark irony of the past decade.” In addition, the film appeared on 78 film critics’ top-ten lists. The Social Network will be screened on Thursday, August 14 at 1:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45. Everyone is invited on a drop-in basis. The event is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunc. The next movie in the Piedmont series is Dead Poet’s Society, starring Robin Williams, to be screened on Thursday, September 11th.

articles.text: Craven (Bojana Novakovic), are leaving his home when a shotgun blast kills Emma. Initially Tommy thinks the shot was aimed at him and wonders who from his past (an ex-con seeking his long contemplated revenge) might have tried to kill him. As he looks for the killers (there were two), he begins to discover pieces to the puzzle that are at first perplexing but soon point not to him as the target but to Emma. It turns out that she worked for a major defense contractor, Northmoor, located in Northhampton, and that she was flirting with the idea of becoming a whistleblower. Since this is pulp cinema, there has to be pulp dialogue (here spoken with a Boston accent) wherein the Chief of Detectives says to Tommy, “These guys are armed and dangerous,” and Tommy says, “What do you think I am?” Note the lack of ambiguity. Or when Tommy looks at a corporation CEO, who he senses is somehow involved in Emma’s death, and says, “You had better decide whether you’re hanging on the cross or banging in the nails.” What that means is a bit unclear, but no matter, the pulp imagery is spot on, sounding hardedged and threatening, mirroring Tommy Craven’s persona throughout the film.

Carter knows how to write a captivating romance and Since this is pulp cinema, there has to be pulp dialogue (here spoken with a Boston accent) wherein the Chief of Detectives says to Tommy, “These guys are armed and dangerous,” and Tommy says, “What do you think I am?” Note the lack of ambiguity. Or when Tommy looks at a corporation CEO, who he senses is somehow involved in Emma’s death, and says, “You had better decide whether you’re hanging on the cross or banging in the nails.” What that means is a bit unclear, but no matter, the pulp imagery is spot on, sounding hardedged and threatening, mirroring Tommy Craven’s persona throughout the film. Getting stuck in a nine-day time-loop. Oh, and your grandfather who is planning to announce the sole benefactor of the family inheritance dies each day.” —Jenny Gilroy, E. Shaver, Bookseller, Savannah, GA Is Edge of Darkness violent? Definitely. In the Craven world you can have conversations, brief and to the point, and then the moment is quickly reached when the best response is simply to hit or shoot the bad guy. Sometimes these moments of carnage and gunplay, or the threat of carnage and gunplay, are connected to the plot by the slightest of threads. No worries, though, they’re a rush. This is, after all, a take no prisoners pulpy revenge movie. Edge of Darkness. Starring Mel Gibson, Ray Winstone, Danny Huston and Bojana Novakovic. Directed by Martin Campbell. 1 hr., 57 min. articles.text: On Monday, July 28, at 2:25 pm, an armed robbery occurred in the 100 block of Arbor Drive in Piedmont where suspects stole tools from construction workers at gunpoint. Piedmont Police officers responded and began an investigation which later led to the arrest of four suspects in Oakland and the recovery of a firearm. The two victims were working inside an unfinished garage on Arbor Drive when a black Nissan Altima approached and two men got out. One suspect pointed a firearm at the workers and ordered them not to move while demanding their tools. A victim reported both suspects were armed. A toolbox and a table saw were stolen and then the suspects fled on foot back to the Nissan. A third suspect, who had remained in the driver’s seat, drove away. Just after 7:00 p.m., Piedmont Police officers Singh and Faucher located the suspect vehicle in Oakland on Fruitvale Avenue. Four individuals were detained by Piedmont Police and identified as Serina Vares, Kenneth Vigil, This 9mm handgun was recovered by Piedmont Police while making four arrests in Oakland on July 28. Alberto Sanchez, and Jose Barajasavalos. The individuals were arrested and booked for multiple charges including theft and robbery. The investigation uncovered a loaded firearm and additional evidence connecting the suspects to the robbery. One suspect was later also found to have an outstanding warrant from Piedmont for Felony Reckless Evading Arrest. The suspects were transported two at a time and booked into Santa Rita Jail. Charges included Robbery, Felon in Possession of a Firearm, Possession of a Stolen Vehicle, Vehicle Theft, and Probation Violation, along with multiple outstanding warrants and in-custody holds.

It is relatively easy to critique the creed on the basis that it was written exclusively by males, that the theological debates it tried to resolve seem rather insignificant to people of a much later time and place and that any effort to put the faith into words is by definition incomplete and inadequate. Still, meaningful cultural exchange and unforgettable memories. But it was Tallinn, and Laulupidu, that brought everything into focus. From spontaneous singing on the grass to processions through the rain-soaked streets of Old Town, PEBCC singers experienced firsthand how song can unite generations and nations. “The moment the flame was lit and the whole crowd began singing, I understood what this meant to them,” said one singer. “I’ll never forget it.” As PEBCC looks ahead to future exchanges, including its own Golden Gate Festival in July 2026, the lessons of Laulupidu will continue to resonate: that music has the power to transcend language, to carry history, and to forge lifelong friendships. PEBCC looks forward to welcoming national and international choirs to the Bay Area for a week of public concerts, friendly competitions, connection, and shared song. articles.text: Garbage, recycling collection resumes in Piedmont Residents throughout Piedmont saw trash pile up this month as sanitation workers went on strike across northern California. During the strike, City staff spent their time negotiating with the solid waste collection company, Republic Services, to advocate for service in Piedmont. The regional sanitation worker strike began on Tuesday, July 8 in Stockton. In support of the Stockton strike, Republic Services workers in the Bay Area joined the regional work stoppage, with the “sympathy strikes” affecting as many as 30 cities in the region, including Fremont, Newark, and Piedmont. Two days after work ceased, City staff managed to negotiate with Republic Services for limited black bin pickup service on July 10, with extremely limited recycling pickups in the days after. Much of this service was reportedly carried out by members of Republic Services management, in lieu of the striking sanitation workers. “From the first day of the symBlue garbage trucks were back on their regular collection routes as of July 21.
articles.title: Sanitation worker strike ends

articles.text: Keeping with summer tradition, the City of Piedmont has hired a herd of nearly 200 goats to control the weeds in Moraga Canyon ahead of the upcoming fire season. Starting in early July, the goats were let loose onto the hillside behind the Corporation Yard in a flurry of black, white, and brown fur. The stubby-horned lawnmowers have worked across this area for the past weeks, moving soon across the road to tackle the hillside above Blair Park. Each year, the City of Piedmont competitively bids on the services of these goats in the employ of Ecosystem Concepts, a local vegetation management company. The goats are almost always in high demand for a number of reasons – they are inexpensive, better for the environment, and take care of challenging areas that would otherwise require mechanical equipment. The herd’s vegetation-eating efforts are crucial to fire prevenA pair of goats team up to take down a bush. tion, especially in the hot summer months. In the coming weeks, goats will chew their way through the overgrown brush, weeds and the lower limbs of trees behind the Corporation Yard to create a “fuel break” through which wildfires are less likely to burn. Officials hope that this effort will provide a critical buffer for homes up the hill in the event of a fire. The annual grazing usually takes around two to three weeks. The furry lawncare advocates eat for roughly eight hours in a day, with a break for rest between their morning and afternoon shifts. This work goes hand-in-hand with fuel load reduction work implemented earlier this year, clearing shrubs and pruning trees A herd of goats takes a break after a long day of work.

articles.text: On March 25, State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond announced 336 elementary schools selected for the 2025 California Distinguished Schools Program. None of Piedmont’s three elementary schools – Beach, Wildwood, and Havens – were included. The omission may come as a surprise to many, given that Piedmont Unified School District recorded the third-highest scores statewide in both English Language Arts and Math on the 2024 California Assessment of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP) exams. These exams replaced the STAR testing system in 2014. The California Distinguished Schools Program recognizes schools under two categories: “closing the achievement gap” and “achieving exceptional student performance.” Piedmont schools were not eligible for the first category. To qualify for “closing the achievement gap,” a school must enroll at least 40% of students from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds. That designation includes students who qualify for free or reduced-price meals, or whose parents or guardians did not complete high school. In Piedmont, those percentages remain well below the 40% threshold: Wildwood has 2.2% of students in this category, Beach 3.1%, and Havens 1.7%. articles.text: Editor: The city built the existing fence between the sidewalk and roadway from Red Rock Road to Monte Avenue to stop children walking to and from Coaches Field from crossing Moraga Avenue. The City Council considered the fence necessary because Caltrans standards for safe sightlines and stopping distances could not be met on Moraga Avenue at or near Red Rock Road. Recent analyses provided by independent traffic engineers show that violations of those standards remain not only between Monte Avenue and Red Rock Road but also along much of the Blair Park frontage on Moraga Avenue. Despite these violations, the draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan shows an option with 199 homes in Blair Park. Piedmonters presumably value children living in Moraga Canyon as highly as children living in central Piedmont. If so, the Specific Plan would include strategies to protect children living in Blair Park from the danger inherent in crossing Moraga Avenue to Coaches Field or to the existing fenced sidewalk they would use to walk to school and back. pages.text: 2 2 Wednesday, July 30, 2025 Opinion By Jay Russell QUESTION: Ozzy Osbourne, Hulk Hogan and Malcolm-Jamal Warner all passed away last week. Which had the biggest impact on your life? Asked on Monday, July 28, in central Piedmont and by phone. CAROLYN PAN, Portsmouth Road I was so sad to hear about Malcolm’s passing. He will always be Theo Huxtable in my mind. I also used to wrestle in my grandpa’s living room with my brother and cousins and we would fight over who got to be Hulk. SUSY ASCHE, Greenbank Avenue Ozzy 100%! “Mama I’m coming home” is my favorite song. LETTERS - MAIN Safer plan needed for Blair Park pedestrians Editor: The city built the existing fence between the sidewalk and roadway from Red Rock Road to Monte Avenue to stop children walking to and from Coaches Field from crossing Moraga Avenue. The City Council considered the fence necessary because Caltrans standards for safe sightlines and stopping distances could not be met on Moraga Avenue at or near Red Rock Road. Recent analyses provided by independent traffic engineers show that violations of those standards remain not only between Monte Avenue and Red Rock Road but also along much of the Blair Park frontage on Moraga Avenue. Despite these violations, the draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan shows an option with 199 homes in Blair Park. Piedmonters presumably value children living in Moraga Canyon as highly as children living in central Piedmont. If so, the Specific Plan would include strategies to protect children living in Blair Park from the danger inherent in crossing Moraga Avenue to Coaches Field or to the existing fenced sidewalk they would use to walk to school and back. We have, after all, protected children walking from central Piedmont to Coaches Field even though they have little reason to cross Moraga. How, then, can we not protect children required by the Specific Plan to cross the same roadway? Sadly, the only protection offered in the Plan is to “signalize” a crossing at Red Rock Road – a location we know does not meet Caltrans safe sightlines standards. What good does it do to “signalize” an intersection that drivers will not see until it’s too late to stop? The only responsible and decent solution to this conundrum is to adopt the safer option shown in the Plan. That option would move the city corporation yard to Blair Park and locate the 199 homes around Coaches Field. The only argument publicly offered against this alternative is that the city would incur the cost of rebuilding the corporation yard. The city will, however, incur that cost whether or not new housing ever appears in Moraga Canyon. The Community Facilities Element of the General Plan adopted last year identifies the corporation yard as a public safety facility. articles.text: In a time marked by escalating anti-immigrant rhetoric and policies, BBQ Without Borders will return to the Oakland Museum of California on Saturday, August 2, This popular biennial event, presented by No Immigrants No Spice (NINS), is more than just a celebration of food; it’s a powerful affirmation of the immense and often unacknowledged contributions of immigrant communities to our nation’s cultural richness and social fabric. Amidst a social context where immigrants often face disproportionate challenges, including workplace discrimination, difficulties affording basic needs, and fear related to immigration laws, BBQ Without Borders stands as a beacon of solidarity and celebration. This event is a space that uplifts the lived stories and contributions of immigrants who, despite these hurdles, are incredible drivers of growth and innovation. For instance, in 2022, immigrants were estimated to be one-quarter of America’s entrepreneurs, founding 43.8% of the Fortune 500 companies. These immigrant-founded companies employed more than 14.8 million people worldwide and generated over $7 trillion in revenue. Furthermore, immigrants contribute billions of dollars in taxes annually, with undocumented immigrants alone contributing an estimated $96.7 billion in federal, state, and local taxes in 2022. This year’s event, themed “Toward A Greener Future,” will not only highlight the economic and cultural impact of immigrants but also emphasize the valuable sustainable practices they have long contributed. From eco-friendly farming and cooking techniques rooted in ancestral wisdom, no waste whole animal and planting cooking to a deep, inherent respect for nature, immigrant communities offer crucial insights into cooking up a more sustainable tomorrow for all. This focus is particularly urgent as climate-related hazards like floods, storms, and wildfires are already a major driver of global human mobility, playing a role in 26.4 million displacements in 2023 alone. Climate change is increasingly exacerbating displacement, with the World Bank projecting that slow-onset climate disasters could drive internal displacement for as many as 216 million people by 2050 if urgent action is not taken, further underscoring the interconnectedness of climate justice and immigrant rights. Attendees will embark on an unforgettable culinary journey, savoring an incredible array of flavors from a stellar lineup of Bay Area immigrant chefs, including: • Anthony Salguero of Popoca: Bringing Salvadoran-inspired delights to the forefront. • The team at Café Colucci: Serving up their renowned Ethiopian cuisine. • Maria Marquez of Tacos Mama Cuca: Offering delicious traditional and modern Mexican flavors from Sonora. • Desserts from Third Culture Bakery: A sweet Indonesian and Taiwanese inspired finish to an exceptional meal. Beyond the mouth-watering food and vibrant performances, BBQ Without Borders is a critical fundraiser for the East Bay immigrant community. Their ambitious goal this year is to raise $50,000 in mutual aid. “In a time when the narratives around immigration are often distorted, BBQ Without Borders offers a tangible space with a delicious counter-narrative,” said Piedmont resident Dr. Vibha Gupta, founder of No Immigrants No Spice. “We believe that by coming together over food, we can bridge divides, celebrate the cultural richness immigrants bring, and directly support those who are building our communities from the ground up.” BBQ Without Borders will be held on Saturday, August 2 from 3:00 - 7:00 p.m. at Oakland Museum of California. Tickets are now available at https:// events.humanitix.com/bbq-without-borders-2025/tickets, and various ticket tiers are available. Join for an afternoon that nourishes both body and soul, where every bite supports a more inclusive and equitable future. Organizers encourage people to come hungry, leave inspired, and help celebrate the invaluable tapestry that immigrants weave into the fabric of their communities. No Immigrants No Spice (NINS) is a non-profit organization that uses food as a way to highlight the positive impact immigrants have on culture and society. Through events and initiatives like BBQ Without Borders, NINS aims to foster understanding, celebrate diversity, and provide critical support to immigrant communities, including the distribution of micro-grants. Learn more at https://noimmigrantsnospice.org/.
articles.title: Immigrants Without Borders to host BBQ at Oakland Museum

This focus is particularly urgent as climate-related hazards like floods, storms, and wildfires are already a major driver of global human mobility, playing a role in 26.4 million displacements in 2023 alone. Climate change is increasingly exacerbating displacement, with the World Bank projecting that slow-onset climate disasters could drive internal displacement for as many as 216 million people by 2050 if urgent action is not taken, further underscoring the interconnectedness of climate justice and immigrant rights. Attendees will embark on an unforgettable culinary journey, savoring an incredible array of flavors from a stellar lineup of Bay Area immigrant chefs, including: • Anthony Salguero of Popoca: Bringing Salvadoran-inspired delights to the forefront. • The team at Café Colucci: Serving up their renowned Ethiopian cuisine. • Maria Marquez of Tacos Mama Cuca: Offering delicious traditional and modern Mexican flavors from Sonora. • Desserts from Third Culture Bakery: A sweet Indonesian and Taiwanese inspired finish to an exceptional meal. Beyond the mouth-watering food and vibrant performances, BBQ Without Borders is a critical fundraiser for the East Bay immigrant community. Their ambitious goal this year is to raise $50,000 in mutual aid. “In a time when the narratives around immigration are often distorted, BBQ Without Borders offers a tangible space with a delicious counter-narrative,” said Piedmont resident Dr. Vibha Gupta, founder of No Immigrants No Spice. “We believe that by coming together over food, we can bridge divides, celebrate the cultural richness immigrants bring, and directly support those who are building our communities from the ground up.” BBQ Without Borders will be held on Saturday, August 2 from 3:00 - 7:00 p.m. at Oakland Museum of California. Tickets are now available at https:// events.humanitix.com/bbq-without-borders-2025/tickets, and various ticket tiers are available. Join for an afternoon that nourishes both body and soul, where every bite supports a more inclusive and equitable future. Organizers encourage people to come hungry, leave inspired, and help celebrate the invaluable tapestry that immigrants weave into the fabric of their communities. No Immigrants No Spice (NINS) is a non-profit organization that uses food as a way to highlight the positive impact immigrants have on culture and society. Through events and initiatives like BBQ Without Borders, NINS aims to foster understanding, celebrate diversity, and provide critical support to immigrant communities, including the distribution of micro-grants. Learn more at https://noimmigrantsnospice.org/.

The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP): • Identifies the natural hazards that pose the greatest risk to Piedmont • Describes how each hazard would likely impact Piedmont if it occurred • Identifies and prioritizes actions the city and community could take now to prevent or reduce those impacts The draft LHMP is the result of nine months of research, discussion and public engagement. Gathering community input is the final step before the city finalizes the document and submits it to Cal OES for approval. Community members may submit comments online or by email to lhmp@piedmont.ca.gov. A presentation on the draft LHMP was held at the Public Safety Committee meeting on Thursday, July 24, and a meeting of the Hazard Mitigation Planning Committee took place on Friday, July 25. Details about upcoming meetings are available at piedmont. ca.gov/LHMP. Priority actions to reduce risk The draft LHMP identifies 21 actions that could help reduce risk in Piedmont, including: • Strengthening IT infrastructure through redundancy and backup systems • Retrofitting or replacing critical facilities to meet modern seismic safety codes • Conducting annual fire fuel mitigation on city property • Strengthening building and fire codes to require wildfire-resistant construction and more stringent vegetation management standards Including an action in the LHMP does not guarantee implementation. Rather, it helps position the city to apply for state and federal mitigation grants that could support the proposed project. articles.text: “I was so excited my voice wouldn’t come out of my mouth!! I was trying to signal to everyone - it’s there! It’s there! And once we saw it everyone was just jumping!” What exactly sparked this level of excitement from Dr. Alejandra Hernandez, coral reef scientist at the California Academy of Sciences? A huge, deep-dwelling hammerhead shark, spotted on her very first submarine descent! Dr. Hernandez’s work to understand marine ecosystems spans both shallow and deep coral reefs. Using innovative technology including robotics, 3D photography, and genetic sequencing, the team gathers data on the flora and fauna found in these ocean ecosystems, monitoring where corals grow and their health, near the surface and at deeper depths. Academy chair of aquatic biology Dr. Pim Bongaertz explains that sometimes the same species of coral grows near the surface and in the depths. The conditions are so different - how does coral do that? Understanding the answer may enable solutions that increase coral reef resiliency around the world. In search of answers to this and other pressing questions facing marine ecosystems, Drs. Bongaertz and Hernandez have “blue careers,” working to advance marine conservation. Dr. Bongaertz is quick to point out that his lab will not single-handedly solve the critical problems facing coral reefs, rather they are providing an important piece of the puzzle being worked on by scientists all over the globe. Collaboration is a critical ingredient for success, spanning scientists, communities, policy makers, financers, educators and more. All of these collaborators have exciting blue careers too, supporting an entire “blue economy.” To ensure healthy marine life, thriving coastal communities, and a robust “blue economy,” it’s crucial to engage young people. School programs at the California Academy of Sciences offer ocean related museum field trips to K-5 students, opportunities to connect with scientists working in “blue careers,” and more. Through engaging activities and stories students realize science is for everyone and needs everyone! Students also practice the transformative skill of collaboration. A third grader explains: “Collaboration for scientists is important because it can help them finish a task and help others. They can share knowledge with each other. It is important, too, because if they get into a bad situation, they can help each other get out of it.” Interested in seeing what it’s like to descend into the deep in a submarine like Dr. Hernandez, or learn about some of the technology illuminating the secrets of the deep? Unseen Oceans, on view at the California Academy of Sciences through September 7, gives visitors of all ages the opportunity to discover the dazzling creatures and features of the deep ocean, and to explore the exciting, collaborative “blue careers” that await the next generation of scientists as they puzzle out a thriving future for these precious ecosystems. articles.text: questions. All three Piedmont elementary schools were named California Distinguished Schools in 2023, under the same two criteria. That year, 22 elementary schools in Alameda County were recognized, compared to just 13 in 2025. The significant drop has led some to wonder if there was an informal quota by region, or whether the state prioritized schools demonstrating progress in underserved populations. The Piedmont Post reached out to Thurmond’s office for clarification but did not receive a response by press time. The Distinguished Schools program alternates annually between elementary and secondary school recipients. In 2024, middle and high schools were eligible. Piedmont Middle School received the honor in both 2019 and 2021. No awards were given in 2022 due to the pandemic. Selection for the program is based on metrics from the California School Dashboard, the state’s multi-indicator accountability system. “The California Department of Education (CDE) uses multiple measures to identify eligible schools based on their performance on the state indicators as specified on the California School Dashboard,” Thurmond’s press release stated.

articles.text: The opening of a new memorial mediation garden at Piedmont Community Church was celebrated on church grounds during a dedication ceremony on Saturday, July 12. Church members Suzie Skugstad, Paul Schroeder and a host of volunteers dedicated time to create the garden and donations from church members and friends paid for construction. articles.text: Piedmont City Council voted at their meeting on Monday, July 7, to approve a contract for street paving to contractor McGuire and Hester for $1,370,000, with an overall construction budget of $1.5 million. This project will remove and replace asphalt on 10 residential streets this summer, as well as restriping markings on 32 additional roadways. The residential repaving project calls for as much as 2,000 tons of hot mix asphalt in its repairs. It is also expected to have 4,200 square feet of roadway dig-outs, and repair 650 feet of gutter. Work locations are concentrated primarily in the Dracena Park area, between Grand and Highland Avenues. According to the Public Works Department the selection of streets was based upon streets with the most vehicle miles on them. This work is separate from the ongoing Grand Avenue Repavement Project, which is adding pedestrian safety features to the section of Grand Avenue in Piedmont. “We are removing and replacing existing asphalt,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. A work schedule for the project is expected in August. Public Works plans to notify residents of affected streets once the schedule is available, through flyers and other communication methods. For streets near schools, the City plans to coordinate with schools to minimize potential disruptions. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Toledo Blade Tadej Pogačar wins his fourth Tour de France title in six years. Tadej Pogačar continues to prove he’s a once in a generation type of athlete, winning this year’s Tour de France, marking his fourth title in six years. He is now equal on wins with Chris Froome, one behind France’s Jacques Anquetilm and Bernard Hinault, and two back of Belgian legend Eddy Merckx, and Miguel Induráin of Spain. Pogačar won the General Classification’ Yellow Jersey with a 4 minute, 24 second lead over Danish rival Jonas Vingegaard. It now marks the second consecutive year for Vingegaard to trail Pogačar after the Dane beat the Slovenian in 2022 and 2023. He captured four stage wins to help establish a four-minute lead with eight stages remaining. Also winning the Polka Dot Jersey for being the top Mountain Classification rider, Pogačar excelled on the hilly and mountain courses. He won Stage 4’s 108.2 mile hilly course and Stage 7’s 122 mile hilly course before making his push on the Stage 12-13 mountain ride. Pogačar won Stage 12’s 112.2 mile ride through the Pyrenees mountains with a sturdy 2 minutes, 10 second lead on Vingegaard in second. The Slovenian then won Stage 13’s 6.8 mile time trial in the Pyrenees with a 36 second advantage over Vingegaard, creating a 4 minute and 7 second lead in the process. articles.text: Richey recounts attaining No. 1 in the U.S. and subsequent work in mental-health awareness Photo courtesy of Cliff Richey A newspaper clipping of Cliff Richey’s monumental sudden-death victory over Stan Smith at the Berkeley Tennis Club’s Pacific Coast Championship in 1970. [Reprinted from October 2020] Back in the late 60s and early 70s, some of the best tennis players in the world would’ve been gathering in the shadows of the Claremont Hotel at the Berkeley Tennis Club around the start of October. The Pacific Coast Championship ran from 1889 to 2013, it was the second oldest ongoing tennis tourney in the United States and is predated only by the U.S. Open. With the start of tennis’ Open Era beginning in 1968, the final three years of the Pacific Coast Championships’ run in Berkeley from ’68 to 1971 meant the best players in the world were meeting close by. Many inf luential matches were taking place for the endof-year rankings, given an October championship meant it was among the final tournaments to determine the leaderboard. Back in 1970, that meant Cliff Richey squaring off with former Wimbledon and US Open champion Stan Smith for the No. 1 ranking in the United States in the semifinals of the Pacific Coast Championship in one of the most breathtaking matches ever played. Their match ran over four hours long and was perhaps the only time a No. 1 ranking came down to a sudden-death point. The score was 7-6, 6-7, 6-3, 6-4, and 4-4 in the final set with the next point the end-all, win-all. Richey hit a forehand volley for the winner. “Almost any way you cut it, the Pacific Coast Championship in Berkeley was the last event of the year for international players… That year going into the tournament, I knew I was in the running for the No. 1 ranking in the United States,” explained Richey from his home in San Angelo, Texas now 73-years old, describing that the U.S. ranking system. “That match was such an unusual finish; it went literally down to the last ball. I had a second serve in my hand at four points all, six-all in the fifth set after playing for four hours, it was ridiculous!” added Richey about the match. Richey’s victory over Smith also meant that he was on pace to win tennis’ world point system under the International Tennis Federation’s Grand Prix circuit, which was famously the predecessor of the current ATP Tour. “In addition, that match was also important because that was the first year the International Tennis Federation Grand Prix of tennis, which was a point system and started at the French Open and finished in Europe. I knew at the Berkeley event that I was doing well in the Grand Prix. “I went to Europe after beating Stan and beat Ken Rosewall in the semifinals London event, and I knew I had to win two matches in Stockholm the next week. The other player right on my butt was Arthur Ashe, but he had to win Stockholm… So the match against Stan also enabled me to win the Grand Prix,” explained Richey. Richey lost to Hall of Famer Arthur Ashe in the 1970 Pacific Coast Championship finals, but his No. 1 ranking was already solidified the previous round. “All the players, officials, or anybody who was close to the game knew that my match with Stan Smith in the semifinals would be for the No. 1 ranking regardless of what happened in the finals,” he said. Following his tennis career, Richey became an activist for mental health awareness after dealing with bouts of clinical depression. articles.text: In this week’s edition of Piedmont athletes in college, we take a look at Luke Barrett of St. Mary’s basketball team, Max Wagener of University of Redlands’ water polo team, and Nico Defazio of Howard Christian University’s baseball team. LUKE BARRETT Basketball St. Mary’s College Luke Barrett, PHS Class of 2020, finished as a senior leader on St. Mary’s No. 7 seeded team in the eastern bracket. The Gaels beat No. 10 Vanderbilt 59-56 in comeback fashion on March 21 in the Round of 64, but fell to No. 2 Alabama 80-66 the following round. He played a critical part in SMC’s opening round win over Vandy. He sent a pair of assists for 3-pointers in the second half, including one to Augustas Marčiulionis give his team a 53-50 lead with 4:33 left. He also knocked down a 3-pointer to give St. Mary’s a 56-50 lead with 2:01 left. Luke finished with a double-double against Vanderbilt with 12 points, 10 rebounds, and two assists. Against Alabama, he played 37 minutes, logging six points, seven rebounds, and an assist. A look back: Tennis legend Cliff Richey & the Pacific Coast Championships at the Berkeley Tennis Club Richey recounts attaining No. 1 in the U.S. and subsequent work in mental-health awareness Photo courtesy of Cliff Richey A newspaper clipping of Cliff Richey’s monumental sudden-death victory over Stan Smith at the Berkeley Tennis Club’s Pacific Coast Championship in 1970. By Jonathan Comeaux [Reprinted from October 2020] Back in the late 60s and early 70s, some of the best tennis players in the world would’ve been gathering in the shadows of the Claremont Hotel at the Berkeley Tennis Club around the start of October. The Pacific Coast Championship ran from 1889 to 2013, it was the second oldest ongoing tennis tourney in the United States and is predated only by the U.S. Open. With the start of tennis’ Open Era beginning in 1968, the final three years of the Pacific Coast Championships’ run in Berkeley from ’68 to 1971 meant the best players in the world were meeting close by. Many inf luential matches were taking place for the endof-year rankings, given an October championship meant it was among the final tournaments to determine the leaderboard. Back in 1970, that meant Cliff Richey squaring off with former Wimbledon and US Open champion Stan Smith for the No. 1 ranking in the United States in the semifinals of the Pacific Coast Championship in one of the most breathtaking matches ever played. Their match ran over four hours long and was perhaps the only time a No. 1 ranking came down to a sudden-death point. The score was 7-6, 6-7, 6-3, 6-4, and 4-4 in the final set with the next point the end-all, win-all. Richey hit a forehand volley for the winner. “Almost any way you cut it, the Pacific Coast Championship in Berkeley was the last event of the year for international players… That year going into the tournament, I knew I was in the running for the No. 1 ranking in the United States,” explained Richey from his home in San Angelo, Texas now 73-years old, describing that the U.S. ranking system. “That match was such an unusual finish; it went literally down to the last ball. I had a second serve in my hand at four points all, six-all in the fifth set after playing for four hours, it was ridiculous!” added Richey about the match. Richey’s victory over Smith also meant that he was on pace to win tennis’ world point system under the International Tennis Federation’s Grand Prix circuit, which was famously the predecessor of the current ATP Tour. “In addition, that match was also important because that was the first year the International Tennis Federation Grand Prix of tennis, which was a point system and started at the French Open and finished in Europe. I knew at the Berkeley event that I was doing well in the Grand Prix. “I went to Europe after beating Stan and beat Ken Rosewall in the semifinals London event, and I knew I had to win two matches in Stockholm the next week. The other player right on my butt was Arthur Ashe, but he had to win Stockholm… So the match against Stan also enabled me to win the Grand Prix,” explained Richey. Richey lost to Hall of Famer Arthur Ashe in the 1970 Pacific Coast Championship finals, but his No. 1 ranking was already solidified the previous round. “All the players, officials, or anybody who was close to the game knew that my match with Stan Smith in the semifinals would be for the No. 1 ranking regardless of what happened in the finals,” he said. Following his tennis career, Richey became an activist for mental health awareness after dealing with bouts of clinical depression. He’s off to play collegiate rugby with the California Golden Bears on at UC Berkeley also named Witter Field. At Piedmont High, Ashton was a two-way starter at running back offensively and linebacker defensively. He earned first-team All-League honors at both positions and was our honorable mention for Athlete of the Month last November. He helped lead Piedmont to a 10-2 overall record, the WACC Mission Division title, and reaching the Division 7 NCS Semifinals as the No. 3 seed. Piedmont’s 42-46 NCS win over No. 6 Fortuna marked the school’s first postseason win since 2017. Ashton ran for three touchdowns and 91 yards in PHS’ 31-7 win over Newark Memorial to secure the WACC Mission Division and followed up with three touchdowns game in their win over Fortuna. This summer I am doing a mix of weight lifting and on and off field conditioning. I am recording all of my workouts through an app that uses my body weight percentage to compile a weight ratio and rep range for each individual lift that I do. When I am out of the weight room, I am working on my explosiveness, mobility, and speed. This consists of doing hill sprints, stair workouts, and band exercises. What are your fitness goals for the summer? This summer I am focusing on gaining as much strength as possible. I am trying to gain weight while staying in shape and putting on as much muscle as possible. To do this I focus on my nutrition intensely. My overall goals are to get my “Drive Strength” lifts as high as possible, things like bench press, back squat, and shoulder press. How are you measuring your development? I measure my development through an app issued by Cal Rugby called Bridge Athletic. This app tracks my weight, the weight I am doing for each individual lift, and the amount of reps I can do. It all gets put into a system that creates a progressive overload mixed with high intensity to help me output maximum strength. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? For right now I do all of my workouts alone tracked through my app. My coach reviews my performance each week. In August, I will begin workouts with the team and on field training. The advice I would offer to young athletes is consistency and grit. Constantly going to the gym and eating right is so important in developing your progress. Even if you only have 30 minutes to workout, everything counts. An athletes’ body lives off of consistency and pushing it to its limits day in and day out. If you want to achieve your goals you must possess both of those characteristics every day in your life. pages.text: Wednesday, July 30, 2025 15 HIKING WITH JON Alpine lakes on the Five Lakes Trail near Lake Tahoe By Jonathan Comeaux This week we delve into one of the most unique trails in Northern California. In the fifth of six features of trails near Lake Tahoe, we focus on the Five Lakes Trail with connects a batch of alpine lakes in the Granite Chief Wilderness, just north of Lake Tahoe in Olympic Valley. The Five Lakes Trail is a 4.8 mile hike in total and provides around 1,100 feet of elevation gain. It’s a good location to get accustomed with hiking in high elevation. Our day starts at 6,450 feet of altitude, topping out at near 7,600 feet. It also connects with the historic Pacific Crest Trail. The trail goes on the southern ends of the KT-22 and Washeshu mountain peaks. To your left will be views of the pine-treed strewed mountains of Scott Peak and the mosaic of jagged rock cliff faces toward Ward Peak. But given that the location is surrounded by resorts and the tourist towns of Truckee, Tahoe City, Kings Beach and other North Lake Tahoe destinations, this hike can be a traffic jam. We passed 105 other hikers in the trek toward the summit and One of the five alpine lakes was still covered in snow as of May 2025. This lake is marshier, but equally as picturesque. The view of Ward Peak on the right. You’ll pass under a tramway toward the summit of KT-22 Mountain peak. Staff Photos The Five Lakes Trail of Alpine Meadows in north Lake Tahoe provides a 1,100 foot climb to a group of alpine lakes. One of the five accessible lakess is among the three that are swimmable. The backdrop is Washeshu Peak. another 51 on the way back toward the car—bringing an average of 31.5 people per mile. This means patience while passing others is of utmost importance. Long portions of the hike are less than six-feet wide, making you stepping aside for groups a certainty. I passed at least three groups of over 10-people and many families with children miserably making their way up the mountainside. Faster hikers may find themselves behind slower traffic without a clear pathway around. But at the summit, a group of five alpine lakes are waiting for you. Despite the foot traffic, you can easily find your own area on one of the three swimmable lakes. Finding all three could be tricky for some. The largest lake lays right off the main trail; hugging its eastern shore brings you to another interconnecting swimmable lake. Perhaps the most hidden lake is just east of there, staying on its eastern shore takes you to an open ridgeline where you’ll find the green valley of Alpine Meadows below you. The first mile of your course gains near 660 feet; 430 of that comes in the initial half mile, then a quick gain of near 200 feet up two switchbacks. The next mile mostly levels out, gaining another 370 feet to the group of lakes. Most your journey is in open space, so prepare with sunscreen and proper hydration. When we returned to the Five Lakes Trail in May 2025, snow was still present along the trail and at the lakes. Now at the end of July, the trails and lakes should be clear of any snow. According to Granite Chief Wilderness officials, camping at the Five Lakes Basin—600 feet away from the lakes’ shorelines—is permitted without the need of acquiring wilderness permits. Proper food storage and only gas powered stoves are required. The Chronicle’s Tom Steinstra ranked Five Lakes as Tahoe’s No. 10 best hikes in 2012. This is our fifth of six features of popular trails around Lake Tahoe. See The Post’s June 25 issue for Eagle Lake near South Lake Tahoe, July 2 feature of the Rubicon Trail around Emerald Bay, July 9 feature of the popular swimming hole at Horsetail Falls, and July 23 for a feature on Washeshu Peak. Next: Final Lake Tahoe feature on August 6 will be the unique Donner Pass Trail outside of Truckee. Look for this sign off of Alpine Meadows Road to start your hike.

articles.text: “Sip and Stroll” held Friday, Aug. 8 The 31st annual Sculpture in the Garden at Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek ends Sunday, August 10. The event is the nonprofit’s longest-running annual art exhibit and sale that celebrates sculptural pieces with the natural, arid beauty of the garden. This unique exhibit features 50 art installations and sculptures by over 30 craftspeople, ranging in design and materials used. A range of returning local artists, as well as newcomers, are participating this year. Sculpture in the Garden also serves as a fundraiser for Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery. All artwork is available to purchase, and proceeds from this exhibit go back into the Garden to help protect the plant collection, promote education and support preservation. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, was a pioneer in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public, made possible through fundraisers like Sculpture in the Garden. A Sculpture in the Garden ‘Sip and Stroll’ is held Friday, August 8, from 5:30 p.m. to 8 p.m. Ticket-holders may enjoy a complimentary drink and browse the garden pathways and sculpture art display. Sculpture in the Garden is on view through August 10 and is open to the public during regular garden hours, Wednesday through Sunday, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. The event is free with regular Garden admission. The nursery is located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek. For more information, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/event/2025-sculpture-in-thegarden/. articles.text: Husband and wife textile artists Agus Ismoyo and Nia Fliam host a batik workshop at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco this Sunday, August 3. Batik fabricmaking, originating from Indonesia and Java, has been celebrated for centuries. It still remains a large part of the culture of Indonesia and is widely used in celebrations and rituals, including marriage ceremonies and religious observations. The fabric is made using a wax and resist dyeing technique and has been mastered by artists and families for over 2000 years. Ismoyo and Fliam have been producing batik textiles in their Yogyakarta, Indonesia studio since 1985. They use the traditions of Ismoyo’s ancestors, batik makers in the court city of Solo in Java, and other historical batiks as contemporary art. Their studio produces high-end batik fabrics and paintings along with a range of wearable art and interior decor. The artists will offer a hands-on workshop at 1 p.m. inviting guests to create their own batik patterns. The workshop is suitable for families with children of all ages. The workshop will be followed by storytelling. The workshop is part of the museum’s free “First Sundays,” an event that invites visitors to enjoy cultural celebrations, hands-on workshops, dance and music performances, food popups and tastings, group tours, and other community events, as well as the museum’s world-renowned collection and special exhibitions. For more information, visit https://calendar.asianart.org/ event/batik-workshop-with-agusismoyo-and-nia-fliam/.
articles.title: Batik artists host workshop at Asian Art Museum this Sunday

articles.text: Docent tours held Tues through Sun Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art, the first exhibition to highlight Thiebaud’s extensive reinterpretations of works by his artistic heroes, leaves the Legion of Honor on August 17. Docent tours are held Tuesday through Sunday through Friday, August 15. The exhibition includes 65 pieces by Thiebaud, representing his wide-ranging reinterpretations of old and new European and American artworks spanning from 1957 to 2020. Thiebaud was an American painter known for his colorful works depicting commonplace objects like pies, pastries, and hot dogs, most often associated with the Pop art movement because of his interest in objects of mass culture. Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art is the first exhibition to spotlight his extensive involvement with art history throughout his six-decade-long career until his death in 2021. The exhibition is a facet of the “Legion of Honor 100,” a yearlong centennial celebration of San Francisco’s fine arts museums and its collections. “As a self-identified ‘thief,’ who mined the work of his predecessors and contemporaries, Wayne Thiebaud’s practice was deeply rooted in his study of art history, but this aspect of his work has never been explored,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Over the course of the next year, as we reflect upon the Legion of Honor’s legacy as a center of art historical research and inspiration, Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art couldn’t be more timely.” Exhibition curator Timothy Anglin Burgard said Thiebaud’s engagement with art history at large “revealed his belief that the world of art transcended limiting definitions of time and place, as well as progress.” “Viewed from this perspective, the entire global history of art, encompassing every movement and style, was as accessible, relevant, and inspiring to Thiebaud as contemporary art,” he said. Special exhibition tickets are required to join docent-led tours. Tours are held Tuesdays through Sundays, at 11:30 a.m. and 1:30 p.m. Docents will be available in galleries to answer questions between August 2 and August 15. pages.text: 18 18 Wednesday, July 30, 2025 Arts & Entertainment Sculpture in the Garden ends Aug. 10 at Ruth Bancroft garden “Sip and Stroll” held Friday, Aug. 8 By Allyson Aleksey The 31st annual Sculpture in the Garden at Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek ends Sunday, August 10. The event is the nonprofit’s longest-running annual art exhibit and sale that celebrates sculptural pieces with the natural, arid beauty of the garden. This unique exhibit features 50 art installations and sculptures by over 30 craftspeople, ranging in design and materials used. A range of returning local artists, as well as newcomers, are participating this year. Sculpture in the Garden also serves as a fundraiser for Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery. All artwork is available to purchase, and proceeds from this exhibit go back into the Garden to help protect the plant collection, promote education and support preservation. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, was a pioneer in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public, made possible through fundraisers like Sculpture in the Garden. A Sculpture in the Garden ‘Sip and Stroll’ is held Friday, August 8, from 5:30 p.m. to 8 p.m. Ticket-holders may enjoy a complimentary drink and browse the garden pathways and sculpture art display. Sculpture in the Garden is on view through August 10 and is open to the public during regular garden hours, Wednesday through Sunday, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. The event is free with regular Garden admission. The nursery is located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek. For more information, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/event/2025-sculpture-in-thegarden/. Batik artists Nia Fliam and Agus Ismoyo Batik artists host workshop at Asian Art Museum this Sunday By Allyson Aleksey Husband and wife textile artists Agus Ismoyo and Nia Fliam host a batik workshop at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco this Sunday, August 3. Batik fabricmaking, originating from Indonesia and Java, has been celebrated for centuries. It still remains a large part of the culture of Indonesia and is widely used in celebrations and rituals, including marriage ceremonies and religious observations. The fabric is made using a wax and resist dyeing technique and has been mastered by artists and families for over 2000 years. Ismoyo and Fliam have been producing batik textiles in their Yogyakarta, Indonesia studio since 1985. They use the traditions of Ismoyo’s ancestors, batik makers in the court city of Solo in Java, and other historical batiks as contemporary art. Their studio produces high-end batik fabrics and paintings along with a range of wearable art and interior decor. The artists will offer a hands-on workshop at 1 p.m. inviting guests to create their own batik patterns. The workshop is suitable for families with children of all ages. The workshop will be followed by storytelling. The workshop is part of the museum’s free “First Sundays,” an event that invites visitors to enjoy cultural celebrations, hands-on workshops, dance and music performances, food popups and tastings, group tours, and other community events, as well as the museum’s world-renowned collection and special exhibitions. For more information, visit https://calendar.asianart.org/ event/batik-workshop-with-agusismoyo-and-nia-fliam/. articles.text: Free concert in Golden Gate Park Sept. 7 San Francisco Opera’s 103rd season opens on Friday, September 5 with the company’s annual opera ball, featuring Music Director Eun Sun Kim conducting Verdi’s Rigoletto. Tickets for the San Francisco Opera’s annual ball, the company’s biggest fundraiser, are available online now. The ball is held at both City Hall and the War Memorial Opera House with proceeds benefiting the artistic initiatives of San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Opera Guild’s education programs. Guests will be greeted with a festive cocktail reception followed by a dinner crafted by local chefs served in San Francisco City Hall’s rotunda. The opening night performance of Verdi’s masterpiece Rigoletto closes out the evening. The opening weekend celebrations continue on Sunday, September 7 where Kim conducts the orchestra at Golden Gate Park, featuring stars from the fall season for the popular Opera in the Park concert, now in its 50th year. Highlights of the company’s 103rd season are the world premiere of The Monkey King by composer Huang Ruo and librettist David Henry Hwang, and a new production of Richard Wagner’s final masterpiece Parsifal. Saturday matinee performances have been added to the 2025-26 season schedule for the first time in many years, joining the popular Sunday matinee slots. The Saturday matinee performances are Rigoletto (September 13), Parsifal (October 25) and The Barber of Seville (June 6 and 20). Opera subscriptions and single tickets for concerts this year are available at (415) 864-3330 and sfopera.com. Opera ball tickets may be purchased online at https://www.sfopera.com/seasons/opera-ball/. The annual Opera Ball is held at San Francisco City Hall.
articles.title: SF Opera’s annual ball kicks off 2025-26 season on Sept. 5

articles.text: Woodminster Summer Musicals presents Lin-Manuel Miranda’s 2005 musical In the Heights with performances on select dates August 8 through 17, closing out the company’s summer season. Miranda’s critically-acclaimed musical love story is set over the course of three days involving characters in the largely Dominican American neighborhood of Washington Heights in Upper Manhattan, New York City. The score features hip-hop, salsa, merengue, and soul elements that are commonplace in Miranda’s works. In the Heights was nominated for thirteen Tony Awards and won four, including Best Musical. Woodminster Summer Musicals events are held at Woodminster Amphitheater, an outdoor amphitheater in Joaquin Miller Park, Oakland. Woodminster is a nonprofit organization that has presented summer musicals at the amphitheater for over 50 years, traditionally featuring three plays or musicals over summer months. In the Heights closes out Woodminster Summer Musical’s 58th season. The musical is performed August 8 through 10 and August 14 through 17.
articles.title: Woodminster presents In the Heights Aug. 8 - 17

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse’s production of My Fair Lady, based on the film adaptation of George Bernard Shaw’s 1913 play Pygmalion, is showing onstage now through September 13. My Fair Lady originally premiered on Broadway in 1956, telling the story of Eliza Doolittle, a Cockney flower girl who takes speech lessons from professor Henry Higgins, a phonetician, so that she may pass as a lady. The legendary original production received unanimous glowing reviews since its opening and won six Tony Awards, including Best Musical, and ran for 2,717 performances making it the longest-running musical in Broadway history at the time. The musical features a beloved score including classic songs “I Could Have Danced All Night,” “Get Me to the Church on Time,” “Wouldn’t It Be Loverly,” “On the Street Where You Live,” “The Rain in Spain,” and “I’ve Grown Accustomed to Her Face.” The score of My Fair Lady was among the most successful ever to emerge from the American musical theatre with more than Photo by Jessica Palopoli Jillian Smith as Eliza Doolittle in San Francisco Playhouse’s My Fair Lady five million copies of the Broadway-cast recording sold. San Francisco Playhouse’s production is directed by Artistic Director Bill English, with music direction by Dave Dobrusky and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The ensemble includes Jillian Smith as Eliza Doolittle and Adam Magill as Henry Higgins, with Julio Chavez, Heather Orth, Jill Slyter, Jura Davis, Kareem Jenkins and Andy Collins rounding out the ensemble. The show is on stage six days a week; Tuesday through Sunday. For showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/2024-2025-season/my-fair-lady/.
articles.title: SF Playhouse: My Fair Lady playing through Sept. 13

articles.text: Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon in The Trip to Spain When the first of these road trip movies appeared in 2010 and Steve Coogan and Bob Brydon took a culinary tour of England, I missed it. That film was followed in 2014 by visits to similar Michelin restaurants and five star hotels as they wandered through Italy. That led to The Trip to Spain, their third adventure-lite excursion through the rolling, bucolic hills of Spain, once again taking a week to stop at historic stone hotels, each at least several hundred years old, as well as renowned restaurants that serve cuisine on white oval plates that prove to be works of art. But the essence of these trips – adapted from a BBC series – is the conversation that Coogan and Brydon engage in as they sit across from one another, their elbows leaning on white table clothes while sipping robust local wines. So therein is the full reveal. There is no plot per se. Nada. Okay, there is a fragile, oblique theme in The Trip to Spain, one hidden in all their smart banter and endless impressions of the likes of Michael Caine or Sean Connery, enhanced with spot on Mick Jagger mimicry. That theme? It’s about confronting the reality that they have arrived at that point in life just beyond middle age. And as much as that seems to matter to them, the improvisational dialogue never takes a deep dive into this existential question, one that is instead studiously ignored in favor of verbal play and clever ripostes. There are private moments when the two pause and make contact with family back home and in a way those conversations are more engaging than the riffs that take place over dinner. I know that sounds heretical, for it is these back and forth musings and comedic retorts that take stage center and engage what I can only assume is an acquired taste. I do acknowledge that British humor can be dry as day-old toast. Sara Couden, contralto Zachary Gordin, piano

articles.text: The debut Prime streaming series Ballard is based on the best-selling novels written by the prolific Michael Connelly. It is not only exceptional in plotting and overall production but in characterization. It introduces Connelly’s first lead female character, detective Renée Ballard. It follows the compelling Prime series The Lincoln Lawyer and Bosch/Bosch Legacy, each based on novels by Connelly. Ballard is set in Los Angeles where, for reasons explored in some detail in the series, Ballard is given the lead in LAPD’s Cold Case division. She and a crew of volunteers and three reserve officers are given the task of taking deep dives into murders committed years ago and never solved. Though underfunded, and located in an expansive basement which is filled with shelved boxes of dormant cases. Ballard and team bring to each unsolved a renewed determination, state-ofthe-art technology (e.g. DNA/Ballistics), and what is referred to as the “murder book,” meaning the investigation’s detailed chronology and summary assembled by the original assigned detective. Ballard also finds herself coping with the seemingly inherent sexism of the LAPD.
