articles.text: Guillermo del Toro’s reimagined Oscar-winning Pinocchio is based on the classic Carlo Collodi’s children’s book, written in But parents should know that this stop-motion version, while immensely creative, is not your grandfather’s Pinocchio. Disney The reframed story opens by introducing the audience to Geppetto (David Bradley), an elderly Italian woodcarver, and his much-adored young son Carlo. The time is the early 1900s and the world is on the cusp of WWI. Geppetto has been hired to carve a massive crucifix for the local church. Of course Carlo is at his side, helping, his favorite pine cone always nearby. While working, Carlo hears the sounds of planes overhead and tells his father who grows concerned. He tells Carlo that they must leave the church and hurry home. Just as they are leaving, Carlo remembers he has forgotten his pine cone and runs back into the church to find it. Meanwhile one of the planes has dropped a bomb that hits the church, killing Carlo who is still inside. Geppetto, stunned and knocked off his feet by the blast, finds the body of Carlo lying near a pew. Holding his son in his arms, he is inconsolable, his grief and sense of loss are beyond comprehension. Tearfully, he buries Carlo along with the pine cone, and so years pass. Geppetto’s sadness only increases and he takes to drink, trying to lose himself in the bottle. Italy, now controlled by Il Dulce, has become a fascist state while supporting Germany as it prepares for WWII. And then, unexpectedly, in a grief-stricken drunken rage, Geppetto goes to Carlo’s grave site and with an ax chops down the pine tree that has grown by Carlo’s tombstone. In a haze of anger and grief, he spends a fevered night carving a wooden puppet from the trunk of the tree. Recall that this is del Toro, and the wooden boy bears little resemblance to Carlo. His legs are long and spindly, his nose too long, his body round and wooden. And, of course, there is no star for Geppetto to wish upon. But in the early dawn while Geppetto sleeps there appears a blue fairy (Tilda Swinton). And while Sebastian J. Cricket (Ewan McGregor), the story’s narrator, watches, life is bestowed on the wooden marionette. And so begins the strange, melancholy journey of Pinocchio, an undisciplined boy who brings only chaos into the old woodcarver’s life while Geppetto feels helpless to control him. The villagers think of the wooden youngster as a demon. The embedded question going forward is will Pinocchio become the boy prescribed by the Blue Fairy (truthful and obedient), or will he fall under the spell of a cohort of unsavory characters? That is the tale that unfolds. Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio. Directed by Guillermo del Toro and Mark Gustafsen. A stop-motion animation. With voices of Gregory Mann, Ewan McGregor, David Bradley. 1 hr., 57 min. PG-older kids, tweens. Released in 2022. Now streaming on Netflix/Apple/Fandango. A scene from Disney Animation’s Bolt Bolt is a family-friendly Disney animated story that kids will thoroughly enjoy. The feature begins with a 7-year-old girl named Penny (Miley Cyrus) who spots a puppy she insists she simply has to adopt and decides to call him Bolt (John Travolta). Actually the pooch is a White Swiss Shepard. Five years later, Penny and Bolt star in a hit television show in which the pair fight crime and block the evil plans of Dr. Calico (Malcom McDowell). In order to get the best performances from Bolt, the director convinces Bolt that he does have the actual super powers he displays in each episode, an example would be his “super bark.” Penny is dismayed, realizing that her pooch can never leave the set least he discover that his powers are not real. In one episode, a cliffhanger, Penny is “kidnapped,” Bolt thinks it actually took place and sneaks off the set believing she must be rescued. Instead he bumps his head, falls into a packing crate of peanuts, and is mistakenly shipped to New York City. Lost, he befriends a street-smart cat named Mittens (Susie Essman). A scene from Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio
articles.title: MOVIES FOR KIDS Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio

articles.text: He convinces her he has to get back to Hollywood and Penny. And so the adventure begins in earnest. Meanwhile, back in Hollywood, a White Swiss Shepard is found to replace Bolt so the television show can continue, in spite of Penny’s initial reluctance. Mittens and Bolt hit the road with a stopover at a trailer park in Ohio where they confront a series of close calls involving animal control and where they meet a hamster named Rhino (Mark Walton). Eventually, the dynamic trio continue on what proves to be a cross-country journey, headed for Hollywood, the television show set, and most of all Penny. Of course, there is one final harrowing moment on the set shortly after their arrival; however, this is Disney and the story has a perfect ending involving a reunion between Bolt and Penny and the adoption of rhino and Mittens by Penny. Bolt. Directed by Chris Williams and Byron Howard. With voices of John Travolta, Miley Cyrus, Susie Essman. Walt Disney animation. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released in 2016. Streaming on Disney+/Fandango/Apple/Prime.
articles.title: Bolt a kids’ delight

The time is the early 1900s and the world is on the cusp of WWI. Geppetto has been hired to carve a massive crucifix for the local church. Of course Carlo is at his side, helping, his favorite pine cone always nearby. While working, Carlo hears the sounds of planes overhead and tells his father who grows concerned. He tells Carlo that they must leave the church and hurry home. Just as they are leaving, Carlo remembers he has forgotten his pine cone and runs back into the church to find it. Meanwhile one Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio of the planes has dropped a bomb that hits the church, killing Carlo who is still inside. Geppetto, stunned and knocked off his feet by the blast, finds the body of Carlo lying near a pew. Holding his son in his arms, he is inconsolable, his grief and sense of loss are beyond comprehension. Tearfully, he buries Carlo along with the pine cone, and so years pass. Geppetto’s sadness only increases and he takes to drink, trying to lose himself in the bottle. Italy, now controlled by Il Dulce, has become a fascist state while supporting Germany as it prepares for WWII. And then, unexpectedly, in a grief-stricken drunken rage, Geppetto goes to Carlo’s grave site and with an ax chops down the pine tree that has grown by Carlo’s tombstone. In a haze of anger and grief, he spends a fevered night carving a wooden puppet from the trunk of the tree. Recall that this is del Toro, and the wooden boy bears little resemblance to Carlo. His legs are long and spindly, his nose too long, his body round and wooden. And, of course, there is no star for Geppetto to wish upon. But in the early dawn while Geppetto sleeps there appears a blue fairy (Tilda Swinton). And while Sebastian J. Cricket (Ewan McGregor), the story’s narrator, watches, life is bestowed on the wooden marionette. And so begins the strange, melancholy journey of Pinocchio, an undisciplined boy who brings only chaos into the old woodcarver’s life while Geppetto feels helpless to control him. The villagers think of the wooden youngster as a demon. The embedded question going forward is will Pinocchio become the boy prescribed by the Blue Fairy (truthful and obedient), or will he fall under the spell of a cohort of unsavory characters? That is the tale that unfolds. Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio. Directed by Guillermo del Toro and Mark Gustafsen. A stop-motion animation. With voices of Gregory Mann, Ewan McGregor, David Bradley. 1 hr., 57 min. PG-older kids, tweens. Released in 2022. Now streaming on Netflix/Apple/Fandango. Bolt a kids’ delight A scene from Disney Animation’s Bolt By Chris Honoré Bolt is a family-friendly Disney animated story that kids will thoroughly enjoy. The feature begins with a 7-year-old girl named Penny (Miley Cyrus) who spots a puppy she insists she simply has to adopt and decides to call him Bolt (John Travolta). Actually the pooch is a White Swiss Shepard. Five years later, Penny and Bolt star in a hit television show in which the pair fight crime and block the evil plans of Dr. Calico (Malcom McDowell). In order to get the best performances from Bolt, the director convinces Bolt that he does have the actual super powers he displays in each episode, an example would be his “super bark.” Penny is dismayed, realizing that her pooch can never leave the set least he discover that his powers are not real. In one episode, a cliffhanger, Penny is “kidnapped,” Bolt thinks it actually took place and sneaks off the set believing she must be rescued. Instead he bumps his head, falls into a packing crate of peanuts, and is mistakenly shipped to New York City. Lost, he befriends a street-smart cat named Mittens (Susie Essman). He convinces her he has to get back to Hollywood and Penny. And so the adventure begins in earnest. Meanwhile, back in Hollywood, a White Swiss Shepard is found to replace Bolt so the television show can continue, in spite of Penny’s initial reluctance. Mittens and Bolt hit the road with a stopover at a trailer park in Ohio where they confront a series of close calls involving animal control and where they meet a hamster named Rhino (Mark Walton). Eventually, the dynamic trio continue on what proves to be a cross-country journey, headed for Hollywood, the television show set, and most of all Penny. Of course, there is one final harrowing moment on the set shortly after their arrival; however, this is Disney and the story has a perfect ending involving a reunion between Bolt and Penny and the adoption of rhino and Mittens by Penny. Bolt. Directed by Chris Williams and Byron Howard. With voices of John Travolta, Miley Cyrus, Susie Essman. Walt Disney animation. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released in 2016. It would certainly help if Socrates had been a music critic. His questions would force us to think. There were two inspiring concerts during the past week. One was at the Piedmont Piano Company and the other was in our Piedmont Center for the Arts. Both venues are similar and showcase “candidates for superstardom”. The concert at Piedmont Piano Company featured a joint recital with pianists Rachel Breen and Sergey Belyavsky. It was obvious from the start that the two pianists are equally matched and have a great working relationship. It turns out that the two of them are, in the words of Herb Caen, “an item.” Their ascent to pianistic superstardom is via the international piano competition highway. Musical competitions have become one of the best ways to achieve fame and success. Since there were no printed programs, each pianist had a chance to introduce their pieces. Even though the concert had a “carnival“ inspiration, the first piece was a piano Sonata by Mozart played by Rachel Breen. She told the audience that this particular Sonata is fresh and imaginative – and that’s the way she played it. More than that, she made the modern concert grand piano sound like a piano from Mozart’s day. Individual artistry came into play in many ways. I was impressed with the way Breen presented conversational musical dialogues. Another important aspect was that she took time to express the music. All too often, modern players choose tempos that are much too fast, perhaps to impress the audience. Unfortunately, the music is torn asunder. When the Mozart Sonata was concluded, Sergey Belyavsky took the stage and performed Schumann’s monumental Carnevale. This concert featured Festival Opera in a salon series entitled Baroque Queens. It was a vocal concert which featured mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz and an ensemble of three musicians, Festival Opera General Manager Zachary Gordin on harpsichord, Jon Mendle played the lute and Joshua Minkus-Mahoney was the cellist. Printz has a rich voice with deep contralto qualities and a ringing top register. But I confess that hanging out with these two Brits for almost two hours, interspersed with a travelogue of Spain, can be tedious and at times seem a bit self-indulgent. One other obser vation: though the food served looks tasty and so nicely presented, and Brydon is ostensibly going to write restaurant reviews (Coogan is writing a memoir), little is ever said about the food itself. They taste it, nod appreciatively, but are too busy relishing their conversations to comment on what’s before them. My last observation: there were times when I felt that the insipid/clever/smart discussions were a way of avoiding what was really on their minds: old age, meaning mortality. Coogan does say, “If you’re ripe, is it better to be plucked or just drop?” But having said that, they quickly move on to a back and forth, return service, run to the net repartee focused on Roger Moore as James Bond and the Moors. They avoided saying s’mores. But I waited for it. Given the last scene of The Trip to Spain, expect a fourth film, likely set in Morocco. How that comes about given the final set up, well, we’ll see. articles.text: Last week’s walkers has a special guest. Piedmont Scout Sammy Ragones partnered with Piedmont’s Public Works Department for his Eagle Scout Project to build new batting cages at Coaches Field. This type of project is required to reach the highest rank in Scouting. Sammy was going to meet the walkers at the cage, talk about his Scouting experience and the project, and show them the work he did. Since the group was going to Coaches Field via Moraga Avenue, they could also check on the eaglets in their Mountain View Cemetery nest with a Moraga stop. Some background on Scouting in Piedmont was shared before the walkers got started. The Rev. John Stuchell of Piedmont Community Church started a local scouting program in October 1910 with 25 boys and parents. This was the same year that Boy Scouts was formed in the United States. Later, Piedmont decided to establish its own council separate from the Oakland-Piedmont Council and on March 21, 1921 the Piedmont Council was chartered by Boy Scouts of America as its 42nd Council. Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander was a driving force behind creating Piedmont’s council. The Piedmont Council is one of the smallest in the U.S. but today it serves over 1,000 youth in diverse programs ranging from Cub Scouts and Boy Scouts to coed teen programs including crews for Community Service, Sea Scouts, and Police Explorers. The walkers headed off to Coaches Field. At Moraga and Monte Avenue there were the seemingly ever-present eagle watchers with binoculars, telescopes, and cameras looking for the bald eagles and their offspring. A large, gray eaglet wing was seen occasionally flapping on a distant branch and a surprising light shower of small, white feathers blew in the breeze toward the group. The group continued to Coaches Field for a different kind of eagle watching. Soon-to-be Eagle Scout Sammy Ragones was at the new batting cages with his mother, Leora, waiting for the walkers. After introductions, Sammy told us about his Scouting experience that started in 6th grade as a Cub Scout. Sammy is now in Troop 15 and has a 50-mile hike of Mt. Whitney planned for later this summer. His Eagle project was building new baseball batting cages. The new cages replaced the original ones with new turf, nets, and space for a second batter. Piedmont Scout Sammy Ragones partnered with Piedmont’s Public Works Department for his Eagle Scout Project to build new batting cages at Coaches Field. This type of project is required to reach the highest rank in Scouting. Sammy was going to meet the walkers at the cage, talk about his Scouting experience and the project, and show them the work he did. Since the group was going to Coaches Field via Moraga Avenue, they could also check on the eaglets in their Mountain View Cemetery nest with a Moraga stop. John Stuchell of Piedmont Community Church started a local scouting program in October 1910 with 25 boys and parents. This was the same year that Boy Scouts was formed in the United States. Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander was a driving force behind creating Piedmont’s council. The Piedmont Council is one of the smallest in the U.S. but today it serves over 1,000 youth in diverse programs ranging from Cub Scouts and Boy Scouts to coed teen programs including crews for Community Service, Sea Scouts, and Police Explorers. The walkers headed off to Coaches Field. At Moraga and Monte Avenue there were the seemingly ever-present eagle watchers with binoculars, telescopes, and cameras looking for the bald eagles and their offspring. A large, gray eaglet wing was seen occasionally flapping on a distant branch and a surprising light shower of small, white feathers blew in the breeze toward the group. The group continued to Coaches Field for a different kind of eagle watching. Soon-to-be Eagle Scout Sammy Ragones was at the new batting cages with his mother, Leora, waiting for the walkers. After introductions, Sammy told us about his Scouting experience that started in 6th grade as a Cub Scout. Sammy is now in Troop 15 and has a 50-mile hike of Mt. Whitney planned for later this summer. His Eagle project was building new baseball batting cages. The new cages replaced the original ones with new turf, nets, and space for a second batter. Sammy chose the batting cages as his Eagle project to help benefit the Piedmont Baseball-Softball Foundation with whom he has played baseball for 10 years. He is also now on the high school baseball team. The project builds on the service of Troop 15 Eagle Scout Alexander Menke who built the original batting cage for his Eagle project in 2006. After receiving the endorsement of both the Park and Recreation Commissions, the City Council allocated $50,000 for the new cages and the Baseball Foundation raised $11,000 in community donations to supplement the project. Sammy planned, organized, and managed this extensive community service project. The previous batting cage was almost 20 years old. The new cages are 12 feet high and the city flattened the surface to provide for the larger cages and added a two-foot retaining wall. Electrical power was added for the pitching machines. Sammy worked with his Scout volunteers to prepare the site and the cage construction and earth work was performed by a City contractor. The Scouts dismantled the original cage last December, removed the old nets, poles, mats, and fencing, and then installed new nets and turf. The cages are now open and being used. Sammy took the walkers inside them for an inspection. The group returned to the Exedra on Moraga and had another chance to see the eaglets. The two that hatched in May and had grown dramatically. They typically fledge at between 10 and 14 weeks after they hatch and were in that process. It can be gradual, with the young ones initially “branching” out to nearby areas before fully taking flight. They often remain nearby for several weeks or months as they learn to hunt and fly from their parents. Parents continue to feed their eaglets even after they leave the nest. The young bald eagles are dark in color but develop their characteristic white head and tail at about four to five years. After getting some more good looks at the birds, the walkers retraced their steps back Highland for their returned to the Exedra. Bruce Markham hired Bryan Del Bondio who served as president of the winery for four decades. Markham became known for its excellence with Bordeaux varietals, especially Merlot. It became one of the first Napa Valley wineries to produce a varietal labeled Merlot. In 1990 Markham’s Merlot was honored as “Merlot of the Year.” In1993 Del Bondio hired Kimberlee Nicholls as enologist and she was promoted to head winemaker in 2001 – becoming one of the first women in the valley to lead a winery of Markham’s stature. Now 32 years later Kimberlee Nicholls is still at the helm as the winery continues to thrive, adding new vineyards and exploring new offerings to spotlight the terroirs of Markham’s acclaimed estate vineyards. In an industry known for flighty transitoriness, Nicholls’ steadfast, stable leadership has helped Markham thrive in the difficult, turbulent world of the fine wine business. In 2018 as Markham celebrated its 40th anniversary vintage, Kimberlee and the Markham team made the bold decision to reduce its annual production by half. Now 32 years later Kimberlee Nicholls is still at the helm as the winery continues to thrive, adding new vineyards and exploring new offerings to spotlight the terroirs of Markham’s acclaimed estate vineyards. In an industry known for flighty transitoriness, Nicholls’ steadfast, stable leadership has helped Markham thrive in the difficult, turbulent world of the fine wine business. In 2018 as Markham celebrated its 40th anniversary vintage, Kimberlee and the Markham team made the bold decision to reduce its annual production by half. The plan was to make less wine, but better wine and they also made major investments in the winery, buying new equipment and using exclusively French oak barrels while replanting vineyards and adopting modern viticultural practices. “Along with our amazing team, our estate vineyards have always been the heart and soul of Markham,” said Kimberlee. “As the stewards of these vineyards for decades, we have developed an intimate understanding of these sites, their sweet spots and best blocks, and the way that each individual vineyard expresses itself in the bottle. The results have exceeded all expectations.” Markham Winery is on Hwy. 29 just north of St. Helena. They have an outdoor seating area for tasting as well as a spacious lightfilled, tasting room. Markham Winery 2812 St. Helena Hwy North St. Helena, CA 94574 Appointments: markhamvineyards.com The cheese and charcuterie platter at Markham. Markham Winery, one of Napa’s first, was built in 1879. • 2023 Markham Sauvignon Blanc, $25 The Sauvignon Blanc was handed to us out in front of the winery before we entered the tasting room. The combination of a warm sunny day and the refreshing blast of the cool wine was marvelous. The wine shows pure, floral, citrus-driven aromas, transitioning to a beamingly bright tensile palate lined with peaches, apricots and mouthwatering acidity. The finish continues this live-wire energy, concluding with a tangy, refreshing vibrant finish. • 2023 Markham Chardonnay District Series Oak Knoll, $45 This is a traditional big powerful Chardonnay that is 100% barrel fermented in 50% new oak. It is scented of croissant, butter and lemon cream pie with ripe tropical fruit touches in the background. Full-bodied with a creamy texture, it has good layers of ripe fruit, creamy and honeyed in the mouth with a long finish. An impressive old-school Chardonnay effort. • 2023 Frenchman’s Blend, $42 Named after Jean Laurent the wineries French founder, this is an unusual blend of two thirds Sauvignon Blanc and one third Chardonnay. It is made in concrete spheres without any oak influence. This is the opposite of the Chardonnay. It is sleek, crisp and acidic, smelling of tart Granny Smith apples. In the Kimberlee Nicholls, Head Winemaker at Markham since 2001. mouth it is pure and clean – a vibrant one-note symphony. This is the perfect porch pounder for a hot summer day. • 2022 Markham Merlot Napa Valley, $32 This wine blended from several of the Markham Napa Valley vineyards is fermented in stainless steel and represents their entry-level wines. It is medium garnet colored with scents of black cherries, tobacco, mint and olives. The medium-bodied palate offers moderately concentrated cherry flavors. It’s structured by soft tannins and juicy acidity and a smooth satisfying finish. The airy tasting room at Markham Winery. • 2021 Markham Marked Parcels Merlot, $75 This wine from the Yountville Ranch Vineyard is a big step up in intensity from the wine above. It opens with a rich layered bouquet of plums, boysenberries, dark chocolate and tobacco. The palate offers a big fruit forward presence combining a broad, seamless mouthfeel and impeccable precision. All it needs is a plate of beef bourguignon. • 2021 Markham Marked Parcels Cabernet Sauvignon, $90 The wine is concentrated on the nose with aromas of cassis, violets, raspberry and layers of freshly turned earth. In the mouth the wine shows typical Cabernet flavors of blackberry and eucalyptus. It is leafy, and a little minty with supple tannins on the long savory finish. • 2019 Markham The Character, $130 A blend of the five major Bordeaux varieties with Merlot being predominant, The Character is their flagship blend and is aged in 100% new French oak. Unfurling with aromas of spices, smoke, dark berries, licorice mingled with delicate floral top-notes, its full-bodied, deep and concentrated with a velvety attack that segues into an elegantly structured and energetic mid-palate. The wine is well framed by soft tannins concluding with a penetrating, perfumed finish. Would show well in a blind tasting of top tier right bank Bordeaux.

articles.text: In a world that often overlooks the creativity and curiosity of older adults, Stagebridge stands as a joyful, defiant exception – celebrating the power of storytelling, performance, and personal growth at every stage of life. Last month a full house of more than 70 people packed the Stagebridge theater to enjoy the Performing Arts Summer Cabaret, an afternoon of vibrant storytelling, heartfelt songs, poignant acting, and hilarious improvisation. Featuring 30 talented students, all over the age of 60, the event was a reminder that the stage is never too far out of reach, no matter when you start. But Stagebridge isn’t slowing down. As you read this, the Stagebridge Performing Arts Summer Camp is underway, inviting a dynamic community of older adults to dive into everything from musical theatre and clowning to storytelling, playback theater, and choral singing. It’s a camp experience like no other—one that encourages adults to discover something new, flex creative muscles, and maybe even tap dance a little along the way. “This isn’t just about performance, it’s about connection,” says Eleanor Clement Glass, Stagebridge Board Member. “Our students find confidence, community, and pure joy in these classes. You’re never too old to try something new or return to a dormant talent - singing, acting, or dance” Stagebridge is uniquely dedicated to the 50+ community and to lifelong learning, with all performing arts classes and events designed to celebrate the voices, perspectives, and experiences of older adults. Whether you’re stepping into the spotlight for the first time or returning to a long-lost love of the arts, Stagebridge provides a welcoming, vibrant space to grow. Interested in joining the fun? Fall classes are just around the corner! Learn more about Stagebridge and all upcoming programs at www.stagebridge.org. Stagebridge is America’s oldest performing arts nonprofit for older adults and is based in Oakland. info@stagebridge.org The Performing Arts Showcase by Stagebridge on June 29 highlighted a variety of classes. Pictured are vocalists in one of Scrumbly’s singing classes.

articles.text: As Americans, we can take pride in the fact that we are a nation of givers. And as the economy improves, charitable giving is on the rise. In fact, according to the National Philanthropic Trust in 2023 total charitable giving from U.S. individuals, corporations, foundations, and bequests exceeded $557 billion with 67% coming from individuals.1 While money may be tight for many Americans, it’s nice to know that there is a way to support a favorite charity without having to worry about the impact it could have on your budget. How? By giving the gift of life insurance. Here are just a few ways you can use this proven method to contribute money to your favorite causes: • Donate an existing policy — If you already have a policy and no longer need the death benefit, you can gift the policy to your desired charity, which may give you some tax benefits. The charity will receive the full benefit amount when you die. • List the charity as a beneficiary — As the owner, you remain in control of your policy and can leave money to as many beneficiaries as you like: children, grandchildren— even multiple charities. Or, you can name a single charity the sole beneficiary, and it will receive the entire amount. • Purchase a separate policy — There are times when it makes sense to have separate policies: one for loved ones and one for charitable gifts. This technique can prove especially helpful if you would like to retain ownership of one policy, but not the other. • Create a Charitable Remainder Trust —-While this planned-giving tool is designed to shelter appreciated assets such as stocks and real estate, you can also incorporate life insurance if it’s set up properly. Be sure to consult a trusts and estates advisor before pursuing this approach. Giving life insurance can be a lasting legacy to support causes dear to you. Depending on the method you choose, it may also offer a variety of tax benefits. articles.text: Eventually, we all reach a point where it’s time to make a change and downsize—whether that means moving into a smaller home or condo, relocating to be closer to children/grandchildren, or transitioning to an independent living community that offers connection and a sense of belonging. You’ll likely have many questions about the downsizing process. Over the past year, I’ve covered a variety of topics to help guide you through this transition and am always happy to answer any questions when the time comes for you to make your move. Here’s one important aspect of selling a home to consider: understanding the buyer mindset in our area. Even the nicer homes can take a bit longer to sell these days. Here are a few reasons we counseled our clients to reduce the price; and within an hour, activity picked up and we had multiple showings, two offers and went into contract shortly thereafter. Here’s Why: You might imagine a buyer would just make a lower offer on a home. In our area, things just don’t seem to change. While in other parts of the country buyers do make lower offers, we have always been unique. We also led the way providing disclosures ahead of time in order to obtain non contingent offers. It irritated our Contra Costa and San Francisco agents until they started following suit. Why a price reduction can be a powerful strategy. • Most Buyers Do Not Want to “Offend” the Seller. Many buyers (and even their agents) hesitate to write low offers. They fear being rejected or seen as disrespectful. Instead of writing a lower offer, they often just move on to homes priced within their perceived value range. Believe me, agents do encourage agents/ buyers to come to the table. • The Market Has Spoken. You’ve had showings but no offers, which likely means buyers see better value elsewhere. A price adjustment isn’t a failure; it’s a strategic move to reposition your home to meet the market where it is today, not where it was a month ago. • Perception Is Everything. A listing that lingers over 30 days can develop a stigma— buyers may assume something’s “wrong” even if there isn’t. A fresh price can create urgency and renew interest, especially among those who may have seen the listing before. • Our Goal Is To Spark Action, Not Wait. Ultimately, the goal is to get you the highest possible price in today’s market. Strategic pricing is what drives competition—when buyers see value, they act quickly. Sometimes, a small price correction can lead to multiple offers or a faster sale than continuing to wait at a stagnant price. And so it is! A quick note to buyers: Don’t wait. Make the offer before you risk losing the home or facing competition. You might have had the chance to negotiate—before it was too late. articles.text: Dear Abby: Can dogs get the flu? My sweet Lucy seems to have a cough and isn’t very energetic. Should I take her to the vet or just wait it out? Worried, – Cindy and Lucy the Lab Also, keep her away from other pups while she’s under the weather so she doesn’t pass it on. It’s been flu after flu this year. Don’t wait. Go Dog, Go! (to the Vet) –Abby Dear Cindy and Lucy: Yes, dogs can get the flu—and the symptoms can look a lot like other less serious doggy colds. But if Lucy has a wet or dry cough, low energy, a fever, loss of appetite, or a runny nose, take her to the vet ASAP. Canine flu can sometimes turn into pneumonia, and nobody wants that. It’s important to get a proper diagnosis so you know how to help her feel better. Dear Abby: I wanted to tell you that a neighbor was hit by a car today at the corner of Sea View and LaSalle. She was walking her dog and said it seemed like a car had stopped, but then the driver headed into the intersection and hit her. She was taken to Highland Hospital – hopefully it’s not too serious. pages.text: Wednesday, July 30, 2025 27 Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I would like to write memoirs for my family. It seems like I’m always having to click in several places when I want to save my work, when I want to cut something or copy and paste, etc. I spent so much time with this busy work that I am not spending enough time writing. Is there some way for me to speed up and smooth out my workflow? –Arthur, Piedmont Dear Arthur: When we used pen and paper, all we had to worry about was not losing the notebook we were writing in. But with computers, there are many more points of failure. And there are also many more tasks to protect what we’re doing, to edit our work, and to save our work. I think with what you describe, you would really benefit from learning a few keyboard shortcuts. Keyboard shortcuts are keyboard combinations that do the same tasks as you do when clicking around the computer. For example, when you’re writing a document in Microsoft Word, to save your work, you must go to the top of your screen, click on File, then click on Save. A shortcut using your computer keyboard would be to hold the Command button down with your thumb, and press the letter S. It doesn’t sound like it would save much time, but when you’re saving your work every few paragraphs, it is faster. The same kind of process goes for Copy and Paste. If you want to copy a selection in your document, you can highlight it with your cursor, go up to the word Edit choose Copy then click your curser in the document where you want to paste this text, and then back up to Edit and Paste. Or you can highlight it with your cursor, press Command C then click where you want it pasted and click Command V. There are so many possibilities of functions and shortcuts using what Mac calls modifier keys, these are the Function (fn or Globe icon), Control, Option, Shift, and Command keys. Depending on the second key that you press, usually a letter, you can control much of your work without going up to the top menu bar. Add to make add to make things even faster, many of these options are available in a contextual click. The contextual (sometimes called secondary) click is something you can set up on your mouse or trackpad. Any of you who were or still are PC users, have been able to access this by clicking the right side of your mouse, sometimes called a right click. This is something that can be set up on your Mac in System Settings, Mouse or Trackpad Settings. By Abby, a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: Can dogs get the flu? My sweet Lucy seems to have a cough and isn’t very energetic. Should I take her to the vet or just wait it out? Worried, – Cindy and Lucy the Lab Also, keep her away from other pups while she’s under the weather so she doesn’t pass it on. It’s been flu after flu this year. Don’t wait. Go Dog, Go! (to the Vet) –Abby Dear Cindy and Lucy: Yes, dogs can get the flu—and the symptoms can look a lot like other less serious doggy colds. But if Lucy has a wet or dry cough, low energy, a fever, loss of appetite, or a runny nose, take her to the vet ASAP. Canine flu can sometimes turn into pneumonia, and nobody wants that. It’s important to get a proper diagnosis so you know how to help her feel better. the lower right or left, or several other possible gestures. I like the term contextual because depending on where you are positioning your cursor, you will get different options. For example, if you use a secondary or contextual click on an empty spot on your desktop, you will see the option to clean up your folders, create a new folder, or change your wallpaper to name a few. If you click on text in your document after you highlight it, you will see the Cut, Paste (after you have copied something), Copy options. Apple has a whole list of keyboard shortcuts, and instructions on how to use them here: https:// support.apple.com/en-us/102650 It takes some time to become comfortable with these shortcuts, but if you go to the website above, you will see there are more than you will ever use. articles.text: Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on July 13, 2022. France celebrates National France Day on July 14, and Paris is the pinnacle of some magnificent pomp. The nation’s republic is deeply rooted in self-governing principles when the Paris mobs showed their grit and stormed Versailles and kidnapped the king, their outrage erupting over heavy taxes and a population dying of starvation. Paris mobs had terrified the crown for a century. Versailles was built for the king to get far away from the madding crowds, and plenty grand to house the nobles at close range. When an armed crowd sacked the medieval fortress, the commoners cheered, and the symbol of tyranny was taken down, stone by stone. A century later, the National Assembly chose a national date, and the Fête happened to share the Bastille Day remembrance date without being about the Bastille. Salut, heureux quatorze juillet, rather than a happy Bastille Day. The Paris extravaganza boasts the most lavish parade in the world, and speeches by dignitaries are broadcast to the nation. The Fête is joyous and starts with a traditional military ceremony and full-dress parade down the Boulevard Champs Elysée. Jet propelled planes flying at low altitudes and trailing the tri-color streams thrill the audience. Picnickers vie for the prime spots on the grassy knolls at Champ de Mars, with their blankets and food baskets, though wine and champagne and all alcohol is banned from the park. A formal classical concert begins shortly after 9 pm. Earlier, the music sets are by popular deejays. Fireworks fire off around 11 pm over the Eiffel Tower and Trocadéro Garden. And around midnight from 700,000 to as many as a million people begin to find their way home. They proceed largely on foot, at least to reach an open Metro station and queue for the regional commuter trains. The Paris Insider Guide suggests where to situate in Paris for the best views of the fireworks. Cross the Seine to the Trocadéro esplanade, but one must arrive early for this popular perch. Sacre Coeur church in Montmartre is at a high point, and the Parc de Belleville in the 20th district. The top floor of the Tour Montparnasse has a 360º nighttime view at the price of a fourstar dinner. The bridges of Paris offer a mostly unobstructed view, especially Pont des Arts, Pont de la Concorde, and Pont Alexandre III. Two years ago in 2020, for the first time since the end of World War II, a restricted military marched in parade dress and reduced by half in respect to the year of Covid-19. One year ago, 2021, the vigorous full program was restored, but the crowds were curtailed while mask requirements were still in effect. In midMarch, France suspended the Full military parade to the Arc de Triomphe la Fête Nationale Française. The Alpha Jet E (patrol) of the Patrouille de France. requirements for vaccine passes, and the nation celebrated. The coronavirus is not defeated, only weakened, yet commerce is back in full swing. Tourism has returned in full force to France, and café society is back in swing. Possibly, travelers have taken note that the U.S. dollar is at $1.02 per euro and has rapidly spiked to near parity, a dramatic climb for the U.S. dollar since just February when a Euro transacted at $1.14. Parity hasn’t occurred since 2002. In the 2008 global financial crisis, according to Bloomberg, a euro was transacting at $1.60. The current euro drop is attributed to Europe’s exposure to the economic effects of Russia’s war in Ukraine, and an anticipated rise in the cost of natural gas products for heating this coming winter. Summer months are typically the season when European nations build up gas surpluses, and the source of whip-saw prices is suspected to be manipulation by Russia, which denies accusations. Higher energy prices are beleaguering several EU nations that refused Russia’s demands to pay in Russian rubles. At the same time, the U.S. Federal Reserve is raising interest rates faster than the European central bank. Just in June, European consumer prices jumped 8.6%. The European Union has the challenge of keeping disparate economies in a shared monetary system, and though euroskeptic politicians are in France and Italy, the fiscal union is intact. The writer and conjoint Michael Mathews decamped to Paris, The City of Light, La Ville-Lumière. We are perpetual sojourners in a foreign clime. Comments to pkf.empower@ gmail.com. articles.text: Havens’ Avenue of Palms was for sale in 1922. They hired Houghton Sawyer, Albert Farr and Engineer Robert E. Carney to design a model city center. Continuing Farr’s Spanish Mission design at City Hall, their Master Plan called for an elaborate Exedra at the entrance to Piedmont Park, a grand threestory City Hall, additions to the current City Hall, a library, museum and municipal garages. They planned to re-route the streetcar line into a tunnel where passengers could enter and exit streetcars at an elegant plaza with a fountain at the park level. Passengers would not have to cross the streetcar tracks. The Master Plan was to be completed in phases, with each building to be approved by voters before construction. The grand three-story City Hall was scaled down to the present onestory Community Hall. Voters approved the first phase in 1924 which included funds to build the Exedra and the Community Hall. Later units of the Master Plan were never realized. School construction took precedence. The Junior High School and Wildwood School were built in 1923. Later bond issues failed to pass, and the Depression ended all thoughts of grand new construction. Piedmont’s new Community Hall and Exedra opened on April 3, 1925. Civic leaders and residents entered the newly landscaped Piedmont Park through the Exedra, which reporters compared to the “Arch of Triumph.” Guests admired Howard Gilkey’s new landscape design, with its rose garden behind the Exedra, extensive lawns and flowering shrubs along the path to the hall. The Community Hall was dedicated as a meeting place and social hall for all Piedmont residents. The lower level of the hall became the new armory for Piedmont’s Battery D of the 143rd Field Artillery. Piedmont Park had been saved The original Piedmont High School designed by William Weeks in 1921. from development. Only two small parts of the original park were sold to real estate developers. The land that became Guilford Road was sold as “Guilford Place” in 1921, and the land that became Palm Drive was sold as the Lower Piedmont Park Tract in 1922. Today, a few palm trees survive on Palm Drive from Havens’ “Avenue of Palms.” The new Community Hall and Exedra in 1925. articles.text: Frank C. Havens opened Piedmont Park in 1898 with a new Clubhouse, the mineral springs, a rustic teahouse, and the beauty of the ravine, waterfalls and meandering paths through bucolic Bushy Dell Canyon. Havens added “The Maze” (1904), an “Avenue of Palms” to the Maze from Grand Avenue, a Japanese Tea House (1907) and the Piedmont Art Gallery (1907). He added a bandstand for Sunday concerts, rustic park benches the upper park and exotic plants including Queen palm trees, Canary Island date palms, cordyline and banana trees, orchids and roses. Piedmont Park thrived until 1916. Visitors enjoyed an afternoon in the park, ate lunch in the Clubhouse or enjoyed tea in one of two teahouses, listened to Sunday concerts at the bandstand, marveled at Havens’ collection in the Piedmont Art Gallery, got lost in the Maze and wandered the paths throughout the ravine. reported that lawsuits totaling $90,000 were filed against Frank C. Havens. The Anglo-California Trust Company held the mortgage on the park for $172,000, and neither the interest nor the principal had been paid. The park was to be sold at a foreclosure auction in 1917. Havens had auctioned off his art collection, and now he was selling Piedmont Park to raise funds. In 1916, Piedmont Park was for sale. The School Board voted to purchase some of the park land for a new high school and athletic field. They wanted to buy 13 acres, but Havens would not sell less than 27 acres. The city of Piedmont wanted to save the park from development, but did not have the funds to purchase the remaining parkland. In November of 1916, Piedmont voters defeated a measure to raise funds to purchase the parkland. Piedmont Park land was still available in 1921 when Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander and others offered to purchase 14 acres of the park if the city would reimburse them. This plan allowed the entire 27-acre parcel to be sold. The School District could buy the 13 acres they wanted, and the city would have its park. Alexander purchased the land for the city in 1921 and one year later voters passed a bond issue, and the city reimbursed Wallace Alexander and his partners in full. Piedmont High School In 1921, construction began immediately on the high school. Architect William Weeks designed a reinforced concrete school with terra cotta trim for 500 students. The auditorium spanned the front of the school with two stories of classrooms behind. Two wings held more classrooms. Clinical depression has 10 or 12 criteria that lasts a various amount of time. It is a bona fide medical illness; it’s like in America we’re allowed to be sick from the Adams Apple down but not the Adams Apple up. It can happen to anybody. Richey recounts some of his experiences with depression and what led to him writing the book. “I had episodes throughout my life. In tennis, my last six years of the tour, I had lost my game; I couldn’t get my backhand back. That’s why I got depressed; I had lost what was most valuable to me: my skill… I had a three year breakdown at my worst,” said Richey, describing some situations from his book. “I’ve spoken at 60 or so events over the last 10 years and hosted some golf events. I wrote the book as a mental-health book, the desire was to help others who suffered like I did. It just so happened that my daughter had a year off from being a professor at Texas A&M. She did a wonderful job of putting it together, it’s my tennis career and depression running on parallel tracks, meeting at the end,” he added. Pacific Coast Championship history In 1971, the final year at Berkeley, Australian legends Rod Laver and Ken Rosewall squared off in what became the “Rocket” Laver’s sixth singles title of the year. The doubles’ title in ‘71 was another all-Australian exhibit with Laver and Roy Emerson defeating Rosewall and Fred Stolle. It was held in multiple venues and held its last event at the SAP Center in San Jose, starting at the Old Del Monte Lodge in Monterey in 1889, moving to the Hotel Rafael in San Rafael from 1890 to 1899, and then to Berkeley from 1900 to 1930 for its initial stay. From there, the PCC played in Alamo from 1931-1933, returned to Berkeley from 1934-1941, went to San Francisco in ’42-’48, then back to Berkeley from 1949 through 1971. The Cow Palace and Bill Graham Civic Auditorium then hosted from 1973 to 1993; then moved to San Jose with the opening of the HP Pavilion. That was its downward phase when it was classified as an ATP 250 series tournament. During its time in San Francisco, John McEnroe dominated the event with 14 combined singles and doubles titles, five in singles. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council unanimously appointed Frederick W. Shavies II as the city’s next Chief of Police at its regular meeting on Monday, July 7. Shavies, who began his tenure on July 22, brings nearly two decades of law enforcement experience and most recently served as Deputy Chief of Police in Oakland. Widely respected for his strategic leadership and commitment to community policing, Shavies has led complex investigations, managed high-profile events, and implemented forward-thinking crime prevention and engagement strategies. “Piedmont is incredibly fortunate to welcome Frederick Shavies as our next Chief of Police,” said Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen. “He brings exceptional law enforcement experience, a strong commitment to equity and accountability, and a proven ability to lead with integrity. His familiarity with our community and ability to build trust make him the right person to lead the department into its next chapter.” Frederick Shavies began as Piedmont’s new Chief of Police on July 22.
articles.title: City Council selects Frederick Shavies as Piedmont’s next Police Chief

articles.text: Highly regarded Chief honored in City Council Chambers The City of Piedmont hosted a retirement reception for its retiring Police Chief, Jeremy Bowers, outside of City Hall on July 7 before the City Council meeting. The meeting itself began with a ceremonial item, honoring Bowers for his years of service to the Piedmont Police Department. Refreshments were served on the patio in front of City Hall while friends and community members congratulated Bowers on his retirement and offered well-wishes for his family’s next chapter. “This has always been and always will be more than just a job to me,” said Bowers in thanks to the community. “I hope you know, as a community, the impact you had on my career. When I look back at my time in Piedmont, it’s more than being a member of the Piedmont Police Department – it’s being a memPolice Chief Jeremy Bowers delivers heartfelt words about his time working in Piedmont. ber of Piedmont that I’ll always take with me.” Born to a military family on a U.S. Army base in Wurzburg, Germany, Bowers was raised in Boulder, Colorado before moving to California to study Social Science and Criminal Justice at San Francisco State University. Bowers was hired by the San Jose Police Department, and worked there for 18 years, rising to the rank of Lieutenant. Bowers later went on to earn a bachelor of science in Administration of Justice Friends and residents gather outside City Hall to congratulate Jeremy Bowers on his retirement.

articles.text: City advice for pruning trees and clearing debris As grazing goats begin clearing dry grasses in Moraga Canyon, it’s time for Piedmont residents to prepare their own yards for fire season. The East Bay hills have seen major wildfires over the past 150 years. Lessons from those events—and recent fires across California—are clear: when residents actively manage the vegetation around their homes, communities are better protected. • Wildfire prep starts at home: Piedmont urges residents to prune trees, clear debris, and maintain defensible space around homes. • City is at work: Crews deploy goats, clear brush, and trim street trees as part of year-round fire prevention efforts. • Help is available: Free yard inspections and wildfire safety resources are offered at piedmont.ca.gov/vegetation. Tips for preparing your yard While the gold standard is to clear all vegetation within five feet of your home, even small steps can improve your home’s chance of surviving a wildfire. The city encourages residents to take these fire-smart actions over the next few weeks: • Create defensible space: Remove branches that hang over your roof or are within 10 feet of your chimney. articles.text: A wiser person than I once noted that when children hear a good story they don’t respond, “Explain it to me,” but rather “Tell It Again.” I keep this bit of wisdom in mind every year when it comes time for the five days of Vacation Bible Camp at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church. It is important to remember that the stories of the Bible are more enduring than our interpretations of them, no matter how “kid-friendly” our interpretations may be; that the narratives of the Scripture far outshine our explanations of them, no matter how theologically profound our explanations are. There is comfort in this. If we can just tell the stories, the stories will do their life-shaping work. Tell it again By Pastor Jim Hopkins A wiser person than I once noted that when children hear a good story they don’t respond, “Explain it to me,” but rather “Tell It Again.” I keep this bit of wisdom in mind every year when it comes time for the five days of Vacation Bible Camp at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church. It is important to remember that the stories of the Bible are more enduring than our interpretations of them, no matter how “kid-friendly” our interpretations may be; that the narratives of the Scripture far outshine our explanations of them, no matter how theologically profound our explanations are. There is comfort in this. If we can just tell the stories, the stories will do their life-shaping work. They will get into the heads, hearts and minds of the leaders as well as the young people, the teachers, as well as the students. We who lead don’t have to be experts in Bible, theology, or child psychology, we simply need, gently and humbly, to give voice to the stories. This is especially true on Thursdays, the day most curriculums focus on the death and resurrection of Jesus. While I personally struggle with interpretations that suggest Jesus’ crucifixion was a price he paid for our sins, for others such interpretations are life giving and inspiring. Conversely, I am drawn to interpretations of the crucifixion that suggest it is a portrayal of the depths to which God suffers with us. For others, such interpretations are overly vague and abstract. In this regard it is important to note that historically Christianity as a whole has never been able to develop an explanation of the meaning and significance of Jesus’ death so satisfactory that it has been declared to be the final word on the matter. Still, it tells the story. It is equally important to note that when children hear the accounts of the crucifixion they are far less interested in its theological interpretations than in the crown of thorns, the nails, the cross and the cries of Jesus. Likewise, they are far less interested in the explanations of the resurrection than they are in the See Religion Corner on page 3 CYNTHIA CEE, Piedmont Pines We have been traveling for two weeks so it hasn’t affected us. articles.text: It’s so odd to think about these words, let alone type them. After almost four years, I’ll be delivering my last round of papers in the coming weeks. The choice has been affected by outside decisions. I would gladly have delivered the paper until I developed arthritis or my hair turned gray. Working for the paper has given me some truly incredible opportunities and opened up some wonderful conIf I’d never started to deliver papers, I would not have had the courage to submit an article about my Scout troop’s weekend outing at Kirby Cove. The article was sent to someone I am now proud to call not only my boss, but a treasured friend – Mr. Gray Gray has become one of my greatest supporters and helped me once more on my scouting journey when he sponsored me for the 2023 National Jamboree. Additionally, he allowed me to put pamphlets into the papers in order to fundraise further. Forever supportive of my writing and praising my articles, I do not believe my experience with the Post would have been half as enjoyable without his continued engagement. The Post has also been a source of connection, and I’ve bonded with many Piedmont residents over it. From the people to whom I deliver the papers and the adults in my scout troop, it always makes for an interesting and delightful conversation. I’ve become familiar with many of the people on my paper route, connecting with them over the smallest of things. To catalog all of my memorable experiences with the readers of the Post would fill an entire 32-page issue with no room for ads, but each one has been unique and altogether enjoyable – from receiving yearly turtle bark around the holidays from a treasured family friend and subscriber to being stopped on the street by a man who proceeded to give me $20 and tell me how much he appreciated my timely deliveries. I’ve found connections in the other delivery kids too. It’s a simpler connection, in the way I know my route is always covered, and in the way there’s no hesitation to take on a route in upper Piedmont because they forgot at the last minute before summer camp. In the way you smile at the other kids picking up their papers or folding them on the benches. And finally, delivering for the Post has taught me so much, not only in the literal sense of responsibility and what it means to have people depend on you, but also more indirectly. It’s helped me sharpen my soft skills in striking up conversation and writing emails. Truly, it’s helped me communicate better overall. The depths of my gratitude to the Post have no end, but I would like to try and humbly recognize just how incredible their impact has been on me. Thank you for all you have done, Piedmont Post. articles.text: Editor: I think I speak for most in the community when I express my joy that there are now bald eagles taking residence in Piedmont. I humbly request a few safety considerations: Risk to pets: According to the Raptor Project, bald eagles can carry more than their body weight — one bald eagle was found to have carried an object weighing 12 pounds. But this doesn’t mean we need to put leashes or harnesses on our cats; rather keep an eye on them. Risk to ecosystem: bald eagles do not harm the environment, but their presence could create a competitive challenge against other birds of prey like local hawk species; and could pose a danger to small mammals like squirrels. Consider closing the lids to your compost bins so that animals displaced by the eagles don’t forage in your refuse. In summary, bald eagles represent freedom, strength and independence; may we enjoy these birds and be reminded of their grandeur. –Jay Bohanion

As of Friday, July 18, the City announced that trash collection will be continuing, including backyard pickup. Organics collection resumed on Thursday, July 17. All households in Piedmont should have received at least one trash (black bin) collection since July 8. Any residents who have had no waste collection should use the City’s online self-reporting tool to notify City staff immediately so service to their address can be prioritized. The online self-reporting tool can be found at https://bit.ly/ PiedmontWastePickups. Republic Services has stated that normal service is expected to resume on Monday, July 21. Keep carts out until collected and report pickup status City staff have been working actively with Republic Services to ensure continued collections in Piedmont since a regional work stoppage began on July 8. Ongoing documentation about where service has occurred is an important tool. Residents can support documentation efforts by reporting collections received at https://bit. ly/PiedmontWastePickups. Residents should keep carts out on the curbside until they are collected. Once a waste stream is collected, bring that cart in until the next regular collection day. These indicators provide valuable information as staff work to confirm collection status reports and coordinate with Republic Services to prioritize areas most in need of service.

articles.text: On Monday, September 1, Children’s Fairyland turns 75 and will celebrate with a full day of family fun from 10 a.m.- 4 p.m. The Labor Day event will feature performances by DJ Lance Rock, Prescott Circus, and Daisy the Clown, with hands-on activities, interactive art, a brand-new bilingual puppet show, giveaways, special guests, and a parade through Oakland. “This isn’t just a birthday party, it’s our love letter to the generations of families that have supported Children’s Fairyland,” said Kymberly Miller, CEO of Fairyland. “For 75 years, Fairyland has been a place where kids and families fall in love with storytelling, make cherished memories, and feel safe to play, explore, and connect. This celebration honors our past, reflects on our growth, and opens a new chapter in Fairyland’s story.” The 75th Birthday Party kicks off at 9:30 a.m. with a Parade to the Birthday Party, co-hosted by BART and Fairyland. Starting at the 19th Street BART Station, the parade winds its way to Lake Merritt and ends at the Fairy Gates. DJ L a nce Ro ck , t he Emmy-nominated host of the hit Nick Jr. Series “Yo Gabba Gabba!,” brings his signature mix of music, storytelling, and dance to Fairyland’s Festival Stage. He’ll perform live twice, at 1:00 p.m. and 3:00 p.m., each followed by a meet and greet. The birthday party will also premiere “Tío Conejo’s Big Wish,” Fairyland’s first fully bilingual puppet show based on a folktale from Cuba. The show will run through October 26th, with daily performances at 11:00 a.m., 2:00 p.m., and 4:00 p.m. A live show by Prescott Circus at noon will feature Oakland youth performers showcasing acrobatics and juggling. A bubble-filled performance by Daisy the Clown at 2:30 p.m., blending balloon twisting, magic, and playful chaos. Daisy is a beloved performer known for creating interactive and creative fun for kids of all ages. Puppet Playdates with Quercus, Fairyland’s fuzzy mascot, occur at 11:20 a.m. and 2:20 p.m. Children’s Theatre interactive performances of “Teddy Bear’s Wish” start at 11:30 a.m. and 12:30 p.m. The activities include art stations, a giant birthday card for Fairyland, a community-painted mural, and a Birthday Adventure Passport activity, where kids collect stamps after completing activities and prompts, then turn it in for a limited-edition 75th anniversary button. All kids will take home special goodie bags. Children’s Fairyland opened its gates on September 2, 1950 as the country’s first storybook theme park, built specifically for young children. Fairyland quickly became a cherished part of Oakland’s identity and cultural landscape, igniting imaginations, shaping childhoods, and inspiring countless theme parks around the world. The idea for creating a storybook theme park in Oakland began in 1948, when local nursery owner Arthur Navlet envisioned a place where children could play freely and safely through a world built just for them. With support from the Lake Merritt Breakfast Club, Oakland Parks Superintendent William Penn Mott Jr., and a dedicated group of community members, the dream for Children’s Fairyland took shape. Since then, Fairyland has remained a cherished part of Oakland’s cultural landscape, attracting nearly 200,000 visitors annually to explore the park’s 10 acres. Over the years, it has grown to include cultural celebrations, literacy programs, puppet education, summer camps, and one-of-a-kind performances that reflect the diverse cultural heritage of the Bay Area. The park has remained true to its roots over the decades, providing hands-on, screen-free experiences that inspire imagination, creativity, confidence, and a lifelong love of learning. Buy tickets in advance at Fairyland.org Celebrate 75 years of Fairyland on Labor Day, September 1.

articles.text: The usage and possession of smartphones and other mobile communication devices on school grounds remained a hot topic for much of last school year as Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) sought to comply with Assembly Bill 3216, the Phone-Free Schools Act. In Piedmont next year, only high school students will be permitted to use cell phones, and only: before school, after school and during lunch. A full ban of smartphones and mobile communication devices is planned for 2026-27 year. The statewide bill requires school districts to adopt, by July 1, 2026, “a policy to limit or prohibit the use by its pupils of smartphones while the pupils are at a school site.” During the May 28 school board meeting, board members gave their final thoughts before the district approved Board Policy 5131.8. “I hope that we are going to be innovative and think about the culture change of this in our implementation,” said board member Susy Struble. “To me the biggest issue here is the distraction and the lessening of our kids’ ability to have deep focus and pay attention.” A Cell Phone Task Force was assembled in 2024 including parents, and staff from every school site. The task force met on multiple occasions between December 2024 and February 2025 to explore research, consult other districts, and draft policy options; they then presented an update to the board on March 12. “Student input has been an important part of our cell phone policy development,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. “I met with middle and high school students last year, including invitations to participate in a survey and to join our cell phone workshop. The Board and I also met with the journalism class in the spring to hear additional feedback about how to engage more students. Next year, I plan to hold several meetings in the fall for students and parents to continue to gather feedback on the policy.” For the 2025-26 school year the policy states “Smartphones and other mobile communication devices shall not be used in any manner that infringes on the privacy rights of any other person. • Primary and middle school students shall have their personal devices off, or silenced, and stored during the instructional day. • High School students shall have their phones, smartphones, and smart devices turned off, or silenced, during instructional time unless instructed by a school administrator, or teacher or authorized by the district. High School Students shall be able to use their devices before school, during lunch, and after school.” The district’s decision comes amid a broader national shift toward phone-free schools. In California, Assembly Bill 3216 reflects growing concern about the impact of device use on student focus, mental health, and classroom behavior. Several districts, including Los Angeles Unified and San Mateo Union High School District, have already adopted stricter phone policies ahead of the state’s July 2026 compliance deadline. Piedmont’s policy includes the following four exceptions for student device use. 1. In the case of an emergency, or in response to a perceived threat of danger; 2. When a teacher or administrator grants permission to the student to possess or use a mobile communication device, subject to any reasonable limitation imposed by that teacher or administrator; 3. When a licensed physician or surgeon determines that the possession or use is necessary for the student’s health and well-being; 4. When the possession or use is required by the student’s individualized education program. The policy received a lengthy first reading discussion during the school board meeting on May 14, which included some dissenting opinions from parents and students. The meeting’s recording is available at Piedmont.granicus. com/player/clip/3069?view_ id=9&redirect=true When school starts up in 19 days, on August 11, there will certainly be a learning curve for students to adjust to the new policy, and for staff on how to enforce the policy. “One thing I learned was that we have policies in place that are not consistently enforced,” said board member Ruchi Medhekar. “The fact that there is a difference from classroom to classroom, from grade to grade, to me, is not in the spirit of the existing policy.” Medhekar also spoke out against teachers giving “device time” as a reward for finishing work early. Board member Max Roman put some of the onus on the board itself to help with the small changes next year and bigger changes a year away. “We could do a better job at creating spaces and things for kids to do, at passing and lunch periods, where they now tend to look at their phones,” said Roman. “I actually suspect that the kids will end up rediscovering the joy of talking to each other with their faces,” added Roman.

articles.text: A March 27 decision by Piedmont School Board and the high school athletic director Tyler Small to not bring back 17-year veteran Girls’ Soccer Head Coach, Dan Chubbock received lengthy criticism during the April 23 school board meeting. The issue was not included on the meeting’s agenda, so a line of soccer players and parents paraded to the microphone to speak out against the decision during public comment for items not on the agenda. “I want to address the abrupt firing of our coach and set the record straight on him.” said Darcy McKee, a junior and a captain of the team. “His team talks are a perfect balance of expectation and encouragement. It is so motivating to see how invested he is in our every performance.” “I was planning to play soccer again next season as a junior with coach Dan and the team, but with this recent decision, I am unsure if I will be playing,” said Chloe Toyama. “[Chubbock] always brought positivity, laughter and a competitive spirit that pushed us to grow and succeed,” added Ellia Kwan. The many comments of praise also introduced another thread of emotion – the shock and frustration of another Athletic Director, Tyler Small, for making such an unpopular decision In his first year as AD. Piedmont parent, PHS alum, and Piedmont Soccer Club board member Jonathan Essner asked the school board to handle situations like these with more grace, respect and professionalism. “Dan was fired from his role in a three-minute phone call with the athletic director. I was taken aback, left to think something egregious had taken place given the unceremonious nature of the dismissal,” said Essner. “For Tyler to not rehire Dan for the poor atmosphere on girls’ soccer, without consulting anyone on the team about [the] atmosphere is wrong and he (Small) has made a mistake,” said senior Ava Sauer. “Compounded with his many scheduling errors all season erodes my faith in Tyler as an athletic director.” Tim Lasocki, a girls soccer parent and the President of the Piedmont Soccer Club reminded the school board that two years the PHS girls soccer team and Chubbock were coach were honored in City Hall for winning sectionals and a day in their honor was created. “The athletic director, Tyler 17-year veteran Girls’ Soccer Head Coach Dan Chubbock was let go after this year. Small, collected no feedback from players or families before releasing the 17-year head coach of the program,” said Lasocki. School board members sat and listened to 17 minutes of rebuke from the soccer community but did not respond under provisions of California’s Brown Act. The job posting for Chubbock’s post is still active and can be seen at Edjoin.org/Home/JobPosting/2065995. “[Girls soccer] was not broken, but it could be now,” said soccer parent and videographer Neil McKee.
articles.title: Support for PHS soccer coach Dan Chubbock

articles.text: In June 2025 a team of high schoolers led by Piedmont Community Service Crew member Nathan Bekele embarked on a three-week journey to Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, partnering with St. Paul’s Hospital and Melu’e Foundation, one of the country’s few autism centers. The group’s goal was to raise awareness, deliver supplies, and provide hands-on support for children with developmental disabilities. The trip began with strong community support, centered around the “Taste of Ethiopia” at Lemat Restaurant in Berkeley. It raised $35,000 through ticket sales and a lively art auction featuring Ethiopian artists, including one who grew up at Melu’e Foundation. Reflecting on the challenge and growth of volunteering abroad, Piedmont High School student Kidus Yalew shared, “Going to Ethiopia was a hard challenge, but it showed me that even far from home, friendship can feel like family. We spent our days helping out at the hospital and spending time with autistic kids. I saw how just being there for others can bring hope, even on the tough days. I realized resilience isn’t about handling everything on your own, it’s about serving together, leaning on each other, and finding strength in community.” Funds from the fundraiser helped pay six months’ rent for Melu’e Foundation and supplied essential therapy equipment, computers, furniture, and care packages for pediatric oncology units at St. Paul’s Hospital and Tikur Anbessa Specialized Hospital (Black Lion Hospital). During the trip, while shadowing under doctors in the ICU at St. Paul’s Hospital, the team came across a 16-year-old girl diagnosed with Guillain-Barré Syndrome. Her condition was rapidly worsening, and the medicine needed to stabilize her was far beyond her family’s financial reach. Moved by the urgency of the situation, the team took immediate action by texting their donor support group in the U.S. and raising $3,000 in a single afternoon to cover the full cost Chloe Park (left), TJ Park, Amanuel Girma, Lucas Bekele, Nathan Bekele, Ethan Mesfin, Joaquin Fierro, Theodros Girma, Gabriella Mesfin, and Kidus Yalew of her life-saving treatment. The experience became a defining moment of the trip, highlighting the impact of compassion, quick action, and community support in saving lives. Coronado High School student Gabriella Mesfin, a relative of Bekele, described the emotional impact of working directly with the children. “Working with the children was a meaningful experience. One moment that stood out was seeing their joy during our time together. This cause matters because it brings hope to those in need. pages.text: Wednesday, July 23, 2025 7 PCSC Trip Recap: Autism Awareness and Service Initiative in Ethiopia By Nathan Bekele In June 2025 a team of high schoolers led by Piedmont Community Service Crew member Nathan Bekele embarked on a three-week journey to Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, partnering with St. Paul’s Hospital and Melu’e Foundation, one of the country’s few autism centers. The group’s goal was to raise awareness, deliver supplies, and provide hands-on support for children with developmental disabilities. The trip began with strong community support, centered around the “Taste of Ethiopia” at Lemat Restaurant in Berkeley. It raised $35,000 through ticket sales and a lively art auction featuring Ethiopian artists, including one who grew up at Melu’e Foundation. Reflecting on the challenge and growth of volunteering abroad, Piedmont High School student Kidus Yalew shared, “Going to Ethiopia was a hard challenge, but it showed me that even far from home, friendship can feel like family. We spent our days helping out at the hospital and spending time with autistic kids. I saw how just being there for others can bring hope, even on the tough days. I realized resilience isn’t about handling everything on your own, it’s about serving together, leaning on each other, and finding strength in community.” Funds from the fundraiser helped pay six months’ rent for Melu’e Foundation and supplied essential therapy equipment, computers, furniture, and care packages for pediatric oncology units at St. Paul’s Hospital and Tikur Anbessa Specialized Hospital (Black Lion Hospital). During the trip, while shadowing under doctors in the ICU at St. Paul’s Hospital, the team came across a 16-year-old girl diagnosed with Guillain-Barré Syndrome. Her condition was rapidly worsening, and the medicine needed to stabilize her was far beyond her family’s financial reach. Moved by the urgency of the situation, the team took immediate action by texting their donor support group in the U.S. and raising $3,000 in a single afternoon to cover the full cost READ IT IN THE POST E v e n t C a l e n d a r Chloe Park (left), TJ Park, Amanuel Girma, Lucas Bekele, Nathan Bekele, Ethan Mesfin, Joaquin Fierro, Theodros Girma, Gabriella Mesfin, and Kidus Yalew of her life-saving treatment. The experience became a defining moment of the trip, highlighting the impact of compassion, quick action, and community support in saving lives. Coronado High School student Gabriella Mesfin, a relative of Bekele, described the emotional impact of working directly with the children. “Working with the children was a meaningful experience. One moment that stood out was seeing their joy during our time together. This cause matters because it brings hope to those in need. Helping raise $3,000 for the 16-year-old showed me how powerful community support can be,” she said. The team’s efforts received national coverage on Ethiopian television, reaching tens of thousands of viewers and helping break the stigma around autism in the country. The trip concluded with a final ceremony, where Bekele, local hospital leaders, and nonprofit directors emphasized the ongoing commitment to autism advocacy. This initiative demonstrates how young people can foster meaningful change through cross-cultural partnerships, compassion, and perseverance—lessons that will continue to inspire all involved for years to come. articles.text: Photo by Gerald McKeegan, Chabot Astronomer Images of the Ring Nebula captured by Chabot’s telescope, Nellie. early astronomers who mistook them for forming planets. The Ring Nebula looks like a smoke ring, but we’re likely viewing an hourglass-shaped cloud from one end. Its vibrant colors (red hydrogen, turquoise-green oxygen, and traces of carbon and neon) tell us about its composition and structure. The life cycle of stars Stars up to eight times the Sun’s mass die in this quiet way. Their white dwarfs will cool over trillions of years, eventually becoming black dwarfs. But because the universe is still young in cosmic terms, all white dwarfs that have ever formed are still glowing today. Tips for summer stargazing Use a telescope to discover planetary nebulae, globular clusters, and galaxies. No telescope? Find a dark sky and bring a camera. Summer is ideal for widefield shots of the Milky Way as we face its center. You can catch Vega and Lyra rising in the east after dusk. Join Chabot astronomers and staff for free telescope viewing every Friday and Saturday from 7:30–10:30 p.m. (weather permitting). And if you’re ready to go deeper, check out Unveiling the Universe: Astrophotography 101, a new summer course through Oakland Space Academy for high school students and adults. Participants only need their phone. (Laptops and light sunset dinner included!) In this course, participants will learn the basics of astrophotography so that they can capture the galaxy for themselves! View the link: https://chabotspace.org/programs/ events-listing/ Wherever you are, head outside, look up, and let the universe unfold.
