pages.text: 10 10 Wednesday, July 23, 2025 Summer Thoughts ® What stars leave behind Summer evenings open a window into the deeper universe. At Chabot Space & Science Center, we spend these nights gazing into the cosmos and invite you to do the same. Whether you’re looking through a telescope or simply lying back to watch the stars, this season is perfect for connecting with the universe while spending time with the “astronomer next door”. The Ring Nebula: A star’s last breath A highlight of the summer sky is the Ring Nebula, a beautiful remnant of a dying star in the constellation Lyra. Look for Lyra high in the eastern sky around 9:00PM. Its brightest star, Vega, glows bluish-white and points the way to the Ring Nebula. Though invisible to the naked eye, you can see it through our observatory telescopes or with your own, available in our gift shop! The Ring Nebula lies 2,500 light-years away. Unlike explosive supernovae, most stars end their lives slowly. After billions of years, they expand into red giants, shedding their outer gas layers over thousands of years. What remains is a white dwarf: a hot, dense stellar core. The radiation from this core lights up the gas, forming a glowing cloud we call a planetary nebula. articles.text: Shavies describes his approach to policing as rooted in collaboration – bringing together law enforcement, residents, and community partners to build safer neighborhoods. “I am honored to have been chosen to serve as the next Chief of Police for the City of Piedmont,” Shavies said. “I am excited to bring my experience in community safety, law enforcement leadership, and officer development to a city and department I have long admired. I look forward to building on Piedmont’s many strengths and guiding the department forward.” The city retained executive search firm Teri Black & Company to conduct a nationwide search following the retirement announcement of former Chief Jeremy Bowers earlier this year. Shavies was selected after several rounds of interviews with a professional panel, city leadership, and the City Council. “Among a strong pool of candidates, Frederick Shavies stood out as an exceptional leader with the experience, values, and knowledge to guide our Police Department going forward,” said City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore. Outgoing Chief Bowers also praised the appointment. “I’m pleased to congratulate Frederick Shavies on his appointment,” Bowers said. “Throughout my tenure, I have had the opportunity to work with Deputy Chief Shavies and I have always found him to be a trusted colleague whose competence, professionalism, and steady leadership have earned my deep respect.” Captain Chris Monahan served as interim Chief of Police between July 18, when Bowers retired, and July 22, when Shavies officially assumed the role. “Dude says when the men were separated from the boys, we were among the adolescents.”

If Pogačar wins it all, as expected, it will mark his fourth win of Le Grand Tour, putting him in rarified air with Chris Froome and behind five-time winners like France’s Jacques Anquetilm and Bernard Hinault, Belgium legend Eddy Merckx, and Miguel Induráin of Spain. Pogačar won Stage 4 to put himself in second place and then regained the Yellow Jersey the following day in a 33-km time trial. On July 14’s Bastille Day mountain course on Stage 12 from Auch to Hautacam along the Pyrenees, Pogačar dominated the field by attacking the final 12 km to establish a 2 minute, 10 second lead Vingegaard. He then won the following 10.9 km mountain course time trial to pad nearly two minutes to his advantage up to 4 minutes, 7 seconds. Pogačar’s Stage 12 victory marked a bit of redemption for him after falling behind on the same course in 2022, which wound up costing him the title to Vingegaard. “From the very first time I got to ride on that climb, I was looking forward to racing here and it came in the Tour de France 2022. At the time, I was giving everything to get back the Yellow Jersey but Jumbo were too strong. I had almost already forgotten about this, I was just looking forPhoto courtesy of UAE Team Emirates Tadej Pogačar leads the General Classification standings and is poised to claim his fourth Tour de France title. We had this stage in mind for a long time. We did a super job with the team and I’m super happy to win here and to take time on my rivals,” he added. The final five stages of the 112th La Grande Boucle starts a flat 160.4 km Stage 17, while the back-to-back mountain courses in Stages 18-19 could either be Pogačar solidifying his victory or Vingegaard fighting from behind. Stage 18’s 171.5 km course features three steep ascents with grades of 5.5 percent, 7.9 percent, and 6.5 percent and a summit finish. articles.text: Layth Haddawy (middle), a PHS senior, stands on the podium with his first-place medal after winning the 2025 USPA National Championship. Piedmont High School senior Layth Haddawy has quickly ascended up the rankings entering the third year of his competitive powerlifting career. On July 8 he won the U.S. Powerlifting National Championship in Las Vegas in the age 16-17 category. Haddawy lifted a combined total of 1,118 pounds, including 380 pounds in the squat, 253.5 pounds on the bench press, and a 485 pound dead lift. Haddawy won in a field of three, receiving a score of 395.87 and beating the second-place lifter by 58 points. “I am very proud of this achievement and feel gratified in knowing that I was able to compete in a more competitive division than last year and manage to place better,” Haddawy said. Layth last competed in the USPA Get Bent’s Spring Break in Oakland on April 5 where he lifted 1,085 total pounds. Three months later, Haddawy increased his squat by 28 pounds and his bench by 5.5 pounds. Haddawy hit three reps in the squats at the 2025 National Championship, increasing his weight each time by lifting 341 pounds, 363 pounds, and finishing by jumping 17 pounds to 380. “When I first started powerlifting, my squat had been the lift that I had the least experience with out of the three. So over the last year, I have put far more effort into improving my squat. The large jumps among the three reps were because I was conserving energy for the last rep,” Haddawy said. At last year’s USPA National Championship, Haddawy finished second in a field of 10, but he later learned he was dealing with a fracture in his pelvis. An MRI revealed Layth suffered an avulsion fracture, which is when a fragment of bone or muscle breaks away from the main bone. He spent the following months rehabbing and training for his next event in April 2025. articles.text: Staff Photos Tanya Kononova graduated from Piedmont High School in 2024 and competed on the Highlanders’ tennis team for two years after coming to Piedmont as a Ukrainian refugee. [Updated from August 2022] Tanya Kononova graduated from Piedmont High with the Class of 2024 and made a big name for herself as a standout tennis star, earning the Western Alameda County Conference’s Player of the Year award in 2022 as a junior after winning the league’s individual tournament’s singles bracket while she finished second the following year. She just finished her freshman year at San Diego State. Her path from Europe to the Highlanders’ tennis team wasn’t the typical journey like foreign exchange students who come to Piedmont High. For Tanya and her family, they never envisioned staying in California as a refugee prior to February 24, 2022—the day Russia invaded her native country of Ukraine. She arrived to Piedmont on July 22 of 2022 from Odesa, a city on the southern shore of Ukraine. Kononova turned up to coach Jim Landes’ tennis clinic a week later, instantly impressing him. “It was the week I had the high school girls warm up clinic, one week before tryouts. I told her to come the next day and she showed up to the clinics every day. Right then and there, I knew she was a very good player the first time she hit. That was a good warm up for her to meet some people,” said Landes. Departing from her country is an unimaginable experience to those of us here tucked away in the hills. Kononova and her mother, Olga Charugina, packed what they could and drove to the border of Moldova three weeks after the Russians invaded. Her father is still in Ukraine as men under the age of 60-years old were kept from leaving the country. She stayed in Moldova with relatives for two months and was forced to wait at the border for 13 hours before passing into the neighboring country. She described the experience of leaving Ukraine. “It was very scary to be leaving the Ukraine because we were afraid of being hit by bombs. There were so many people waiting at the border trying to get out,” said Kononova when speaking through a translator. Tanya and her family then decided to relocate to Bulgaria from May through July 2022 after a town administration building nearby in Moldova was targeted by Russian artillery. They had no connection to anyone in the country, forced to forge their own way. “We had no relatives there [in Bulgaria]. We had a place where we lived with me, my mother, my grandfather and my grandmother,” said Kononova. When initially leaving Odesa, she and her family were forced to quickly throw together their belongings because of fear that the Russians would siege the city. They only grabbed two suitcases with just some items to get by, like some clothes, textbooks, and her cell phone before making their way to Moldova.
articles.title: Tanya Kononova details her journey as a Ukrainian refugee and Piedmont tennis player

articles.text: All interested Piedmont High and Millennium High girls who want to play flag football in the upcoming Fall 2025 season are invited to attend a preseason training and conditioning camp. The coaching staff is committed to making this third season of PHS girls flag football a place where all girls continue to become better all-around athletes, mentally and physically, using their football knowledge to improve all parts of their lives. Preseason training will be held: • July 28 - 31 (Monday - Thursday) from 3-5 p.m. at Witter Field • Aug. 4 - Aug. 7 (Monday - Thursday) from 3-5 p.m. at Witter Field Training will include strength conditioning, agility, and football skills including flag pulling and throwing and catching. Both new and returning athletes should plan to attend. The first official day of practice for the upcoming season will be the first day of school, August 11, from 4-6 PM at Witter Field. articles.text: Piedmont Swim Team, a yearsound organization, will host tryouts on August 19-21 at Montclair Swim Club, 1901 Woodhaven Way. Tryouts will be from 4:00- 6:30 pm on all three days. Swimmers will be grouped by age and given a 30-minute time slot. The coaching staff expects that swimmers (ages 9 and over) to be available on all three days to get a clear sense of swim competency and coachability, which will help with group placement. Swimmers ages 8 and under are only expected to come for two days, August 19-20. PST is comprised of eight swim groups (Green, Blue, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, YRHS (year-round high school) and Titanium). For more information about the expectations of the differing groups, please refer to the PST 2025-2026 Handbook found on the website at the bottom of the article. Please note that PST is a yearround swim team (see exception below*). This tryout is for the 2025-2026 swim season. Practices for all accepted swimmers will begin on 8/23/25. For families joining PST in our younger groups, Green and Blue only, we realize the commitment to a competitive swim team might not be fully appreciated. As a way to support and encourage new swimmers to discover their love for swimming, PST will offer shorter terms for Green group families (12 weeks in the fall, 12 weeks in the spring, and 8 weeks in the summer). You can register for the fall session only or choose to continue on. The Blue group will have a 6-month trial that runs August to February. In January, Blue group swimmers and their guardian(s) will meet with their swim coach and decide if PST’s competitive swim program is the correct environment for their swimmer to thrive. Swimmers in the Blue group can opt to leave the team in February or continue on. This family trial is only available to swimmers who are new to PST and who participate in our Blue group. Starting in year two, Piedmont Swim Team is hosting tryouts on August 19-21. Photo courtesy of Piedmont Swim Team

14 Wednesday, July 23, 2025 Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 18th year. Current and former college athletes as well as high school athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmont-post.com. SAM SHELBY Football increasing my speed and endurance. How are you measuring your development? We use catapults/VBCs, which track your speed both on the field and in the weight room. I measure my development with the numbers given by our devices and my weight on the scale. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working with The Hun football coaches as well as the strength and conditioning coaches. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I reached a top speed of 22.2 MPH during one of our field workouts. It was the top speed of the team thus far. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Never be afraid to bet on yourself. Piedmont High Class of 2025 The Hun School, Class of 2026 Sam Shelby finished his high school career as the Post’s Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year after being an influential two-sport athlete in track and football. On the gridiron, Shelby was Piedmont’s primary playmaker as a receiver on PHS’ WACC Mission Division title-winning team. He finished the season with 66 receptions for 1,157 yards and 10 touchdowns, to go along with one rushing touchdown. As the Highlanders’ place kicker, Shelby converted 59 of 61 point after attempts. He helped Piedmont win the WACC Mission Division title, marking its second-consecutive league banner after winning the Shoreline the previous year. In track, Shelby entered the spring with a full head of steam after missing most of his junior year due to an injury. He qualified in three events at the North Coast Section Meet of Champions. Sam Shelby just graduated from Piedmont High. Staff Photo Individually, he placed sixth of 21 in the 400 with a time of 49.64 at the event. He helped the 4x100 team place ninth of 24 in 42.89, while the 4x400 team ran a 3:27.66 in the preliminaries to finish sixth of 22, while they placed ninth in the finals in 3:30.57. He was also third of 41 in the 200 meter dash at the WACC Championship with a time of 22.26. Sam’s 200 time of 22.26 and 400 time of 49.64 are both school records. He came just .02 shy of matching Kevin Hogan’s 1959 record of 22.24 in the slightly-longer 220 yard event. He details his workout regimen ahead of his senior year at the Hun School in Princeton. What is your workout program this summer? This summer, I am training with the Hun Football team [at Princeton] both on the field and in the weight room. Typically, we spend the mornings in the weight room and the afternoons on the field. What are your fitness goals for the summer? To put on more weight while Photo courtesy of Chico State Breah Bell, PHS Class of 2024, just finished her freshman year on Chico State’s track and field team. BREAH BELL Track and Field However, my track program is something I designed myself. Most of it consists of 200 repeats and broken 400s, but I am looking forward to adding some more technique in there to really make sure I’m ready to tackle all sorts of sprints next season. What are your fitness goals for the summer? Sprint endurance has got to be the biggest thing for me. With our teams’ new recruits, my 4x100 relay spot is in jeopardy, and I refuse to give up my anchor spot without putting in as much effort as I can. If I can perfect my sprint endurance as well as my top end speed, I’ll be able to maintain my spot, and hopefully run sub 12 next season too! How are you measuring your development? Time trials are the best way to keep track of one’s progress. For example, Week 1, maybe I run a 27 second 200. After 3-4 weeks, I’ll run another trial, and hopefully it’ll be down to 26 seconds. I also hope to visually see muscle growth, which has always been a bit of a challenge for me because of my height. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’m mostly working on my own. I think it’s important to work on your own though because it builds discipline as well as a genuine passion and commitment towards your work. Working alone has definitely grown my love for track. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I can’t deny that my first season at Chico State was kind of a bummer. But I also am proud of where I started that year. I broke the 12.5 barrier and joined the 12-low crew. With a new personal record of 12.4, I am now .38 seconds from joining Chico State’s top 10 All-Time 100m runners. That’s my goal for next season. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? My best piece of advice is to stick with it. Nobody plays a sport because it’s easy. We play these sports because we love them. It’s competitive, it’s exciting, but it’s also hard, both mentally and physically. That being said, the true separation between mediocre athletes and true star players is simply passion, dedication and commitment. Work on that craft, even when nobody else is watching. JORDAN ALEMANIA Football Piedmont High Class of 2025 The Hun School, Class of 2026 Jordan Alemania was another member of Piedmont’s football team in the fall of 2024, earning first-team all-league honors on both defense and offense. The Highlanders went 10-2, won the WACC Mission Division title, and reached the semifinals in the D7 North Coast Section postseason as the No. 3 seed. Alemania made his most noise as a defensive lineman, often wreaking havoc off the edge. One of his best performances was recording three sacks in a dominant 31-7 win over Newark Memorial to help capture the league title. Piedmont’s 42-26 win over No. 6 Fortuna in the first round of the NCS tournament marked the school’s first postseason win since 2017. What is your workout program this summer? This summer, I have been working out on my own and with the Hun football team. Our program is being run by a strength and conditioning coach with a combination of weights, jumps, and sprints. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals are to put on good weight while staying explosive and quick. How are you measuring your development? I am measuring my development by using force plates and tracking my speed with a catapult device. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working out with my team and doing skill specific training with a group of De La Salle and Cal football players. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I hit a 495 pound barbell squat. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Don’t overthink it. Keep working hard and your chance will come. articles.text: In this week of Hiking with Jon we delve into our fourth of six features of trails near Lake Tahoe, to include one of the tallest peaks in California, Washeshu Peak (formerly Squaw Peak) at Palisades Tahoe in Olympic Valley. If you are in the North Lake Tahoe area, take a hike with a million-dollar view atop Washeshu Peak at over 8,000 feet in elevation. Palisades Tahoe Olympic Valley is a popular destination for Piedmont residents on ski week. But during the summer months, the region becomes a prime hiking location with wildflowers and sweeping awe striking views of Lake Tahoe and Desolation Wilderness. articles.text: Dolly Parton The San Francisco Symphony, joined by a cast of guest vocalists and musicians, will perform hit songs by iconic country pop music star Dolly Parton in a special multimedia concert on Friday, August 1 entitled Dolly Parton’s Threads: My Songs In Symphony. The innovative and unique concert features the country legend on screen, leading audiences in a visual-musical biopic and through key highlights of her storied sixty-year career. Symphony musicians will play alongside solo artists including vocalists Hollie Hammel, Julie Williams and Katelyn Drye; guitarists Derek Drye, Lindsey Miller, Dean Berner; bassist Gary Lunn, and percussionist Chris Leidhecker. Conductor Jack Everly, principal conductor of the Indianapolis Symphony and the Naples Philharmonic, leads the artists and San Francisco Symphony featuring Parton’s hit songs “Jolene,” “Coat Of Many Colors,” “I Will Always Love You,” and more. Parton is one of only a handful of individuals to receive at least one nomination from all four major annual American entertainment award organizations, including an Emmy, GRAMMY, Oscar, and Tony. Her career spans 60 years and 49 albums, and her music has influenced generations of pop, country, blues and soul recording artists. She also founded a number of charitable and philanthropic organizations, including the Dollywood Foundation which brings education and poverty relief to her hometown in east Tennessee. All songs performed at the Dolly Parton’s Threads: My Songs In Symphony concert are written by Parton unless otherwise noted. Orchestral arrangements are by David Hamilton. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco. Visit https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2024-25/SWTS25-Dolly-Parton to purchase tickets, or call the box office at (415) 864-6000. Tickets are limited.
articles.title: SF Symphony performs Dolly Parton hits in Aug. 1 concert

articles.text: Korsa Musical Theater, a Bay Area musical theater training company, concludes its 20th season with a production of Oklahoma! at the Pinole Valley High School Theater. Tickets are available for three more performances, including two 7 p.m. performances on July 25 and 26; and a 2 p.m. matinee on July 28. Oklahoma! is the first musical written by Rodgers and Hammerstein, a theater-writing team of composer Richard Rodgers and lyricist-dramatist Oscar Hammerstein II. The 1943 musical is based on Lynn Riggs’s 1931 play Green Grow the Lilacs and follows the story of farmgirl Laurey and cowboy Curly’s budding romance, threatened by a brooding ranch-hand named Jud. The play ran for over five years on Broadway, a record that would not be bested until My Fair Lady’s initial run in 1956. Korsa Musical Theater’s production features a cast of 33 student performers age 13 through 20, led by a team of professional directors including award-winning Director Susannah Martin, Music Director David Möschler, and Choreographer Janet Collard. The production also includes a 30-piece live orchestra, with five student instrumentalists playing Robert Russell Bennet’s original score. Tickets are available online at www.korsamt.org or at the door one hour before curtain. Ticket prices are $18–$40, with discounts for students, seniors, military, teachers, and groups. Pinole Valley High School Theater is located at 2900 Pinole Valley Road in Pinole. Photo courtesy of Korsa Musical Theater Korsa Musical Theater’s production of Oklahoma! features a cast of 33 student performers.
articles.title: Play ends July 27 in Pinole

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company’s production The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe is playing onstage now through August 10. The one-woman stage show The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe was originally written by Jane Wagner and turned into a critically-acclaimed film in 1991. The show is often praised, and considered controversial at the time, for its feminist material including the compressed history of the feminist movement offered in Act 2. Writer and comedian Marga Gomez stars in Wagner’s iconic play as Trudy, an eccentric bag lady who serves as a bridge between Earth and the cosmos. The protagonist becomes a whole cast of comedic, quirky characters, weaving together tales of a punk-rock rebel, wealthy Californian socialites, and feminist reactionaries. “There are so many Signs of Stupid Life in 2025 that I am excited to revive this iconic play to experience something way more intelligent,” Gomez shared. “I first saw [the play] on Broadway when I was hitting open mics and working odd jobs. I was Marga Gomez in Aurora’s The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe awed. I had goosebumps. If anyone told me back then I would be performing Jane and Lily’s iconic characters someday I would have freaked out.” Gomez is an acclaimed comedian known for her dynamic storytelling and brings her unique voice to this one-woman tour de force. She is the recipient of the GLAAD Media Award for Theatre. “I couldn’t be more thrilled to see Marga Gomez stepping in to Lily Tomlin’s iconic role,” said Josh Costello, Aurora’s Artistic Director. “Anyone who has seen Marga perform knows she is a Bay Area treasure. There has always been a connection between Lily Tomlin’s work and Marga’s, so it’s fitting that Marga will be the one to perform Search for Signs at Aurora.” Visit https://www.auroratheatre.org/search-for-signs for showtimes and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Aurora’s The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe now playing through Aug. 10

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) welcomes Bay Areabased funk and soul artist Rojai this Friday as part of the museum’s free “Friday Nights” series. Jairo Vargas, who goes by the stage name Rojai, merges elements from funk, soul and R&B to create a raw and unique sound that evokes the musical spirit of San Francisco, where he was born and raised. Rojai is the leader and vocalist for the acclaimed San Francisco bands Bayonics, The Pocket (formerly Hot Pocket) and Starship Connection. Rojai performs with The Pocket this Friday at OMCA, following a Reggaetón dance lesson led by Sara Templeton. “Friday Nights” is a free community-gathering evening event series held every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout spring and summer, featuring live music, immersive arts activities and late-night museum access with the purchase of a museum ticket. Concerts begin at 7 p.m. Bring a blanket and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s large lawn, where live music and entertainment takes place throughout the evening. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from a stationed food truck on-site. A rotating list of vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon Streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. Friday Night events are always free and open to the public, but late-night museum access requires a ticket purchase. Visit https://museumca.org/event/friday-nights-at-omca-with-rojai-inthe-pocket/ to learn more about this Friday’s featured artists. Photo courtesy of Oakland Museum of California Rojai performing with The Pocket

articles.text: Event is part of TIM’s free public programs Author Liz Schott leads a discussion on Dorothy Wright Liebes’ legacy and involvement in the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition this Saturday, July 26, at Treasure Island Museum. The event is part of the museum’s free summer programming that aims to inform residents and visitors of the island’s historical relevance. Liebes, known as “the mother of modern weaving,” opened her first weaving and textile design studio on Powell Street in San Francisco in 1930. Her innovative designs and textiles adorned high fashion and commercial clothing, and then grew to become integral elements of architectural projects. Liebes embarked on a six-week journey across Europe in prepation took place over the course of eight months on San Francisco’s newly-minted purpose-built Treasure Island, and Liebes was tasked with gathering pieces that conveyed her vision for the role of handcraft in modern design. Author Liz Schott is the event’s featured speaker. Schott is writing a biography of Liebes’ legacy and the textile designs that became so widely recognized that they were dubbed the “Liebes Look.” She received the Hazel Rowley Prize in early July for her biography of Dorothy Wright Liebes. articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) will present a new exhibition, People Make This Place: SFAI Stories, celebrating the legacy of students and artists associated with the San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI), which ceased operation in 2022. The San Francisco Art Institute was one of the oldest art schools in the United States and the oldest west of the Mississippi River. Despite the university’s influence in the local and global art world, the private college closed permanently due to declining enrollment, high real estate costs, and challenges related to the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic. Notable alumni include Annie Leibovitz, Paul McCarthy, Rita Keegan, Alice Brown Chittenden, Clark Hobart, Percy Gray and more. The school employed influential artists and thinkers of the 1950’s Beat Movement, when San Francisco was a leading producer of important figures. SFAI faculty David Park, Elmer ing works by Joan Brown, Miguel Calderón, Imogen Cunningham, Mike Henderson, Candice Lin and Carlos Villa. The exhibition also includes a range of archival materials drawn from the museum’s library and permanent collection, as well as the San Francisco Art Institute’s Legacy Foundation and Archive. In celebration of the opening weekend of People Make This Place: SFAI Stories, SFMOMA will host a special film screening with Becky Alexander and Jeff Gunderson, the team behind the San Francisco Art Institute Legacy Foundation and Archive. Gunderson and Alexander will share films and stories highlighting the history and significance of the campus and take questions. The screening is free and open to the public, museum admission is not required. The screening takes place Sunday, July 27, 2025, at 2 p.m. To learn more, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/ people-make-this-place-sfai-stories/. The exhibition is on view July 26 through July 2026. articles.text: George MacKay stars in 1917 the awful, a killing field of stasis that continued beyond all reason. This is the context for Mendes’ most remarkable film, 1917, set in northern France, at the height of the war. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, July 23, 2025 MOVIES FOR ADULTS 1917 – Remembering World War I By Chris Honoré Before discussing writer/ director Sam Mendes’ film 1917, I feel I would be remiss not to mention Peter Jackson’s extraordinary They Will Not Grow Old. He was given access to hundreds of archival WWI news footage from Britain’s Imperial War Museum – scratched, grainy, and hand cranked film that he, using state-of-the-art restorative technology, not only colorized but literally brought back to life. It’s as if he opened a portal in time and we see young Brits gathered on a battlefield, waiting, some, breaking the fourth wall, staring into the camera, smiling, their youthful faces filled with an optimistic eagerness that would soon be devastatingly transformed. WWI, which began in July of 1914 and lasted until November or 1918, was one of the deadliest wars in history. Nine million combatants and seven million civilians were killed as a direct result. Indirectly, 50 to 100 million deaths occurred worldwide, attributed to what was referred to as the “Spanish Flu,” the pandemic thought to have begun in the damp, muddy, disease-ridden trenches, conditions that were almost as lethal as the withering machinegun fire, shelling and chlorine gas faced by the troops. WWI was an extraordinary display of nationalistic hubris, bordering on a collective insanity in which millions of men, on all sides, were sacrificed for mere yards of soil. It was a nightmare of George MacKay stars in 1917 the awful, a killing field of stasis that continued beyond all reason. This is the context for Mendes’ most remarkable film, 1917, set in northern France, at the height of the war. The story is deceptively simple: two young soldiers – Lance Corporal Schofield (George McKay) and Lance Corporal Blake (Dean Charles Chapman) – are ordered by their general to deliver a letter to a command post some eight miles away, instructing the commanding officer to stand his troops (two battalions, numbering 1,600 men) down. They are told that all lines of communication have been cut. The intelligence in the letter explains that the Germans have fashioned a trap and should the dawn assault take place, casualties will be grave. The caveat is that to arrive at the command post, the distance to be crossed is, in truth, a No Man’s Land, comprised of German troops (thought to have retreated), desiccated terrain and trenches. The general adds that among the battalions waiting is Corporal Blake’s brother. And so, the two climb up a ladder onto the lip of a deep trench, urging one another on, Schofield expressing his reluctance, yet both feeling the urgency of their mission. What they leave behind are green fields and wildflowers; it’s a beautiful spring afternoon in April. But what they find as they move ever deeper into enemy territory is a landscape of utter destruction – deep craters filled with water and bodies, dead horses, stretching barbed wire, and a horror of mud, death and unrecognizable carrion covered with flies and feeding birds. Hell has been there and left. Their sense of urgency is palpable; to fail would be catastrophic; they must survive in order to deliver the letter carried inside Corporal Blake’s tunic. Any hint of exposition – backstory, shared memories of origin or tales of home – is inconsequential. What we hear are the sounds of their breathing, the rasp and clank of their gear as Blake and Schofield crouch forward, bayoneted rifles ever at the ready. This is the narrative arc. However, what writer/director Sam Mendes and legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins do, from the outset, is create the illusion that the camera is the third person on the journey and the entire film is shot in one long take, never cutting away. Of course, that is not the case, but the impact of this most effective photographic technique (not a conceit) is striking. In other words, 1917 is a truly visual film, and it is the camera that propels it forward, Blake and Schofield moving constantly, the story revealed as they grimly survey all that is before them. And so, the question posed is: can Mendes and Deakins capture and then sustain the attention of the audience as the fraught images escalate, the faces of the two made grimly fearful by what they witness, leaving them to wonder what, among all this carnage, awaits them. I would judge that 1917 is an engaging, photographic marvel and a marvelous achievement, possessing a wonderful score by Thomas Newman and truly fine performances by both MacKay and Chapman. 1917. articles.text: Sophie and the Rising Sun is set in a small coastal South Carolina town named Salty Creek. It’s autumn, and the year is 1941. The film opens with a bus stopping brief ly and leaves behind a semi-conscious, injured man lying in the grass near the bus stop. A number of locals who witnessed this unexpected moment gather around the man and notice that he is Asian and assume he is, to use their word, a “Chinaman.” Someone leans down and asks him his name. The man struggles to whisper, “Ohta.” Perplexed, uncertain as to what to do with the man, three prominent townsmen approach long-time resident Ann Morrison (Margo Martindale) who is recently widowed and has a cottage behind her house, currently being used for gardening supplies. Explaining that the man needs a place to recover they ask her if he might stay in her cottage. Out of concern and generosity, she agrees and understanding that Mr. Ohta (Takashi Yamaguchi) will need care has her maid begin to look after him. And so the story begins to unfold. We soon learn that living next to Mrs. Morrison is a young woman, Sophie Willis. She lost her husband in WWI, and now supports herself by fishing lobsters just off the coast during the week, and on Sundays, carrying her easel and paints, captures on canvas the ocean and the surrounding wildlife. Slowly Mr. Ohta begins to mend and reveals not only his quiet decency, but his skills as a gardener, a talent that surprises and pleases Mrs. Morrison for she too finds refuge in simply caring for her plants. Of course, Sophie and Mr. Ohta meet and she discovers that he shares her love of painting and their paths cross each Sunday morning. What changes the warm, heartfelt arc of the narrative is December 7, 1941. Mr. Ohta tells Ann that he is not Chinese but Japanese and was born in America. The townspeople of Salty Creek initially react to the presence of Mr. Ohta with curiosity and even suspicion, with the attack on Pearl Harbor ot soon emerges as gossipy, racist and xenophobic with the exception of Ann, her newly hired maid Salomé (Lorraine Toussaint), and Sophie. These women soon begin to comprehend the risk involved for Mr. Ohta should he remain in Salty Creek. Sophie and the rising Sun is not only an exceptionally fine film, with strong performances (look for Margo Martindale). At this moment it is also timely. Sophie and the Rising Sun. Written and directed by Maggie Greenwald. Starring Julianne Nicholson, Takashi Yamaguchi, Margo Martindale. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated R. Released in 2017. Now streaming on Prime/Fandango/ Apple. articles.text: Gerard Butler and Jonny Weston in Chasing Mavericks Chasing Mavericks is a family friendly, classic sports story, reminiscent of those inspirational films that were so ubiquitous in the 70s and 80s. The field of play, however, is not a grassy pitch or an oval track; rather, it’s based on a true story set in a famous surfing spot, just north of Half Moon Bay, Ca., known for its monster-size 30 foot waves (some peaking over 60 feet) and a dangerous, life threatening undertow. It’s called Mavericks. The focus of the film is a teenager, Jay Moriarity (Johnny Weston), whose dream is to ride the seemingly impossible northern Pacific break. He quickly learns that to ride and survive the El Nino created waves will require not only extensive training and endurance, but the ability to hold one’s breath for some four minutes or risk drowning. The narrative opens with 9-year-old Jay attempting to rescue the small dog of his childhood friend, Kim (later portrayed by Leven Rambin), that has has fallen into the surf. Jay is saved from the surging waves by a crusty old surfer, Frosty Hesson (Gerard Butler), who years later reluctantly agrees to mentor Jay, after he persistently shares with Frosty his unyielding desire to surf Mavericks. And so the adventure begins with Frosty putting Jay through a rigorous training regime, insisting that he must learn not only the basics of big wave riding, but must practice those skills that will help him survive the harrowing, unforgiving waves should he wipeout and find himself in the grip of what’s called the “spin cycle.” Frosty also loans Jay his “big gun” long board, and Jay’s single-parent mom (Elisabeth Shue) buys him a weather radio for his 16th birthday, allowing him to track the storms that produce the huge surf. Of course, after months of practice, the singular storm arrives and Jay’s opportunity presents itself. Mavericks is ready; however, will Jay be ready, and will he be able to master the mythical monsters that form and crash with a Zen-like intensity that must be seen to be believed. Meanwhile, Frosty and Kim stand on shore and watch Jay paddling toward his destiny. Chasing Mavericks. Directed by Curtis Hanson, Michael Apted. Starring Gerard Butler, Johnny Wesson, Elisabeth Shue. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG. Released in 2012. Streaming on Disney+/ Fandango/Prime/Apple.

articles.text: Weekends until August 25, 11–2 p.m. Nepalese Art Exhibit This exhibition brings together Nepali artists living in the USA as first-generation immigrants. The body of works displayed explores the paradoxes of diasporic life—particularly the process of building identity amid pressures to conform to dominant cultures and homogeneous identities. Drawing inspiration from everyday life and personal experiences, this exhibition reflects the tension between strong attachment to the culture left behind and the process of assimilating into a new society. As the result of seven months’ research on Nepali Diaspora artists and their works, based in the Bay Area and beyond, by Fulbright Visiting Scholar Swosti Rajbhndari Kayasth with San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum, the show has provided a platform for artists to express their unique experiences and perspectives, often highlighting the complexities of navigating multiple cultures and identities. articles.text: Nikola Printz Festival Opera continues its 2025 season with a Salon Series of Sunday afternoon concerts in Piedmont featuring some of the Bay Area’s rising stars and critically acclaimed artists. The concerts will be at Piedmont Center for the Arts on July 27, August 24, and September 28. The series offers intimate, artist-curated performances that highlight rare repertoire and virtuosic collaboration between talented singers and musicians alike. At the conclusion of each concert, the audience is invited to stay for a post-performance reception with the artists. Festival Opera General Director Zachary Gordin said, “This new format encourages programming a broader variety of vocal music: art song, arias and scenes from operas, solo cantatas, complete short operas, and even some gems from genres outside of the classical music spectrum. The artists and programs we present this year are all very dear to me, and the singers are absolute stars of their respective voice types. They are sure to offer memorable and impactful performances which our audience can witness up-close in this chamber music venue.” Baroque Queen Sunday, July 27, 4 p.m. Rising star and critically acclaimed mezzo-soprano Nikola Printz joins musicians Joshua Mikus-Mahoney (cello), Jon Mendle (theorbo and Baroque guitar), and Zachary Gordin (harpsichord) for a performance of musical gems by Monteverdi, Handel, Purcell, more—composers who shaped the early days of opera with their dramatic musical storytelling. Accompanied by a small baroque banda, Nikola Printz brings their dynamic artistry to revive the voices of legendary heroines, sorceresses, and queens from the past. American Song Cycles Sunday, August 24, 4 p.m. The Salon Series continues with a powerful afternoon of music by renowned soprano Carrie Hennessey and acclaimed pianist Daniel Lockert featuring two magnificent works by American composers. Experience encore performances of Julia Seeholzer’s Portraits of Disquiet, a gripping reflection on our modern world, and Jake Heggie’s At the Statue of Venus, a poignant and humorous journey of anticipation and self-discovery. Shawnette Sulker Sara Couden Carrie Hennessey Bel Canto Forever Sunday, September 28, 4 p.m. A celebration of soaring vocalism with soprano Shawnette Sulker and contralto Sara Couden, accompanied by Zachary Gordin at the piano. The program includes 19th century Bel Canto music of Rossini, Bellini, Delibes, Meyerbeer with dazzling duets, arias, soaring melodies and vocal fireworks that define the art of bel canto, beautiful singing. Individual tickets for each Salon concert are affordably priced at $40 and available online at www.festivalopera.org. The Piedmont Center for Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Ave, Piedmont.

articles.text: On a quiet, winding stretch of Buena Vista Way, perched high in the leafy solitude of the Berkeley Hills, lies a residence so richly steeped in history and architectural splendor that even longtime locals may pass by unaware. Shielded by a stately gate and set among old-growth redwoods and oaks, this Berkeley Landmarked home, known as Hume Cloister, is not simply a house—it is a living artifact, a Gothic revival echo of medieval France brought to life with Californian soul. Located at 2900 Buena Vista Way, the estate defies expectations. While Berkeley is no stranger to idiosyncratic homes or storied pedigrees, the Hume Cloister occupies a category of its own. Built in 1929, the estate was the brainchild of Samuel and Portia Bell Hume, an intellectual power couple whose academic and professional contributions still ripple through the University of California system and beyond. Its design, inspired by a 13th-century monastery the couple visited in Toulouse, France, is the work of noted Bay Area architect John Hudson Thomas, a master of eclectic historical revival styles. The result is a residence that would not feel out of place in the French countryside but instead finds itself gazing across the San Francisco Bay. In its construction and setting, the home is an act of artistic ambition and a deeply personal vision. Samuel Hume, a dramatic literature scholar, art curator, and rare book dealer, spent much of his professional life elevating the cultural landscape of California. He served as a professor at UC Berkeley and as director of the Berkeley Art Museum. His wife, Dr. Portia Bell Hume, was a pioneer in psychiatry and mental health education, notably one of the first women to teach in the medical school at UC Berkeley. Together, they envisioned a sanctuary that would not only serve as a home but also as a space for intellectual reflection, creativity, and retreat. And a sanctuary it is. Sited on more than two-thirds of an acre, the Hume Cloister commands unobstructed panoramic views stretching from the San Mateo Bridge to Mt. Tamalpais and beyond. From the main terrace, the Golden Gate Bridge appears perfectly framed, like a painting made by nature and architecture working in concert. The dramatic elevation provides not just vistas but a sense of quiet serenity, rare commodities in today’s ever-expanding world. The house itself is an architectural narrative told in stone, wood, and wrought iron. Upon entering, visitors are met with the scale and craftsmanship of another era: vaulted ceilings soar 25 feet overhead, while massive fireplaces anchor the living spaces. Wrought-iron chandeliers of cathedral scale cast shadows that evoke a sense of monastic calm. Stone arches and a spiral staircase offer a tactile link to the medieval structures that inspired the Humes nearly a century ago. Thomas’s design placed emphasis on balance between grandeur and intimacy. The grand living room leads to a mezzanine library and office space with commanding views over the bay—a setting easily imagined as the workspace for a scholar of literature, or a psychiatrist drafting the early contours of a mental health curriculum. The library is equipped to house more than 2,000 books, and the view from this elevated perch—particularly during the golden hours of early morning and dusk—is nothing short of meditative. At the heart of the residence lies its most distinctive feature: a cloister-style courtyard, modeled At the heart of the residence lies its cloister-style courtyard, modeled directly after those in European monasteries. directly after those in European monasteries. Lined with arched colonnades and featuring a stone wishing well at its center, the courtyard exemplifies the home’s spiritual and architectural mission. It is a space designed not just for contemplation but for communion—with nature, history, and the self. While the architecture pays tribute to medieval sensibilities, the home’s current iteration is anything but antiquated. The present owner has undertaken a comprehensive 7+ year restoration and modernization effort, preserving the historic character while introducing contemporary amenities. The kitchen features a Wolf range, Sub-Zero refrigerator, and custom millwork beneath a louvered ceiling and skylight— marrying utility and aesthetics in a way that honors both the old and the new. Each of the five en-suite bedrooms has been updated with toptier finishes, including custom tilework, copper showerheads, and heated floors. The grounds of the estate are equally evocative. Beyond the cloister courtyard, a series of outdoor spaces reveal themselves: a greenhouse and planting beds ideal for an amateur horticulturist; a bocce court tucked beside a small redwood grove; and a restored koi pond, arched bridge and a fountain gently bubbling at its center. Next to it, the adjoining en-suite guestroom shares similar amenities and access to the deck and koi pond. In addition to these 2 spacious bedrooms, the main level includes 2 other en suite bedrooms, allowing privacy and space for family and friends alike. Additionally, a full guest house off the enclosed driveway includes a full kitchen, living room, large bedroom, laundry facility, and full bath. The private quarters and public spaces alike follow a rhythm of light and shadow, openness and enclosure, that makes the home feel both expansive and profoundly personal. It is this harmony between history and modernity, privacy and connection, place and purpose that makes the Hume Cloister so exceptional. More than just a home, it is an architectural expression of two lives lived with intellect, intention, and imagination. For Samuel and Portia Hume, the Cloister was not only a residence but an embodiment of ideals: beauty, scholarship, and sanctuary. That such a place remains largely unknown, even to longtime Berkeley residents, only adds to its mystique. Tucked away behind its gate, with only the parts of the building and Spanish tile roof peeking above the trees, the Hume Cloister asks nothing of the world but offers so much to those who step inside. It stands as a testament not only to a particular architectural style but to a world view that holds that the spaces we inhabit shape the lives we lead. As real estate in the Bay Area continues to evolve, and as historical preservation faces increasing challenges, the Hume Cloister is a rare and precious reminder: that the past, when thoughtfully preserved and lovingly restored, can inform a richly modern life. It is a living museum, yes, but also a home, warm and welcoming, prepared to host the next chapter in its storied life. Whether for a discerning collector, a lover of history, or simply someone in search of unparalleled peace and beauty above the fray, the Hume Cloister offers a singular opportunity. In a region defined by innovation and speed, it is a place of stillness, where every stone and beam seems to whisper, “Slow down. You are home.” Listing Agents: Anian Tunney & Adrienne Krumins The Grubb Company 510-339-0400 The grand living room leads to a mezzanine library and office space.

pages.text: Wednesday, July 23, 2025 27 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers explore Bellevue, Sharon Avenue By Dick Carter There was good summer turnout of 40 walkers and four K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday for the Walking on Wednesdays weekly walk. The group was pleased Monica Katzel was visiting family and walking with them for the first time. She reported that former walker Christine Caliste, who lived and worked with the Katzel family and retired to her native Granada, is well, enjoying retirement, and remembers the walkers fondly. Two streets the group hadn’t walked this year were Bellevue and Sharon Avenues. Bellevue has many beautiful and interesting homes. Sharon was developed by early Piedmonter William Sharon and has some interesting history. The group went up Sierra Avenue to the 217-foot path between 17 and 29 Sierra to Mountain Avenue, then to the street triangle where Bellevue intersects with Mountain. They checked on the island oak in the triangle’s center which replaced a Sequoia last year that had been in this intersection for generations. The oak is native to California, and it is hoped it will thrive in this small island that has no regular source of water. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation raised over $8,000 from neighbors for the tree’s planting and care for at least two years. The group went up Bellevue and came to the front gate of a beautiful mansion that is down a long driveway. From the front yard there is a majestic view of San Francisco. On a past walk late friend and walker Will Adams pointed out that the house was placed on the lot specifically so that the driveway entrance would provide the wonderful view. The walkers climbed to the top of Bellevue and went down the steep Pacific Avenue to Dormidera and Sharon Avenues. At Sharon, the history of its development was shared based on an article by Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi in the society’s magazine. William Sharon was born in 1852 and grew up on an Ohio farm. In 1872 he went to San Francisco and then Virginia City, Nevada to work for his uncle, who was a successful banker and silver mine owner. Sharon married Lillian Mygatt in 1876 and became successful in finance and mining too. He was also elected to the Nevada State Senate in the 1880s. The Sharons initially lived in Virginia City, but they wanted their children to attend better schools and bought a home in Oakland in 1890. In 1893 the Sharons purchased nine acres in the Piedmont hills on Mountain Avenue. They built a magnificent three-story house in the middle of their land and called it Casa Montana. With their seven children, Lillian’s mother, a housekeeper, cook, and gardener they moved into it in 1898. However, in 1914 the new City of Piedmont imposed a new property tax based on the size of the property, and the Sharons’ taxes increased dramatically. So, in 1915 the Sharons subdivided their land in a development they called Sharon Terrace. It had 20y lots with frontages on Mountain, Sharon, Dormidera, and Pacific Avenues. Some family members built homes on them, and the driveway to Casa Montana became Sharon Avenue. Sharon died at his home in 1926, but Casa Montana continued as a family home. Developer George Windsor purchased the remaining land and built his own home at 11 Sharon and the house at 7 Sharon on spec. He later also built homes at 40 and 44 Sharon. Sadly, Windsor demolished Casa Montana in 1936. The mansion was replaced by three homes at 27, 33, and 37 Sharon. Today, only three Sharon family members’ houses, those at 235 Mountain and 56 and 52 Sharon, remain on the former Casa Montana property. The group saw where Casa Montana once stood, and the remaining historic homes. The walkers took a side trip up Sharon Court, and by chance long time Piedmont recreation coordinator Janet Epstein and husband George were outside their home. Janet told the walkers about the Piedmont Seniors’ group activities that she has managed since 1996. After the unexpected visit with the Epsteins, the group returned to Sharon Avenue. They went down Sharon’s hill to Mountain and enjoyed a lovely, cloudy view of the Bay Bridge along the way. The group noted the 235 Mountain house that was built in 1912 by a Sharon family member. The group got in some additional steps going up Craig Avenue to Highland before their usual noontime return to the Exedra. articles.text: The Taste of Sonoma is the county’s largest wine gathering Every year I look forward to the Sonoma County Vintners “Taste of Sonoma” grand tasting. Held on an expansive grass lawn at Kendall-Jackson winery in Santa Rosa, the best wineries of Sonoma County gather to show off their current vintages. There are three enormous tents filled with I would guess nearly 200 wineries. Unlike other tastings there seems to be no limit on the number of wines a winery can pour, with some wineries bringing 6 or 7 different bottlings. What is amazing to me Is the viticulture area and vast diversity Sonoma has in geography and weather. It seems whatever grape you want to grow there is an area of Sonoma County that is suitable to it. We now know that Pinot Noir and Chardonnay tends to thrive in cooler climates so there is a tent for the cool Gaps Crown and Sonoma Coast AVAs. Cabernet tends to thrive in the warmer Alexander Valley so there is a tent for that. Zinfandel and Syrah do well in the Dry Creek and Russian River valleys and those AVA’s are represented as well. I know of no other place on earth that has greater geographic and climatic diversity than Sonoma County. The other great thing about the Taste of Sonoma tasting is the food and creature comforts. There were six food trucks serving a variety of delicious offerings from ceviche to pulled pork to mac and cheese. And unlike other wine tastings where there is rarely a place to sit down, the Taste of Sonoma has numerous lounges with comfy sofas and chairs for outdoor seating. There is also a VIP lounge where selected wineries pour their premium wines. All in all, it was one of the best organized tastings I have attended. The hardest part is choosing which wines to write about. There were way more good wines poured than I have room for in this article. But at the end of the day some wines lingered in my mind. They had something special about them that made them memorable. Those are the wines I present to you below. ers. The palate is medium bodied with very fine tannins and a lovely caressing texture in the mouth, fine tension and poise with crisp, red-berried fruits on the shimmering finish. • 2020 Meadowcroft River Trace This lovely wine is a Grenache, Syrah, Mourvedre blend from San Joaquin and Contra Costa Counties. It features ample vanilla and warm spice notes overlaid on an exotic bed of cherries and blueberries. Its medium bodied and supple on the palate, with a peppery tang to the lingering finish. Should drink well for 7 to 8 years. • 2023 Williams Selyem Pinot Noir Westside Road Neighbors The Westside Road Pinot has a voluminous bouquet with crushed strawberry and red currant scents intermingling with tobacco and fennel. The palate is well-balanced and the red fruit is full and rich in the mouth. The finish is long, complex and satisfying. • 2021 Weather Pinot Noir Lares Vineyard For the second year in a row this Weather Pinot was a standout to me. It pops out of the glass with succulent dark cherries and spice box notes. Medium-bodied the palate offers flavors of raspberry with a soft tannic edge. It shows seductive florals with spicy flavors and ends with a foodfriendly finish. Try with some grilled salmon. • 2020 Zialena Cappella Originally a sacramental wine from Italian Swiss Colony this new version of Cappella is a blended red wine whose contents change each year. The wine has plum and blueberry aromas framed by cedar and vanilla with some briary flourishes. It is medium to full-bodied and boasts a supple creamy texture yet remains bright and fresh on the fruity finish. Aromatically dynamic it segues to generous peaches and honeysuckle. The palate explodes with flavor, its pure concentrated fruits refreshed by tangy acidity

The medium bodied palate features concentrated red berry fruit, earth and cherry flavors. It’s structured by velvety tannins and mouthwatering acidity and has a long, perfumed finish • 2024 Three Sticks Castenada Rose Crafted from a field blend of Red Rhone varieties using the saignee vinification method. It has enticing aromas of strawberries and watermelon. On the palate it is medium-bodied layered and concentrated concluding with a long, sappy finish that would make it able to stand up to heartier foods. • 2023 Enkidu Sauvignon Blanc Starts with an exotic and flashy nose with tangerine citrus notes, nectarines and tropical aromas. Similarly, the palate is impressive in its amplitude while remaining perfectly focused through the bright, chiseled and layered finish. This is a perfect example of what a Sonoma County Sauvignon Blanc should be. • 2023 Salty Goats Pinot Noir Fort Ross-Seaview From a vineyard at 1100ft elevation and 3 miles from the Pacific this cool climate Pinot was aged for 12 months in 30% new French oak and has an enchanting vanilla kiss on the voluptuous cherry nose. This has touches of pine and pepper on the nose highlighting black cherries, earth and black olives. It’s impressively full-bodied and richly concentrated without seeming heavy or overdone, finishing supple and velvety on the lingering finish. Should do well in the cellar for well over a decade. • 2023 Longboard Albarino Elieo Vineyard So nice to see this Russian River vintner taking a chance with a “weird” varietal. Of course, Albarino is not weird Each winery was pouring multiple wines in Spain or Portugal where they have been producing it for centuries. Sort of like a cross between Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling it’s a lovely wine with green apple and pear aromas. In the mouth the wine is clean and focused with melon and peach fruit and a soft, round mouthfeel leading to a crisp finish. • 2023 Sean Minor Grenache Rossi Ranch Grenache is such a lovely varietal I was surprised that there were not more representatives at the tasting. Glad to come across this one from the historic Rossi Vineyard. It screams of varietal character showing notions of vanilla, strawberries, cherries plus some floral notes. It’s medium-bodied, silky and expansive on the palate and vibrant on the finish. A perfect pizza wine. • 2024 Pride Mountain Viognier Viognier is a notoriously difficult grape to produce and very few New World versions come close to the magnificence of France’s Condrieu. Pride is the exception to the rule. It has lovely scents of peach, pear and honeysuckle. The full-bodied round palate offers ripe peach and apricot fruit tempered by good acidity and a long savory, satisfying finish. Consistently excellent year after year. See Wine Corner on page 29

articles.text: “The first time we left, we hurried to pack in one night because everybody was afraid that the Russians would eventually take Odesa, so we left very quickly. We basically narrowed things down to what would fit in two suitcases,” said Kononova. There was a moment when Tanya traveled back to her home in Odesa for a week in order to grab more belongings. She visited a friend at the city center when a rocket struck a building close by. Speaking through a translator, Kononova details the emotions she experienced: “When we were leaving for Moldova, I didn’t feel that much. But we had to come back to Odesa for a week and that’s where it really hit me… I went shopping with a friend and when we were in a store, we were notified to go to a shelter because they detected a missile. We laughed and didn’t go anywhere, but then we heard an explosion which felt like it was right next to us. There were four more explosions, and it was one of the days they bombed one of the many residential areas in Odesa. I couldn’t sleep that night, and kept moving my bed away from the window. That’s when we understood that we needed to leave,” she explained. Kononova’s family and friends have been widespread, while some are still residing in Odesa. Her best friend is now living in London, while other friends have scattered around Europe and some family still lives in Moldova. Tanya and her mother moved into her uncles’ home in Piedmont and have since taken up residence at a separate home in town. “Some people moved entire families; some moved just their kids… I’m still in touch with all of my friends; one of my friends was able to fly into Bulgaria to visit me,” said Kononova. When entering the States last year, it marked the first time Kononova swung a racket since departing her country in February 2022. She began playing tennis when she was six years old and continued at the club level through her teenage years. Playing for Piedmont High helps provide an outlet for Tanya in a foreign place so far from home. “It’s completely different from the places I was at before. But, I think it’s a nice place to stay and it feels like you’re safe here. The people are quite happy to see you… Playing on the team definitely makes me feel like someone stands for me. It feels like you’re not alone and it’s less stressful. It’s more fun,” said Kononova. Kononova then burst onto the scene in the fall of 2022 as Piedmont’s incumbent No. 1 singles starter, showing her fierce style and fiery passion on the courts on Tanya Kononova is a former WACC Champion and competed at No. 1 singles for two years. articles.text: “It took three months to rehab from my hip fracture. After my hip was healed, I assumed training would resume as normal. But throughout preparing for my last two meets, I learned I can still be prone to strains and injury in that region. Even though I am recovered, I still need to train in a way that can keep my hips healthy and working,” Haddawy said. Haddawy first started competing as a high school sophomore and lifted in the 132 pound division in last year’s National Championship. Adding 16 pounds to his frame meant Layth didn’t have to sacrifice strength to deal with the rigors of a challenging weight-cut, which can prevent lifters, along with wrestlers and professional fighters, from competing at full strength. “Being able to compete without having to do as near drastic of a water cut helped a lot as I had noticeable less fatigue as well as being able to replenish energy far easier,” Haddawy said. His gym, Get Bent Training in Oakland, also won the team category for the National Championship in competition with two other gyms. “It means a lot to me to be able to compete and represent my gym and coaches alongside the people that I train with every day. The team championship is a great reward for my coaches who put in a lot of work with little recognition,” Haddawy said. Layth now plans the next step of his powerlifting career in joining Powerlifting America, which will give him a better chance at landing a position on Team USA. “My plan for the future is to leave the current federation I compete in, USPA, and switch to Powerlifting America. A win at Powerlifting America would put me on Team USA and give me the opportunity to compete internationally,” Haddawy said. Layth Haddawy and his team, Get Bent Training.
articles.title: Layth Haddawy

pages.text: 32 32 Wednesday, July 23, 2025 Jeremy Bowers Continued from page 1 at Sam Jose State and a masters degree in Criminology, Law and Science at UC Irvine. “I remember when Jeremy joined our department,” said former Piedmont Mayor Teddy King. Speaking to Bowers, she said, “You were part of a revolution in policing here along with your predecessor, the great Rikki Goede. The two of you… have transformed this department into one that is responsive, forward-looking, community oriented, and progressive in all the best ways…You make me proud as a Piedmonter, and as an Alameda county resident. I’ve loved hanging out with you and your beautiful family for all these many years. I hope we get to stay friends for a long, long time to come.” Bowers joined the Piedmont Police Department as a captain in September 2014 and was appointed chief two years later when Goede retired. As Chief, Bowers led the Piedmont Police Department in significant investments in technology as a force multiplier, establishing Piedmont’s public safety camera system. He also oversaw expansion of dispatch staffing for the first time since 1978 and the construction of the new 911 Dispatch Center, which is expected to be complete this fall. “When we heard Chief Bowers was retiring, we were immediately moved to express our gratitude and appreciation,” said Jennifer Alderman, representing the Jewish Community of Piedmont. Alderman and others presented Bowers with a specially commissioned piece of art by Bay Area artist Nina Bonos, depicting a hamsa – a traditional Jewish symbol for good fortune, safety and protection for the journey ahead. “I’ve spent many times with Jeremy and previous [City] Administrators going through issues, and it’s his insightfulness, his willingness to make decisions, his open-mindedness that always struck me. Those are criteria of leadership,” said former Police Chief Jeremy Bowers (left) receives a piece of art from representatives of Piedmont’s Jewish community. Piedmont mayor Bob McBain. In terms of accolades, Bowers was the recipient of the Movers of Mountains Award in Public Safety and Community Bridge Building from the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Association of Santa Clara Valley. Earlier this year, Bowers was honored by the San Francisco District Attorney’s office with the Hometown Hero Award for his efforts in community engagement and his work partnering with residents and local schools to address gun violence. “I’ll be honest with you,” said Chief Bowers. “Every day I ask myself if I am doing enough? Every day I have doubts if I’m doing enough for my men and women, or the community, or my peers in the city. I think, quite frankly, that’s been my secret to success. I never feel like I’ve arrived – I always feel like there’s more to give. “Up to my last day here, and probably after my last day here, I’ll be questioning if I did enough – because I care.” Bowers closed with thanks to his wife Tricia and children Jordan, Andre and Anjali. Bowers also expressed confidence in Piedmont’s police staff and incoming leadership with the City’s next police chief, Frederick Shavies. The packed City Council chambers delivered Bowers a heartfelt standing ovation at the end of his speech. As a part of the proclamation, Mayor Betsy Andersen declared July 7, 2025 as “Jeremy Bowers Day.” “Chief Bowers, you’ve done enough,” assured Mayor Andersen. “You’ve arrived.” Where in the World Are We? articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a youth-led Venturing unit of Piedmont Scouts, served thousands of hotcakes for Fourth of July parade goers on Friday morning, July 4. The crew’s Pancake Breakfast sold around 360 breakfast plates and fueled the fun of Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade. More than full tummies and scrumptious fixings went into the event, it required hard work. PCSC members, led by Advisor Ken Li, arrived at the Veterans Hall at 6:30 a.m. to prepare for the big feast. At that hour many parade goers were blissfully sleeping through silenced workday alarms. The work involving 10 PCSC crew members and five adults started the afternoon of the July 3. That Thursday, the group of 15 worked six hours setting up the kitchen and the hall for the following day. They washed and cut up the fruit, set up the tables with chairs, tablecloths and decorations, and prepped all the utensils. PCSC took over the Pancake Breakfast in 2016 from the Recreation Department, and has done it every year since, except in 2020 due to Covid. In 2021 PCSC persevered to host the event as a Waldo Avenue block party. For the crew of around 130 members, events can sometimes be an all-hands on deck inviting the middle school Piedmont Service Club and other volunteers. “People who have done it before, especially the ones that are really involved in planning and running it, they’ll say ‘Oh! The pancake breakfast is one of my favorite things to do’,” said Li. This year’s event threw some curveballs at the volunteer crew. The normal breakfast rush at 9:00 a.m. didn’t happen. When the clock hit 9:30 a.m., Crew Adviser Li got a little worried. But crew members adapted by sending out missionaries, of sort, to recruit customers. Li told his crew, “Hey, we have all these volunteers waiting to serve. Let’s send a bunch of them out with signs.” The teens put down their serving spoons, made some signs, and sent out four crew members to get the attention of potential customers outside. pages.text: Volume 27, No. 38 Piedmont, California July 9, 2025 91¢ Piedmont Post Piedmont Post A Community Newspaper Serving the Citizens of Piedmont Pancake Breakfast draws big crowd on the Fourth By Jay Russell Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a youth-led Venturing unit of Piedmont Scouts, served thousands of hotcakes for Fourth of July parade goers on Friday morning, July 4. The crew’s Pancake Breakfast sold around 360 breakfast plates and fueled the fun of Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade. More than full tummies and scrumptious fixings went into the event, it required hard work. PCSC members, led by Advisor Ken Li, arrived at the Veterans Hall at 6:30 a.m. to prepare for the big feast. At that hour many parade goers were blissfully sleeping through silenced workday alarms. The work involving 10 PCSC crew members and five adults started the afternoon of the July 3. That Thursday, the group of 15 worked six hours setting up the kitchen and the hall for the following day. They washed and cut up the fruit, set up the tables with chairs, tablecloths and decorations, and prepped all the utensils. PCSC took over the Pancake Breakfast in 2016 from the Recreation Department, and has done it every year since, except in 2020 due to Covid. In 2021 PCSC persevered to host the event as a Waldo Avenue block party. For the crew of around 130 members, events can sometimes be an all-hands on deck inviting the middle school Piedmont Service Club and other volunteers. “People who have done it before, especially the ones that are really involved in planning and running it, they’ll say ‘Oh! The pancake breakfast is one of my favorite things to do’,” said Li. This year’s event threw some curveballs at the volunteer crew. The normal breakfast rush at 9:00 a.m. didn’t happen. When the clock hit 9:30 a.m., Crew Adviser Li got a little worried. But crew members adapted by sending out missionaries, of sort, to recruit customers. Li told his crew, “Hey, we have all these volunteers waiting to serve. Let’s send a bunch of them out with signs.” The teens put down their serving spoons, made some signs, and sent out four crew members to get the attention of potential customers outside. That tactic worked, as they eventually sold 360 plates to paying customers, netting them around $4,000. articles.text: Editor: As a 33 year-long Piedmont resident in Sidney and Irene Dearing’s neighborhood, I vehemently oppose the design and installation of this permanent public memorial for them. Why was the neighborhood never consulted about it? I do applaud honoring the Dearings, maybe in an effort to atone for the misdeeds of Piedmonters of the past, however, this work of art is no way in harmony with the character of our neighborhood, or this beautiful city we live in. The proposed design would do well in modern cities such as Brasilia or Dubai, but clearly not here. I doubt the Dearings would enjoy looking at it, defacing this little gem of a park, and upsetting its magnificent redwoods.. Because this creative artist has cleverly designed these statement pieces with enclosed benches, trash will accumulate within the sculptures. In addition, the walls made with wood, with attract vandalism, such as graffiti. The structures will require quite a bit of maintenance, and painting over the years. A beautiful bronze plaque, telling the story, would be infinitely more appropriate. Neighborly Yours, Dr. Jean-Pierre L. articles.text: New batting cages have been finished at Coaches Field after months of work by Piedmont’s Public Works Department, partnered with Piedmont Scout Sammy Ragones for his Eagle Scout Project. The new cages replace the original ones with new turf, nets, and space for a second batter. Ragones chose the batting cages as the site for his Eagle project to help benefit the Piedmont Baseball-Softball Foundation (PBSF), with whom he has played baseball for 10 years. The project builds on the legacy of Troop 15, where Eagle Scout Alexander Menke built the original batting cage for his Eagle project in 2006. Ragones first approached the City with his proposed project in 2023. After receiving the endorsement of both the Park and Recreation Commissions, the City Council allocated $50,000 in last year’s budget for the cage replacement. The Piedmont Baseball-Softball Foundation (PBSF) raised $11,000 in installation of new batting cages. community donations to supplement the project. articles.text: Zeppelin is a sweet, scruffy teddy bear of a dog, who is about 2.5 years old and 56 lovable pounds (working on that weight loss journey!). This guy has a playful side and is good at making dog friends in playgroups and in his foster home. He can be shy on first meetings, but he quickly warms up when people are patient and can offer tasty treats. Zeppelin knows sit, down, and shake, and absolutely loves couch cuddles. He’s house trained, able to hang out at home when his foster is away, and even charming enough to win over his foster’s bossy resident dog with his easygoing nature. articles.text: The City of Piedmont released a video update for the pool project in its Community Pool Project Newsletter on July 3. The video comes in lieu of the promised official project update in City Council chambers, which has been pushed back to August. The pool’s project budget remains at $34.9 million, after being funded by $25.1 million in bonds and interest from measure UU. The last pool update, at the March 3 City Council meeting, reported June 2 as the expected completion date for pool construction. The video, uploaded to the City’s youtube channel, introduces project executive Joshua Kaiser, taking over after the untimely passing of George Sanen. The video can be found at https:// youtu.be/EzfLfUnWneA?si=723pcv-NDHBMFTHN. Longtime Piedmont resident Don Chandler spoke about the pool project at the City Council meeting on Monday July 7 – the meeting for which the City had previously promised an official update. “I’m very disappointed that there’s no update at this meeting on the pool progress,” said Chandler, a respected commercial architect with projects around the world. “I saw a video on the City website generally praising the project with very little information regarding the latest update.” for the pools to be filled with water in August. This would allow the pool to begin system testing, also known as “commissioning,” which will take a minimum of six weeks.
