articles.text: Let’s be real: If I’m starving and exhausted on a Wednesday night, I will 100% grab that frozen burrito out of the freezer and call it dinner. But would I call it good? Not exactly. Now imagine a different kind of meal. One where you take your time browsing the local farmers market, choosing tomatoes that feel just right, chatting with the sourdough guy — maybe even planning your menu based on what looks and smells the freshest. You get home, put on music, chop, stir, simmer. The scent fills your kitchen, and when you sit down to eat, it’s not just a meal — it’s an experience. That’s slow food. And it’s not just about what you eat; it’s about how you make it. Here’s the thing: Creativity works the same way. In the age of AI, we’re all standing in the metaphorical freezer aisle. You want a poem? A song? A logo? A painting? A marketing campaign? AI can crank it out in seconds. And just like that frozen burrito, it might do the job. But if we rely only on the fast, easy version, we lose something essential: the process. Creativity isn’t just about the final product — it’s about what happens in your brain (and your heart) when you take the long way. When you doodle without a plan. When you write a story, then rewrite it, then throw it away and start over. When you try to paint the sunset and realize halfway through that it looks more like a lopsided pumpkin — but keep going anyway. Just like slow food, slow creativity feeds us in a different way. It keeps the curious, nonlinear, playful parts of our minds alive. It teaches us patience and perseverance. It helps us make meaning — not just output. AI is here to stay, and it’s a powerful tool. But if we only use it as a shortcut, we risk turning the most human parts of ourselves into frozen meals. Efficient? Yes. Predictable? Sure. But kind of bland — and definitely not inspiring. So let’s start a movement. Call it From Scratch. Call it Slow Made. Call it Brain to Page. Call it whatever you want. But the next time you sit down to make something, pause for a moment. Give yourself permission to linger. To explore. To savor the process. Because that’s where the flavor is. Nina Meehan is a Speaker, Consultant and Workshop Leader with a specialization in the 3Cs: Creativity, Communication and Connection. https://ninameehan. com/
articles.title: Slow Creativity in the Age of AI

Throughout the summer the Post prints a sampling of letters written by kids attending Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s residential camp at Lake Vera outside Nevada City in the Sierra foothills. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. A new session opens like a storybook, pages fluttering in the warm wind. Counselors from across the globe greet their campers not just with words, but with a quiet understanding… We’re about to create something extraordinary. And oh, the story we’re writing. A story where cabin mascots (is that a… dog-deer?) come to life, skeletons duel under the treetop canopy, and mythical creatures whisper clues to secret missions. Nerf darts fly like comets from atop the Giant Swing, and campers cackle as they rescue their counselor from kidnap, making a daring escape. Whimsy isn’t just present – it leads the way. But amidst the thrill, a quieter magic revealed itself. Campers wrapped up like a bow in an aerial silk, testing gravity and grit. Another sinks their teeth into a Chaindle, an innovative creation See Postcards from Camp on page 9 Oak campers show off their newly acquired aerial prowess. Two Camp Augusta staff as Windborn, the foe campers face in our Tuesday EP: ‘Stormforged.’ Campers watch the fog rise as they combine special ingredients with liquid nitrogen to make ice cream. During an EP station, campers learn how to saw through a wooden plank.

Around the craft shack table, laughter leaves campers in stitches and campers leave stitches in embroidery hoops. A group stirs ice liquid nitrogen, watching fog curl up like a potion… Ice Cream will be the product. Session 3 has a reminder for us: joy wears many faces. Sometimes it’s wild-eyed and sprinting across the field. Sometimes it’s gentle, like a new note played on an unfamiliar instrument. And sometimes, joy shows up in surprise - in the unexpected wakeup, the intimate nighttime embers, the moment where normalcy disappears and the extraordinary takes over. Li said many people at the breakfast only see the steam coming off the pancakes and the delicious food, but there is so much more in motion. “This is a major fundraiser for community service that’s done by youth, not just done by youth, but planned as well. There’s all this kind of youth empowerment [happening], to practice their leadership skills,” said Li. articles.text: Piedmont Fencing Club trains at the Piedmont Community Church. The Piedmont Fencing Team recently traveled to Milwaukee, Wisconsin for the 2025 National Championships hosted by USA Fencing. Summer Nationals are considered as a marquee event for youth fencers, with 6,000 competitors from across the country. Representing Piedmont was rising PHS freshman Maya Dvoiris and elementary student Ian Stock. Dvoiris competed in the Cadet Women’s Foil and Youth 14 Women’s Foil categories, while Stock was in the Youth 10 Men’s Foil event. Dvoiris finished 176th of 262 athletes in the Cadet Women’s Foil and 217th of 299 in the Youth 14 Women’s Foil. She reached the Tableau knockout stages in both events. In the Cadet Women’s Foil pool play, Dvoiris opened with a 5-3 win over Olivia Chang of Golubitsky Fencing in Orange County and followed up with a 5-3 victory over Mia Bertolini of Marx Fencing in Massachusetts. She followed with four losses, but had close 5-3 defeats to Reese Samala of Cleveland Fencing Academy and Annika Krahe of Brooklyn Bridge Fencing Club. Maya moved onto the tableau stage with the 174th seed and faced No. 81 Haley Pedersen of United Fencing Academy, losing 15-9. In the Y-14 Women’s Foil, Dvoiris won two of six matches. She dominated Kenzie Lin of Renaissance Fencing in Michigan 5-1 and followed with a 5-4 win over Pelu Akinbamiro of Fort Bend Fencing in Houston. She had a narrow 5-4 loss to Zoya Baulin of Manhattan Fencing Club. She faced No. 39 Maya Photos courtesy of Piedmont Fencing Team Orbe-Austin of Peter Westbrook Fencing in New York after receiving the No. 217 seed. Dvoiris played her opponent close to a 12-7 loss. Stock won one of his six matches, a victory that came in dominant fashion with a 5-1 drubbing of Ben Brown of Fioretto Fencing Academy in Florida. Among his losses was a narrow 5-4 battle against Lionel Fang of Mid Island Fencing Academy in New York. He received the No. 138 seed in the tableau and faced Zhengxuan Lin of Bay Area Fencing Club in Los Gatos, losing in a 10-6 contest. Piedmont Fencing Club next competes on August 30-31 in the Fortune ROC/RJCC/RYC in Ontario, California. For more information on Piedmont Fencing Club, visit www. piedmontfencingteam.com. Maya Dvoiris (right) competed in the Cadet Women’s Foil and Youth 14 Women’s Foil categories at the National Fencing Championships in Milwaukee.

articles.text: Coach Jordan Seiden gathers the football team at the Lake Tahoe Football Camp. Piedmont High’s football team recently traveled to South Lake Tahoe for the Lake Tahoe Football Camp June 16-19 at Lake Tahoe Community College. The response was strong with 39 players from varsity and junior varsity rosters. Piedmont competed with 15 other schools in 7-on-7, 11-on-11, and in an offensive line vs. defensive line event called “Trench Wars.” “It was great for the kids to get a week together,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “We were the smallest team, but the boys really went up there and competed. We grew a lot and saw areas that we need to work on. We had our ups and downs, and we expected that. It’s early in the summer, so we only have so many plays installed.” Head track coach Pouyan Assadi, a varsity assistant, also made the trip. “The 72 hours we were in Tahoe, I genuinely believe was 4-6 weeks of practice crammed into one,” Assadi said. “There were 16 individual teams that, including teams from Wyoming, Idaho, and Nevada. This is the place you want to go if your team wants to get better.” The camp gave coach Seiden to take a look at his roster ahead of 2025 season, when the Highlanders will undergo vast changes. They lost a total of 16 seniors from last year’s WACC Mission Division title-winning team. The only returning fulltime two-way starter is offensive and defensive lineman Adrian Kondakov. “One of the biggest things about the offensive line is continuity. That group has to work together and they did well. Adrian is our leader and just goes out there and gets it done. He’s like a bear pushing his cubs to where they need to go. He’s really stepped up all summer. We’re going to have four new starters, and Adrian is the only player back who was a full-time starter,” Seiden said. The camp offered sophomore Jimmy Lagios, the younger brother of three-year starting quarterback Markos Lagios, and opportunity to show his skills. Returning to potentially making an impact to their offense is Xavier Henderson and Rehan Mumtaz. Piedmont earned five AllCamp honors, including Lagios, Kondakov, and offensive and defensive lineman Chase Knapp in the varsity level, and quarterback Jonah Cha-Foster and tight end and linebacker Mason Gray in the junior varsity level. “Jimmy did really well; he was great. Guys are going to get a lot of reps, so we need to make sure everyone can handle that. We came back healthy and will get Photos by JC Curran back to work this week,” Seiden said. The Highlanders will continue with their own training camp through the summer until the start of padded practice in mid-August. “These are the dog days of the summer. It’s grinding, paying attention to detail, and spending a lot of time in the weight room. We need to get our bodies ready to go,” Seiden said. Jimmy Lagios, a sophomore and younger brother of last year’s quarterback, Markos Lagios, is looking to being the team’s new quarterback. Rehan Mumtaz a rising junior, makes a run in the Lake Tahoe football camp.
articles.title: PHS gets early start at Lake Tahoe Football Camp

Levi finished her junior year with a .462 batting average on 18 hits, five doubles, two triples, scored 10 runs, and 11 RBIs. PHS gets early start at Lake Tahoe Football Camp Coach Jordan Seiden gathers the football team at the Lake Tahoe Football Camp. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s football team recently traveled to South Lake Tahoe for the Lake Tahoe Football Camp June 16-19 at Lake Tahoe Community College. The response was strong with 39 players from varsity and junior varsity rosters. Piedmont competed with 15 other schools in 7-on-7, 11-on-11, and in an offensive line vs. defensive line event called “Trench Wars.” “It was great for the kids to get a week together,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “We were the smallest team, but the boys really went up there and competed. We grew a lot and saw areas that we need to work on. We had our ups and downs, and we expected that. It’s early in the summer, so we only have so many plays installed.” Head track coach Pouyan Assadi, a varsity assistant, also made the trip. “The 72 hours we were in Tahoe, I genuinely believe was 4-6 weeks of practice crammed into one,” Assadi said. “There were 16 individual teams that, including teams from Wyoming, Idaho, and Nevada. This is the place you want to go if your team wants to get better.” The camp gave coach Seiden to take a look at his roster ahead of 2025 season, when the Highlanders will undergo vast changes. They lost a total of 16 seniors from last year’s WACC Mission Division title-winning team. The only returning fulltime two-way starter is offensive and defensive lineman Adrian Kondakov. “One of the biggest things about the offensive line is continuity. That group has to work together and they did well. Adrian is our leader and just goes out there and gets it done. He’s like a bear pushing his cubs to where they need to go. He’s really stepped up all summer. We’re going to have four new starters, and Adrian is the only player back who was a full-time starter,” Seiden said. The camp offered sophomore Jimmy Lagios, the younger brother of three-year starting quarterback Markos Lagios, and opportunity to show his skills. Returning to potentially making an impact to their offense is Xavier Henderson and Rehan Mumtaz. Piedmont earned five AllCamp honors, including Lagios, Kondakov, and offensive and defensive lineman Chase Knapp in the varsity level, and quarterback Jonah Cha-Foster and tight end and linebacker Mason Gray in the junior varsity level. “Jimmy did really well; he was great. Guys are going to get a lot of reps, so we need to make sure everyone can handle that. We came back healthy and will get Photos by JC Curran back to work this week,” Seiden said. The Highlanders will continue with their own training camp through the summer until the start of padded practice in mid-August. “These are the dog days of the summer. It’s grinding, paying attention to detail, and spending a lot of time in the weight room. We need to get our bodies ready to go,” Seiden said. JOJO MURPHY Basketball Piedmont High Class of 2022 Seattle University Class of 2026 JoJo Murphy transferred to Seattle University’s basketball team after finishing his junior year at Chico State. At Chico Murphy won the California Collegiate Athletic Association Player of the Year award and was the Division 2 California Collegiate Athletic Association’s Men’s Basketball West Region Player of the Year. Murphy led the entire CCAA with an average of 20.5 points per game and a .395 3-point shooting percent. He scored 20 or more points 16 times, was a threetime CCAA Men’s Basketball Player of the Week winner and earned CCAA All-Tournament honors. He was named the CCAA’s Freshman of the Year in 2023 and was first-team All-CCAA, while earning an honorable mention for All-CCAA in 2024. Murphy was a top recruit for Seattle University in the transfer portal. He’s now set to play Division 1 basketball in the Western Athletic Conference with the Redhawks. He details his journey to Seattle and workout regimen ahead of his Division 1 debut. What is your workout program this summer? An old friend and current overseas hooper, Kyree Brown, was a key mentor prior to coming to Seattle. He’s a Berkeley High grad and Seattle U alum, and gave insight to his lifting tendencies and how to read the game as a veteran point guard. Shooting at Laney College and morning lifting sessions in Concord were key tune ups for live games at the San Francisco Pro-Am and various open runs at different colleges throughout the Bay. What are your fitness goals for the summer? Transferring from a Division 2 school to D1, the physicality and Photo courtesy of Chico State Athletics JoJo Murphy, PHS Class of 2022, embarks on his first season at Seattle University after transferring from Chico State. speed of the game will ramp up. Conditioning and dietary habits are vital for making the jump. How are you measuring your development? At Seattle, our everyday habits are tracked. From shooting workouts, to weight room progress and tracking wins within the team. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Prior to coming to Seattle, training in the Bay was spontaneous through different cities. Now, I’m in Seattle with our coaching staff. articles.text: The chamber music festival Music in the Vineyards kicks off its 31st season in Napa Valley on August 1. The series of live performances traditionally showcases distinguished chamber musicians as well emerging young talent during its four-week season, with concerts held at popular wineries and vineyards throughout the valley. This year’s featured artists include the Borromeo String Quartet, Pacifica Quartet and Ariel Quartet, as well as Pavone String Quartet, a group of undergraduate students at the world-renowned Shepherd School of Music at Rice University. The Pavone Quartet is winner of Music in the Vineyards’ 2025 Fellowship Quartet competition and will perform on August 11. Since the festival’s inception in 1995, wineries in Napa Valley continue to lend their space for MITV musicians to perform live, offering a uniquely Northern Californian festival experience. With complimentary wine tastings at each intermission and breathtaking views of the Napa Valley, this unique combination of wine country ambiance and great musicianship allows audiences to experience chamber music in small intimate settings. Music venues this year include Clos Pegase Winery, Frog’s Leap Winery, Hess Persson Estates, Domaine Carneros, Louis M. Martini Winery, Maxville Winery, Stag’s Leap Wine Cellars, Hudson Ranch, Ehlers Estate, Markham Vineyards, Hudson House at Beringer Vineyards, Spottswoode Estate, Silverado Vineyards, and Inglenook. For more information on Music in the Vineyards and to purchase tickets, visit www. musicinthevineyards.org. Borromeo String Quartet will perform at Music in the Vineyards this season.
articles.title: Music in the Vineyards concerts begin August 1

articles.text: Korsa Musical Theater, a Bay Area musical theater training company, concludes its 20th season with a production of Oklahoma! showing July 18 through 27 at the Pinole Valley High School Theater. Oklahoma! is the first musical written by Rodgers and Hammerstein, a theater-writing team of composer Richard Rodgers and lyricist-dramatist Oscar Hammerstein II. The 1943 musical is based on Lynn Riggs’s 1931 play Green Grow the Lilacs and follows the story of farmgirl Laurey and cowboy Curly’s budding romance, threatened by a brooding ranch-hand named Jud. The play ran for over five years on Broadway, a record that would not be bested until My Fair Lady’s initial run in 1956. Korsa Musical Theater’s production features a cast of 33 student performers age 13 through 20, led by a team of professional directors including award-winning Director Susannah Martin, Music Director David Möschler, and Choreographer Janet Collard. The production also includes a 30-piece live orchestra, with five student instrumentalists playing Robert Russell Bennet’s original score. The run consists of four 7 p.m. performances on July 18, 19, 25, and 26; and two 2:00 p.m. matinees on July 20 and 28. Tickets are available online at www.korsamt.org or at the door one hour before curtain. Ticket prices are $18–$40, with discounts for students, seniors, military, teachers, and groups. Pinole Valley High School Theater is located at 2900 Pinole Valley Road in Pinole. Photography by Jonah Pagenhart Evie Mitchell and Maddox Scardina in Korsa Musical Theater’s Oklahoma!
articles.title: Korsa Musical Theater presents Oklahoma! in Pinole July 18 - 27

articles.text: Cal Performances welcomes former artist-in-residence Angelique Kidjo and world-renowned cellist Yo-Yo Ma to UC Berkeley’s historic Greek Theatre in a special Labor Day weekend performance on Saturday, August 30. Kidjo is a four-time Grammy winner and has earned recognition over the years for projects like Yemandja, the artist’s first major foray into stage acting, and a reboot of the Talking Heads’ classic 1980 album Remain in Light, both part of the Cal Performances 2021–22 season. The Benin-born singer was also named one of Time magazine’s “100 Most Influential People of 2021” for her work as a performer, teacher, and cultural ambassador. Her latest recordings incorporate West African music, Afrobeat, Afro-pop, hip hop, and R&B. Ma has performed as a soloist with orchestras around the world. He has recorded more than 90 albums and received 18 Grammy Awards. In addition to recordings of the standard classical repertoire, he has recorded a wide variety of folk music such as American bluegrass music, traditional Chinese melodies, the tangos of Argentinian composer Astor Piazzolla, and Brazilian music, and remains one of the world’s most well-respected cellists. The Labor Day concert is Cellist Yo-Yo Ma with Angelique Kidjo part of Cal Performances’ Illuminations: “Exile & Sanctuary” programming for the 2025–26 season, a theme that aims to “connect seven unique performances to academic research” on the UC Berkeley campus, focusing on physical displacement, rupture of identity, and “a stripping away of the familiar that leaves an individual or community without a sense of belonging.” The performance connects centuries of interaction between African musical idioms and western music, highlighting exile and sanctuary as both a refuge and a creative space for artists. Ma and Kidjo use the Baroque sarabande dance form and its possible African antecedent, a dance to worship the Congolese spirit Zarabanda as a method to showcase the qualities that connect different cultures, genres, and musical traditions. “Every day there are moments when all of us can feel we are on the inside of something and also when we feel we are on the outside of something,” Ma said in a statement. “To be able to understand both at the same time and oscillate between the two gives us a larger perspective on the world.” “If your mind is open, and there is no fear, it’s easier to listen, and to question yourself,” Kidjo added. Tickets are likely to sell out fast. Tickets for all performances are available at calperformances. org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday–Friday, 12–5:30 p.m. and Saturday–Sunday, 1–5 p.m.
articles.title: Yo-Yo Ma comes to Greek Theatre on August 30

Yo-Yo Ma comes to Greek Theatre on August 30 By Allyson Aleksey Cal Performances welcomes former artist-in-residence Angelique Kidjo and world-renowned cellist Yo-Yo Ma to UC Berkeley’s historic Greek Theatre in a special Labor Day weekend performance on Saturday, August 30. Kidjo is a four-time Grammy winner and has earned recognition over the years for projects like Yemandja, the artist’s first major foray into stage acting, and a reboot of the Talking Heads’ classic 1980 album Remain in Light, both part of the Cal Performances 2021–22 season. The Benin-born singer was also named one of Time magazine’s “100 Most Influential People of 2021” for her work as a performer, teacher, and cultural ambassador. Her latest recordings incorporate West African music, Afrobeat, Afro-pop, hip hop, and R&B. Ma has performed as a soloist with orchestras around the world. He has recorded more than 90 albums and received 18 Grammy Awards. In addition to recordings of the standard classical repertoire, he has recorded a wide variety of folk music such as American bluegrass music, traditional Chinese melodies, the tangos of Argentinian composer Astor Piazzolla, and Brazilian music, and remains one of the world’s most well-respected cellists. The Labor Day concert is Photography by Jonah Pagenhart Evie Mitchell and Maddox Scardina in Korsa Musical Theater’s Oklahoma! A Tribute to Harry Warren Cellist Yo-Yo Ma with Angelique Kidjo part of Cal Performances’ Illuminations: “Exile & Sanctuary” programming for the 2025–26 season, a theme that aims to “connect seven unique performances to academic research” on the UC Berkeley campus, focusing on physical displacement, rupture of identity, and “a stripping away of the familiar that leaves an individual or community without a sense of belonging.” The performance connects centuries of interaction between African musical idioms and western music, highlighting exile and sanctuary as both a refuge and a creative space for artists. Ma and Kidjo use the Baroque sarabande dance form and its possible African antecedent, a dance to worship the Congolese spirit Zarabanda as a method to showcase the qualities that connect differSalvatore Antonio Guaragna (1893-1981) Featuring the In the Tradition Piano Trio ent cultures, genres, and musical traditions. “Every day there are moments when all of us can feel we are on the inside of something and also when we feel we are on the outside of something,” Ma said in a statement. “To be able to understand both at the same time and oscillate between the two gives us a larger perspective on the world.” “If your mind is open, and there is no fear, it’s easier to listen, and to question yourself,” Kidjo added. articles.text: Visit the San Francisco Botanical Garden in Golden Gate Park this Saturday, July 12, for a free expert-led discussion on growing and maintaining succulents. Succulents can be found within each continent except Antarctica and particularly thrive in California’s varied climates. They are favored by gardeners for their ability to store water in their leaves, allowing for less frequent watering and maintenance. These characteristics, resilient properties and slow growth make succulent species a great plant for first time plant owners and novice gardeners who want to learn more about plants. Succulent plants also come in a wide variety of shapes, colors, and sizes, making them a popular addition in arid-climate gardens. UC Master Gardener Janice Moody and San Francisco Succulent Society member Jeff Harter will lead a free discussion on these versatile plants and offer tips for growing and maintaining them in your containers or landscape. Moody became a UC Master Gardener in 2010 and then started Seascapes Succulent Nursery and Garden Design in 2016, located in Half Moon Bay. Harter has grown his own garden in 800 square feet of San Francisco soil for over a decade, starting in 2012 when he replaced his lawn with terraces and mulch. His fascination with succulent and bromeliad species has led him to fill his garden with diverse succulents such as gasteria, haworthia, crassula, and aloe. RSVP is required for this event. The discussion takes place in San Francisco Botanical Garden’s plant shop at 11 a.m. Admission to the Garden is free for San Francisco residents, veterans, Museums for All/EBT participants, and Gardens members. articles.text: Oakland Museum of California docent Avril Angevine leads a gallery tour of female artists this Saturday, July 12. The tour is free for OMCA members. Guests will explore the backgrounds of some of California’s best but least known women artists, including Sonia Getchoff, Viola Frey, Carmen Lomas Garza, Hung Liu, Margaret Peterson, and Ann Weber. The museum highlights major female and female-identifying artists from California and in 2022 highlighted five lesser known women artists in its Gallery of California Art, featuring Liu, Dorothea Lange and new artwork by Rosie Lee Tompkins. The Oakland Museum of California also exhibited artwork by international artist and activist Angela Davis, who was the feature of its special exhibition Angela Davis–Seize the Time in 2023. Angevine is a lifelong art aficionado with a particular interest in modern, contemporary, and California art, who speaks on art subjects at various locations in the Bay Area, including the OLLI programs at Santa Clara University, Dominican College, San Francisco State, and the Fromm Institute. Angevine is also a museum guide at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) and the Sonoma Valley Museum of Art. The tour begins at 12 p.m. on Saturday. Tour spots are limited, a sign-up sheet will be available at the Ticketing Desk when checking in on July 12. For more information, visit https://museumca.org/event/ member-tours-women-artists-ofthe-omca-gallery-of-californiaart/. articles.title: Oakland Museum exhibit of female artists

articles.text: Materialized Thoughts, an art exhibit coming to the Piedmont Center for the Arts, brings together Nepali artists living in the USA as first-generation immigrants. The body of works displayed explores the paradoxes of diasporic life—particularly the process of building identity amid pressures to conform to dominant cultures and homogeneous identities. Drawing inspiration from everyday life and personal experiences, this exhibition reflects the tension between strong attachment to the culture left behind and the process of assimilating into a new society. These artworks investigate the nuanced realities of diasporic life – living in between cultures, constantly navigating the differences and similarities between homeland and host land, and the ongoing process of carving out a new identity. This exhibition is the culmination of the research on Nepali Diaspora Artists based in the Bay Area and beyond, conducted by Swosti Rajbhandari Kayastha as a Fulbright Visiting Scholar, 2024- 25, with the Asian Art Museum, San Francisco. The research was conducted over seven months in 2024-2025. This exhibition is the first of its kind, featuring artworks selectively by Diaspora Nepali Artists, showcasing diverse cultural narratives, challenging dominant art world narratives, and fostering dialogue about identity, displacement, and belonging. This exhibition has provided a platform for artists to express their unique experiences and perspectives, often highlighting the complexities of navigating multiple cultures and identities, seeking to play a crucial role in cultural preservation, documentation of history, and promoting cross-cultural understanding. Through such exhibitions by diaspora artists, you can help gain a deeper understanding of cultural identity, witness artistic innovation, and engage with important social issues. They also foster empathy and understanding of shared human experiences, challenges, and triumphs, providing an opportunity to celebrate the diversity of artistic talent and contribute to a more inclusive art world. Supporting diaspora artists can contribute to a more inclusive and globally oriented art world, enriching the cultural landscape and contribute to a broader understanding of the diaspora’s impact on contemporary culture and society.
articles.title: Nepali art exhibit at Piedmont Center for the Arts

articles.text: World-renowned classical guitarist Derek Gripper from South Africa is set to play at the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) on July 12. After quickly selling out of tickets for his 8:00 p.m., a 5:30p.m. show was added. Tickets are selling fast, with the classically-trained musician on the verge of becoming PCA’s first ever double-sold-out show. Gripper is a guitarist and composer renowned for his unique ability to transcribe and perform complex West African kora music on the classical guitar. His work bridges the gap between different musical traditions and has garnered international recognition for its innovation and virtuosity. Gripper gained widespread attention from his ability to translate arrangements from the African kora, a 21-string harp, featured on his 2012 album One Night on Earth, a recording so unexpected that celebrated guitarist John Williams said, “It seemed absolutely impossible until I heard Derek Gripper do it.” Gripper said his project was about creating previously unseen connection between African oral traditions and Western classical music, bridging the gap between different ways of listening and understanding. Along the way, Gripper has performed with legendary musicians like John Williams and Toumani Diabaté’s Symmetric Orchestra, sharing stages from Carnegie Hall to Shakespeare’s Globe. The journey from kora to guitar came full circle last year, when Gripper partnered with kora legend Ballaké Sissoko on a joint tour and album. Though the two musicians did not share a language, they were able to play music together with beautiful improvisation. No two shows on that tour were alike, but their 2024 album Ballaké Sissoko & Derek Gripper remains for music lovers to enjoy. “It was a very natural project – we just had to sit together,” explained Gripper. “…It’s a project that was done very much in the moment. We don’t talk about music much at all because we don’t share a language.” Tickets are available at concertsinamerica.com while supplies last. famous for having one rehearsal and one performance. But Mr. Patterson (sometimes spelled Paterson) operated a company that was completely integrated racially. As for food, there was everything your taste buds could imagine. He was a very lively guy. He was a virtuoso playing the banjo, organized orchestras, and wrote and produced countless shows. He said that Piedmont was too quiet in the summer. Something needed to be done. That’s why he organized the Fourth of July parade. Let’s take a look at the results. Some people might say that Piedmont is a superb city. articles.text: Cary Grant in the iconic scene from Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest I would suggest that each of Alfred Hitchcock’s films, to include North By Northwest, is a master class in taut, well-plotted, compelling storytelling and often mirror the noir genre of the 1940s (e.g. Double Indemnity, The Big Sleep). Vertigo, Rear Window and, of course, the breathtaking Psycho are only a few examples of this auteur’s years of filmmaking. NXNW opens with Roger Thornhill (Cary Grant) having lunch with business associates in a white tablecloth New York restaurant. He is unexpectedly paged, excuses himself, and finds that there are two men waiting for him who refer to him as a Mr. Kaplan. Trying to explain that his name is Thornhill not Kaplan, he is nevertheless roughly escorted from the restaurant and shoved into a waiting car. Ignoring his protests, he is driven to a mansion where he is taken inside and told to wait in the library. Finally a man enters, greets him as Kaplan and introduces himself as Phillip Vandamm (James Mason) who ignores all of Thornhill’s attempts to convince him that they have the wrong man. And so begins what proves to be a complex narrative involving a murder at the United Nations, an escape by Roger, and a long train ride where he meets an attractive woman, Eve Kendall (Eva Marie Saint), who surprisingly agrees to help Roger. The story unfolds and unexpectedly cuts to Mt. Rushmore, and involves not only Eve, but a government agent referred to only as the Professor (Leo G. Carroll). The tone and content of North the film’s publicity poster that shows Cary Grant running across a rural plowed field dressed in his signature gray suit, white shirt, tie. Just behind him is a crop-duster, taking aim, clearly intending to kill him. The look on Grant’s face conveys the improbable and frightening predicament in which he finds himself. Eventually, the mystery is revealed and Roger and Eve are back on that now familiar train sharing a sleeping car. Their denouement moments together were already established by an earlier bevy of double entendres which only hinted at their mutual attraction. But then hinting is all that the writers and Hitchcock had to work with in the 40s and 50s. We’re no longer in Kansas, Toto. North By Northwest. Directed by Alfred Hitchcock. Starring Cary Grant, Eva Marie Saint, James Mason. 2 hrs., 16 min. Released in 1959. Streaming on Tubi/ Fandango/ Prime/apple tv.

Vertigo, Rear Window and, of course, the breathtaking Psycho are only a few examples of this auteur’s years of filmmaking. NXNW opens with Roger Thornhill (Cary Grant) having lunch with business associates in a white tablecloth New York restaurant. He is unexpectedly paged, excuses himself, and finds that there are two men waiting for him who refer to him as a Mr. Kaplan. Trying to explain that his name is Thornhill not Kaplan, he is nevertheless roughly escorted from the restaurant and shoved into a waiting car. Ignoring his protests, he is driven to a mansion where he is taken inside and told to wait in the library. Finally a man enters, greets him as Kaplan and introduces himself as Phillip Vandamm (James Mason) who ignores all of Thornhill’s attempts to convince him that they have the wrong man. And so begins what proves to be a complex narrative involving a murder at the United Nations, an escape by Roger, and a long train ride where he meets an attractive woman, Eve Kendall (Eva Marie Saint), who surprisingly agrees to help Roger. The story unfolds and unexpectedly cuts to Mt. Rushmore, and involves not only Eve, but a government agent referred to only as the Professor (Leo G. Carroll). The tone and content of North By Northwest is best captured by the film’s publicity poster that shows Cary Grant running across a rural plowed field dressed in his signature gray suit, white shirt, tie. Just behind him is a crop-duster, taking aim, clearly intending to kill him. The look on Grant’s face conveys the improbable and frightening predicament in which he finds himself. Eventually, the mystery is revealed and Roger and Eve are back on that now familiar train sharing a sleeping car. Their denouement moments together were already established by an earlier bevy of double entendres which only hinted at their mutual attraction. But then hinting is all that the writers and Hitchcock had to work with in the 40s and 50s. We’re no longer in Kansas, Toto. North By Northwest. Directed by Alfred Hitchcock. articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Only Yesterday Only Yesterday was written and directed by Isao Takahata who cofounded the remarkable Studio Ghibli with Hayao Miyazaki. When released in Japan in 1991, it was a box office sensation, yet, surprisingly, failed to reach the U.S. until 2016. If the works of Miyazaki and Takahata have captured the imaginations of your youngsters, then Only Yesterday is a must see. It’s extraordinary, an example, once again, of the stunning artistry and story telling that has become the brand of Ghibli. The film’s narrative touches on adult themes while focusing on a hybrid protagonist: a 27-year-old woman and a 10-year-old girl. The story begins with Taeko Okajima (Daisey Ridley), a kind of Japanese everywoman, an office worker and life-long resident of Tokyo. She departs by train for a vacation trip in the country to visit relatives, intending to help with the seasonal harvest of safflowers. On her journey, while travelling through the night on a sleeper car, headed for the rural town of Yamagata, she begins to reminisce about her childhood: a strict father, puberty, bad grades, first crushes, insecurities, the mockery of mean girls, all told from the point-of- view of a 10-year-old who is negotiating the 5th grade. These images, beautifully animated, lyrical, and are blended seamlessly with the reactions of the older, increasingly reflective Taeko. At one point she says, “I didn’t expect to bring my fifth-grade self along for the trip.” She is met at the Yamagata train station by a young man, Toshio (Dev Patel), a friend of the family, with whom she strikes up a friendship and it’s with him that she begins to share her very personal and conflicted memories. During her stay in this bucolic setting, walking the fields of flowers, enveloped by the soft hillsides, she grows ever more wistful about her past. She reflects on her dreams from childhood, her hopes and dreams, some splashed, and wonders if the life she is living in Tokyo is truly one she wishes to continue. And there is, of course, her growing fondness for Toshio. Only Yesterday is a work of art, wonderfully told, absent intensely imagined, suspend-your-disbelief characters. Instead, the fable moves gently, at times sadly, from the present to the past and back with calm tenderness. Only Yesterday. Written and directed by Isao Takahata. Animé by Studio Ghibli. With voices of Daisy Ridley, Dev Patel and Ashley Eckstein. 1 hr. 58 min. Rated PG. Released in 2019. Streaming on MAX/Roku/apple tv/Prime/ Fandango/Hulu

articles.text: Captain America: The First Avenger is, at least initially, set in New York City. The year is 1942. Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) and his best friend, Sgt. Bucky Barnes (Sebastian Stan), are downtown attending a future technology exhibition, and happen to pass a military recruitment station. War is in the air, Bucky is about to ship out for Europe, and countless men are enlisting, with the exception of Steve who suffers from asthma, and weighs in at some 98 pounds. It’s not for trying that he’s not in uniform, and to his chagrin he’s been rejected multiple times. As it happens, also attending the exhibition is Dr. Abraham Erskine (Stanley Rucci), a brilliant inventor and genetic scientist, working on a special “super soldier” experiment for the Strategic Scientific Reserve. The project is under the command of Col. Chester Phillips (Tommy Lee Jones). Dr. Erskine happens to overhear a conversation of regret between Bucky and Steve, and looking at the scrawny Steve decides he might be perfect for his special serum and what are referred to as “vita rays.” Pulling a few strings with Col. Phillips, the scientist manages to get Steve into the program. Ever hopeful, willing to try anything to enlist, he agrees. Stretched out on a table, machinery begins to hum and spark, the serum/vita rays are administered, and to his Chris Evans in Captain America: The First Avenger surprise, Steve emerges much taller, more muscular, with an ability to now run at a tremendous speed. In other words, he has been indeed transformed into a super soldier. Amazing at the result, the army decides to dress him in stars and striped tights, hood, provide him with a shield and send him cross-country to advertise for war bonds using the name Captain America. The best part of Captain America: The first Avenger is the transformation of weakling Steve Rogers into his alter ego: he’s now a square-jawed, humble, even shy superhero who soon is sent out to fight for truth, justice, and the American way. Soon he confronts his uber-nemesis and Nazi provocateur, the villainous, megalomaniac Red Skull (Hugo Weaving) and his army of thugs called Hydra, all ensconced in Red Skull’s alpine forest retreat where he is conducting his own experiment: a blue-cube that will enable him to take over the world. Of course, the story – a big, bold, razzle-dazzle adventure – has plenty of action, chase scenes, shootouts, a submarine, aircraft, and even a fight on top of a Nazi blimp, all leading to a spectacular showdown between Captain America and Red Skull. And there’s even a touch of romance between MI 16 Brit spy, Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell), who has been assigned to the Strategic Reserve. Kids will love this origin film, one that will soon be followed by The Avengers, introducing lots of superheroes. Stay tuned. Captain America: The First Avenger, Directed by Joe Johnson. Starring Chris Evans, Hayley Atwell, Hugo Weaving. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG. Released in 2011. Streaming on Fandango/ Prime/Disney+/apple tv.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group met at the Exedra on Wednesday, July 2, to enjoy an early summer walk together on a lovely morning. With the Fourth of July just two days away, the group was already getting into the spirit. There was an excellent holiday-week turnout of 42 walkers — and four K-9 best friends. The group welcomed Charlie, along with Lynn and Dave Holzman, who brought Pepper and Fiona for their first walk with the group. Before the usual 10:30 a.m. start, Peggy Shultz, a physical therapist, led a helpful refresher on fall prevention and safe walking exercises. As the group gathered, someone pointed out a fun fact: July 2 was the 183rd day of the year in the Gregorian calendar, meaning 182 days remained — it was the halfway point of the year. With noon being the group’s typical finish time, they could officially celebrate a “Happy New Half Year.” The group was also reminded that they’d soon be walking in the Fourth of July Parade — and a bit of Piedmont parade history was shared. The city’s first official parade took place 60 years ago, in 1965, thanks to Dick Johnson, then-chairman of the Recreation Commission. Johnson’s El Cerrito Avenue neighborhood had already been celebrating Independence Day since the mid-1950s with its own kids’ bike parade, watermelon-eating contest, and water balloon toss. Mary Ellen Sherry and Dorothy Carter, who lived on the block, had taken part in similar festivities elsewhere and wanted the same for their street. Alongside neighbors like Dick Carter and Patty Edmonds, they created the El Cerrito event. Johnson pushed to expand it citywide, giving rise to the Piedmont parade we know today. In honor of that legacy, the walkers headed to El Cerrito Avenue to see where it all began. From there, they made their way to Mesa Avenue, where they would gather on Friday to join the parade. Nearby, they paused to spot a local treasure — a pair of bald eagles and their two eaglets nesting in a eucalyptus tree at the edge of Mountain View Cemetery. The eaglets had hatched in May and were first spotted by the group in early June. Since eaglets typically don’t fledge for 10 to 14 weeks, the birds were still at home — and the walkers hoped for another look. Along the way, they stopped at the under-construction aquatics center on Magnolia Avenue, where cement was being poured and the site was buzzing with activity. The walkers continued to the 300 block of El Cerrito — the birthplace of Piedmont’s first July 4 street celebration nearly 70 years ago — then crossed Oakland Avenue to Blair Avenue, up Dracena Avenue, and across to Park Way. Climbing Park past Highland, they arrived at 22 Mesa Avenue for a group photo. Before heading toward the eagle’s nest, a bit of ornithological trivia was shared: the bald eagle became the symbol of the United States when it was chosen for the Great Seal in 1782. It was Walkers: Melba Yee, Bill Ahen, Alicia Rivera, Noemi Alvarado, Ken Moy, Quincy Dong, Helen Dong, Kat Lang, Stella Houston, Tina Shum, Diane Jimenez, Alissa Quan, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Peggy Shultz, Sherry Jacobs, Mark Davis, Chuck Oraftik, Cathy Laymon, David Haecker, Debbie Powell, Liza Dalrymple, Dave DeRoche, Joyce Ahern, Rick Eigenbrode, Caskey Weston, Laurie Leonard, Lisa Leonard, Mike Gallant, Laura DuDell-Foley, Russ Nelson, Jack Fischrup, Tracy Lee, Marianne Jakus, Pat Nicholas, Denny McGee, Judy Wong, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Charlie, and Lynn and Dave Holzman with their K-9 best friends Pepper and Fiona were walking with them for the first time.

The word “bald” originally meant “white” in Old English, referring to the eagle’s distinctive white head. Lori Austin, who had recently returned from Africa, shared a photo of the African fish eagle, which also has a white head and chest. Interestingly, it took six years of Congressional debate before the bald eagle was formally chosen as the national emblem. Benjamin Franklin wasn’t a fan — he wrote that the eagle was a “bird of bad moral character” and preferred the turkey, calling it “more respectable.” Though the bald eagle has long symbolized America, it was only in December 2024 that Congress officially designated it as the national bird. After reaching Mesa, the group went down to Moraga Avenue, up a block to Monte Avenue, and looked across to the eucalyptus trees for a glimpse of the eagles. Several enthusiasts with binoculars were already there. The eaglets occasionally popped their heads above the nest, noticeably larger than a month before. articles.text: It was a typical cool, foggy summer morning in the East Bay as I drove over the Bay Bridge into San Francisco. I was headed for Fort Mason, and my head was full of memories. More than 20 years ago, the first big tasting I attended as a new wine writer was the annual Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) tasting at Fort Mason. I was astounded by the size of the event — not one, but two of the huge festival pavilions were packed with winery tables pouring their Zins. The first hour was reserved for the trade and media, and the place was already lively. But at the designated hour, the general public was let in – and the pavilions exploded with people eager to sample. The atmosphere was euphoric, and more than a few attendees over-served themselves. But I must say, it was a great party. (I, of course, was soberly hard at work finding the best Zins for my readers.) pages.text: Wednesday, July 9, 2025 27 The Wine Corner Best New Zinfandels By Pierre DuMont It was a typical cool, foggy summer morning in the East Bay as I drove over the Bay Bridge into San Francisco. I was headed for Fort Mason, and my head was full of memories. More than 20 years ago, the first big tasting I attended as a new wine writer was the annual Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) tasting at Fort Mason. I was astounded by the size of the event — not one, but two of the huge festival pavilions were packed with winery tables pouring their Zins. The first hour was reserved for the trade and media, and the place was already lively. But at the designated hour, the general public was let in – and the pavilions exploded with people eager to sample. The atmosphere was euphoric, and more than a few attendees over-served themselves. But I must say, it was a great party. (I, of course, was soberly hard at work finding the best Zins for my readers.) Over the past 20 years, the ZAP tasting has moved around quite a bit – Rockwall Winery, the Palace Hotel, a fancy SF restaurant, and most recently, COPIA in Napa. This year, they’re back at Fort Mason, but instead of the giant pavilions, the event was held in a medium-sized room near restaurant row. There was a line to get in, and the crowd was enthusiastic. Inside, about 50 wineries were pouring, and the room was comfortably packed with tasters. As usual, I found old favorites I’ve written about before – and some new producers that were exciting to discover. Many good wines were poured, but what I present below are the memorable wines — the ones that stuck with me at the end of the day because they were truly special. I encourage you to seek them out. • 2023 Once and Future Zinfandel Bedrock Vineyard This is the second year in a row that Joel Peterson founder of Ravenswood new project Once and Future has been in the top Zins. The juice from these 135-year-old vines sees a good percentage of new French oak and the blackberry and cassis nose shows a touch of sweet vanilla. It is rich and full in the mouth with exceptional balance and structure. This Zin is delicious now and will last for a decade in the cellar. • 2023 Williams Selyem Zinfandel Belloni Vineyard This marvelous Zin from Russian River’s famed Belloni Vineyard is wonderfully aromatic with raspberries and strawberries on the nose. In the mouth you find big dark fruit flavors with a wonderfully dense fine-grained tannin structure and great presence on the palate. Try this with some grilled pork ribs. • 2021 Terra D’Oro Zinfandel Deaver Vineyard Coming from a 135-year-old vineyard in the Amador foothills the wine has kaleidoscopic aromas of boysenberry jam, beef, lavender, and peach. The medium-bodied palate features generous floral flavors. It has a silky texture, bursts of mouthwatering acidity and a long, spicy finish. • 2021 Gluntz Zinfandel Dante Dusi Vineyard The Dante Dusi vineyard in Paso Robles has near iconic status as a fount of powerful oldstyle Zinfandel that is not for the faint of heart. The wine is bursting with boatloads of plum, blueberry, and raisin fruit - full and round in the mouth. Drink this big boy over the next 3 or 4 years. flavors, and earthy layers add complexity. It has great acidity and silky tannins leading to a smooth finish. Would partner great with a hearty beef stew. • 2023 St. Amant Heritage Red (BEST VALUE) The St. Amant Heritage blend from Lodi features Zin mixed with Alicante Bouschet and Petite Sirah. It has scents of tar, cherries and forest floor undertones. The medium-bodied palate offers complex, layered flavors that range from sweet fruit to earth and spice. It has a softly chewy texture and a perfumed finish. • 2021 J. Dusi Paper Street Zinfandel The Paper Street Zin is a stunner, delivering waves of herbscented fruit ranging from blueberries to plums and even hints of nectarine. It’s full-bodied and concentrated, silky-textured and long on the mouthwatering finish. • 2019 David Clinton Zinfandel Teldeschi Vineyard The Teldeschi Vineyard in Dry Creek Valley has produced a deeply fruited Zin with open-knit aromas of mixed berry jam, cassis, dried flowers and leather. The palate offers layer after layer of spicy, floral fruit. It’s structured by fine tannins, good acidity and a long, detailed finish. Should last in the cellar for five or six years. • 2023 Peachy Canyon Zinfandel Nancy’s View I have been a fan of Peachy Canyon wines for many years now. The wine hails from the Adelaida District near Paso Robles and reveals aromas of wild berries, blueberries and tea leaves. The medium-bodied palate is bursting with robust berry • 2018 Three Zinfandel Live Oak In 1885 Italian immigrants planted vines in the sandy soil of northern Contra Costa County near Oakley. Today these ancient vine grapes are highly sought after by such esteemed producers as Ridge Vineyards. This bottle has scents of cherries, licorice and potpourri. The medium-bodied palate is smooth and supple with a deep core of savory fruit, bright acidity and a long latent finish. Delicious stuff. • 2021 Summit Lake Zinfandel This Howell Mountain estate is celebrating their 50th vintage with this bottling. It is a medium bodied effort displaying a classic perfume of cherry, raspberry and briery fruit as well as soil notes. Dense with excellent purity, abundant spice, unobtrusive tannin, and a peppery finish this concentrated mountain grown Zinfandel will drink well for 5-7 years. • 2021 Kokomo Zinfandel Timber Crest Vineyard The Kokomo Zin is dark purple in color with a gorgeous nose of saddle leather, spice box, black cherry and blackberries. The attack is sweet but not cloying and the finish is full-bodied rich, and explosive. It will drink well for a decade or more. • 2021 Dashe Zinfandel Todd Brothers Ranch This Alexander Valley Zin has long been one of my favorites. It has 7% Petite Sirah added for depth and complexity and is aged in 20% new French oak. It exhibits copious quantities of sweet black cherry and blackberry fruit as well as a hint of raspberries in its big, peppery bouquet. Medium to full-bodied, elegant, concentrated and powerful, it would make a great partner to a grilled leg of lamb. • 2021 We Know Jack Zinfandel Rockpile is one of the newest AVAs established in 2002. I have been very impressed by the beauty and power of the Zins from that area. This bottling is a perfect example of what Rockpile has to offer. Its saturated ruby/ purple color is followed by a big, peppery, spicy nose with underlying minerals and black fruits. There is very good density in this appealing wine. • 2022 Trentadue “La Storia” Zinfandel The ever-reliable Miro Tcholakov winemaker at Trentadue Winery has again produced a marvelous Zinfandel. It has effusive aromas of cherry pie and stone fruits on the nose, while the medium to full-bodied palate is supple, framed by silky-textured tannins leading to a long, elegant finish. • 2018 Covenant Landsman Berkeley based Covenant Winery has produced an interesting blend of 65% Zinfandel, 18% Petite Sirah and 17% Grenache. It is medium garnet-purple colored with kirsch, raspberry pie and spice box scents plus tobacco, leather and olives. The palate is full, rich, firm and chewy with savory layers and a long finish. articles.text: When Frank C. Havens opened Piedmont Park in 1898, only the Clubhouse, the rustic teahouse, the mineral springs and the beauty of the ravine, waterfalls and wandering paths were there to attract visitors to the park. Havens continued to add more attractions to draw visitors to Piedmont Park and to the city itself. Many visitors enjoyed the weather and views and decided to build their homes here. Frank Havens and his Realty Syndicate was there to sell them a home site. In 1904 he built “The Maze.” Gardeners planted a large circular hedge maze in the natural bowl where Witter Field stands today. This privet maze challenged all who entered to reach the bright red pagoda at the center. Ladders strategically placed throughout the Maze allowed those feeling hopelessly lost to climb a ladder to the top of the hedge and get their bearings. And true to the nature and design of mazes, the Maze in Piedmont was a double challenge; the return trip out of the Maze was just as challenging as that to the center. lower entrance to Piedmont Park. Havens developed a lane from Grand Avenue to the Maze and on to the park paths. He lined it with palm trees, some of which still survive on what is now Palm Drive. The Maze from 1904 is now the location of the high school’s Witter Field. One year after the 1906 earthquake and fire in San Francisco, Havens added more attractions to Piedmont Park. Many refugees from San Francisco fled to the East Bay, and Havens wanted to draw them to Piedmont and sell them property for building homes. In keeping with the Victorian interest in the exotic, Havens added a Japanese Tea House. Built as a replica of the late-fifteenth century Silver Pavilion in Kyoto, Japan, the teahouse opened in 1907 where today’s Japanese Tea House stands. (The current tea house was moved to Piedmont Park in 1976 from an estate where Piedmont Middle School now stands.) A Japanese gate led to a Japanese-style garden with ponds and a moon bridge. Stickwork fences, pillars and benches complemented these Japanese grounds. Also in 1907, Havens built his Piedmont Art Gallery on the site of today’s tennis courts in the park. The spacious art gallery had a large skylight and was built to display Havens’ collection of 375 pieces of art by English, French, Russian, American and other painters. Two additional gallery wings extended beyond the main gallery. Eleven countries in all were represented by this collection. The centerpieces of Havens’ collection were 162 large Russian masterpieces that were exhibited at the 1904 St. Louis Exposition. After the exposition, the paintings were stored in Canada. In order to avoid paying customs This rustic teahouse was built near today’s bus shelter. fees on the paintings, they were unscrupulously appraised far below their value. Havens and his agent then snatched them up at a fraction of their worth. Havens was particularly fond of California impressionists, and his collection also included work by William Keith, Charles Rollo Peters, Gordon Couts, Thomas Hill, Xavier Martinez and others. Xavier Martinez and Gordon Couts lived and painted in Piedmont at this time. Havens’ art collection was said to be one of the finest collections in the country. Havens charged admission to the Art Gallery, and artist Richard Partington, Havens’ sister-in-law Carrie Sterling and son Seyd Havens served successively as curators of the gallery. In 1916, Havens had plans to develop the park into residential home sites. He sent his paintings to San Francisco where they were auctioned off. Some paintings went to private collectors, some to the new Oakland Art Museum, and many went to the de Young Museum in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. If you enjoy reading these history columns twice monthly, consider becoming a member of the Piedmont Historical Society and receiving the annual newsletter. For more information on Piedmont’s history and the Historical Society, see: Piedmonthistorical. org, or contact Gail Lombardi at lombardg@pacbell.net. articles.text: The Fourth of July Parade Committee has announced that this year’s Grand Marshal will be Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers who will be retiring this month after 11 years working for the Piedmont Police Department. “It’s an honor,” said Bowers. “It’s another opportunity to engage and say thank you, quite frankly, to a community that’s been very rewarding and healthy to work in and work with.” “He’s retiring and he has served our community well, and we’re extremely appreciative of his great service,” said Parade Committee Chair Kathy Kelleher. A Grand Marshal is chosen every year by the Committee to be honored by the community. Those selected ride in a parade car as part of the Fourth of July Parade festivities and join members of the Fourth of July Committee on the reviewing stand in front of the police station. With Chief Bowers approaching retirement effective July 17, the community-oriented police chief was an obvious choice for the parade. Earlier this year, Bowers was honored by the San Francisco District Attorney’s office with the Hometown Hero Award for his efforts in community engagement and his work partnering with residents and local schools to address gun violence. “I was fortunate because I started with a great situation, and I’ve been most satisfied with Staff photo Jeremy Bowers, Chief of Piedmont Police Department, has been named Grand Marshal of this year’s Fourth of July parade.

Hamburgers and hot dogs from Piedmont’s Scout troops are expected to keep parade-goers and crows in the park well fed. “I think it’s going to be a little bit bigger than last year,” said Kathy Kelleher, Chair of the Fourth of July Parade Committee and daughter of parade founder

articles.text: The California Repercussions stage and marching band is set to return to Piedmont for its 58th annual Fourth of July Parade this Friday. The band will entertain parade-goers with classic and popular tunes alike. Based in the San Francisco Bay Area, the Repercussions are a 50-piece band made of equal parts brass, woodwinds, percussion, and party. For over 30 years the Repercussions have had the pleasure of playing for many discriminating clients and events such as the NFL Pro Bowl, the San Francisco Giants, the National Mayors’ Conference, and Oracle Corporation. The band has also thrilled crowds on international tours in London, Munich, Spain, Australia and Brazil. The band is composed of former college marching band members, primarily UC Davis, who may have graduated from school but never fully grew up. The Repercussions are known to have fun during their performances, waving horns in the air, dancing, and laughing their way along. Though the band is large, it promises not to be a constant wall of sound: the band mixes the power tunes in with others that feature a section of the band or a talented soloist. The California Repercussions will be marching in the Piedmont 4th of July Parade this year. Look for them as the final entry.
articles.title: Repercussions marching band to play in Fourth of July Parade

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) will host its annual pancake breakfast in Veterans Hall on Friday morning, July 4, from 8:00 – 10:30 a.m., complete with pancakes, sausages, fresh fruit, orange juice and coffee. Adult tickets are $15 (ages 15+) and youth tickets will be $10 (ages 3-14). Children under three can eat for free. The Pancake Breakfast is a decades-old Fourth of July tradition in the city. The event was hosted by the Piedmont-Montclair Rotary Club for many years and briefly by the Recreation Department, which passed the tradition on in 2015 to the Community Service Crew, a coed Venturing unit of Piedmont Scouts under the leadership of Ken Li. “I’ve met people who say they’ve been coming for many, many years,” said Li about the event’s popular community appeal. “I suppose it’s an extension of the parade, so people sometimes will host and get friends to come over and visit with them while they watch the parade, and they plan to come to the breakfast before the parade.” The Pancake Breakfast is one of the PCSC’s largest fundBowers Grand Marshal. ...... 1 Question Man. ................. 2 Letters.......................... 3 Climate Corner................ 5 Schools......................... 6 Postcards from Camp. ........ 8 Pancake breakfast . .......... 10 PPD Blue...................... 11 Sports. ......................... 12 Hiking with Jon. .............. 15 Museums. ..................... 16 Music . ......................... 17 PCA events.................... 19 Movie reviews................ 20 Indie Next book list.......... 22 Wed. RELIGION CORNER Miracles and wonders By Dr. William McNabb Recently I had a successful heart ablation to correct Ventricular Tachycardia, an ailment I did not even realize I had until recently. At 8:00 a.m. I was wheeled into the Cath Lab at Summit Hospital in Oakland. At 3:00 p.m. the same day I was at home eating a hamburger. (The burger was not mentioned in the after-visit list of things to avoid.) This morning, I am reflecting on how this slow-motion miracle occurred. My cardiologist inserted electrodes on catheters into my groin and neck. They made their way to my heart where they had a Star Wars type light saber battle with a small spot on my ventricular wall that Darth Vader had taken over and was trying to lead a rebellion against my atria the rightful command central for my heart’s electrical signals. The entire war took place without my even knowing about it because of my excellent anesthesiologist, Dr. Yann. I have written before in previous hospital reports about how I was wonderfully taken care of by some nurses who all had uplifting Biblical names. Grace (unmerited forgiveness), Emmanuel (God with us), Angela (angel). They were immigrants from Nigeria, Eritrea and Mexico. This time my excellent nurses were Lan (China) and Raphael (Philippines). The brilliant general of this cardiac Star Wars battle was my cardiologist Dr. Rajan Shah from Iran. It is beyond tragic to think that if it were up to the vile Mr. Trump this man and those nurses may not have been welcomed in this country. I call what happened to me yesterday a slow-moving miracle. Perhaps it began in the 17th century when William Harvey, an English doctor, first described the circulatory system. Then discovery after discovery. I wonder what doctor first said, “maybe we can snake a wire through a vein into the heart and shock it into behaving correctly.” And what wonderful scientist invented these drugs that can put you to sleep instantly and wake you with no pain, grogginess or memory of what scary things just happened See Religion Corner on page 3 DICK CARTER, Florada Avenue Being in last year’s Piedmont parade with our Walking on Wednesdays group is one favorite. It was more fun than sitting in my lawn chair and just watching, and we’re marching together again this year. We had friends and family in town from across the country and we all had a great time at the Piedmont Parade, TOM RAMSEY, City Council Member Our first Piedmont Parade 20+ years ago. When Bowers’ predecessor, Riki Goede, first suggested he move from the San Jose Police Department to join Piedmont’s police force, Bowers initially dismissed the idea. “The thought of leaving San Jose was something that I never considered,” said Bowers. “However, after learning more about the city and taking stock of personal and professional considerations, I made the decision to apply.” In the end, Bowers moved to Piedmont in search of a healthy and meaningful work-life balance. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council adopted a City budget for 2025- 2026 fiscal year at their regular meeting on Monday, June 16. The annual budget serves as a major policy document and describes how Piedmont intends to deliver its services and fund infrastructure in the coming year. The City’s $40.5 million General Fund budget includes the first year of new revenue from Measure F, a 20% increase in the Municipal Services Parcel Tax passed by voters in March 2023. Measure F funds will provide $538,000 in the coming year, which the City used to fund two additional 911 dispatch positions and an expansion of the Police Department’s automated license plate reader (ALPR) program. The FY2025-26 budget looks to maintain service levels citywide, prioritizing high quality service delivery, fiscal responsibility, and planning for the future while bringing several multi-year major projects to completion, including the City’s new community pool, the relocation of the 911 dispatch center, and the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Successful completion of the pool and dispatch center projects remain the City’s top priorities, followed by: • Installation of the Dearing Memorial at Triangle Park • Planning for a future public safety building to replace aging structures that do not meet modern standards for critical facilities. Additionally, next year’s budget focuses on investment in public spaces citywide. Capital improvements planned for the coming year include: • Repaving 1.9 miles of streets, re-striping an additional six miles of streets, and repairing 1,800 feet of sidewalk • New playground equipment at the Linda Beach Tot Lot and Piedmont Park • Upgrades to flood-prone storm drain infrastructure at eight locations across the city • Pathway repairs in Piedmont Park, similar to those recently completed at Crocker, Dracena, and Linda Parks • Four “DC fast charging” electric vehicle charging stations in the Civic Center Looking further ahead, the budget includes the development of a Sustainable Park Management Plan, identifying the management practices and future improvements needed to ensure Piedmont’s public spaces remain vibrant and support community needs long into the future. Adoption of the budget follows two City Council study sessions, review by the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, and two public hearings.
articles.title: City investing in public spaces

articles.text: Business owners can now apply for, renew, and pay annual tax for their City of Piedmont business license entirely online. The City’s new tool, launched in May, replaces a cumbersome paper-based process, providing community members a faster, simpler way to manage business licensing and rental taxes. Business owners no longer need to download forms, write checks, or visit City Hall in person. Through the new online portal, business owners can: • Apply for a new business license • Pay their annual business license tax, including rental business tax • Close their City of Piedmont business or rental account • Update contact information and business details All actions and payment history are stored in one place, accessible 24/7 from any device. Community members who need assistance using the online system can get help by calling a dedicated support number at (510) 250-1975 or by visiting City Hall, where staff can assist business owners with completing the process using the public online service kiosks located in the lobby. Licenses required for all businesses operating in Piedmont All businesses operating in Piedmont – including rental property owners – must have a valid business license. This includes, but is not limited to: • Home-based businesses (includes 1099 self-employment) • Online storefronts or “influencers” with a Piedmont business address • Landlords operating longterm or short-term rentals • Contractors and consultants working in Piedmont, even if located elsewhere Businesses that fail to obtain a license are subject to late fees and penalties. Learn more about licensing requirements and compliance at piedmont.ca.gov/BusinessCompliance. Part of a broader effort to modernize services The launch of online business licensing continues Piedmont’s work to make City business more accessible and user-friendly. This system joins the NextRequest public records portal, Piedmont Police CitizenConnect online incident map, and eTRAKiT online building and planning permit portal in a growing collection of digital services. Building on these efforts, a new City website is currently in development and scheduled to launch later this year.
articles.title: Piedmont’s Online Business License tool removes paper from the application process

articles.text: Piedmont Climate Fellow shines a light on what happens to plastic recyclables after the blue bin Ever wonder what happens to plastic after you put it in your blue recycling bin? The answer is more interesting than you might think. Piedmont’s recycling is sorted at Republic Services’ West County Resource Recovery Facility (WCRR) in Richmond. From there, plastics are bundled by type and sent out to be sold. The markets that accept different types of plastics constantly fluctuate. The types of plastic in highest demand are Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) – used for water bottles, soda bottles, and food containers – and High-Density Polyethylene (HDPE), commonly used for shampoo bottles, laundry detergent, and household cleaners. Republic Ser vices uses AI-powered arms to seamlessly identify PET plastic at its sorting facility, pulling out and bundling the most valuable plastics for shipment while ejecting other materials to avoid cross-contamination. These robots are currently being trained to collect HDPE plastics as well. For other types of plastic – often found in single use plastic bags, clamshells, packaging foam, and disposable drinking cups – recycling markets are more fluid. Even after placing these in a blue bin, likelihood of reprocessing may be slim and there’s a good chance they will find their way to a landfill. You can avoid the stress of wondering where these materials will end up by looking for ways to forgo them altogether. We call this strategy “stop or swap.” To “stop” is the act of eliminating a plastic good or material from your daily routine, opting for reusables instead. These can include stainless steel water bottles, tote bags, and reusable food containers. Where reusables aren’t an option, like when you’re buying milk at the grocery store, try to “swap.” Swap is the act of choosing plastics that have a stronger recycling market. For example, rather than purchasing milk in a carton, try to buy milk that comes in a glass bottle or #1 (PET) plastic jug. I want to close by reiterating that despite market fluidity, it is essential that as a community, we preserve our practices of placCity of Piedmont Climate Fellow Andrew Kaplowitz ing plastic goods in the blue bin. However, that isn’t to say we can’t implement change in our spending habits. Through the installation of stop and swap strategies, Piedmont can lower its environmental footprint by reducing the quantity of plastic that ends up in our landfills. If you are still unsure about how to dispose of waste and recyclables, StopWaste provides a tool called RE:Source, which is a search engine that allows you to input any type of item and see how it gets sorted in your community. articles.text: On March 4 this year Piedmont Unified School District said goodbye to two veteran Human Resource (HR) Managers, Kim Randlett and Suzanne Binder. Randlett has since been hired back in an elevated role as HR Director. On July 1 Randlett officially completed her first day in the new role which has many more responsibilities. Randlett had been handling contracts and HR details for all classified staff for 13 years and will now also be in charge of hiring and onboarding the other half of district contracts, those of teachers and certificated faculty. The school board brought her back after she applied for and officially secured the new job title on May 14. “Kim is just really the best. She is truly a rock star in terms of not only her expertise, but her skillset, and relationships with our staff,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. “She has such respect from all of our staff and it’s because she knows so much and really has a service attitude.” Randlett earned a degree in business from Webster University and holds a certificate from the ACSA Personnel Academy. Her Piedmont tenure began in 2007 as a Havens paraeducator. She moved into the district office in 2011 to support assistant superintendents Michael Brady and Randall Booker. The new role has 24 essential tasks. Randlett, well-respected within the district, will also be in charge of Title 9, administering grievance and disciplinary procedures for employees, and public record requests. Another new essential job responsibility for the Director will be as a liaison for union groups, and leading labor negotiations for PUSD. “I really pride myself on good relationships, my clear communication with staff and union leadership. I look forward to working with CSEA and APT the next coming school year. My door is always open, anytime anyone has any questions they can come anytime,” said Randlett in the May 14 board meeting. The Director will also take charge of job descriptions & salary schedules for district employees. The HR department will be augmented by an entry-level HR job under the Director, instead of having two managers. The job posting for the Payroll Technician II / Personnel Attendance role was posted June 25 at Edjoin.org/ Home/JobPosting/2107454 with an annual salary scale of $73,742- $90,648.
