articles.text: Crucial—but often invisible—skills that let teenagers truly lift off A fledgling hawk’s wings look full long before it can soar. Hidden among the downy coverts are “primaries” and “secondaries”—the true flight feathers that bite the air and hold the bird aloft. Our kids, too, can appear ready for the big sky: decent grades, solid friendships, a résumé of clubs. Yet many stall once the thermals of late adolescence hit. Below are four less-obvious “feathers” parents can help cultivate—capacities that research links to stronger well-being and real-world traction. 1 Feedback Fluency Most teens dread criticism, yet the ability to seek and digest honest feedback predicts healthier self-concepts and lower depressive symptoms a year later. Coach your teen to ask three questions after any project—“What worked? What didn’t? What one change would have the biggest payoff?” Model the posture by soliciting their critique of your own decisions around the house. 2 Radical Responsibility & Clean Communication Blame feels lighter in the moment, but longitudinal data show that adolescents who practice taking full ownership for outcomes develop steadier social responsibility values in emerging adulthood. Pair that ownership with “clean” communication: when your head and your heart match your words and your actions. Having internal integrity in this way combined with seeking the lessons in challenging moments places cornerstones in the foundation of budding wisdom. 3 Expansive Curiosity Curiosity isn’t a trait; it’s an approach that can be trained. Teaching students the Question Formulation Technique boosted dispositional curiosity across an entire semester, which in turn lifted academic engagement. Help teens broaden and deepen their questioning by scheduling weekly “wonder walks”: 20-minute strolls where the only rule is to generate ten genuine questions about what they see or read. Curiosity widens the runway for future passions they can’t yet imagine. 4 Humble Collaboration Intellectual humility—the willingness to give up being right in order to stay connected— correlates with sharper critical thinking and more resilient relationships. Families can practice it with a simple ritual: in any debate, each side must restate the other’s viewpoint to their satisfaction before replying. The habit trains teens to treat disagreements as design sessions rather than zero-sum games. Take-Off Checklist (Next 30 Days) • Feedback Friday: over pizza, everyone shares one success and one improvement from • • • • the week. Ownership Ledger: teen logs daily instances of blame shifted and accepted; review patterns weekly. Question Jar: place a mason jar on the table; whoever contributes the most new questions in a week picks Friday’s dessert. Debate-and-Restate Night: choose a low-stakes topic (pineapple on pizza). Practice the humility ritual. Mentor Map: together, list five adults outside the family whom your teen trusts; draft a plan to ask one for feedback on a current goal. Why start now? Wisdom doesn’t appear when a driver’s license turns into a mortgage; it grows from thousands of small flights in safe airspace. By seeding feedback fluency, radical responsibility, expansive curiosity, and humble collaboration during the high-school years, you give your child the aerodynamic edge they’ll need when the winds pick up—and the confidence to leave the nest on their own power. Randall Grayson Ph.D (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over 20 years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about summer program, family camps, and twoweek sessions can be found at www.campaugusta.org.

articles.text: On June 8 and 9 Alice followed the rabbit all the way to Piedmont as Pinecones and Portals Hiking Theater Company acted out the popular children’s tale Alice in Wonderland with Piedmont Park doubling as Wonderland. Children, pets, parents and guardians followed Alice and her friends on an interactive walking adventure of moving theatrics called Alice Piedmont Recreation Department put on the moveable feast of the eyes and ears, which left patrons enchanted. The act opened with Molly Armstrong, playing Pip the narrator, climbing on and all around the Exedra’s vase in search of the audience Kids were instructed to grab hold of a rope while the stroller and wheelchair friendly adventure moved from the sand park towards Piedmont Park’s bandstand. The company’s founder, Juliana Frick played Alice who happens to eat a magic cookie that shrank her before our very eyes into Amalia Luma Kessinger-Frick, of third grade size. Juliana Frick is an award-winning physical theater artist, and acrobat that grew up touring with acclaimed youth-troupe Circus Smirkus from the age of nine. In 2017, Frick was diagnosed with a rare illness that caused profound hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction. As a chronically ill and late-deafened adult, Juliana is a proud Disabled artist who strives to make the creative process and performance accessible to all. Little Alice and Alice led the adventure down into the park at the looping pace of the accordion, played by Jonathan Kipp. The white rabbit, frantic as always, raced over the expansive Piedmont Park lawns while the crowd, and a bus load of Camp Augusta campers waiting to ship out, looked over quizzically. Characters from Wander Land led families through park paths, on the banks of Bushy Dell Creek, as the tale unfolded all around, incorporating clowning, inventive puppetry, and live music. articles.text: St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland is partnering with the office of Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee to host a community Ceasefire Teach-In on Saturday, July 19, at the church on 114 Montecito Avenue. This neighborhood event is part of the Ceasefire Teach-In Series, an initiative by Mayor Lee and her Public Safety Working Group to engage local communities in meaningful dialogue about ending gun violence in Oakland. Speakers will include Mayor Lee, Oakland Police Chief Floyd Mitchell, and Violence Prevention Chief Dr. Holly Joshi, along with other public safety leaders. Together, they will describe the data, strategies, and evolution of Oakland’s Ceasefire program. “We are deeply committed to peace and justice in our community,” said the Rev. Dr. Mauricio Wilson, rector of St. Paul’s Episcopal Church. “We are grateful for the opportunity to host this vital conversation and invite all of our neighbors to join us.” RSVPs are encouraged at bit.ly/OaklandMayorCeasefireTeachIn or by email to ddaavis-howard@oaklandca.gov. For more information on Oakland’s Ceasefire Strategy, visit https://www.oaklandca.gov/Public-Safety-Streets/Crime-Prevention/Oakland-Ceasefire-Strategy.
articles.title: St. Paul’s Episcopal Church to host Ceasefire dialogue on Oakland gun violence

articles.text: Staff Photos Aubrey Turner, PHS Class of 2020, appeared with Oakland Soul in its W League season. Aubrey Turner graduated from Piedmont High in 2020, signing on with the University of Portland to play Division 1 collegiate soccer. Now five years since she graced the halls of PHS, Turner returned to the Bay Area to play professionally for Oakland Soul of the USL W League. “It’s a surreal feeling to walk out on the pitch for a home game and to see the number of fans Soul has. It shows how Oakland has always cared about its teams and always comes out strong,” Turner said. Although she only appeared once for Soul before aggravating an injury, Turner was able to get back on the field and train with the club. “I started training with Soul in March and right before our first game, I hurt my ankle. I have a history of ankle injuries, so that told me I need to take time to get healthy if I want to continue playing,” Turner explained. After concluding her collegiate career with the Pilots in the fall of 2023, Turner traveled to Europe to play professionally with F.C. Famalicã, a team in the top tier of Portuguese football and located in the northern Portugal city of Vila Nova de Famalicão. With the help of an agent, Turner landed a workout at F.C. Famalicão and impressed their coaching staff enough to earn a roster spot. “It was December 2023 and I was deciding on whether to use my fifth year or play professionally. I was put in touch with an agent and I went on trial with Famalicão. They were interested in me and that’s how I wound up in Portugal,” Turner said of her time in Portugal. In 2024, Turner had four appearances at Famalicão for a total of 84 minutes. “I always wanted to live abroad and I was able to do that outside of soccer. I lived in Porto and a lot of the area reminded me of Northern California. During the drive, I would think, ‘This place looks just like home.’ Europe’s style of play is possession-based and they concentrate on the technical aspect. One thing that jumped out at me were the tricks the Portuguese girls would do in juggling circles,” reflected Turner. Playing just 30 minutes away from the city of Porto, some of Aubrey’s favorite memories were watching her favorite team, Arsenal, play FC Porto in the Champions League and, of course, eating delectable Portuguese food. “Portugal itself is beautiful, I want to go back. The food is amazing; I’m still trying to find a good natas place out here. I went to a Porto vs. Arsenal game, that was fun to just watch the fan base environment out there. The fans are screaming and singing nonstop. They know every chant and sway back and forth,” Turner said. With Oakland Soul, Turner was able to suit up with fellow Aubrey Turner describes her career after returning from playing professional soccer in Portugal.

articles.text: With only so many of our end-of-year awards to go around, some of the mighty contributions made throughout the year tend to get lost on the shuffle. In this article, we reflect on three athletes who were either entering their first year as a starter or getting time in their PHS athletic career. Three who made a huge impact included Amalia Gray of the cross country and track teams, Luca LaForte of the tennis team, and Abigail Jacoby of the water polo and swim teams. AMALIA GRAY Cross Country, Track and Field Amalia Gray burst onto the scene as a sophomore distance runner, becoming one of the best performers on the team. We named her our honorable mention for Athlete of the Month in November. She qualified for the prestigious CIF State Cross Country Championship at Woodward Park, where she finished 101st of 201 runners with a time of 20:24.5. To get there, she finished 14th of 127 at the NCS Championship at Hayward HS with a time of 21:25.3. At the WACC Championship, also at Hayward, Gray placed 16th of 40 in 20:16.9. In track last spring she reached the NCS Bayshore Area Championship in the 3200 meters, finishing 12th of 19 with a time of 12:35.28. At the WACC Championship, she placed 13th of 26 in 12:50.24. Photo by Becky Spies Amalia Gray reached the CIF State Cross Country Championships last fall as a sophomore. at No. 2 doubles with Bini. LaForte represents a potential bright future for Piedmont High’s tennis team, earning starts alongside fellow freshmen Ben Davis, Joey Assalian, Emilio Misra, and Robert Piniella. ABIGAIL JACOBY Water Polo, Swimming Abigail Jacoby, an incoming senior, isa two-sport athlete on the water polo team in the fall and swimming team in the spring. She earned first-team All-League honors for swimming and an honorable mention on water polo. In the fall, Jacoby led the girls’ water polo team to a 10-12 overall record, achieving the school’s most wins since 2017. They finished the WACC Championship Tournament in fifth place after defeating Encinal 6-5 in the fifthplace final. She scored three goals and a steal in Piedmont’s tournament win over Encinal, while she also logged three goals and two assists in their 11-9 win over Lick-Wilmerding in first round of the consolation bracket. In swimming, Jacoby was a WACC champion in the 200 individual medley with a time of 2:19.06 in a field of 22 swimmers. She was also a member of two second-place finishes on relay teams. Her 200 medley team of Cynthia Wu, Sam White, and Sydney Olson finished with a time of 1:56.50 in a field of 19 teams, while her 200 freestyle team of Wu, Olson, and Charlotte Zhang finished in 1:43.88 against 17 other teams. LUCA LAFORTE Tennis Luca LaForte was a standout freshman on the tennis team last spring, emerging as a top doubles starter in his debut season. He earned an honorable mention for All-League honors. Some of his best performances include a 6-2, 6-1 at No. 1 doubles with Gianluca Bini against Lick-Wilmerding and a 6-1, 7-6 (8-6) win against Castro Valley Staff Photos Luca LaForte was a standout freshman on the tennis team last spring. By Jonathan Comeaux Aubrey Turner graduated from Piedmont High in 2020, signing on with the University of Portland to play Division 1 collegiate soccer. Now five years since she graced the halls of PHS, Turner returned to the Bay Area to play professionally for Oakland Soul of the USL W League. “It’s a surreal feeling to walk out on the pitch for a home game and to see the number of fans Soul has. It shows how Oakland has always cared about its teams and always comes out strong,” Turner said. Although she only appeared once for Soul before aggravating an injury, Turner was able to get back on the field and train with the club. “I started training with Soul in March and right before our first game, I hurt my ankle. I have a history of ankle injuries, so that told me I need to take time to get healthy if I want to continue playing,” Turner explained. After concluding her collegiate career with the Pilots in the fall of 2023, Turner traveled to Europe to play professionally with F.C. Famalicã, a team in the top tier of Portuguese football and located in the northern Portugal city of Vila Nova de Famalicão. With the help of an agent, Turner landed a workout at F.C. Famalicão and impressed their coaching staff enough to earn a roster spot. “It was December 2023 and I was deciding on whether to use my fifth year or play professionally. I was put in touch with an agent and I went on trial with Famalicão. They were interested in me and that’s how I wound up in Portugal,” Turner said of her time in Portugal. In 2024, Turner had four appearances at Famalicão for a total of 84 minutes. “I always wanted to live abroad and I was able to do that outside of soccer. I lived in Porto and a lot of the area reminded me of Northern California. During the drive, I would think, ‘This place looks just like home.’ Europe’s style of play is possession-based and they concentrate on the technical aspect. One thing that jumped out at me were the tricks the Portuguese girls would do in juggling circles,” reflected Turner. Playing just 30 minutes away from the city of Porto, some of Aubrey’s favorite memories were watching her favorite team, Arsenal, play FC Porto in the Champions League and, of course, eating delectable Portuguese food. “Portugal itself is beautiful, I want to go back. The food is amazing; I’m still trying to find a good natas place out here. I went to a Porto vs. Arsenal game, that was fun to just watch the fan base environment out there. The fans are screaming and singing nonstop. They know every chant and sway back and forth,” Turner said. articles.text: How humbling is the Beautiful Game? Through the CONCACAF Gold Cup quarterfinals, only one of my predictions came true when Mexico beat Saudi Arabia. As for the other three quarterfinals matches, each of them went to penalty kicks. The United States edged past Costa Rica 4-3 on June 29 after ending regulation and extra time in a 2-2 draw, Guatemala upset Canada 6-5 in PKs after ending extra time 1-1 the same day. The previous day, Honduras upended Panama 5-4 in penalties after also ending extra time in a 1-1 tie. The U.S. now faces Guatemala in the semifinals today, July 2, while Mexico takes on Honduras. If things go as expected, it will set up another tantalizing rivalry match with the Stars and Stripes against El Tri of Mexico for the championship, to be played in Houston on Sunday, July 6. Against Costa Rica, the U.S. dominated possession at 64 percent of the ball and continuously tested the defense with 18 shots, only four were on target. Costa Rica, meanwhile, only had seven shots with three on target, but held an initial 1-0 lead after scoring in the 12th minute before the United States answered with Diego Luna’s goal in the 43rd and Maximillian Arfsten’s goal early in the second half in the 47th. 14 Wednesday, July 2, 2025 Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 18th year. Current and former college athletes as well as high school athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmont-post.com. JACK STEIN Cross County, Track & Field Piedmont High Class of 2022 Pomona-Pitzer Class of 2026 Jack Stein, PHS Class of 2022, just finished his junior year on Pomona-Pitzer’s cross country and track teams. In cross country last fall, he finished the season by helping his school place third of 32 teams in the Division 3 NCAA Championship on November 23. Stein finished the race 28th of 294 athletes with a time of 24:34.3 on the 8K course. Stein also competed in track in the 5K and 10K events at the SCAIC Track and Field Championship on April 26-27. He finished the 5K seventh of 44 runners with a time of 14:57.80. He was second of 16 runners in the 10K, clocking a 30:57.88. As a sophomore, Stein helped the Sagehens claim the 2023 Division 3 NCAA Championship by defeating Wisconsin La Crosse by just one point, 158-159, where the former Highlanders’ star finished as Pitzer’s fifth-best runner—meaning his time of 25:49.3 was what they ultimately needed to win the title. Stein graduated from Piedmont High as its All-Time record holder in the 1600 and 3200 meters with respective times of 4:14.77 and 9:12.62. He also won the WACC Cross Country championship with a time of 15:34.76, was second of 144 in the NCS Championship in 15:29.4 and placed 12th of 209 at the CIF Championship, clocking a 15:43.4. What is your workout program this summer? I am currently going into my senior cross country season for Pomona-Pitzer. The goal of my workout program this summer is to build a strong base of fitness in preparation for races this fall. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals are to stay healthy, run lots of miles, and get sufficient nutrition and sleep. How are you measuring your development? I plan how many miles I want to run on a weekly basis and track them on Strava. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? My coach has given me a training plan but I am executing it on my own. I’ve been running with past and current teammates to keep me company. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Last November, I received All American honors after finishing 28th at the NCAA Division 3 Cross Country Championships in Terre Haute, Indiana. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Set goals and be consistent. Every day ask yourself - what am I doing today to achieve that goal? NATALIA MARTINEZ Basketball Jack Stein (right) is set to start his senior year at Pomona-Pitzer College. He was the Post’s 2022 Co-Athlete of the Year and holds multiple records at Piedmont High. Piedmont High Class of 2024 San Diego State Class of 2028 Natalia Martinez, PHS Class of 2024, closed an impressive freshman season on the San Diego State women’s basketball team. They won the Mountain West Conference as the No. 4 seed and earned a No. 14 ranking in the NCAA’s Spokane 1 bracket. The Aztecs finished their season with a 25-10 record. San Diego State went up against No. 2 LSU, which made it to the Elite Eight, losing 103- 48. Martinez was in the starting five, playing 27 minutes for seven points, one rebound, and one assist. As the No. 4 seed in the Mountain West Tournament, SD State beat No. 5 New Mexico 63-53, upset No. 1 UNLV 71-59, and won the title against No. 2 Wyoming 72-68. She logged six points and two assists on Wyoming. She set a Mountain West Conference record on January 18’s 85-66 win over Utah State, when she became the first player to sink six 3-pointers in a conference game, to go along with nine rebounds and seven assists. In her record-setting performance, Martinez finished with 22 points, converting 7/8 from the field and 6/7 for 3-pointers. She also added one steal and a block, and hit one of her 3-pointers from nearly 30 feet. Martinez finished her debut year with 252 points, shooting 39 three-pointers and a sterling 41 percent shooting percentage from beyond the arc and 44 percent from the field. She also logged 68 rebounds, 49 assists, 20 steals, and seven blocks. What is your workout program this summer? My summer started up around May, so I was able to do multiple workouts a day at Piedmont High School and Laney College. My workouts would consist of shooting, break down dribbling moves, and different finishes under the rim. In July, I’ll be back at SDSU to work out and practice with my team. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals this summer is to gain muscle, so I have been lifting a lot more consistently. How are you measuring your development? I’m able to measure my development by playing against other people, like current college players or even pro players to see what I have improved on and what I need to do better. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? She is the Post’s only back-to-back winner of the Athlete of the Year award winner (2023 and 2024). Gardere, my high school coach. I also go to Evolve Performance on Piedmont Ave to lift. the USPA National Championships next week on July 9 in Las Vegas. We also won the Mountain West championship and were able to compete in March Madness! What is your workout program this summer? I train the squat, bench, and deadlift 2–3 times per week, along with accessory work on days that are not focused on powerlifting. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Advice I would offer to younger athletes is to work hard. Remember, hard work isn’t hard when you’re having fun. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goal is to win or place on the podium at the USPA Drug Tested Nationals and achieve a 1,200 pound total. How are you measuring your development? I’m motivated by seeing how much my strength increases over time. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I train at a gym called Get Bent in West Oakland with my two primary coaches: Jason Romero and James Cunningham. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Another major goal of mine is to reach a 400 DOTS score. DOTS is a scoring system in powerlifting that uses your body weight and total to calculate performance. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Prioritize stretching and staying flexible. It’s much easier to prevent an injury than to recover from one. He last competed on April 5 in the USPA National Tested Get Bent’s Spring Break in Oakland. In the Age 16-17 category at 148 pounds, Haddawy hit a combined total of 1,085 pounds, including 352 pounds in the squat, 248 pounds on the bench press, and a 485 pound dead lift. Layth found power lifting after competing on Piedmont High’s junior varsity football team in 2023. Instead of standing out on the field, he found he was always lifting more weight than his football teammates, leading him to Get Bent Gym in Oakland. articles.text: With the summer in full swing, we delve into our second of six features of trails around Lake Tahoe with the lengthy but awe-striking Rubicon Trail around Emerald Bay. The Rubicon Trail is a 5.9 mile out-and-back (11.8 round trip, 1,350 feet in elevation gain) trail that stretches around Emerald Bay with a 360 degree view of Fannette Island, enabling hikers to see the historic Vikingsholm mansion. It includes the quant and quiet Emerald Bay Boat Camp, with countless places to rest beside the crystal blue water on the way to the Rubicon Point Lighthouse. Starting from the parking lot in the Upper Eagle Point Campground, the Rubicon Trail goes 1.6 miles beside Lake Tahoe with before reaching Vikingsholm—a 38-room mansion built in 1929 on the shores of Emerald Bay. It was the summer home of Mrs. Lora Josephine Knight. She inherited her fortune from the passing of her former husband William Henry Moore, whose law firm had controlling interest in U.S. Steel, Union Pacific, Rock Island Railroad and the National Biscuit Company (later named Nabisco). She was among the primary financial backers of Charles Lindbergh’s trans-Atlantic flight The view from the starting point at Upper Eagle Point Campground. Two hikers on the way up to Fannett Island’s Tea House.

articles.text: Visit the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco on Sunday, July 6 for a film screening of Disney’s Mulan followed by a family-friendly magazine workshop and collection tour. Mulan, based on the Chinese legend of Hua Mulan, broke new ground as a Disney film when it premiered in 1998. Fa Mulan, the protagonist, became the first Disney princess of East Asian descent and was conceived by animators and writers as more of a warrior-heroine than a princess. Variety’s Todd McCarthy praised the character at the time for inspiring “a turn of the circle from such age-old Disney classics ... in which passive heroines were rescued by blandly noble princes.” The museum will host a screening and singalong of Mulan in Samsung Hall at 11:30 a.m. The screening will be followed by a ‘Zine’ lesson suitable for children ages 6 to 16 in the Koret Education Center. Tours will be held throughout the day, including a docent tour of Yuan GoangMing: Everyday War at 11 a.m., and a collection tour at 2 p.m. The event is part of the museum’s Free First Sunday, where museum admission is free and visitors are encouraged to enjoy cultural celebrations, hands-on workshops, live dance and music performances, food pop-ups and tastings, and other community events, as well as the museum’s world-renowned collection and special exhibitions. For more information, visit https://calendar.asianart.org/ event/free-first-sunday-july-6/ ?_ga=2.87740504.1995936897. 1751218276-1505381405.17512 18276. A still from Disney’s Mulan (1998)

articles.text: The 31st annual Sculpture in the Garden at Ruth Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek, exhibiting a range of returning local artists and newcomers, kicked off last week and continues through August 10. Sculpture in the Garden is the nonprofit’s annual art exhibit and sale that celebrates sculptural pieces with the natural, arid beauty of the garden. This unique exhibit features art installations and sculptures by local craftspeople, ranging in design and materials used. The event also serves as a fundraiser for Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery. All artwork is available to purchase, and proceeds from this exhibit go back into the Garden to help protect the plant collection, promote education and support preservation. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, was a pioneer in her All sculptures are available for purchase. The 31st annual event features artwork by new and returning artisans. focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public, made possible through fundraisers like Sculpture in the Garden. Sculpture in the Garden is on view through August 10 and is open to the public during regular garden hours, Wednesday through Sunday, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. The event is free with regular Garden admission. The nursery is located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek. For more information, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/event/2025-sculpture-in-thegarden/.

articles.text: Legion of Honor, one of the Fine Arts museums of San Francisco, is currently exhibiting more than 250 personal photographs by Paul McCartney in a never-before seen collection entitled Paul McCartney: Photographs 1963–64: Eyes of the Storm through July. The exhibition includes the Beatles’ songwriter and singer personal captures as well as video clips, archival materials and more that offer a behind-the-scenes look at the meteoric rise of one of the world’s most celebrated and popular bands. Images span December 1963 through February 1964 and chronicle the Beatles’ journey to megastardom. Photographs were taken by McCartney with a single-lens reflex camera, which were introduced in the 1950’s as part of a new generation of handheld cameras. Sally Martin Katz, Legion of Honor Assistant Curator of Photography, said that McCartney acquired the camera in 1963 at a time “when many were experimenting with this newly popularized medium.” “The technology of the 35mm handheld camera allowed for a spontaneity in picture-taking, leading to the emergence of a snapshot aesthetic that embraced imperfection,” Katz said. “McCartney’s pictures reflect this new spirit in photography, as well as the literal blur of travel that The Beatles were experiencing, rapidly moving from one place to another.” Katz added that the exhibition, which includes photographs printed for the first time, captures “Beatlemania in full force.” “They depict the frenzied crowds chasing the band down the New York City streets, for example, and the swarms of people greeting them at the Miami airport,” she said. “The Beatles were at the eye of the storm they created: thousands of eyes were looking to capture that storm, and McCartney, with his camera, returned their gazes.” Visit https://www.famsf.org/ exhibitions/paul-mccartney-photographs to learn more. pages.text: 16 16 Wednesday, July 2, 2025 Arts & Entertainment Asian Art Museum hosts Mulan screening and workshop July 6 By Allyson Aleksey Visit the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco on Sunday, July 6 for a film screening of Disney’s Mulan followed by a family-friendly magazine workshop and collection tour. Mulan, based on the Chinese legend of Hua Mulan, broke new ground as a Disney film when it premiered in 1998. Fa Mulan, the protagonist, became the first Disney princess of East Asian descent and was conceived by animators and writers as more of a warrior-heroine than a princess. Variety’s Todd McCarthy praised the character at the time for inspiring “a turn of the circle from such age-old Disney classics ... in which passive heroines were rescued by blandly noble princes.” The museum will host a screening and singalong of Mulan in Samsung Hall at 11:30 a.m. The screening will be followed by a ‘Zine’ lesson suitable for children ages 6 to 16 in the Koret Education Center. Tours will be held throughout the day, including a docent tour of Yuan GoangMing: Everyday War at 11 a.m., and a collection tour at 2 p.m. The event is part of the museum’s Free First Sunday, where museum admission is free and visitors are encouraged to enjoy cultural celebrations, hands-on workshops, live dance and music performances, food pop-ups and tastings, and other community events, as well as the museum’s world-renowned collection and special exhibitions. For more information, visit https://calendar.asianart.org/ event/free-first-sunday-july-6/ ?_ga=2.87740504.1995936897. 1751218276-1505381405.17512 18276. Ruth Bancroft 2025 “Sculpture in the Garden” launches with new and returning artists By Allyson Aleksey The 31st annual Sculpture in the Garden at Ruth Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek, exhibiting a range of returning local artists and newcomers, kicked off last week and continues through August 10. Sculpture in the Garden is the nonprofit’s annual art exhibit and sale that celebrates sculptural pieces with the natural, arid beauty of the garden. This unique exhibit features art installations and sculptures by local craftspeople, ranging in design and materials used. The event also serves as a fundraiser for Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery. All artwork is available to purchase, and proceeds from this exhibit go back into the Garden to help protect the plant collection, promote education and support preservation. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, was a pioneer in her All sculptures are available for purchase. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public, made possible through fundraisers like Sculpture in the Garden. Sculpture in the Garden is on view through August 10 and is open to the public during regular garden hours, Wednesday through Sunday, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. The event is free with regular Garden admission. articles.text: Paul Simon American singer-songwriter Paul Simon, who rose to fame in the 1960’s as part of the folk-rock duo Simon & Garfunkel, will perform three concerts at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco July 19, 21 and 22 as part of his “Quiet Celebration” spring and summer tour. The legendary artist and Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductee wrote the duo’s hits, including “Bridge Over Troubled Water,” “Mrs. Robinson,” before embarking on his own successful solo career in 1971. Simon’s “Quiet Celebration” tour, his first since 2018, features the live debut of his Grammy-nominated album, Seven Psalms, along with a celebration of his timeless classics. Simon has contended with severe hearing loss and has chosen intimate venues with optimal acoustics for this tour, his team said in a statement. The band traveling with Simon includes talented musicians such as Caleb Burhans, Jamey Haddad, Gyan Riley, Mick Rossi, Andy Snitzer, Nancy Stagnitta, Mark Stewart, Eugene Friesen, Steve Gadd, and Matt Chamberlain. The San Francisco Symphony does not appear in the concerts at Davies Symphony Hall. Simon recently cancelled his June 28 and 29 shows scheduled at Philadelphia’s Academy of Music following “chronic and intense back pain.” “Today it became unmanageable and demands immediate attention,” reads a statement on Simon’s social media account Instagram. “Unfortunately we have to cancel these shows at this time, as we don’t have the ability to reschedule them.” The post continued, “However, we are hopeful after this minor surgical procedure which has been scheduled in the next few days, Paul will be able to complete the tour as well as look into returning to make up these dates.” Tickets can be purchased by visiting https://www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2024-25/ Paul-Simon. Ticket-holders may be entitled to refunds if San Francisco shows are cancelled.

articles.text: The iconic Fillmore Jazz Festival returns to San Francisco for its 36th year on July 5 and 6. Fillmore Jazz Festival is the West Coast’s largest free, ongoing jazz festival. The event attracts more than 50,000 attendees annually, and spans twelve blocks on Fillmore from Jackson to Eddy with two main stages at California and Eddy. Select performances are held inside the Calvary Presbyterian Church and Jones Memorial United Methodist Church. This year’s theme is “Lift Every Voice,” drawing inspiration from the famous hymn based on the poem by NAACP leader James Weldon Johnson in 1900. “Lift Every Voice and Sing” was first performed by schoolchildren in celebration of Abraham Lincoln’s birthday and over time became a rallying cry during the Civil Rights Movement. Today it remains a powerful symbol of Black pride, perseverance, and hope and was referred to as the Black national anthem by the NAACP. Fillmore Jazz Festival’s 36th engagement features an eclectic lineup across multiple music venues, showcasing the talents of more than 25 local and nationally-renowned artists. The festival also offers more than 140 arts and crafts booths, 25 food vendors and face painting and activities for kids. The event is free and no registration is required. The festival begins at 10 a.m. and ends at 6 p.m. both Saturday, July 5 and Sunday, July 6. Visit https:// www.fillmorejazzfest.com to learn more.
articles.title: Fillmore Jazz Festival returns to San Francisco July 5-6

articles.text: Valley of the Moon Music Festival kicks off its 11th season in Sonoma County, entitled “Liaisons,” on July 12. The festival runs through July 27 and features 10 performances, 3 lectures, and events highlighting “musical relationships across time and place.” Under the artistic direction of cellist Tanya Tomkins and fortepianist Eric Zivian, this year’s festival celebrates chamber music across centuries and continents. Valley of the Moon will present ten concerts that highlight historical instruments, offering guests a rare opportunity to enjoy classical music as originally intended. Valley of the Moon is nestled in the heart of Sonoma County’s wine country and brings together new artists, world-renowned classically trained musicians and music lovers in intimate settings. Each concert at the Hanna Center Auditorium in Sonoma County is followed by a complimentary wine reception. This year’s performances feature pre-concert lectures hosted by Harvard musicologist Kate van Orden, who Mads Tolling performs a free family concert on July 27. offers her historical insights into program choice and performance. Valley of the Moon will host a free family concert on July 27 featuring Grammy Award–winning jazz violinist Mads Tolling. Tolling is an internationally renowned violinist and composer, a two-time Grammy award-winner, and the 2016 DownBeat Critics Poll Rising Star winner. He is best known for his work with the Turtle Island Quartet, Stanley Clarke, Bob Weir, and local groups including the all-star San Francisco String Trio. A pay-what-you-choose concert at La Luz Center on July 17 will spotlight Spanish-speaking composers, performed by artists including Marc Teicholz and Beneath a Tree, with commentary in Spanish and English. Valley of the Moon Festival concludes on Sunday, July 27 with “Inspirations,” a program featuring Tchaikovsky, Mozart, and Haydn in a celebration of intergenerational musical influence performed by the full Festival ensemble. For full schedule, tickets, and more information, visit https://valleyofthemoonmusicfestival.org. The music festival kicks off July 12.
articles.title: Valley of the Moon Music Festival kicks off 11th season July 12

articles.text: Materialized Thoughts, and art exhibit currently on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, brings together Nepali artists living in the USA as first-generation immigrants. The body of works displayed explores the paradoxes of diasporic life, particularly the process of building identity amid pressures to conform to dominant cultures and homogeneous identities. Drawing inspiration from everyday life and personal experiences, this exhibition reflects the tension between strong attachment to the culture left behind and the process of assimilating into a new society. These artworks investigate the nuanced realities of diasporic life – living “in between” cultures, constantly navigating the differences and similarities between homeland and host land, and the ongoing process of carving out a new identity. The themes of “double-consciousness” – being “here and there” at the same time. This exhibition is the culmination of the research on Nepali Diaspora Artists based in the Bay Area and beyond, conducted by Swosti Rajbhandari Kayastha as a Fulbright Visiting Scholar with the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. The research was conducted over seven months from November 2024 to June 2025. This exhibition is the first of its kind, featuring artworks selectively by Diaspora Nepali Artists, showcasing diverse cultural narratives, challenging dominant art world narratives, and fostering dialogue about identity, displacement, and belonging. This exhibition has provided a platform for artists to express their unique experiences and perspectives, often highlighting the complexities of navigating multiple cultures and identities, seeking to play a crucial role in cultural preservation, documentation of history, and promoting cross-cultural understanding. Through such exhibitions by diaspora artists, you can help gain a deeper understanding of cultural identity, witness artistic innovation, and engage with important social issues. They also foster empathy and understanding of shared human experiences, challenges, and triumphs, providing an opportunity to celebrate the diversity of artistic talent and contribute to a more inclusive art world. Supporting diaspora artists can contribute to a more inclusive and globally oriented art world enriching the cultural landscape and contribute to a broader understanding of the diaspora’s impact on contemporary culture and society.
articles.title: Nepali art exhibit in Piedmont

articles.text: Saturday, July 12, 5:30 and 8:00 p.m. Derek Gripper Guitar Concert Derek Gripper is a South African classical guitarist and composer renowned for his unique ability to transcribe and perform complex West African 21-string kora music on the classical guitar. His work bridges the gap between different musical traditions and has garnered international recognition for its innovation and virtuosity. It is about creating connection — between African oral traditions and Western classical music, between different ways of listening and understanding. Along the way, Gripper has performed with legendary musicians like John Williams and Toumani Diabaté’s Symmetric Orchestra, sharing stages from Carnegie Hall to Shakespeare’s Globe. Note: 8 pm show is sold out. Early show at 5:30 added. articles.text: The arts are a two-way street. Some entertainers make a fortune while others starve. In the first category is a mediocre violinist of worldwide popularity. According to his publicity, it costs about $1 million to bring him to the stage. Not exactly a bargain in my opinion. On the other side of the street there are many examples of artistic inspiration. pages.text: Wednesday, July 2, 2025 19 The Musical Gourmet Artistic inspiration By Joseph Gold The arts are a two-way street. Some entertainers make a fortune while others starve. In the first category is a mediocre violinist of worldwide popularity. According to his publicity, it costs about $1 million to bring him to the stage. Not exactly a bargain in my opinion. On the other side of the street there are many examples of artistic inspiration. These folks operate on a very limited budget. They do a great service to their communities and to audiences in general. An opera performance in Reedley, California on Saturday evening is a perfect example. General admission was only $50 and included the opera performance and a very high-quality dinner as well. Rosalinda Verde Alexander is the founder of the Visalia Opera Company and serves as its Executive Director. The wonder of it all is that she is a fine singer and also a good fundraiser. In addition to these things, she is a teacher in the public schools and an inspiration to her students and to adults everywhere. Alexander has close contact with “special needs students.” She engages them to be part of the concert program. It was delightful to see them on the stage. The concert performance included scenes from some very popular operas. All of the singers were outstanding vocally. In particular, were full-voice tenor Peter Girardot, Oakland-based The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet mezzo soprano Linda Baird, and Alexander. In case you didn’t know, opera was the most popular form of entertainment for at least 300 years. Opera singers were also the highest paid entertainers. No one made more money than opera singers. Opera was popular for many reasons. Composers could poke fun at every aspect of human life… and not be arrested. Politics was often the subject of opera. All that opera composers had to do was change the names of places and people …voila! And there was nothing the big shots could do about it. You name it and opera had it. History, geography, political satire, extravagant dancing, and beautiful costumes. As a social media, opera taught people how to behave as well as how not to behave. Opera companies could be very agile and were able to travel very easily. During religious holidays such as Lent, composers adapted their operas. The result was oratorio. Composers were very good at “rolling with the punches”. Reedley, California is a very interesting place. We tend to forget that the Central Valley was financially very well off. For example, a famous violin dealer came every year to sell his expensive instruments in the Central Valley. Other characteristics of these small towns are the courteous and polite people. They are culturally minded and very often quite generous. In order for their operas to be a success, they need a very adept coordinator, and Rosalinda Verde Alexander is that. She coordinated every aspect of the musical portion of the program, found a performance space, got three musicians to be the “Orchestra” of the evening, and supervised both the box office and the restaurant. As for the audience… Pay your entrance fee and sit down at an elegant supper club… enjoy the show. After the performance, all of us went to a local pub for even more celebration. Perhaps in the future, the Visalia opera company will have more than one performance. Generosity pays dividends. Rosalinda Verde Alexander is a woman of many abilities. She is the founder and executive director of Green Rose Productions, which is the Visalia Opera Company. She is an inspiring teacher in the public schools and is a very fine singer and a manager of all aspects of musical production. articles.text: Roy Scheider and Robert Shaw in Jaws The now iconic film Jaws was released on 464 screens simultaneously on June 20, 1975. It was the No.1 film in America for 14 weeks and went on to generate three sequels. The story, set on a quiet New England tourist island called Amity, finds its primal sweet spot in the first harrowing scene and never relents. Its late at night and we see a teenage beach party underway. A girl and boy are flirting, he’s drinking, and when he approaches her, she impulsively gets up and runs toward the water, leaving him and her clothes behind. She dives into the darkness of the ocean and begins to swim slowly out toward a ringing navigation buoy, pausing only to tread water. The only sound is the hollow clang of the bell until we hear the soft yet ominous background score of John Williams. The girl, having reached the buoy holds onto it and suddenly her calm face grimaces and then is frozen in fear and terror. Her boyfriend, now standing near the water, unaware, calls out to her. The audience watches as she is lifted and pushed through the water, terrified, and suddenly is pulled beneath the surface. That riveting moment frames the entire narrative, reminding the audience that below the all but flat and seemingly benign surface of the waves is an unseen lethal presence. The grim remains of the young woman are discovered the following morning, and the Amity Police Chief, Martin Brody (Roy Schieder), is called to investigate. It’s a ghastly scene and he stares out at the ocean. His first impulse is to close the beaches. But the Mayor (Murray Hamilton) and the city council reject the idea; it’s the beginning of the high tourist season. What occurred is a one-off, an accident they insist. Chief Brody is uncertain; however, he relents. To assuage both Brody and the council, an ichthyologist, Matt Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss), is hired as is a crusty local fisherman called Quint (Robert Shaw), both are tasked to join the search for what is now assumed to be a rogue great white who is deadly and territorial and referred to by Hooper as an eating machine. articles.text: The film If Beale Street Could Talk opens with a quotation from author James Baldwin: “Beale Street is a street in New Orleans where my father and Louis Armstrong were born. As was jazz. Every black person in America was born on Beale Street, whether in Jackson, Mississippi, or in Harlem, New York. Beale Street is our legacy.” And it is that legacy that writer-director Barry Jenkins (Moonlight) explores, his film a painful and aspirational adaptation of Baldwin’s 1974 novel. As well, it makes explicit that Beale Street is not so much a street but a remarkable metaphor for a life experience, viewed through the prism of what it means to be black in America. The film opens with Tish (Kiki Layne), 19, and Fonny (Stephan James), 22, walking through a park. Immediately it is clear that they are deeply in love. In voice over, Tish explains that they have been friends since childhood and with age their connection has changed, morphing into an all encompassing love while they move ever so cautiously toward consummating their feelings and making love. As Tish explains, this is the world they move in and so profound is their attachment that it’s as if they possess a luminescent halo that surrounds them, one defined by hope and joy. Watching them standing together, embracing, foreheads touching, it’s obvious that Beale Street is a deeply emotive love story. KiKi Layne and Stephan James in If Beale Street Could Talk Randy Wilk and Kalim Winata provided support and sponsorship for Materialized Thoughts at Piedmont Center for the Arts.

articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Coco The story of Coco follows a 12-year-old boy named Miguel Rivera (Anthony Gonzalez) who lives in the small Mexican town of Cecilia. He dreams of one day becoming a musician, exactly like the legendary Ernesto De La Cruz (Benjamin Bratt), an iconic guitar player. Miguel secretly practices while studying video footage of Ernesto. There is, however, a problem, and it is not a small one: the Riveras are shoemakers. They are part of the artisan trade community, and theirs is a tradition that has been proudly passed along from one generation to the next. The expectation is that Miguel will be what the Rivera men were before him, shoemakers. Music playing is strictly forbidden. Meanwhile, Miguel yearns to participate in a talent show to be held in the town plaza on the Dia De Muertas, a day when those who are deceased visit the living. His ancient great grandmother, Coco (Ana Ofelia Marguia), the strict matriarch of the Rivera family, and the daughter of Miguel’s great-great grandmother, Imelda, sternly supports the family’s ban on music playing. In preparation for the Dia De Muertas, the Riveras have created an elaborate shrine with the photos of deceased family members. Miguel, if he going to be in the talent show, realizes he will need a guitar. He goes to the tomb of Ernesto and there finds his guitar, which he steals. At that quirky moment Miguel is transported to the Land of the Dead and it is there that he meets all of his past relatives who are preparing for their journey on this very special day. When he meets up with his great-great grandmother, Imelda (Alana Ubach), she makes it clear that he must quit music. Of course, she has a dark history with musicians. During his adventure, Miguel hooks up with a scallywag called Hector (Gael Garcia Bernal), and also has a sidekick, a spifffy dog. There is one caveat to Miguel’s family reunion with those who have passed away, and that is he must return to the Land of the Living by dawn or he will remain forever in the Land of the Dead. All he needs is a blessing from a deceased relative. And so, his journey continues. This is a beautifully animated feature film, one of Pixar’s best, filled with vibrant colors, cultural themes, wonderful songs, and amazing alebrijes (folk art sculptures). Of course, the embedded importance of family runs throughout the story, as well as the importance of following your dreams, all of it leading Miguel to finding peace in the Land of the Living. Coco. Directed by Lee Unkrich. Pixar/Disney Animation. Starring Anthony Gonzalez, Gael Garcia Bernal, Benjamin Bratt. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. Released in 2017. Now streaming on Disney+/Prime/Fandango. articles.text: The Eagle Huntress, set in the stark Altai Mountains of the Mongolian steppes, is, in so many ways, extraordinary. When commenting on the vast, isolated plains and unforgiving snow-covered mountains, director Otto Bell said, “It’s not the end of the world, but you can see it from there.” This breathtaking film is intermittently narrated by Daisy Ridley in English, with subtitles. The sweeping cinematography, by Simon Niblett, is gorgeous, at times involving a drone for aerial shots of eagles in flight, their grace and beauty something to behold. But at the center of this beautifully rendered documentary is a 13-year-old girl, Aisholpan Nurgaiv, who explains to her father, Nurgaiv, that she wishes to follow him in what is a centuries old tradition. She wants above all to become an eagle huntress. He tells Aisholpan that for generations only men have been allowed to use eagles to hunt small game for fur and meat. She has heard of the annual Golden Eagle competition and appeals to her father to let her train an eagle and enter the contest. Of course, the tribe’s council of elders opines about a young woman, a girl, actually, joining the 70 other hunters who will arrive in the provincial capital of Olgii to compete. Women, they insist, are too fragile and lack the stamina and strength to hunt with raptors, birds that can stand almost three feet tall, with wingspans of six feet or more. But Nurgaiv encourages his daughter, who is hardworking, ever cheerful, unexpectedly intrepid and resolutely committed to becoming the first female eagle huntress. And so, with the help of her father, who is a gentle and supportive coach and clearly cares deeply about his child, they set out to find and capture an eaglet, one still in its nest, somewhere high in a mountain crevice. What is remarkable about this journey on horseback is not only the effort by Aisholpan, as she rappels down a fissure with her father high above on belay, but the nature of their interaction. Nurgaiv encourages, always kind, and Aisholpan perseveres. She finds there are two eaglets in Aisholpan Nurgaiv in The Eagle Huntress

articles.text: The Indie Next List has fresh reading recommendations every month. Check out their newest iteration of hot-off-the-press literature recently published by respected writers. The Indie Next List of new releases is curated by independent bookstore owners and staff of only new releases. July’s list should be of great use in augmenting summer reading lists fit unwinding on a beach towel with fantasy, romance and even the combination of the two, romantasy. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received praise from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small book store culture. I Gave You Eyes and You Looked Toward Darkness Lethem (Transl.), Graywolf Press, Fiction “I insist that you’ll be obsessed with this magnificent, slim book. Curious, disgusting, beautiful and resoundingly feminist — this is a book to captivate your hungering Madeline Miller readers, your Oyeyemi fans.” —Dustin Kurtz, Literary Arts, Portland, OR The Girls Who Grew Big Fiction “Just as she did in Nightcrawling, Leila Mottley gives voice and understanding to parts of life that our culture often tells us to ignore. The book is full of life and heart and hope.” —Beth Black, The Bookworm of Omaha, Omaha, NE The Enchanted Greenhouse Romance “This cozy fantasy in the world of The Spellshop is the first notes of birdsong mixing with winter sunshine. It’s a snowy evening spent in front of a fireplace, with fresh bread, warm soup, and the comfort of quiet company. A balm for a weary soul.” —Jericha Harriman, Northshire Bookstore, Saratoga Springs, NY The Satisfaction Café “For fans of Jonathan Franzen, Kathy Wang delivers a stellar debut. Her keen observations on everyday life are on full display with Joan Liang and her unexpected life journey where she must seek the satisfaction that lies within.” —Susan McBeth, Adventures A Marriage at Sea Books, Biography “A raw telling of the fight a young couple endures physically and mentally as their boat is capsized by creatures in the middle of the sea. Reads like a novel — it’s crazy this is a true story!” —Alex Hammett, Serendipity Books, Chelsea, MI Hazel Says No Hanover Square Press, Fiction “Told from multiple characters’ perspectives, this is a downright titillating story about family and community, choices and growth. Readers will root for Hazel and her entire family from beginning to end in this page-turning drama.” —Liz Whitelam, Whitelam Books, Reading, MA Sunny Side Up Books, Fiction “Very rarely do we ever fit into a mold. This book completely forges a new path in accepting yourself and others for who we are. Beauty is in the eyes of the beholder and this is just what the doctor ordered!” —Suzanne Lucey, Page 158 Books, Wake Forest, NC Finding Grace Martin’s Press, Fiction “I have never gasped as loudly as I have at the conclusion of Finding Grace’s first chapter. At that point, I was all in. Rothschild’s elegant prose and sense of place and time root the reader in this incredibly vivid story of love, loss, and the history that we are willing to rewrite.” —Megan Birch-McMichael, The Silver Unicorn Bookstore, Acton, MA These Summer Storms Books, Fiction “Alice travels home to the family island for the funeral of her eccentric, billionaire tech father. As old wounds reopen and family drama compounds, we learn the inheritance game is afoot. Will Alice play? Hang on for the ride!” —Sierra Hollabaugh, The Bookery Cincy, Cincinnati, OH The Compound House, Fiction “Lily wakes up in a middle-ofthe-desert house as a cast member on a mysterious reality show that’s part Survivor, part Truman Show, part Love Island. I was uneasy (a good thing) from page one of this unpredictable tale that unfurls with mounting dread and razorsharp societal commentary.” —Joelle Herr, The Bookshop, Nashville, TN Daikon Press / Simon & Schuster, Fiction “A historical novel that really opens your eyes to what Japanese people experienced at the end of WWII. Daikon fills in the emotion that strict history does not. Wonderful characters and beautiful writing!” —Becky Anderson, Anderson’s Bookshops, Naperville, IL Party of Liars Thriller “Everyone loves a Sweet 16! Perfect for fans of Samantha Irby, Jenny Lawson, and Maria Bamford.” —Mara Panich, Fact & Fiction Downtown, Missoula, MT Make Your Way Home Books, Short Stories “I mean it when I say this book is breathing life into me. Walkers view design award winners By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group is not surprised when unexpected, happy things happen on their walks of Piedmont streets. Last Wednesday some serendipitous encounters added significantly to their walk enjoyment. There was a large turnout of 55 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra for the fun. Before they started walking it was noted that the group will walk again together in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade. The walkers were in the parade last year and participants noted how much fun it was. They hope for a big turnout again this year. It was then shared that each year the Planning Commission and City recognize a small number of Piedmont projects that they feel represent the highest level of design excellence in residential construction, landscaping, and sustainable home improvements with their Design Awards. Last year the commission introduced Sustainability Awards to celebrate property owners who have incorporated green elements into their homes. Walker Jim Kellogg is a former planning commissioner. He said the selection process is for city staff to nominate their favorite projects from all those that have been reviewed by the commission and for the commissioners to pick the winners. To be eligible, a project must conform to Piedmont’s design and planning guidelines and must have completed construction in the previous calendar year. Last year the commission introduced Sustainability Awards to celebrate property owners who have incorporated green elements, like heat pumps, solar panels, and greywater systems, into their homes. The walkers could see two of the four 2025 Design Awards winners on a loop in the northwest part of town. Additionally, the group could go see a Sustainability Award winner. The first home for the walkers to see was the winner of the Excellence in Comprehensive Remodel with Integrated Accessory Dwelling Unit at 224 Greenbank Avenue. By coincidence, David Lee, the homeowner, was outside working. After introductions, David told the group about his project. The house’s footprint had to stay the same, so the crawlspace at the house’s front was cleared and used for more room and an ADU. New windows matched existing ones and solar and a heat pump were part of the project. The neighbors were supportive of the effort. It took one year, but David said he was glad they did it and would do it again. After thanking David, the walkers went down to Grand Avenue, up Cambridge Way, and over to York Drive. The next destination was 47 York Drive and on the way there was another house to see – the home of Piedmont realtor Stacey Isaacs and Chuck Wolf. As the walkers approach the now complete, modern, beautiful house, they had their second happy surprise of the morning. Stacey had seen them coming, came out to welcome them, and shared the project’s story. Stacey and Chuck bought the original house six years ago. They liked that the lot was deep and level and intended to remodel the house. Some projects were started but they came to realize that to have the house the way they wanted, it would be better to take the old house down and start all over. That’s what they did. They first built an ADU to live in during the two years of new house construction. The project took more time and money than they had expected, but the house is spectacular. After sharing the history, Stacey provided the group’s third surprise of the morning. She generously invited the 55 walkers to come inside. It was an offer they couldn’t refuse. The home is an open-concept jewel. It’s beautifully detailed and furnished and flows nicely from the front to the backyard with the ADU on the side and a raised swimming pool of a modern designed at the back. The walkers greatly enjoyed Stacey’s open house and had to be reminded that there was another house to see on the block. Thanks were given to Stacey and Chuck for their hospitality and group made their way up to 47 York. This house was the winner for Excellence in for a Second Story Addition. The walkers enjoyed seeing the seamlessly added second floor to the house. It was a good thing property owners Kevin Ma and Liana Wu were not there to talk about their project because the unexpected and happy visits with David, Stacey, and Chuck had taken a good piece of the morning. There wasn’t time to go up to Estrella Avenue and see James Glauber and Tracy Lieu’s City Sustainability Award winner on Estrella Avenue. It would have to be part of a future Wednesday walk. The group retraced their steps back York to Cambridge and then returned to the Exedra via, Blair, San Carlos, Oakland, El Cerrito, and Magnolia Avenues. The walkers should have expected it was another walk of surprises and fun. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Wednesday Walkers with homeowner David Lee on Greenbank Avenue. articles.text: On, June 25, Oakland Zoo and The Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) announced the piloting of a new Wildlife Confiscations Coordinator position, based at the Oakland Zoo, to support the work of AZA’s Wildlife Confiscations Network. The position will simplify the process of providing care and placing of animals confiscated from the illegal trade in California, serving as a centralized, statewide point of contact for wildlife law enforcement officers seeking trusted animal care facilities. Oakland Zoo joined AZA’s Wildlife Confiscations Network in 2024 and has since responded to 15 requests from the Network, including cases involving a marmoset, 60 venomous snakes, spider monkeys, and an 8-month-old tiger cub. The Zoo is the first facility in California to pilot a regional confiscations position. “Through the Wildlife Confiscations Network, we’ve built a coalition of trusted facilities ready to provide expert care for confiscated wildlife in need,” said Dan Ashe, President and CEO of AZA. “This new position at the Oakland Zoo strengthens that safety net by ensuring not only the immediate rescue and placement of wildlife trafficking victims, but also the lifelong, quality care they deserve, all while enabling California law enforcement to focus their efforts on bringing traffickers to justice.” After a two-year successful pilot program in Southern CalDr. Alex Herman, VP of Vet Services, says hello to a tortoise rescue.

articles.text: Comic actor Bill Murray called Kung Fu Hustle “the supreme achievement of the modern age in terms of comedy,” and the American filmmaker James Gunn called it “the greatest film ever made.” Can Kung Fu Hustle possibly live up to such praise? You can judge for yourself, right in your own hometown, because Kung Fu Hustle is the choice of this month’s Piedmont Flix Fest. One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. Released in 2004, and written produced and directed by Stephen Chow, it stars Chow, one of entertainment’s martial arts greats, in the leading role of Sing, in a madcap mashup of gangland encounters in Shanghai. It features lots of sizzling king fu encounters that may remind you of the spectacular feats in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon. Kung Fu Hustle was nominated as the Best Foreign Language Film of 2006 by BAFTA and the Golden Globes. Roger Ebert described it as “Jackie Chan and Buster Keaton meet Quentin Tarantino and Bugs Bunny.” Another critic said she was torn between shouting Wow! and laughing out loud. Flix Fest films are free and usually screen at 1:00 p.m. but because of a scheduling conflict, King Fu Hustle will be shown at a changed time, at 4:15 p.m. on July 10th. The screening takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors for this showing will open at 4:00. The event is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks. The next movie in the Piedmont series is The Social Network, to be screened on August 14th. ®

The position will simplify the process of providing care and placing of animals confiscated from the illegal trade in California, serving as a centralized, statewide point of contact for wildlife law enforcement officers seeking trusted animal care facilities. Oakland Zoo joined AZA’s Wildlife Confiscations Network in 2024 and has since responded to 15 requests from the Network, including cases involving a marmoset, 60 venomous snakes, spider monkeys, and an 8-month-old tiger cub. The Zoo is the first facility in California to pilot a regional confiscations position. “Through the Wildlife Confiscations Network, we’ve built a coalition of trusted facilities ready to provide expert care for confiscated wildlife in need,” said Dan Ashe, President and CEO of AZA. “This new position at the Oakland Zoo strengthens that safety net by ensuring not only the immediate rescue and placement of wildlife trafficking victims, but also the lifelong, quality care they deserve, all while enabling California law enforcement to focus their efforts on bringing traffickers to justice.” After a two-year successful pilot program in Southern California, AZA’s Wildlife Confiscations Network, in partnership with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, has become a proven model for coordinating support for law enforcement agencies tasked with caring for seized wildlife. Since its launch, the Network has assisted with more than 135 wildlife trafficking cases and placed over 4,600 animals into quality care. To expand this effort and address the specific needs across the state, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has formally partnered with the Network to pilot the California Wildlife Confiscations Coordinator role, strengthening California’s regional response to illegal wildlife trade. “The establishment of this new position streamlines the process for law enforcement, which is often burdened with finding qualified facilities to provide care for these animals,” said Sara Walker, senior advisor on wildlife trafficking at AZA. “It allows law enforcement to prioritize the investigation and prosecution of individuals involved in wildlife trafficking, guarantees that the animal’s health and wellbeing are prioritized after discovery, and ensures that confiscated wildlife will not re-enter the illegal trade.” See Oakland Zoo on page 32 Dr. Alex Herman, VP of Vet Services, says hello to a tortoise rescue. articles.text: John Hardgrove of Fairview Avenue, Piedmont from the University of Denver in 1965; as a student, he had also dabbled in acting with the university’s theater department. But his real passion was advertising. His career began at Guild, Bascom & Bonfigli, a storied firm of its day, where he worked as a graphic designer, followed by a stint at Dancer Fitzgerald Sample. In 1968, John became creative director at San Francisco’s Aviva Toy Company, which produced toys based on Charles Schulz’s beloved Peanuts comic strip. A dog lover and gifted illustrator, John played a central role in bringing Snoopy off the page and into the physical world, shaping Schulz’s iconic beagle into toys and merchandise that became part of daily life for millions. In 1977, John opened his own agency, The Design Bunch, specializing in print advertising and design. He moved to Piedmont and commuted to work from Oakland by ferry, accompanied by his dog du jour. After 50 productive years, John retired in 2015, celebrating the occasion with a grand party in Alsace, France. The AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am Tournament illustration, designed by John Hardgrove He then devoted himself to watercolor painting – a passion he had discovered later in life. In 1992, he enrolled in evening classes at Piedmont Adult School, and five years later, one of his golf paintings was selected for the official poster and program cover of the AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am Golf Tournament. The honor made John a mini-celebrity and gave him the chance to mix with the likes of Clint Eastwood and Kevin Costner, just a few of the tournament’s many high-profile guests. John went on to specialize in painting golf courses, landscapes, and, most notably, dog portraits. A lifelong dog lover, he considered those portraits family treasures. But his subject range was much larger. I remember a delightful portrait of Queen Elizabeth that John painted for her jubilee, which hung above his mantelpiece. His dining room table was always piled with sketches and drying watercolors. John was also known among California car enthusiasts as the owner of a 1954 powder-blue Jaguar XK 120 convertible. pages.text: Wednesday, July 2, 2025 25 Remembering John Hardgrove By Anastasia Edel I met John and his dog Charlie in the summer of 2016: two eternal bachelors wearing red bandanas, walking along Palm Drive. It was an election year, so my husband and I often talked politics with John while our terriers waited patiently on the sidewalk, Charlie often lying on my feet; I can still remember the feel of his bristly brown coat on my skin. John and Charlie lived on Fairview, just a few minutes up the hill. Before too long, we received an invitation for a glass of wine. Our friendly neighbor turned out to be the owner of a magnificently landscaped garden, which over the years I came to call “Hardgrove’s Park.” Sprawling over 8,000 square feet, it was laced with winding sand paths and so many flowering plants that something was always in bloom: lavender, roses, sunflowers, geranium, pink bougainvillea, climbing sweat peas, violet and blue petunia – a symphony of colors. Clusters of pale-yellow angel trumpets hung over the garden swing, and in season, a bowl of ripe figs stood in the small kitchen. It was in that garden that I listened to stories from John’s life – as vibrant and full as the place itself, rich with art, commerce, and adventures. Born in 1941 to Robert Snyder Hardgrove, a real estate firm owner, and Eleanor (Farquhar) Hardgrove, a social worker and a Red Cross volunteer, John grew up in Ohio, the middle of three brothers. He earned a master’s degree in communication arts John Hardgrove of Fairview Avenue, Piedmont from the University of Denver in 1965; as a student, he had also dabbled in acting with the university’s theater department. But his real passion was advertising. His career began at Guild, Bascom & Bonfigli, a storied firm of its day, where he worked as a graphic designer, followed by a stint at Dancer Fitzgerald Sample. In 1968, John became creative director at San Francisco’s Aviva Toy Company, which produced toys based on Charles Schulz’s beloved Peanuts comic strip. A dog lover and gifted illustrator, John played a central role in bringing Snoopy off the page and into the physical world, shaping Schulz’s iconic beagle into toys and merchandise that became part of daily life for millions. In 1977, John opened his own agency, The Design Bunch, specializing in print advertising and design. He moved to Piedmont and commuted to work from Oakland by ferry, accompanied by his dog du jour. After 50 productive years, John retired in 2015, celebrating the occasion with a grand party in Alsace, France. Snoopy as World’s Greatest Golfer, designed by John. The AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am Tournament illustration, designed by John Hardgrove He then devoted himself to watercolor painting – a passion he had discovered later in life. In 1992, he enrolled in evening classes at Piedmont Adult School, and five years later, one of his golf paintings was selected for the official poster and program cover of the AT&T Pebble Beach National Pro-Am Golf Tournament. The honor made John a mini-celebrity and gave him the chance to mix with the likes of Clint Eastwood and Kevin Costner, just a few of the tournament’s many high-profile guests. John went on to specialize in painting golf courses, landscapes, and, most notably, dog portraits. A lifelong dog lover, he considered those portraits family treasures. But his subject range was much larger. I remember a delightful portrait of Queen Elizabeth that John painted for her jubilee, which hung above his mantelpiece. His dining room table was always piled with sketches and drying watercolors. John was also known among California car enthusiasts as the owner of a 1954 powder-blue Jaguar XK 120 convertible. Quite possibly the classiest car ever made, it had been driven by the likes of Clark Gables, Humphrey Bogart and Frank Sinatra, and earned John numerous awards, including several at car shows hosted by Piedmont. He once took me for a spin in his immaculately maintained treasure, its brilliant blue the color of California sky. We drove to Orinda, drawing enthusiastic honks at intersections and turning quite a few heads. Held in my passenger seat by a rough airplane-grade seat belt, I felt like a Hollywood star riding beside a Bogart-style dandy – aviator glasses, bright neck scarf, and leather gloves to match his jacket – at least until the Jaguar lost power climbing a steep hill. Somehow, John (then in his late 70s) managed to keep the heavy beast from sliding backward and coaxed it to the top. At that point, we agreed it was time to leave the Orinda hills and return to Piedmont. On the way back, he told me he had been driving his Jaguar to Fort Ross with other owners of John’s award-winning Jaguar XK-120 on Palm Drive antique sports cars. It must have been a spectacular sight – provided you knew how not to tumble off the steep cliffs on Route One north. John clearly did. When I asked if my daughter could include his Jaguar in her prom pictures, not only did he agree, he brought out movie props to set the mood. The photos turned out so splendid they would have made James Bond weep. A generous man, John loved entertaining. His 80s birthday party was a jolly affair with 37 guests – neighbors, fellow artists, and friends, some of whom had flown in from Europe, a continent John loved and travelled extensively. Poor Charlie was so agitated by all the commotion that he abandoned his giant fish toy and followed John everywhere through the garden, howling, standing on his hind legs, and waving his front paws until John finally let him jump into his lap. There they sat together on the swing – a man and his dog, two lifelong friends. Both would be gone within three years – John first, Charlie shortly thereafter. This June marks the first sad anniversary of their departure. But this is how I want to remember John – happy in his garden, surrounded by his paintings and those who loved him, Charlie in his lap, his beautiful car waiting in the garage, ready for another adventure. pages.text: Wednesday, July 2, 2025 31 Parade Preview Continued from page 1 Dick Johnson. “It’s going to be great – we’ve got a lot of good entries.” The Fourth of July Parade is Piedmont’s largest annual event, drawing an estimated 3000-4000 participants and viewers each year. This year’s theme is “Traditions Thrive in 2025.” Parade entries prepare for friendly competition as they compete for the Highland Cup, Highland Saucer, Highland Spoons and the ribbon awards. Results will be announced sometime after the parade. Parade goers will have a chance to see the winners of the float contest marching in the parade on the morning of July 4. Advance float judging will take place on the evening of July 3 for three awards that will be publicly displayed during the parade: Most Artistic, Most Consistent with Theme and Best Spirit. Marshal will be Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. As is tradition, Bowers will be featured as a prominent rider near the front of the parade in one of the parade’s dignitary cars. The parade will once again host a diverse lineup of classic cars ranging from 1960’s Thunderbirds to sleek mid-90’s Volvos and Jaguars. The Piedmont Community Band, the city’s only musical organization that can claim a single yearly rehearsal, will be joining the parade once again. The band is comprised of volunteer amateur and professional musicians who enjoy playing music while marching in formation, dressed in blue pants, white shirts and a red kerchief. The fan-favorite Balloon Platoon, dressed in cartoonishly oversized sailor outfits with inner tubes, will be celebrating 50 years of whimsical marches and twenty-one mop salutes in the parade this year. “A lot of hard work goes into it, but having people who have familiarity with the City has been really helpful,” said Kelleher. The Piedmont Post will provide free programs for all attendees at the parade. The Highland Cup (left), Highland Saucer and Highland Spoons are presented each year to the best entries in the 4th of July Parade.

Oakland Zoo Continued from page 24 Lola, a rescued tiger, was rehabilitated at the Oakland Zoo. Beyond the Wildlife Confiscations Network, Oakland Zoo has played a crucial role in rescuing and caring for a diverse range of animals, including insects, amphibians, primates, and birds. Since 2021, the Oakland Zoo has received over 100 requests from wildlife agencies, advocacy groups, and animal rescue organizations for assistance with rescue efforts. These efforts aim to support victims of the wildlife pet trade, roadside zoos, and other criminal activities. “With Oakland Zoo’s decadelong history of animal rescue and efforts to end the wildlife trade, it is essential to continually expand the Zoo’s role in combating this tragic industry. We are proud to be part of the Wildlife Confiscations Network, which has united our efforts toward a common mission and offers us a new opportunity to help save more wildlife that are victims of trafficking,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. Funding for the position is provided by the CDFW and is focused primarily on requests for triage and temporary holding of trafficked or illegally held animals within the state of California. This role is distinct from the Zoo’s other wildlife rescue programs. Azules, an endanger female spider monkey, was brought to the zoo on January 2 after being rescued by California Highway Patrol following a New Years Eve arrest. Yellow-naped amazon parrot, Brock, is now an Oakland Zoo resident after being rescued from the illegal wildlife trade industry. Where in the World Are We?
